messages.content: Bali has some places way cheaper than the famous ones. Any reason not to go budget?

Cheaper can be fine, but bungee is one activity where you should check before you book. Look for a long operating history, recent reviews that mention safety checks, clearly retired or logged cords, and staff who weigh you and double-check every connection. If a place can't tell you how often its cords are replaced, or the setup looks improvised, spend the extra money on the established operator.
can i just learn BASE from youtube and practice off a bridge? courses are like $3000

No, this is one of the fastest ways people die in the sport. Packing, slider configuration, delay timing and off-heading recovery all need hands-on instruction and someone checking your work in person. A YouTube video can't spot a line twist in your pack job or tell you your exit is pitching you toward the object. The course costs a lot less than the alternative, so save up and do it right with a recognized first jump course.
Wakeboarding tomorrow but my neck's stiff from a whiplash-type fall last week. Big deal?

It could be, so I'd give it a miss. Neck injuries from a hard whiplash fall sometimes need assessment, and wakeboard crashes can snap your head around hard. If you have numbness, tingling in your arms, severe pain or headaches, see a doctor before doing anything. Even if it's just muscle strain, wait until you have full pain-free movement before you get back on the water.
I've been doing BASE for 3 years and I feel like I'm getting bored. Thinking of trying lower objects to get the rush back.

Be careful with that reasoning, because chasing a rush is a pattern behind a lot of experienced jumpers' accidents. If you want new challenges, look at improving accuracy, new legal sites, tracking or wingsuit progression on big exits, all with mentors who've done them. Lowering your altitude margin just to feel something removes the buffer that protects you on a bad day. Sometimes boredom is a sign to take a break, not to raise the stakes.
can i fly with a mild hangover? just a small coastal soaring session

Give it a miss. Even a mild hangover slows your reactions and dulls your judgement, and dehydration makes it worse. Coastal soaring looks gentle, but it involves flying close to cliffs and other pilots, where a moment of slow reaction matters. Drink some water, eat something, and fly tomorrow with a clear head.
Can I wear my regular life jacket from boating?

Probably not ideal. Whitewater PFDs are cut shorter for paddling movement, fit snugly so they won't ride up in a swim, and often have a rescue harness and pockets for safety gear. A loose boating vest can slip over your head in turbulent water, so get a proper Type III or V whitewater PFD fitted at a paddle shop.
Plantar fasciitis. Training for Kilimanjaro in 3 months. Help.

Three months is workable if you start managing it now. Do daily calf and plantar fascia stretches, roll the arch on a frozen bottle, wear supportive boots with good insoles, and avoid going barefoot on hard floors. Swap some of your hiking volume for cycling or swimming to keep your fitness while the foot settles, and see a podiatrist about orthotics or taping. Build back to long hikes in your actual boots well before the trip, because summit day is long and the descent is brutal on feet.
how long should i rest between dives

A common rule of thumb is to rest at the surface for at least twice your dive time, and longer for deeper or tougher dives. That means after a 1 minute dive you rest 2 minutes or more. As the session goes on and you get tired, lengthen your rests. If you're still breathing hard or feel off, wait longer or call it a day.
hey can i bring my gopro on my first tandem?

Almost certainly not, because most dropzones forbid student and tandem passengers from carrying cameras. Loose camera mounts can snag lines or distract you, which is why USPA guidance recommends at least 200 jumps before flying with a camera. If you want footage, book the handcam or outside videographer package instead, since they're experienced and know how to get good shots safely.
Is paragliding over water risky?

It can be. If you land in water, the wing and lines can tangle around you and drag you under, which is a real drowning risk even for strong swimmers. Avoid flying over water unless you have plenty of altitude to reach land comfortably, or you're on a supervised SIV course with a rescue boat and flotation gear. If you do end up heading for water, unclip your leg straps and chest strap before touching down only if you're very close and have practised it, and get out from under the wing quickly.
My friend has an old rig in his garage from the 90s, says it's fine. Could I learn to pack it and use it?

Don't jump that rig without a full inspection by a certified rigger, and honestly, it probably isn't airworthy. Gear from the 90s may have degraded fabric and webbing, old canopies that aren't suited to students, and no working AAD. Learn on modern student gear at a dropzone first, and if the old rig matters to you, let a rigger decide whether any part of it is still usable.
Thinking about wreck penetration on an upcoming trip, guide says it's no big deal. Thoughts?

Going inside a wreck without specific training is one of the classic ways divers die. Silt-outs, entanglement and losing the exit happen fast, and in an overhead environment you can't swim straight up. Swimming through wide, open, well-lit swim-throughs with a qualified guide is a different thing from real penetration. Go no further than you can see daylight, and take a wreck course if you want to go further.
My friend blacked out last week but is fine now. He wants to dive again tomorrow. Too soon?

If he hasn't seen a doctor, he should before diving again, because a blackout can involve water aspiration and lung issues that show up later. If he gets the all-clear, he should come back conservatively, with shallower, shorter dives and longer rests. He should also take an honest look at what caused it: hyperventilation, fatigue, cold or pushing too hard. And make sure his buddy is trained in rescue.
how do i learn a kong vault without eating the box lol

Start on something low and soft, like a padded vault box or a stack of mats, and practice diving your hands to the far edge of the obstacle so your hips have room to pass over. Most face-plants come from placing your hands too close and not pushing, so think "reach and shove" rather than "plant and pray." Build up with dive rolls on grass and cat passes before adding speed, and only move to hard surfaces once you can land it consistently on the soft stuff.
want to skate at night, any tips

Night skating is fun but visibility is everything, so wear something reflective and put a light on yourself or your board so drivers can actually see you. Stick to routes you already know in daylight, because cracks and rocks are much harder to spot in the dark. Softer wheels in the 78a to 85a range will help you roll over debris you can't see.
my coach says salt tabs are a scam. true??

Not a scam, but they're often overused. Most people get plenty of sodium from sports drink and real food, so tabs matter more for heavy, salty sweaters in long hot races. The bigger danger in ultras is actually drinking too much plain water, which can dilute your blood sodium. Drink to thirst and take sodium in modest amounts rather than slamming tabs on a schedule.
Can I just use my resort skis for touring if I get some of those adapter things?

Frame adapters like the Daymaker or Trekker do work for short, occasional tours, but they're heavy and clunky, and alpine boots without a walk mode make long climbs miserable. They're fine for trying out touring before you spend a lot of money. If you're hooked, a dedicated tech or hybrid binding setup will make the whole thing far more enjoyable. Whichever you use, you still need avalanche gear and training before you go anywhere near avalanche terrain.
how often should i change oil on my crf250r

Most riders change the oil on a CRF250R every 3 to 5 hours of ride time, and do it more often if they ride hard, ride in sand or race. These high-revving four-strokes don't hold much oil and break it down quickly, so cheap frequent changes are much easier on your wallet than a top-end rebuild. Change the filter every other oil change, and check your manual for the transmission oil interval, since on that bike it's a separate compartment.
Can I teach myself paragliding from YouTube videos? Lessons are crazy expensive where I live.

Videos are great for theory, but they can't replace an instructor watching your launches and talking you through your first flights on the radio. Most serious injuries happen to self-taught pilots who misjudge conditions or botch a launch they never properly drilled. If cost is the issue, look for a school abroad offering a full licence course in one or two weeks, which is often cheaper than piecemeal local lessons. Keep the YouTube habit for supplementing what you learn, not replacing it.
can i just wear my bike helmet for downhill

For cruising around flat streets it's fine, but for actual downhill you want a full-face helmet. Most downhill crashes involve sliding or tumbling face-first at speed, and a bike half-shell leaves your jaw, teeth and chin completely exposed. Look for a certified full-face skate or motorcycle-style lid; a decent one costs less than one dental reconstruction.
just got my first longboard, wanna go down the big hill near my house tonight. tips?

Hold off on the big hill tonight, especially in the dark when cars and road debris are hard to see. Spend your first sessions on a gentle slope in daylight learning to footbrake, carve to control speed and do a basic slide, then step up gradually once you can stop reliably. Wear a helmet and pads from day one, and if you can, ride with someone more experienced who can show you the ropes.
Is it okay to do a cave dive with a slight cold if I'm clearing my ears fine?

It's best to skip it, because even mild congestion can cause reverse blocks on ascent, which is especially dangerous in a cave where your ascent is limited. Colds can also affect your breathing and decision-making. Wait until you've fully recovered, and the caves will still be there.
Can I climb Aconcagua solo with no guide? I've done a few 4000ers in the Alps.

People do climb Aconcagua independently, but jumping from Alpine 4000ers to a nearly 7000 m peak alone is a big step. The altitude, brutal wind and cold are a different league, and on your own nobody will notice if you start making poor decisions from hypoxia. A smarter move is joining a logistics-supported expedition or climbing with an experienced partner, and getting a 6000 m peak like Huayna Potosí or Chimborazo under your belt first.
I want to hit a rail I've never tried in icy conditions, it's my last day of the trip

I'd skip the new rail today. Ice makes approaches faster and less predictable and makes landings punishing, so it's about the worst setup for a first attempt. Spend your last day lapping features you already know and enjoying them, and save the new rail for softer snow when you've got time to learn it properly.
Is surfing big waves with a GoPro mouth mount a bad idea?

Yes, a mouth mount in big surf is risky because a heavy wipeout can slam the camera into your teeth or jaw. It also makes it harder to take a good breath before going under, which matters a lot in heavy water. Use a helmet mount or a board mount instead, and accept that big waves will take some cameras no matter what.
What's the best shoe for parkour? Budget around 80 bucks.

Look for a flat, flexible shoe with a grippy gum-rubber sole, decent heel cushioning, and a snug fit without a bulky toe. Purpose-built options like Feiyue-style shoes or the cheaper models from parkour-specific brands work well, and running shoes with low, wide soles are fine too. Skip shoes with deep tread lugs or thick stacked heels, since they reduce your ground feel and roll your ankle more easily on precision landings.
Can I swim in a river after heavy rain? It looks fine.

It's best to wait a few days, because rivers after heavy rain often run much faster than they look and can carry hidden debris. Runoff and sewage overflows also push bacteria levels up, which can make you ill. Check the local water quality alerts and flow levels, and go back when the water has cleared and calmed.
My boyfriend soloed a 200 ft route last weekend and posted it. I'm terrified. How do I bring it up?

Your fear is reasonable, and it's fair to tell him directly that it scares you and why. Approach it as a conversation rather than an ultimatum. Ask what draws him to it, how he prepared, and whether he'd consider sticking to roped climbing or using rope-solo systems. If he's committed to it, you're allowed to decide what level of risk you can live with in a partner.
I climb 5.11 trad comfortably. Is soloing a 5.6 I've done 20 times reasonable?

You're in the zone where experienced climbers do make that choice, but the risk never goes away. A broken hold, a wasp, a wet patch, or a moment of distraction can kill you on a 5.6. If you do it, inspect the route on a rope right beforehand, pick perfect conditions, and be honest with yourself about why you want to. Many strong climbers decide that taking a quick rope or a self-belay setup gives them most of the flow with far less consequence.
is skating at night ok? there's this sick empty parking garage

It can be fun, but the main risks are poor lighting hiding cracks and debris, and drivers not expecting someone on a board, especially on ramps between levels. Make sure it's actually legal to skate there or you could get kicked out or fined. If you go, bring a friend, wear light-colored clothing or lights, check the ground in the light first, and stay off the ramps where cars come around blind corners.
anchor bolts at the crag look rusty, probably fine for one top rope session right?

Don't trust visibly rusty bolts. Corrosion can weaken them in ways you can't judge by eye, especially near the sea. Skip that route, or back the anchor up with trad gear if you're properly trained to build one. Report the bolts to the local climbing association or the rebolting fund so they get replaced.
do pros wear any protective gear

Professional cliff divers mostly wear only swimwear, but they rely on years of training, coaching and divers in the water who are ready to help immediately. Some wear tape or supports on their wrists and ankles. For recreational jumpers, water shoes and a wetsuit in cold water are worth considering, and a safety spotter is the most important protection.
is it ok to climb with a hangover lol

Light gym bouldering is your call, but don't belay or lead anyone. A belayer's slower reaction time and lapses in focus are exactly how drops happen. Being hungover also makes you dehydrated and clumsy, which isn't ideal for falling well. Drink water, eat something, and maybe make today a mellow session.
hey can i belay my friend while wearing crampons and standing right under them

Keep the crampons on if the ground is icy, but don't stand directly underneath. Ice falls constantly while someone climbs, so set up off to the side, out of the fall line, and keep your helmet on. Find a stable stance, and anchor yourself if the base is sloped or slippery so you don't get pulled off your feet.
My paddle partner refuses to wear a PFD, says he's a strong swimmer. Thoughts?

Swimming ability barely matters in whitewater, because aerated water is less buoyant, currents are stronger than any swimmer, and a knock on a rock can leave you dazed. Strong pool swimmers drown in rivers all the time. Tell him plainly that you won't paddle with him without one, since a rescue for him also puts you at risk.
I'm the most experienced in my group so they all just follow my call. Kind of stressful honestly.

That's a real hazard, because the expert halo makes groups stop questioning decisions, and accident studies show it clearly. Set it up so everyone voices concerns before each slope and anyone can veto without having to justify it. It takes pressure off you, and pushing them toward their own avalanche training means you aren't the only safety net.
best lights for cave diving?

You'll want a primary canister or high-output handheld light around 1500 to 3000 lumens with a focused beam for clear signaling, plus two independent backup lights clipped to your harness. Brands like Halcyon, Light Monkey, OrcaTorch and Divesoft are popular. Your instructor will have opinions on beam angle and mounting, so check with them before you buy a primary.
What's the fastest way to get better at corners? I keep washing out on berms.

On berms, washing out usually means you're braking in the turn or not committing your weight to the bike. Finish your braking before the entry, look through to the exit, and press your outside foot and inside hand into the bike so the tires bite into the berm wall. Practice on one corner, lap it a dozen times, and a coach can spot your specific mistake in minutes.
how tight should a harness be

Do the waist belt up above your hip bones, snug enough that you can only slide a flat hand underneath. It shouldn't be able to slip down over your hips even if you hang upside down. The leg loops can be a little looser, and you should be able to fit a flat hand under those too. Double-check that every buckle is doubled back or properly locked, as the manufacturer instructs.
What causes most wingsuit skydiving accidents?

The main problems are deployment issues like line twists or poor body position, canopy collisions or traffic problems at the dropzone, and pilots moving to larger suits before they're ready. Altitude awareness is another big one because the suit makes freefall last longer. The fix is boring but effective: progress suit size slowly, follow dropzone flight patterns, and keep high deployment altitudes.
how long does the whole thing take start to finish

Plan on one to three hours in total, including check-in, weigh-in, the safety briefing, harness fitting, the queue and getting back up or out after your jump. The free fall itself lasts only a few seconds, and the bounces maybe a minute. Busy seasons and weather holds can stretch the wait, so don't schedule anything tight right after.
Is it ok to touch the coral if I'm careful?

Best not to. Even a light touch can damage the protective mucus layer and kill coral polyps that took years to grow, and some corals and things living on them can sting or cut you. Work on your buoyancy so you can hover without needing to hold on, and if you really need to steady yourself, use one finger on bare rock.
how big is too big for a 52 year old guy whos been surfing 30 years

There's no hard number, but your limit is the size where you can comfortably handle a two-wave hold-down and paddle back out without panicking. For some surfers that's 15 feet, for others it's 30. At 52, your recovery, cardio and any medical issues matter more than raw experience. Get a checkup, keep your breath and fitness training sharp, and size up gradually with a solid crew around you.
Detailed one: I'm full cave certified, 60 cave dives, planning to push past a restriction I've never done in a known Florida system. Buddy wants to go no-mount with one tank. Thoughts?

No-mount through an unfamiliar restriction is a big step up, and doing it with a single tank leaves you with no redundant gas source in the worst possible place. Stick with two independent cylinders, even if you're pushing one ahead of you, and stage your gas planning conservatively. A good idea is to run the restriction first with someone who knows it, or get a sidemount and no-mount specialty course before going for it.
Thinking about proximity flying in the mountains after my first season. Worth it?

After just one season, that's way too early. Proximity flying is extremely unforgiving, with tiny margins for error, and most fatalities come from pilots who moved too fast. Spend several more seasons building precision, glide control and BASE skills, then progress under the direct guidance of experienced mountain pilots on forgiving lines first.
How do I do a whip

Before you even think about whips, you need to be smooth and very comfortable on the jump, landing straight consistently, because a whip that's not brought back in time means landing sideways. Start by adding small amounts of lean and bar input off a mellow tabletop where landing matters less, and focus on getting the bike straight well before the landing. A coach or experienced rider watching you can save you from learning the hard way.
my buddy has a bungee cord and wants to jump off the old train bridge near us this weekend. we'll measure it first, it'll be fine right

Please don't do this. Getting the stretch right depends on a cord rated for your exact body weight, a correct calculation of how far it extends under load, rigging that won't fail and someone trained to set it all up. An ordinary bungee cord and a tape measure can't account for any of that, and a small mistake means hitting the ground or the bridge structure. Book a real jump instead. You'll get the same thrill without betting your life on guesswork.
My dad is 72 and wants to bungee for his birthday. Is that nuts?

Not nuts at all. Plenty of people jump in their 70s and 80s, and most operators don't set an upper age limit. Some will ask for a doctor's note above a certain age, though. The real questions are his heart, blood pressure, bones and back, so have him get checked by his doctor first. With the all-clear, it makes a fantastic birthday story.
how long does cave cert take

Typically about 8 to 10 days total if you do cavern, intro to cave and full cave together, though many people spread the levels out and dive between them. Some instructors require extra days if your buoyancy or trim isn't solid yet. It's worth taking the time, because rushing through means less real experience at each stage.
is it true you should drink as much water as possible during a hot ultra

No, and that idea genuinely hurts people. Overdrinking plain water during long events can cause hyponatremia, a dangerous drop in blood sodium that can lead to confusion, seizures and death. Drink to thirst, typically somewhere around 400 to 800 ml an hour depending on heat and your size, and get sodium in through electrolyte drinks, salt tabs or salty food.
Need you to just tell me how to start soloing, no lecture.

Fair enough, here's the short version. The people who survive soloing start by climbing roped for years, then solo terrain far below their limit that they've already climbed many times on rope, and they back off at the first doubt. So the actual first step is to lead a lot outdoors with experienced partners. There's no faster path that doesn't hugely raise your odds of dying.
can i use a snorkel on deep dives

Use it at the surface for breathing up, but take it out of your mouth before you dive. Diving with a snorkel in your mouth can let water flood in if you black out, and it gets in the way of recovery breathing at the surface. Many freedivers clip the snorkel to their mask strap or drop it entirely for line diving.
Is Island Peak a good first 6000er for someone who's done some UK winter climbing?

It's a popular choice, and your winter background helps with crampons and axe work, though the summit ridge and fixed lines mean you should be comfortable jumaring and on steep snow. Combining it with the Everest Base Camp trek gives you excellent acclimatization beforehand. Go with a reputable operator and a climbing Sherpa, and make sure they include a proper skills refresher at base camp.
Weight belt question - should I overweight a bit so it's easier to get down?

No. Weight yourself so you're neutrally buoyant at around 10 meters, or about a third of your target depth. That way you stay positive near the surface, which is exactly where you want to float if you black out. If you're overweighted, you'll sink if you lose consciousness, and the extra lead also makes the ascent harder at the moment you have the least oxygen. Use a quick-release rubber belt, and make sure both you and your buddy know how to dump it.
I'm 58, decent diver, never been in an overhead. Too old to start cave?

Plenty of people start cave diving in their fifties and beyond, so age alone isn't the issue. Get a dive medical first, since the gear is heavy and the dives can be long and cold, and be honest about fitness, heart health and any medications. Start with a cavern course and see how you feel before committing to full cave.
I'm claustrophobic but want to try cave diving. Bad idea?

Not necessarily, but be careful, as panic is one of the most dangerous things that can happen in a cave. Start with open water and cavern dives where you can see daylight, and talk openly with an instructor about your claustrophobia. Some people find they're comfortable underwater even with tight spaces, while others realize it's not for them, and both outcomes are completely fine.
Bought a 450 as my first dirt bike because everyone says you grow out of a 250 too fast. Mistake?

Honestly, for most new riders a 450 is a lot of bike, since it makes so much power so quickly that a nervous grab of throttle can loop you or send you into a tree. If you're keeping it, ask a dealer about a throttle tamer or a mellower map, ride in a big open area, and get a few lessons before touching jumps. A 250F would let you learn the skills faster and with fewer scares, and swapping now is cheaper than a hospital bill.
whats the fastest way to learn a backflip, i want it by next weekend

A week is too tight to learn a backflip safely on your own. Rushing it is how people over-rotate onto their necks or under-rotate onto their faces. The fastest safe route is a few sessions at a gymnastics or parkour gym, where a coach can spot you and you can drill it into a foam pit. If you have natural air awareness you might land it with a spot quickly, but don't take it to hard ground until you can land it cleanly every time.
How long does it take to get good at parkour?

Expect the basics like vaults, precisions and safety rolls to feel solid after six months to a year of consistent training a few times a week. Truly advanced skills usually take several years, because your tendons and joints adapt more slowly than your muscles do. Training with a coach or a community can speed things up a lot, mainly because you'll get feedback and won't waste months reinforcing bad habits.
is training alone okay

For low-risk skills on familiar ground, sure. For anything with height, new jumps or flips, train with someone else, because if you get hurt alone, help might not come quickly. When you do go solo, tell someone where you are, carry your phone, and stay within your proven ability.
Thinking about building a jump line in the woods behind my house. Any tips?

Start small with tabletops instead of gaps, because they're far more forgiving if you come up short, and build longer, smoother landings than you think you need. Make sure you have permission to use the land, pack the dirt firmly, and keep the runout clear of trees and rocks. Ride with someone around in case you crash, and keep a first aid kit and phone nearby.
Going to try my first tabletop jump this weekend. Any tips?

Start by rolling the tabletop a few times at low speed so you know exactly how long the top is and where the landing starts. Stand up with your weight centered and knees bent, and keep the throttle steady on the face instead of chopping it, because chopping the throttle is what makes the front end dive. Add a little speed each pass until you're landing on the downslope. If you're nervous, ask an experienced rider to go ahead of you so you can match their speed.
Training for my first 5k open water race. How should I practice sighting?

Build it into every swim: every 6 to 10 strokes, lift just your eyes above the surface like a crocodile, then roll into your breath. Pick big landmarks like buildings or trees rather than the buoys themselves, which are hard to see over chop. Practice in the pool by sighting on an object at the end of the lane, then rehearse in open water with a buddy. Good sighting can easily save you a few hundred metres of zig-zagging in a 5k.
is it ok to climb with a hangover

Light bouldering on easy problems is usually fine, but your coordination and judgment will be worse than usual. Skip lead climbing and belaying, since those depend on attention and quick reactions to keep other people safe. Drink plenty of water, keep the session short, and save anything hard for another day.
Fingers have been aching after sessions, especially my ring finger at the base. I climb 5 days a week. Push through it?

Don't push through it, because pain at the base of the ring finger is a classic early sign of pulley strain, and climbing through it is how a minor tweak becomes a rupture that costs you months. Five days a week also leaves your tendons almost no recovery time, since they adapt much more slowly than muscle. Cut back to two or three days, avoid crimps and small pockets for now, and see a physio, ideally one who works with climbers, if the pain is sharp or doesn't clear in a week or two. A sudden pop or bruising means stop and get it checked right away.
is it dumb to swim across the lake alone at 6am before anyone's around? it's only like 800m

It's not dumb to want that quiet swim, but going completely alone with nobody watching is the part to fix, because cramps or cold shock can turn 800m into a long way fast. Tow a bright swim buoy, wear a colored cap, and tell someone your route and the time you expect to be back. Ideally get a friend to paddleboard or kayak alongside, which keeps the magic of the empty lake without the risk.
what should i do if i land flat on my back

First, get to the surface and to shore, and have your friends help if you're dazed. If you have intense back pain, numbness, tingling or difficulty breathing, keep still and call emergency services, because you could have a spinal injury. Even if you feel okay, watch for blood in your urine or worsening pain over the next day, since a hard flat landing can bruise internal organs.
should i ride with a broken finger if i tape it

I'd hold off until a doctor says it's healed enough. Gripping the bars and working the clutch or brake puts a lot of stress on fingers, and a crash could make the break much worse or require surgery. Riding with a weak grip also makes it harder to control the bike. Most finger fractures heal in a few weeks, so give it time.
can i practice tricks in the trees

Butters, small ollies off rollers and slow presses are fine in open, mellow glades, but tree riding plus trick attempts is a bad combo. Trees don't give you room to slide out of a fall, and tree wells can be deadly in deep snow. Keep the flashy stuff to open groomers and the park, and keep tree runs about control.
Is sauna training actually legit for heat acclimation or is it bro science?

It's legit, and it's backed by research. Spending about 20 to 30 minutes in a sauna right after a run, several times a week for two or three weeks, increases plasma volume and gives you real heat adaptations. It works best combined with some training in actual heat, since it doesn't fully mimic running hot. Start short, hydrate well afterward, and get out if you feel dizzy.
Is a terrain trap really that big a deal on a small slope?

Yes, a small slide that ends in a gully, creek bed or tree well can bury you deeply because all the debris piles into one spot. Lots of fatal burials happen on small, short slopes for exactly this reason. Pay as much attention to what's at the bottom of a slope as to how big it is.
is skydiving actually dangerous or is that overblown

It's riskier than everyday activities, but much safer than most people think. In the US the fatality rate runs at roughly one per few hundred thousand jumps, and tandem jumps are statistically even safer. Most fatalities among experienced jumpers involve canopy errors near the ground, which is why training and good judgment matter more than luck.
is a backflip off a 8m cliff doable if I can do one on a trampoline

Trampoline skills don't translate cleanly. Off a cliff you have no rebound, the timing is different, and over- or under-rotating at 8 meters means a flat back or face slap that can really hurt you. If you want to learn, do it off springboards and low platforms at a dive pool, ideally with a coach, and only take it to cliffs once you're landing it consistently.
can I ride alone at private land? nobody else rides near me

You can, but riding alone in the dirt adds real risk, because if you get hurt or pinned under the bike, nobody may be around to help. If you do go solo, tell someone where you are and when you'll be back, carry your phone on your body instead of on the bike, and consider a crash detection app or wearable. Stick to riding you know you can handle, and save new jumps or hard sections for days when someone else is with you.
can i ride a cheap hardtail on the black runs

Black downhill runs on a cheap hardtail are asking for trouble. The frame, wheels, brakes and fork usually aren't built for those impacts, and the lack of rear suspension makes the bike harsh and harder to control at speed. Ride greens and blues on it to build skill, then rent a proper downhill bike when you're ready for the black runs. You'll ride better and the bike won't fail on you.
best way to keep my hands from freezing while belaying? they get numb fast

Bring a warm belay jacket, ideally a big synthetic puffy, and put it on the moment you stop climbing, since your core temperature drives your hand warmth. Carry two or three pairs of gloves and swap to a dry pair, and pack thick mittens for long belays. Keep your fingers moving and eat and drink regularly to keep generating heat. If you start losing dexterity, tell your partner, because belaying with numb hands isn't safe.
do wingsuits glide far enough to cross a valley

A good pilot in a large suit can reach glide ratios around 2.5:1 to 3:1, and that sounds like a lot, but crossing terrain depends on wind, sink rate, altitude, and the exact line. Miscalculating a glide is one of the classic ways wingsuit BASE jumpers die. That kind of flying is only for very experienced pilots who have scouted the line and have mentorship.
want to try grinding a handrail asap whats the quickest way

There's no real shortcut, but the fastest safe route is to learn grinds on a low ledge or flat bar first so you understand how to lock in and balance. Once you're comfortable doing 50-50s and boardslides on a flat bar, try a small rail with a few steps and a clear runout. Wear a helmet and pads, because handrail falls often happen sideways and fast, and a botched one can be brutal on your ribs and groin.
What's the deal with weighing yourself during ultras?

Some races weigh you at checkpoints to catch problems early. Losing more than about 3 to 5 percent of your start weight suggests dehydration, while gaining weight points to overdrinking and hyponatremia risk. Small drops of 1 to 2 percent are normal and fine. If medical staff flag you, listen, because the scale is catching something you might not feel yet.
Can I do a pool freediving course if I'm not a great swimmer?

Yes, many people start that way. Most entry courses only require you to be comfortable in the water and able to swim a modest distance, often 200 meters or so with fins or without. Tell the instructor upfront and they'll adapt. Spending some time building basic swim fitness first will make the course far more enjoyable.
First time swimming in a lake this weekend, water's about 14°C. Should I just dive in to get it over with?

Don't dive in. Sudden immersion in water that cold triggers a gasp reflex and rapid breathing that can make you inhale water before you've even started swimming. Walk in slowly, splash your face and neck, and give yourself a minute or two of calm breathing before you put your head under. The shock passes in about 90 seconds if you let it, and you'll swim much better for it.
My girlfriend wants me to quit wingsuiting since a friend of ours died BASE jumping. I only do skydives with the suit. How do I explain the difference?

Be honest that the main risk difference is terrain. Wingsuit skydiving happens high above the ground with lots of altitude and a reserve parachute, while wingsuit BASE involves low altitude and proximity flying, where a small mistake is often fatal. Still, wingsuiting isn't risk-free, so listen to her fears and share what safety habits you actually follow. If she's still struggling, a calm conversation with your coach or a friend in the sport might help her see the realities.
I'm 16 and my buddy says we should paddle out at the big reef break tomorrow since the swell is 20 feet. We've surfed 8 foot beach breaks. Good idea?

Skip it and watch from the cliff instead, because jumping from 8 foot beach break to 20 foot reef is a leap that seriously injures experienced surfers. The hold-downs, the shallow reef and the sheer volume of water moving are a completely different game from what you've trained for. Spend this swell watching where the locals sit, how they pick waves and where they get caught inside. Then build up gradually through 10 to 15 foot days with someone experienced alongside you.
I'm 17, really want to do Mount Elbrus this summer with my friends who are also 17. No guide. Thoughts?

Elbrus is deceptively dangerous: it looks like a simple snow slope, but it kills people every year, mostly in whiteouts where climbers lose the route and wander into crevasse fields. With no high-altitude experience and no guide, the odds are against you. Join a guided group, many of which take younger climbers with parental consent, and you'll get the experience while someone who knows the mountain watches your back.
Riding a jump with wet heavy snow. Should I go faster than usual?

Probably a bit, because slow snow kills speed, but don't just guess. Take a test run or two where you roll the jump without airing it to feel how much speed the snow is costing you. Wet snow can also be grabby on landings, so keep your weight centered and your knees ready to absorb. If you can't judge it confidently, skip the bigger features that day.
how high can a beginner safely jump from? going to a quarry this weekend

Start at around 3 to 5 meters and stay there until your entries are consistently clean and controlled, because impact forces climb fast with height and a sloppy landing at 10 meters can easily injure you. Quarries are especially risky since they often hide submerged machinery, rebar and ledges, so have someone check the landing zone with goggles first. Never jump alone, and skip the jump entirely if you can't confirm the depth.
Is it normal to be scared of boxes? I keep chickening out at the last second.

Totally normal, and bailing at the last second is actually riskier than committing, because that's when you catch an edge. Start on the widest, lowest, flattest box in the park and just ride straight across it with a flat base, no tricks, until it feels boring. Keep your knees bent, your weight centered, and your eyes on the end of the box rather than your feet. Confidence comes from repetition on features well within your ability.
I'm 16 and my parents won't let me go to a parkour gym. Any way to learn at home safely?

You can build a lot of the foundation at home with low-risk training. Practice bodyweight strength like squats, push-ups and pull-ups, along with balance on low edges, precision jumps on flat ground, and safety rolls on grass or a mattress. Avoid flips and anything high until you have proper coaching. Showing your parents you're training sensibly might also help convince them to let you go to a gym later.
my 9 year old wants to learn to drop in on the 6 foot quarter pipe at the park this weekend, he can barely ollie yet. is that ok?

I'd hold off on the 6 footer for now and start him on a 2 to 3 foot ramp, because dropping in is about committing your weight forward and that's much less scary and less punishing on a small ramp. Get him in a helmet, knee pads and wrist guards, and have him practice the motion on flat ground or grass first by leaning onto the front truck. Once he's dropping in confidently and rolling away clean on the small ramp, moving up a size at a time is the right progression, and his ollie doesn't need to be perfect for this.
is it ok to skate on the road if there's no sidewalk

It depends on your local laws, since some places ban skateboards on roads, so check that first. If it's allowed, ride in the same direction as traffic, stay as far right as is safe, and avoid busy roads, hills that can push you into traffic, and riding at dusk or night. Wear a helmet and bright clothing, and use lights after dark. If the road is fast or has no shoulder, carry the board instead, because cars won't expect you.
how far out should i go

Only as far as you could comfortably swim back if you got tired, cramped, or the conditions changed. A good starting rule is to swim parallel to the shore within your depth or close to it, rather than heading straight out. Build up distance over several sessions, and always tell someone your plan and wear a bright cap or tow float so you can be seen.
Ankle harness or body harness, which is less scary?

Most people find the body harness less scary because you feel more secure and you rebound upright, not dangling by your feet. Ankle attachment gives you the classic swan-dive feel and a cleaner flying sensation, but hanging upside down at the end bothers some people. Both are safe when a good operator sets them up, so pick whichever lets you actually step off the edge. Lots of first-timers go body harness and switch to ankle next time.
My dad is 72 and wants to skydive for his birthday. Is that crazy?

Not crazy at all, and plenty of people in their 70s, 80s and even 90s have done tandem jumps. The main concerns are the landing, which can be hard on hips and knees, and any heart conditions. Have him get a checkup and doctor's clearance first, and tell the dropzone his age so they can pair him with an experienced instructor who's good at sliding landings.
First time on class II next weekend, super nervous. Anything I should know?

Being nervous is normal and actually useful, because it keeps you paying attention. Go with experienced paddlers, wear a fitted PFD and helmet, and practice your wet exit before you hit the rapids. If you swim, float on your back with your feet up and downstream, hold onto your paddle if you can, and swim aggressively toward an eddy or the shore.
Is it safe to fly over the sea?

Flying along the coast in good conditions is common and pleasant, but flying out over open water is risky. If you have to land in water, the wing and lines can drag you under fast. Unless you're doing a supervised SIV course with rescue boats, keep within easy glide of land. If you're flying near water regularly, consider a flotation device and a hook knife.
What happens if the cord snaps?

With a reputable operator it's extremely unlikely. Cords are logged, retired after a set number of jumps well below their failure point, and often made of hundreds of bundled strands rather than one. Most serious bungee accidents in history came from human error, like the wrong cord length or a connection that wasn't secured, rather than a cord snapping. That's why staff who double-check everything matter more than anything else.
Wrists are killing me from falling during park practice, any advice?

Get some wrist guards, which are cheap and do a lot to prevent the common snowboard wrist fracture. Try to fall onto your forearms or roll onto your back rather than reaching out with straight arms. If the pain is sharp, swollen or not improving after a few days, get it checked, because scaphoid fractures often feel like a sprain and can go wrong if ignored.
heard a big whumpf when we were skinning up today. kept going and nothing happened lol

That whumpf was a weak layer in the snowpack collapsing under you. It's about as clear a warning sign as nature gives, so you got lucky rather than proving it was fine. Whumpfing and shooting cracks mean the snowpack is primed for a slab to release, and on a steeper slope that collapse could have taken the whole thing. Next time treat it as a cue to back off to low-angle terrain with nothing steep overhead and call it a day.
is it safe to skate on a mini ramp without a helmet if it's only like 3 feet

I'd still wear the helmet, because on a mini ramp the most common bad fall is slipping out backward and hitting your head on the coping or flat, and that happens at even 3 feet. A lot of serious head injuries happen at low heights simply because people let their guard down. A helmet is cheap insurance, especially while you're still learning to fall.
how long after acl surgery can i race again

Most surgeons and physical therapists say roughly nine to twelve months, and the timeline should be based on passing return-to-sport strength and stability tests, not just the calendar. Going back too early is one of the biggest risk factors for re-tearing. Follow your rehab program closely and get your surgeon's clearance, then start with easy trail riding and add track time gradually before you race.
Thinking of soloing the Flatirons third class routes in Boulder. I hike a lot but don't climb. Okay?

The Third Flatiron's standard route is low fifth class, so it's harder and more exposed than its reputation suggests, and people die there regularly. With no climbing background, go with a guide or an experienced friend on a rope for your first time. Many Boulder climbers do solo it eventually, but only after climbing it roped and knowing the descent, and the rappels have caught people out. Avoid it when the rock is wet or icy.
What's the deal with the 'hook breathing' thing after surfacing?

Recovery or hook breathing is a technique you do right after surfacing to get oxygen back to your brain faster and lower the risk of blackout. You take a quick inhale, hold briefly with slight pressure, then exhale passively, and repeat for several breaths. Make it a habit on every dive, even easy ones. Your buddy should watch you through it for at least 30 seconds.
partner wants to lead and me to belay but i weigh 50 kg and he's 90. issue?

That weight difference matters, because a hard fall can yank you off your feet into the wall or the first bolt. Use a ground anchor or an Ohm, which is a resistance device clipped to the first bolt, and stand close to the wall rather than far back. An assisted braking device helps too. Practice some controlled falls together so you know what the pull feels like before he goes for anything at his limit.
Is it ok to drink some alcohol before climbing to stay warm?

No. Alcohol actually lowers your core temperature by dilating blood vessels in your skin, which raises the risk of hypothermia and frostbite. It also slows your reactions and dulls your judgment, which you need sharp on ice. Bring a warm, non-alcoholic drink and save the beer for after.
My 15 year old wants to try ice climbing with his friends who have 'done it a couple times.' Should I let him?

Your instinct to pause is a good one, because a couple of days out doesn't give teenagers the skills to build anchors in ice, judge ice quality, or spot overhead hazards like falling ice. A better first step is a guided intro day or a youth ice clinic with a certified guide, where he'll learn proper crampon and tool technique on toprope with someone who knows how to read conditions. Plenty of ice festivals and guide services run beginner programs, and he can go with his friends if they want to join. Once he has some real instruction behind him, outings with experienced partners make a lot more sense.
I tore my A2 pulley 6 weeks ago, feels fine now. can i go back to crimping?

Feeling fine is not the same as being healed, since pulley tears usually need around two to three months or more before you can load them fully, depending on severity. Go back gradually with open-hand grips and easy climbing first, then add crimps over several weeks, stopping at any sharp pain. Taping with H-taping can help for a while. A hand physio who knows climbing can grade the injury and give you a specific return plan, which is well worth it to avoid a re-tear.
Spearfishing tomorrow, any tips to stay down longer for the big fish?

Spearfishing kills more breath-hold divers than any other activity, because the focus on a fish makes you stretch dives and ignore your body's warnings. Dive with a buddy using one-up one-down, take longer surface rests than feel necessary, and set a rule that no fish is worth extending a dive. You get longer bottom time by relaxing and moving efficiently, not by pushing through the urge to breathe.
Is it safe to do parkour on roofs if I'm careful? I've been training for 3 months.

No, three months isn't nearly enough for rooftops, and even experienced traceurs treat height as a separate skill with zero margin for error. A fall from a single storey can cause spinal injuries, and roofs add unknowns like rotten surfaces, loose gravel, skylights and trespassing problems. Keep building your precision and confidence at ground level, where a missed jump costs you a scraped shin instead of your life. If height work ever interests you, learn it later under a coach who can judge your consistency honestly.
my buddy says we can just solo the easy WI2 approach gully unroped to save time. thoughts

Low-angle ice still kills people, because a slip on a hard surface turns into a long, fast slide you can't arrest. Unless you're both very experienced and the ice is in great condition, rope up or at least simul-climb with protection in. The time you save soloing isn't worth the consequences of one catch on a crampon point. If speed matters, start earlier instead.
I'm 52 and finally want to try free soloing before I'm too old. Thoughts?

Wanting a big adventure at 52 is great, but free soloing is the one that can't be done halfway or late. Being experienced with a rope is what makes soloing possible at all, so if you're new, you'd be starting a multi-year process. Try a guided multi-pitch climb, an alpine ridge, or a via ferrata instead. They'll give you plenty of exposure and accomplishment with a safety system in place.
how do i do a precision jump

Stand with your feet together, swing your arms back, then drive them forward as you jump off both feet. Aim to land on the balls of your feet, knees bent, so you stick the landing without wobbling. Start with gaps of a foot or two on flat ground, using lines or cracks as targets. Only add height or narrow rails once you can stick ten landings in a row without stepping.
how do you check depth before jumping

The most reliable method is to swim down yourself with goggles and confirm both the depth and that the bottom is clear across the whole landing area. A weighted rope with marked meters works as a quick backup, but it can miss rocks between measurement points. Recheck every time you visit, because water levels and debris change with rain, tides and seasons.
how do i know if a cliff edge is stable

Look for cracks, loose stones, crumbling soil, or overhangs, and avoid edges that are wet, mossy or sandy underfoot. Test your footing a step back from the edge before committing, and launch from a solid, well-used spot rather than the very lip. If the rock looks rotten or recently broken, find another place to jump.
Detailed one: 34F, mild hamstring strain sprinting for an obstacle race 9 days ago, no bruising, walking fine, mild tightness when I stretch. Race in 3 weeks. Plan?

That sounds like a mild grade 1 strain, and three weeks is a realistic window if you progress carefully. Over the next week, focus on pain-free hamstring loading like bridges, hamstring slides and eventually Nordics, plus easy jogging. Then build back up to strides and short sprints only once fast running feels normal. Skip aggressive static stretching for now, since it irritates a healing strain more than it helps. On race day, warm up thoroughly and ease off the all-out sprints if it tightens up.
dude theres an antenna near my town nobody guards it, thinking about jumping it this weekend solo

Don't do that, and please don't do it solo. Antennas have guy wires that are hard to see and deadly to hit, the landing areas are often fields with power lines, and climbing them is trespassing that can bring serious legal trouble. If you're already a trained BASE jumper, find out about the object from experienced local jumpers and go with them. If you're not, an FJC is the only sensible next step.
going solo touring tomorrow, conditions look good. any tips?

Solo touring removes your only realistic rescue, so if you go, set your margins much wider than you would with a partner. Stick to low-angle terrain under about 30 degrees with nothing steep above you. Leave a detailed plan and return time with someone, and carry a satellite messenger like an inReach. Honestly, finding a partner is the better call, but if you're going alone, ski it like a burial isn't an option, because effectively it isn't.
can i hold my breath underwater on scuba to save air

Never, because holding your breath while ascending even a meter or two can overexpand your lungs and cause an air embolism. To save air, breathe slowly and deeply, stay warm, move slowly and fix your buoyancy so you're not finning against it. Good air consumption comes with relaxed experience, not tricks.
How often should I replace my harness? I've had mine 7 years and it looks fine.

Most manufacturers recommend replacing a harness every five to ten years, and sooner if it's been used often or exposed to sun, chemicals, or big falls. Seven years with regular use is a good time to retire it, especially if you see fraying, fading, or stiff webbing. A harness is relatively cheap compared to the risk of a failure.
Thinking of running a desert ultra solo, unsupported, in July. Good idea?

That's genuinely dangerous, and I wouldn't do it. Unsupported desert running in peak summer means you can't carry enough water, and if you develop heat illness alone, there's no one to cool you or call for help. If you want a big desert challenge, choose a supported event or go with a partner, plan water caches and an escape route, carry a satellite messenger, and run at night or in a cooler month.
Pulled hamstring sprinting for a parkour gap. How long till I can jump again

That depends on the grade. A mild strain might be two to three weeks, and a bad one can take months, especially if you felt a sharp pull or see bruising down the back of the thigh. Start gentle movement and isometric holds early, then build up through eccentric work like Nordics and progressive running before any explosive jumps. Sprints and gap jumps come last because that's exactly where hamstrings re-tear. A physio can grade it and give you a timeline you can trust.
Had ACL reconstruction 5 months ago. Feel strong. Surgeon says 9 months but I want to ski in a month. Thoughts?

Listen to your surgeon, because the graft is actually at its weakest during this remodeling phase, even though your leg feels great. Reinjury rates drop sharply for people who wait at least nine months and pass strength and hop testing, and skiing is one of the highest-risk sports for ACL tears. Use this month to keep pushing your rehab, because that's what protects your knee long-term.
temps went above freezing yesterday, ice should still be fine today right

Not necessarily, because a thaw can leave ice detached, rotten or hollow even after it refreezes overnight, and the risk is worse on routes that get sun. Look closely when you get there: dripping water, rotten-sounding thuds when you swing, cracks at the top, or chandeliers peeling away are all reasons to pick something else. If in doubt, go for a shaded, thicker line or just top rope something conservative for the day.
is it legal to do parkour in public places

Usually, but it depends on the place. Public parks and plazas are generally fine as long as you aren't damaging anything or putting other people at risk. Private property, including many malls and office complexes, means you need permission, and security can ask you to leave or call the police. Be respectful, leave when you're asked, and never climb onto roofs or structures you don't have access to.
Doing static apnea in my bathtub to train. Totally safe since I can just lift my head, right?

Unfortunately not, because when you black out you don't get to lift your head. People have drowned doing breath-hold training alone in bathtubs and pools. Do your static training dry, lying on a couch or bed, or in water only with a trained buddy watching you closely. Dry CO2 and O2 tables work your breath-hold just as well with no drowning risk.
what happens if i panic and grab the cord

Grabbing the cord is a common instinct, and it can cause rope burns or tangle your arms, which is why the crew tells you to keep your arms out wide or crossed on your chest. Listen closely to the briefing and practice the arm position before you step up. If you do grab it, let go and stay relaxed, because the system will still slow you down. The jumpmaster will talk you through the recovery.
teenager here, parents say downhill is too dangerous. how do I convince them

Show them you're taking it seriously: suggest a coached session at a reputable bike park, wear full protective gear, and agree to start on beginner trails. Parks with staff, patrol and medics are much safer than random backyard jumps, which can reassure them. Invite them to come watch your first day, because seeing the setup often changes their mind.
Just got back from a concussion 3 weeks ago. Can I start hitting jumps again?

Only once a doctor has cleared you for full contact or impact activity, not just normal day-to-day life. A second concussion before the first has healed can be much more serious, and jumps carry real fall risk. If you get the all-clear, ease back in with smooth riding and small features before going back to anything big. And replace your helmet if it took the hit.
is it safe to ski in trees during high avalanche danger

Trees help less than people think, and only dense trees will anchor the snowpack. Sparse or open glades can still slide, and getting swept into trees causes severe trauma. On a high danger day, low-angle trees well away from any big slopes or runout zones are a reasonable option, but avoid steep glades and stay out from under avalanche paths.
My regulator free-flowed on my last cave dive and I handled it but I'm kinda shaken. Normal?

Totally normal, and the fact that you handled it means your training worked. Get the regulator serviced before your next dive, and talk the incident through with your buddy or instructor to lock in what went right. If the anxiety sticks around, do a couple of easy cavern or open water dives to rebuild confidence before going back into the cave.
I'm worried I'll panic if I flip. How do I get over that?

Practice wet exits and rolls in a pool or flatwater with an instructor until flipping feels routine. A big part of the fear comes from not knowing what will happen, so get used to being upside down in a controlled setting. Breathing calmly and taking a beat before you exit or roll will help a lot.
How do I flock with other wingsuiters without crashing into them?

Start with small, organized flocks led by an experienced flight leader, and agree on the plan, break-off and deployment separation on the ground. Approach from behind and slightly below the person you're joining, never from above where you can't be seen. Before deploying, turn away and clear your airspace, because wingsuit collisions often happen at breakoff.
how fast do street luge riders actually go?

Competitive street luge riders regularly hit 60 to 70 mph on steep race courses, and the fastest recorded runs have pushed past 90 mph. Most recreational riders on typical hills sit somewhere in the 30 to 45 mph range, which is still plenty fast when you're lying a few inches off the pavement. Those top speeds only happen on closed courses with hay bales, marshals and cleared roads, never on open streets.
My son crashed and his helmet hit the ground hard but he says he's fine, no headache. Can he keep riding today?

Pull him for the day. Concussion symptoms often show up hours later, and kids tend to downplay them so they can keep riding. Watch him tonight for headache, nausea, confusion, unusual sleepiness or mood changes, and get him seen right away if any appear. Replace that helmet either way, because a hard impact can crush the liner even when the shell looks fine.
I blacked out briefly at the surface yesterday but my buddy got me. I feel fine now. Can I dive today?

Sit today out. A blackout means you went well past your limit, and diving again right away raises your risk while your body and judgment reset. If you inhaled any water, felt short of breath, coughed, or have chest discomfort, get checked by a doctor, because lung problems can show up hours later. When you return, dive more conservatively and work out with your buddy or an instructor what pushed you over.
Is free soloing more dangerous than BASE jumping?

Both are among the deadliest activities in sport, and precise statistics are hard to pin down because few people do either. The difference is that BASE has gear and training progression, while soloing has no backup if anything goes wrong. Many well-known practitioners of each have died, including some of the most experienced. Neither is something to get into casually, and both need years of foundation in a related discipline.
how do I survive a two wave hold down

Stay as relaxed as you possibly can, because panic burns oxygen fast. Let the wave release you instead of fighting, then swim calmly toward the surface or pull your vest if you're disoriented or running low. Train for it beforehand with breath-hold courses that simulate stress, since that's what builds the calm you need. Always surf with partners or water safety watching, because a quick rescue after a two-wave hold-down can be the difference.
Is cave diving in Mexico safer than Florida?

Neither is inherently safer; they're just different. Mexican cenotes tend to be shallow and clear with lots of decoration, while Florida springs are often deeper with stronger flow and siltier passages. The risk depends on your training, planning and staying within limits, so choose sites that match your certification and dive with local guides the first time.
what's the deal with helmets? nobody wears them at my local crag

Wear one anyway. Rockfall and dropped gear happen at any crag, and lead falls can flip you upside down. Belayers are exposed too, since they stand right under the route. Modern helmets are light and comfortable, so it's easy protection to add.
ok honestly what's the fastest way to heal a sprained ankle so i can get back to parkour

The fastest legit route is controlled early movement, not total rest: protect it and use compression for the first couple of days, then start range-of-motion work and walking as pain allows. From there, progress to balance drills and calf raises, then hops, and only go back to precision jumps once you can hop and land on it confidently without pain. Rushing the landing stage is what leads to repeat sprains, so a physio-led plan really is the quickest path back.
My buddy is acting drunk and stumbling at 5,300m but swears he's fine. We're supposed to summit tomorrow.

That sounds like it could be HACE, and a person with brain swelling often can't judge their own condition, so don't take his word for it. Test him by having him walk heel-to-toe in a straight line; if he can't, or he's confused or unusually sleepy, he needs to go down right away, even at night, with someone accompanying him. Call your guide or rescue service now and give him oxygen or dexamethasone if either is available. The summit isn't happening for him tomorrow, and getting him lower fast could save his life.
is it fine to skip the beacon if I'm only skiing trees today? avy danger says moderate

Bring it anyway, because trees don't stop avalanches and moderate danger still means human-triggered slides are possible on specific features. Glades on steep slopes slide regularly, and a tree well or a slide into timber is often worse than open terrain. Beacon, shovel and probe go on every tour, and so does a partner who actually knows how to use them.
do i need special insurance for big wave surfing trips?

Yes, a lot of standard travel insurance excludes extreme sports, so check the policy for big-wave surfing specifically. Look for one that covers medical evacuation, because remote spots can mean a helicopter or boat ride to a hospital. It's well worth paying for, given what can happen out there.
Is towing in easier than paddling for big waves? Thinking of skipping the paddle stuff.

Tow-in makes catching huge waves easier, but it adds risk and skill requirements of its own. You need a trained ski driver, rescue sled skills, and the ability to handle much faster speeds on a heavy tow board. Most respected tow teams were strong big-wave paddle surfers first, because that's where you learn to read the ocean and survive wipeouts. Skipping that foundation is exactly how people get hurt.
partner wants me to belay him with a grigri but i've only ever used an ATC. how different is it, can i just figure it out?

A GriGri works differently enough that you shouldn't figure it out on a live climber. The feeding technique is different, and the classic danger is holding the cam open while lowering or short-feeding, which disables the assisted braking. Have your partner or gym staff walk you through the correct thumb-on-cam feeding method and practice catches and lowers with him close to the ground first. Keep your brake hand on the rope the whole time, exactly like with an ATC.
How long do I have to dig someone out if they're buried?

Survival odds drop sharply after about 10 to 15 minutes, mostly from asphyxiation, so speed is everything. That's why your partners, not a rescue team, are the victim's best chance, and why everyone needs a beacon, shovel and probe and has practiced using them. Practice beacon searches regularly until you can find and dig out a buried target well inside that window.
do i really need a neck brace or is that just marketing

It's not pure marketing, but the evidence is mixed. Some studies and plenty of riders credit braces with limiting extreme neck movement in crashes, and critics worry about load moving to other parts of the spine. If you wear one, get it properly fitted so it works with your helmet and chest protector. Treat it as a reasonable extra layer, not a requirement that outranks good boots, a quality helmet and riding within your limits.
What's the deal with neck braces? Worth it or hype?

They're worth considering, and many riders and teams treat them as standard gear. A well-fitted brace like a Leatt or Atlas is designed to limit extreme head movement in a crash and reduce the risk of serious neck injury. The research is still developing, so they aren't magic, but plenty of riders feel the added protection justifies the cost. Get one fitted properly with your chest protector so it doesn't shift around.
can i ride with a cracked rib if i tape it

No. Taping doesn't stabilize a rib fracture, and riding a bike that's slamming through whoops can turn a cracked rib into a displaced one that punctures a lung. Get it checked so you know what you're dealing with, then plan on roughly six weeks off. Fitness work that doesn't hurt is fine while it heals.
can I use a sit on top for class 3

You can, and some people do run class III on whitewater-specific sit-on-tops, but a recreational sit-on-top from the beach is a different story. Those tend to be long, wide and hard to maneuver, and you'll get dumped and separated from the boat a lot. If you want to stay on top, look for a purpose-built whitewater sit-on-top with thigh straps, though most paddlers find a proper whitewater kayak gives far better control. Either way, build up on class II first.
Is a 150 foot bridge too low for a first BASE jump?

Yes, it's far too low for a beginner. At that height you'd be on a static line or direct bag with almost no time to deal with a malfunction or a bad opening. First jumps are usually done from objects several hundred feet high with a clean landing area, under an instructor who has chosen the site. Leave low objects for years later, if you ever do them.
is it ok to just skip drinking for the first 10 miles of a hot 50k so i dont have to stop to pee

No, that's backwards, because you'll start a deficit you can never catch up on once the day heats up. Drink to thirst from the start, roughly 400 to 800 ml per hour depending on heat and your size, and take sodium along with it. Needing to pee early is actually a decent sign you're on track, and a 30-second stop costs far less than a DNF from heat exhaustion at mile 25.
whats the highest bungee jump in the world

The Macau Tower jump is the highest commercial jump from a building at 233 m, and a few bridge and gorge jumps, like Zhangjiajie in China at around 260 m, claim even higher drops. Bloukrans Bridge in South Africa at 216 m is the classic big bridge jump. All of them are run by experienced operators, but they're not great first jumps, so many people do a smaller one first to learn how they handle it.
Do I need to stretch to be good at parkour?

You need mobility more than extreme flexibility. Focus on hips, ankles, wrists and shoulders, because those joints take the most load during landings, vaults and climbs. A short routine of dynamic warm-ups and some post-training stretching will help you move better and reduce strain. You don't need splits, but stiffness does increase your injury risk.
is sidemount or backmount better for cave diving?

Both work, and lots of excellent cave divers use each. Sidemount wins in low or tight passages and makes reaching your valves easier, while backmounted doubles are simpler to manage in big open systems like many in Florida. Choose based on the caves you plan to dive and get proper instruction in that configuration before taking it underground.
is it dumb to climb ice alone in a remote area if I'm only toproping

Solo toproping isn't inherently reckless with a solid self-belay setup, but going alone in a remote area adds risks your rope system can't solve. If a falling chunk of ice hits you, a crampon catches and twists your leg, or you get stuck hanging and can't get down, nobody's there to help, and cold can turn a minor injury into an emergency quickly. Practice solo toproping at a crag with other climbers around, use two independent self-belay devices, and always tell someone exactly where you are and when you'll return. Carrying a satellite messenger is a smart addition anywhere without cell coverage.
is it really necessary to double check knots, I've done it 100 times

Yes, every single time. Experienced climbers are the ones who get caught by an unfinished knot after a distraction. A quick partner check of harness, knot, and belay device takes ten seconds and catches the mistakes routine hides. Make it a habit you never skip.
how often should i practice with my beacon

Do at least a few practice sessions before each season and keep refreshing during the season. Many people do a quick drill before most tours. Practice single and multiple burials, fine searching, probing and strategic shoveling, because digging takes longer than searching in real rescues. Many areas have beacon parks where you can practice for free.
detached retina surgery 6 months ago, healed fine. bungee ok now?

Run this past your eye surgeon specifically before booking. The pressure changes in your head when you hang upside down and the jolt of the rebound are exactly the kind of stress retina specialists warn about, even after good healing. Many operators list recent eye surgery as an exclusion, so a clear written okay is essential before you jump.
Thinking of jumping a building at night to avoid security lol. Tips?

I'd skip it. Night jumps make it much harder to read the landing area, see obstacles and judge wind, and rushing an illegal jump to dodge security creates exactly the stress that causes mistakes. If you're new, building jumps should come after solid experience on legal, forgiving sites. Stick to legal objects and daylight until you have a lot more jumps.
I'm 16 and my friends want to duck the ropes at our local hill after a big dump. I don't want to look like a wimp. What should I do?

Out-of-bounds terrain right after a big storm is exactly where slides kill unprepared groups, and ducking ropes usually means no beacons, no rescue plan, and nobody coming to look for you. Saying you're not going isn't wimpy; it's what experienced backcountry skiers do on high-hazard days. Ski the fresh snow inside the boundary with them, and if you want to get into backcountry skiing for real, push for an intro avalanche course together.
Fastest way to get to wingsuit BASE? I want to fly Lauterbrunnen next summer.

There isn't a safe fast way. The widely respected path is 200+ skydives, then 200 or more wingsuit skydives, then a BASE first jump course, then plenty of slider-up and slick BASE jumps before you ever combine the two. For most people, that takes several years, not one summer. Lauterbrunnen will still be there. Build the skills in that order and treat the timeline as part of what keeps you alive.
Trying to learn a 180 off a small kicker but I keep under-rotating and landing sketchy. Any tips?

Most under-rotation comes from not winding up before the lip. Pre-rotate your shoulders slightly against the spin direction on the approach, then unwind them as you pop and let your hips follow. Keep your eyes looking over your lead shoulder toward the landing, because your body goes where your head turns. Practice ground 180s on flat snow until the motion feels automatic.
I'm 47 and want to get back into motocross after 20 years off. Am I too old?

Plenty of riders your age are out there, and vet classes are some of the most competitive at local tracks. Be honest that your reflexes and recovery aren't what they were, so start on a bike with manageable power, like a 250F instead of jumping straight on a 450. Book a day at a riding school to clean up your technique, and get your fitness up first, because tired riders crash. Get modern gear too, since neck braces and boots have come a long way in 20 years.
best boots for 6000m peaks

For most 6,000 meter peaks you'll want a double boot or a very warm insulated single boot rated for serious cold, like the La Sportiva G2 Evo, Scarpa Phantom 6000 or similar. They need to be crampon compatible and fit well with thick socks so your toes aren't cramped, because tight boots cause frostbite. Try them on in a shop with your expedition socks and break them in on long hikes before the trip.
first time ice climbing next weekend with a guide, what should i actually wear?

Dress in layers you can climb in. A synthetic or merino base, a light fleece, and a softshell or hardshell on top work well, plus a big puffy jacket to throw on while you belay or rest. Bring two pairs of gloves, a thin dexterous pair for climbing and a warm pair for standing around, because the thin ones will get soaked. Your guide will usually supply boots, crampons, a helmet and a harness, but confirm that ahead of time so you're not scrambling at the trailhead.
Fingers are killing me after 3 days straight at the gym. Push through or rest?

Rest. Finger pulleys and tendons adapt much more slowly than muscle, and three days straight is a classic route to a pulley strain. Take at least two days off and stick to a rest day between sessions for now. If you get sharp pain at the base of a finger, or a pop, stop climbing and see a physio who knows climbing injuries.
My son hit his head skating, he's acting fine but threw up once. Wait and see?

Don't wait. Vomiting after a head hit is a warning sign for concussion or something more serious, so take him to urgent care or the ER now, even if he seems okay. Watch for confusion, worsening headache, drowsiness or more vomiting on the way. Keep him off the board until a doctor clears him.
I'm 19 and I feel like I'm wasting my youth if I don't do something crazy like free solo.

Your youth is better spent building a climbing life you can enjoy for the next 50 years than gambling it on a single route. There's plenty of wild, committing adventure out there with a rope, like big walls, alpine routes, remote first ascents, and desert towers. Try climbing El Cap over a few days or learning to climb in the mountains, which is about as crazy as it gets while still giving you a margin. The climbers people admire most are usually the ones who are still around.
how often should i replace my griptape

Replace it when it stops holding your shoes during flicks or slides, usually when the grit is visibly worn smooth in your foot spots. For someone skating several times a week that might be every few months, though many people just ride the tape until the deck itself breaks. A quick fix is scrubbing it with a grip gum or a wire brush to bring back some bite.
Why do my forearms get so pumped ice climbing? I rock climb 5.11.

Almost everyone over-grips their tools at first, and that's what's pumping you out. Rock strength doesn't fully transfer to ice. Hang on straight arms, let your legs push you up in solid steps, and hold the tools as loosely as you safely can. Shaking out each hand at good rests helps a lot too, and it gets dramatically better within a few sessions.
I keep getting a squeeze feeling in my chest at depth, kinda tastes like blood after. normal?

No, that sounds like a lung or trachea squeeze, which is a barotrauma injury. Stop diving deep for now, and see a doctor if you're coughing blood, short of breath or in pain. When you come back, rebuild depth slowly, work on thoracic flexibility and stay relaxed at depth. Talk it through with an instructor too, since tension and fast depth progression are the usual causes.
best shoes for beginner

Go for a comfortable, flat-lasted shoe with velcro, such as the La Sportiva Tarantulace, Scarpa Origin or Black Diamond Momentum. They should feel snug with your toes slightly flexed, but not painful, because aggressive downturned shoes won't help you yet and will make you hate climbing. Try several pairs on in a store, since sizing varies a lot between brands.
best way to corner on berms without washing out

Look through the turn to the exit, not at your front wheel, and do your braking before the berm so you roll in off the brakes. Enter a bit high, drop your outside pedal or keep them level with heels down, and push your weight into the bike so the tires bite the berm wall. If you keep washing out, check your tire pressure and tread wear too, since hard, worn tires slide easily.
38, never skated, is it stupid to start now

Not at all, loads of people pick it up in their thirties and forties and enjoy it. Your body won't bounce back from slams like it did at fifteen, so wear a helmet, wrist guards and pads, and spend your first few weeks on balance, pushing and turning before chasing tricks. Going to a skatepark early in the morning when it's quiet, or booking an adult beginner lesson, makes the start much less intimidating.
