just tell me the fastest way to get licensed

Do AFF at a busy dropzone with good weather in a sunny region, take time off work, and jump as many days in a row as possible. Consistency matters more than anything, because long gaps cause rusty skills and repeated levels. Some people finish the 25 jumps for their A license in one to two weeks this way, but go at the pace your instructors set rather than trying to rush past their signoffs.
Feet first or head first?

Feet first, every time, unless you've been trained in diving. Headfirst entries on unknown water are a classic cause of spinal injuries, and even at moderate heights a bad angle can hurt your head or neck. Keep your body straight, legs together, arms tight to your sides or crossed over your chest, and point your toes.
Should I stretch before or after training?

Do dynamic movement before training, such as leg swings, arm circles, light jumps, and easy rolls to warm up your body for the session. Save longer static stretches for after training or a separate mobility session, since holding stretches right before explosive work can reduce your power a bit. A proper warm-up of ten to fifteen minutes is one of the simplest ways to cut your injury risk.
Terse question: wingsuit BASE, how many jumps first?

Common guidance is at least 200 wingsuit skydives and around 200 BASE jumps before your first wingsuit BASE jump, done under a mentor on a well-known exit. Many careful jumpers wait longer. Wingsuit proximity flying has killed a lot of very skilled people, so don't let anyone rush you.
Do I need a vario as a beginner?

Not for your first training flights, since instructors usually guide you by radio and you're learning to feel the air yourself. Once you start soaring and thermalling, a vario becomes really useful, because it beeps when you're climbing and helps you find and centre thermals. A basic model or a decent phone app is enough to start. Pair it with an instrument that shows airspace and altitude once you begin flying cross country.
How long after getting my P2 should I wait before flying thermals midday in summer?

There's no fixed timeline, but most instructors want you to build plenty of airtime in calmer morning and evening conditions first, often 30 to 50 flights. Strong midday summer thermals can be punchy and turbulent, and a newer pilot can get overwhelmed fast. Ease in by flying earlier in the day as thermals are building, ideally with a mentor or instructor nearby. Taking an SIV course before tackling strong conditions is also a smart move.
Weather looks gusty, around 20 mph, but I drove 3 hours. Should I push the DZ to let me jump? I'm licensed.

Don't push it, because if the DZ or your own limits say no, the drive doesn't change the physics of landing in strong gusts. Gusty wind is a common cause of hard landings and collapses near the ground, even for experienced jumpers. Use the day for packing practice, a canopy talk or tunnel time if there's one nearby, and come back when it's calmer.
first time doing a lake swim this weekend, any tips? kinda nervous

Nerves are normal and actually useful, so channel them into a simple plan. Swim parallel to the shore in water where you could stand up, wear a bright swim cap, and tow a tow float so boaters can see you and you have something to rest on. Go with a buddy, start with just 10 to 15 minutes, and get out while you still feel good rather than pushing to the point of shivering.
how high is too high for a first cliff jump? my friends are doing 15m tomorrow

For a first jump, 3 to 5 meters is plenty, and 15 meters is a serious height where you hit the water at roughly 60 km/h and a bad entry can mean cracked ribs, a concussion or worse. Start low, get your feet-first entry clean and consistent, and work up over multiple sessions rather than matching your friends on day one. There's zero shame in watching them go from the 15 while you nail a few from lower ledges.
chain keeps coming off when I land jumps

A chain that throws on landings is usually too loose, so set the slack to the spec in your manual, which on most MX bikes is measured with your hand under the swingarm behind the slider. Also check rear wheel alignment, worn sprockets with hooked teeth, and the chain guide and roller. A worn guide is a very common culprit. Get it fixed before your next ride, because a thrown chain can lock the rear wheel or hurt your leg.
My buddy wants to tow us behind a car on our boards to get speed. Good idea?

No, skitching behind a car is one of the fastest ways to get badly hurt, because you have zero control over the vehicle and a small bump or sudden brake can throw you under it. It's also illegal almost everywhere. If you want speed, find a proper hill, build skills step by step and ride with good gear and spotters.
My stomach always shuts down in hot races and I can't eat after about hour 6. Help

Heat reduces blood flow to your gut, so this is extremely common. Slowing your pace a bit when it's hottest is often the biggest fix. Take small amounts of food often rather than big portions, use liquid calories and cold, easy foods like watermelon, broth or gels, and train your gut by eating on hot long runs. If the problem keeps happening even with those adjustments, a sports dietitian can help you build a plan.
I'm 52, overweight by maybe 40 lbs, and my daughter wants me to try climbing with her. Is that a dumb idea?

Not dumb at all. Top-rope climbing at a gym is one of the most beginner-friendly ways in, since the rope takes your weight and you can stop and rest whenever you need to. Start on the easiest routes and focus on pushing with your legs instead of pulling with your arms, which spares your shoulders and elbows. If you have any heart, joint or blood pressure concerns, a quick check-in with your doctor beforehand is sensible. Otherwise, go, and let your daughter show off a little.
Cased a double yesterday, landed hard on the face, my wrist is swollen and clicky but I can still grip. Ride tomorrow?

Skip tomorrow and get that wrist X-rayed, because swelling plus clicking after a casing is a classic sign of a scaphoid fracture, and those often feel manageable at first. A scaphoid fracture that gets missed and keeps getting loaded can lose its blood supply and turn into months of surgery instead of weeks in a cast. One missed ride day is nothing compared with that.
can i ride a penny board for my commute

Yes, a penny board is fine for short commutes on smooth paths, and its size makes it handy to carry. The short wheelbase and small wheels make it twitchy at speed and easy to stop by cracks or pebbles, so keep the speed modest and watch the ground. If your commute is long or the pavement is rough, a slightly bigger cruiser with softer wheels will be much more comfortable and stable.
how to wheelie a 250f

Practice in a big, open, flat area in second gear. Sit back a little, cover the rear brake with your foot, and give a firm throttle blip while pulling on the bars, or fan the clutch for a smoother lift. The rear brake is your safety net, because tapping it drops the front instantly if you go too far, so practice using it on small lifts before you ever go higher. Keep the lifts small until finding the brake becomes automatic.
what's a terrain trap and why does everyone harp on them

A terrain trap is any feature that makes an avalanche far more dangerous, like a gully, creek bed, depression, cliff or tree band, because debris piles up deep there or you hit something. A small slide that would just knock you over on an open slope can bury you several meters deep in a gully. Always ask what happens if this slides, and where does it take me.
quick: do i need a jet ski buddy for 15ft days or is that overkill

On 15 foot days at a heavy break, it isn't overkill, and many serious crews treat water safety as standard. If a ski isn't possible, at least surf with experienced partners and agree on a plan for spotting each other and doing rescues. Don't paddle out alone on days that size.
My ear squeezes on the way down but if I push through it pops eventually. Is that fine?

No, pushing through pain is how divers end up with ruptured eardrums or middle ear barotrauma. Equalize early and often, starting at the surface and every meter or so on the way down. If it hurts, ascend a little until it eases and try again. If it still won't clear, end the dive. That's a call experienced divers make all the time.
My wingsuit zips are kind of sticky and one arm cutaway handle is frayed. Fine to jump?

Don't jump it until it's sorted. Sticking zippers and a frayed arm release can stop you from getting your arms free in an emergency, which is exactly when it matters most. Get the suit inspected or repaired by the manufacturer or a qualified rigger or wingsuit technician. Until then, ground the suit.
Race director said they might cancel for heat but I trained a year. Can I go run the course anyway?

I get the frustration, but running it unsupported on the day the RD judged too dangerous to staff is a bad bet. With no aid stations, no medical and no sweeps, a heat problem on remote trail can turn serious fast. Ask about deferral or a shorter alternate, and put that fitness into a fall race.
Should I bring my own dexamethasone and nifedipine for an expedition? Never used them.

Carrying them is common and sensible for expeditions to remote high altitude, but you should get them from a doctor who explains exactly when and how much to use. Dexamethasone treats HACE and severe AMS, and nifedipine helps with HAPE, but both buy time for descent rather than cure the problem. Keep them in an easy-to-reach spot in your pack, make sure a teammate knows where they are and how to use them, and check for interactions with any medication you already take.
pregnant, 10 weeks, booked a dive trip months ago. ok to go?

The firm medical advice is no scuba diving during pregnancy. There isn't enough research to show it's safe, and there's concern about bubbles affecting the fetus, which can't filter them the way your lungs do. Snorkeling is generally fine, so you can still enjoy the reef from the surface. Check with your OB, and see if the dive shop will credit your booking for a future trip.
I have type 1 diabetes. Am I allowed to skydive?

Many people with well-controlled type 1 diabetes skydive. The main concern is a hypo in freefall or under canopy, when you need full mental clarity. Talk to your endocrinologist first. Then plan your blood sugar for the jump day, check your levels before boarding, and tell the dropzone and your instructor about your condition. Some countries and organizations require a medical sign-off for solo training, so ask the dropzone what paperwork they need.
I've got high blood pressure but it's controlled with meds. ok to jump?

Possibly, but check with your doctor first, because the sudden head-down drop and rebound cause a real spike in blood pressure. Many operators list high blood pressure on their medical declaration and may ask for a doctor's note. If your doctor clears you, tell the crew about it on the day so they're aware.
how cold is too cold for open water without a wetsuit

Below about 15°C, most people without cold-water experience will feel cold shock and lose strength in their hands and arms quickly. Below 10°C, even acclimatised swimmers usually limit themselves to a few minutes. Build up gradually over weeks, enter slowly so your breathing settles, and get out while you still feel in control rather than when you start shivering hard. Have warm layers and a hot drink ready, because you'll keep cooling for a while after you leave the water.
can i put my kid's dirt bike in the bed of my truck with just bungee cords

Use ratchet or cam-buckle tie-downs instead of bungees, because bungees stretch and let the bike bounce loose over bumps. Put the front wheel against the bed wall or in a wheel chock, run two straps from the handlebars with soft loops out to the front corners, and compress the forks about a third of the way. Add a rear strap so the back end can't swing. Check them after the first few miles, since straps tend to settle.
how do i stop spinning too far on 360s

Over-rotation usually comes from throwing too much wind-up, so take a smaller rotation into the takeoff and let your head lead the spin. Spot your landing early and stop the spin by opening your shoulders back toward the slope. Practicing on a small jump with a clean landing helps you find the right amount of rotation.
Is it ok to skate on the street next to traffic since there's no sidewalk on my road

That's genuinely risky, because drivers don't expect a skateboarder, and a small rock or crack can drop you into the lane. If you must ride a road, stick to quiet streets with light traffic, ride with the flow, wear bright clothing, and stay off it entirely at night or in bad visibility. It's better to find a route through bike paths or quieter streets, even if it's longer, or just carry the board along the sketchy stretch.
My 15 year old wants to try ice climbing this winter. Is that crazy?

Not crazy at all, plenty of teens climb ice and love it, especially on top rope at a guided intro day where the gear and anchors are handled by a pro. Book a beginner course with a certified guide or a reputable ice park rather than letting them learn from friends, since the first few days are where people pick up good or bad habits with crampons and tools. Make sure they wear a helmet and dress in layers, and they'll probably come home hooked.
My 11 year old wants to hit the big jumps in the terrain park after watching YouTube. He's been riding two seasons. Is that crazy?

Two seasons is a solid base, but big jumps are a different skill set, and kids tend to underestimate the speed and air time involved. Have him master the small features first, with clean takeoffs, controlled straight airs and consistent landings, before moving up a size. A park-specific lesson or kids' freestyle camp is honestly the best investment here, because coaches teach speed checks and how to read the landing. And make sure he's wearing a helmet every single time; wrist guards are a smart add too.
I've got a 50k this weekend and it's forecast 38C. I haven't done any heat training. I'll be fine right? I'm pretty fit

Fitness helps, but it doesn't replace acclimation, and unacclimated fit runners are a classic heat stroke case because they can push hard enough to overheat. Treat it as a run for finishing, not racing: start much slower than usual, walk the climbs, use ice and water on your skin at every aid station, and keep your electrolytes up. If you get confused, stop sweating, feel chills or get dizzy, drop out and get help. Seriously consider switching to a shorter distance or deferring if that's an option.
rope burn on my hand from belaying lol does that mean im doing it wrong

It probably does, since rope burn usually comes from catching or lowering by letting the rope slide through your hand without enough control from the device. Lower slowly and steadily with the brake strand held down in the braking position, and let the device do the friction work rather than your grip. Belay gloves help a lot on long lowers. Ask gym staff to watch your belay, because a couple of corrections now fixes it quickly.
is it fine to swim across the bay alone at dawn, it's only like 1.5km

I'd skip the solo crossing, because the middle of a bay is where you're farthest from help and least visible to boats, and dawn light makes that worse. Cramp, cold or a sudden current can turn 1.5 km into a serious problem when nobody knows where you are. Get a kayaker or paddleboarder to escort you, or join a local group that does the crossing. If you can't arrange that, swim along the shoreline instead, wear a bright cap and buoy, and tell someone your route and your finish time.
Quick q: how much water per hour in 100 degree heat?

Somewhere around 400 to 800 ml an hour covers most people, but it depends heavily on your size and sweat rate. Weigh yourself before and after a hot training run to estimate your own losses, then aim to replace most of them, not all of them. Drink to thirst, and if your hands swell or you're gaining weight during the race, back off the fluids.
Low clouds rolling up the hill while I'm waiting at launch. Wait or bail?

If the cloud is reaching launch, bail or wait it out on the ground. Launching into cloud or getting enveloped right after takeoff means you lose all visual reference, and that's genuinely dangerous near terrain. Cloud filling in from below can also cut off your landing field. Give it time and see whether it lifts and clears properly, and if it doesn't, walk or drive down.
I have asthma that's well controlled. Can I still do high altitude stuff?

Many people with well-controlled asthma climb high successfully, and the cold, clean mountain air is sometimes easier than city pollution. The risk comes from cold, dry air triggering attacks, so see your doctor beforehand to set up an action plan, possibly with a step-up in preventer medication. Carry your inhalers somewhere warm like an inside pocket, because they can fail in the cold, and travel with partners who know your plan.
how long before i can do a 360

There's no set timeline, but most people need solid 180s both ways and comfortable switch riding before a 360 feels natural. Expect to spend weeks or more of park sessions getting there, depending on how often you ride. Practice on small jumps, keep your speed modest, and focus on a strong wind-up and keeping your eyes leading the spin. Trying it before your 180s are clean usually means landing sideways and catching edges.
is it dumb to skate in the rain

It's not dumb, but it's a lot sketchier, because wet pavement and painted lines get really slick and your wheels lose grip without much warning. Water also wrecks bearings and can make decks go soggy and lose their pop. If you do go, ride slowly, avoid painted surfaces and metal plates, and dry off your bearings afterward.
my 14yo wants to go to the skatepark alone. it gets pretty crowded. am i overreacting being nervous

It's normal to be nervous, but a 14-year-old going alone is pretty common, and you can make it a lot safer with a few simple ground rules. Insist on a helmet, have them share their location or check in at set times, and make sure they know skatepark etiquette, like waiting your turn and not standing in landing zones, since collisions cause many park injuries. Going together for the first visit or two helps you see the crowd and the vibe for yourself. Quieter weekday mornings are a good way to start.
can i just use my regular hiking boots with strap on crampons for ice climbing

Not for real vertical ice. Flexible hiking boots let the crampon flex and pop off, and your calves will be screaming within a few minutes of front-pointing. You want stiff, crampon-compatible mountaineering boots with automatic or semi-automatic crampons that have aggressive front points. Most guide services and gear shops rent boot and crampon combos, so try that before you buy anything.
operator says too windy, cancelled. it's barely breezy down here, can i push them

Don't push them. Wind at jump height is often far stronger than at ground level, and gusts can swing a jumper into the structure or make the recovery dangerous. A good operator canceling for weather is exactly the judgment you're paying for. Ask to reschedule or get a refund, and keep that operator on your list for the next try.
I crashed yesterday and hit my head pretty hard. Helmet's cracked but I feel totally fine, riding again tomorrow. Need a new helmet first?

Yes, replace the helmet, because a cracked helmet won't protect you again, but more importantly, don't ride tomorrow. A hit hard enough to crack a helmet can cause a concussion even if you feel fine, and symptoms often show up later. Get checked by a doctor before you ride again, and follow a proper return-to-sport protocol, because a second head injury on top of an unhealed concussion can be dangerous.
Should I scout every rapid or is that overkill?

Scout anything you can't see the bottom of, any rapid you've never run, and anything that's changed level since you last saw it. On runs you know well at a familiar flow, boat scouting from eddies is usually fine. When in doubt, get out and look; it costs five minutes and has saved plenty of lives.
first time outdoor bouldering this weekend. what do i need

At minimum, bring a crash pad, or two if you can borrow a second, plus your shoes, chalk and a brush for cleaning holds. Bring a friend to spot and move the pad, because outdoor landings are uneven and rocky in a way gym floors never are. Pick problems well below your gym grade, since outdoor grades often feel stiffer, and check the top-out and the way down before you commit. Pack out all your trash and brush off your tick marks when you leave.
Signed up for my first triathlon. The swim is the bit I'm dreading. tips?

Practise in open water a few times beforehand, ideally in the wetsuit you'll race in, so race day doesn't feel completely new. Start at the side or the back of the pack to stay out of the washing-machine chaos at the start. Settle into a steady pace rather than sprinting. If it all gets too much, roll onto your back or wave to a safety kayak, since they're there exactly for that and you won't get disqualified for resting.
My 12 year old wants to do a sea swim race this summer. She's a strong pool swimmer. Good idea?

It can be a great goal, but pool strength doesn't fully prepare a swimmer for waves, cold, murky water and no wall to grab. Look for a junior or short-distance event with good safety cover, and get her a few supervised sessions with an open-water club or coach first. That way she can practise sighting, mass starts and handling chop in a controlled setting. If she enjoys those sessions and stays calm, she'll be in a much better position on race day.
train alone or with a group?

A group or class is better, especially early on, because other people spot your bad habits, push you to progress sensibly, and can help if you get hurt. Training solo is fine for conditioning and low-risk drills. If you do train alone, tell someone where you are and keep the riskier stuff for sessions with others.
My hands get painfully cold then hot when ice climbing. Is that frostbite?

That's almost certainly the screaming barfies, the brutal rewarming pain when blood rushes back into cold hands, and it's normal rather than frostbite. Keep your arms loose, shake out often, and swing into the climb with warm hands to cut down how bad it gets. If you ever see white, waxy or numb patches that stay that way after warming, that's when to treat it as frostbite and get it checked.
Street luge vs downhill skateboarding, which is more dangerous?

They're roughly comparable, but the risks differ. Luge riders are lower and more stable, so they tend to go faster with fewer random falls, though they're nearly invisible to cars and hard to stop quickly. Standup downhill involves more falls but they're usually slides you can manage with good technique and gear. In both sports, the biggest danger by far is riding open roads with traffic, not the discipline itself.
My 10 year old wants to hit the big kickers in the terrain park. He's fearless. Should I let him?

Fearless is exactly why you should slow him down a bit. Have him master the small and medium jumps first, landing every one cleanly with control of his speed, before he moves up a size. Big park jumps need a precise approach speed, and kids tend to case the knuckle or overshoot the landing. A park lesson or youth freestyle program will move him up safely and quickly, and a helmet is non-negotiable.
what tire pressure for downhill?

Most riders run roughly 22-28 psi rear and 20-25 psi front with tubeless tires, depending on weight and conditions. Go lower for grip in wet and roots, higher for rocky terrain to avoid pinch flats and rim damage. Inserts like CushCore let you run lower safely. Test and adjust on a familiar trail.
Can I swim in the river after the storm? Water looks fun and fast.

I'd skip it until the river has settled for a few days. After a storm the flow is stronger than it looks, there's debris and hidden branches in the water, and runoff often carries sewage and farm waste that can make you seriously ill. Fast, brown water is exactly the condition that catches out confident swimmers. Wait for it to clear and drop, and check your local water quality reports before going back in.
What's the cheapest way to get into paragliding without cutting safety corners?

Take a certified course, since many schools rent you gear during training, so you don't have to buy anything up front. Afterwards, buy a recently inspected secondhand beginner wing (EN-A) along with a harness that has a back protector and a reserve, ideally with your instructor's help. Join a local club too, because you'll get site access, mentoring and good used gear leads. Skipping lessons or buying unknown old gear is where cheap turns expensive.
My girlfriend froze at the top and now feels embarrassed. How do I help her get past the fear?

Freezing is a healthy reaction, so let her know there's nothing to be embarrassed about. Next time, have her start much lower, around 2 or 3 meters, and stack up easy successful jumps so her confidence grows with her skill. Never count down or pressure her, because forced jumps are where people panic in the air and land badly.
temps are hitting 8C this afternoon but the route is in the shade, still good to go right?

I'd be cautious, because air temperature affects the whole formation, not just the ice your tools hit. Warm air can loosen the attachment points of pillars and curtains and release ice from above even when your section is shaded, and freestanding features are especially prone to collapse during a warm spell. If you go, choose fat, well-attached ice, avoid pillars and anything with sun-exposed ice hanging above it, and plan to finish early before afternoon warming peaks. If you're hearing dripping water, cracking, or seeing hollow, sagging ice, take that as your signal to bail.
what's the deal with leashless tools, should a beginner use them?

Most modern tools are leashless, and beginners do fine with them. They make it easier to switch hands, shake out, and place screws. The catch is that dropping a tool is a real possibility, so many people use a tether or umbilical, especially on multi-pitch routes. Learn on top rope first and you'll build grip confidence before it matters.
Is there any shortcut to get good at big waves fast? I don't wanna wait years.

Honestly there's no safe shortcut, because the ocean knowledge, breath control and judgment big waves demand only come from time in the water at gradually increasing sizes. What you can do is speed up that path with focused training, coaching, safety courses and surfing with experienced chargers who can mentor you. Surfers who rush the process are the ones who end up badly hurt.
what's the oldest age you can bungee jump

Many operators have no strict upper age limit, and people in their 80s and 90s have jumped. Some do ask older jumpers for a doctor's note or set their own cutoff, so check the specific site. What matters more than age is health: heart conditions, high blood pressure, osteoporosis, and joint or back issues are the usual concerns. If you're fit and your doctor is fine with it, age alone shouldn't stop you.
what does 'line arrow' mean

A line arrow is a small plastic marker clipped onto a cave guideline, and it always points toward the nearest exit. Divers use them at junctions and personal markers, and in zero visibility you can feel them to know which way is out. Never move someone else's arrow, because their life could depend on it.
Can I dive with a perforated eardrum if I wear earplugs?

No, because earplugs can't seal a perforation against pressure, and water entering the middle ear can cause severe vertigo underwater, which is genuinely dangerous at depth. Most perforations heal in a few weeks, and you need an ENT or dive medicine doctor to confirm it has closed before you dive again. Stay surface-side until then.
Got a heavy chest cold but I'm also dealing with a minor sinus squeeze injury from last week. Dive trip leaves Friday

With a recent sinus barotrauma and congestion, equalizing will be hard and you risk a worse squeeze or a reverse block on ascent, which can be painful and dangerous. Decongestants can wear off mid-dive, so don't rely on them. See a doctor, ideally one who knows dive medicine, before Friday. If you're still congested, sit out the first days of the trip or snorkel instead of diving.
skating without a helmet is fine if im just cruising right

Cruising is actually when plenty of serious head injuries happen, because a pebble or crack can stop your wheels dead and pitch you forward before you can react. You don't need full trick gear to cruise, but a helmet is worth wearing every time, since a fall onto pavement at even jogging speed can cause a concussion or worse. Find a lightweight skate helmet that fits well and you'll forget it's there.
how do the red bull divers survive 27 meters??

Years of progressive training, mostly from springboard and platform diving backgrounds, plus near-perfect body control so they hit feet first, rigid and vertical at around 85 km/h. The water below is deep and checked, and safety divers are in the water ready to reach them within seconds. Even with all that, they still pick up injuries, so it's not a height for anyone without that preparation.
Best boots for Denali?

You want a true double boot or an integrated triple-style 8,000 m boot, because Denali's cold is brutal and frostbite is common. Many guides consider the La Sportiva G2 Evo, the Scarpa Phantom 6000 or similar, the minimum, and some climbers go up to an Olympus Mons-class boot for extra margin. Fit them with the socks you'll actually wear and break them in on long winter hikes before the trip.
Worth doing a big wave risk assessment course?

Yes, it's one of the best investments you can make. Courses like BWRAG cover CPR, rescue techniques, ski operations, and incident planning, and those skills save lives in the lineup. Many crews expect members to have one.
what happens if a sherpa says no to my summit attempt

You listen. Sherpa guides see weather, snow conditions and climber fatigue with decades of experience, and when they call it, it's because they've seen people die from pushing on. Most reputable operators back their guides' calls completely. Arguing your way past that decision is one of the most dangerous moves you can make on a big mountain.
Can I fly home the same afternoon after two dives this morning? Flight's at 4pm.

That's cutting it too close. After multiple dives, DAN and most training agencies recommend at least 18 hours before flying, because the lower cabin pressure can trigger decompression sickness from nitrogen still in your tissues. Either move the flight to tomorrow or skip the second dive and make tomorrow a dry day. A missed flight is annoying, but a bend at 35,000 feet is a real emergency.
can i jetski for my mate at a big wave spot if i've only driven skis on lakes

Please don't make this your first time driving in surf. Picking someone up in the impact zone means reading sets, getting in and out between waves and handling a rescue sled under pressure. A mistake there can get you both badly hurt. Take a dedicated ski rescue and tow course and get hours on smaller swells first. Your mate's life literally depends on your driving.
sauna for heat acclimation, how long

Start with 15 to 20 minutes right after an easy run and build toward 30 to 40 minutes over a week or two, about four to six sessions a week. Get out immediately if you feel dizzy, nauseated or your heart is pounding. Drink and take some salt afterward, and skip it if you're sick or underslept.
How do you share air in a cave with zero visibility?

Teams practice it in training: the diver out of gas signals by touch, takes the donor's long hose regulator, and the two exit together along the line in a touch-contact position. The long hose, usually around two metres, lets you move in single file through narrow passages. It's a skill you need to drill repeatedly with an instructor until it's automatic, because in a real emergency there's no time to work it out.
Is there a big-wave surfing course I can take?

Yes, programs like Surf Survival, XPT and various big-wave safety courses run around the world, teaching breath-hold, rescue, hold-down survival and how to work with a water safety team. They're taught by experienced big-wave surfers and lifeguards. If you're planning to surf big waves seriously, one of these courses is one of the best investments you can make.
beacon shovel probe. do i really need all three or can i skip the probe

You need all three, and the probe is not the one to skip. A beacon gets you close, but the probe pinpoints the victim and how deep they are before you start digging. Without it you waste precious minutes shoveling in the wrong spot, and burial survival drops sharply after about 15 minutes. A good probe weighs a few hundred grams, which is nothing for what it does.
How do I get into proper high diving rather than just jumping off random cliffs?

Start at a pool with a diving club. Learning platform diving from 3, 5 and 7.5 meters gives you the body control and entry technique high diving is built on. Gymnastics or trampoline training helps with air awareness. From there, some clubs and high-diving camps offer coached progression to greater heights with proper safety cover.
is a cheap $30 board from walmart okay to start?

It's usually not worth it. Those boards tend to have hard plasticky wheels, gritty bearings and stiff trucks that make skating harder and less safe, because they stop suddenly on small cracks. A complete from a skate shop costs around $80 to $120 and rides dramatically better. A used board from a skater friend is also a great option.
Group of 5, one person is way less experienced than the rest. How should we handle that on avalanche terrain?

Plan the day around the least experienced person's skill and comfort, not the strongest skier's ambition. Make sure they know how to use their rescue gear, include them in decisions so they feel free to speak up, and pick terrain everyone can manage confidently. On any avalanche slope, expose one person at a time and regroup in safe spots out of the runout.
elbow pain on the inside after climbing, ignore it?

Don't ignore it. Pain on the inner elbow often points to golfer's elbow, a tendon overuse issue that gets stubborn if you push through it. Cut back on hard pulling, especially crimping and steep terrain, and see a physio for a proper diagnosis and loading program. Caught early, it usually responds well.
can i use my phone instead of a transceiver, there's an app

No. Phone apps aren't reliable avalanche transceivers, aren't compatible with the 457 kHz standard everyone else's beacon uses, and batteries die fast in the cold. Get a modern three-antenna digital beacon and practice with it. Keep your phone away from the beacon while touring too, since electronics can interfere with searching.
Buddy says I should just send the big gap jump on my first day at the park, it's only like 20 feet. Thoughts?

Don't do it on day one. A 20-foot gap punishes coming up short, so you need consistent speed control and pop on tabletops first, which takes multiple sessions to build. Ride the tabletop version of the line or the smaller jumps until you're landing smoothly every time, then watch others hit the gap so you can judge the speed before you even think about it. Your buddy won't be the one in the ER.
Water's 14C, I only have a 3mm. Fine for a quick session?

That's too cold for a 3mm on a freediving session. Cold makes you burn oxygen faster, shortens breath-holds and can trigger shivering and poor judgment. A 5 to 7mm open-cell suit, plus a hood, makes a huge difference at 14C. If you go anyway, keep it short and shallow, and get out at the first sign of shivering.
Im 52 and overweight, thinking about trying bouldering. Am I going to wreck myself?

Plenty of people start bouldering in their fifties, and the easy grades are very approachable at any size. The main risks are falls and overloaded joints, so begin on the lowest problems, climb down instead of jumping, and quit while you still feel fresh. Spend a few sessions building technique before you try anything powerful, because your tendons adapt more slowly than your muscles. If you have heart, back or joint problems, a quick check with your doctor first is worth it.
There's an avalanche warning in the area but our ice route is just a short waterfall in a gully. Should be fine?

Gullies are actually terrain traps, so a short waterfall can be one of the riskier places to be if there's loaded snow above it. Check what's above the route and the approach on a map and in the avalanche forecast, because a slide that starts far out of sight can sweep straight down your line. With an elevated warning, pick a route with no avalanche terrain above it, or hire a guide who knows the area, and carry beacon, shovel and probe if you're in avalanche terrain at all.
is a weight belt ok to wear or should i skip it

A weight belt is fine and often necessary, but weight yourself so you're positively buoyant at the surface and neutral at around 10 to 12 meters, never heavy at the top. Overweighting makes you sink if you black out near the surface and makes the ascent harder. Use a rubber belt with a quick-release buckle so you or your buddy can drop it fast.
how high can you safely drop from with a roll?

There's no universal safe number, because it depends on your conditioning, your landing surface and how clean your technique is, but most beginners shouldn't drop from above about hip height for a long time. A roll spreads out the impact, but it doesn't erase it, and drops beyond your conditioning will wreck knees, ankles and heels over time. Build up in small increments, a few inches at a time, and only progress when your landings are silent and controlled every single rep.
Throat feels kinda squeezed and I tasted blood after a deep dive. Normal?

No, that's a sign of a lung or airway squeeze, meaning a barotrauma injury from going deeper than your body has adapted to. Stop diving and see a doctor, especially if you're coughing blood, have chest pain or have trouble breathing. Expect to take at least a couple of weeks off, and when you come back, build depth much more gradually, with an instructor helping you work on flexibility and staying relaxed.
Coughing up pink frothy stuff at 5200m. Probably just the dry air right?

No, pink frothy sputum is a warning sign of HAPE, fluid in the lungs, and it can kill quickly. Descend now, with someone else, by at least 500 to 1,000 metres, and use oxygen or a Gamow bag if your team has one. Contact rescue or your expedition doctor immediately, and don't wait until morning.
is it ok to skip knee pads once you're experienced

Plenty of experienced riders still wear knee pads or leathers, because experience doesn't stop a wheelbite, a rock or a car. What changes is that skilled riders choose gear that matches their speed and terrain. At downhill speeds, protection is just part of the setup.
My buddy says throw bags are pointless because people just swim to shore anyway. True?

Not true. A throw bag is one of the most important rescue tools you can carry, especially for tired swimmers, swims in cold water or swims above more rapids. Carry one, practice throwing it, and learn to belay a swimmer so you don't get pulled in yourself.
My 14 year old wants to start downhill skating and I'm honestly scared. Is there any safe way to do this?

There's a much safer way to do it, and it starts with gear and a learning path rather than a hill. Insist on a certified full-face helmet, slide gloves with pucks, and knee and elbow pads, then have them learn foot braking and the Coleman slide on a gentle, low-traffic slope before going anywhere steep. Many cities have longboard clubs or skate shops that run beginner sessions, and kids who learn alongside experienced riders pick up good habits fast. It's also worth agreeing on a firm rule together: no open-road runs where cars can come around a corner.
what's the deal with Perrine Bridge, is it legal?

Yes, the Perrine Bridge in Twin Falls, Idaho, is one of the few places in the US where BASE jumping is legal year-round without a permit. That's why many First Jump Courses run there. It's about 486 feet over the Snake River with a decent landing area, but the river is cold and fast, so a water landing is a real danger. Jump it with locals or an instructor first so they can brief you on winds and outs.
Is river swimming after heavy rain okay?

I'd give it a few days. Rain makes rivers faster and colder, carries debris along, and often washes in sewage and farm runoff, which can make you ill. Currents you can't see from the bank can catch even strong swimmers. Wait until the water has dropped and cleared, and check the local water quality reports before you go back in.
can i run a desert ultra fasted to train fat adaptation

Not a hot race day, because adding a fasted state to heat stress makes low blood sugar, poor decisions and dropping out much more likely. If you want to experiment with fat adaptation, do it on shorter, cooler training runs with food on hand. In a hot ultra, aim for steady carbs, around 60 to 90 grams per hour if your gut tolerates it, because the heat already makes eating hard enough.
Do I need a buddy in caves or is solo ok if I'm careful?

Start with a buddy, and plan to stay with one for a long time. Solo cave diving does exist, but only very experienced divers with fully redundant gas, lights and skills do it, and they accept a higher risk. Early on, a trained teammate is your backup gas supply and a second brain when something goes wrong.
Got certified 6 years ago, haven't dived since. Can I just jump on a boat dive in Thailand?

Do a refresher first. Most shops call it ReActivate or a Scuba Review, and it's usually a half day. Six years is long enough for skills like mask clearing, buoyancy and handling an out-of-air situation to get rusty, and those are what you need when something goes wrong. Many reputable operators will require one anyway, and it makes the rest of your trip more relaxed.
what happens if i get line twists in BASE?

Line twists in BASE are serious because you might be heading toward the object while you're still sorting them out. The standard approach is to look up, check your heading, steer away from the wall with rear risers if needed, and then kick out of the twists. Your first jump course should drill this, and practicing the motions on the ground helps you react fast. Good body position at deployment and a careful pack job are the best prevention.
hit my head skating, wasnt wearing a helmet, had a headache since and feel kinda foggy. its been a few hours

A headache and foggy feeling for hours after a head hit are concussion symptoms, so get checked by a doctor or urgent care today instead of waiting it out. Go to the ER right away if you get vomiting, worsening headache, confusion, slurred speech, unusual drowsiness, or weakness on one side. Don't skate, drive, or drink alcohol until you've been evaluated, and have someone stay with you for now. And wear a helmet once you're cleared, because a second hit before the first heals can be much worse.
what does HAPE actually feel like

High altitude pulmonary edema usually starts as breathlessness that doesn't settle when you rest, a dry cough that later turns wet or frothy, and a big drop in how far you can walk before stopping. People often notice a gurgling sound in the chest, lips or nails turning bluish, and a racing heart while lying still, and it tends to get worse at night. It can kill within hours, so the treatment is to descend immediately, ideally at least 500 to 1,000 meters, and use oxygen if you have it rather than waiting to see if it improves.
how many big breaths should i take before going down to stay longer

None. Taking fast, deep breaths before a dive is hyperventilation, and it's one of the main causes of blackout. It lowers your CO2, so your urge to breathe gets suppressed while your oxygen keeps dropping, and you can pass out before you feel any warning. Breathe slowly and relaxed for a couple of minutes, take one full final breath, and let a course teach you proper breathe-up technique.
Can I dive the day after a long-haul flight or should I wait?

Diving the day after a long flight is generally fine, since the no-fly concern runs the other way, from diving to flying. The real issue is that you'll likely be dehydrated and jet-lagged, and both raise your risk of decompression sickness and poor judgment. Drink plenty of water, get a proper night's sleep, and make your first dive an easy, shallow one.
Got dragged during ground handling yesterday and hurt my wrist. Normal?

It happens, but it's a warning sign that the wind was too strong or that you need better technique for killing the wing, like pulling one brake hard or grabbing the rear risers. Get the wrist checked if it's swollen or painful after a few days. Before you go again, practice depowering with an instructor in lighter conditions. Wearing a helmet and gloves during ground handling also helps.
I keep hearing 'climb high, sleep low.' What does that actually mean in practice?

During the day you hike to a point several hundred meters above camp, spend an hour or two there, then come back down to sleep. That brief exposure triggers your body's adaptation, and sleeping lower, when breathing is naturally shallower, keeps you out of trouble. On the EBC route, for example, people stay two nights in Dingboche and spend the rest day hiking up Nangkartshang hill.
What's the deal with arm pump and how do I stop it?

Arm pump happens when your forearm muscles fill with blood faster than it can drain, usually because you're gripping the bars too hard and staying tense. Relax your grip, squeeze the bike with your knees and legs, and breathe steadily. Build forearm and general cardio fitness, warm up before riding, and stay hydrated. If it's severe and persistent even with good technique, talk to a sports medicine doctor, because some riders have a condition that needs medical evaluation.
I want to go to 40m on my next trip. I'm advanced certified, 25 dives. What do I need?

Take the Deep Diver specialty first, since 40 meters is a real step up from 30 and narcosis, gas consumption and decompression limits all get much tighter down there. Your air disappears fast at that depth, so you'll want solid buoyancy, a carefully planned gas reserve and a computer you understand well. Build up gradually with an instructor rather than jumping straight to 40.
do I really need a helmet at the skatepark if I'm good at falling

Yes, because even skilled skaters can't always control how they fall, especially when a wheel catches or they slip off coping backwards. Most head injuries at parks happen from backward slams onto concrete, where no amount of skill lets you roll it out. A good-fitting helmet is cheap insurance, and pros wear them for the same reason.
My buddy packed my rig for me, is that fine for my first few jumps?

Learn to pack your own rig and do it every time, with an experienced jumper checking your work while you're new. Your buddy may be good, but you need to know the job was done right and understand your own gear inside out. Many BASE fatalities trace back to packing errors, so make this part of your training.
Are night jumps hard? I want to try one at 40 jumps

At 40 jumps you're not there yet. In the US, a B license is required and USPA expects you to finish night jump training first. At night your depth perception and canopy traffic awareness both suffer, and you need to be very solid with landing patterns before you add darkness. Work toward your B, then do the night jump course with an instructor when it comes up.
I'm 67 and want to start winter sea swimming with a local group. Any concerns?

That's a great thing to take up, and a group is the right way to do it. Cold shock causes a spike in heart rate and blood pressure, so check in with your doctor first, especially if you have any heart or blood pressure issues. Then start in autumn so you acclimatize as the water cools, keep winter dips to a few minutes, and enter slowly while you control your breathing. Have warm layers and a hot drink ready, and let the group know it's your first season.
What's the deal with cornices?

Cornices are overhanging lips of wind-drifted snow on ridgelines, and they can break much farther back than you'd expect, dropping you with them or setting off the slope below. Stay well back from the edge on the windward side, since you often can't tell where solid ground ends. Also avoid traveling under them, especially on warm days or after big wind events when they're most likely to collapse.
Is 45 too old to start parkour? I'm reasonably fit, run 3x a week.

Not at all, and plenty of parkour gyms run adult or masters classes full of people in their 40s and 50s. Your running base helps, but expect your wrists, knees and Achilles to need time to adapt to landings and quadrupedal work, so build up slowly over months rather than weeks. Focus first on precision landings, safety rolls, balance and low vaults, and leave big drops for much later, if ever. A good coach will tailor progressions to your joints, which is worth more than any app or video.
Can I do two tandem jumps the same day?

Yes, many dropzones allow it if there's space on the loads, and some even offer a discount on the second jump. Stay hydrated and eat something between jumps, because the adrenaline crash can leave you tired. If the first jump left you dizzy or nauseous, give it a day instead.
dude I can hold my breath 4 min on land, so I can go to 30m right?

Not yet. Static breath-hold on land doesn't translate directly to depth, because diving adds exertion, cold, pressure and equalization, all of which burn oxygen much faster. Work up depth gradually, a few meters at a time, on a line with a trained buddy, and get a course to learn proper technique. Rushing depth is how people end up with squeezes or blackouts.
how long till i can do flips and stuff

It varies a lot, but most people working with a coach can land a basic backflip within a few months to a year, depending on their background. Getting there safely means trampoline and mat work first, along with spotting. People who skip those steps tend to land on their neck, so the slower route really is the faster one in the long run.
Kickflip tips? Been trying for 3 weeks

Three weeks is totally normal, so don't sweat it. Put your front foot just behind the bolts with your toes hanging slightly off the heel edge, then pop and flick off the corner of the nose, outward and slightly forward rather than straight sideways. Keep your shoulders level over the board, because leaning back is the number one reason people land in the splits or step off.
I'm 16 and the guys at the track are doing the big triple. I can clear doubles fine. Should I just send it?

Don't send a triple just because others are doing it. Coming up short on a triple is one of the most common ways riders get seriously hurt, because you land on the face of the last jump. Being comfortable on doubles is the right foundation, but before trying it, make sure you can consistently hit the exact speed and line those guys use. Watch their approach, ask one of the fast riders to pace you, and if possible, work with a coach who can tell you when you're ready.
Is Denali a good first big mountain? I've done some 14ers in Colorado.

Not really, since Denali is a major jump from Colorado 14ers: it's an arctic, heavily glaciated peak that demands crevasse rescue skills, cold weather camping, sled hauling and two to three weeks of self-sufficiency. A better path is to build glacier experience on peaks like Rainier or Baker, take a crevasse rescue course, and maybe do a 6,000 meter peak in South America like Aconcagua or Chimborazo first. When you do go to Denali, going with a guided outfitter for your first attempt is the smart call for most people.
should i stretch before or after training

Do dynamic movement like leg swings and joint circles before training, and save long static stretches for after or for a separate mobility session. Long holds right before explosive jumps can briefly dull your power. A consistent mobility routine a few times a week is what really keeps your hips, hamstrings and ankles happy.
what's deep water soloing and is it safer

Deep water soloing means climbing sea cliffs ropeless over deep water, so a fall ends in a splash rather than on the ground. It's much safer than regular free solo, but it carries its own hazards: water that's too shallow, tides, hidden rocks, and bad landings from height that can injure your back or ears. Go with locals who know the venue, check depth and tides every time, and keep your first climbs low. Majorca and Thailand's Tonsai area are classic places to try it.
im at 140 jumps and feel super solid. any way to get into a wingsuit early?

Honestly, no reputable instructor will put you in a suit at 140, and that's a good thing. The extra jumps aren't busywork. They build the deployment and malfunction reflexes you'll need when you're tired, off heading or pulling with a wing on your body. Use those 60 jumps deliberately: do some tracking jumps, take a canopy course, and practice clean, stable pulls.
how high can you safely highball boulder

There isn't a fixed safe height, because risk climbs steeply above about four to five meters and depends heavily on the landing, the number of pads and good spotters. Highballs need several pads covering the fall zone, experienced spotters, and a problem you could downclimb or have rehearsed, ideally on a toprope first. Work up gradually, and only once falling, spotting and pad placement are second nature to you.
Cheapest way to climb Aconcagua? Thinking of going solo no permit to save cash.

Skipping the permit isn't worth it, because rangers check at the park entrance and camps, you can be fined and removed, and the permit pays for the rescue and medical services that save climbers there every season. Solo on Aconcagua also means no one to notice early altitude symptoms. To cut costs legally, go in the shoulder season when permits are cheaper, use the Normal Route, skip a full guide but hire mules and base camp services, and team up with other climbers so you're not truly alone.
quick q is it ok to swim after a few beers at the beach

Not really, because alcohol slows your reactions, impairs judgement and speeds up heat loss, and it plays a part in a lot of drownings. Even a couple of drinks can make you overestimate how far you can swim or underestimate the conditions. Save the beers for after your swim, or just paddle in the shallows if you've already had a few.
My friend says you should just dive deep when a huge set comes so it passes over you. True?

Diving under helps, but on truly big waves the turbulence can reach well below where you can dive, so it's not a guaranteed escape. The better plan is good positioning so you don't get caught inside, plus knowing the channel and the safest escape route. If you do get caught, ditch your board if needed, take a good breath, dive as deep as you comfortably can and stay relaxed through the tumble.
quickest way to get comfortable with my canopy before base

Sign up for canopy courses at your dropzone and practice accuracy landings on every skydive, aiming for a small target with different wind directions. Work on flat turns, rear riser control, and braked flight so you can steer away from objects fast. Being able to land precisely in tight spaces matters more for BASE than any freefall skill.
do i need special ropes for ice climbing

Use a dynamic rope with a dry treatment, which stops it from absorbing water and freezing stiff. Many ice climbers use half or twin ropes on multipitch for longer rappels and protection from sharp ice and tool strikes. For toproping or single-pitch, a dry single rope of about 9 to 9.8 mm is a great all-around choice. Never use static rope for lead climbing.
friend says we can ride on the abandoned quarry, no one checks. good idea?

I'd skip it. Quarries often have unstable edges, hidden drop-offs, loose rock and water-filled pits, and riding there is usually trespassing, which can mean fines or a seized bike. If someone gets hurt, help could be far away and no one may know where you are. Find a legal track or riding area instead, where conditions are maintained and other people are around.
Can I learn to do flips off cliffs by just watching YouTube videos and practicing?

Videos are great for understanding technique, but flipping off cliffs is not something to learn by trial and error. A slightly over-rotated or under-rotated flip means you hit the water at speed on your back, face or head. Learn rotations on a trampoline or at a diving pool with a coach first, and only take a flip to a low cliff once you can land it consistently into deep water.
Can I take my certification test in a quarry or does it have to be the ocean?

A quarry is completely fine. Many people certify in quarries or lakes, and the skills transfer directly to the ocean. Cold-water, low-visibility training can even make you a more capable diver. Just do one or two easy guided ocean dives on your first trip so you can get used to surge, currents and saltwater buoyancy.
can i use my skydiving rig for a BASE jump if i just take the reserve out

No. Skydiving rigs and canopies aren't built for BASE. BASE gear uses a larger pilot chute, a specific container and bridle setup, and a canopy designed for fast, on-heading openings at low airspeed, which skydiving gear doesn't do reliably. Jumping modified skydiving gear off an object is a well-known way to get a slow or off-heading opening into the wall, so buy proper BASE gear and have an experienced rigger or instructor check it.
Divemaster on our boat keeps skipping the buddy check and rushing everyone in. Am I overreacting?

You're not overreacting. A buddy check takes thirty seconds and catches things like an air valve that's turned off or a loose weight belt, which cause real accidents. Do the check with your buddy yourselves no matter what the boat crew does, and if the overall attitude feels sloppy, mention it to the operator or choose a different one next time.
My 16 year old son told me he wants to free solo when he's older. Should I be panicking?

No need to panic, since lots of young climbers say this after seeing Free Solo, and most never do it. The best thing you can do is support his climbing in a structured way, like a gym team, a mentored outdoor program, or an AMGA-certified guide, so he builds skills and judgment around experienced adults. Talk with him openly about risk instead of forbidding it, because forbidding it tends to drive it underground. Kids who are surrounded by a good climbing community usually absorb a healthy respect for the consequences.
Can you recommend a gym that teaches free soloing

You won't find gyms that teach free soloing, because no reputable business can safely or legally run ropeless instruction at height. What you can do is build the skills that soloists rely on: outdoor trad and multipitch courses through a certified guide service, mentorship from experienced local climbers, and plenty of highball and deep water soloing at established spots. If you're in the US, an AMGA-certified guide is a good place to start for real outdoor skills.
how do you butter

A butter is pressing onto your nose or tail while riding so the other end lifts off the snow, and spinning or pivoting on that pressed end. Start on a gentle slope at slow speed and shift your weight over your front foot until the tail comes up, keeping your arms balanced. Once you can hold the press, add a small shoulder rotation to pivot around. Flatter, softer boards make it much easier.
Running Badwater-style desert ultra next spring. How long should heat acclimation take before race day?

Plan on 10 to 14 days of consistent heat exposure. Most of the plasma volume and sweat-rate adaptations show up in that window, though full acclimation keeps improving out to around three weeks. Aim for 60 to 90 minutes a day of moderate running or sauna and hot-bath sessions after training, and time it so your last big heat block ends a week or so before the race. Acclimation fades within a couple of weeks without exposure, so don't finish it too early.
speed wobbles are terrifying. how do i stop them

Wobbles usually come from tension and loose trucks, so bend your knees, put more weight on your front foot and try to relax. Tighter kingpins or stiffer bushings help a lot, and wider stances add stability. Most importantly, if you're getting wobbles, you're going faster than your setup and skill can handle, so back down to slower hills until you can ride them smoothly.
should I tape my fingers every session to prevent injury

Taping every session won't prevent pulley injuries, and studies show it gives only a small amount of support. Tape is useful for protecting split skin or flappers, and as a light aid when you're coming back from an injury under a therapist's guidance. Proper warm-ups, building up crimp volume gradually and taking rest days do far more to keep your fingers healthy.
First time in the park. Etiquette?

Stand where riders above can see you, and call out or raise a hand before dropping in so others know you're going. Never stop or sit on the landing or just after a feature, and clear out of the way quickly if you fall. Watch a few runs first to learn the flow and the speed people take into each feature, and start on the smallest ones while you get comfortable.
teen here (16). parents said no to paragliding. how do i convince them

Show them you're serious about the safe route, not the risky one. Research certified schools near you, many of which accept students around 14 to 16 with parental consent. Bring a parent to a tandem flight or an intro day so they can meet the instructors, see the gear and ask their own questions. Parents usually soften when they see structured training, proper equipment and qualified people involved, so let them see that before pushing.
how windy is too windy for BASE

There's no single number, but many jumpers call it off once steady winds get past about 10 to 15 mph or gusts become unpredictable, and much lower at cliffs where turbulence and rotor come off the terrain. Wind direction matters as much as speed, since a tailwind or crosswind at the exit can push you toward the object on opening. If you're even asking yourself whether it's too windy, it probably is. Walking down is always an option.
Is a lights-out drill really necessary? Seems dramatic.

It's essential, because sooner or later light failure or a silt-out puts you in the dark, and you want your hands already trained to find the line and follow it calmly. Practicing in training turns a potential panic into a routine procedure. Many cave divers repeat the drill on occasional easy dives to keep the skill sharp.
I've got 200 logged dives, mostly wrecks. Can I teach myself cave diving with videos and go with an experienced buddy?

Your wreck experience will help with buoyancy, but please don't self-teach this one. Cave courses drill no-visibility line following, gas-sharing exits and lost-line drills under an instructor's watch, and you can't practice those properly from videos. An experienced buddy isn't trained to teach or evaluate you either. With your log you'll probably move through cavern and intro to cave quickly, so take the course.
I keep panicking under water when I get held down even on 8 foot days. How do I fix that before going bigger?

That's the right thing to fix before sizing up, because panic burns oxygen faster than anything else. A proper breath-hold and apnea course will teach you to relax your body under stress, and dry CO2 tables at home build tolerance safely. Keep surfing the 8-foot days until hold-downs feel uncomfortable rather than scary, and don't move up until that shift has actually happened.
Can I fly the same day as freediving?

For normal recreational freediving, flying the same day is generally considered fine, unlike after scuba. If you did many deep, repetitive dives, though, there's some decompression risk, so give yourself a margin of several hours or more before the flight. Also watch for ear or sinus trouble, since flying with congestion or a barotrauma injury can make things worse.
How many lights do I actually need for cave diving? Seems like overkill to carry three.

Three is the standard for good reason: one primary and two backups, so you can still exit safely after a double failure. Lights do fail, usually at the worst moment, and in a cave without light you can't read your gauges, see the line or signal your buddy. Backups are small and cheap compared to what's at stake, so carry all three and check them before every dive.
Just tell me the trick to not getting hurt when I hit the water. Quick.

Go in vertical and feet first, with your legs together, toes pointed, body tight and arms pressed to your sides or crossed over your chest. Squeeze your glutes so the water doesn't hit you somewhere painful, and keep your chin neutral. Most injuries come from leaning or flailing in the air, so commit fully to the jump and stay rigid until you're under.
I'm open water certified and found a cool cenote on vacation. Can I just swim into the cave part if I stay close to the entrance?

Stay in the open water and cavern zone where you can see daylight, and only go there with a guide. The cave section past the light zone is where open water divers die, usually because silt gets kicked up and they lose the way out within seconds. Most cenotes have certified cavern guides who will show you the beautiful parts safely, and if you get hooked, take a proper cavern course before going any further.
is it normal for my fingers to be sore days after climbing

General tiredness and soreness in your fingers a day or two after a session is normal, especially when you're new. Pay attention to sharp or localized pain at the base of a finger, a pop you heard or felt, swelling, or pain when gripping, since those can be pulley injuries and need rest and possibly a physio. Take rest days between sessions so your tendons can catch up with your strength.
Is it bad to dive with a cold?

Yes, skip it. Congestion makes equalizing hard or impossible, which raises your risk of ear and sinus barotrauma. Decongestants can wear off mid-session and cause a reverse block on the ascent. Wait until you're fully clear, it's only a few days lost.
My instructor seems sloppy, skipping preflight checks. Should I worry?

Yes, take that seriously. Preflight checks catch tangled lines, unclipped buckles and other problems that cause real accidents, and a good instructor models them every time. Raise it directly, and if nothing changes, switch to another school certified by your national association. You can also report your concerns to that association.
how many skydives do i actually need before i can start BASE? my buddy says 50 is fine

Fifty is too few, and no reputable first jump course will take you with that number. Most require at least 200 skydives, and many mentors want 300 or more with plenty of accuracy work and canopy flight on smaller, faster wings. BASE gives you no reserve and almost no altitude to fix problems, so the canopy skills you build in skydiving are what keep you alive. Get the numbers in properly and arrive at a course already bored of landing on a target.
Is beer at the aid station a good idea mid race in heat?

Mostly no. Alcohol increases fluid loss and dulls your judgment, which is exactly what you don't want in the heat. A sip after the finish line is the place to celebrate. Stick to electrolytes, cola, and real food during the race.
is night swimming in the ocean dangerous

It carries more risk, mainly because nobody can see you, including boats and anyone trying to help, and it's harder to judge distance and conditions. If you want to try it, go in a group, stay close to a beach you know well, and wear lights on your cap and tow float. Pick a calm night and keep it short, and skip it in surf or currents.
best way to learn a backflip on a snowboard fast?

There's no safe fast track for inverts, because under-rotating a backflip can land you on your head or neck. The proven route is to practice on a trampoline with a snowboard-style trainer board, then move to an airbag or water ramp session with coaching before you ever try it on snow. Once it's consistent there, take it to a clean medium jump with a soft landing, and make sure you're wearing a helmet and you aren't riding alone.
is it dumb to try a backflip off a wall if i've never done a backflip on flat ground

Yeah, skip that one for now, because a wall flip adds height and rotation timing you haven't built yet, and under-rotating usually means landing on your head or neck. Learn a standing backflip first on a trampoline or a sprung floor with a coach spotting you, then progress to flat ground with mats. Once that's solid, a coach can walk you through wall flips safely.
Swam out of my boat for the first time today, scraped my leg up, feeling shaken. Is this normal?

Completely normal. Pretty much every whitewater paddler has swum plenty of times, and feeling rattled afterward is part of it. Clean that scrape well, since river water can carry bacteria, and keep an eye on it for redness or swelling. Next time out, drop back to an easier run for a session or two to rebuild confidence, and consider practicing swims deliberately in a safe rapid so the next one feels familiar.
I want to swim the English Channel next year. I've done 5k in a lake. How hard can it be?

It's a huge step up, because the Channel is around 34km in cold, tidal and often rough water that usually takes 10 to 20 hours. Most successful swimmers train for two or more years, build up to six-hour qualifying swims in water under 16°C, and work with an experienced coach. Pilot boats are often booked years in advance, so it's sensible to set a realistic date. Doing a 10k and then a longer marathon swim first will show you how your body copes with the distance and the cold.
What's a jump spool for?

A jump spool bridges a short gap between two lines, for example going from the main line onto a side tunnel, so you keep a continuous guideline back to the exit. You tie into the first line, run to the second, and tie in again. Navigating junctions like this is taught on cave courses, along with the marker system you use to show your way home.
what's the deal with nitrox, is it worth getting certified

Yes, especially if you do several dives a day. Nitrox has less nitrogen than air, so you get longer no-decompression limits and often feel less tired afterward. The trade-off is a shallower maximum depth because of oxygen toxicity, which is why the course teaches you to analyze your tank and calculate your MOD. It's a short, cheap course with a big payoff on dive trips.
I got caught in what I think was a rip current yesterday and panicked. Managed to get back but I'm shaken. What should I have done?

I'm glad you got out, and being shaken afterwards is a normal reaction. The key with a rip is not to fight it head-on toward shore. Float to save energy, stay calm, then swim parallel to the beach until you're out of the pull, and wave and shout for help if you're tiring. Next time, swim between the lifeguard flags and spend a minute watching the water before you go in. Rips often look like calmer, darker channels where the waves aren't breaking.
what's the minimum group size for whitewater

Three boats is the classic minimum. If someone swims, one person can help the swimmer while another chases the boat or sets safety. Two can work on easier water with experienced paddlers, but it leaves very little margin if something goes wrong. Make sure everyone in the group knows basic rescue and carries a throw rope.
Are slide pucks on gloves really necessary or just for show?

They're genuinely necessary for hands-down slides, because they let your hand glide on the pavement instead of grinding skin and fabric away. Without them you'll wreck your hands and lose control mid-slide. Get gloves with replaceable pucks and swap them out when they wear thin.
My 15 year old wants to bungee jump on our trip to New Zealand. I'm terrified. Should I say no?

You don't have to say no out of fear alone, because the big New Zealand operators run some of the most tightly regulated jumps in the world. Most allow teens around 14 or 15 with parental consent and minimum weight requirements, so check the specific site's rules. If you want extra peace of mind, go watch a few jumps together first and ask the crew how they check gear and weigh jumpers, since seeing the process usually calms nerves on both sides.
do i need a neck brace

They aren't mandatory, but many downhill riders wear one, especially racers and those hitting big jumps, since the research suggests they may reduce some neck injuries in certain crashes. If you ride fast or big features, it's worth trying one on at a shop to make sure it fits with your helmet and body armor. Either way, a good full-face helmet and riding within your skill level do more to protect you.
Ultra in 2 weeks, plantar fasciitis flared. Cortisone shot then run?

Doctors are often cautious about cortisone in the plantar fascia right before a big event, because it can weaken the tissue and raises the risk of rupture under long loading like an ultra. Talk it through honestly with a sports doctor rather than treating the shot as a quick fix. In the meantime, calf stretching, plantar loading exercises, supportive shoes and cutting your mileage can calm it down. If it's severe, think seriously about dropping to a shorter distance or deferring your entry.
Water looks dark and deep so I assume it's fine right?

Dark water tells you almost nothing, since murky or shaded water can hide rocks, logs or a shallow ledge just under the surface. Before anyone jumps, someone needs to swim the exact landing spot and dive down to feel for the bottom, or use a weighted rope to measure. It takes five minutes and it's the single biggest thing that separates a fun day from a hospital trip.
torn ACL, had reconstruction 5 months ago. feel great. ski season starts next month, surgeon is being conservative saying wait till 9 months. thoughts?

Your surgeon is right. Feeling great at five months is normal, but the graft is still weak and remodeling, and the research on re-tear rates is clear that going back before about nine months raises the risk a lot. Skiing is one of the worst sports for ACL loading, with twisting falls and binding issues. Use the time to pass proper return-to-sport tests on strength symmetry and hop testing. You could plan a late-season return on mellow groomers if you're cleared.
Thinking of buying a used carbon wetsuit off marketplace for cold water. Good idea?

It can work, but check it carefully. Open-cell freediving suits tear easily and can lose thickness with age, so look for rips, compressed neoprene and a snug fit. A suit that's too loose flushes cold water and steals your breath-hold, so fit matters more than price. For genuinely cold water you probably want 5 to 7 mm.
Im fit from crossfit, can I skip surf specific training for big waves?

CrossFit gives you a solid base, but it won't replace surf-specific training. Big-wave surfing demands paddle endurance, breath-hold under stress and comfort being thrashed underwater. Add long paddling sessions, swim conditioning, breath-hold training with a buddy or course, and lots of time in progressively bigger surf. Raw strength helps far less than lung capacity and ocean knowledge when you're held down.
Helmet is 7 years old but looks perfect, no crashes. Still good?

Replace it. Most manufacturers recommend replacing a helmet about every five years because the EPS liner and the adhesives break down from sweat, heat and UV even when the shell looks flawless. A new helmet costs a lot less than what an old one might fail to prevent, and modern helmets also come with better rotational-impact tech.
I'm terrified of heights but my girlfriend booked us a jump for our anniversary. Will I be okay??

Plenty of people who are scared of heights still jump, and the fear usually peaks at the edge and disappears once you're falling. The jump masters deal with nervous first-timers all day and will talk you through it without rushing you. You can still back out on the platform, and good operators won't pressure you. If you'd rather not, tell her honestly, because a scary experience you didn't choose isn't much of a gift.
Detailed question: I've done ~40 jumps between 5-9m with clean entries. Want to progress to 12-15m. How should I approach that?

Progress in small steps, around 10, then 11 to 12, and stay at each height until several jumps feel boringly clean, since mistakes punish you much harder up there. Film your entries to catch subtle tilts, and work on core strength and holding a rigid body in the air. At 12 meters and up you really want a spotter or swimmer in the water and verified depth of 5 meters or more. A session with a high-diving coach would be well worth it at this stage.
I'm terrified of getting the bends. I panic just thinking about it. Is it as common as I think?

It's actually rare in recreational diving, roughly a few cases per ten thousand dives, and most of those come from pushing limits. Stay within your computer's no-decompression limits, ascend slowly, do a three-minute safety stop at 5 meters, stay hydrated and don't fly too soon, and you've removed most of the risk. If the anxiety is strong, tell your instructor, because extra pool time to build calm is completely normal.
There's another party climbing directly above us on the only route at the crag. Should we just start up behind them?

I'd wait or pick another line. Anyone climbing above you will knock down ice with every tool swing and kick, and on a narrow route there's often nowhere to get out of the debris path. If you have to wait, belay well off to the side and out of the fall line. Once they're higher, finished, or rappelling down, it's much safer to start your climb.
can i drink the night before my first jump? like a few beers

A couple of beers is generally fine, but don't show up hungover or still drunk, because dropzones will turn you away and they're right to. You'll want to be sharp, hydrated and rested, especially for AFF, where you need to remember procedures. Keep it light, drink water, and get a solid night's sleep.
Can I ride motocross with a cast on my wrist if I tape it up good

No, riding with a broken wrist risks re-injuring it and making a minor fracture a surgery, and you won't have the grip or control to ride safely. Wait until your doctor clears you, then come back gradually to build up your grip strength again. Missing a few weeks is annoying, but it beats months off later.
18, trying to learn a frontside 360 on a medium jump. I keep under-rotating. tips?

Under-rotating usually comes from not winding up enough on the approach or from opening your shoulders too late.
