Set your edge and pre-wind on the takeoff, pop with your legs, and keep your head turning to spot the landing over your shoulder. If you can't land it on a small jump first, go back there, because under-rotating on a medium jump lands you on your edge with real speed.
Are cheap Amazon down suits good enough for 7,000m?

Usually not. Above 7,000 meters you're dealing with life-threatening cold and wind, and bargain suits often use poor-quality down that's overstuffed in some spots and thin in others, with flimsy zippers that can fail when your hands are numb. Frostbite and hypothermia are serious risks at that height, so invest in proven brands built for 8,000 meters, or rent from a reputable outfitter in Kathmandu if cost is the issue.
how do i get faster on downhill without crashing more

Speed mostly comes from braking less in the right places, not from riding harder. Brake hard and early before a corner, then release and let the bike carry speed through it, and look far ahead to the exit instead of at the ground in front of your wheel. Session one short section repeatedly until you can ride it smoothly, because smooth is fast. A single coaching session will often find more time for you than a whole season of trial and error.
how do I do a nose press on a box

Approach straight with a flat base, then once your board is on the box, shift your weight forward over your front foot until the tail lifts. Keep your knees bent, your shoulders square to the box and your eyes looking at the end of the feature. Practice the press on flat snow first so you know where your balance point is before you try it on the box.
how do i learn to fall properly

The core idea is to roll rather than catch yourself, so if you're falling forward, tuck and take it on your shoulder and side instead of slapping your hands down. On ramps, wear knee pads and practice knee-sliding down the transition on purpose, since that's the safest bail. Practicing falls deliberately on grass or a padded surface feels silly but builds the reflex for when it actually counts.
quick q, is it ok to swim right after eating?

Yes, the old 30-minute rule is mostly a myth and you won't drown from a sandwich. A big heavy meal can make you feel sluggish or crampy, so eat lightly beforehand if you're doing a longer swim. The bigger thing to avoid is alcohol, which genuinely affects your judgement and how your body copes with cold.
my friend says if I just commit 100% to a jump I'll make it

Commitment matters, but only for jumps you've already proven you can make. Hesitating mid-jump really is dangerous, so traceurs are right to value committing. That only works when you've built the distance safely somewhere else first. If you're relying on commitment to get you over a gap you've never cleared before, you're gambling, not training.
quick: caffeine in hot ultras, yes or no

Yes, in moderate doses it still helps alertness and performance in the heat and won't meaningfully dehydrate you. Save it for later in the race or overnight sections, and stick to doses you've tested, around 1 to 3 mg per kg spread over hours. Going overboard can wreck your stomach and spike your heart rate, which the heat already does plenty of.
I'm 52 and used to cliff jump in my twenties. Anything I should know before getting back into it?

Restart lower than your old comfort zone, around 3 to 5 meters, and work back up gradually, because your spine, joints and reaction speed aren't what they were at 25. If you have back problems, osteoporosis or heart concerns, check with your doctor first, since the impact and cold-water shock are real stresses. Your experience still counts, so expect your technique to come back faster than your tolerance for hard landings.
How do I tell if a slope is 30 degrees without an inclinometer?

Rough tricks like the pole method can get you in the ballpark, but people consistently underestimate slope angle by eye. A slope angle app on your phone or a cheap inclinometer is worth carrying, and planning with slope-angle shading on maps like CalTopo is even better. When in doubt, assume it's steeper than it looks.
First time going to a bike park this weekend. Rented a full-face but my buddy says I can skip the knee pads since I'm just doing green trails. True?

Wear the knee pads. Beginners fall most often on green trails, usually at low speed onto knees and hands. Pads are light, cheap to rent, and you'll forget you have them on after ten minutes. Add gloves too if you don't have them, since palms take a beating in slow-speed tumbles.
how often should I jump to stay current

There's no fixed rule, but frequent jumping keeps your emergency reactions and canopy skills sharp, and long gaps are when mistakes creep in. If it's been months, do some skydives first and come back on an easy, familiar object before anything challenging. Being current matters most on low or technical jumps, where reaction time is everything.
Detailed question: I'm 30, climb 5.12 sport, 5.10 trad, 6 years in. I'd like to solo some long 5.5 ridge routes in the Sierra for the alpine experience. Where do I draw the line?

With your background, soloing easy alpine ridges is something a lot of mountaineers do, but where you draw the line should depend on consequences, not grade. Treat loose rock, route-finding errors, weather and fatigue as the real crux, and carry a light rope and small rack so you can rope up for anything exposed or uncertain. Start on well-traveled classics like the Cathedral Peak SE Buttress in good conditions, tell someone your plan, and turn back the moment rock quality or your focus slips.
How cold is too cold for ice climbing?

There's no hard cutoff, but below about -20°C ice gets brittle and dinner-plates easily, and frostbite becomes a real risk. Wind makes it worse. On very cold days, choose shorter, sunny routes, layer up and turn back early if anyone's fingers or toes stop rewarming. Plenty of climbers wait for the -5 to -15°C range, when ice is plastic and enjoyable.
what does nitrox actually do for me

Nitrox has more oxygen and less nitrogen than air, so you absorb nitrogen more slowly and get longer no-decompression times, especially on repeat dives around 18 to 30 meters. The trade-off is a shallower maximum operating depth because of oxygen toxicity, so you need the certification to learn to analyze your tank and set your computer correctly. It's one of the most useful courses a recreational diver can take.
Thinking of doing Mount Rainier as my first glacier climb. Guide or no guide?

For a first glacier climb, go guided, or at least take a proper crevasse rescue and glacier travel course before going independent. Rainier has serious crevasse danger, rockfall and fast-changing weather, and it's killed many experienced climbers. A guided climb with a skills seminar will teach you rope travel, self-arrest and how to read the route, which sets you up to do it yourself later.
I'm an experienced resort skier, black diamonds no problem. Can I just go out the backcountry gate?

Your skiing ability is real, but it doesn't help you judge avalanches. Many accidents involve strong skiers who assume skill equals safety. Beyond the gate there's no ski patrol and no avalanche control, so everything from route choice to rescue falls on you and your partners. Take an avalanche course and go out with a guide or experienced partners first. That way your skiing gets used on terrain you actually understand.
Thinking about running a waterfall soon. I've been paddling a year.

Waterfalls bring serious risks like spinal compression, pitoning and getting stuck in undercut caves, and one year of paddling usually isn't enough for that jump. Build solid class IV skills first, then start with small, well-known drops under the guidance of experienced creek boaters. Scout thoroughly, set safety at the bottom, and practice good tuck technique so you protect your back and face.
Gonna solo the first pitch of a route I've never been on, it's rated 5.6 and I climb 5.11 so should be fine right

Grade margin helps, but onsight soloing is where a lot of accidents happen, because you don't know where the loose blocks, wet sections or sandbagged moves are. Old 5.6 routes can be polished, run out and confusingly rated, and an unknown crux with nothing below you is a different experience from a 5.11 on rope. Climb it on lead first, then decide whether to come back without the rope. That one rope lap costs you an hour and takes away most of the unknowns.
Is reverse bungee safer than regular?

Reverse bungee, where you're launched upward, isn't inherently safer. It just puts different stresses on your body. The acceleration is sudden and strong, which can be hard on your neck and back. As with standard bungee, safety depends mostly on the operator's equipment and procedures, so choose a well-established one.
I flipped and hit my head, felt dizzy after but fine now. Keep paddling tomorrow?

Dizziness after a head hit can mean a concussion, and paddling with one raises the risk of worse injury and another swim. Get checked by a doctor, especially if you have headache, nausea, confusion or vision changes. Take a few days off and only return once you're symptom-free and cleared.
fastest way to learn a backflip on concrete this weekend

A backflip on concrete in one weekend is how people end up with neck injuries, so I'd skip that timeline entirely. The good news is that a parkour or gymnastics gym can probably get you landing assisted flips into a foam pit or onto a mat within a session or two, with a coach spotting you. From there, most people need several weeks of consistent reps on soft surfaces before it's safe to take outside. If you want to spend this weekend productively, book an intro session and work on your back-tuck jumps and set height.
Could I solo a route at night for the vibe if I know it well?

Skip this one. Darkness takes away your ability to spot wet patches, loose rock, or a misplaced foot, and a headlamp narrows your vision exactly when you need full awareness. Even routes you know feel different at night, and fatigue and cold make it worse. Climb it at night on a rope, which still gives you an incredible atmosphere with a real safety margin.
Cramped up my calf at like 10m yesterday and had to kick up with one leg. Scared the crap out of me lol

That's a scary moment, and you handled it right by staying calm and getting up. Cramps usually come from dehydration, cold, overusing your muscles, or fins that are too stiff, so drink more water, keep your session shorter, consider a thicker suit, and try softer blades. Work on stretching that calf before diving, and if it keeps happening, stay shallow until you figure out what's causing it, with your buddy watching closely.
Is one tank enough for a short cave dive if I turn around early?

No, cave diving standard practice is redundant gas, meaning doubles or sidemount with two independent tanks and regulators, because a single failure in an overhead environment can be fatal. Most cave divers plan with the rule of thirds: one third in, one third out, and one third held in reserve for emergencies. Turning around early doesn't protect you from a free-flow or an entanglement, so get trained in a proper redundant setup before going anywhere you can't reach the surface directly.
climbing trip to joshua tree, never done trad. can i just borrow cams and figure it out?

No. Placing gear is a skill where a bad placement looks fine until it rips out in a fall, and Josh's flared cracks are notoriously tricky to protect. Hire a guide for a day or two, or go with an experienced trad partner who'll check every placement while you practice on the ground and then on mock leads. Meanwhile, Josh has excellent top-rope options and a lot of bouldering, so you'll still have a great trip.
Can I solo a WI2 if I'm a solid WI4 top roper?

I wouldn't. Top roping WI4 doesn't prepare you for the consequences of soloing, where a popped placement or a shattering foothold means a fatal fall even on easy ice. Ice conditions change daily, and WI2 can be brittle or hollow on a given day. Build experience by leading easy routes with good protection first; that's how you develop the judgment soloing demands.
I want to explore a cave nobody's mapped yet. how do i get into that?

Exploration is the far end of cave diving, so the path is years of experience within established systems first. After full cave certification, build up hundreds of dives, add skills like stage diving, scooters, survey and often rebreathers, and join an established exploration team as a support diver. The good teams mentor people who show discipline and patience, and nobody sensible heads into virgin cave alone or undertrained.
is wingsuit flying expensive

Yes, it adds up fast. Getting to 200 jumps typically means AFF plus jump tickets, gear rental or purchase, and coaching, often around $10,000 to $15,000 or more depending on where you are. A new wingsuit runs about $1,000 to $2,500 on top. Don't skimp on coaching or gear checks, since those are the costs that keep you safe.
should i lean back if i feel unstable at speed

No, leaning back is one of the most common causes of speed wobbles and crashes. Keep your weight centered or slightly forward over the front truck, stay low and relaxed, and steer gently. If you still feel unstable, slow down and look at tightening your bushings or adjusting your setup.
is a throw rope something I really need to carry or is it more for guides

Every whitewater paddler should carry a throw rope, because the person most likely to rescue you is your buddy, not a guide. Get a decent throw bag and practise throwing it until you can reliably hit a target at 15–20 meters. A swiftwater rescue course is the best way to learn to use it safely, because ropes in current can be dangerous if you misuse them, especially if you tie yourself to one. It's cheap insurance and makes you a better paddling partner.
My running coach says pain is weakness leaving the body. Lump on my shin hurts when I press it. Keep going?

No. Pinpoint pain over a bone, especially with a lump, is a classic sign of a stress fracture, and running on it can turn into a full break. See a sports doctor and ask about imaging, since early X-rays can miss stress fractures. Pain from hard effort is normal, but localized bone pain isn't something to push through. A good coach should back you on getting it checked.
should my 6 year old wear wrist guards or are they overkill

They're definitely worth it, wrist fractures are among the most common skateboarding injuries, especially for kids who instinctively throw their hands out when they fall. Pair them with a properly fitting helmet and knee and elbow pads. Kids usually stop complaining about them once they see that falling doesn't hurt as much.
how hot is too hot to race

It depends on humidity as much as temperature, which is why races often use the wet bulb globe temperature (WBGT). Once WBGT goes above roughly 28C, the risk of heat illness climbs steeply, and many events modify or cancel around 32C. On a personal level, if you're not acclimated and it's both very hot and humid, dropping to a shorter distance or skipping the race is the smart call, not the weak one.
I'm 16 and really want to get into BASE. What's the fastest path?

Right now your path runs through skydiving, and most dropzones won't let you jump solo until 18, so use the time to get into great shape, learn about weather and gear, and maybe try tunnel flying, which is often open to younger flyers. Once you're eligible, build a solid skydiving foundation with a lot of canopy work before even thinking about a BASE course. Rushing this sport is how people get hurt, and the jumpers who last are the ones who took the long route.
wingsuit + GoPro on first jump?

Leave the camera off your first wingsuit flights. Cameras add snag hazards and distraction, and most dropzones follow the guidance of 200 jumps before flying with a camera anyway. Get comfortable in the suit first, and ask your coach to film you if you want footage.
Detailed question: what's the realistic timeline from first skydive to wingsuit BASE if I'm fully committed?

Fully committed jumpers often take three to five years or more, and taking longer is not a weakness. A rough path is AFF and roughly 200 skydives, then wingsuit training and at least 200 wingsuit jumps, plus a BASE first jump course and many slider-up BASE jumps before combining. Find a mentor who will slow you down when you're tempted to rush, because experience and judgment count more than milestones.
I've climbed for 3 years. My crew is pressuring me to solo a 5.7 with them tomorrow. I don't really want to.

Then don't, and that's a completely legitimate reason on its own, because soloing only works when you're fully committed and clear-headed. Going up because of peer pressure is one of the worst setups possible for ropeless climbing. Bring a rope and offer to lead or top-rope the route while they do their thing. A good crew will respect that, and if they don't, it says more about them than you.
What do I need to check before jumping an unfamiliar cliff?

Check the exit for loose rock and the slope of the wall below, so you know how far out you need to clear. Then check the landing area for size, obstacles and outs if you're off target, along with wind direction and any rotor risk. Get local beta from jumpers who know the object, and never jump something new alone. If anything feels unclear, walking down is always an option.
i keep doing wall runs but cant get past like 2 steps. hacks?

Usually the problem is that you're kicking too low or too close to the wall, so take a slightly faster approach and plant your first foot at about waist height with the ball of your foot. Push up rather than into the wall, and drive your arms upward to reach the top as you step. Two steps is normal for a while, and most of the height comes from that first explosive push. Practice on a wall with a good grippy surface and a soft landing below.
Quick q: can I drink a couple beers before an evening river swim? Just to loosen up

Save the beers for afterwards. Alcohol slows your reactions, makes you lose body heat faster and makes you worse at judging currents and distance, which are all things a river punishes. A lot of river drownings involve drinking, even in strong swimmers. Have one when you're dry and warm on the bank instead.
ugh everyone's so dramatic, it's literally a 5.4, i climb 5.10

Fair, the grade gap matters, and easy terrain is where a lot of seasoned climbers solo. The catch is that 5.4 routes often have the most loose rock, lichen and polished holds, and nobody escapes a broken hold. If you're going to do it anyway, pick something you've climbed recently on rope, go in dry conditions, test every hold, and back off at the first hint of doubt. Quietly roping up for the crux is still the smart move.
what's the deal with swim buoys, do I actually need one or is it just for show

They're genuinely useful. A bright tow float makes you far more visible to boats and paddlers, and you can rest on it if you get cramp or need a breather. Most also have a dry pocket for your keys or phone. It won't save you from everything, but for a few quid it's one of the best safety buys in open water.
Feeling tingling in my shoulder and kind of tired two hours after my third dive today. Probably nothing right?

Treat it as possible decompression sickness and act now rather than waiting. Breathe 100 percent oxygen if the boat or shop has it, drink water, and call DAN's emergency line or local emergency services so they can direct you to a hyperbaric chamber. Early treatment works far better, and getting it checked costs you nothing if it turns out to be minor.
Dove a cave on my intro cert and saw a passage past my limits. It looked easy. Worth sneaking a peek next time?

No, stick to your limits. Intro cave limits on gas, distance and navigation exist because the next steps like jumps, gaps and complex navigation are where divers get lost or run low on gas, even in passages that look easy. Finish your full cave training and you can explore that passage properly, with the skills to get back out.
What's the right landing approach in a strong wind?

Land into the wind with plenty of height margin, because your ground speed will be low and you may drift backward if you're over the landing field too far downwind. Expect rotor and turbulence behind trees, hedges and buildings, so pick a spot well clear of obstacles. Once you're down, turn and kill the wing fast with the rear risers or C's so you don't get dragged. If the wind is near your limit, a top landing or not flying at all may be the smarter call.
Landed hard yesterday and my back aches a bit. Can I fly today?

Get it checked by a doctor before you fly again, especially since back injuries from hard landings can be more serious than they first feel. Flying with an injury also means you might not be able to react well in the air or handle another rough landing. Rest is the safe call for now. Once you're cleared, look at what caused the hard landing and practise your approach and flare.
gimme the fastest way to train my mental game so I can solo by fall

There's no fast track that makes soloing safe, and rushing the timeline is the real danger. If you want a stronger mental game, lead climb outdoors a lot, practice controlled lead falls with a good belayer, and climb routes near your limit where you have to stay calm. That will make you a much better climber by fall. Leave soloing out of the plan until your experience is measured in years.
I'm 45, climbed trad for 20 years, and I've been thinking about soloing a few classic easy routes I know by heart. Thoughts?

With your background, you understand the stakes better than most, so the real question is whether the risk is worth it to you and the people who depend on you. If you go ahead, experienced soloists keep to routes far below their limit, recently rehearsed on rope, in perfect dry conditions, and they'll turn around without ego. Many also start with rope-soloing systems or short sections close to the ground. That lets them check how their head handles it before committing to anything high.
Sprained ankle 4 days ago, still swollen. Trail race in 10 days. How do I make it?

Ten days might be enough for a mild sprain, but still being swollen at day four suggests it's at least moderate. A technical trail is the worst place to test it. Keep up compression and elevation, start gentle range-of-motion and balance work as soon as it's tolerable, and get it looked at to rule out a fracture if walking is still painful. Unless you can hop on it, cut side to side and run downhill without pain by race week, drop to a shorter distance or skip it. A re-sprain on rocks could cost you the whole season.
What's the best boat for a beginner?

A modern river runner or creek-style boat is usually the best choice, because they're forgiving, stable and easier to roll than low-volume playboats. Sizing to your weight and height matters more than brand, so demo a few at a shop or club. Buying used is fine, just check for cracks and a solid outfitting setup.
is soloing a 20 foot route fine since it's short?

Twenty feet is high enough for a fall to break your ankles, back or skull, especially onto an uneven landing. Short routes are better treated as highball boulder problems, with several pads, an experienced spotter and a careful look at the landing zone. Many climbers toprope anything over about 15 feet. That's not paranoia, just experience.
How deep can I go on my open water cert? My buddy wants to hit 35m on a wall dive.

Open Water certification qualifies you to 18 meters, and 35m is beyond even the 30m limit of an Advanced cert. At that depth you deal with real nitrogen narcosis, faster gas consumption, and very short no-decompression times, and you haven't been trained for any of them. Tell your buddy you'll do the wall at 18m, and take the Advanced course if deeper dives appeal to you.
is a used DH helmet from facebook marketplace ok? half price

Usually not worth the risk. You can't know if it's taken a hit, and impact damage inside the foam is often invisible. Helmets also degrade with age, so check the manufacture date on the label if you're tempted. A new budget full-face certified to ASTM F1952 or EN 1078 is a far better buy than a mystery used one at half price.
Someone in my group always says 'never stand up in fast water.' Why??

Because of foot entrapment, which is one of the most common ways people drown in rivers. If your foot wedges between rocks while you're standing or walking in current, the water can push you face-down and hold you there, and it's incredibly hard to rescue. When you swim, stay on your back with your feet up and downstream until you reach slow water that's about knee-deep or less. Your friend's giving you genuinely life-saving advice.
difference between longboard and skateboard for just getting around campus

For campus commuting a cruiser or longboard is usually the better pick, because the softer, bigger wheels roll over cracks and pebbles smoothly and you can cover distance with less pushing. A regular street skateboard is lighter and easier to carry into class, but its small hard wheels catch on rough ground. A mini cruiser around 27 to 32 inches with soft wheels is a nice middle ground if you need to carry it a lot. Whatever you pick, learn to foot brake before you ride anywhere busy.
i'm 16 and want to go climbing outside with friends who are also beginners. we've all climbed at the gym. can we just go?

Outdoor climbing adds hazards that gyms don't have, like building anchors, judging rock quality, and dealing with rope stretch on longer routes. The best option is to go with an experienced adult, guide, or join a youth outdoor climbing program before heading out on your own. Once you've learned how to set up and clean anchors safely, you'll have a lot more fun and be much safer.
I keep going over the bars on landings. What am I doing wrong?

Usually this comes from landing nose-heavy, often from rolling off the throttle on the jump face or leaning too far forward. Stay on the throttle steadily up the face and keep your body centered, using rear brake taps in the air to bring the nose down if needed. Step back to smaller jumps until you're landing smoothly, and get someone to film you so you can see it.
What's a highball and is that basically soloing?

A highball is a tall boulder problem, often 15 to 30-plus feet, climbed with crash pads and spotters. The top of a tall highball can carry consequences close to soloing, because pads only help so much from that height. Climbers work up to them gradually with lots of pads, experienced spotters, and often by inspecting the top on a rope first. Treat highballs as a serious step up from normal bouldering.
spring touring—when should I be off sunny slopes?

In spring you should be off steep sun-facing slopes before they warm through, which on a warm day often means by late morning. Watch for rollerballs, pinwheels, and boots or skis sinking deep into wet snow, since those signal that wet slide danger is rising. Start early, plan routes that follow the sun, and give serious thought to whether it actually froze overnight, because a poor refreeze means the danger rises much sooner.
Buddy says we don't need to scout a rapid if there's a guidebook description. True?

Guidebooks are a good starting point, but they can't tell you about the tree that fell in last month or how the rapid looks at today's level. Scout anything you haven't run recently, anything blind, and anything rated at the top of your ability. Ten minutes on the bank is a small price compared to finding a new strainer from inside your boat.
throttle sticks open sometimes on my crf, still rideable til i fix it?

Park it until it's fixed. A sticking throttle is one of the most dangerous failures a bike can have, because it can send you into a berm wall or a tree. Check the cable routing, look for a kinked or dry cable, make sure the throttle tube isn't rubbing the bar end, and see that the slide moves freely in the carb or throttle body. This is usually a cheap and quick fix, so there's no reason to risk it.
what does the hook breath do

Hook breathing helps you recover after you surface. You take a quick inhale, hold briefly with a little pressure, as if you're bearing down, then exhale passively, and repeat a few times. That keeps pressure on your lungs and pushes oxygen-rich blood back toward your brain at the exact moment you're most likely to black out. Make it automatic, and do it after every dive even when you feel fine.
Is it cheaper to rent gear or buy used when i get my license?

Rent for your first 50 to 100 jumps, since your canopy needs will change quickly as you progress and you'll learn what you actually like. When you do buy used, have a rigger inspect everything before you hand over money, especially the date and service history of the AAD and the condition of the reserve. Never buy gear without a qualified inspection, because a bargain container that doesn't fit your canopies is no bargain at all.
My clutch hand gets numb and arm pump is killing me after 10 mins

Arm pump usually comes from death-gripping the bars, so focus on gripping the bike with your legs and keeping your arms loose with elbows up. Check that your levers are angled so your wrists stay fairly straight and adjust the clutch if it's very stiff. Riding regularly and doing cardio helps a lot, and warming up before riding can reduce pump. If numbness persists off the bike, have a doctor check for nerve issues.
My son just told me he wants to start BASE jumping in a wingsuit. He's 22 and has done maybe 50 skydives. I'm terrified. What should I say?

Your fear is reasonable, because 50 skydives is nowhere near enough for wingsuit BASE, which is one of the deadliest activities in sport. The accepted route is hundreds of skydives, at least 200 wingsuit skydives, and a dedicated BASE first jump course before even thinking about combining the two. Rather than forbidding it, ask him to talk with experienced wingsuit BASE mentors about that progression, since hearing the timeline from people he respects often lands better than hearing it from a parent.
quick q how many screws do i need to lead a 30m pitch

Most people carry 8 to 12 screws for a full 30 m pitch, plus enough to build a solid anchor, typically two or three more. Bring a range of lengths, since thinner ice needs stubbies. If you're asking this before your first lead, get a few mentored leads in with an experienced partner first, because placing screws efficiently while pumped is a skill of its own.
dash vault vs speed vault which should I learn first

Learn the speed vault first, because it's easier, more forgiving, and teaches you how to clear an obstacle with one hand while staying sideways. The dash vault, where you go over feet first and push off with both hands behind you, is trickier to time and can catch your feet if you misjudge the obstacle. Use a low, solid box or railing at roughly hip height and practice both sides. Once speed vaults feel automatic, the dash is a lot easier to learn.
Anxious first-timer here, going to a gym tomorrow and scared of heights. Any tips?

That's really common, and gyms are a good place to work through it. Start on easy top-rope routes, climb a bit higher each time, and practice sitting back into the rope low down so you learn to trust the gear before you're up high. Breathe slowly, look at the holds instead of the ground, and know that coming down from any point is completely fine. Let staff know you're nervous, because they're good at helping first-timers relax.
is night swimming in the ocean a terrible idea

It's riskier, because boats and anyone on shore can't see you, you can't see waves or rips coming, and getting your bearings becomes much harder. If you really want to try it, join an organised night swim with safety kayaks, or go with experienced people at a calm, familiar spot. Wear a light on your cap or buoy and stay close to the shore. Swimming alone in the dark is the part to avoid completely.
Are cheap Everest operators really that bad? 25k vs 60k packages.

The price difference often shows up in exactly the things that matter most: oxygen quantity, Sherpa-to-client ratio, guide experience, weather forecasting and rescue backup. Cheaper operators frequently have fewer bottles per client and less flexibility to wait out bad weather or turn people around early. Some budget operators are solid, so instead of chasing the lowest price, ask about oxygen allocation, guide qualifications, summit success and incident history, and talk to past clients.
Should I tell my buddy my target depth before each dive?

Yes, always. Telling your buddy your planned depth and time lets them time their meet-up on your ascent and know when something is going wrong. Agree on hand signals and a protocol beforehand. Clear communication before each dive is one of the simplest ways to make freediving safer.
do I need shoes?

Water shoes are a good idea for most spots, since you're often climbing over sharp rock, barnacles or slippery ledges to get up and out. They also protect the bottoms of your feet on landing from higher jumps. Choose a snug pair that won't fly off when you hit the water.
What muscles should I train for parkour?

Prioritize your legs and posterior chain with squats, lunges, step-ups and calf raises, because jumping and especially landing put huge loads on them. Add pulling strength with pull-ups and rows for climb-ups and wall runs, pushing strength with push-ups and dips for vaults, and plenty of core work like hollow holds and hanging leg raises. Don't skip ankle and wrist conditioning; those small joints take a beating and are where many beginners get hurt first.
can kids wear arm bands in the sea?

They can, but don't treat them as safety equipment. Armbands can slip off, deflate or float a child into deeper water, and they give kids and parents a false sense of security. In the sea, stay within arm's reach of young children whatever they're wearing. If they need flotation, a properly fitted children's life jacket is much safer.
how long do ice screws take to place, i'm slow and getting pumped

Placing a screw well should take a skilled climber 15 to 30 seconds, and speed comes with practice. Try it on the ground or on top-rope in a relaxed setting until you can do it smoothly. Make sure your screws are sharp, clear a stance or rest spot before placing, and keep your arms straight on the tools to conserve energy. If you're getting badly pumped on lead, that's a sign the route is above your current level, and you're better off building endurance on top-rope first.
Can I use my regular skateboard for downhill or do I need a longboard?

A regular street skateboard has short trucks and tiny hard wheels, so it gets twitchy and loses grip fast, and wobbles start at fairly low speeds. A proper downhill longboard with stable trucks and bigger soft wheels is much more controllable once you're moving. Keep the street deck for parks and flatground, and use a dedicated downhill setup for hills.
operator said they don't do backup harnesses, is that normal

It depends on the setup, but many reputable operators use a secondary attachment or a full-body harness alongside an ankle connection, so it's fair to ask why they don't. A good operator should give you a clear answer about their safety system and maintenance routine. If the explanation is vague or dismissive, I'd find a different operator.
I want to film a wingsuit flight over my city skyline. Legal?

Almost certainly not without major permissions, since flying over a city involves airspace rules, aviation authorities, and landing-area problems. In the US you'd need FAA coordination and city or property approvals, and landing options in a city are dangerous if anything goes wrong. Professional demo teams pull that off with months of planning, so stick to dropzone flights.
My friend died base jumping last month. I've been jumping for 5 years. Should I quit?

I'm really sorry about your friend. You don't have to decide right now, and taking time off to grieve and think about your risk tolerance is completely reasonable. Talk with people you trust, both inside and outside the sport, and be honest with yourself about why you jump and what you're willing to risk. Whether you quit, take a break or come back more conservatively, it's a legitimate choice, and if you go back, make sure you're mentally ready first.
I'm 52, decent rock climber, out of shape-ish. Can I pick up ice climbing this winter?

Definitely, lots of people start in their fifties, and your rock background with ropes and belaying gives you a big head start. Ice relies more on solid footwork and calf endurance than raw arm strength. A guided intro day or two-day course will get you going safely, and some easy stair climbing or calf raises beforehand will make those first sessions much more enjoyable.
whats the max height i can drop from without hurting myself

There's no universal number, because it depends on your conditioning, your technique and the surface you're landing on. For most beginners anything above about hip height onto concrete is already asking for heel bruises, shin splints or worse, even if it feels fine the first few times. Build up in small increments over weeks, land on the balls of your feet with your knees bending to absorb the impact, and roll out of anything that feels heavy. The damage from big drops often shows up in your joints years later, so experienced traceurs keep their big drops rare.
how do i get over being scared of steep rollers

Start by finding a short roller with a clean runout that you can walk down and inspect, then ride it slowly with your weight back, heels dropped, and arms and legs loose. Look at where you're going rather than at the front wheel, and feather both brakes evenly instead of grabbing the front. Repeat it until it feels boring, then move to a slightly steeper one; fear fades fastest with small, successful reps rather than one big leap.
Do I need a special canopy for wingsuit jumping?

You don't need a special canopy, but you want one that opens reliably and on heading, so an elliptical or highly loaded canopy isn't ideal. Many wingsuiters use docile, moderately loaded canopies and longer bridles, and some prefer a larger pilot chute for cleaner extraction. Have your rigger and wingsuit coach review your setup before your first flight.
is cliff jumping at night a cool experience or a terrible idea

It's mostly a terrible idea. You can't see the water surface well enough to time your body position, you can't spot obstacles or check your landing, and anyone helping you won't see where you go under. If you want something memorable, try a sunset session at a spot you already know well, and be out of the water before it gets dark.
I just want to go ASAP without all the waivers and medical questions. Any place that skips that?

Don't look for one, because a place that skips those steps is a place to avoid. The forms and weigh-in are how they pick the right cord and catch conditions that could turn a fun jump into an injury. At a good operator the whole check-in takes 10 to 15 minutes. It's the quickest way to get airborne safely.
Can parkour help with my anxiety? I'm 16 and kinda nervous about trying something new

Plenty of people find it really helps, because parkour is all about breaking scary things into small steps you can actually handle, and that confidence carries over into the rest of life. A beginner class at a parkour gym is a great place to start, since everyone there was nervous once and coaches are used to people who need to go slowly. Nobody expects you to jump anything big; early sessions are mostly crawling, balancing, and small vaults. If your anxiety feels heavy most days, it's also worth talking to a doctor or counselor alongside it, since movement works best as part of the support rather than all of it.
How old do you have to be to skydive? My son is 15 and desperate to go.

In the US and many other countries the minimum age is 18 at most dropzones, and that's a USPA requirement for member dropzones. Some countries allow younger tandem jumpers with parental consent, so check the specific rules where you are. A great bridge in the meantime is indoor skydiving in a wind tunnel, which kids can do from a young age and which builds real body-flight skills he can use later.
can you fly a wingsuit with a camera on your helmet right away?

Hold off on the camera at first. Most guidance is to wait until you have plenty of wingsuit jumps, and many drop zones also require around 200 total skydives before flying with a camera at all. Cameras add snag risk and distraction, and helmet cameras can cause line twist or entanglement issues on deployment. Let your instructor film your early flights, and add your own camera once your flying and pulls are boringly consistent.
We're on a tight budget. What gear can I skimp on for my daughter and what can't I?

Don't skimp on the helmet or boots, buying new certified ones that fit properly, since those protect against the most serious injuries. Goggles, gloves, and a chest protector are essential too but good used or budget options work fine. Jerseys and pants are where you can save the most, since used or entry-level sets protect just as well.
what size deck should i get im 6'1 size 12 shoe

With size 12 feet you'll be most comfortable on a deck around 8.25 to 8.5 inches wide, which gives your feet enough room without the board feeling sluggish. Go toward 8.5 if you mostly cruise or skate transition, and toward 8.25 if you're mainly working on flip tricks. Match the truck width to the deck so the wheels sit roughly flush with the edges. Height matters much less than foot size here, so don't overthink it.
Is it ok to surf big waves alone if I'm careful?

No, big-wave surfing alone is a genuinely bad gamble no matter how careful you are. A hold-down, a knock to the head or a broken leash can turn into drowning in seconds. Nobody being there to see it means nobody pulls you out. Always surf with at least one buddy who knows to watch you, and ideally a water safety team on a ski at heavier spots.
my daughter (7) wants to drop in on the mini ramp at the skatepark. how do i know when shes ready

She's ready when she can comfortably ride the ramp from the flat bottom, pump up partway, and turn around on the transition without wobbling. Before that, have her practice standing on the coping with the tail locked, and ideally a coach or experienced skater can hold her hands for her first few drop-ins. Full pads and a helmet are a must, and knee slides on pads give her a safe way to bail. Start on the smallest ramp in the park and let her set the pace, because forcing it tends to create fear that sticks.
What vitamins or supplements help with breath hold?

No supplement meaningfully boosts breath-hold. The real gains come from structured training, cardio fitness and learning to relax under pressure. Avoid anything sold as an oxygen booster, because it's mostly marketing. If you're curious about nutrition for training, a sports dietitian can give you a sensible plan, but focus your energy on proper breath-hold coaching.
Why are cenotes in Mexico so popular for cave training?

The Yucatan has huge, well-mapped systems with crystal-clear fresh water, warm temperatures and generally permanent guidelines, which makes them ideal for learning. There's also a big community of experienced instructors and established dive centers. Just remember that easy conditions can create complacency, and divers still die there every year, often from going past their training.
is 5.6 easy enough to solo safely if i climb 5.10 on toprope

Grade gap alone doesn't make a solo safe. A wet hold, a snapped flake or a moment of panic can take out a strong climber on easy terrain. Top-rope numbers also overstate your outdoor ability, because you've never had to commit without a rope above you. If you're curious about moving on easy terrain, lead a lot of 5.6 outside first and see how it feels mentally. Many experienced climbers still decide soloing isn't worth it.
is proximity flying worth learning

Proximity flying has killed a lot of very experienced pilots, often world-class ones, because the margins for error are basically zero and terrain and conditions are unforgiving. If it's something you want long-term, the path takes years of wingsuit BASE, careful line scouting, and mentorship from people who've survived it. Most flyers get plenty of thrill from formation flying and acrobatic skydiving, which is a much safer place to push your skills.
Can I use a pool noodle instead of a buoy to save money?

A noodle is better than nothing for a quick rest, but it's not very visible to boats and it's awkward to tow, so it can slip away from you. A basic tow float costs about the same as a takeaway and does both jobs much better. If you're swimming anywhere with boats or paddlers, it's worth spending the bit extra.
how long should screws stay in for a top rope anchor before i check them

Check them every few climbs, or more often if the sun is on them or temperatures are near freezing, because ice softens and screws can melt out. If you see the hanger getting loose, water around the screw or melting, reset it in fresh ice. A tree or bolt backup is always worth using if available.
my wheels are making a gritty grinding noise

That's almost always dirty or dry bearings, especially if you've ridden through dust or puddles. Pop the wheels off, pry the shields off the bearings, soak them in isopropyl alcohol or a bearing cleaner, let them dry fully, then add a couple drops of skate bearing lube. If they still feel rough or have play after cleaning, just replace them, since decent bearings are cheap.
My daughter (17) wants to start paragliding lessons. I'm terrified. How do I know if a school is any good?

Check that the school is certified by the national association, such as USHPA, BHPA or your country's equivalent, and that instructors hold current ratings. Ask about the student-to-instructor ratio, whether students use radios on every flight, what their weather go/no-go rules are, and how old the training gear is. A good school will happily answer all of this and will cancel days when conditions are marginal. Visiting a training session lets you watch how carefully they run things.
my wingsuit is torn on the arm wing a little. can I fly it like that once?

Don't fly it until it's repaired. A small tear can grow under the high air pressure of flight, create asymmetry and make the suit hard to control, especially during deployment. Get it to the manufacturer or a qualified repairer, since it's usually a quick and cheap fix.
What percent of free soloists die?

There's no reliable percentage, because nobody tracks how many people solo, but the list of elite soloists who've died is grimly long. Dan Osman, Derek Hersey, John Bachar, Dean Potter, and Brad Gobright all died climbing in ways connected to ropeless risk-taking. Many of them were among the best in the world, which shows that skill alone doesn't protect you. That history is the most honest statistic available.
Teen here (16). Friends want to climb a quarry wall with no gear, it's like 30 feet. Parents don't know.

Thirty feet without a rope is easily high enough to cause a serious injury or death, and quarries are especially bad because the rock is often loose and may never have been checked by climbers. Many quarries are also on private property with drop-offs or water hazards you can't see well. Suggest a climbing gym instead, where you all get the same rush on solid walls with ropes and staff, and many gyms let 16-year-olds climb with a parent's signed waiver. You can say no and still make it a good day.
rigger says my reserve repack is due next week but i have a boogie this weekend. 1 week over is fine right?

No, an out-of-date reserve makes your rig illegal to jump, and any reputable dropzone will ground you if they spot it at the boogie. The repack cycle exists because the reserve is your last line of defense. Call your rigger today and ask whether they can fit you in before the weekend, since most will rush a repack for a modest fee.
headache at 4200m, otherwise fine. push on tomorrow or nah

Nah, stay put. A headache at that altitude is the classic first sign of acute mountain sickness, and going higher while symptomatic is how mild AMS turns into something serious. Hydrate, rest, take ibuprofen or paracetamol, and only continue if it fully clears; if it gets worse or you get nausea, confusion or stumbling, go down right away.
ok be honest, what actually kills people in big wave surfing

Usually it's drowning from long hold-downs, often made worse by getting knocked unconscious by the lip, the reef or your own board. Two-wave hold-downs and getting caught inside on a set are the classic scenarios. That's why serious crews rely on inflation vests, breath-hold training, jet ski water safety and partners who keep eyes on each other at all times.
Can I just rent gear and dive solo off the beach near my rental? Done 40 dives, feel solid.

Forty dives is a good start, but solo diving at an unfamiliar site with rental gear stacks the risks, since nobody is there to share air or help if you get tangled. If you want to dive independently, take a self-reliant or solo diver course and carry a redundant air source like a pony bottle. For this trip, grab a local buddy or a dive shop guide, and you'll learn the site's currents and entry points too.
Can I do it the day after a big rugby game? Bit banged up.

I'd give it a few days if you're sore or have any possible injury, especially in your neck, back, shoulders or ankles. A jump will take whatever's tender and stress it hard, and a concussion from the game would make it a clear no. Book it for when you're feeling normal again so you can actually enjoy it.
just bought a hangboard, planning to do it daily for gains. I've been climbing 4 months

Put the hangboard aside for now, because four months is generally too early. Your muscles strengthen much faster than your tendons and pulleys, which is how newer climbers end up injured. Most coaches suggest at least a year of consistent climbing before structured hangboarding. Even then, two or three short sessions a week is plenty, never daily. Climbing more routes will make you stronger right now.
ears hurt at like 4m every time. can i just push through it

Don't push through it, because pain means your ear isn't equalized and forcing deeper can rupture your eardrum or injure your inner ear. Equalize early and often, starting right at the surface and every meter or so before you feel any pressure. Go down feet-first on a line if head-down is giving you trouble. If you still can't clear, look into learning the Frenzel technique, and see a doctor if the pain lingers after a dive.
My ears hurt at around 4m every time. Should I just push through it?

Don't push through ear pain, because forcing it is how people rupture eardrums or injure their inner ear. Equalize early and often, starting right at the surface and then every meter or so. Go down feet first or slowly so you have time to equalize, and stop and come up a little if it won't clear. If it never clears, a freediving instructor can teach you the Frenzel technique, and an ENT can check for congestion or structural issues.
Our group always skis together in a bunch so nobody gets lost. Good idea?

Sticking together is great for flat travel, but on avalanche terrain bunching up means one slide could bury everyone, leaving no one to dig. Expose one person at a time on any slope steep enough to slide, and regroup in safe spots out of the path. Keep visual contact so you're spread out but never separated.
should I pee in my wetsuit to stay warm lol

It's a time-honored tradition, and it gives you a brief bit of warmth, but it won't stop you from getting cold over a longer swim. If you're cold enough to be thinking about it, that's a cue to keep the swim short. Rinse your suit well afterwards, unless you want it to stink.
my wrists hurt after a session of vaults. normal?

Some soreness is common when you're new because your wrists aren't used to taking that load. Sharp pain, swelling, or pain that lingers for days isn't normal, though. Warm up your wrists with circles and gentle loaded stretches on hands and knees before each session, and cut back on vault volume for a bit. If the pain persists or you notice clicking or weakness, see a doctor or physio, since wrist injuries can get worse if you train through them.
Perforated eardrum from a surf wipeout. Doc said keep it dry. Can I scuba if I wear a hood?

No, a hood won't seal water out, and diving with a perforated eardrum risks infection and severe vertigo when cold water reaches the middle ear. Vertigo underwater can cause panic and a rapid ascent. Stay out of the water until your doctor confirms the eardrum has fully healed, which often takes a few weeks to a couple of months. Then ease back in with shallow dives and gentle equalizing.
Can I fly home the same afternoon after my last dive? My flight's at 4pm and I finish diving around noon.

That's cutting it too close, and you'd be risking decompression sickness at cabin altitude. The standard guidance is a minimum 12-hour surface interval after a single no-decompression dive and 18 hours after multiple dives or multiple days of diving. Make your last dive the day before you fly, or swap that final morning for a snorkel.
My boyfriend says I'm overreacting, he likes to swim way out past the swimmers' flags. Am I?

No, you're not overreacting. The flags mark the area lifeguards are actively watching, chosen because it's the safest stretch, and going beyond them means nobody may notice if he gets into trouble. Strong swimmers get caught by currents, cramps or cold all the time, and it's the confident ones who drift outside the safe zone. If he wants longer swims, a local open-water club or a buddy with a tow float is the way to do it.
I'm 64 and have mild high blood pressure, controlled with meds. My friends do sea swimming year round and want me to join. Worried about the cold.

You're right to think about it, because cold water spikes your heart rate and blood pressure sharply in the first minute or two. Have a word with your GP first, and mention both your blood pressure medication and the cold, since some drugs change how your body responds. If you get the all-clear, start in late summer when the water is warmest and let your body adapt as the season cools. Enter slowly, stay in for just a few minutes at first, and swim with your friends rather than going out alone.
I am 52 and have a history of lower back problems. Can I still try cliff jumping on holiday in Croatia?

Talk to your doctor before you go, because the impact on entry compresses the spine even at modest heights. If you get the all-clear, keep to low jumps of 2 to 4 meters with very strict feet-first form and a tight core. If any position hurts, skip it. Many spots in Croatia have guided jumping tours where locals know the safe ledges, and that's a good way to try it carefully.
is it ok to ride the park with a slightly sprained wrist

I'd sit it out, because downhill puts constant load on your wrists through braking and impacts, and a weak wrist can cause a crash or turn a minor sprain into something worse. Rest it, get it checked if it's not improving within a few days, and come back when you can grip the bars firmly without pain. A week off now beats a season off later.
Is it true BASE has a fatality rate way higher than skydiving?

Yes, and the gap is large. Studies of sites like Kjerag in Norway have estimated roughly one fatality per 2,300 jumps, while skydiving in the US runs about one per several hundred thousand jumps. You have lower altitude, no reserve, objects close by and often bad landing areas, so mistakes that would be survivable in skydiving can be fatal. Anyone who takes up BASE should understand and accept that difference first.
Is chalk necessary or just a style thing?

Chalk really helps by absorbing sweat and keeping your hands dry, which gives you better grip and confidence on holds. It's not mandatory, but most climbers use it for both safety and performance. Just use it sparingly and brush off excess chalk from holds when you're done, especially outdoors.
teenager here, my mates and i want to paddle out on the biggest swell of the year this weekend, we've never surfed anything over 8 ft

Stepping from 8 feet to the biggest swell of the year is a huge jump, and that's the kind of session where people drown. Go watch from shore, see how the experienced surfers handle it, and surf a smaller nearby spot that's working. Keep building up through bigger days over seasons, and you'll get to the huge ones.
Is it bad to jump into a river after heavy rain?

Yes, you should usually avoid it. Heavy rain brings stronger currents, debris like branches and logs that can be hidden underwater, and murky water that hides the bottom, even if the depth went up. Wait until the river settles and clears, then recheck the landing zone.
quick q, do i need a reserve for base

BASE rigs don't use a reserve, because most jumps are too low for one to deploy in time. That's why so much of BASE comes down to perfect packing, a clean exit and solid deployment technique. You have one canopy, and it has to work, so careful packing and good training are what keep you safe.
can I skip the lesson? I've watched a ton of videos

Videos help, but a lesson gives you real feedback on your body position and braking, which you can't see yourself. Most beginners pick up bad habits that are hard to fix later. Even one session is a big step up. Many parks bundle lessons with rental and lift tickets.
My buddy says audible altimeters are for noobs. Do I need one in a wingsuit?

Yes, wear one, and your buddy is wrong on this one. Wingsuit flights are long, and it's easy to get absorbed in navigation or flying with others and lose track of altitude. A good audible with set alerts for break-off and pull is cheap insurance that experienced flyers use too. Pair it with a visual altimeter you check regularly.
Is skating at night ok if the area's well lit?

It can be, but even in good lighting, cracks, pebbles and wet patches are much harder to spot, and drivers see you less easily. Wear bright or reflective clothing, add a small light to your board or yourself, and ride routes you already know well. Keep the speed down compared to daytime, and avoid busy streets if you can.
Is there a way to learn rails without falling on them?

Mostly, yes, if you start with wide, low boxes and only then move to rails. Practice tail and nose presses on flat snow, and get comfortable riding with a flat base, since edges are what make you slip. Many parks have flat-down, ground-level features that let you fall onto snow rather than metal. A short park lesson also helps you learn how to bail safely when you do fall, because you will at some point.
My son is 19 and just told me he wants to get into cave diving. I'm terrified. Is it as deadly as people say?

Cave diving has a scary reputation, but the large majority of deaths involve divers without cave training who break basic rules like running a continuous guideline, keeping gas reserves and staying above safe depths. Properly trained cave divers who stick to those rules have a far better record, and the training is long, demanding and designed to weed out complacency. If he goes through a reputable instructor and progresses slowly from cavern to full cave, you can be worried in a normal parental way rather than terrified, and it might help to talk to his instructor together.
One of my buddies got knocked out and we couldn't find him for like 20 seconds yesterday. He seems ok now. Anything we should do?

Get him checked by a doctor right away, because a loss of consciousness and possible water inhalation can lead to delayed complications like a concussion or secondary drowning symptoms. Watch for trouble breathing, coughing, chest pain, confusion or unusual tiredness, and go to the ER if any appear. For future sessions, think seriously about taking a big-wave safety or CPR course together and setting up a proper rescue plan.
can i use my skydiving rig for a base jump just once

Don't do it, because skydiving rigs aren't designed for BASE. They're built to open at higher speeds and higher altitudes, and they include a reserve and deployment setup that can work against you on a low, slow object jump. BASE rigs use specific containers, larger pilot chutes, and canopies with features that improve heading control on opening. Borrowing or buying proper BASE gear through a course is the only sensible way to do it.
Can I wear my street motorcycle helmet for motocross?

It'll protect your head, but it's not ideal, since street helmets are heavier, less ventilated, and don't have the peak and wide eye port for goggles that motocross needs. You'll overheat quickly and fog up, which is a real problem when you're working hard on a track. If you're riding regularly, get a proper certified MX helmet, and use your street lid only if you're just trying it once.
What tire pressure should I run for muddy tracks?

Most riders run around 12 to 13 psi as a starting point, and some drop slightly in the mud for a bit more grip and flex. Going too low risks pinch flats and rim damage, so don't go much below about 10 or 11 unless you're running rim locks or mousses. Check your tire manufacturer's recommendation and adjust in small steps.
should i drink coffee before a solo or will it make me shaky

If you normally have coffee, keep the dose close to your usual so you avoid both withdrawal and extra jitters, since adrenaline plus too much caffeine can make your hands and legs shaky at exactly the wrong time. Skip pre-workout supplements or energy drinks before anything ropeless. Test your routine on roped days first so you know how your body reacts on the wall.
is parkour safe for girls?

Just as safe as it is for anyone else, and there are plenty of brilliant female traceurs and coaches out there. The risks come down to progression and technique, not gender, so the same rules apply: build strength first, start small, and learn landing and rolling properly. Some people prefer women-only classes or jams, which many parkour gyms run, especially for getting started. Upper body strength sometimes takes a bit longer to build for climb ups, but that just means more pull-up work, not a barrier.
what should a cliff diving buddy actually do

Your buddy should watch from where they can see both the jumper and the landing zone, and keep eyes on the water until you've surfaced and given an okay signal. Ideally one person stays in or near the water ready to help, and someone knows the exit route and has a phone to call emergency services. It also helps if at least one person in the group knows basic water rescue and first aid.
Teen here, my parents say big-wave surfing is suicide. How do I convince them it's not?

Show them that you're taking safety seriously, because that's what actually changes parents' minds. Talk about doing a surf survival course, wearing a flotation vest, always surfing with experienced people and building up gradually rather than jumping into giant days. It's also worth asking them what would make them comfortable, maybe meeting an experienced mentor or coach. Real progress and responsible choices will convince them far more than arguments.
I'm 58 and terrified but my daughter booked me a tandem flight for my birthday. Is it actually safe?

Tandem flights with a licensed commercial pilot have a good safety record, and you'll mostly just sit in the harness and enjoy the view. Tell the operator about any knee, back or heart issues beforehand, since you'll need to take a few running steps on launch and landing. Feeling nervous is completely normal, and most first-timers say the fear fades within seconds of lifting off. Happy birthday, and enjoy it.
safest way to fall when a jump goes wrong

Learn the parkour roll, which turns impact into momentum by rolling diagonally across your back from one shoulder to the opposite hip, keeping your head tucked and away from the ground. Practice it on grass or mats until it's automatic, because in a real bail you won't have time to think. Never reach out with straight arms to catch yourself, since that's how wrists and collarbones break. Equally important is learning to abort early: if your takeoff feels off, bail by stepping short rather than committing to a jump you're going to miss.
I'm a guide. Clients sometimes ask me to teach them to free solo. What's a good way to respond?

A clean answer is that you teach people to climb well, and that soloing is a personal decision you won't coach anyone into. Then redirect to something real, like efficient movement, footwork and lead head, all of which they want anyway. Some guides also show clients highball bouldering or deep water soloing as safer ways to get that thrill. Being firm and friendly at the same time usually lands best.
Are cave line markers actually important or just nice to have?

They matter a lot. Directional markers called arrows point the way out and let you navigate back even when visibility is bad, and personal markers called cookies show where your team has gone. Placing and reading them correctly is part of what keeps you from following the wrong line at a junction, so take the time to learn and use them properly.
Is it worth getting a neck brace? Seems overkill.

It's a personal call, and the evidence on neck braces is still debated, so many experienced riders go without one. If you ride high-speed race tracks or big jumps regularly, a properly fitted brace is a reasonable extra layer. Make sure it doesn't restrict your vision or helmet fit. For most park riding, a good full-face helmet and solid technique matter more.
My ears hurt after jumping today. normal?

Some pressure or water in the ears is common, but real pain, hearing loss, ringing, dizziness or any fluid or blood coming out could mean a perforated eardrum. In that case, keep water out of your ears and see a doctor rather than jumping again. Next time, keep your head neutral on entry, and consider earplugs designed for water sports if your ears are sensitive.
I've been surfing 3 years, mostly head-high beach breaks. Thinking of paddling out at a big-wave spot this winter when it hits 20 feet. Good idea?

Jumping from head-high beach breaks to 20-foot surf skips about four rungs of the ladder, and that gap is where people drown. Spend this winter surfing overhead to double-overhead reefs and points, and start breath-hold and hold-down training with a certified course like those run by big-wave coaches. Go to the big spot on a big day to watch from the channel and learn the lineup, but leave the board on the beach until you've built up through the intermediate sizes.
Dad here. Son wants to race at 12. How do I know he's ready?

He's ready to race when he can ride consistent laps at practice, control the bike under pressure and handle starts and corners with other riders around. Racing adds stress and close contact, so it helps to take him to a few races to watch first. Consider coaching sessions to build his skills and confidence, and start with a novice or beginner class. Make sure his gear fits well and is in good condition.
Can I drink a couple beers between dives on a liveaboard?

Save the beers for after your last dive of the day. Alcohol dehydrates you and affects your judgment, and dehydration is thought to raise decompression sickness risk. It can also hide early symptoms you'd otherwise notice. Most liveaboards have a 'once you drink, you're done diving for the day' rule for exactly this reason.
Thinking of doing a tandem flight in Turkey, Oludeniz. Any tips for picking an operator?

Oludeniz is a fantastic site, but it's busy, so be choosy about who you fly with. Pick an operator whose pilots hold proper tandem ratings, and ask about insurance, gear age and how many flights each pilot does per day. Read recent reviews, and be wary of anyone dramatically cheaper than the rest. A good operator will also cancel without fuss if conditions are poor.
My partner freedives and I'm terrified every time. How do I know he's being safe?

That fear makes sense, and some simple questions will tell you a lot. Ask whether he's certified, whether he always dives with a trained buddy on one-up, one-down, and whether he trains depth on a line with a lanyard. If the answers are yes, he's following the practices that prevent most accidents. If he dives alone or spearfishes solo, that's the habit worth pushing him to change.
Our group has two people with beacons and two without. Can we still go?

No, everyone needs a beacon, shovel and probe in avalanche terrain, because anyone could be buried and anyone could be the rescuer. If people are missing gear, rent or borrow it before you go, or pick terrain well away from any avalanche paths. It's not worth the risk of an incomplete rescue team.
32 weeks pregnant, my partner wants to jump on our babymoon, can i at least do a small one

No, this one's a firm no while pregnant, at any height. Every reputable operator excludes pregnancy, because the sudden deceleration and harness pressure pose real risks to the placenta and the baby. Cheer your partner on from the viewing deck and maybe book something calmer for yourself, like a scenic gondola ride. The bungee will still be there after the baby arrives.
How many people should be in a whitewater group?

Three boats is the bare minimum, since one person can go for help while another assists the injured paddler. Four to six is often ideal on harder water, with clear roles for lead and sweep. Keep everyone in visual contact and agree on hand signals before you push off.
do I need a coach or can I learn off youtube

YouTube is great for understanding technique, but you'll learn safer and faster with real feedback, whether from a coach, clinic, or experienced local riders. They can spot bad habits like leaning back or stiffening up before they cause crashes. Many crews welcome beginners and will show you good spots to practice. Use videos to study, then practice with people.
wheelie tips? want to learn on my 250f

Start in second gear on flat, open ground at low speed, and cover the rear brake with your foot, because the rear brake is what brings the front end down if you go too far. Give it a blip of throttle and pull back a little to lift the front a few inches, then put it down. Practice that many times before trying to hold it longer. Learn the rear brake first, and wear your full gear, since looping a wheelie is a common way to get hurt.
Is a cheap analog beacon fine or do I need a modern digital one?

Get a modern digital three-antenna beacon, because they're much easier to use under stress and handle multiple burials far better. Old analog units take a lot of practice to use well, and many are past their service life. Buy new or lightly used from a trusted source and check that the firmware is up to date.
how old do u have to be to skydive

In the US most dropzones require you to be 18, since that's the United States Parachute Association standard for both tandem and solo jumping. Some countries allow younger jumpers with parental consent, often from 16, but it varies by dropzone and local law. Call the place you're considering and they'll tell you their exact rule.
First solo flight tomorrow, super nervous, any tips?

Nerves are normal and actually helpful, because they keep you sharp. Get a good night's sleep, eat breakfast, drink water and do your preflight checks slowly and deliberately, especially your leg straps. Trust your instructor on the radio and focus on one thing at a time: a clean inflation, a calm launch, and then flying your landing pattern. If anything feels off on the day, it's completely fine to wait, and you'll be grinning once you're in the air.
teenage son (16) wants to do Mont Blanc with his mates this summer, no guide. how worried should i be

Fairly worried, unless they already have real glacier and crevasse-rescue experience. Mont Blanc's Goûter route has rockfall in the Grand Couloir that kills people every year, plus crevassed glaciers and weather that can turn fast. A much better plan is a guided course or ascent with an IFMGA guide, who can teach them the skills properly and judge the conditions. That gives him the adventure while sharply cutting the risks.
What's a slider-off jump and when should I use it?

Slider-off means removing the slider so the canopy opens much faster, which you use for low jumps or short delays where a slower opening wouldn't leave enough altitude. The tradeoff is harder openings and a higher chance of off-heading or line problems. Get trained by an experienced jumper before trying it, and don't treat slider-off as a license to go lower than your skills allow.
I have high blood pressure but it's controlled with meds. Can I still jump?

Talk to your doctor before you book. Bungee causes big spikes in heart rate and blood pressure, plus a strong jolt and rush of blood to the head, and many operators list high blood pressure among their exclusion conditions. Even if yours is well controlled, a doctor who knows your history is the right person to say yes or no. If they clear you, tell the operator anyway, because they're relying on you to disclose it.
how do I check avalanche risk before an ice climb

Start with your regional avalanche forecast the day you go and look specifically at the aspects and elevations of your approach, route, and descent. Many ice climbs sit in gullies or below big snow slopes, so even when the ice is perfect, the terrain above can slide and funnel right through your line. Watch for recent heavy snowfall, strong wind loading, rapid warming, or signs like cracking and collapsing snow. If you climb in avalanche terrain, carry a beacon, shovel, and probe, know how to use them, and consider an avalanche course before heading out.
how do i make my homemade luge sled faster

Good bearings, quality urethane wheels and a stiff, low frame make the biggest difference, but speed is the easy part on a luge. Put your effort into braking and steering first: proper foot braking with reinforced shoe soles, solid trucks, and a frame that won't flex or snap. Have an experienced builder or local luge rider look over a homemade sled before you take it down anything serious, since frame failures at speed are brutal.
what kind of training should I do in the off-season for big waves

Focus on cardio, breath-hold and strength work for paddling. Running or swimming builds the aerobic base you need to keep paddling out set after set. Supervised apnea and CO2 tables are worth adding too. Mix in pool rock running, but only with a buddy, and take a big-wave safety course before winter so you go in prepared.
wanna try acro. I have about 40 flights. ready?

Not yet. Most pilots have a few hundred flights and solid SIV experience before getting into acro. Acro involves deliberately putting the wing into extreme manoeuvres where mistakes can be serious, so the foundation matters. Build experience, do a couple of SIV courses, and then learn acro over water with a specialist instructor.
what happens if the main parachute doesnt open

You cut it away with the cutaway handle and deploy the reserve, a drill students practice over and over on the ground. Most rigs also have an AAD that fires the reserve automatically if you're still falling fast at low altitude, and many have an RSL that pulls the reserve when you cut away. Reserves are packed by certified riggers and are very reliable.
can i jump a wingsuit at a DZ that's new to me without anyone checking me out?

Most drop zones will want to see your logbook and wingsuit experience, and they often require a checkout jump or briefing first. Expect that and welcome it. Even if a DZ doesn't require it, ask for a briefing on the aircraft, the exit order, the landing area and the local flight patterns. Wingsuit traffic rules vary a lot between drop zones, so this matters.
Is it safe to freedive with a cold?

Better to skip it. Congestion makes equalizing hard or impossible, and forcing it can cause ear or sinus barotrauma. Decongestants can wear off mid-dive and cause a reverse block on the way up. Rest until your head is clear, then ease back in with shallow dives.
can i just watch youtube videos to learn lead climbing then try it at the gym

Videos are a good way to get familiar with clipping and falling, but lead climbing is one skill you really need to learn in person. The risks are specific, like back-clipping, z-clipping, getting your leg behind the rope, and a belayer who short-ropes or gives a hard catch, and someone has to watch you and correct you in real time. Most gyms require a lead test anyway, and a lead course is usually just a session or two. Take the class and use YouTube to review what you learned.
What do wingsuit pilots wear under the suit?

Most wear comfortable, thin athletic layers that don't bunch under the suit, plus proper jumpsuit-compatible shoes. In colder conditions or higher altitudes, add a thin warm layer, but avoid bulky clothes that interfere with your range of motion. A full-face helmet, altimeter and audible altimeter are pretty standard too.
can i use my skydiving canopy for BASE to save money

Generally no. BASE canopies are designed for fast, on-heading openings at low altitude and usually come with different rigging, a single-canopy container, and features like a tail gate or specific slider setups. A skydiving main isn't built for that and can open slow or off heading in ways that are deadly near an object. Buy or borrow proper BASE gear set up by someone who knows what they're doing, as used gear can save money if a qualified rigger looks it over.
Is fear in big waves a sign I shouldn't be out there?

Fear is normal and healthy, and it keeps you alert. Panic that freezes you or makes you take bad waves is a sign to scale back. Grow your comfort zone slowly, and listen when your gut says sit one out.
My canopy opened 90 degrees off heading on my last jump. Got away with it. Do I need to change something?

Yes, take that seriously rather than chalking it up to luck. Off-heading openings usually come from body position at deployment, an uneven pack job, brake settings, or a canopy that just needs a tweak, so go through it with your mentor or the person who taught you to pack. Video of your exit and opening helps a lot in finding the cause. Practice your off-heading recovery on paper and in your head too, because the next one could point you straight at the wall.
what's the safest way to bail if I'm going too fast

If you have time, bail early onto grass or a soft shoulder, and stay low with your hands and gloves ready to slide. Try to slide on pads and gloves rather than rolling or reaching out with stiff arms. Keep your chin tucked and let your gear take the hit. The best bail is the one that happens before you're way out of control.
Quick: can I use my belay loop and carabiner to clip into an anchor or should I use a PAS?

Either can work. A PAS or a sling girth-hitched to your tie-in points is common, and many climbers simply use a clove hitch with the rope instead, which is dynamic and adjustable.
