The key rule is to never shock-load a static tether like a Dyneema sling by climbing above the anchor, since even a short fall onto one can fail or cause injury. Use a locking carabiner and stay tight to the anchor.
can i just skip skydiving and go straight to base? seems faster

No, and that shortcut is behind a lot of beginner deaths. BASE gives you seconds and no reserve parachute, so you need canopy control, body position and malfunction responses that skydiving teaches with far more margin for error. Build your skydiving base first and then do a proper first jump course. It's slower, but it's the version where you stay around to keep jumping.
can my 6 year old just learn on a balance bike then go straight to motocross

A balance bike is a great start because it teaches balance, but the next step should be a small, throttle-limited bike like a PW50 or an electric kids' bike such as a STACYC or KTM SX-E. Keep the throttle limiter set low and supervise on flat, open ground before going anywhere near jumps or a track. Make sure your kid has full properly fitted gear from day one, and consider a kids' training school to learn the basics properly.
We forgot the probe. Shovels and beacons only. Still tour?

Without probes, your rescue time goes up badly because you can't pinpoint the burial and you'd dig blind. If you go, stay in genuinely low-angle terrain with nothing steep above or connected, where a slide isn't realistically possible. Otherwise call it, since a probe is cheap and the outing will still be there next week.
Parkour or freerunning — which is safer for a beginner?

Parkour fundamentals are usually the safer starting point. Parkour focuses on efficient movement like vaults, jumps and landings, while freerunning adds flips and acrobatics that need more coaching to learn safely. Most coaches have beginners build parkour basics first, then add freerunning skills later in a gym setting.
can I bring my gopro on the jump

Usually only if it's a mount the operator approves, like a secure chest or wrist strap they fit themselves. Loose handheld cameras are often banned because a dropped object from that height can seriously injure someone below. Many sites also sell their own video packages, and those angles are often better than a selfie cam anyway.
do i really need knee pads

Yes, knees hit the ground in almost every downhill crash, and pads can be the difference between walking away and needing stitches or surgery. Modern pedal-friendly pads are light enough to wear all day. Get a pair with a hard or impact-foam cap that stays put when you pedal.
Is it safe to ski a slope that already has tracks on it?

Tracks mean the slope held for those skiers, not that it's safe for you. Many fatal avalanches happen on slopes with existing tracks, since a deep weak layer may finally fail on the fifth or tenth rider, or you hit a thinner trigger spot they missed. Tracks are useful information but they're not a stability test. Make your own decision based on the forecast, observations and terrain.
lanyard yes or no for depth training on a line

Yes, wear a lanyard when diving on a line in open water, especially in current or poor visibility. It keeps you attached so your buddy or safety diver can pull you up quickly if something goes wrong. Use a quick-release system you've practiced detaching, and attach it to your wrist or ankle in a way that won't snag.
Can I just wear a regular life jacket from my fishing boat for kayaking rapids?

I wouldn't. Fishing-boat vests are usually bulky, ride up when you swim in current, and restrict the arm movement you need for paddling and rolling. A whitewater-specific PFD is cut short so it doesn't snag on the spray skirt, has adjustable side straps to keep it snug in turbulent water, and often includes a quick-release rescue belt. It's one of the most important pieces of gear you'll own, so it's worth the roughly $100–200.
can i just wear a bike helmet for downhill

For mellow carving, a certified bike helmet beats nothing, but once you're actually going downhill it isn't enough, because most real crashes hit the face and chin. A certified full-face helmet is the standard for anything fast, and many riders use a moto or downhill-MTB style lid. Pair it with slide gloves, and add knee and elbow pads or leathers as your speed goes up. Faces are expensive to fix.
Can I climb with long nails?

You can, but long nails often break, catch on holds, or make it harder to crimp securely. Most climbers keep their nails trimmed short for better grip and fewer injuries. If you really want to keep them longer, try filing the edges smooth and avoid tight crimpers.
I keep freezing at the edge and my friends are pressuring me. Should I just force myself?

No, don't jump because of pressure. Fear at the edge often means your body isn't sure about the height yet, and hesitating mid-jump is how people slip or land badly. Go back to a lower spot, get several clean jumps in, and move up only when you feel steady.
how do I stop arm pump, it ruins every moto

Arm pump mostly comes from gripping too tightly, so focus on squeezing the bike with your knees and keeping your grip on the bars loose. Warm up properly with ten minutes of light riding or cardio before your first moto, and stay hydrated. Over time, more seat time and general cardio help far more than forearm curls. If it's severe and nothing helps, see a sports doctor about compartment syndrome before considering surgery.
thinking of skitching behind my buddys car just in the parking lot, slow speed. bad idea?

Yes, it's a bad idea, even slowly, because you can't control your speed, the driver can't see you well, and any crack or pebble sends you down right next to a moving vehicle. Skitching causes a lot of severe and fatal skateboarding injuries, and the parking lot doesn't change those risks much. If you want that pulled feeling, try pushing with a longboard pole or towing behind a friend on a bike on a closed path. Either way, keep cars out of it.
is flying near clouds okay if theyre not that big

Stay well clear and keep a close eye on them, because small cumulus can grow fast, and the lift under them can get strong enough to pull you up into the cloud, where you lose all visual reference. Pilots call this cloud suck, and it can turn dangerous quickly. If clouds are building fast or getting darker underneath, land early. Your local airspace rules also usually set a minimum cloud clearance distance, so learn those for where you fly.
Gauge is right at the low end of the recommended range. Go or nah?

Usually go. Low water often means slower current and more forgiving rapids, but expect more rocks, more scraping and possible pinning spots where water flows through narrow slots. Watch for undercut rocks and sieves that tend to show up at lower levels. Check recent trip reports or a local club for wood updates before you put on.
Is it ok to paddle class III solo if I've got a good roll?

A good roll is great, but it doesn't help if you get pinned, swim, or hit your head, and class III has enough features where that happens. Paddling solo means nobody can throw you a rope or help you recover gear and get to shore. Run class III with at least two other boaters who know rescue, and keep solo paddling for water you'd be comfortable swimming.
what's a good warmup before training

Spend about ten minutes raising your heart rate with jogging or jumping jacks. Then do dynamic mobility like leg swings, hip circles, arm circles and wrist rolls. Finish with some low-intensity versions of what you'll train, such as small jumps, light landings and easy vaults. Skip long static stretches beforehand, because they can dull your power and reaction time.
My daughter fell during parkour and hit her head, she says she's fine but she seems a little confused. Should I worry?

Yes, confusion after a head hit is a sign of possible concussion or something more serious, so get her checked by a doctor today rather than waiting it out. Go straight to the ER if she starts vomiting, gets very drowsy, has a worsening headache, slurred speech, or unequal pupils. Keep her off training and screens until a doctor clears her, because a second hit before she's healed can be dangerous.
My partner refuses to wear a helmet outdoors, says only beginners do. How do I convince him?

Tell him rockfall and dropped gear don't check anyone's grade, and that helmets protect leaders who flip upside down in a fall, which happens to strong climbers too. Many top professionals wear them on sport and trad routes, so it's a habit of experience rather than a beginner's crutch. Modern foam helmets are light enough that you forget they're on. In the end it's his head, but you can set your own rules, like insisting on helmets at crags with known loose rock.
is diamox cheating

Not at all. Acetazolamide just speeds up the natural acclimatization process, and many doctors and guides recommend it, especially on itineraries with fast altitude gains. It doesn't replace a sensible ascent rate, though, and it won't mask serious illness. Talk to a doctor first, since it's prescription-only and doesn't suit everyone, particularly people with sulfa allergies.
I'm 58 with mild high blood pressure, controlled with meds. Can I start cave training?

Plenty of people start cave training later in life, but you should get cleared by a doctor familiar with dive medicine before signing up. Cave dives can be long, cold and physically and mentally demanding, so your cardiovascular health and medications matter. If you're cleared, pick an instructor who goes at a sensible pace and be honest with them about your health.
what's the best way to clean an air filter on a dirt bike

Wash a foam air filter in a dedicated filter cleaner or warm soapy water, squeezing it gently instead of wringing or twisting it, then rinse and let it dry completely. Once it's dry, oil it evenly with proper foam filter oil, work it into the foam, and squeeze out the excess so it's tacky but not dripping. Grease the sealing rim before you reinstall it, and keep a spare oiled filter in a bag so you can swap one in at the track. Never use gasoline, because it breaks down the foam and the glue.
Ugh. Just tell me the fastest way to boost my breath hold, I've got a competition in 3 weeks.

Three weeks is enough to get sharper but not enough to transform your breath hold, so focus on relaxation, a clean breathe-up and dry CO2 and O2 tables done lying down at home. Do your wet training only with a trained buddy, and don't make big jumps in your max, because overreaching right before a comp is how people end up blacking out. Make sure you sleep well and arrive rested. Announce a conservative performance that you know you can surface from cleanly, since a clean white card beats a red card every time.
how do i keep my hands from getting screaming barfies

Keep your blood flowing before you climb by staying warm at the base, eating, drinking, and swinging your arms. Climb in thinner gloves but put warm belay mittens on between pitches. Avoid overgripping and let your arms hang down when you can rest, because tension and raised hands cut circulation. The screaming barfies still happen sometimes, and the pain usually means blood is returning, so ride it out. Numbness that won't recover is a sign to stop for the day.
what are thermals

Thermals are columns of rising warm air that form when the sun heats the ground unevenly, for example over dark fields, rocky slopes or car parks. Paragliders circle inside them to gain height, which is how pilots stay up for hours and fly long distances. They can also be turbulent and punchy, especially at midday in summer, which is why beginners usually fly mornings and evenings when the air is gentler.
What's the most dangerous type of BASE object?

Cliffs and other terrain jumps are generally the riskiest, especially with wingsuits, because the object is close, the landing areas are tough and the conditions change. Buildings and antennas carry real risk from off-heading openings and tight landings. Big bridges are often considered the most forgiving for learning because they usually have clear space and water or open ground below. Every object needs proper assessment, so 'safest' only ever means relatively safer.
Want to free solo a 5.6 I've top-roped like 20 times. Thoughts?

I'd strongly advise against it, because no matter how easy the route feels, a single broken hold, slip, or moment of cramping has no margin for error. Even elite soloists have died on routes far below their limit. If you want that free, flowing feeling, try lapping the route on top rope, linking it with a quick self-belay system under instruction, or exploring deep water soloing in a safe setting.
how long is a typical first jump course

Usually about five to ten days, depending on the school, the weather and how many jumps they fit in. Expect a lot of ground training on packing, emergency procedures, object assessment and landing areas, followed by a series of jumps from carefully chosen sites. Pick an established instructor with a strong safety record over whoever is cheapest or closest.
Which is better for a first time: tandem or static line?

Tandem is easier and gives you a full 60 seconds of freefall with almost no training, so it's the better pick if you just want the experience. Static line or AFF makes sense if you want to become a licensed skydiver, since you'll be in control of your own parachute right away. Lots of people do a tandem first to make sure they love it, then sign up for AFF.
What's a restriction in a cave?

A restriction is any part of the cave narrow enough that two divers can't swim side by side, or where you have to squeeze, remove gear or swim in single file. They increase risk because sharing gas is harder and silt can trap you in no visibility. Navigating them safely takes specific training, so plan conservatively and only enter restrictions you've been trained for.
is it bad to climb when I'm hungover?

It's not a great idea, especially for leading or belaying, since dehydration and slower reaction times can affect your judgment and grip. If you're feeling rough, stick to easy bouldering or take a rest day and focus on rehydrating. Your partner's safety depends on your belay, so only belay if you're fully alert.
My son is 16 and wants to tandem, can he?

In the US, USPA dropzones require jumpers to be at least 18, with no parental-consent exception. Some countries, such as parts of Europe and Australia, allow younger tandem jumpers with parental consent, so it depends on where you are. If you're in the US, a wind tunnel session is a great way for him to experience freefall until he's old enough.
Worried about my 17 yo son wanting to do a summer 50 miler. Should I let him?

Teens can handle ultras, but heat adds real risk, and a 17-year-old's judgment about pushing through is usually the weak link. Check the race's age minimum, because many 50 milers require runners to be 18. If he's set on it, have him do a sports physical, build up through hot 50Ks first and go with an experienced pacer or crew. A cooler-season first 50 miler is honestly the smarter path.
hey quick one, whats SIV

SIV stands for Simulation d'Incident en Vol, basically a course where you practise collapses, stalls, spins and reserve deployment over water with an instructor guiding you by radio and a rescue boat below. It teaches how your wing behaves in bad situations and how to recover calmly. Most pilots take one after they've built some airtime, and it's one of the best safety investments in the sport.
how do i ollie higher? mine are like 3 inches

Height comes from the snap and the slide working together, so pop the tail hard and fast, then drag the side of your front shoe up the grip tape all the way to the nose. The real secret is sucking your knees up toward your chest after the pop, because the board can only rise as high as your feet let it. Practice on grass or carpet first to drill the motion without the board rolling away, then take it to flat ground.
im 52 and want to start freediving, is that too old

Not at all, plenty of people start in their fifties and do great, since the sport rewards calm and technique more than raw power. Get a medical check first, especially of your heart, blood pressure and ears, because breath-holds put real stress on the cardiovascular system. Then do a beginner certification course where an instructor can build up your depth and times gradually and safely.
I keep missing my roll in the rapid even though I can roll in a pool. Help?

That gap is totally normal, because aerated water, disorientation and panic all shrink your margin compared to a pool. Try practicing in moving water in safe flat spots with a friend nearby, and do repeated rolls on both sides when you're tired. Setting up deliberately and waiting a second before sweeping helps a lot, and a session with a coach can catch small form errors fast.
Is it smarter to start fast while it's cool in the morning and bank time before the heat?

It's tempting, but it usually backfires. Going hard early raises your core temperature, burns through your carbs and leaves you more depleted right as it gets hot. A steady, moderate start with aggressive cooling once the sun comes up nearly always beats banking time, so make the most of the cool hours by eating, drinking and running comfortably.
whats a good deployment altitude for wingsuit

Most dropzones want wingsuit pilots fully deployed by around 4,000 to 5,000 feet, with beginners typically breaking off and starting deployment higher than that. Wingsuit deployments take a bit more time and need a stable, symmetrical position, so give yourself margin. Follow your dropzone's rules and your instructor's numbers, which can vary by location.
My son wants a street luge for his birthday. He's 12. Is that okay?

A 12-year-old can get into luge or downhill, but only with close supervision and proper gear like a full-face helmet, gloves and pads. Start him on mellow hills away from traffic, and ideally find a local club or experienced riders who can teach him the basics. Treat the board as the start of a skill-building process, not something to ride alone on the street right away.
My friend says we can just rig a bungee off the old railway bridge near us with climbing rope and some stretchy cord from a hardware store. Cheaper than paying $150. Thoughts?

Please don't. Real bungee cords are rated for your exact weight and drop length, and operators calculate the stretch so you stop well short of the ground or water. Hardware store cord and climbing rope can't do that, and a few meters of error is the difference between a thrill and a fatal impact. The $150 is paying for engineering and inspected gear, so save up and do it at a licensed site.
lol can i just drink pickle juice the whole race for salt

Pickle juice is fine as an occasional boost, and a lot of runners swear it helps cramps, but it's not a complete plan. It has a lot of sodium and no real calories or carbs, and large amounts can upset your stomach. Pair it with a proper electrolyte drink and food so you're covering energy and fluid, not just salt.
how long do i actually have to wait to fly after diving, my flight's tomorrow afternoon

The standard guideline is at least 12 hours after a single no-decompression dive and at least 18 hours after multiple dives or multiple days of diving. Longer is better, and many divers and operators treat 24 hours as the safer default. If you dived several times today, skip any morning dive tomorrow and you'll be fine for an afternoon flight.
do i actually need an inflation vest or is that just for pros

If you're surfing waves big enough to hold you down for more than a few seconds, an inflation vest is standard kit, not a pro accessory. It gets you to the surface faster after a bad wipeout, which is exactly when you're most oxygen-depleted and disoriented. Buy a reputable brand, learn how to pull the cord and repack the CO2 canisters, and practice deploying it in controlled conditions before you trust it in real surf.
Throw bag or no throw bag for a casual float day on class II?

Bring the throw bag, since class II still has swims, pins and foot entrapment hazards, and a rope is the fastest way to help someone from shore. Keep a river knife on your PFD so you can cut the rope if it ever wraps around someone. Practicing a few throws before you launch takes ten minutes and makes the bag actually useful.
My 13 year old wants to start whitewater with me. How do I keep it safe?

Start with a kids or youth whitewater course with a certified instructor so they learn wet exits, rolling and swimming technique properly, and make sure their PFD, helmet and boat actually fit their size. Keep the first season on flatwater and easy class I-II with a couple of experienced adults around, and set clear rules about scouting and portaging. Kids often progress fast, but let their skills, not their enthusiasm, set the pace.
My partner refuses to go down even though she's confused and stumbling. What do I do??

Confusion and stumbling at altitude point strongly to HACE, and impaired judgment is part of the illness, so you can't wait for her to agree. Get help from your guide, other climbers or a rescue service now, give dexamethasone and oxygen if you have them, and start descending with her, physically assisted if needed. Even a few hundred meters can make a big difference, and every hour counts.
My 15 year old son wants to go cliff jumping with his friends this summer at a quarry. I'm terrified. What should I actually worry about?

The biggest killers at quarries are hidden underwater hazards like submerged machinery, rock ledges and debris, plus very cold water that can trigger cold shock even in summer. Ask that someone checks the landing zone by swimming it first, that they stick to low heights, never jump alone, and stay sober. A spot where jumping is supervised or officially allowed is far safer than an abandoned quarry, so it's worth steering him toward one.
How do I know if an ice pillar is safe to climb?

Free-hanging pillars and ones that have only partly connected to the ground are the most likely to fail, especially when temperatures swing. Signs to worry about are cracks, hollow sounds, water running inside, and a narrow base. Many experienced climbers avoid them except in stable, cold conditions. If you're not sure, don't climb it. Pick a route with fat, well-bonded ice.
there's a road near me with basically no cars at night, perfect for bombing. good idea?

Night is actually the worst time for it: you can't see gravel, cracks or wildlife, and the one car that does show up won't expect a person lying low in its lane. "Basically no cars" is exactly how most serious skate-car collisions happen. If you love that road, ride it in daylight with a spotter at the bottom or a friend radioing traffic, or better yet find a local club that organizes closed-road freerides.
ankle harness or body harness, which is safer

Both are safe when a reputable operator fits them properly, and many sites use ankle attachments with a backup body harness. If you have ankle, knee or hip issues, ask for a body-harness jump, which spreads the load differently and is often available. The bigger safety factor is the quality of the operator, not which style you pick.
I have mild asthma, controlled with an inhaler. Can I still learn to freedive?

Many people with well-controlled asthma do freedive. Even so, get a check from a doctor first, ideally one who knows diving medicine, because cold water and exertion can trigger an attack. Be upfront about your asthma on your course medical form, and bring it up with your instructor before you start. If you get the all-clear, start easy, and skip diving any day your asthma is flaring.
my friend died BASE jumping last year and now i'm scared to jump again. is that normal?

Completely normal, and I'm sorry about your friend. Fear after a loss is your mind processing something real, not a sign of weakness. Take as much time as you need, talk to people who knew them, and consider speaking with a counselor if it's weighing on you. If you do go back, start slow with forgiving objects and trusted mentors, and know that choosing to step away is also a valid and brave decision.
can i just skip electrolytes and drink a ton of water during a 50k in 95 degree heat

Please don't. Drinking large volumes of plain water over hours of heavy sweating is exactly how runners end up with exercise-associated hyponatremia, which can cause confusion, seizures and death. Drink to thirst, and pair your fluids with sodium from capsules, drink mix or salty food, roughly 300 to 600 mg per hour depending on how salty a sweater you are. If you start gaining weight during the race or your hands swell badly, back off the fluids.
Got held down for two waves today at a reef, came up fine but my head still hurts a lot 3 hours later and I feel a bit confused. normal?

It's not something to wait out, because persistent headache and confusion after a hold-down can point to a head injury, near-drowning after-effects, or water in your lungs. Get checked at an urgent care or emergency room now and tell them exactly what happened. Have someone drive you, don't sleep it off alone, and stay out of the water until a doctor clears you.
Is sidemount or backmount better for caves?

Both work well. Sidemount is great for tight, low passages and gives you two fully independent regulators that are easy to reach, while backmount doubles are more common in big, open cave systems and simpler to manage at first. Many divers start in whichever configuration their instructor teaches and add the other later. Pick a good instructor first and let the configuration follow.
How deep do people go in caves?

Most recreational cave dives stay within about 30 to 40 meters, well within air or nitrox limits. Exploration teams go far deeper using trimix, rebreathers and long decompression, sometimes beyond 200 meters, but that's the extreme end of an already advanced sport. Depth training comes separately and only after solid cave experience.
rule of thirds. explain quick

You use one third of your gas going in, one third coming out, and keep the last third in reserve for emergencies like sharing air with your buddy. You turn the dive as soon as either diver hits their turn pressure, no discussion. Many cave divers use even more conservative margins in siphons, with mismatched tank sizes or with high-flow situations.
My doc offered a cortisone shot in my knee so I can ride the enduro race next weekend. Seems like a no-brainer?

It's not a no-brainer. Cortisone can calm inflammation, but it also dulls the pain that's protecting the knee, and racing hard in the days right after an injection can damage tendon or cartilage that's already compromised. Ask your doctor directly what the underlying problem is and whether high-load riding that soon is safe for that specific diagnosis. If the answer is fuzzy, sitting this race out is probably the cheaper option long-term.
how high can a beginner safely jump from? like whats the max

Start in the 3 to 5 meter range, roughly a high-dive platform, and stay there until your feet-first entries are consistently clean. Most people feel ready for more long before their body control is, and somewhere above 10 meters the impact gets serious enough to injure you if your form breaks. Work up a meter or two at a time, and only from spots where depth and conditions are known.
Good turnaround time rule for summit day?

Set a hard turnaround time before you start and stick to it, no matter how close the summit looks. On big peaks like Everest that's often around 11 a.m. to 1 p.m., so you can get down before darkness, exhaustion, or afternoon weather catch you. Lots of fatal accidents happen on the descent after people pushed past their deadline, so treat it as non-negotiable and agree on it with your team ahead of time.
What lights do I need for cave diving

You need a strong primary light, usually a canister or high-output handheld, plus at least two backup lights, each able to last the whole dive on its own. Mount the backups so you can reach them instantly, often clipped to your chest D-rings or harness. Losing light in a cave is an emergency, so the redundancy isn't optional.
Just bought a new beacon. What do I need to do before using it?

Read the manual cover to cover, put in the recommended batteries, and check that it switches between transmit and search reliably. Practice searching with it several times before taking it into avalanche terrain, ideally with your touring partners so everyone knows each other's gear. And do a group beacon check at the trailhead every single day.
can i free solo the flatirons as a beginner? everyone says the first flatiron is easy

Lots of people do scramble the First Flatiron, but it's still a long, exposed route where falls are fatal, and people have died there. As a beginner, climb it roped with an experienced partner or hire a Boulder guide, which is a great way to see it safely. Hold off on going ropeless until you've built real outdoor experience and know the route intimately.
Race director says the heat index will hit 110 and may black-flag the event. I've trained all year. Should I push to start if they allow it?

If they allow it, start with a radically adjusted plan rather than your goal pace, and be genuinely willing to drop. At a 110 heat index, your training fitness matters less than how conservatively you pace, cool and fuel. Slow way down, use ice at every station, and treat any confusion, stopping sweating or nausea you can't control as an automatic stop. And if they black-flag it, accept the call, because a DNF beats an ICU visit and there will be other races.
I'm 16 and want to try a precision jump onto a railing. Any tips?

Make sure you're consistent at sticking precision jumps onto lines on the ground before ever trying a rail, because a rail adds balance demands and a much smaller margin for error. Start with a low, solid rail that's knee-height or lower with grass or a soft surface around it, and land on the balls of your feet with your knees bent. Wobbles happen, so practice bailing safely by stepping off forward or back rather than trying to save every landing.
How do you know when to turn around?

Set a firm turnaround time before summit day and stick to it, no matter how close the top looks, because most fatal accidents happen on the descent when people run out of time, energy or oxygen. Also turn around if you have symptoms of altitude illness, the weather turns bad or someone in your team is struggling badly. The summit is optional, but getting down is mandatory.
Crashed yesterday, hit my head pretty hard but helmet took it. Felt a bit dizzy then fine. Going riding again today, cool?

Not cool. A hard hit with dizziness can mean a concussion, and a second impact before you've healed can be seriously dangerous. Get checked by a doctor before riding again, and expect to rest for at least several days even if you feel fine. Replace that helmet too, since it's done its job and won't protect you the same way again.
Is water touch bungee more dangerous than normal?

It adds some complexity because the cord length must be calibrated precisely to your weight so you just dip in rather than hit the water hard. Experienced operators do this routinely and it's very safe when done right. Make sure your weight is measured on site, not just taken from what you say, and only do it at a place known for water touches.
I'm so scared of falling on lead on ice. Is that normal or am I just a wimp?

That fear is healthy, not wimpy. Falling on ice is far more dangerous than on rock because crampons catch and break ankles, and tools can injure you. Experienced ice climbers treat 'the leader must not fall' as a real rule and only lead routes well within their ability. Spend plenty of time on top-rope, lead only easy grades at first, and you'll build the confidence that comes from real competence.
is it safe to swim alone in the sea if im a strong pool swimmer

Pool strength doesn't transfer as cleanly as people think. Currents, chop, cold and having no wall to grab change everything, so swimming alone is how strong swimmers get into trouble. Go with a buddy or a local swim group, wear a bright cap, and tow a swim buoy so boats and people on shore can see you. Once you know a spot well, staying close to shore and telling someone your exact plan is the bare minimum.
Can I skitch behind my friend's car, he'll go slow

Skip it. Even at low speed you can't react to potholes, gravel or sudden braking, and when you fall you're right next to moving wheels. People get seriously hurt or killed doing this every year, often at speeds they thought were safe. If you want that towing feeling, try a skate park with a friend pushing you, or learn to pump on a bowl.
We are three friends, mid 30s, wanting to try a 7000m peak. Recommendations?

Lenin Peak in Kyrgyzstan and Muztagh Ata in China are the classic first 7,000ers. Both are non-technical and well supported by expedition companies, and Muztagh Ata is a good option on skis. Before committing, make sure each of you has done a 6,000 m peak, because many people learn about their own altitude tolerance the hard way. Book with an established outfitter for permits, base-camp logistics and rescue arrangements, and agree on turnaround rules as a group before you leave.
I'm 58 and pretty fit, is it too late to start ice climbing?

Not at all. Plenty of people start in their 50s and 60s, and ice climbing rewards technique and patience more than raw power. Start with a guided intro day on top rope, focus on footwork so your legs do the work, and build up gradually to spare your shoulders and elbows. If you have any heart or joint concerns, a quick check with your doctor beforehand is worth it.
Is it smarter to run at night during a hot multiday race?

Often yes, because moving during cooler hours and resting through the peak heat is a common, sensible strategy in desert stage races. Just check the race rules on night travel and carry a reliable headlamp plus backup batteries. Fatigue and navigation errors go up at night, so stay with others where you can.
My instructor says I'm not ready for high flights yet but I've done 30 bunny hill flights and feel totally ready. Can I just go to the mountain launch myself?

Listen to your instructor on this one. They've watched your launches, your landings and your decision-making, and they're seeing things you can't see from inside your own head. Mountain flying adds turbulence, landing field selection and much bigger consequences for small mistakes, so ask them specifically what skills they want to see from you before signing off. That gives you a clear goal instead of a vague 'not yet.'
should i wear a wetsuit or go skins for a 2 hour swim in 17C water

For two hours at 17°C, wear a wetsuit unless you're well acclimatized and have done long skins swims in similar temperatures. Heat loss adds up steadily over that time, and mild hypothermia sneaks up on you by slowing your stroke and blurring your judgment. If you're building toward a skins swim, increase your skins time gradually with support nearby. A wetsuit also adds buoyancy, which is useful on a long swim.
What do free soloists do to train mentally?

Serious soloists put in massive amounts of rehearsal, climbing a route roped over and over until every move is automatic, and then they visualize it in detail. Many keep journals and practice staying calm under stress, and they're ruthless about backing off when something feels off. Honnold famously talks about expanding his comfort zone slowly over years rather than forcing through fear. Those habits are worth borrowing for any climbing, since visualization and honest self-assessment will make you a better roped climber too.
what's a delay and how long should mine be on my first jumps

Delay is the time you free fall before deploying your pilot chute, and on first jumps from a bridge or span it's usually very short, often zero to two seconds, sometimes using a static line or PCA. Longer delays need more altitude and more experience, because your speed grows quickly and so does the risk of an off-heading opening. Your instructor will set delays based on the object height, and you should never stretch them on your own.
thinking about buying a used yz250 off facebook, what should i check

Do a cold start so you can hear how it fires up and idles. Check the compression with a gauge too, since a healthy one usually reads somewhere around 150 psi or more, and ask when the top end was last done. Look for a bent subframe, play in the steering head and swingarm bearings, leaking fork seals, a slipping clutch, and whether the VIN is legible and matches the paperwork. Take a short ride if the seller allows it, and walk away if the title or the story doesn't add up.
What's a malfunction like in a wingsuit vs regular skydiving?

The emergency procedures are basically the same: identify, decide by your altitude, then cut away and deploy your reserve if needed. The wingsuit adds complications. Your arms may be restricted until you unzip them, and line twists can be more common if your body position at deployment isn't symmetrical. That's why pulling high, de-arming first and drilling emergency procedures in your suit on the ground matter so much.
I'm 58 and want to start cold water swimming for my health. Anything I should know?

It's a brilliant thing to take up, but cold shock puts a real strain on the heart, so check in with your doctor first, especially if you have any blood pressure or heart issues. Start in autumn while the water is still relatively mild, and let your body adapt as the temperature drops. Go with a group or a buddy, keep your first dips to a couple of minutes, and focus on slow, controlled breathing as you get in. Local cold-water swimming groups are usually very welcoming to beginners.
What should go in a whitewater first aid kit?

Pack a waterproof kit with blister and wound care, an elastic bandage, a SAM splint, trauma shears, gloves, an emergency blanket, and any personal meds like an epinephrine pen. Add a whistle, a lighter, and a headlamp, plus a phone or satellite messenger in a dry bag. A wilderness first aid course will tell you how to actually use it on a remote riverbank.
is a 3mm wetsuit enough for 18°C water

For most people that's on the chilly side, especially across multiple dives. A 5mm or a 7mm with a hood is usually comfortable at 18°C, and getting cold underwater speeds up your air use and dulls your judgment. If you run warm and it's one short dive, a 3mm with a hooded vest can work.
my friend says he can teach me to pack my own main, he has like 200 jumps. that ok?

Learning to pack from an experienced jumper is common, but do it properly. Your dropzone may require you to be signed off as a packer, and in the US it's a skill on the A-license card. Have your friend or a certified coach watch you pack several times before you jump your own packs, and make sure you know how to check that the closing loop and pin are right. Mains are packable by the jumper, but reserves always go to a certified rigger.
do I need to spot first or can I just send it, the water looks deep

Always check it first, because deep-looking water is one of the most common traps in cliff jumping. Dark or murky water can hide boulders, logs and sandbars just a meter or two down. Get in and swim the landing zone, ideally with goggles, before anyone jumps.
is wearing a helmet in the park actually necessary or is it just for beginners

It's necessary, and pros wear them too. Park falls often mean catching an edge or landing on the back of your head on hard-packed snow, and that's where concussions and worse happen. A modern helmet is light and warm and you'll forget it's there. Add wrist guards if you're learning rails or new jumps.
Can I do a 40m deep dive on air if I go slow and watch my gauge?

Going slow doesn't solve the main problems at 40m. On air you'll have significant narcosis that dulls your judgment, very short no-decompression limits, and you'll burn through gas fast. That depth is the recreational limit and needs Deep Diver training, solid experience, a planned gas reserve and ideally a guide. Work up to it gradually with the training rather than trying it on your own.
do i actually need a helmet if im just cruising around the neighborhood

Yes, cruising is actually where a lot of serious head injuries happen, because a pebble or crack can stop your wheels instantly and pitch you forward before you can react. You don't need full pads for casual riding, but a helmet takes zero effort and covers the one injury you can't walk off. Get one certified for skating or multi-sport and you'll forget it's even there.
I'm 19 and I've been bouldering for 8 months, sending V5 indoors. How long until I can start free soloing outdoor routes?

V5 in eight months is real progress, but indoor bouldering and outdoor soloing are almost different sports, so the honest answer is years, not months. Before soloing anything, you'd want a long apprenticeship on rope outdoors, learning rock quality, friction on real stone and how your head handles exposure on routes far below your limit. Most people who solo seriously have climbed the specific route many times on rope first and solo only terrain several grades easier than their max. Get into trad or sport climbing outside with experienced partners or a guide, and let that foundation build for a good while.
whats the most common way people get hurt base jumping

Landing injuries are the most common, especially ankles, legs, and backs from rough terrain, bad approaches, or turbulence near the ground. The most deadly accidents are usually object strikes from off-heading openings, plus wingsuit terrain impacts. Strong canopy control, careful landing area choice, and conservative weather decisions prevent much of this.
Do cave divers really use gold line arrows and cookies

Yes, line arrows point the way to the nearest exit, and cookies are non-directional markers used to show personal ownership or mark routes. They're a vital part of navigation, especially at junctions or in poor visibility. Using them properly takes training, so practice under an instructor before relying on them.
whats the rule of thirds

It's a gas planning rule where you use one third of your starting gas going in, one third getting out, and keep the last third as a reserve for emergencies like helping a buddy who's lost their gas. You turn the dive as soon as either diver hits their first third, whichever comes first. In siphons or with mismatched tank sizes divers often plan even more conservatively, and a cave course will teach you how to adjust it properly.
Just tell me the fastest way to get to 30m. I'm at 15m now and getting bored.

There's no safe shortcut to 30 meters. Getting there takes adaptation in your lungs, equalization technique like mouthfill, and relaxation, and if you rush you risk lung squeeze, ear damage and blackout on the way up. Taking a course at the next level is the quickest realistic path, since an instructor can work on your equalization and set up safe progressive depth sessions with a line and proper safety. Most divers build up a few meters at a time over weeks and months.
Sprained thumb from a ski pole fall. Snowboarding instead tomorrow, no poles needed. Smart workaround?

Not really. Snowboarders put out their hands a lot when they fall, and a thumb that's been hurt in a ski pole fall may be skier's thumb, a UCL tear that sometimes needs surgery if it isn't treated. Get it examined, especially if pinching or gripping is weak or painful. If it turns out to be minor, a thumb spica splint and riding with wrist guards is the safer way to get back out. If you skip the check now, you could end up with a thumb that never pinches properly again.
Do hats and arm sleeves make you hotter or cooler?

Cooler, as long as they're light-colored and you keep them wet. A white hat and sleeves block direct sun and act as evaporative coolers when soaked or stuffed with ice. Dark or dry fabric in full sun can actually trap heat, so soak them at every aid station.
I'm 52 and haven't ridden in 15 years. My son wants me to do a downhill day with him. Am I crazy?

Not crazy at all, plenty of riders start or return in their fifties. Book a half-day lesson or skills clinic first, because modern bikes and trail features have changed a lot in 15 years and a coach will rebuild your fundamentals fast. Stick to greens and easy blues, ride at your own pace rather than your son's, and stop while you still feel fresh. Most injuries happen on that one last tired run.
can i jump if i've been drinking a bit, like one beer for nerves

Skip the beer. Reputable operators won't let anyone jump who's had alcohol, and staff will refuse you if they suspect it. Even a little affects your blood pressure, judgment, and how you follow instructions on the platform, which matters when timing and position count. Deep breaths and talking with the crew work better for nerves.
found a used wing online for 300 bucks, 12 years old, seller says it flies fine. good deal for a first wing?

Probably not. Paraglider fabric loses strength and gets more porous with age and UV exposure, and a 12-year-old wing may well fail a porosity or line-strength check. Only consider it if it has a recent professional inspection report, and even then an older design is less forgiving than modern beginner wings. Ask your instructor to help you find a newer used EN-A wing; it'll cost more but you're betting your life on it.
Fell off a boulder problem yesterday and landed weird on my ankle. It's swollen and bruised and hurts to walk. Ice and keep climbing?

Significant swelling, bruising and pain when walking after a bouldering fall means you should get it checked before you climb on it again. Bouldering falls cause a lot of ankle fractures and bad ligament tears, and walking on an untreated one can turn a six-week injury into a chronic problem. Get an X-ray, ideally from a sports medicine doctor or an urgent care clinic. Ice, elevate and keep weight off it until then.
Hot ultra in 3 days and I have a cold. Run it?

If it's just a mild head cold with no fever, you can probably start with a conservative plan. But if you have a fever, body aches or chest symptoms, skip it, because illness increases your risk of heat illness and can make your heart work harder than usual. Hydrate well, sleep a lot and be honest with yourself about how you feel on race morning.
Thinking about bungee in a country with lax safety rules because it's cheaper. Bad idea?

It's not automatically bad, but you need to vet the operator more carefully when local regulation is weak. Look for long-running companies with international reviews and transparent safety practices, and ideally membership in a recognized bungee association. Check that staff re-weigh you, explain the gear, and double-check attachments. If anything feels rushed or improvised, walk away and accept losing the deposit.
my friend says you should exhale before surfacing to save time. true?

Not quite. Exhaling right before or at surfacing can drop your lung oxygen at the worst moment and raises blackout risk. Surface, then do hook breathing, which means quick passive exhales and strong inhales with a held pressure, for several breaths. Your buddy should watch you for at least 30 seconds afterward.
My son just told me he's planning to take up wingsuit flying and I'm terrified. Is it as deadly as it looks on YouTube?

Those viral clips are mostly wingsuit BASE and proximity flying, which carry a much higher fatality rate than wingsuit skydiving from a plane. Skydiving with a wingsuit at altitude, after the required jump experience and proper coaching, is a fairly controlled extension of regular skydiving. The most useful thing you can do is ask him how he's training and encourage him to stay in the skydiving environment rather than drifting toward BASE or terrain flying.
Booked a liveaboard and I get seasick badly. Anything that won't wreck my diving?

Non-drowsy options are your friend. Many divers do well with meclizine or a scopolamine patch, but try any medication on land first so you know how it affects you before you take it near a dive. Stay on deck looking at the horizon, eat light and keep hydrated. If you're vomiting or exhausted, sit out that dive, because seasickness underwater is miserable and risky.
Ok I watched some youtube videos. Ready to lead my first ice route this weekend? Done some top roping.

Probably not yet. Videos are great for ideas, but leading ice takes judgment about ice quality, solid screw placement and calm movement under pressure, which only come from practice. Get several days of top-roping under your belt, practice placing screws from a stance, then take a lead course or mock-lead with a guide. Your first leads should be on easy, fat ice well below your top-rope limit.
There's a local spot where people jump off a bridge into a river. It's illegal but everyone does it. Worth it?

I'd pass. Bridge jumps over rivers tend to combine shallow or changing depth, currents, snags and debris you can't see, and the fact that it's illegal usually means no one is checking any of it. Rivers change after every storm, so 'everyone does it' tells you little about today's conditions. Find a legal spot with known depth and calm water.
My instructor wants us to do a drill sharing air while following the line blind. Kind of scared, is that normal?

Yes, that's a standard, very important cave course drill, and it's normal to feel nervous about it. It simulates the worst realistic scenario, an out-of-air buddy in a silt-out, and practicing it in training is what keeps people alive. Tell your instructor how you feel so they can walk you through it step by step; feeling the stress in a controlled setting is the point.
Doing a self-supported 40 mile desert run solo next week, any tips

Solo and self-supported in the desert is where things go wrong fast, so share a detailed route and check-in times with someone and carry a satellite messenger or PLB, since cell coverage is often nonexistent. Cache water in advance or carry far more than you think you need, along with electrolytes and a bailout plan. Start before dawn to beat the worst heat. Better yet, bring a partner, because heat illness clouds your judgment exactly when you need it.
should i learn on a jib board or all mountain

If you're mostly riding the park and doing butters, presses and boxes, a soft jib board makes learning easier and more forgiving. If you also want to ride the whole mountain, a softer all-mountain or twin board is the better all-round choice. Most people learning tricks do great on an all-mountain twin with a medium-soft flex.
dude theres a dam with a really cool pool below it, can we swim there

Stay out of the water below dams. They often have recirculating currents that can trap even strong swimmers, and the water level can rise suddenly when the gates open. A lot of them have no-swimming signs for exactly that reason. Find a calmer spot upstream or a designated swimming area instead.
How do I get over fear of falling? I freeze up every time I try something new

It helps to practice falling on purpose, like running out or rolling onto your knee pads on a ramp, so falling stops feeling like the worst outcome. Break each trick into small steps and make the first versions really easy, like trying it stationary or on grass. Wearing good gear makes a real difference in confidence too, and it's normal to need lots of reps before your brain trusts a new move.
I'm 58 and moderately fit. Too old to start cave diving?

Not at all, plenty of people start cave diving in their fifties and sixties. The main requirements are good health, solid buoyancy and a calm, methodical mindset, and age often helps with that last one. Get a dive medical with a doctor familiar with diving, especially for heart health, then build your skills patiently.
I'm a woman on birth control pills. Any altitude concerns?

Estrogen-containing pills slightly raise the risk of blood clots, and altitude, dehydration and immobility in a tent can add to that. For most healthy women this isn't a reason to stay home, but talk to your doctor before a big expedition, especially above 5000 m or on long trips. Stay hydrated, move around regularly and know the signs of a clot, such as a painful, swollen calf or sudden breathlessness.
what altitude do tandems usually jump from

Most tandems exit somewhere between 10,000 and 14,000 feet, which gives roughly 30 to 60 seconds of freefall. The parachute is typically deployed around 5,000 feet, followed by about five minutes under canopy. Some dropzones offer higher jumps for an extra fee, but anything much above 15,000 feet requires supplemental oxygen.
rain all night, park is open. still worth going?

It can be a great day, but ride a level or two below your usual and expect less grip, especially on roots and rocks, which turn slick. Wet-weather or mud tires help a lot. Brake earlier and stay off the brakes in the middle of corners and over roots. Many parks close their steepest or most technical trails after heavy rain, and that is a good signal to stay off them too.
I'm 16. Can I take a cave course?

Most agencies require cave divers to be at least 18, though a few allow cavern training a bit younger with parental consent. Use the next couple of years to rack up open water dives, take advanced and nitrox courses, and work hard on buoyancy and trim, since that's what separates good cave students. You'll arrive at your cave course far more prepared than most.
I fractured my collarbone mountain biking 5 weeks ago. Doc said 8 weeks min. Indoor trainer ok?

An indoor trainer is usually fine and a great way to keep your fitness up, because there's no crash risk and you can ride sitting fairly upright. Check with your doctor first, since leaning on the bars can stress the fracture depending on where it is and how it's being treated. Keep the riding easy, skip sprints where you yank on the bars, and stop if you feel pain at the break. Stick to the 8 weeks before you go back on dirt, since a second crash onto an unhealed collarbone often means surgery.
my board's grip tape is peeling and the deck has a crack near the truck. still good?

The grip tape is just cosmetic and easy to replace, but a crack near the truck bolts is a real problem since that's where the board takes the most stress. It could snap suddenly when you land or push, which is a nasty way to fall. I'd swap the deck now and move your trucks and wheels over, which is cheaper than a full complete.
hurry up, quick checklist before we leave the car?

Do a beacon check at the trailhead with everyone in send and receive mode, confirm shovels and probes are actually in the packs, and agree on the plan and the turnaround time. Make sure someone outside the group knows where you're going and when you'll be back. Two minutes here is cheap insurance.
can i learn tricks on rented gear or do i need a park board

You can definitely learn the basics like ollies, butters and small jumps on rental gear, especially a softer, shorter board. Rentals usually set the board up with a stance aimed at cruising, so ask the shop for a duck stance with the bindings centered, which makes riding switch and spinning easier. Hold off on buying a park board until you know you love park riding.
can i ride downhill with my regular half shell trail helmet or do i really need a full face

For lift-served downhill, wear a full face. The speeds are higher, and going over the bars face-first onto rocks is common enough that jaw and teeth injuries are a real risk. A half shell is fine for mellow trail riding, but it leaves your whole lower face exposed. If you don't want to buy one yet, most bike parks rent full-face helmets cheaply. A convertible helmet with a removable chin bar is also a good middle ground if you ride both kinds of terrain.
can i have a couple beers between dives on the boat

Skip them until you're done for the day. Alcohol dehydrates you, impairs your judgment and may raise your decompression sickness risk, which is a bad trade on a dive boat. Have your beer once the gear's rinsed.
how do pros make tricks look so easy

Mostly thousands of repetitions, starting with tiny versions of the trick on small features and working up over years. They also do a lot of off-snow training like trampolines, airbags and strength work, so their bodies know the movement before they try it on snow. What looks effortless is really very solid fundamentals plus good judgment about when to back off.
Chilblains on my toes after a winter climb. Same as frostbite?

No. Chilblains are an inflammatory reaction to cold and damp at temperatures above freezing, so they're itchy, red or purplish and annoying but rarely serious. Frostbite is actual freezing of tissue, typically numb, white, waxy or hard skin that can blister and blacken. If you notice blisters, discoloration or lingering numbness, see a doctor promptly.
Quick q: do wingsuits have built in safety features like parachutes?

No, the wingsuit itself has no parachute; you wear a normal skydiving or BASE rig, and the suit is designed to work with it. Many skydivers use an AAD, which fires the reserve if you're still falling fast at low altitude, though it's not a reason to fly casually. You still need training, good gear and solid deployment skills.
whats a good surface interval between dives

A common rule of thumb is to rest at the surface for at least twice as long as your dive lasted, so a one-minute dive means two minutes of recovery. For deeper or longer dives, take more than that, and many people use three times the dive time or a set rest at depth. Your heart rate should be back to calm before you go down again. Shortchanging recovery is one of the quiet ways oxygen debt builds up across a session.
can you cliff jump in winter

You can, but cold water changes the risk a lot. Cold shock can make you gasp involuntarily on entry and lose muscle control within minutes, so wear a wetsuit, keep jumps low, and make sure the exit is quick and easy. If you've never trained for cold water, an organized coasteering group with proper kit is the way to go.
I'm 52 and tore my calf a bit trail running. Doctor said grade 1. How soon can I get back to hills?

Grade 1 calf strains usually settle in two to four weeks. Hills are one of the last things to bring back, because uphill running puts the calf through a lot of load and stretch. Start with walking and flat easy jogs once you can do single-leg calf raises pain-free, then add gentle inclines over a week or two. At 52, tendons and muscle take a bit longer to remodel, so a slower return beats a re-tear that sets you back twice as long. A physio can give you a progressive calf-loading plan, and that's worth doing.
WHY do I keep getting a headache after every dive??

The most common causes are skip breathing (pausing between breaths to save air), which builds up CO2, plus a too-tight mask strap, clenching your mouthpiece, or dehydration. Breathe slowly and continuously, loosen your mask, and drink more water before you dive. If the headaches are severe, come with confusion, numbness or unusual fatigue, or keep happening anyway, see a dive medicine doctor, because those can be signs of decompression illness.
Why do I need an AAD? Seems like a crutch. Old timers didn't use them.

Plenty of old timers didn't come home, and AADs have saved hundreds of lives since they became standard. It's not a crutch but a backup for when you're unconscious, disoriented, or simply lose track of altitude, which can happen to anyone. Most dropzones require one anyway, so keep it and keep it serviced.
is it ok to run off the edge or should i just step

Take one or two controlled steps and push out firmly so you clear the rock face, which often slopes outward below the lip. A full sprint on wet, slippery rock risks a fall at the worst possible moment. Before you go, look straight down to see what you need to clear.
Mom here, my daughter is crewing her first hot 100. What should I watch for?

Watch for confusion, slurred speech, stumbling, sudden irritability, stopping sweating or skin that feels hot and dry, since these can mean serious heat illness. Vomiting, swelling or very little urine are other red flags. Keep ice, cold fluids and salty food at every crew stop, and don't be afraid to get race medical involved early. Pulling her when something's wrong is a loving call, not a failure.
can I put bigger wheels on my street board so it rolls better over rough roads?

Yes, softer and slightly bigger wheels, around 54 to 56mm with a 78a to 87a durometer, will make a street board roll much more smoothly over rough ground. The catch is wheel bite: with larger wheels, the wheel can hit the deck during a sharp turn and stop it dead, which throws you. Add riser pads of about 1/8 inch, or tighten the trucks a little, to keep clearance. Test it with some hard carves at slow speed before you trust it at speed.
is it ok to have a couple beers between dives on a liveaboard

Save the beers for after your last dive of the day. Alcohol dehydrates you, slows your thinking and is linked to a higher risk of decompression sickness, and those are bad things to stack on top of repeat dives. Most good liveaboards have a 'once you drink, you're done diving' rule for exactly this reason. Enjoy the sunset beer once your gear is rinsed.
Is it okay to swim at night in the sea? Full moon, flat calm, pretty much ideal

It can be magical, but nobody can see you, boats and lifeguards included, and you'll struggle to judge distance or spot a hazard. If you're going to do it, stay in shallow water close to shore, wear a light or glow stick on your cap and buoy, and have someone on the beach watching. Leave longer swims for daylight.
Explain cutaways like I'm 5

If your main parachute opens badly and won't fly right, you pull one handle to release it completely and then a second handle to open your spare parachute, the reserve. Skydivers practice this over and over on the ground until it's automatic. You also decide by a certain height, so you're never stuck figuring it out too low.
friend dared me to do a cat leap across an alley between two buildings 3 floors up. i can do the distance on the ground easily. thoughts?

Don't do it. Being able to do the distance on the ground doesn't tell you how you'll perform under the fear, wind and wobbly grip of three floors up, and if you miss, the fall is likely to be fatal. Experienced traceurs train a jump at ground level for a long time before even considering height, and they often still decide against it. A dare isn't a reason to risk your life, so do a cooler line at ground level and film that instead.
What's the deal with slide gloves? Do I really need them?

Yes, if you're riding downhill at all you want them. Slide gloves have hard plastic or delrin pucks on the palms so you can put your hand down and slide to scrub speed or recover from a loss of traction, which is the core of most braking and turning techniques. Without them, one bail at speed can take the skin clean off your palms. They're cheap, so buy a pair before your first real hill session.
Is K2 harder than Everest?

Yes, by a large margin, since K2 is steeper, more technical, has worse weather and fewer fixed routes, and its fatality rate has historically been much higher than Everest's. Even with modern fixed ropes and oxygen, it demands very solid 8,000 meter experience and technical climbing skills. Most climbers do several big expeditions, including at least one 8,000 meter peak, before even considering it.
first time at a bike park next weekend, should i just rent a downhill bike or bring my trail hardtail?

Rent the downhill bike, or at least a full-suspension enduro rig, because a hardtail on lift-served trails will beat you up and make braking bumps far harder to control. Most parks rent a package with the bike, full-face helmet and pads, which is the smart move for a first visit anyway. Spend your first few laps on the green flow trails to learn how the bike behaves before you step up.
how long do skateboard bearings last

Decent bearings usually last anywhere from several months to a couple of years, depending on how much you skate and whether you ride through dirt and water. You'll know they're done when they feel gritty, sound grindy, or stop spinning freely even after a clean. Cleaning them with isopropyl alcohol and re-lubing every month or two stretches their life a lot. Replacing them is cheap, so don't push through badly seized ones that make your board stop suddenly.
I keep going over the bars on steep sections. what am I doing wrong

You're probably too far forward or grabbing the front brake hard. Drop your heels, push your hips back, and keep your arms loose and bent so the bike can move under you. Use both brakes smoothly and do most of your braking before steep sections. A coach can spot exactly what's happening in a run or two.
Western States heat this year looks brutal. Should I bail if it's over 100F?

Not necessarily, because people finish in that heat every year, but you have to race it as a heat race, slower and with relentless cooling. Use every stream, ice station and sponge, hold back through the canyons, and accept a slower goal time. Decide your stop criteria now, like confusion, no peeing for hours or vomiting you can't control, so you're not deciding with a cooked brain.
My 10 year old keeps jumping between playground equipment. Should I stop him or let him?

Let him move, because that kind of play builds coordination, strength and risk judgment, but you can steer it so it stays sensible. Encourage him to practice jumps at low heights first and land softly on the balls of his feet, and keep him off anything slick or wobbly. If he's hooked, many parkour gyms run kids' classes that channel the energy into proper technique and teach landing skills that reduce injuries.
honestly isnt it my life and my choice

It is your choice, and nobody can make it for you. It's worth weighing honestly, though: the downside is permanent, and it lands on the people who love you and whoever has to recover you. If you're set on climbing, give it the respect of years of roped mileage first, and make sure your reasons hold up once the initial excitement wears off.
My buddy says to just send the big gap jump and commit. I've never jumped more than a couple feet. Should I?

No. Gap jumps punish hesitation, and if you come up short the landing hits you instead of the other way around, so your first one shouldn't be a big one. Build up on tabletops, which let you roll out safely if you case them, until you can consistently land them at the right speed. Then try a small gap whose landing you've ridden first so you know the speed it needs. Following a confident rider in at matched speed helps a lot, but only once your skills are ready.
I'm 13 and I climb at the gym. I want to free solo the tree in my yard which is like 40 feet. is that ok

Forty feet is high enough for a fall to cause serious injury or worse, and tree branches can snap without warning, so please don't climb it without protection. Tell a parent you want more height and challenge. Ask about joining a youth climbing team or trying outdoor climbing with a coach and ropes. You'll get the same excitement and actually get to keep climbing for years.
Flying into Lukla next month for EBC. What's the actual rule for how fast I can gain altitude without getting sick?

The standard guideline is that once you're above about 3,000 meters, your sleeping altitude shouldn't rise more than 300 to 500 meters per night, with a rest day every three or four days or after every 1,000 meters gained. You can hike higher during the day as long as you come back down to sleep, which is why the classic EBC itineraries include acclimatization days in Namche and Dingboche. Resist the urge to skip those, because they're what makes the difference between enjoying Kala Patthar and turning around sick at Lobuche.
best way to get stronger fingers fast? thinking of hangboarding daily

Daily hangboarding is a fast way to get injured, not stronger, because finger tendons and pulleys adapt over months, not weeks. If you've been climbing consistently for at least a year, two short sessions a week of controlled hangs on a decent edge are plenty, and you should leave reps in the tank. If you're newer than that, just climbing a lot, especially on varied terrain, builds finger strength more safely. Patience here saves you a season on the sidelines.
How often do I need to repack my reserve?

The usual standard is every 6 to 12 months, depending on the manufacturer and your national association, and sooner if it gets wet, sandy or compressed for a long time. Many pilots do it at a repack clinic, where you can throw your reserve from a harness hanging under a simulator, which is great practice for the real thing. Write the date down and treat it as non-negotiable maintenance.
can i reuse an old harness i found at a garage sale? looks ok

Skip it, because with secondhand gear you don't know its age, how it was stored, its fall history or what chemicals it may have touched. Nylon weakens with UV exposure and age even when it looks fine, and harnesses usually have a lifespan of only several years to ten. A new harness doesn't cost much, and it's the one piece of gear holding you in the air, so buy one you know the history of.
I'm 67 and want to start sea swimming this summer. Any reason I shouldn't?

Lots of people start sea swimming in their sixties and love it, so there's no reason in principle why you shouldn't. Because cold water puts a sudden load on the heart, it's worth a quick check with your doctor first, especially if you have any heart or blood pressure issues. Start in summer with short dips in calm water, go in gradually, and swim with a group or a buddy. Local sea swimming groups are usually very welcoming to beginners.
impatient: whats the cheapest way to get into BASE fast

There isn't a safe fast track, because the time you spend skydiving is the part that keeps you alive. The cheapest route that still makes sense is to log your 200+ skydives efficiently, buy a used container from a reputable rigger when you're ready, and pay for one quality FJC instead of trying to learn for free. Cutting corners in BASE usually doesn't save money, it ends in an injury or worse.
Weight limit for tandem? I'm 240 lbs.

Most dropzones cap tandem students at around 220 to 230 lbs, and some charge a surcharge or require a specific instructor above 200. At 240 you may still find a dropzone that can take you, since a few go up to 250 or 260 with larger equipment. Call ahead and give your honest weight, because the limits exist for the gear's ratings and the safety of your landing, and fudging the number puts both you and your instructor at risk.
My dad is 58 and wants to take a freediving course on our holiday. He's fit but has high blood pressure. Should he?

He can probably do it, but he should see his doctor first, ideally one with dive medicine experience. Breath holding and the dive reflex put real strain on the heart and blood pressure. Some blood pressure medications can also change how his body responds underwater. If he gets cleared, a gentle intro course in calm water is a great way for him to try it. He should tell the instructor about his condition upfront.
can i practice precision jumps on wet rails

Avoid it, especially if you're still learning, because wet metal can be dangerously slippery and the usual result is a fall onto the rail. Use wet days for ground-based drills, conditioning or precision jumps on dry concrete lines or a rough, grippy surface instead. Even experienced traceurs test wet surfaces very carefully and use small, low-risk jumps. A slip on a rail can easily mean a broken shin or a nasty fall.
how long does someone survive buried in an avalanche

Survival chances fall off steeply after about 15 minutes, mostly from asphyxiation, so speed matters more than anything else. That's why companion rescue is what saves lives, since organized rescue teams almost never get there in time. Your group has to be able to find, probe and dig someone out within minutes, which takes the right gear and plenty of practice.
Pool won't let me practice breath-hold. Can I just do it quietly when lifeguards aren't looking?

Don't sneak it. Lifeguards often can't tell a breath-holder from a drowning swimmer, and a silent blackout is exactly what makes this dangerous. Look for a local freediving club or pool session run by instructors, which most cities have, where training is supervised. Do dry tables at home in the meantime.
How did Honnold prepare for El Cap specifically?

He spent about two years rehearsing Freerider on a rope, memorizing every hold and sequence, especially the crux Boulder Problem pitch. He had already soloed many hard routes and climbed El Cap on a rope dozens of times, and he kept detailed journals of each move. He even backed off a solo attempt partway in 2016 because it didn't feel right. That combination of years of preparation and a willingness to retreat is the part people usually overlook.
Can I ride motocross on public roads if I put a license plate on it?

Not just by adding a plate. A motocross bike needs to be properly registered and street-legal, which usually means lights, mirrors, a horn, DOT tires and a road-rated title. Some states allow dual-sport conversions, but the rules vary a lot, so check with your DMV first. Riding an unregistered MX bike on the road can get it impounded, and your insurance won't cover you if something happens.
ugh my hands got frozen and now they're burning and throbbing, normal?

That's usually the screaming barfies, the painful rush as blood returns to cold hands, and it's very common in ice climbing. It typically peaks for a minute or two and then fades. If your fingers stay numb, look white, waxy, or grayish, or blister later, that points to frostbite. Warm them gently and get medical attention rather than rubbing them or using direct heat.
my gf wants to jump but can't really swim. she'd wear a life jacket, that ok?

Not off a cliff. A life jacket hitting the water from height can ride up hard into the chin and neck and cause injuries, and if she can't swim she can't handle the exit or a surprise current. Let her build swimming confidence first, or go with a guided coasteering outfit that uses proper gear and jumps from low heights with instructors in the water.
There's a gap between two walls near my school about 2 meters apart and 1.5 meters high. Everyone says I can't make it. How do I train to prove them wrong?

Forget proving anyone wrong, because ego is the fastest way to get hurt in parkour, and a gap at height punishes a miss hard. Mark out the exact same distance on flat ground with chalk and practice until you can land it consistently, sticking the landing on a line twenty times in a row with room to spare. Then test it on low walls at the same distance before considering the real one, and only go for it if you would bet on landing it every time.
is it okay to have a couple drinks before to calm my nerves

Skip the drinks. Operators will refuse to let you jump if they think you've been drinking, and they're right to. Alcohol affects your blood pressure and your judgment, and it can make the head rush and nausea much worse. If you want to calm your nerves, eat a light meal, drink water and take some slow breaths on the platform instead.
I'm open water certified and found a cool cave entrance on vacation in Mexico. Can I just swim in a little way to look around?

Don't do it, even a little way. Untrained open water divers going a short distance into caves are the single biggest category of cave diving deaths, because silt-outs, disorientation and the lack of a direct path to the surface turn 'just a peek' into a trap within seconds. If you want to see the cenotes, book a guided cavern tour with a certified cavern guide, where you stay within sight of daylight and follow a fixed line.
I'm 58, decent shape, had a stent put in three years ago. Thinking about Aconcagua. Crazy?

It isn't automatically crazy, but Aconcagua at nearly 7,000 meters puts serious strain on the heart, so this has to start with a cardiologist, ideally one who knows altitude physiology. Ask for an exercise stress test and an honest talk about what reduced oxygen will do to your particular heart. If you get the green light, a lower objective like Kilimanjaro or a 6,000-meter peak in Bolivia first would show you how your body handles altitude before you commit to something that big and remote.
First time outdoors next month, going with friends who've climbed in the gym for a year. Anything I should know?

Gym experience doesn't automatically carry over outside, because setting up anchors, cleaning routes and judging rock quality are separate skills that gyms never teach. If nobody in the group has proper outdoor training, hire a guide for the first day or join a club trip so someone experienced checks the anchors and your systems. Everyone should wear a helmet, since loose rock and dropped gear are the big outdoor hazards. Pick well-traveled, easy crags so you're learning the systems instead of fighting the grade.
honest question: is ice climbing more dangerous than rock climbing?

In general it carries more risk, mostly because of the hazards you can't fully control. Ice can fracture, detach, or fall from above; screws vary in reliability depending on ice quality; leader falls are much more likely to cause injury; and cold, avalanche terrain, and short days add more problems. That said, much of that risk can be reduced through solid instruction, conservative route choices, and staying on toprope or well within your grade when you're learning. Plenty of people climb ice for decades safely because they treat conditions with respect.
what PSI for tires on hardpack

Start around 13 to 14 psi front and rear on hardpack, then adjust based on feel. Higher pressure helps guard against pinch flats and rim damage on rocky or square-edged hardpack. If the bike feels skatey with no grip, drop a pound at a time, but going much below 12 without a mousse or tire balls risks flats and dinged rims.
What's rope soloing and is it a good compromise?

Rope soloing means climbing alone while protected by a rope, either toprope soloing with a device like a Micro Traxion or lead rope soloing with a self-belay system. It's a solid compromise for climbers who want solitude and flow, though it still has real risks if the setup is wrong. Learn the systems from an experienced mentor or guide, use a backup device, and practice on terrain where mistakes are survivable. Many people find it's the solo experience they wanted in the first place.
Snowmobiling into backcountry skiing access, do I need the same avalanche gear?

Yes, the full kit: beacon, shovel, probe, and ideally an airbag, carried on your body and not strapped to the sled, since you can get separated from the machine. Sleds can get you into big avalanche terrain fast and highmarking puts heavy loads on slopes, so sledders are overrepresented in avalanche deaths. An avalanche course built for motorized users is worth it.
I'm 13, can I go cliff jumping
