You can try low jumps of a couple of meters if an adult who knows the spot is there with you, the depth is checked and you're a confident swimmer. Avoid big jumps until you've built up experience and your body has more strength to absorb impact. Many places run summer camps or guided sessions for kids your age, which is a great way to learn properly.
I'm 52, been surfing for 30 years, want to try my first real big-wave session. Too old?

Plenty of people surf big waves well into their 50s and 60s, and your water knowledge counts for a lot. Ask a doctor for a cardiac check before you start serious breath-hold work, since hold-downs put a heavy load on the heart. Then do a big-wave survival course and build up through progressively bigger days with a good crew, and age won't be your main limit.
is it ok to bomb my street at night, there's basically no traffic

I'd skip that, because at night drivers can't see you, you can't read the pavement, and "basically no traffic" is exactly when the one car shows up. A low rider at speed is nearly invisible, and gravel or cracks you'd normally avoid become crash triggers. If you want empty roads, look into local sessions or organized closed-road events, or ride in daylight with a spotter at blind corners. Lights and reflectors help, but they don't make a night hill bomb safe.
ok real talk how many solo climbers actually die

Nobody keeps an exact count, but the list of elite soloists who've died is long, including Dean Potter, Derek Hersey, John Bachar, Brad Gobright and many others, all highly experienced. That's the uncomfortable truth: at the top level, the activity has a strikingly high fatality rate over a career, because a single mistake or random event is fatal. Most longtime climbers would tell you skill lowers the odds but doesn't remove them.
Can I use a cheap fitness tracker to monitor my oxygen sat on a climb?

It can give you a rough trend, but wrist-based SpO2 readings get unreliable at altitude, especially with cold fingers and movement. A proper fingertip pulse oximeter is cheaper than you'd think and much more accurate. Even then, use it as one piece of information alongside how you actually feel, because a low number by itself doesn't diagnose altitude sickness.
I'm 42 and never skated but downhill looks amazing. Too old?

Definitely not too old, and plenty of riders start in their 30s and 40s. Start with a stable longboard on flat ground and gentle hills, learn foot braking and carving, then move on to slides before chasing speed. Wear full pads and a good helmet from day one, since you'll heal slower than a teenager, and look for a local longboard group or lesson to learn faster with fewer falls.
Doing my first desert ultra next spring (Marathon des Sables style). How long should I heat acclimate beforehand?

Aim for 10 to 14 days of heat exposure, since most of the adaptation (lower heart rate, earlier and more dilute sweating, expanded plasma volume) happens in that window. If you can't train somewhere hot, do 45 to 90 minute sessions in heat at home, like overdressed runs, an indoor trainer in a warm room, or sauna sessions right after easy runs. Time it so your last block ends within a week or so of the race, because the adaptations start fading after a couple of weeks without heat.
Avalanche gear for ice climbing? I thought that was only for skiing.

Many ice routes sit in gullies or under slopes that collect snow, and climbers get caught in avalanches more often than people realize. If your approach or route has any avalanche terrain above it, carry a transceiver, shovel and probe, check the local forecast, and know how to use them. An avalanche awareness course is well worth taking if you're going to climb beyond roadside crags.
Can I do a backflip off the platform on my first jump?

Save the tricks for later. Your first jump should be a simple, clean exit in the position the jump master tells you, so you get a feel for the fall and the rebound. Flips change how you load the cord and increase the chance of tangling or a jarring rebound. Most operators only allow styled jumps once you've done a few, and only if they offer them.
Ok real talk, how many ibuprofen can I take to get through a marathon on a sore knee

Don't use ibuprofen to push through a race. Taken during endurance events, it raises the risk of kidney injury, especially when you're dehydrated, and it masks the pain that's warning you the knee is getting worse. If the knee hurts enough that you need painkillers to run, have it looked at before the race, and consider deferring or switching to a shorter distance. Running a marathon on a masked injury is how a few weeks off turns into a season off.
There's a low-head dam on our local river that looks like it'd make a cool little drop to paddle. Thoughts?

Don't run it. Low-head dams are called drowning machines because the uniform backwash forms a recirculation that traps boats and swimmers, and even strong swimmers and rescuers die in them every year. They look deceptively mild, which is exactly why they're so dangerous, so portage well around it and give it a lot of room on the approach.
There's a flooded mine near my town that locals swim into. Thinking of diving it with a buddy this weekend, we're both rescue certified.

Please don't, at least not like this. Flooded mines combine every cave hazard with unstable ceilings, hanging debris, old cables, possible bad air pockets and often unknown layouts, and rescue certification doesn't cover overhead diving. If mine diving interests you, get cave-trained first, then look for organized, surveyed mine sites that are managed by experienced teams.
elbow tendinitis from climbing. physio said rest 4 weeks. any way around it

Rest doesn't have to mean doing nothing. Ask your physio whether you can do eccentric wrist exercises or isometric holds, since those are often part of tendon rehab anyway. Cardio, legs, core and antagonist push work are also usually fine. The thing to avoid is climbing through the pain, because tendons heal slowly and chronic elbow tendinopathy can drag on for many months if you rush. Four focused weeks is cheap compared to a lost year.
Is it okay to skydive while pregnant? Only 8 weeks.

No, dropzones won't take pregnant jumpers at any stage. The harness pressure, the opening shock and the risk of a hard landing are all real hazards to a pregnancy. Save the jump for after the baby is born and you've got your doctor's okay to return to activity.
do I actually need an inflatable vest or is that just for pros

If the waves are big enough that a long hold-down is possible, you want one, pro or not. An inflation vest can get you to the surface faster after a bad wipeout. But it isn't magic, and it can fail or get torn. Pair it with a proper safety course so you know when to pull it, and service the CO2 cartridges before every swell.
i just got my A license, can i jump at a different dz alone?

Yes, an A license lets you jump at any USPA dropzone, but expect a gear check and checkout briefing when you arrive. Ask about the landing area, the hazards and the traffic pattern, and consider doing a jump with a coach your first time there. New areas with unfamiliar winds and outs catch a lot of fresh A-license holders off guard.
Is deep water soloing a safer way to get the solo feeling?

Yes, deep water soloing is the best way to get that ropeless freedom with a much safer outcome when you fall. It still has real risks, so check the water depth at the actual tide, scout for submerged rocks, avoid falling from very high, and learn to land feet-first with your body tight. Go with experienced people at established venues like Mallorca or Thailand's Railay, and always have a swimmer or a boat nearby. It's a genuinely fun way to push moves without a rope.
I keep catching my edge landing 180s and slamming hard. it's getting kind of scary

That usually means you're landing short of rotation or on an edge instead of a flat base, so the downhill edge digs in. Commit to the full 180 by keeping your head and shoulders turning until you're facing the new direction, and aim to touch down flat with your weight centered. Drop back to a smaller feature or flat-ground spins for a bit to rebuild confidence, and take a day off if you're sore, because tired legs make edge catches much more likely.
I've done 40 cavern dives, I think I'm basically ready for cave without paying for another course honestly

Cavern experience is a good base, but it doesn't prepare you for the cave environment, and skipping the training is how experienced divers end up in accident reports. Cave courses drill lost-line, lost-buddy, zero-visibility and gas-sharing exits that you won't learn in the light zone. Your 40 dives will make the intro and full cave courses go smoothly, so take them, it's money well spent.
best place in the world to learn big wave surfing as a beginner?

There isn't really a beginner big-wave spot, but some places are a good stepping stone, like Waimea Bay on smaller days or spots in Portugal and Mexico with established crews and good safety culture. The best place to learn is wherever you can surf with experienced people who'll guide your progression and look out for you. Before traveling, master overhead to double-overhead surf at home first.
is it legal to skate on the sidewalk

It depends entirely on your city, since some ban sidewalk skating downtown or in business districts and others allow it everywhere. Check your local municipal code or just search your city name plus skateboard ordinance. Where it's allowed, yield to pedestrians, slow down around driveways, and step off in crowded spots.
quick one: how deep can open water certified divers go

The recommended limit for Open Water divers is 18 meters, or about 60 feet. To go to 30 meters, take the Advanced Open Water course, which includes a supervised deep dive. Beyond that you'll want Deep Diver training, since nitrogen narcosis and gas consumption really start to matter there.
can i do parkour with flat feet

Yes, lots of traceurs have flat feet and train without trouble. Strengthen the small muscles in your feet and ankles with barefoot balance work, towel scrunches and calf raises, and increase jumping volume gradually so your arches and shins have time to adapt. If you get persistent arch, shin or knee pain, a sports podiatrist can check whether support or a specific exercise program would help.
Weather says cumulonimbus possible this afternoon. Morning flight ok?

A short morning flight can be fine, but plan to be on the ground well before clouds start towering, which often happens by late morning on these days. Cu-nim can create massive gust fronts and cloud suck that can pull a paraglider up uncontrollably even miles away. Watch the sky constantly, and land the moment cumulus start growing tall and dark. If in doubt, skip the day.
What's a gun and why does everyone use them for big surf

A gun is a long, narrow, thick surfboard with a pointed nose and tail, built to paddle fast and get into big waves early. Big waves move fast, so you need that extra length and paddle speed to catch them before the lip throws, and the narrow shape holds a line at high speeds. It's the standard tool for paddling big surf, and riding a shortboard out there is asking for trouble.
what should my first ice climbing rack look like

For leading moderate single pitches, start with about 10 to 12 screws, mostly 13 and 16 cm with a couple of 19 or 22 cm for anchors and V-threads. Add a V-thread hooker, some cord for threads, a few alpine draws, a couple of locking carabiners, and screamers if you want extra peace of mind on thin ice. Buy quality screws with crank handles, since fast placement matters when you're pumped. If you're still learning, rack up on toprope or with a mentor's gear before spending hundreds.
best beginner wingsuit?

Start with a small, forgiving first flight suit like the Squirrel SPRITE or Phoenix-Fly Prodigy, or a similar entry model from TonySuits. Smaller wings give you an easier exit, simpler deployment and more room to make mistakes. Most first flight courses provide a suit, so fly a few before buying and ask your coach which size and model fits you.
what's a PCA and why would i use one

A PCA, or Pilot Chute Assist, is a static line from the exit point to your pilot chute that pulls your canopy out as you fall. It's used on very low objects and in first jump courses so you don't have to throw your pilot chute while you're still learning stable exits. It lets students build up to freefall delays safely, so trust your instructor's judgment on when to move off it.
What's the best way to train lung capacity on dry land?

Try CO2 and O2 apnea tables done dry while lying down, plus interval cardio like running or swimming to raise your tolerance under exertion. Breathing apps such as STAmina structure the tables well. Never do breath-hold work in water, a bath, or a pool alone, because shallow-water blackout gives no warning and kills strong swimmers every year.
Can I take ibuprofen during a hot 100 miler for my knees?

Skip it during the race. NSAIDs combined with dehydration and long hot efforts raise your risk of acute kidney injury, which does happen to ultrarunners. If you really need something, acetaminophen in normal doses is the safer choice mid-race. Better still, deal with the knee issue with a physio before race day.
Any problem swimming in a lake with blue-green algae warnings?

Yes, stay out. Blue-green algae can produce toxins that cause rashes, vomiting and in bad cases liver or nervous system damage, and swallowing even a little water is enough to make you ill. It's also very dangerous for dogs, so keep them away too. Wait until the warnings are lifted, or find another spot for now.
I just bought a 10 foot gun but have never surfed over 6 ft. Can I take it out at a big reef this weekend to learn?

Owning the board doesn't change the jump from 6 feet to a big reef, which is a much heavier and more dangerous wave. Take the gun out on overhead days at a forgiving point or beach break to get used to its paddle speed and turning before you think about the reef. Build up gradually through the sizes, and get some breath-hold training in along the way.
brakes feel spongy halfway down the mountain. keep going?

Stop somewhere safe and let them cool for at least ten minutes. Spongy brakes on a long descent usually mean overheated fluid, and they can fade further or fail at the worst moment. When you set off again, brake in firm, short bursts instead of dragging the brakes the whole way, which is what cooks them. If they still feel soft once cooled, walk the steep sections or take the easiest route down, and get them bled before your next ride. Don't risk a technical section on brakes you can't trust.
whats the fastest way to learn to grind a rail

The fastest way is starting low, so skip the big handrail and use a flat bar a foot or so off the ground until 50-50s feel boring. Wax it, come in at a slight angle with decent speed, ollie up so both trucks lock on, and keep your weight centered over the bar. Learn to bail by stepping off to the side early, and wear a helmet, because rail slams tend to throw you sideways or onto your hip and head.
I sprained my ankle 2 weeks ago, it's mostly better. Can I go back to jumping?

Mostly better isn't quite ready for impact, because ankles that are rushed back tend to get re-sprained and can become chronically unstable. Before jumping again, you should be able to walk, jog, hop on that leg, and balance on it without pain. Ease back in with low drops and balance work, and if it's still swollen or unstable, get a physio to check it out and give you a rehab plan.
How do I know when I'm ready for the medium park line?

A good benchmark is that you can land straight airs, grabs and 180s on the small jumps consistently, under control, without thinking too hard about it. You should also be able to judge your speed so you clear the knuckle every time. Watch a few riders on the medium line first, and if a coach or experienced friend can check your riding, their read is valuable.
My 12 year old son keeps jumping between the garage roof and the shed roof after watching YouTube. How worried should I be?

Pretty worried, honestly. Roof gaps are among the most common ways kids get seriously hurt doing parkour, because a missed takeoff on shingles or a gutter that gives way means falling headfirst onto concrete from height. Rather than just banning it, which often pushes it out of sight, find him a local parkour gym or a youth class with certified coaches, where he can do the same jumps over foam pits and learn proper progressions. Most kids who get real coaching quickly lose interest in the shed roof once they can see how much there is to learn on the ground.
Shoulder dislocated surfing last month, popped back in on its own. Feels ok now. Paddling out tomorrow, any tips?

The biggest tip is to get it assessed first if you haven't already. First-time dislocations in active people have a high recurrence rate, and the shoulder can feel fine while the capsule and labrum are still damaged. Paddling and duck diving put repeated overhead load on exactly that position, and a dislocation out in the water is genuinely dangerous. A physio can test its stability and give you a rotator cuff strengthening program, and many people do return to surfing within a few months. Until then, small mellow days close to shore are the most I'd risk.
what's the difference between parkour and freerunning

Parkour is about getting from point A to point B as efficiently as possible using vaults, jumps, and climbs, while freerunning adds acrobatic and expressive moves like flips and spins that aren't necessarily efficient. In practice the line is blurry, and most people train a mix of both. If you're new, it's worth focusing on parkour fundamentals first, since solid landings and body control make the flashy stuff far safer later. Flips in particular should be learned in a gym with mats before you take them outdoors.
I panicked a bit on my last dive and shot up from like 12m. Felt fine after. Do I need to worry?

You were lucky, but a rapid ascent from 12m can cause a lung overexpansion injury or decompression sickness, and symptoms sometimes show up hours later. Watch for chest pain, breathing trouble, confusion, numbness or joint pain over the next day, and call DAN or a doctor right away if any appear. Before diving again, do a refresher with an instructor focused on staying calm and controlling your ascent. Panic is very fixable with practice.
Cheapest way to get into diving? I don't want to spend a fortune on gear.

Start by renting everything except a mask, which you should buy and have fitted properly because a leaky mask ruins dives. Do your Open Water course somewhere affordable like Honduras, Egypt or Thailand, or do the theory online and the checkout dives locally. Buy a dive computer next, since it's the most personal piece of safety gear. Leave the regulator and BCD for later. Avoid buying used regulators unless they come with fresh service records.
im 35 and never skated. too old to learn downhill?

Not at all; plenty of people start downhill in their 30s and 40s, and adults often progress well because they're patient about fundamentals. Just accept that your body recovers slower, so invest in good pads, a full-face helmet and slide gloves from day one. Spend your first few weeks on flat ground and tiny hills learning stance, carving and foot braking before chasing speed.
What did Honnold do to prepare for El Cap?

He climbed Freerider many times on rope over about two years, rehearsing and memorizing every crux sequence, especially the Boulder Problem and the Enduro Corner. He also kept a detailed journal of the moves, trained finger strength obsessively, and backed off his first attempt when it didn't feel right. That depth of preparation is a big part of why his climb stands out, and it isn't a blueprint most climbers should follow toward soloing.
There's a quarry near me with crystal clear water. Signs say no swimming but tons of people do it. Worth it?

I'd give it a miss. Quarries are notoriously dangerous: the water gets brutally cold just below the surface, there are sheer underwater drop-offs and old machinery, and they usually have no easy way out and no lifeguards. They account for a lot of drownings every summer, often of strong young swimmers. Look for a managed open-water venue or lake nearby instead, where you get the same clear-water feel with safety cover.
Diving in a 2-knot current tomorrow, drift dive. Any tips? A bit nervous.

Drift dives are fun once you relax into them, so go with the current rather than fighting it. Stay close to your guide and buddy, descend promptly as a group, and carry a surface marker buoy and a whistle so the boat can find you. Keep your buoyancy neutral and your hands off the reef, and if you get separated, do your safety stop and surface with the SMB up.
honestly the swell is maxing and I'm getting impatient, how do I know when it's too big?

It's too big when waves are closing out across the whole bay, the channel is breaking, or the locals and experienced crew are staying on the beach. If you're unsure whether you could make it out, survive a set on the head, or get back in, it's too big for you. Sit this one out and watch from shore. There will be better days.
can I skateboard 2 weeks after an ACL reconstruction if I go easy

No, that's way too early. The graft is weak in the first months, and one awkward bail could rip it out and put you back in surgery. Most surgeons clear board sports somewhere around 6 to 12 months, after strength and stability testing. Follow your surgeon's and physical therapist's timeline, and use the rehab time to build leg strength.
We're doing a multi-pitch route. Any tips for anchors between pitches?

Use two well-placed screws in solid ice at least a body length apart. Equalize them and clip yourself in before you take your partner off belay. Set the anchor off to the side of the fall line so ice knocked off by the leader doesn't hit the belayer, and check the screws periodically on warm days, since they can melt out. If the ice is thin or rotten, find a better spot or go down rather than trusting a sketchy anchor.
Ran a hot 50 miler yesterday and today my legs are super swollen and my pee is dark brown. Just sore right?

Not necessarily. Brown urine and swelling after a hot ultra are classic signs of rhabdomyolysis, where damaged muscle floods the kidneys and can cause acute kidney injury. Go to an urgent care or the emergency department today and tell them you ran an ultra, because they'll want to check your CK levels and kidney function. Hold off on ibuprofen until you've been seen.
do you have to sign a waiver

Yes, basically every operator will make you sign a waiver and fill out a medical declaration. Read it properly and be honest about health conditions, because they use that information to keep you safe, not just to cover themselves. If you lie about something like a heart condition, you're the one who carries the risk.
Found a 150ft antenna near my town. Good first jump?

No. 150 feet is extremely low and leaves almost no margin for a slow opening, a line twist or an off-heading. Antennas also bring guy wires, which are a serious entanglement hazard, and they usually involve trespassing. Do your first jumps through a course at a big, legal bridge like Perrine in Idaho, where you get height and an experienced instructor next to you.
do i need to worry about jellyfish

Most stings are just painful rather than dangerous, but it's worth checking local advice, because some regions have species that can be serious. If you get stung, rinse with seawater rather than fresh water, carefully remove any tentacles, and soak the area in hot water if you can. Get medical help if you have trouble breathing, chest pain or a strong reaction spreading beyond the sting.
whats AFF

AFF stands for Accelerated Freefall, the most common way to learn to skydive solo. You jump from the start with your own parachute while one or two instructors hold onto you in freefall, then they gradually let you fly on your own over a series of levels. It typically takes seven or eight jumps to finish the levels, followed by more supervised jumps before you earn your A license.
I fell and scraped my leg pretty bad. Should I keep riding?

Stop and take care of the scrape first, since riding with a fresh wound risks infection and more pain. Clean it with water, cover it and watch for signs of infection like spreading redness, swelling or pus. If it's deep, keeps bleeding or has gravel stuck in it, get it looked at by a doctor before you skate again.
There's a ton of icicles hanging above the route. Climb anyway?

I'd steer clear, especially if it's warm or the sun is hitting them. Falling icicles and ice daggers are one of the leading causes of serious ice climbing injuries, and a big one can kill even through a helmet. Choose a route that isn't threatened from above, or come back on a colder, shadier day. If you're unsure, it's a good call to walk away.
my daughter (9) is obsessed with climbing everything. would parkour classes be good for her?

Probably, yes. Kids' parkour classes are great for channeling that energy into safe, controlled movement. A good kids' program teaches landing, balance and spatial awareness through games, and it helps kids learn where their limits are. Look for a gym with specific youth coaching and low ratios, and ask to watch a class first.
My friend wants to film me on a drone at a 15 foot reef break, I'm a strong 10 foot surfer. Worth it for the clip?

Don't pick your first 15 foot reef session based on getting a clip. A jump of that size on reef needs your full attention on wave selection and safety, not on performing for a camera. Get a few sessions in at that size first with experienced surfers around. Once you're comfortable, then bring out the drone.
is it ok to surf with a cracked rib if i go easy

Not really, because paddling loads your ribs on every single stroke and a wipeout or a board to the chest could displace the crack and injure your lung. Cracked ribs usually need about six weeks, and a doctor should confirm it's a simple fracture before you even think about the water. While you wait, walking and leg work will keep your fitness up without risking a much longer layoff.
Is it okay to freedive with a cold if I take a decongestant?

Better to skip it. Decongestants can wear off mid-session, which leads to reverse blocks on ascent where trapped air hurts or damages your ears and sinuses. Congestion also makes equalizing harder and more likely to cause barotrauma. Wait until you're fully clear, and you'll enjoy the dives far more anyway.
Quick question, can I freedive the day after scuba diving?

Freediving right after scuba carries some risk, because you still have residual nitrogen and the repeated ascents can add to your decompression stress. A common recommendation is to wait at least 24 hours after scuba before deep freediving, and longer after repetitive or deep scuba days. Check what your training agency recommends, and if you're unsure, use that day for a shallow, easy session or just rest.
rotor's slightly bent, rubs a bit. ride the park anyway?

A slight rub from a mildly bent rotor can usually be trued with a rotor tool or adjustable wrench, and it's worth doing before the ride. If the bend is significant, the rotor is cracked or bluish from heat, or the pads are badly worn, replace it rather than gamble on it. Brakes are the one thing you can't afford to have fail on a descent. Most park shops can sort it out quickly.
Is skitching behind a car as dangerous as people say

Yes, it's one of the most consistently deadly things you can do on a board. You're hidden from the driver, a pebble at that speed throws you under or behind traffic, and there's no way to stop safely if the car brakes. If you want that speed rush, learn downhill skating on a closed or quiet road with proper gear instead.
What are auto belays and rope solo setups? Are they safer than free soloing?

Yes, by a huge margin. An auto belay is a gym device that lowers you if you fall, and rope soloing outdoors uses a fixed rope with a self-locking device so you're protected without a partner. Rope soloing still needs careful setup, a backup device and good anchors, so learn it from a guide or experienced mentor before trying it.
My ears hurt at about 4 meters every time. I just push through it and it eventually stops. Ok?

Don't push through it. Pain that stops on its own can mean your eardrum has ruptured, and that can cause vertigo underwater, which is dangerous on a breath hold. Equalize early and often, starting right at the surface and every meter or so after that, and if it won't clear, come up a little and try again rather than forcing it. If it keeps happening, a freediving instructor can teach you the Frenzel technique, and it's worth seeing an ENT to make sure your ears are healthy.
lead climbing outside first time, gym lead certified. anything different?

Quite a bit. Outdoor bolts are spaced farther apart, ledges and slabs make some falls riskier, and clips can be awkward, so start on routes several grades below your gym max and choose well-traveled, well-bolted sport lines. Make sure your rope is long enough to lower off, tie a stopper knot in the end every time, and learn cleaning and lowering at the anchor before you need it, ideally from a mentor or guide on the ground. Wear a helmet, since rockfall and dropped gear happen outside in a way they don't in the gym.
dude im gonna jump the stairs at school, 7 stair, been skating 2 months, any tips

Two months in, a seven-stair is a big jump in risk, and that's where people snap ankles, break wrists or eat the bottom of the stairs head first. Work up from a curb to a three-stair and then a five, making sure you can ollie them consistently and roll away clean before going bigger. When you finally try the seven, wear a helmet and wrist guards and have a friend nearby, and check that the run-up and landing area is clear and smooth.
do i need a helmet on class II

Yes. Class II still has rocks just under the surface, and the most common time to hit your head is when you flip in shallow water. A properly fitted whitewater helmet is cheap insurance, and most outfitters and clubs require one anyway.
I'm 62 and want to try whitewater kayaking. Too old?

Not at all. Plenty of people take it up in their 60s and paddle for decades. Start with a beginner course, focus on technique over strength, and choose a forgiving, stable boat. If you have heart, shoulder or back issues, check in with your doctor first, since cold water and swims are a real physical stress.
I want to buy a used kayak online for whitewater. What should I check?

Look for cracks, deep gouges or thin spots on the hull, especially under the seat and at the ends, by holding the boat up to a light, and avoid boats with soft spots that flex too much. Check that the outfitting is intact, meaning the seat, bulkhead or foot braces, hip pads and grab handles, since those matter for both control and safety. Make sure the size fits your weight range, because a boat that's too small or too big will behave badly. If you can, bring an experienced paddler along to look it over and sit in it first.
can I skip the safety ski guys if I'm just paddling and not towing

On genuinely big days, jet ski safety is just as important for paddle surfers, because they're the ones who get you out of the impact zone after a bad wipeout or a two-wave hold-down. Plenty of serious paddle sessions have safety skis in the channel for exactly that reason. If you can't arrange one, team up with others who have, or keep the size where you can confidently self-rescue.
Is it ok to use my skydiving rig for BASE? Don't want to buy new gear yet.

No, a skydiving rig isn't built for BASE. BASE rigs have one large canopy designed for fast, on-heading openings at low airspeed, with a bigger pilot chute and a different deployment system. A skydiving setup can open too slowly or snivel at the speeds you'll be falling. Buy or rent proper BASE gear, ideally a rig your course instructors recommend for beginners.
Water's high after the storm and the run is supposed to be epic right now. Our group is mostly class II-III paddlers. Go or no go?

For a mostly class II-III group, high water after a storm usually means no go, or at least pick a lower, easier section. Flood flows push the difficulty up a class or more, bring in fresh strainers and wood, and make swims longer and rescues much harder. Check the gauge against the known safe range for that run, and if it's above it, save the epic day for when your group can actually handle it.
What's the deal with speedbar? Should beginners use it?

The speedbar is a foot stirrup that lowers the angle of attack, making the wing fly faster, which is useful for penetrating headwind or getting out of sink. The trade-off is that a wing on speedbar is more prone to collapses, and those collapses tend to be more dynamic. Beginners should learn to use it gradually in smooth air under instructor guidance, and should ease off it in turbulence. It's a skill to build, not something to fear or ignore.
Wingsuit pilot here, how do I avoid getting too tired on long flights?

Fatigue usually comes from tension, so practice relaxing your arms and keeping pressure on the wings without fighting the suit. A well-fitting suit and good core and shoulder conditioning help a lot, as does keeping jumps short while you build endurance. If you're fatigued, it affects deployment, so don't push yourself to fly long when you're tired.
my buddy says we can just dig a pit and if it looks fine we're good

Pits are useful, but a single pit is one data point from one spot, and snowpacks vary a lot even across one slope. A pit can look great while a weak layer lurks 50 meters away. Use pit results alongside the avalanche forecast, recent avalanche activity, cracking or whumpfing, and the weather. If the forecast says a persistent weak layer is in play, a reassuring pit shouldn't override that.
is wingsuiting worth it

For a lot of people, yes; it's one of the most rewarding ways to fly your body, with long freefalls and a real feeling of gliding. It requires serious commitment, including hundreds of skydives, money and continuous training. If you do it with patience and good coaching, open-sky wingsuiting can be a fantastic and reasonably safe hobby.
I had a retinal detachment repaired two years ago. Can I bungee?

Talk to your ophthalmologist before you book, because sudden deceleration and the rush of pressure to the head are exactly the kind of strain eye surgeons worry about after a detachment. Most operators list eye conditions on their medical declaration for that reason. If your specialist clears you in writing, you'll have a clear answer either way. A tandem swing or zipline could still give you the adrenaline with far less head-down force.
How do I clear a 70 foot double? I can do 40s fine.

The jump from 40 to 70 feet is bigger than it sounds, because the speed and commitment needed go way up and casing a 70 can end your season. Work up gradually on intermediate jumps in the 50s and low 60s, and get your speed reference by following a faster rider who clears it a few times. A session or two with a motocross coach is worth it at this stage, since they can spot body position and throttle habits that will bite you on bigger gaps. Never try it when the track is chopped up late in the day or when you're tired.
I'm 68 and in decent shape. Too old for a tandem?

Plenty of people jump tandem in their 70s, 80s and beyond, so age alone usually isn't the issue. What matters is whether you can lift your legs for landing and whether you have any heart, back, joint or osteoporosis problems. Check with your doctor, and tell the dropzone your age and health history when you book so they can match you with an experienced instructor.
How do I get better at holding my breath fast? Competition in 6 weeks

Six weeks is enough for real gains if you train smart: dry CO2 and O2 tables a few times a week, plus relaxation and breathing work. Most improvement comes from staying calm and efficient, not from forcing longer holds. Do all your wet training with a qualified buddy or coach. Don't try to set personal bests in training, and leave the max attempt for competition day with safety divers present.
Kinda worried. My friend top-roped me today and kept a lot of slack the whole time. Normal?

No, on top rope the belayer should keep the rope fairly snug, so a fall only drops you a short distance. Big loops of slack can let you swing into the wall or even hit the ground near the start. Tell your friend directly, or ask gym staff to watch them belay and give some coaching. If it continues, find a different belayer.
I'm 160kg and really want to bungee. Any place that'll take me?

Most sites cap out between 100 and 150 kg because cord systems are rated for specific weight ranges, so options will be limited. Some operators with heavier-rated cords or body harness systems may go higher, so call around and ask directly. If no place can take you, try a swing or a zipline in the meantime, since many of those have higher limits and give a similar rush.
I'm 55, any special advice for getting into downhill?

Start slow with coached sessions and easy trails, and wear good armor. Strength and mobility work off the bike, especially for legs and core, helps a lot with control and injury prevention. Recovery takes longer, so pace your days and take breaks. Plenty of riders your age ride bike parks regularly and love it.
how many ice screws do I need for a single pitch WI3

For a typical 30 to 40 meter WI3 pitch, a rack of 8 to 10 screws covers protection plus an anchor, though it depends on how often you place. Mostly bring 13 and 16 cm screws, add a couple of 19 or 22 cm ones for anchors in good thick ice, and carry a 10 cm stubby for thin spots. Save two solid screws for the anchor and keep your spacing tight down low, where a fall would put you on the ground or a ledge. If the ice is thin or chandeliered, bring extras, because you'll be placing more often and backing up dubious screws.
My girlfriend wants me to quit BASE after our baby is born. How do people deal with that?

It's a really common crossroads, and plenty of jumpers do scale back or stop when kids come along. It's worth sitting down together and talking honestly about the actual risk, what the sport means to you, and what she needs to feel okay. Some people quit, some move to the most conservative jumping possible, and some switch back to skydiving, which still offers flight with a reserve. Whatever you choose, make it a decision you make together, not one you hide.
keep swallowing water and panicking in open water but fine in pool. why??

That's really common, and it's usually the cold, the lack of visibility and having no wall to grab that throw off your breathing. Work on exhaling steadily underwater so you're ready to inhale cleanly, and breathe away from the waves by bilateral breathing. Start in shallow water near shore and rest on a float whenever you need to. A coached open-water session can help a lot with the confidence side.
My dad is 62 and signed up for a desert 100K this spring. He has high blood pressure meds. Should I be worried?

It's worth a conversation, not panic, because plenty of runners in their sixties finish hot ultras safely. Some blood pressure medications, especially diuretics and beta-blockers, affect fluid balance, sodium levels or heat tolerance, so he should talk to his doctor specifically about racing in heat. He might also ask for a sweat-rate and electrolyte plan built around his meds. Encourage him to run conservatively and treat dropping at an aid station as a smart option, not a failure.
First time surfing 12 foot waves tomorrow, nervous as hell. Any tips?

Nerves are normal and actually useful, so channel them into watching the lineup for at least 20 minutes before paddling out to spot sets, rip channels and where people get caught. Stay a little wide and deeper than you think at first, let a couple of sets pass, and commit fully when you do go, because hesitation on the takeoff causes most bad wipeouts. Paddle out with a friend who knows the spot, and if conditions feel beyond you, it's completely fine to just watch.
do I really need a spotter for downhill if I know the hill?

Yes, especially for blind corners or intersections, because a single unexpected car can be deadly no matter how well you know the hill. A spotter with a radio or clear hand signals can warn you about traffic you can't see. Even experienced riders use spotters on open roads.
I keep getting water up my nose and it hurts. How to stop that?

Breathe out slowly through your nose as you enter the water, or pinch your nose with one hand while keeping your elbow tight to your body. A nose clip is the easiest fix and lots of jumpers use them. Make sure your entry is vertical, because even a slight tilt forces water up your nose.
Im 67 and in decent shape, too old for a tandem?

Not at all, people well into their 80s and 90s do tandems regularly. The main concerns are bone density, back and neck problems, heart conditions and hip flexibility, since you need to lift your legs for landing. Get a quick check with your doctor, mention any joint issues to the dropzone when you book, and you'll very likely be good to go.
What injuries are common in cliff jumping?

The most common are bruising, back and neck strain, burst eardrums, and compression injuries to the spine from landing in a seated position. Higher jumps or bad entries can cause broken ankles, cracked ribs, concussions and lung contusions, and hitting the bottom or a rock causes the really serious spinal injuries. Good form, verified depth and sensible heights prevent the vast majority of these.
Quick question: two stroke or four stroke for a beginner

Four-strokes are usually the friendlier choice for beginners, since their smooth, predictable power and engine braking are easier to learn on. Two-strokes are lighter and cheaper to rebuild but have a sudden powerband that can catch new riders out. Either works, but a 250F is a solid all-round starter for most adults.
My PFD is from like 2005, still good?

Old PFDs lose buoyancy as the foam compresses, and the fabric and buckles can degrade from UV and wear. Check for fading, tears and stiff or flattened foam, and do a float test in calm water to see whether it still holds your head up comfortably. If it's questionable, replace it with a whitewater-specific vest, since it's the most important piece of gear you own.
Whats the easiest spin to learn first

A frontside 180 is the usual first spin because you can see where you're going the whole time. Practice it on flat ground first, then off a small roller: wind your shoulders slightly the opposite way, pop, let your shoulders lead the rotation and your board will follow. Land on a flat base with your knees soft and ride away switch, so get comfortable riding switch beforehand.
My 16 year old son wants to do Kilimanjaro with his school group. The 5 day Marangu route. Is that safe? I'm worried sick.

Your instinct is reasonable, because five days is the fastest common itinerary and has noticeably lower summit success and higher rates of altitude sickness than longer routes. A healthy 16-year-old can safely climb Kilimanjaro, but a 7 or 8 day route like the Lemosho or Machame with a climb-high-sleep-low profile is much safer. Ask the school or operator directly about their altitude protocols, whether guides carry pulse oximeters and oxygen, and how they handle turning a student around, and push for the extra days if you can.
just tell me quick, do I need to do anything to prepare

Eat a light meal a couple of hours before, drink water, and wear snug clothes and secure shoes or go with what the operator provides. Empty your pockets and remove glasses or loose jewelry. Be honest about your weight and any health conditions when they ask.
What should be in a high altitude med kit?

The core high-altitude drugs are acetazolamide, dexamethasone and nifedipine for AMS, HACE and HAPE, along with painkillers, antibiotics for gut and chest infections, rehydration salts, blister care and a pulse oximeter. Get the prescription items and the doses from a travel or wilderness medicine doctor, ideally someone who knows altitude. A wilderness first aid course before the trip is just as valuable as what's in the bag.
I'm 62 and want to start climbing. Too old?

Not at all; plenty of people start climbing in their sixties and keep climbing for decades, and it's great for strength, balance, and mental sharpness. Start on top rope or auto-belays at a gym, progress gradually, and give your tendons and joints extra recovery time between sessions. If you have any heart, joint, or bone health concerns, a quick check with your doctor beforehand is worthwhile, and an intro lesson will get you climbing with good technique from day one.
Back from a long break with tendon pain in the knee. Want to do a big skimo race. Too ambitious?

Probably, because patellar tendon pain plus a big jump in training load is a recipe for a flare-up. Build up gradually, use isometric holds like wall sits for pain relief, and progress to heavier strengthening under a physio's eye. Choose a shorter race this season and save the big one for when the tendon can tolerate full volume.
thinking about towing my 14 yr old into some 15 footers, hes ripping. yay or nay

Nay for now. Even if he's ripping, tow surfing 15-footers comes with speeds and hold-downs that demand more ocean experience and physical maturity than a 14-year-old usually has. Let him keep building on smaller big days with paddle surfing and safety training, and get him around experienced mentors. The tow stuff will still be there when he's truly ready.
Lower back tweaked deadlifting. BJJ tournament next week. Grind through?

A tweaked back in BJJ is risky, because you can't control the loads when someone's stacking you or cranking a guard pass. If the pain is improving, you can move freely, and you have no leg pain, numbness or tingling, you might be okay by next week, but test it with full-intensity rolling first. If you're still guarding the movement, sit this tournament out. Any shooting leg pain or numbness means see a doctor first, not compete.
best first BASE canopy for someone around 180 lbs?

Most beginners go with a 7-cell BASE canopy sized for a conservative wing loading, often around 230 to 260 square feet for your weight depending on the model. Popular choices include the Ace, Hybrid or Dolphin, but the right size depends on your gear, exit weight and the objects you'll jump. Ask your course instructors or the manufacturer to size it for you rather than guessing.
Can I climb Elbrus in winter alone? Looks like a walk-up on YouTube.

Winter turns Elbrus into a serious mountain, with temperatures often below minus 30, brutal wind and very short weather windows, and climbers die there every year, often when whiteouts hit on the broad, featureless upper slopes. Going alone means no one helps if you get lost or hurt, and rescue in winter can take a long time. If you really want winter, go with an experienced local guide and carry a GPS track, but summer is a far better first attempt.
Thinking about Mont Blanc as my first big mountain, I've done a bunch of hiking. Can I do it without a guide?

Mont Blanc's normal route crosses the Grand Couloir, a rockfall gully that has killed many climbers, and the upper glacier involves crevasses and exposed ridges. Hiking experience doesn't prepare you for crampon technique, ice-axe arrest or reading rockfall conditions. For a first attempt, hire an IFMGA guide, who will also make you do an acclimatization climb first, or spend a season building alpine skills on easier peaks. Lots of hikers die there every year thinking it's a walk-up.
Getting back on the bike after a bad crash with road rash and a sprained wrist. Mostly it's in my head though. Advice?

That's really common after a hard crash, and it's worth taking seriously. Make sure the wrist is genuinely healed and you can brake and grip confidently, then start on quiet roads or a trainer before rejoining group rides or descents. Rebuild your confidence in small steps, like familiar routes, easy pace and a riding buddy you trust. If you're still freezing up on descents after a few weeks, a skills coach or even a chat with a sports psychologist can help a lot.
What's the deal with tucking? Do I need to?

Tucking means crouching low with your arms back to cut wind resistance, and it makes you go noticeably faster. You don't need it until you can handle your current speed comfortably, because adding speed you can't control is how people end up crashing. Learn braking and sliding first, then use the tuck as a tool once you have control.
Going to Florida springs next month, just got full cave cert. Any tips for the first dives?

Congrats, and keep your first dives well inside your training: shorter penetrations, simple main-line routes and conservative gas plans while you get used to diving without an instructor. Florida springs often have strong outflow, so going in can be hard work while the trip out is fast, which makes gas consumption easy to misjudge. Dive with an experienced local buddy if you can, and build complexity slowly.
how long after scuba diving do i need to wait before skydiving

The common guideline is at least 24 hours after diving before you go to altitude, and longer if you did multiple dives or decompression dives. The lower pressure at jump altitude can cause nitrogen still dissolved in your body to form bubbles, which is decompression sickness. If your trip has both, schedule the skydive first or leave a full day of buffer after your last dive.
My 13 year old son keeps jumping between garage roofs with his friends after watching YouTube. I'm terrified. What do I do?

Banning it outright usually just pushes it out of sight, so the better move is to redirect the energy into a proper parkour class or gym, where he'll learn the same moves on padded equipment with coaches who teach progression and how to fall. Most cities have parkour academies or freerunning sessions at gymnastics clubs that take teens. Be honest with him that roofs are where the serious injuries happen, because fragile surfaces, gutters and gaps are easy to misjudge. Kids who train properly tend to get more cautious, not less, because they learn how much skill those YouTube clips actually take.
what durometer wheels for downhill grip

For grip-focused downhill, most riders use wheels in the 75a to 80a range, with wider contact patches and square lips for maximum hold. Harder wheels and rounded lips slide more easily, which suits freeride. Your weight, the road surface and the temperature all matter, so start in the middle and adjust.
Thinking about jumping at a cheap unregulated place abroad, way cheaper than home. Any red flags to watch for?

Watch for no reserve or AAD on the tandem rig, instructors who can't show valid tandem ratings, rushed briefings, and planes that look poorly maintained. Ask which certification body they follow, such as USPA, BPA, or APF equivalents, and check recent reviews and any incident history. If anything feels off, walk away, because the savings aren't worth it on gear where your life depends on the details.
whats the best wetsuit thickness for cold big wave spots like mavericks

At Mavericks, most people wear a 4/3 or 5/4 full suit with booties, and often a hood in the colder months. Water there can sit in the low 50s Fahrenheit. A good fit matters as much as thickness, because a loose suit flushes cold water during long hold-downs. Many surfers wear an inflation vest under or over the suit, so make sure your setup works together.
is it ok to go out after a couple of beers if the surf's pumping

No, alcohol and big surf don't mix. Even a couple of beers dulls reaction time and judgment, and it cuts your breath-hold and your ability to stay calm during a hold-down. Sit this session out or wait until you're fully sober. The swell will be there again.
i fell on my wrist trying a frontside 360 yesterday and it's still swollen. is it fine to ride today

Take today off and get it checked, especially if it's still swollen. Snowboard wrist injuries are often small fractures that feel like a sprain, and riding on one can make it much worse. Ice it, keep it elevated and see a doctor or the ski patrol clinic if the swelling hasn't gone down. When you go back, wrist guards are worth it.
I'm 7 months postpartum and want to do a hot 50K. Anything special?

Check with your doctor or a pelvic floor physio first, especially if you're breastfeeding, since that increases your fluid and calorie needs significantly in the heat. Build up gradually, as your heat tolerance and recovery may feel different than before. If you're nursing, plan extra fluid and calories and figure out pumping logistics. Be generous with yourself on pacing, because finishing comfortably is a real win here.
Feeling tingly in my arm and really tired about an hour after my second dive. Overthinking?

Treat that as possible decompression sickness and take it seriously now. Get on 100% oxygen if the boat or shop has it, lie down, drink water, and call the DAN emergency hotline or local emergency services to get evaluated near a hyperbaric chamber. Don't wait to see if it passes, because early treatment makes a big difference.
honestly how do people not freak out about what's underneath them in deep water

Lots of people do at first, and it's a completely normal fear. What helps most is gradual exposure. Swim parallel to the shore where you can stand up, then slowly move out deeper as you get comfortable. Focus on your stroke and your breathing rather than looking down, and swimming with a group helps a lot. The feeling usually fades with time.
Long story short I get massive nausea after mile 30 in the heat every time. Can't eat. What do I do?

Nausea in the heat usually means your gut isn't getting enough blood because you're overheating or pushing too hard, so the first fix is slowing down and cooling aggressively with ice. Switch to small, frequent bites of easy carbs, like gels, watered-down sports drink or broth, instead of big portions of solid food. Ginger chews help some runners. If it keeps happening even at slow paces, see a sports dietitian, who can help you train your gut over the next few months.
im 14 and want to freedive w friends at the lake this summer no adults lol how dangerous is it really

Honestly, it's one of the riskier things you could do at a lake. Blackouts happen without warning, even to good swimmers, and lake water is often too murky for friends to spot someone underwater. If you're into it, get a parent to help you sign up for a junior freediving course, where you'll learn real techniques and how to rescue a friend. Until then, keep breath-hold games out of the water entirely.
trekking to Annapurna Base Camp with my 12-year-old, too much?

ABC tops out around 4,130 m, and many fit kids handle it well on a slow itinerary. The main concern is that children may not describe their symptoms clearly, so watch for irritability, poor appetite, unusual tiredness or sleep problems, and be ready to descend early. Use a 10 to 12 day plan with a reputable guide, and stay flexible about cutting the trip short.
what's the best way to learn an ollie

Start stationary on grass or carpet so the board can't roll away while you learn the timing. Put your back foot on the tail, your front foot just behind the front bolts, then snap the tail down and slide your front foot up toward the nose to level the board out. Once you can pop and land cleanly standing still, try it while rolling slowly on smooth pavement. Expect it to take weeks, which is completely normal.
its 11pm, can I skate the empty road outside my house

It's risky because drivers aren't expecting a skater at night and you're hard to see. If you do go, stick to a quiet street, wear bright or reflective clothing, and put front and rear lights on yourself or your board. Better yet, find an empty lit parking lot or a lit skatepark. Keep your speed low, since small cracks and rocks are hard to spot in the dark.
I want to fly over the sea cliffs near my town. No one flies there. Any tips?

Unflown sites are unflown for a reason, so treat this as an expert-level question rather than an adventure. Coastal cliffs can have rotors, sea breeze shifts and no bailout landing zones, plus possible airspace or legal restrictions. Talk to your local club or a regional instructor about whether it's even feasible. Unless you're very experienced, stick to established sites with known landing areas.
Me and my friends wanna build a jump in the backcountry. Any tips?

Backcountry jumps are a lot of fun, but they come with avalanche risk and no ski patrol nearby. Make sure your group has avalanche training, beacons, shovels and probes, and check the local avalanche forecast before heading out. Pick a spot with a safe, clear landing and run-out away from trees and cliffs, and build the landing steep enough to absorb impact. Start small and test it before anyone tries anything big.
I'm open water certified but my buddy cancelled. Can I just solo dive off the beach, it's only 10 meters?

I'd skip it. Open water certification trains you to dive with a buddy, and at 10 meters an entanglement, a free-flowing regulator or running low on air is far more serious with nobody there to help. If you really want to explore solo diving, take a dedicated self-reliant course and carry redundant air. Today, ask the local dive shop whether they can pair you with a buddy or a guide.
What wheels for sliding vs grip?

For grip, go with softer wheels around 78a to 80a with sharp lips and a wider contact patch, which hold well through corners. For sliding, harder wheels around 80a to 86a with rounded lips break traction more predictably and smoothly. Many riders keep two sets and match them to the hill. Whatever you run, a predictable slide is safer than a wheel that grips unexpectedly and then suddenly lets go.
Can I teach myself wingsuiting from videos if I'm already an experienced skydiver?

Videos are great supplementary material, but your first flights should be with a certified wingsuit instructor. That's the norm, and many drop zones require it. The course covers things that videos can't check, like your exit position, how you release the arm wings before pulling and how you handle instability. It's one or two days and a few jumps, and it removes most of the beginner mistakes that actually hurt people.
Ok real talk, my group wants to keep climbing but one guy is acting kind of drunk and wobbly at camp 2. We're 300m from the summit push camp.

Stumbling and drunk-seeming behaviour at altitude points to HACE, swelling of the brain, which is a true emergency. He needs to go down now, with at least one or two strong people, and not be left alone or told to sleep it off. Give dexamethasone and oxygen if you carry them, and call for rescue support. The summit will still be there next season, and he may not be if you push on.
what's the difference between a slider up and slider down jump

With slider up, the slider stays on the lines to slow the opening. You use it for longer delays where you have more airspeed. Slider down, or slider off, gives a much faster opening for low jumps and short delays, at the cost of a harder snatch and a greater chance of line twists or line overs. Which one you need depends on object height and delay, and that decision is best learned with an instructor instead of guessed.
Flying into Lukla next month for EBC. I'm fit, runner, 3 marathons a year. Can I skip the acclimatization days to save time?

Skip them and you're gambling, because marathon fitness does almost nothing to protect you from altitude sickness, and fit people often get into trouble precisely because they feel strong and push too fast. Above 3,000 meters the standard rule is to raise your sleeping altitude no more than 300 to 500 meters a day, with a rest day every three or four days, which is why Namche and Dingboche have built-in stops. If time is the real constraint, shorten the trip by flying out of Lukla sooner rather than cutting days on the way up.
going to my first downhill race next month, what should i expect lol nervous

Expect a friendly crowd, lots of waiting around, practice runs and a mandatory rider meeting where they go over the course, hazards and flag signals. Bring full leathers or approved protective gear, a full-face helmet, spare wheels and slide pucks, and plenty of water. Take your practice runs slowly to learn the lines, and don't feel pressured to keep up with fast riders on day one.
Climbing partner keeps shrugging off my concerns about the avalanche forecast. He's way more experienced. Should I just trust him?

Experience counts, but so does your gut, and any safe team works on the principle that one person's no is enough to turn around. Lay out your concerns specifically by pointing to the forecast, recent snowfall or loading on the slope, and ask him to explain his reasoning. If you're still uneasy, it's completely legitimate to stay back, because avalanches don't care how experienced anyone is.
I keep hearing about weighing yourself mid-race. Why bother?

It's a quick check on whether your fluid intake is in the right range. Losing more than 2 to 3 percent of your body weight means you're getting dehydrated. Gaining weight during a long race is actually a red flag for overdrinking and hyponatremia. Know your starting weight and compare at aid stations, along with how you feel.
what's the deal with auto belays, are they safe?

Auto-belays are very safe when used correctly, and most accidents happen because someone forgot to clip in before climbing. Always check that the carabiner is locked onto your belay loop, and many gyms have a gate or mat system that reminds you. Treat clipping in like your partner check and confirm it every single time.
quick q: does bungee hurt

Not really, for most people. The bottom of the fall feels like a firm but smooth tug, then you bounce a few times, and the main discomfort is blood rushing to your head while you hang upside down. Some people get a bit of a headache or sore legs afterward, but that's usually it.
short question, do ice screws go in angled up or down

Place them roughly perpendicular to the ice surface, or angled very slightly downward from the hanger, which means pointing slightly upslope into the ice. Studies have shown that pulling force on screws placed that way is strong, while placements angled steeply up or down are weaker. More important than the exact angle is good-quality ice, so clear away rotten surface ice before you place.
Pulled my hamstring sprinting. How fast can I get back to kitesurfing?

That depends on the grade, but a mild strain usually needs two to three weeks and a moderate one six or more. Kitesurfing loads the hamstring hard during edging and when you get yanked, so you want full pain-free stretch and strength before you go. A physio can grade it and give you a progressive loading plan, which also cuts the high reinjury rate hamstrings are known for.
What's the deal with landing on the downside of a jump?

Landing on the downside spreads the impact and keeps the bike stable, so it's the safest way to land. Landing flat or casing puts a big shock through the bike and your body and can cause crashes. Aim for consistent speed and form so you land in the same spot each time. If you're unsure about a jump, roll it until you've built up the skills to clear it.
I'm 52, strong resort skier, never been in the backcountry. Where do I even start?

Start with an intro avalanche awareness session and then a full AIARE 1 or national-equivalent course, which pairs classroom work with field days on skins. After that, hire a certified mountain guide for your first few tours so you can watch how a pro reads terrain and makes decisions. Your resort skiing will carry you a long way, but backcountry snow and touring fitness take some adjusting, so plan on mellow terrain your first season.
how long does the freefall last on a tandem?

From the usual 10,000 to 14,000 feet you get about 35 to 60 seconds of freefall, depending on the exit altitude. After that the canopy ride lasts around four to seven minutes, which is when you can actually chat and take in the view. Some dropzones charge more for higher altitude, and if you can afford it, the extra freefall is usually worth it.
sprained my wrist skating 3 days ago, still swollen and hurts to grip stuff. just tape it and skate?

Don't skate on it yet. Swelling and grip pain three days out can mean a fracture, especially the scaphoid bone, which often looks like a sprain and heals badly if ignored. Get it checked by a doctor and probably x-rayed. If it does turn out to be a sprain, rest it until gripping is pain-free, then wear wrist guards when you return.
can I learn tricks if I have a weak knee from a previous injury?

You can, but talk to a physio or sports doctor before you start throwing jumps. They can tell you what your knee can handle and give you strengthening work for your quads, hamstrings, and hips, which helps a lot. Stick to ground tricks and small features at first, and consider a knee brace if they recommend one. Progressing slowly is much better than reinjuring it mid-season.
how much does weight matter

A lot. The cord is chosen or adjusted for your exact weight so you stop at the right point, which is why operators weigh you on the day instead of trusting the number you give them. Most sites have a minimum of around 35 to 45 kg and a maximum somewhere near 120 to 150 kg. Be honest and check the limits before booking so you don't get turned away at the top.
Is BASE jumping legal in the US?

It depends on the location. It's legal at some sites, like the Perrine Bridge in Twin Falls, Idaho, and on a lot of BLM land, but it's banned in national parks such as Yosemite and illegal on most private property without permission. Fines, confiscated gear and arrest are real possibilities, so check local regulations and talk to local jumpers before going anywhere.
Is it fine to ride in normal hiking boots? MX boots are like $400

Skip the hiking boots, because feet and ankles are some of the most commonly injured body parts in motocross, and hiking boots won't stop your ankle from twisting or your shin from getting crushed under a footpeg. You don't need $400 boots, though. Entry-level MX boots from brands like Alpinestars, Fox or Gaerne run around $150 to $200, and lightly used pairs are often much cheaper. Boots are one piece of gear worth buying before anything fancy.
My 17 year old son just told me he wants to surf Jaws next winter. He's a good surfer at our local beach break. Should I be terrified?

Your concern is reasonable, because the gap between a good beach-break surfer and someone ready for Jaws is years of progression, not one winter. A realistic path runs through bigger and bigger reef and point breaks, a water-safety certification, a tow-team or jet-ski support relationship, and time spent at outer reefs watching before ever paddling out. Talk with him about building toward it with a coach and a big-wave survival course, which shows you're taking his goal seriously and gives him the safest route to it.
can i freedive with a cracked rib

Don't. A cracked rib limits how fully you can breathe up and how well your chest copes with pressure at depth, and a displaced fragment can damage the lung, which is extremely dangerous underwater. Ribs usually take about six weeks to heal. Get cleared by a doctor before you go back to depth or do any packing or stretching work. Easy walking and dry breath-hold relaxation that doesn't hurt are fine meanwhile.
Just tell me the max depth for cave diving on air, I don't need a lecture.

Most training agencies set about 30 metres as the recommended limit for air because narcosis gets significantly worse beyond that, and in a cave that impairment can be deadly. Some divers go a bit deeper, but anything past around 30 to 40 metres should be done on trimix with the right training. In short, stay at 30 metres or shallower on air in caves.
I'm open water certified and found a cool cenote with a cave entrance. Can I just peek inside a few meters with a flashlight?

Don't go in, even a few meters, because the overhead environment is exactly where open water divers die, and most cave fatalities involve untrained divers who only meant to take a quick look. Silt kicks up instantly, visibility can drop to zero, and without a guideline you can lose the exit in seconds. Stay in the cavern zone where daylight is clearly visible with a certified cavern guide, or book a cavern course if the caves really call to you.
hill bombing tonight with no helmet, need tips to go faster

Please grab a helmet before anything else, because at hill bomb speeds a fall onto pavement without one can cause a serious brain injury in an instant, and that's not something good technique can undo. For speed control, learn to slide or carve before you bomb, pick a hill with a clear runout and no cross traffic, and have a friend spot the bottom for cars. Bigger, softer wheels and a lower, stable stance will help you stay planted, but only push your speed as far as you can confidently stop.
My 11 year old is begging to bungee on vacation. Is that ok?

Many reputable operators accept kids around 10 to 14 and up with parental consent, as long as they meet the minimum weight. Check that specific site's rules, and look for a well-established outfit rather than whichever stall is cheapest. Talk it through with your kid first so they know they can back out at the edge with zero shame, because a forced jump is no fun for anyone.
Booked a tandem in Nepal, operator seems cheap and has no reviews. Worth the risk?

Spend a bit more on an established, well-reviewed operator. In Pokhara there are many reputable companies with licensed pilots, good equipment and insurance, so cutting corners isn't necessary. Ask about the pilot's certification and the gear's condition, and check for reserves. The view's the same, but your safety margins are much better.
Solo touring tomorrow. Any tips?

Going solo means there is nobody to dig you out, so a burial is almost certainly fatal, and your margins have to be far wider than usual. Keep to low-angle terrain well away from any avalanche paths, leave a detailed plan and a return time with someone, and carry a satellite messenger or PLB. Ideally, find a partner, but if you're going alone, treat tomorrow as a mellow mileage day rather than a skiing objective.
I'm 52, climbed trad for 25 years, lead 5.10 comfortably. Thinking about soloing some 5.5 classics I know well. Thoughts?

With 25 years of trad and a big grade margin, you're in the profile of people who solo easy classics, but the risks that remain are the ones experience can't fully cancel out: a hold breaking, a wet patch, a bad day. Pick routes you've climbed many times recently, check conditions on the day, and set a firm rule to back off at the first sign of doubt or fatigue. Also be honest with yourself about age-related changes in grip endurance and recovery, and rerun the routes on rope this season before going ropeless. It's your call, but go in with a plan to retreat, not just a plan to top out.
Had a panic attack mid-lake last week. Scared to go back. What do I do?

That's really common and very fixable. Go back with a friend and swim close to the shore in water you could stand up in, and roll onto your back to float the moment you feel your breathing speed up. Practise breathing out slowly into the water, because panic usually comes from shallow, gasping breaths. Wearing a wetsuit and towing a buoy can make you feel much more secure. An open-water coaching session is worth it if the fear sticks around.
I bought a used rig online. Can I just pack the reserve myself to save money?

No. Reserves have to be packed by a certified rigger, and in the US that's an FAA requirement with a 180-day repack cycle. Before you jump that used rig at all, have a rigger fully inspect it, checking the harness, the container, the AAD service dates and the canopy condition. A rigger inspection costs far less than what you could lose with a hidden flaw in gear you didn't see built.
Feeling a little dizzy and breathless climbing stairs at our hotel in Cusco, normal?

Yes, that's completely normal at 3,400 meters, especially in your first day or two. Take things slow, drink water, skip alcohol on the first night, and give your body time to adjust. Watch for signs like a severe headache, vomiting, being breathless while resting, or confusion; if those show up, see a doctor, and Cusco has clinics that know altitude illness well.
Pretty sure I cracked a rib in a bike crash. Doc says nothing to do but wait. Can I keep training indoors?

Easy indoor training on a turbo or stationary bike is usually fine if breathing doesn't hurt too much, but keep the intensity low so you're not heaving air. Avoid anything with impact, twisting or a risk of falling for about six weeks while it heals. If you get breathlessness, chest pain that's getting worse, or you start coughing up blood, go straight to urgent care.
can two people ride on my dirt bike

Most dirt bikes are designed for one rider, with no passenger seat or pegs, so doubling up affects handling, braking and suspension and makes crashes more likely. The passenger also usually lacks proper gear and has nothing safe to hold onto. On a track it's generally banned, and on trails it's still a bad idea. If you want to ride together, get a second bike.
my chain keeps dropping on rough sections. annoying but whatever right?

It's more than annoying, because a dropped chain can jam or throw you off balance mid-section. Most DH bikes run a chain guide for exactly this reason, so check that yours is fitted and adjusted, and that your clutch derailleur is switched on. A worn or overly long chain can also cause drops. Any bike shop can sort it quickly.
I'm 58 and on blood pressure meds. Is a desert 100-miler a dumb idea?

It's not automatically dumb, but you need your doctor in on it before you commit. Some blood pressure meds, especially diuretics and beta blockers, change how you handle fluids, sodium and heat, and a 100 in the desert stresses all three hard. Ask specifically about dose adjustments for long hot efforts and get a stress test if you haven't had one recently. Plenty of runners your age finish these races, and they're the ones who planned around their meds rather than ignoring them.
back's sore after a heavy MTB crash yesterday. just take a few advil and ride?

If it's just muscular soreness, gentle movement is fine. But after a heavy crash, rule out anything worse first. See a doctor if there's pain right over the spine, numbness, tingling, weakness, or pain that's getting worse rather than better. If it's clearly muscular and eases as you move, an easy spin on smooth trails beats a gnarly descent. Save the full-speed riding for when you're not relying on painkillers to feel normal.
how do i know which slopes are wind loaded

Look at which way the wind has been blowing. Snow gets stripped from windward sides and deposited on lee slopes, especially just below ridges and on cross-loaded gully walls. Clues include cornices, pillowy or rounded snow shapes, firm hollow-sounding slabs, and shooting cracks. Wind slabs are often most reactive in the first day or two after loading, so avoid steep lee slopes during and right after windy storms.
ugh cave course is so expensive and takes forever. any way to speed it up or just learn from youtube

Videos are great for previewing skills, but they can't replace an instructor watching you handle a lights-out exit or an out-of-air drill underwater. Some people try to self-teach this sport, and it ends badly far too often. To save money, ask about package deals for cavern through full cave, and practice your buoyancy and kicks in open water beforehand so you need fewer extra training days.
quick: what does recent avalanche activity tell me?

Recent avalanches are the strongest evidence you can get that similar slopes are unstable right now. If you see fresh slides, assume that any slope with the same aspect and elevation could go too. Dial your terrain way back and stick to low-angle slopes.
What's the most common avalanche type that kills people?

The dry slab avalanche is the main killer, usually triggered by the victims themselves or someone in their group. A cohesive slab of snow breaks away over a weak layer, often in one piece, and can be hard to escape. Persistent slabs, which sit on buried weak layers for weeks, are especially dangerous because they're hard to predict. That's why forecasts and courses spend so much time on them.
Do cornices just randomly break?

They can break with little warning, especially during warming, storm loading or under a skier's weight, and they often fracture much farther back from the edge than you'd expect. Stay well back on the ridge, ideally on the windward side, and avoid traveling underneath large cornices on warm days. Cornice falls can also trigger slides on the slope below.
wanna try a bigger suit, been flying my beginner one for 30 jumps. ready?

Maybe, but number of jumps alone doesn't decide it; ask whether your exits, flying and deployments are consistently clean and controlled. Most coaches suggest 50 or more jumps on a beginner suit before stepping up, and ideally coaching on your flights. Get a coach to review video, then make a modest jump to an intermediate suit rather than a big advanced one.
My buddy wants to skip the deco stop on the way out because we'll be close to the exit. Fine?

No, skipping required decompression is a classic route to DCS, and being near the exit doesn't change your tissue loading. Plan your gas so you have enough to complete every stop comfortably, and dive within no-deco limits if you aren't trained for decompression. If your buddy is pushing this, talk it through before the dive, because team plans only work if everyone sticks to them.
Is a sauna suit a good idea for heat training runs?

Wearing one for a few easy, short sessions can mimic heat stress, but it's a blunt tool that traps heat with no escape, so overheating can sneak up on you. Keep it to easy efforts of 30 to 45 minutes, drink beforehand, have someone around or stay close to home, and stop at any dizziness or chills. Post-run sauna sessions or simply running in the hot part of the day are more controlled ways to get the same adaptation.
what's a good ice climbing grade progression for a beginner

Most people spend their first season top roping WI2 and WI3 until it feels steady, then try some WI4 on top rope. Leading usually begins on easy WI2 or WI3 with great gear and a guide or experienced mentor, after much more time top roping. Moving slowly is the norm here, because ice punishes rushed progression more than rock.
Why do wingsuit pilots fly patterns at dropzones?

Wingsuiters cover lots of horizontal distance, so dropzones assign flight patterns to keep them away from other jumpers and the plane's path. Typically wingsuiters exit last and fly a set pattern, often perpendicular to jump run or off to one side.
