Learn your dropzone's pattern and stick to it, because getting lost or flying into other groups' airspace is a real collision risk.
What do I do if my board starts sliding out of control on a corner?

Stay low and relaxed, and try to keep your weight over the board rather than panicking and standing up. If you're losing it, commit to a controlled slide or put your hands down to scrub speed. If it's truly gone, aim your bail toward the softest, clearest area. Most corner crashes come from entering too fast, so brake earlier than you think.
I'm pregnant (second trimester) and have been lake swimming for years. Can I keep going?

Many experienced swimmers carry on through pregnancy, but check with your midwife or doctor, since your situation is what matters most. Avoid very cold water, because cold shock and the strain it puts on your heart and blood pressure aren't ideal right now, and keep your swims shorter and gentler. Always swim with someone, stay close to the shore, and get out if you feel dizzy, overheated or unwell.
lake has blue-green algae warning but only on one side. can i swim the other side?

I wouldn't. Algal blooms drift with the wind and can spread across a lake within hours, and the toxins aren't always visible. Exposure can cause rashes, stomach illness and worse, and it's especially dangerous for dogs. Wait until the warning is lifted and find another spot in the meantime.
im scared of boxes. i fell on one last week and my ribs still hurt

If your ribs still hurt a week later, get them checked before you ride again, since a cracked rib can easily be made worse by another fall. Once you're cleared, start on the widest, flattest, lowest box in the park and just ride straight across it with a flat base, without trying any tricks. Most box slams come from being on an edge or leaning back, so stay centered and look at the end of the feature, not your feet. Confidence comes back fast when the first few runs are boring.
What's proximity flying and how do people get into it

Proximity flying means flying a wingsuit close to terrain like ridges and slopes, usually from BASE exits, and it's one of the highest-fatality activities in adventure sports. People who do it responsibly spend years building up: hundreds of skydives, hundreds of wingsuit skydives, extensive BASE experience and then flying lines with experienced mentors, starting with huge margins. If you're interested, the sensible first step is simply getting excellent at wingsuit skydiving and BASE separately.
Is it smart to bomb a really steep hill to learn how to go fast

No, steep hills are where you find out you can't stop, and the speed wobble that sends people flying usually shows up before they're ready for it. Learn to footbrake and carve to control speed on gentle slopes first, then step up the grade gradually as you get comfortable. If you want to go fast seriously, look into a longboard with proper downhill setup, a full-face helmet and slide gloves, and practice sliding to a stop before you ever point it down anything steep.
Tried a frontside boardslide and ended up slamming my ribs on the rail. Anything I should check?

Ouch, if you have sharp pain breathing deeply, coughing or twisting, or any shortness of breath, get checked out, because cracked ribs and occasionally lung injuries come from exactly that kind of slam. For the trick itself, the slam usually happens when you over-rotate or catch your edge, so start on a wide box and keep your weight centered over the feature. Take a few days off rails until the pain settles.
I'm 45 and want to learn park tricks. Too late?

Not too late at all; plenty of people start park riding in their forties. You'll want to progress more deliberately than a teenager since injuries heal slower, so focus on butters, small boxes and small jumps, and wear a helmet and possibly impact shorts. A park lesson or adult freestyle clinic can save you a lot of bad habits and falls. Ride when you're fresh rather than at the end of the day when your legs are tired.
What's a good way to practice landing without getting hurt?

Start low and focus on silent landings, from curb-height drops to start, landing on the balls of your feet, and letting your ankles, knees and hips absorb the impact together. The quieter the landing, the better you're absorbing the force. Practice rolls on grass or mats at the same time, so that once you start adding height, you have a way to dissipate impact that's beyond what your legs can handle alone.
Can I jump if I'm pregnant? Only about 8 weeks along

No. Every reputable operator excludes pregnant jumpers at any stage. The sudden deceleration and the jolt of the rebound pose a real risk to a pregnancy, even early on. Save this one for after the baby arrives, and it'll still be waiting for you.
I flipped yesterday and panicked so bad I couldn't get the spray skirt off. Shook me up. What do I do?

That's a really common experience, and it's good you're thinking it through instead of brushing it off. Go back to a pool or calm water with an instructor or a trusted buddy standing beside you and practice wet exits over and over until pulling the grab loop is automatic. Check that the loop is always outside the skirt and easy to grab, and that the skirt isn't too tight for you. Once the panic response fades, the confidence usually comes back fast.
can you hurt yourself from just 5 meters?

Yes. At 5 meters you hit the water at around 35 km/h, so a bad entry can still cause bruising, burst eardrums, back strain or worse. The bigger risk at that height is usually hitting the bottom or a hidden obstacle, especially in shallow water. Low jumps are a good place to learn, but they still need good form and a depth check.
I want to hitch a ride by holding onto a car on my longboard to get up the hill faster, chill?

Don't skitch. One pothole, crack or sudden brake from the driver will throw you under the car or into traffic, and that's how people get killed. To get up hills, push, walk, or work out shuttle runs with a friend driving you to the top in the car.
Is there a way to brake on a street luge besides your feet?

On a standard street luge, your feet are the brakes, so you'll want sturdy shoes with thick rubber soles or tire rubber glued on. Some riders practice gentle steering scrubs, but there's no mechanical brake on most sleds. That's exactly why luge should only be ridden where there's a long runout and a closed road, since you can't stop quickly.
is skitching behind a car fun or nah

Skip it, because holding onto a moving car is one of the few skate stunts that regularly kills people. The driver can brake or turn without warning, you have no control over the speed, and one pebble at that pace sends you under a wheel or into traffic. If you want speed, learn proper downhill on a longboard with full gear, which gives you the thrill while letting you control it.
Quick q: deep water soloing, is that a good stepping stone to real soloing?

Deep water soloing is its own great discipline, and you should do it for its own sake rather than as a stepping stone. It has real hazards, like hitting the water badly, shallow spots, tides and cold, so go with locals who know the venue and check depth before you go. It also teaches you nothing about the consequences of falling onto ground, so don't treat confidence gained over water as readiness for a ground-up solo.
Is it safe to let my 6yo ride a PW50 in the backyard?

A PW50 is a great starter bike for a 6-year-old, and the backyard can work if it's flat, open and free of obstacles like trees, fences, pools or roads. Set the throttle limiter screw so the speed is very low to start and supervise every ride. He still needs a proper helmet, goggles, gloves, boots and long sleeves and pants. Check your local noise and property rules too, because neighbors can complain.
is it ok to ride the bike park alone

It's generally fine on busy park days, since the trails get regular traffic and patrol. Still, stick to trails you know and ride within your comfort zone. Tell someone your plan, carry your phone, and save the park patrol number in it before your first run. Avoid the hardest or least-used trails when you're solo, because a crash there could mean a long wait for help. Riding with a friend is still the better option, especially late in the day when the trails thin out.
Should I wear spine protection for park riding?

If you're hitting jumps or rails regularly, a back protector is a smart call. Back and tailbone injuries are common from slams, and a light vest or pad is barely noticeable while riding. Pair it with impact shorts and wrist guards if you're still learning, and you'll recover from falls much faster.
can I take my dirt bike on the road to get to the trails, its like 2 miles

That depends on whether the bike is street legal where you live. A pure motocross bike with no lights, plates or registration almost always can't legally be ridden on public roads, even for a short distance. Riding it anyway can get you fined or the bike impounded, and you may not be insured if something happens. Some places let you dual-sport or plate certain bikes, so check your local DMV rules. Otherwise, a cheap hitch carrier or small trailer is the easy fix.
best cliff diving spots in the world

Well-known spots include Mostar Bridge in Bosnia, Rick's Café in Negril, Jamaica, La Quebrada in Acapulco, the Polignano a Mare cliffs in Italy, and Inis Mór in Ireland, which hosts the Red Bull Cliff Diving series. Places like Mostar and La Quebrada are performed by trained professional divers, so as a visitor stick to the lower ledges or join a supervised session. Always ask locals about tides and depth, because conditions change.
are there any certifications for free soloing

No, there's no certification, school, or guide service that teaches free soloing, which says a lot about how serious it is. The recognized path is building real climbing skills through gym instruction, lead climbing courses, and guided trad and multi-pitch days. Organizations like the AMGA in the US or national alpine clubs elsewhere offer courses that make you a far more competent climber. Any experienced soloing that happens grows out of years of that foundation.
Do you need a license for street luge racing?

You don't need a government license, but most organized races require you to register with the event or a sanctioning body and meet their gear and experience rules. Some may require proof of previous racing or a skills check. Check the rules for each event you want to enter.
is wingsuit flying just for adrenaline junkies?

Not really. A lot of wingsuit skydivers are drawn to the calm, precise side of it: navigation, flying formations with friends and the feeling of a long, smooth glide. Done from a plane with proper progression, it's a skill sport more than a thrill ride. The people who last tend to be the methodical ones who plan carefully.
I get anxious and hyperventilate whenever I start an open water swim. How do I get past it?

That's really common and very fixable, because it's usually triggered by the cold, the dark water or the feeling of having no wall nearby. Get in slowly, splash your face, and float or tread water for a minute while you breathe out long and slow through your mouth before you start swimming. Begin with a few easy strokes of breaststroke or gentle front crawl and build gradually. Regular swims with a supportive group, where you can stop and rest whenever you need to, will steadily take the edge off.
pulse ox says 78% at 4500m. bad?

At 4,500 meters, 78 percent can actually be normal for many people, especially in the first day or two, so the number alone isn't a crisis. What matters is how you feel and the trend: a reading that keeps dropping, or dips into the low 70s and below along with breathlessness at rest, headache or confusion, is a warning sign. Use the oximeter as a supporting tool, trust symptoms more than the number, and descend if you feel sick no matter what it says.
how do I get over the fear of steep rollers. I freeze at the top every time

Start on a shorter, less steep roll-in and session it until it feels boring, then step up gradually. Look at where you want to go rather than the drop itself, get your weight back with heels down and arms slightly bent, and keep a light, steady feather on both brakes instead of grabbing. Walk the feature first so you know what's at the bottom. A skills coach can fix your body position in one session, which kills a lot of the fear fast.
ollie tips?

Shift your weight to your back foot so the nose lifts, then spring off the tail and pull both knees up to your chest. Think of loading the tail like a spring rather than just jumping, and keep your shoulders level so you don't rotate. Practice on flat ground or a gentle slope at slow speed until the pop feels snappy.
I'm 67, in decent shape but have a hip replacement. Can I still do a tandem?

Plenty of people in their 60s and 70s do tandems, but the hip replacement matters most on landing, since you'll need to lift your legs and possibly slide in. Get clearance from your orthopedic surgeon first, then tell the dropzone about the replacement so they can plan for a seated slide landing. Many dropzones ask for a signed medical form for older jumpers anyway, so having your doctor's okay in hand makes everything smoother.
beacon battery at 40%, fine for a day trip?

Check your beacon's manual, but most manufacturers recommend replacing batteries around 50 percent, and many recommend replacing them outright before a big trip. Cold weather drains batteries faster, and search mode uses more power than transmit. Fresh alkaline batteries are cheap, so swap them before you go. Avoid lithium unless your model specifically supports them, since some beacons misread their charge.
I'm diabetic (type 1). Can I do open water swimming safely?

Yes, plenty of people with type 1 swim in open water, but it takes planning, because cold water and hard exercise can drop your blood sugar fast. Talk to your diabetes team about adjusting insulin and carbs. Check your levels before you get in, carry fast-acting glucose in your buoy or with your kayaker, and always swim with someone who knows about your condition and knows how to help.
Should I learn on a longboard or a regular skateboard? I mostly want to cruise to class.

For cruising to class, a cruiser or small longboard is a great choice because the soft, big wheels handle cracks and rough pavement way better than a trick deck. A longboard is more stable at speed, while a smaller cruiser is easier to carry and weave around people on campus. Either way, learn to foot brake before you need it on a hill, and wear a helmet since you'll be around traffic.
I keep getting speed wobbles around 30mph and I almost ate it yesterday. what do i do

Wobbles usually come from tension or weight sitting too far back, so the first fix is to relax your knees and push more weight onto your front foot. On the setup side, tighter trucks, harder bushings or a lower-angle baseplate will make the board much more stable at speed. Until you've sorted it, stay below about 25 on that hill, because a full wobble at 30 can throw you hard.
My buddy says you have to commit 100% or you'll get hurt, so just send it on the 40 footer. True?

Commitment does matter, because hesitating mid-air is dangerous, but the real lesson is to only go big on features you're actually ready to commit to. A 40-foot jump done without working up through the smaller lines is where people break femurs and backs. Hit the small and medium jumps until you're landing them clean every time at the right speed, then step up gradually. Your buddy's advice works for jumps you've earned, not for skipping the ladder.
I'm 16, my parents won't let me do luge. how do i get them to say yes

Show them you're taking it seriously. Put together a plan that includes proper gear like a full-face helmet, leathers and gloves, starting on gentle closed slopes, and joining a local gravity sports club or beginner event. Offer to have them come watch or meet experienced riders. Parents usually relax once they see structure and responsibility rather than a random hill and a homemade sled.
precision jump tips? keep overshooting the rail

Overshooting usually means you're throwing too much horizontal power and not enough height, so aim to arc up and drop onto the rail rather than drive across it. Land on the balls of your feet with your knees deeply bent, and let your hips sink back to absorb the momentum. Practice the exact distance on a painted line on the ground until you can stick it ten times in a row, then move to a low curb, and only then to the rail. Sticking a precision is mostly about controlling where your weight ends up, so film yourself to check whether you're leaning forward at takeoff.
ok honest question. how bad is it if i skip the helmet on a top rope day

Bad, and top rope days are actually some of the worst for this, because whoever's climbing above you is constantly knocking down ice chunks and dinner plates onto the base. Falling ice is the most common way people get hurt at the crag, and it hits belayers just as often as climbers. Wear the helmet the whole time, including while belaying and hanging out at the bottom.
Is it dumb to jump hungover? Booked for tomorrow morning lol

Yes, and most dropzones will turn you away if they think you're still impaired. A hangover dulls your reactions, makes the altitude and canopy ride much more nauseating, and leaves you dehydrated. If you're feeling rough tomorrow, call and reschedule, because it costs you nothing and you'll actually enjoy the jump.
dude can I hit the big gap at the bottom without scouting it? my buddy says it's fine

Scout it first, every time. Gaps can have rutted takeoffs, washed landings, or need a specific speed you can't judge from your buddy's word. Watch a few riders hit it, walk the lip and landing, and only go when you know the speed. Five minutes of looking beats a season of healing.
Can I fly with a hangover? Just a gentle sledge run, nothing crazy.

Skip it today. Even a sledge run needs a clean launch, good reactions and sound judgment, and a hangover dulls all three while dehydration makes you tire faster. Most launch accidents happen in those first few seconds. Rest up and fly tomorrow.
how many liters of water per day up high

Aim for roughly 4 to 5 litres a day above about 4,000 m, because you lose a surprising amount through heavy breathing in dry air. Clear, pale urine is a better gauge than counting litres. At camp, melting snow takes a lot of time and fuel, so budget for both, and drink warm fluids, which are easier to keep going in the cold.
Is it actually dangerous to dive alone if I'm experienced?

Yes, it is, because the problems that kill experienced divers are the ones you can't fix alone: entanglement, an out-of-air emergency, or a medical event like a cardiac issue at depth. Solo diving is a specialty that calls for dedicated training and fully redundant gear, including a backup air source like a pony bottle. Without both, dive with a buddy, even if they're less experienced than you.
Hot ultra in 3 weeks and I haven't done any heat prep. Too late?

Not too late; three weeks is actually plenty. Start now with daily heat exposure, either running in the hottest part of the day at an easy effort or doing sauna or hot-bath sessions after runs, and you'll get most of the benefit in 10 to 14 days. Taper the volume as race day approaches but keep some heat exposure going so you don't lose it.
im 58 and kinda scared of heights, is paragliding even an option for me or am i kidding myself

You're not kidding yourself. Plenty of people start in their fifties and sixties, and many with a fear of heights find flying feels nothing like standing on a ledge, because there's no edge to look over. Start with a tandem flight with a licensed pilot to see how your body and nerves respond. If you love it, a school can start you on gentle training slopes where you're only a few metres off the ground. It's worth a quick check with your doctor about your knees and back, since landings and ground handling can be physical.
Is it true wingsuit BASE has a really high death rate?

Yes, it's one of the riskiest recreational activities measured, with some studies putting the per-jump fatality risk far higher than skydiving. Many experienced jumpers die from small misjudgments in terrain flying, not beginner mistakes. If you're drawn to it, approach it with long, structured progression, and recognize that many skilled pilots choose to stay in skydiving for that reason.
what should i wear for a tandem jump

Wear comfortable, fitted clothes suited to the weather, like athletic pants or leggings and a t-shirt or light long sleeve, since it's colder at altitude. Sneakers with laces are best, so leave sandals, boots with hooks and loose jewelry at home. The dropzone will provide a jumpsuit, goggles and harness.
just tell me how to run a reel, i'll figure out the rest myself

Reel technique really can't be self-taught safely, because the details that keep you alive, like tie-offs, placements, line tension and avoiding line traps, come from supervised practice with someone correcting you. A bad placement can leave you stuck in a restriction or lost following the line by touch in zero vis. Many instructors run land drills and open water reel sessions as part of cavern training, and that's the right way to learn it.
do i really need to check my gear every single jump? feels excessive

Yes, every single time. With no reserve, one worn line, a misrouted bridle, or a pilot chute that's not properly stowed can be fatal, and you only get to miss it once. A proper gear check takes a couple of minutes and is the cheapest insurance in the sport. Do it yourself and get a buddy to check you too.
what happens if the pilot chute gets wrapped around my leg?

A pilot chute in tow or tangled around a limb is a serious emergency, and in BASE you have almost no time to fix it with no reserve. You prevent it through a stable body position at pull, a clean throw away from your body, and a gear setup checked before every jump. Have your instructor teach you the right body position and throw, then rehearse it until it's automatic.
Best way to recover my boat after a swim?

Your safety comes first, so swim to shore or an eddy before worrying about your kayak, and let it go if it's dragging you toward hazards. If conditions are mellow, push the boat ahead of you toward an eddy while kicking. Your group can also bump it in with their kayaks, which is far faster and safer than chasing it down.
Is it okay to practice spins on icy days?

I'd save spins for softer days. Ice makes your edges catch or wash out on takeoff and landing, and falling on ice hurts a lot more than falling on groomed snow. On icy days work on butters, presses and clean riding instead, or call it early. Spring slush and fresh corduroy are much better for learning rotations.
What river grade is good for a first trip with an outfitter?

Start with class I-II on a guided trip or lesson. That level gives you moving water, small waves and eddies to practice on without serious consequences if you swim. Many outfitters run beginner courses on these sections, and once you're comfortable you can step up to easier class III with guidance.
My kid (12) watched Free Solo and now climbs trees with no hands near the top. How do I handle this?

Take this seriously, because a tree fall can easily cause serious injury, but approach it as a sign he's excited rather than a reason to forbid climbing altogether. Get him into a kids' climbing program or a youth team at a local gym, where he can climb hard with ropes and coaching. Set a clear rule that tree climbing stays low and always uses both hands. Kids usually take to the structure once they see how much fun real climbing is.
best way to stop on a skateboard? I keep just jumping off lol

Jumping off is actually a legit bailout, but you'll want a real stop too, and the foot brake is the easiest place to start. Keep your front foot pointed forward over the front bolts, then lower your back foot and drag the sole flat against the ground with gradually more pressure while keeping your weight on the front leg. Practice it at walking speed on smooth pavement until it feels automatic before you rely on it on anything with a slope.
im scared of going fast but my friends keep pushing me. what do i do

Ride at your own pace, seriously. Fear is your body telling you that your skills aren't there yet, and riders who push past that tend to get hurt. Work on braking and slides on smaller hills, and speed will feel comfortable on its own as your control improves. Good riding friends will respect that.
Is it ok to hit the park without a helmet if it's just small jumps

Wear the helmet, because small jumps are exactly where people get casual and catch an edge on takeoff or land on hardpack. Most park head injuries happen at low speed from backslaps or edge catches, not from huge airs. A modern helmet is light and well vented, so there's really no downside.
how do i know if conditions are safe enough to swim today

Check the water temperature, the wind (offshore wind can push you out), the tide times, the swell forecast and any local water quality alerts before you go. Once you're there, watch the water for a few minutes for rips, waves and boat traffic, and ask lifeguards or locals if they're around. If anything makes you hesitate, take that as your answer and swim another day.
is chalk bad to breathe in at the gym? i do like 4 sessions a week

Magnesium carbonate isn't considered toxic, but airborne dust in a poorly ventilated gym can irritate your airways over time, especially if you have asthma. Liquid chalk or a chalk ball cuts down a lot of the dust, and climbing during quieter, less crowded hours helps too. If you notice a persistent cough or wheeze, mention your climbing habit to a doctor. For most people, four sessions a week is fine.
Do I need a knife on my PFD?

It's a good idea to carry a blunt-tip river knife on your PFD for cutting rope in emergencies, like when a throw rope or line gets wrapped around someone. Make sure it's securely mounted and easy to reach with either hand. Practice deploying it so you can use it quickly if needed.
I want to try a deep dive this weekend without my buddy since she's busy, just once. Ok?

Don't do it. Most freediving deaths happen to divers alone, and a blackout at depth or on ascent is fatal without someone to bring you up. Reschedule, or join a local club or dive center where you can be paired with a trained safety diver. Waiting a week is nothing compared with the risk.
There's a storm forecast for late afternoon but the morning looks perfect. I'll be landed by 1pm. Fine right?

Maybe, but be very careful. Storms can develop faster than forecast, and their gust fronts and cloud suck can reach far beyond the cloud itself, which is extremely dangerous under a paraglider. Plan to be on the ground well before the forecast window, watch for cumulus growing tall early, and land straight away if clouds start building. If the forecast says storms are possible from midday, skip the day.
What does a good dive buddy actually do?

A good buddy stays at the surface and watches you through your whole dive. For deeper dives they meet you partway up during the last 10 meters or so, and they keep their eyes on you for at least 30 seconds after you surface, since that's when blackouts usually happen. They should know how to bring an unconscious diver to the surface, protect the airway, and do a rescue, so you should both take a course together. Only one of you dives at a time, while the other watches.
is it ok to skate in the rain

It's best avoided. Wet pavement cuts your grip massively, painted lines and metal covers get slick as ice, and your stopping distance gets longer. Water also wrecks bearings and can make your deck delaminate. If you get caught out, ride slowly and carry the board over anything shiny, then dry your bearings afterward.
Is it fine to hit jumps on a powder day off-piste? Seems softer

Powder landings can be softer, but backcountry jumps come with hidden rocks, stumps and avalanche risk that aren't in the park. Only ride off-piste with a partner, an avalanche transceiver, a shovel and a probe, and the training to use them. If you want soft landings without those risks, look for natural features near the groomed runs inside the resort boundary.
elbow hurts on the inside after lots of climbing, how long to rest

Pain on the inside of the elbow is usually climber's elbow, a medial tendinopathy, and complete rest isn't the best fix. Cut back the climbing that provokes it and start progressive wrist flexor strengthening, often with slow eccentric work, ideally guided by a physio. Expect anywhere from several weeks to a few months, and stay below the pain threshold as you gradually return.
I froze on the exit last time and walked down. Am I a wimp?

Not at all. Walking down is one of the most respected decisions in BASE, and plenty of experienced jumpers do it regularly. Freezing is your brain telling you something isn't right, whether that's your mindset, the conditions or your readiness. Talk it through with your mentor, and come back when it feels clear rather than forced.
I ran a 50 miler in 95 degree heat last weekend and my pee was dark brown afterward. It's normal now. Was that a big deal?

Brown or cola-colored urine after an ultra can mean rhabdomyolysis, which can damage your kidneys, so yes, it was a big deal even though it cleared up. Get a doctor to check your kidney function and CK levels now, especially since you're presumably planning more races. Next time, if it happens during or after a race, seek medical care right away instead of waiting it out.
do bungee cords ever snap

Modern commercial cords almost never snap, because reputable operators track how many jumps each cord has done and retire them well before they wear out. The rare accidents tend to come from too-long cord calculations or attachment mistakes, not the cord itself failing. It's another reason to stick with established operators who keep proper logs.
My son crashed and says he's fine but he can't remember the lap before. Can he keep riding today?

No, memory loss after a crash is a classic concussion sign and he's done for the day, even if he insists he feels okay. Get him checked by a doctor today, and watch for headache, vomiting, confusion, or drowsiness, which mean go to the ER immediately. He shouldn't ride again until a doctor clears him, and his helmet should be replaced since it's taken a significant hit.
quick q - is it ok to hold my breath for a second to take a photo

Don't hold your breath on scuba, even briefly. If you drift up even a meter or so with your lungs full, the expanding air can injure your lungs. Take your shot during a slow exhale instead. Many underwater photographers learn to time their shutter to the breathing cycle, and it actually steadies the camera.
is it cheaper to learn base in europe?

It can be, and places like Norway, Switzerland, and Italy have strong BASE scenes with established courses and mentors, though travel costs often offset some savings. Pick a course by instructor reputation and safety record rather than price. Also check local rules, since access to some sites and landing areas is restricted.
Crashed and hit my head pretty hard yesterday. Helmet looks fine and I feel ok mostly just a bit foggy. Riding again Sunday

Feeling foggy a day after a hard hit is a classic concussion sign, so get checked by a doctor before Sunday, and go straight to urgent care if you have headaches, vomiting or confusion that get worse. A second impact before your brain has healed can be far more serious than the first, which is why return-to-ride protocols usually take at least a week or two of being symptom-free. Replace that helmet too. The impact liner compresses on a hard hit even when the shell looks perfect, so it won't protect you properly the next time.
I'm 52, slightly overweight, on blood pressure meds. Want to try freediving on holiday next month. Realistic?

Very possibly, but see your doctor before you go. Some blood pressure medications, beta blockers in particular, affect how your heart responds to breath-holding and cold water. Get a medical clearance, ideally from someone familiar with diving medicine, and book a beginner course with an instructor rather than trying it on your own. Plenty of people start in their fifties and do well, as long as they progress gently.
I weigh about 245 lbs. Am I too heavy for a tandem?

You might be right at the limit, so call the dropzone before you book. Most tandem weight limits fall between 220 and 250 pounds, and some charge an extra fee near the top end because heavier jumpers put more load on the gear and the instructor. Be completely honest about your weight, because the equipment is rated for specific loads and the limit exists for safety, not judgment.
My friend says hyperventilating before duck diving helps you stay under longer. True?

It does extend your hold, which is exactly why it's dangerous. Hyperventilating lowers CO2, which delays your urge to breathe while your oxygen keeps dropping, so you can black out without warning. Stick to slow, calm breathing before a hold.
how many days a week should i train as a beginner

Two or three sessions a week with rest days between is a great starting point, because your tendons and joints adapt more slowly than your muscles and need time to catch up. On off days, light mobility work or walking is fine. Bump it up gradually once landings feel easy and you aren't carrying soreness from one session into the next.
Do I really need a course or can I learn from YouTube?

YouTube is useful for theory, but get a proper course. The most important skills, like rescuing a blacked-out buddy, recognizing LMC and correct safety protocols, need hands-on practice with an instructor in the water. A two- or three-day entry course is affordable and teaches you the habits that keep people alive. Use videos to supplement it, not to replace it.
What should I do if my wing collapses?

For an asymmetric collapse, your first job is to stop the turn: look where you want to go, shift your weight to the open side, and apply enough brake on that side to hold your heading without stalling it. Most modern wings, especially EN-A and B, will reopen by themselves, and a firm pump on the collapsed side can help if it doesn't. If you're spinning, tangled or close to the ground, throw your reserve early. The best way to really learn this is an SIV course over water with a qualified instructor.
Badwater 135 is my goal in two years. How do I even start heat training for something like that?

Start by building a solid ultra base in normal conditions first, because heat adaptation is a layer on top of fitness, not a substitute for it. Then add structured heat exposure: 60 to 90 minutes of easy running or cycling in the heat, or post-run sauna sessions of 20 to 30 minutes, several times a week for about two weeks before key races. Do a few hot-weather 100Ks and at least one 100-miler before applying, and get a pre-season physical including an ECG, since Badwater stresses your heart and kidneys more than almost anything else you can sign up for.
I panic a little in low vis. Is cave diving a terrible idea for me?

Not necessarily, but it's something to work on before you go near a cave. Build comfort gradually with low-vis open water dives, mask-off drills and blackout line exercises in a pool, ideally with an instructor. Many cave instructors will be frank about whether you're ready and help you get there. If the anxiety doesn't fade with practice, the cavern zone can still be a rewarding place to stop.
Big storm last night. Wind loading on the leeward side. Want to ski it today.

Fresh wind-loaded leeward slopes right after a storm are classic setups for touchy slabs, and this is when human-triggered avalanches peak. Give it a day or two to settle and check the forecast, and in the meantime ski sheltered, low-angle terrain with no steep loaded slopes above you. The powder will still be good on safer terrain while the loaded stuff stabilizes.
My regulator free-flowed at 15m and I panicked. How do I stop this happening again?

Free-flows are scary but very manageable. You can breathe from a free-flowing regulator by holding it slightly out of your mouth and sipping the air. Practice that skill in a pool with an instructor until it feels routine. Make sure your regulator gets serviced on schedule, and if you dive in cold water, use an environmentally sealed reg rated for it, since cold is a common cause of free-flows. A refresher course will help rebuild your confidence too.
quick q, is a regular leash fine for big surf

No, get a big-wave leash, which is thicker, longer and built to handle the massive load of a heavy board in heavy water. A standard leash can snap and leave you swimming in the impact zone, which is a dangerous place to be stranded. Check it for nicks and wear before every session, because big waves find weak points fast.
Doing my first triathlon. Terrified of the mass swim start. Any tricks?

Start at the back or the outside edge of the pack, a few seconds after the gun, and you'll avoid most of the kicking and climbing. Practise sighting and breathing to both sides in open water before race day so you're not learning it in the chaos. If you panic, roll onto your back, breathe and wave to a kayak if you need to; the safety crew are there for exactly that and resting on a kayak usually won't disqualify you. Plenty of experienced triathletes still start at the back on purpose.
climbing w/ a tweaky A2 pulley. how bad is it to keep crimping

Pretty bad, honestly, because crimping loads the A2 pulley harder than almost any other grip, and a tweak is often a partial strain that can go to a full rupture under one hard move. Drop crimps entirely for now and stick to open-hand climbing well below your limit, as long as there's zero pain. If you felt a pop, see bruising, or have pain when you press on the base of the finger, see a hand specialist or a physio who knows climbers. Done properly, rehab usually takes a few weeks. Pushing through it can mean months.
how many big breaths before a dive to go longer? i heard hyperventilating helps

Skip the hyperventilating, because it's one of the most common causes of freediving blackouts. It blows off CO2, which is the signal that tells you to breathe, so your oxygen can run out before you feel any urge. Do a calm, relaxed breathe-up with slow exhales for a couple of minutes, then take one full final breath. Your dives will feel longer simply because you're relaxed.
Should I surf alone on big days if nobody else is out?

No, big surf with nobody out means nobody can help if you get knocked out, held down or lose your board in the impact zone. Even pros won't surf heavy waves without a partner or water safety on a ski. If no one's around, watch it from shore or go surf a smaller, safer spot that day.
quick q: how often should my reserve be repacked

Every six months is common practice, and many manufacturers say no more than twelve. Get it done by a qualified packer, ideally while you watch so you learn how it's done. Also do a repack after any significant wetting or a deployment.
my knees hurt when I land, is that normal

Some soreness after a new session is normal, but pain right as you land usually means your technique or volume needs adjusting. Make sure you're landing on the balls of your feet, with your knees tracking over your toes rather than caving in, and that you're absorbing through your hips as well as your knees. Cut back on drop height and the number of landings for a bit, and add squats and single-leg work to build strength. If the pain is sharp, causes swelling, or the knee feels unstable, see a physio before you keep training.
got stung by a jellyfish at the beach, what do i do

Get out of the water and rinse the area with seawater, not fresh water, which can make remaining stingers fire. Carefully remove any tentacles with tweezers or the edge of a card, then soak the area in hot water as hot as you can comfortably tolerate for about 20 minutes, which helps with most stings. If you have trouble breathing, chest pain, swelling of your face, or the sting covers a large area, get medical help right away.
I'm 64 and in decent shape. Too old to bungee?

Age alone usually isn't the dealbreaker. Plenty of people jump in their 60s, 70s and beyond, though many operators set an upper age limit or ask for a doctor's note over a certain age. What matters more is your heart, blood pressure, back, neck and bone density, since the rebound puts real force on all of them. Get a quick check-up and tell your doctor exactly what you're planning, and if you get the green light, go enjoy it.
Lost altitude awareness on my third wingsuit jump and pulled at 3,000. What went wrong?

Wingsuit flights feel long and the ground looks deceptively far, so it's easy to lose track without strong altimeter habits. Use an audible altimeter set with warnings above your pull altitude, glance at your visual altimeter on a schedule, and debrief this with your instructor. Low pulls are a warning sign, so treat it seriously and simplify your next flights until awareness is automatic.
What's the actual difference between HAPE and HACE? Trying to understand what to watch for in my climbing partner.

HAPE is fluid in the lungs. Watch for breathlessness at rest, a wet cough, gurgling breath, crushing fatigue and sometimes bluish lips. HACE is swelling of the brain. Watch for confusion, odd behavior, a severe headache and loss of coordination. The easiest field test is to have them walk heel-to-toe in a straight line, and if they can't, treat it as HACE. Both can kill within hours, and the treatment for both is to descend immediately, with oxygen, dexamethasone (for HACE) or nifedipine (for HAPE) as bridges to get down, not reasons to stay.
Is Bridge Day a good event for my first ever BASE jump?

Bridge Day can be a good first jump if you go through an organized first jump program there, since it's legal, high, and well supported. It's also crowded and the landing in the river means you'll want to be comfortable with water landings and a boat pickup. Make sure you meet the event's experience requirements and go with an instructor or mentor rather than showing up alone. Approach it as a training jump, not a party.
rip current. what do i actually do

Don't fight it by swimming straight back to shore, because that's how people exhaust themselves. Stay calm, float or tread water, and swim parallel to the beach until you're out of the pull, which is usually only a short distance. If you can't get out, float and raise an arm and shout so a lifeguard sees you. Better still, learn to spot rips before you go in: look for a darker, calmer channel with fewer breaking waves.
Thinking about bombing the big hill by my school tomorrow, never done a hill that steep but how hard can it be lol

Harder than it looks, and the gap between a mellow hill and a steep one is where most bad downhill injuries happen. If you can't do a controlled slide or reliably foot brake from your target speed, you'll hit the bottom faster than you can handle, and there's often traffic or an intersection there. Work up to it over a few weeks on intermediate hills first. When you're ready, ride it with a friend spotting the bottom and full pads on.
Do I need a wetsuit for cliff jumping?

In cold water it's a really good idea. It cuts the risk of cold shock and keeps you functional for the swim out, and a thin suit also cushions scrapes on rocks. In warm water, at least wear sturdy water shoes for the climb and the exit, since slipping on rocks is a common way to get hurt.
how long does it take to get full cave cert

The training itself often takes about a week or two of intensive diving across cavern, intro and full cave courses, but most good instructors want you to have plenty of experience between stages. Realistically, many divers spend months or more getting there, logging dives at each level before moving on. Rushing the process is one of the more common mistakes, so let your skills set the pace rather than the calendar.
Thunderstorms forecast for afternoon but we're planning a multipitch. Start early and risk it?

An early start is fine if you've set a firm turnaround time and the route has easy escape options, but on multipitch rock a thunderstorm is serious, with lightning, wet rock and slow rappels. Choose a shorter route or one where you can bail quickly, and turn back at the first build-up of clouds or thunder, without waiting to see if it passes. Getting caught high on the wall in a storm is a classic accident scenario.
I had a detached retina repaired two years ago. Can I still do a bungee jump?

This one needs your eye doctor's sign-off before you book, because the sudden deceleration and pressure spike from a bungee jump are a known risk for retinal problems. Most operators list prior eye surgery or retinal issues as a reason to get medical clearance or not jump at all. Ask your ophthalmologist directly, and if they're hesitant, a tandem paraglide or zipline can deliver a big thrill without the same jolt.
My brakes feel kinda spongy but I'm heading up the lift in 10 min. Ride it or not?

Don't take spongy brakes down a downhill trail. That usually means air in the hydraulic system or worn pads, and it can get worse fast as the brakes heat up on a long descent. Most bike parks have a shop at the base that can bleed them or swap pads quickly. Losing one lap beats losing your brakes halfway down.
Divers keep talking about the 5 rules of accident analysis, what are they

They come from Sheck Exley's analysis of cave diving fatalities: training, a continuous guideline to open water, proper gas management, staying within safe depths and carrying multiple lights. Most cave diving deaths involve breaking one or more of these rules, often by untrained divers. They're a great summary of why cave diving demands discipline and proper training.
Beginner here, is an online avalanche course enough?

Online courses are a great starting point for theory, but they can't stand in for field training. A proper AIARE 1 or similar course gets you out practicing companion rescue, snow observations and terrain choices with instructors who correct your mistakes. Do the online material first, then take an in-person course before you go into avalanche terrain.
how deep does the water need to be

A common rule of thumb is that the water should be at least as deep as the jump is high for lower jumps, and never less than about 3 to 4 meters even for small ones. For anything over about 10 meters, you want 5 meters or more of verified depth. Always check it yourself by swimming the landing zone or dropping a weighted line, because water levels change with tides, seasons and droughts.
Ran low on air last dive and panicked a little, shot up maybe 10m pretty fast. I feel fine now, 3 hours later. Should I worry?

It's good you're feeling okay, but watch yourself closely for the next 24 hours. Symptoms of decompression sickness can show up later, things like joint pain, tingling, numbness, unusual fatigue, a rash, dizziness or trouble breathing. If any of those appear, breathe oxygen if it's available and call DAN's emergency line or local emergency services right away. Don't dive or fly in the meantime, and work on checking your air more often so you head up with plenty in reserve.
avalanche gear for ice climbing? seems overkill

It's often not overkill, because many ice climbs sit in gullies or under slopes that slide. If the approach or the climb is in avalanche terrain, carry a beacon, shovel, and probe, and check the local avalanche forecast before you go. A lot of ice climbing accidents involve small slides knocking climbers off. Some roadside crags have no avalanche risk, so it really depends on the route, and an avalanche course is well worth taking if you climb in the mountains.
torn ACL, waiting on surgery in 2 months. can i still ski groomers carefully?

I wouldn't. An ACL-deficient knee can give way without warning on a ski turn, and the twisting load can tear your meniscus or damage cartilage, which makes the surgery and your long-term knee much worse. Use the two months for prehab like quad and hamstring strength, range of motion, and stationary biking. Your surgeon will tell you that the stronger you go into the operation, the faster you come out of it.
my 14 yo wants to jump off the 8m cliff all his mates do at the lake. im terrified. should i let him?

Your worry makes sense, because 8 meters is high enough to cause real injuries like compressed vertebrae or a ruptured eardrum from a bad landing, and peer pressure makes kids rush. A good middle ground is to go with him, check the water depth together, and have him build up from 3 to 5 meter jumps until he can consistently land feet-first, body straight and arms tight. If he can't do that cleanly at lower heights, 8 meters should wait.
my son keeps skitching (grabbing onto cars). how do I explain why it's a bad idea without sounding like a nag?

Keep it concrete: at car speed, a pebble or crack under his wheels throws him onto the road, and the driver may not even know he's there, so he could get run over by the car he's holding or the one behind it. Plenty of skaters have died this way, and it's the kind of mistake you only get to make once. It might land better if you offer something he actually wants, like rides to a good skatepark or a downhill session on a closed road with proper gear, so he still gets the speed rush.
How do I train my legs and lungs for big surf in the off season?

Mix interval cardio like hill sprints or rowing to mimic the bursts of paddling and recovery, plus leg strength work such as squats, lunges and jump training to handle drops and impacts. Add dry breath-hold tables at home, and do pool apnea only with a trained buddy watching you. Long paddle sessions and swims in the ocean on smaller days will tie it all together better than the gym alone.
My son just told me he wants to surf Jaws next winter. He's 22 and good but I'm terrified. What should I ask him?

Ask him who he'll be surfing with, whether he'll have a jet ski safety team, and what his training plan looks like for breath-hold, rescue and fitness. Serious big-wave surfers usually work up through other big breaks first and surf in tight-knit crews who watch out for each other. If his answers are specific and he's training with experienced people, that's a good sign. If it's mostly enthusiasm, encourage him to spend a season building up first.
What does 'sighting' mean and how do I practise it?

Sighting is lifting your eyes just above the surface every few strokes to check you're heading for your target, since there's no black line like in a pool. Lift your eyes forward just enough to look over the water, then turn to breathe to the side, so it blends into your stroke. Practise in the pool by looking up at an object at the end of the lane every six to eight strokes. In open water, pick a big landmark like a tall tree or building rather than a small buoy.
can i learn skateboarding from youtube or do i need lessons

Plenty of skaters learn the basics from YouTube, and channels with clear slow-motion breakdowns are genuinely helpful for things like pushing, ollies and stopping. What a lesson gives you is someone who spots your bad habits early, teaches you to fall safely, and gets you comfortable at the skatepark faster. If you're nervous or an adult beginner, one or two lessons followed by YouTube for the rest is a great combo. Either way, film yourself sometimes, since it shows you what you're actually doing.
Quick one: what's a safety stop and do I really need it on a shallow dive?

A safety stop is a pause of about three minutes at roughly 5 meters before you surface. It gives your body extra time to off-gas nitrogen and helps you control your final ascent. It's technically optional on very shallow dives, but it costs you almost nothing and lowers your decompression sickness risk, so make it a habit on every dive.
Is it worth buying a neck brace?

If you ride fast downhill or race, a neck brace like a Leatt is worth considering. Studies suggest it can reduce the risk of some neck injuries by limiting extreme head movement, though it isn't a guarantee. It needs to fit with your helmet and body armor to work properly, so try it on together before buying. For casual park laps, a good full face and body armor matter most first.
teach me how to scrub jumps

Scrubbing is an advanced technique where you lay the bike over on takeoff to stay lower and faster. Before trying it, you should be very comfortable clearing the jump normally at consistent speed. Start on a small, smooth tabletop and practice small amounts of lean while staying relaxed, building up gradually over many sessions. A coach can help with timing and body position and spot mistakes before they cause crashes.
my buddy says helmets are optional on easy rivers lol

Your buddy is wrong on this one, because most head injuries in kayaking happen when people flip in shallow, rocky water, and easy rivers tend to be shallow and rocky. A capsize in two feet of water over cobbles can do real damage. Wear the helmet every time and make sure it fits snugly, so it doesn't slide back when you're upside down.
how long should I wait between jumps

Wait long enough to fully catch your breath, swim out, and watch for anyone else in the landing zone, usually a few minutes. Stop when you're tired or cold, since sloppy form and slower reactions creep in late in the session. Make sure the previous jumper is clear of the zone before you go.
wrist hurts after a fall yesterday, swollen and it hurts to bend it. can I skate today if I tape it?

I'd skip skating today and get it checked, because swelling plus pain when bending after a fall can be a fracture, especially a scaphoid break, which is easy to miss and heals badly if ignored. Ice it, keep it elevated and see a doctor or urgent care for an X-ray. Taping it and skating risks another fall onto an already injured wrist, and a few days off now beats months in a cast later.
I blacked out briefly in the pool doing static apnea but my buddy pulled me up and I'm fine now. Can I keep training today?

No, call it a day. After a blackout, your body needs time to recover, and pushing again the same day raises the risk of another one. If you inhaled any water, watch for coughing, chest tightness or breathlessness over the next several hours, and see a doctor if any of that shows up, since water in the lungs can cause problems later. Next session, back your times off and talk through with your instructor or buddy what led up to it.
Quick q: I wear glasses. Problem?

Not a problem, because dropzones have goggles that fit over glasses. Tell them when you check in and they'll set you up with an over-the-glasses pair that stays put in freefall. If you have contacts, those also work well under regular goggles.
fastest way to learn a backflip on a board? dont want to waste a whole season

The fastest route that doesn't end your season is a trampoline or airbag facility. Plenty of resorts and freestyle centers have bag jumps where you can try flips on an actual board with a soft landing. Get the rotation dialed on a trampoline first so you know where you are in the air, then progress to the airbag. Trying it cold on a snow jump is how people land on their heads, and a neck injury costs you far more than one season.
my 9 yo wants to move from a PW50 to a 110 four stroke, is that too big a jump?

A 110 four-stroke is actually a very common next step from a PW50, as long as your kid can sit on it with the balls of both feet touching the ground and is ready to learn a clutch or semi-auto. Many 110s come with a throttle limiter screw, so set it low for the first few sessions and open it up as their control improves. Start in a big open field rather than a track, and make sure their helmet, boots and chest protector still fit, because kids outgrow gear fast.
How deep can I go after my level 1 course? I hit 16m in the course and want to try 25 next week

Jumping 9 meters in a week is a big leap. Progress in small steps of a few meters, and only once your current depth feels completely comfortable and your equalization is easy. Lung squeeze and blackout risk both climb when you rush depth. Work with a buddy or coach and set a sensible target, maybe 18 to 20 meters, before going deeper.
What's the deal with sleeping above 8000m?

Above roughly 8000 m, the so-called death zone, your body deteriorates faster than it can recover, even on oxygen. Sleep is short and broken, appetite disappears and judgment slips without you noticing. That's why climbers minimize their time up there, push for the summit from a high camp and get back down as quickly as possible.
Can I put a dropper post on my dh bike, everyone says no but why

You can, but there's little point because downhill bikes are lift-served and you keep your saddle low the whole time anyway. A dropper adds weight and another part that can fail in rough terrain. Just slam the saddle down and save the money for something like better tires or a suspension tune.
Lake jumping vs ocean jumping which is safer

Neither is automatically safer. Lakes can hide submerged logs and rocks and are often very cold below the surface, while oceans add swell, currents and harder exits. What matters most is known depth, a clear landing zone, calm conditions and an easy way out. A well-known, regularly used spot is safer than a random one either way.
i had 2 beers at lunch, jumps at 5. fine right?

I'd sit this one out. Alcohol slows your reaction time and decision making, which matters when you have seconds to deal with a malfunction or a tricky landing, and most dropzones forbid jumping after drinking. Do another load tomorrow with a clear head, because the sky will still be there.
pulled with my arm wings still zipped on my last jump lol, canopy opened fine

Glad it opened fine, but take it seriously. Pulling without de-arming, or with restricted arm movement, can make it much harder to deal with a malfunction or reach your handles. Make a firm pre-pull routine: wave off, de-arm, check your altitude, then reach. Practice it on the ground. Talk it through with an instructor so it doesn't become a pattern.
quick q: what's the easiest grade to start free soloing at

There isn't a safe starter grade, because a fall from 30 feet kills you whether the route was 5.4 or 5.12. Experienced climbers who solo usually stick to terrain many grades below their roped limit, on routes they know intimately, and they've spent years building that margin first. If you're new, put that energy into learning to lead and building real mileage on a rope. Bouldering is also a great option if what you're after is the feeling of climbing without gear.
Can I take ibuprofen during a hot ultra for my knee?

Better not. NSAIDs like ibuprofen during long, hot efforts raise your risk of acute kidney injury, especially combined with dehydration, and they may also make hyponatremia more likely. If you need pain relief on course, acetaminophen is a safer choice at normal doses. Get the knee looked at before the race rather than masking it.
I'm at 140 jumps and my buddy says he can teach me wingsuit on the side, no course needed. He's got like 500 wingsuit jumps. Good idea?

I'd pass on that, even though your buddy is clearly experienced. You're under the usual 200-jump minimum, and an informal setup skips the structured first flight course where a certified coach checks your gear, exit plan and emergency drills. Finish your jump count, then do a proper first flight course. Your buddy can be a great mentor once you're through it.
My kid's friend's parent offered to take them outdoor climbing. They're not certified. Should I let them?

Ask some specific questions first: how much outdoor experience the parent has, who will set up the anchors, and whether they'll climb top-rope only on a crag they know well. A long, solid track record of safe, competent climbing matters more than a certificate, but you should be comfortable with their anchor and belay skills. If you're unsure, suggest a guided day instead, or go along to see how they set things up.
quick q does it hurt to land flat

Yes, a lot, and from any real height it can do actual damage. Flat landings from around 8 meters and up can bruise organs, wind you badly, or knock you out. Keep your body vertical and narrow so you slice into the water.
luge question: can I build my own sled from plywood and old skate trucks

You can build a basic buttboard or practice luge that way, and plenty of riders started there, but keep it for low speeds on gentle, closed hills. Plywood flexes and cracks, and cheap trucks and bearings aren't built for luge loads, so things can fail exactly when you're going fastest. For real speed, use a proper aluminum or steel frame, solid luge trucks, quality wheels, and get it inspected by experienced riders before racing. Your sled is the only thing between you and the asphalt, so don't cut corners there.
what's samba

Samba is freediver slang for a loss of motor control, a stage short of a full blackout. It usually happens right after surfacing, when oxygen dips and the diver shakes, twitches or can't hold their head up. It's a clear sign you pushed too hard. Your buddy should support your airway and talk you through recovery breaths, and you should end your session for the day.
How much does it cost to get into paragliding? Like realistically.

Realistically, a full beginner course to your first rating runs roughly 1,500 to 3,000 USD depending on country and school. New gear (wing, harness, reserve, helmet) is typically another 4,000 to 6,000. Some pilots save by buying used, but only do that with an instructor's help, since wing age and line condition really matter for safety. Add travel, site fees and ongoing reserve repacks, and plan for it as an ongoing hobby rather than a one-time purchase.
Can I hit the double black today, I've been riding 2 weeks and feel unstoppable

Two weeks in is the classic window when confidence outruns skill, and double blacks are built for riders with years of experience. Spend the day perfecting the blues and reds you've already ridden, because smooth and fast there is real progress. Watch riders on the double black from the side to see what it actually demands.
front brake makes me nervous, can i just use the rear

You'll want to learn the front, because it does most of your stopping power and relying only on the rear means longer stops and sliding into corners. Practice in a flat, open area using one or two fingers and squeezing progressively rather than grabbing, braking hard in a straight line before you turn. Once you get used to it, you'll feel much more in control and confident.
can I wear just jeans and a hoodie

For slow cruising, sure, but on a real hill denim and cotton tear through in a second and you'll lose skin underneath. At minimum, add knee and elbow pads, slide gloves, and a full-face helmet, and consider hip pads or padded shorts. For serious speed or luge, leathers or a proper abrasion-resistant suit is the standard for a reason. Clothes are cheaper than skin grafts.
ankle or body harness, which is better

Ankle attachment gives you the classic swan dive and the most dramatic feel. A full-body harness spreads the force more evenly and is gentler if you have ankle, knee or back problems. Both are safe when they're fitted properly. Most good operators back up an ankle setup with a body harness anyway, and if they don't, that's worth asking about.
is cavern diving the same as cave diving?

Not quite. Cavern diving stays within the daylight zone, usually with a limited distance from the surface and no restrictions, while cave diving goes beyond natural light into the true overhead environment. Cavern training is a common first step and a great experience in itself, but it doesn't qualify you to go further into the cave.
Can I dive with a cold if I take decongestants?

Don't. Decongestants can wear off at depth, which can cause a reverse block on ascent where trapped air can't escape your sinuses or ears, and that's painful and potentially damaging. If you can't equalize easily without medication, sit the dive out. Missing a day of diving is much better than missing a whole trip with a burst eardrum.
River's running way above normal after the storm. Friends say high water is more fun. Thoughts?

High water after a storm is a different river. It's faster, colder, and full of new wood and debris, eddies disappear, and swims get long and dangerous. Unless everyone in the group has solid experience at that specific flow, wait a few days for it to drop and check the gauge against a guidebook's recommended range. Strainers from storm debris are the big killer here, so scout any blind corners.
My 14 year old wants to freedive with a speargun like his uncle. thoughts?

Start with freediving itself before adding the speargun. Spearfishing makes people push their dives longer and deeper while focusing on fish instead of their own condition, which is why it causes so many blackout deaths. A youth freediving course is a great first step, and many agencies take kids from around 12 to 14. If he spearfishes later, it should always be with an experienced, trained buddy watching him from the surface.
my kid wants a park board for christmas, should I get the stiffest one so it's more stable?

Go the other way. A softer, flexible board is much easier for kids to press, butter, and land with, and stiff boards are less forgiving when they make mistakes. Make sure it's sized properly for their height and weight, usually ending somewhere between chin and nose. A shop can help you pick the right length and flex.
what size board should i get im a size 11 shoe

For street and park skating with size 11 feet, an 8.25 to 8.5 inch deck is a solid range that gives you room for flip tricks without feeling clunky. If you mostly want to ride transition or cruise, going up to 8.5 or even 8.75 adds stability. Match your trucks to the deck width so the wheels sit roughly flush with the edges.
How do I know if the ice is thick enough to place a screw?

Tap with your tool and listen. Solid ice makes a dull, solid thunk, while hollow or detached ice sounds drummy. You want enough depth to fit most of the screw in good ice, and in thin ice you can use shorter screws or tie them off, knowing they're weaker. Learning to judge this reliably takes mentored time on lead, so get an experienced partner to check your placements early on.
honestly how much salt per hour lol everyone says something different

That's because it genuinely varies a lot from person to person. Most runners land somewhere between 300 and 800 mg of sodium per hour in heat, and heavy, salty sweaters sometimes need more. A sweat test, or just paying attention to white salt crust on your clothes and how you feel on long hot runs, will tell you where you fall. Dial it in during training, not on race day.
best exercises to strengthen for climb ups?

Pull-ups, explosive pull-ups, and dips are the core of it, because a climb up is essentially a pull transitioning into a push. Practice muscle-up negatives on a bar or wall, lowering slowly through the transition, which is where most people get stuck. Add straight-arm support holds and wall cat hangs to build grip and shoulder strength. Train these two or three times a week with rest days between, since elbows and shoulder tendons get angry if you jump up the volume too quickly.
what's a dinner plate in ice climbing

It's a big flat chunk of ice that breaks off when you swing a tool, usually because the surface layer is brittle in very cold temperatures. They can be quite heavy and come down on you or your belayer, which is one reason why helmets and belaying off to the side matter. Clean the brittle surface carefully before you commit to a placement.
quick q, can i swim out past the buoys at the beach, i'm a strong swimmer

Usually not a good idea. The swim buoys often mark where boats and jet skis are allowed to start operating, and drivers simply don't expect a head in the water out there. Being a strong swimmer doesn't make you visible. If you want to swim longer distances, look for a local open water group or a designated swim course where boats are kept away and someone is watching.
how long before a beginner should try the terrain park

Once you can link turns confidently on blue runs, stop when you need to and ride switch a little, you're ready for the small features. For most people that's somewhere between a few days and a season of riding. Start with small jumps and wide boxes, read the park etiquette signs, and wear a helmet.
What's the deal with the one up one down rule? My buddy and I usually just dive together to save time.

One up, one down means one of you dives while the other stays at the surface watching. The watcher then meets the diver partway up the final stretch, because that's where most blackouts happen. If you're both underwater at the same time, neither of you can see or rescue the other if something goes wrong. It costs you some dive time, but it's the single habit that keeps freedivers alive, so stick to it every dive.
Thinking of going straight from sea level to Leh and doing Stok Kangri in 3 days, possible?

That's far too fast, since Leh is already about 3,500 meters and Stok Kangri tops 6,100, and people who rush it often get seriously sick. Plan to spend at least two or three full days doing nothing strenuous in Leh, then do some acclimatization treks before attempting the peak, which typically means a total of 8 to 10 days. Stok Kangri has also been closed in recent years to protect the area, so check the current status and look at alternatives like Kang Yatse.
I'm 41 and want to start doing park stuff. Am I crazy or is that doable?

Totally doable, and plenty of riders get into park in their forties. Your recovery time is longer than a teenager's, so progress steadily: start with butters, small side hits and boxes before you work up to jumps. Wear a helmet and consider wrist guards and impact shorts, because they cut down on the bruises and sprains that would otherwise keep you off the snow.
I did my FJC last week, 8 jumps. Want to do a cliff in Moab next weekend alone, thoughts?

Please don't. Eight jumps is very early, and terminal cliff jumps in Moab bring real complications, including object strikes on off-heading openings, tricky landing areas, and remote rescue access. Keep jumping bridges or simple objects with experienced people, and do your first cliffs with a mentor who knows each exit. Your skill builds fastest when you progress steadily and safely.
I slammed on my wrist yesterday and it's swollen and hurts to turn it. Just a sprain probably?

It might be, but swelling plus pain on rotation after a fall onto an outstretched hand is the classic sign of a scaphoid fracture, which often looks like a sprain and can heal badly if it's missed. Get it X-rayed soon, ideally today, and keep it iced and immobilized until then. Wear wrist guards when you're back on the board, since they prevent exactly this injury.
What do I do if I get caught inside on a huge set?

Stay calm and conserve oxygen first, because panic burns air faster than anything. If you can't make it over, ditch your board away from you and dive deep before the wave hits, since the turbulence is weaker down there. Relax through the hold-down, then pull your vest toggle if needed and swim to the surface. Get a breath and look for the next wave and your safety team. A big-wave survival course lets you practice this in a controlled setting before you need it for real.
I have epilepsy, seizure free for 3 years on meds. Can I do a tandem?

Possibly, but you'll need clearance from your neurologist, and many dropzones will ask for a doctor's note. Being seizure-free on medication for three years is a good sign, but the decision belongs to your doctor, who knows your history. Be fully honest on the dropzone's medical form, because they need accurate information to keep you and your instructor safe.
Do ice bandanas actually help or is that just a gimmick

They genuinely help, because cooling your neck and head lowers perceived effort and slows the rise in core temperature. Studies on ice slurries and external cooling show real performance gains in heat. Refill them at every aid station, and pair them with ice in your hat and ice water dumped over your arms and torso.
My buddies want to ride the track after dark with headlamps. Fun or dumb?

Dumb, unless the track has proper lighting. Headlamps don't show depth, ruts or jump faces well enough at motocross speeds, and you'll lose the shadows you rely on to read the terrain. Many tracks also prohibit after-hours riding and have no medical help on site then. If you want night riding, look for a track that runs lit evening practice sessions.
how much does it cost to get into street luge

Expect several hundred to a couple thousand dollars depending on new versus used gear. A sled, full leathers, a full-face helmet, gloves and proper shoes are the core, and the leathers and helmet are where you shouldn't cut corners. Buying a used sled from a club member is a great way to start cheaply.
Is pickle juice for cramps legit?

It can work for some people, and it seems to act through a nerve reflex rather than by actually fixing electrolytes that fast. A small sip is fine to try. Cramps in heat are often more about fatigue and pacing than salt alone, so easing off the pace is usually the real fix.
I panicked underwater and grabbed my instructor. I'm so embarrassed. Should I quit?

Don't quit over that, because instructors see it all the time and it's exactly why they're there. The important thing is to talk it through with them and practice the skill that triggered it in calm, shallow water until it feels routine. Confidence comes from repetition, not from never being scared. Lots of excellent divers had a shaky start.
trying to land a kickflip down a 5 stair tomorrow, ive only landed kickflips on flat like 10 times total. tips??

Honest tip: you're not ready for the 5 stair yet, because ten flat landings means your kickflip isn't consistent enough to trust when you're dropping that far. Get it to where you land most attempts on flat while rolling, then take it up curbs, a single stair, a 3 stair, and so on. When you do go for the 5, wear a helmet and check that the run-up and landing are smooth and clear of people. Working up in steps is how people actually land it without hurting an ankle or a wrist.
I'm 58 and out of shape but really want to try whitewater. Realistic?

Very realistic. Plenty of people start in their fifties and sixties, and good technique matters far more than raw strength. Start with a beginner course from a certified school, maybe try a guided raft trip first to get a feel for moving water, and talk to your doctor if you have heart or shoulder concerns. Building some general fitness and shoulder mobility alongside lessons will make it more fun and help you avoid injury.
headache at 4500m, should i just take ibuprofen and keep going up

Ibuprofen can take the edge off a mild headache, but don't use it as a ticket to keep climbing. A headache at that altitude is often the first sign of acute mountain sickness, so the rule is to stay where you are until it fully resolves and never go higher with symptoms. If it gets worse or you add nausea, confusion or stumbling, descend immediately.
dry breath hold for 6 min every night before sleep, am I overdoing it

If you're doing it lying down, out of the water and somewhere safe, it's generally fine. That said, a nightly max every single time is more grind than training, and progress tends to come from varying your work with CO2 and O2 tables and easier sessions. Stay relaxed rather than fighting through it, and never do it in water or anywhere a blackout could hurt you. If you notice headaches, poor sleep or feeling foggy, back off.
brake pedal goes soft after a few laps, normal?

No, a rear brake that fades after a few laps usually means the fluid is overheating, often because it's old, has absorbed moisture, or has air in the system. Bleed it with fresh fluid of the type marked on the reservoir, and check the pads and the rotor for wear or glazing. Also check whether you're dragging the brake while riding, since that's a common cause. Don't keep riding with a soft brake on a track, because it tends to fail at exactly the moment you need it.
Can I fly straight into La Paz and start climbing Huayna Potosí the next day?

That's asking for trouble, since La Paz alone sits around 3600 m and many people feel rough just walking around town. Give yourself at least four to five days to acclimatize with easy hikes around Lake Titicaca or Chacaltaya before attempting Huayna Potosí. Most reputable guiding companies build that time into their plans for good reason.
Do I really need a neck brace or is that overkill for a hobby rider?

It isn't overkill, but it's also not as clear-cut as helmets and boots, which are non-negotiable. The research suggests braces may reduce some neck and collarbone injuries, and plenty of hobby riders wear one for peace of mind. If you buy one, get it properly fitted with your helmet and chest protector so it doesn't limit your movement or vision, and make sure it isn't eating into your budget for a quality helmet and boots first.
My guide on Kili says if we're slow we might have to turn back before Uhuru. I paid $3k. Can I insist?

You can argue, but it's better not to, because the turnaround time protects you from descending exhausted in the dark and afternoon weather. Guides who enforce it are the good ones, since the money is never worth an evacuation or worse. What you can do is ask today what pace you need, how to manage your breaks, and whether moving earlier helps your odds.
My husband is running a 100 miler in Texas in July and he's 58 with high blood pressure. Should I be worried?

It's reasonable to want some reassurance, and the right move is for him to get a sports medicine check before race day. Some blood pressure medications, especially diuretics and beta blockers, change how the body handles heat and fluid. His doctor can review his meds and maybe suggest an exercise stress test. If he's cleared, he should go conservative on pace in the heat and make sure the crew knows the warning signs of heat illness.
Paddling in my area at dusk, any problem with that?

Plan to be off the water well before dark. Low light makes it hard to read rapids, spot hazards and see a swimmer, and rescues get much harder. Give yourself a buffer for delays like swims, pins or a slow group, and bring a headlamp in your safety kit just in case.
got dizzy and fell onto my head training a flip on grass. feel ok now, maybe a bit of a headache. fine?

Don't brush that off, because a headache after landing on your head can be a sign of concussion even if you feel mostly fine. Stop training for today, have someone keep an eye on you, and get checked by a doctor, especially if you have nausea, confusion, vomiting, blurred vision or a worsening headache, which mean you should get emergency care straight away.
