Don't go back to flips until you're fully symptom-free and cleared. Rest now matters more than one more session.
can i just swim across the bay alone at dawn, its only like 1.5km

I'd skip the solo crossing. Shipping lanes, currents and boats that can't see a swimmer in low light are exactly what turn a 1.5 km swim into a rescue. Get a kayaker or paddleboarder to escort you, wear a bright cap and tow float, and check tide and boat traffic times first. With support it's a great goal, but alone it's an unnecessary gamble.
is nitrox safer? my friend says it lets you dive deeper

Your friend has it backwards. Nitrox gives you longer no-decompression times at moderate depths, but because of oxygen toxicity it actually limits how deep you can go, for example to about 34 meters on 32 percent. It does need a short certification course so you learn to analyze your gas and set your maximum depth correctly. It's well worth doing if you do a lot of repetitive dives.
how do you even jump. like, the lip thing

Start on small tabletop jumps where the gap is filled in, so coming up short won't hurt you. Roll toward the lip neutral with knees and elbows bent, then extend your body upward as you go up the face, like a gentle push, rather than pulling on the bars. Keep your eyes on the landing and absorb with your legs when you touch down. Do lots of reps at slow speed before adding more, and a jump clinic will speed things up a lot.
Helmet, gloves, boots — are boots really necessary?

Yes. Ankle injuries from hard landings are some of the most common paragliding injuries, and sturdy hiking boots with ankle support reduce them a lot. They also protect you on rocky launches and hike-ups. Skip sneakers and sandals, since the cost of decent boots is small compared to a broken ankle.
Is spring corn skiing safe from avalanches?

Safer timing-wise, but not safe by default, because wet slides become the main problem as the sun warms the snow. The trick is to ski aspects when they've just softened and get off them before they turn slushy and deep, which often means early starts and being off sunny slopes by late morning or early afternoon. If you're punching through to your boot tops or seeing rollerballs, it's time to leave.
how do you know if a bolt outside is safe

You can't verify a bolt is perfect just by looking at it, but warning signs include rust, cracks in the surrounding rock, spinning hangers, or old-style bolts, and you should avoid those. Check local climbing guidebooks or websites, which often note routes with questionable or recently replaced bolts. When in doubt, back up with extra protection or pick another route.
Headache at 4,200m on day 3, took ibuprofen and it's gone. Keep going up tomorrow?

A headache that clears completely with ibuprofen and comes with no other symptoms is usually mild AMS, but the safe move is to rest at the same altitude another night instead of climbing tomorrow. If you wake up feeling clear, with good appetite and no nausea, dizziness or unusual fatigue, you can go on carefully. If the headache comes back or anything new appears, especially stumbling, confusion or breathlessness at rest, go down rather than up. Masking symptoms with painkillers and continuing to climb is how mild AMS turns into something serious.
Is there a course or certification for big wave safety?

Yes, there are several good ones, like the Big Wave Risk Assessment Group (BWRAG) safety courses that started in Hawaii, along with breath-hold programs aimed at surfers. They cover CPR, water rescue, jet ski rescue, hold-down training and how to plan a big-wave session. Taking one before surfing serious size is one of the best investments you can make, for yourself and the people you surf with.
Can I fly home the same afternoon after two dives this morning? My flight's at 4pm.

That's cutting it too close. The standard guideline after multiple dives is to wait at least 18 hours before flying, because the lower cabin pressure can trigger decompression sickness from nitrogen still in your tissues. Either move the flight to tomorrow or skip the second dive and plan your diving so your last one is well over a day before departure.
Bike seized up, smells burnt. Can I keep riding to get back to the truck?

Don't keep riding, as a seized engine can lock up and throw you, and running it further could destroy it. Let it cool completely, then check the oil level and coolant, and see if the engine turns over smoothly with the kick starter or in gear. If it still feels tight or noisy, push or tow it back. Have a mechanic inspect it before riding again.
Can I just skip the wetsuit for my first triathlon swim? I hate how tight they feel.

Check the race rules first, because many events make wetsuits compulsory below a certain water temperature. Even where they're optional, a wetsuit adds buoyancy and warmth that make first-timers noticeably calmer. Tightness usually means a poor fit or not pulling the suit high enough through the crotch and shoulders, so try a properly sized one and do a couple of practice swims in it. If you're still miserable after that, a sleeveless model is a good compromise.
Is there any way to land a wingsuit without a parachute?

Only one person, Gary Connery, has done it, and it took a huge purpose-built landing pile of cardboard boxes plus years of planning and expert support. For everyone else, a parachute is essential, and the suit alone simply can't slow you enough to land. Treat it as a historical stunt, not anything to try.
I keep getting pain on the inside of my elbow after climbing sessions. Push through or rest?

Rest it, because that sounds like medial epicondylitis, often called climber's or golfer's elbow, and pushing through usually turns it into a months-long problem. Cut back on hard pulling and steep climbing, and start gentle eccentric wrist-flexor exercises once the sharp pain eases. If it doesn't improve within a couple of weeks, see a physiotherapist who works with climbers, since they can find the cause, which is often grip habits or training volume.
got my first DH bike, set it up myself from youtube. good enough?

YouTube is fine for basics, but get a bike shop to check it before your first park day. Suspension sag, brake bleed, and correct torque on stem and axles really matter at downhill speeds. A loose stem bolt or poorly set fork can cause a crash. It's usually a cheap check and worth the peace of mind.
Is backflip off a cliff something I can learn by just trying it on a lower ledge?

Learn it on a trampoline and a pool diving board first, ideally with a coach, before going anywhere near rock. On a cliff, an under-rotated flip means landing on your back or face, and an outward lean can bring you back toward the rock. Once it's dialed at the pool, try it low with deep water and plenty of clearance from the cliff face.
Is it fine to just train my good arm while my other one heals? Climber with tennis elbow type thing

Yes, training around an injury is smart, and there's even evidence that training one side helps the other keep some strength. Also do lower body, core and antagonist work like push-ups if they don't hurt. For the sore elbow itself, rest alone usually isn't enough. Slow, progressive loading like eccentric wrist exercises tends to help, and a physio can set that up so you don't flare it.
I'm 58 and just retired. Too late to learn kayaking rapids?

Not at all. Plenty of people start in their fifties and sixties and paddle happily for years. Start with a proper beginner course so you learn efficient technique rather than relying on strength, and be honest about any shoulder or back issues, since good form protects those joints. Many clubs have active older members who'd love to bring you along. Progress at your own pace on class I and II, and you may be surprised how much fun it is.
best way to not be scared of jumps? i freeze up

Freezing is normal and often your brain correctly noticing that you're not ready yet, so lower the stakes rather than forcing it. Practice the jump at ground level until it's boring, then raise it in small steps so the only new thing is a little height. Breaking it down like this builds real confidence, and coaches use the same method because it beats just psyching yourself up.
What's the actual difference between wingsuit skydiving and wingsuit BASE in terms of risk?

In skydiving you have thousands of feet of buffer, a reserve parachute, and usually an AAD, so most mistakes can be recovered. BASE gives you one canopy, low altitude, and often a cliff face right beside you, so errors like an off-heading opening or misjudged glide can be fatal within seconds. That's why experienced flyers usually recommend hundreds of wingsuit skydives plus solid regular BASE experience before even thinking about wingsuit BASE, all with mentorship.
I want to film parkour for TikTok but my best moves aren't super flashy. Should I do bigger stuff for views?

Don't level up the risk just for the camera, because chasing views is how a lot of people end up trying moves they haven't really earned. Clean, smooth flows with good angles, interesting locations, and solid editing often perform better than sloppy big moves. Film your training progress too, since people love watching someone build up a skill over weeks.
The route has a huge cauliflower formation and an overhanging dagger above it. My friend wants to climb right under the dagger. thoughts?

I'd stay out from under that dagger. Free-hanging daggers can snap without warning, especially as temperatures change or vibrations from climbing travel through the ice, and anyone underneath would be in a serious fall line. Look for a line that keeps you out of its fall path, or choose another route that day. Belay from a protected spot away from the debris zone as well, since that's where hanging ice ends up if it breaks.
Is Elbrus a good beginner high peak? Heard you can take a snowcat most of the way.

Elbrus is technically simple, but it's no easy hill, and its reputation as a beginner peak lures people into trouble. Riding the snowcat skips some of the effort, but not the altitude, and the weather can turn into a whiteout or bitter wind very fast at 5,642 meters, where people get lost and die every year. Go with a reputable guide, give yourself several days of acclimatization hikes, and make sure you're comfortable using crampons and an ice axe before summit day.
Shark on our dive tomorrow — reef sharks. Should I be scared?

Reef sharks like whitetips and blacktips are generally shy and rarely interested in divers, and seeing one is usually the highlight of a dive. Stay calm, keep your arms close, don't chase or corner them, and listen to your guide's briefing. Avoid splashing at the surface and don't dive where people are feeding fish.
my friend wants us to try roof gaps on our apartment building tonight, he says it's only like 6 feet

I'd pass on this one. A six-foot gap is a jump most beginners could make on flat ground, but at height, in the dark, with unknown roof surfaces, gravel, or loose edges, there's zero room for error, and a slip means a fall of several stories. Experienced traceurs who do roof gaps have usually stuck the exact same jump hundreds of times at ground level and checked the landing in daylight. If you want the thrill, mark out the same distance between two walls at ground level and see how consistent you both really are first.
Can I take my GoPro on my first flights?

Wait until you're comfortable launching and landing. Early flights need your full attention, and fiddling with a camera or worrying about the shot is a real distraction. If you do mount one later, use a secure mount on the helmet or harness, check it can't snag lines, and set it recording before you clip in.
I blacked out on surfacing last weekend but felt fine after. Can I dive again this weekend?

Take this seriously and give yourself a proper break first. Many agencies recommend at least a few days off after a blackout, and you should see a doctor if you inhaled any water, have coughing, chest discomfort or breathing trouble, because lung complications can show up late. When you come back, dive well under your previous limits, look honestly at what caused it, like fatigue, overweighting or pushing too far, and ideally go over it with an instructor.
Is tow-in surfing safer than paddling?

Each style carries different risks, so neither one is simply safer. Tow-in lets you catch much bigger, faster waves with a ski there to pick you up, but the speeds and wave size make wipeouts more violent. Paddle surfing keeps you in smaller waves, though you're more exposed if a set catches you inside. Whichever you do, the safest setup is a trained ski driver with rescue sled experience and a partner who knows the break.
Anyone used those cheap altitude tents at home before a trip? Worth it?

They can help. Several weeks of sleeping in a hypoxic tent gives you partial acclimatization, and some Everest operators now run shorter expeditions built around them. The benefits fade within days to weeks, so time it close to your departure, and it doesn't replace on-mountain acclimatization. If you're doing a standard trek with a sensible itinerary, they're a luxury, not a necessity.
Is it fine to skip leathers for street luge if I wear jeans and a hoodie? Leathers are expensive.

Jeans and a hoodie will shred through in a fraction of a second at luge speeds, and the road will take skin down to the tissue underneath. Leathers or a proper abrasion-rated suit are the core safety gear in this sport, which is why races require them. Used motorcycle leathers are often cheap on secondhand marketplaces and work fine as long as they fit snugly and the seams are intact. Until you have them, keep your speeds very low.
My son just turned 16 and is obsessed with cave diving after watching documentaries. Should I let him?

Wanting it is great, and the best way to channel that is building strong fundamentals rather than jumping into caves. Many cave agencies set a minimum age of 18 for full cave courses, so for now he can get open water and advanced certifications and log lots of dives with a focus on buoyancy control. If he's still keen in a couple of years, a reputable cavern course with a well-reviewed instructor is the right first step, and you can feel good that he's going in trained.
Trad climbing self taught from youtube, placing gear on lead this weekend. any tips

Before you lead on your own placements, get them checked by someone who knows trad, ideally a guide or experienced mentor, because YouTube can't tell you whether your cams are walked or your nuts are about to pop. Ground school, where you place gear at head height, hang on it and have an expert critique it, is the standard way to learn. Then lead well below your grade while you build experience. One or two days with a guide is cheap insurance.
Can I paddle class IV after only one season?

It's possible for a very athletic, well-coached paddler, but most people need a couple of seasons at class III to build reliable rolls, good boat control and river-reading skills. Class IV swims can be long and serious, and you need to be able to help rescue others too. Move up gradually and paddle with experienced groups who can tell you honestly when you're ready.
Quick one - do I need a helmet on class II?

Yes, always wear a helmet on whitewater, class II included. If you flip upside down, your head is right next to the rocks, and plenty of injuries happen on easier rapids precisely because people get casual. A proper whitewater helmet is light and comfortable once it's fitted, so it's a no-brainer.
What do I do if I get my foot stuck in the rocks while swimming?

The best defense is prevention: when swimming in current, keep your feet up and float on your back with your feet pointed downstream, and never stand up in moving water deeper than your knees. If someone does get entrapped, it's a true emergency where every second counts, and rescuers usually use a stabilization line or a snag line to keep their head above water. Taking a swiftwater rescue course is the only realistic way to learn those techniques properly.
Do I need insurance for BASE jumping?

Yes, it's worth looking into, because many standard health and travel policies exclude BASE and rescue costs can be huge, especially abroad. Look for specialist adventure sports coverage that explicitly includes BASE and helicopter rescue. Read the fine print, since some policies cover skydiving but not BASE.
How cold does it get on top of Elbrus in July

Expect around -10 to -20°C at the summit on a typical July morning, and wind chill can make it feel well below -30°C. Storms roll in quickly, and whiteouts on the broad upper slopes have led to fatal navigation errors. Bring full summit layers and mitts, and carry a GPS track along with the willingness to turn back if visibility closes in.
Can I paddle after a couple beers?

Skip the beers until you're off the river, since alcohol slows reactions, impairs judgment and speeds up hypothermia. Whitewater demands quick decisions and good balance, and drinking undermines both. Have a cold one at the takeout instead.
I'm 62 and my grandson wants to take me tandem paragliding for my birthday. My knees aren't great. Should I worry?

Plenty of people your age fly tandem, and the pilot does all the flying, so you mostly need to manage a short run on takeoff and possibly on landing. Tell the operator about your knees when you book, since they can choose a site and day with gentle wind that allows a softer launch, and some offer seated landings. Check with your doctor if you have heart or back issues as well. Then go enjoy it with your grandson.
I'm 58 and out of shape but want to learn ice climbing. Too late?

Not at all, plenty of people start ice climbing in their fifties and sixties. Begin with a guided intro day on toprope, where the guide handles the rope systems and you focus on learning efficient technique, which matters far more than raw strength on ice. Building some general fitness ahead of time, especially leg strength, core work, and grip endurance, will make those first days much more enjoyable. It's also worth a quick check-in with your doctor if you have any heart or joint concerns, since cold and exertion add strain.
Had a back surgery 2 years ago, fully healed. Bungee okay?

Get a doctor's clearance first, ideally from your surgeon or a spine specialist. Bungee puts real compression and whiplash-style forces on your spine, and most operators exclude anyone with back problems or previous spinal surgery unless cleared. Feeling fully healed doesn't always mean the spine can handle that kind of load. Bring written clearance if the operator asks, and be honest on the medical form.
my wing had a big collapse last flight and i got it back out but im kinda shaken. should i just get back up asap?

Being shaken after a big collapse is normal, and it's worth working through before you fly again rather than pushing past it. Talk the flight through with an instructor so you understand what caused it, whether conditions, wing choice or input. If the wing is near the top of your skill range, consider whether it's the right one for you. A SIV course, where you practise collapses over water with professional guidance, is one of the best ways to rebuild confidence, and when you return, choose a mellow day.
I'm 15 and want to get into freediving. Where do I even start?

The best start is a beginner course from an agency like AIDA, PADI Freediver, SSI or Molchanovs. Many accept teens with a parent's consent, and some set a minimum age, so check with local schools. You'll learn safe breathing, equalization and, most importantly, how to rescue a buddy who blacks out. Until then, enjoy snorkeling at the surface with someone nearby instead of practicing breath holds on your own.
How long after a broken collarbone before I can mountain bike again? Mine was 6 weeks ago.

That depends on whether it was surgically fixed and what your follow-up X-rays show. Many people can start turbo or road riding around 6 to 8 weeks, but trail riding usually waits until the bone is solidly united, often 10 to 12 weeks or more. Another crash onto an incompletely healed collarbone can re-break it or bend any plate you have in there. Ask your surgeon for clearance with imaging, and build strength back up before you go anywhere technical.
partner fell and hit a ledge, says he's fine but has a headache. continue climbing?

Stop climbing and get him checked out. A headache after a hit can signal a concussion, and symptoms can worsen over hours. Watch for confusion, vomiting, or drowsiness, and seek medical care promptly if any appear. Don't let him drive.
can i dive with a cold, ears a bit blocked, just a 12m dive

Skip it. Blocked ears mean you probably won't equalize properly, and even 12 meters is plenty deep to cause a barotrauma injury or a reverse block on the way up. Decongestants can wear off mid-dive and make things worse, so don't rely on them. Wait until you can equalize easily on land and your sinuses are clear. A missed dive day is far better than a perforated eardrum.
can I use my regular single tank setup for intro cave

Usually not; most intro cave courses require a redundant gas setup, either doubles or sidemount, because a single first stage failure in a cave can be fatal. Ask your instructor exactly which configuration they want before you buy anything. Many people rent or try both sidemount and backmount doubles before settling on one.
Whats the deal with chalk, do i actually need it

For most people it makes a real difference, because chalk dries sweat and gives you more friction on the holds, especially on small or sloping ones. Get a chalk bag or bucket, chalk up before you start a climb, and don't cake it on, since a thin layer works better than a thick crust. Some gyms require liquid chalk or chalk balls to keep dust down, so check their rules first.
how long should I be able to hold my breath before surfing big waves

Many big-wave surfers train to a static breath-hold of 3 to 4 minutes, but the number that really matters is how you handle a breath-hold while your heart is pounding and you're being thrashed around underwater. Two-wave hold-downs can keep you under for 30 to 60 seconds in chaos, which feels nothing like a calm pool hold. Learn through a proper course like those run by big-wave safety programs, and never do breath-hold training alone in water, because shallow water blackout kills strong swimmers.
what happens if the main parachute doesn't open??

Every sport rig has a second reserve parachute, and on a tandem the instructor is trained to handle this exactly. They cut away the problem main and deploy the reserve, which is packed and inspected by a certified rigger. Most rigs also have an AAD, a small device that fires the reserve automatically if the jumper is still falling fast at a low altitude, so there are multiple layers of backup.
Is a First Jump Course really necessary or can I just learn from YouTube and a friend who jumps?

Take the course, because BASE gear, packing, object assessment and malfunction responses are things you need hands-on instruction and direct feedback on, not video theory. A friend who jumps isn't the same as an experienced instructor who has taught dozens of students and knows how beginners fail. A good FJC also includes supervised jumps from a span or low-risk object, which is the safest place to make your first mistakes.
Ugh, should I take a lesson or can I just watch YouTube and learn myself?

YouTube is great as a supplement, but take a lesson. An instructor will catch bad habits early, teach you wet exits and self-rescue safely, and get you rolling much faster than you'd manage alone. Whitewater also has a lot of judgment-based skills, like reading water and spotting hazards, that you really learn on the river with experienced people. A weekend course will save you months of frustration and keep you a lot safer.
bungee in a third world country with no regulations — just trust the operator's vibe?

Don't rely on vibes. Ask how often they replace cords, whether they weigh every jumper, whether there's a backup harness or attachment, and how long they've been operating, and watch a few jumps to see if staff double-check every connection. Look for recent reviews from fellow travelers too, and if anything feels improvised or rushed, walk away.
is it ok to do parkour at night in the city

Low light makes it much harder to judge distances and spot cracks, wet patches, or loose surfaces, so night training is riskier than it looks. If you do it, stick to spots you know well from the daytime, keep it to low, familiar moves, and train with a friend. Stay off private property, because security and police are far more twitchy after dark.
What's a safety roll and why does everyone keep telling me to learn it?

A safety roll, or parkour roll, is a diagonal roll across your shoulder and back. It turns the force of a landing or fall into forward momentum instead of sending it straight through your joints. People keep recommending it because it protects your knees, ankles and spine on bigger drops, and it can save you when something goes wrong. Learn it on grass or mats until it's automatic on both sides, then move to harder surfaces.
Taking a 4 day self-supported trip next month, first multi-day. Any tips?

Pick a river at least a full grade below your daily limit, because a loaded boat is slower and harder to roll. Pack a group first aid kit, a satellite communicator or PLB, extra paddle, pin kit, and someone who knows how to use it, and leave a detailed float plan with a contact at home. Practice paddling your loaded boat on an easy day run before the trip, and check the gauge and weather forecast right up to launch.
Teammate at 5800m is acting drunk, slurring, can't walk straight. We're tired, what do we do?

Treat this as possible HACE, a life-threatening emergency, and get them down immediately, even at night or when you're exhausted. Give oxygen and dexamethasone if you have them, and call for rescue or a helicopter if you can get a signal. Don't leave them alone and don't wait for them to improve, because every hour counts.
First ultra ever, picked a desert one. Dumb?

Ambitious more than dumb, but heat is a tough variable to add to a distance you've never run. A cooler-weather first ultra lets you learn fueling and pacing without the added risk. If you're set on this one, train specifically in heat, go slow, and treat finishing as the only goal.
Can I use caffeine pills to get through the hot afternoon section?

Moderate caffeine is fine and can help, so stick to around 100 to 200 mg at a time and don't go much over 3 to 6 mg per kg for the whole day. Big doses can upset your stomach and raise your heart rate, which matters more in heat. Test it in training, not for the first time on race day.
My friend got super confused and stopped sweating at mile 40 last summer and the medics took him off course. He's mad and says he was fine. Was he?

No, the medics almost certainly saved him from something serious. Confusion together with hot, dry skin is a classic sign of exertional heat stroke, which is a medical emergency and can cause organ damage or death if cooling is delayed. The fact that he doesn't remember it as bad is part of the problem, because heat stroke impairs judgment. He should talk to a sports medicine doctor before his next hot race, since a previous heat illness can raise the risk of another one.
Can I just take Diamox and go straight up? Seems easier.

Diamox speeds up acclimatization, but it doesn't replace it, and people who use it to justify a rushed ascent still get HAPE and HACE. Use it as a backup to a sensible ascent rate. It also has side effects like tingling fingers, frequent urination and making carbonated drinks taste flat, so try a dose at home first. Get a prescription from a doctor who knows travel medicine, since it isn't right for everyone, especially people with sulfa allergies.
do solo climbers use chalk?

Yes, almost all of them use chalk, usually from a chalk bag on a belt, because dry hands give you consistent friction on every hold. They tend to chalk up at secure rests rather than mid-crux, and they practice that rhythm on roped laps first. On humid days, many soloists skip the route entirely, since chalk only goes so far against sweaty hands and slick rock.
is a trampoline actually useful for snowboard tricks

Yes, it's one of the best tools for learning spins and flips, because you can practice rotation, spotting and body position with a soft landing. Lots of riders use a trampoline board with no bindings to mimic their stance. Start simple with 180s and 360s, and get coaching before attempting flips even on a trampoline, since bad flip landings there can hurt you too.
Bike bogs when I crack the throttle off the bottom, idk what to adjust

A bog when you crack the throttle usually means the bike is running lean or the accelerator pump isn't set right. On a carbureted four-stroke, check the pump timing first, then try richening the pilot circuit or moving the needle clip, adjusting one thing at a time. On a fuel-injected bike, first check for a dirty air filter or a vacuum leak, and if those are fine, it may need a map change. If you're not comfortable working on jetting, a good shop can sort it out quickly.
do the people working there actually check everything every time or is it routine

At a good operator, yes, they do. Standard practice is multiple staff cross-checking harness, carabiners and cord attachment before every single jump, often with a verbal callout. If you notice staff skipping checks, joking around at the edge, or rushing you, that's a legitimate red flag and you're within your rights to walk away.
is it better to jump in morning or later in day

It doesn't matter much safety-wise, but mornings often have calmer winds and shorter queues, which means less waiting around getting nervous. Some sites have better light for photos later in the day. Just make sure you've eaten something light and you're not dehydrated, whatever the time.
Rappelling: do I need a backup knot or autoblock? Seems like overkill

Use both, because many rappelling deaths come from rappelling off the end of the rope or losing control, and those two backups prevent exactly that. Tie stopper knots in both rope ends and use an autoblock, such as a friction hitch below your device, so you won't drop if you get hit by rockfall or need your hands. They take a few seconds each and pros use them as standard practice.
can i jump drunk? need the liquid courage tbh

No, and any decent operator will turn you away if you show up smelling of booze. Alcohol messes with your blood pressure and judgment and makes you more likely to panic or move wrong on the platform. The nerves are part of it, so breathe slowly, don't overthink it, and let the crew count you down.
why do my legs shake so bad going fast

That's mostly nerves and tension, and stiff legs feed directly into speed wobbles. Bend your knees more, keep your weight forward over the front truck, breathe, and look far ahead instead of at your board. If the shakes come from the board itself, tighten your trucks or use harder bushings. Drop back to a speed where you feel loose, then creep up again.
How do I know if a slope is wind-loaded?

Look for signs like cornices, pillow-shaped drifts, hollow-sounding or stiff snow, and cracks shooting out from your skis. Wind-loaded slopes are often on the lee side of ridges and below cornices, where snow piles up. If you suspect wind loading, avoid those slopes or choose lower-angle terrain until conditions improve.
My 12 year old wants to join me for sea swims. She's a strong pool swimmer. Is that okay?

It can be, but pool strength doesn't fully carry over to waves, cold and the lack of a wall to grab. Start her in calm, shallow, lifeguarded water close to shore, with a wetsuit if it's chilly, and stay right beside her. Kids lose heat faster than adults, so keep the first swims short and watch for blue lips or shivering. A junior open-water club session is a great way for her to learn sighting and conditions safely.
can i swim on my period in the ocean

Yes, absolutely. A tampon or menstrual cup works fine in the water, and there's no evidence that periods attract sharks or cause any extra risk. Just swim as you normally would and change your protection afterwards.
Gym bouldering, I keep jumping off from the top. My knees are starting to complain. Normal?

It's common, but it's a warning sign. Repeated drops from the top of the wall add up, even onto padding. Downclimb as far as you comfortably can before letting go, then land on both feet with your knees bent and roll back onto your butt and back to spread out the impact. If the knee pain lingers or you notice swelling, catching, or instability, get it looked at by a physio. In most cases, changing how you fall fixes it.
Got caught in a rip current last weekend and panicked. What should I have done?

The key is not to fight it head-on, because rips can pull faster than even strong swimmers can swim. Float on your back to save energy and calm your breathing, then swim parallel to the shore until you're out of the current, or let it carry you until it weakens. Raise an arm and shout if you need help. Next time, swim at lifeguarded beaches between the flags, since lifeguards know where rips are forming that day.
Water's 11°C. I'm tough, I'll skip the wetsuit.

At 11°C, toughness doesn't stop cold shock, the gasping and fast breathing in the first minute that causes a lot of drownings, and it doesn't stop your arms weakening as you chill. Without a wetsuit you could become unable to swim properly within 10 to 20 minutes, sooner if you haven't built up cold tolerance over the season. If you want to swim without a suit, keep it to a few minutes, stay close to shore, have someone watching, and work up the time gradually over weeks. Bring warm layers and a hot drink, and get dressed quickly afterwards, because you'll keep cooling for a while after you get out.
My buddy solos regularly and wants me to follow him up a 5.7 this weekend. I've only top roped. He says it's easy.

Pass on this one, because having only top-roped means you haven't experienced real exposure or climbed on outdoor rock without a safety net. Easy for him after years of experience isn't easy for you, and the pressure of keeping up with someone is exactly how accidents happen. Ask him to take you up the same route on a rope instead, which is a great way to learn from him. If he's a good friend, he'll respect that.
Ears hurt at around 3m every time. Should I just push through it?

No, pushing through ear pain is how you rupture an eardrum or damage your inner ear, and that can sideline you for months or longer. The pain means you aren't equalizing early or often enough. Start equalizing at the surface and keep doing it every meter or so on the way down, before you feel any pressure. If you still can't clear, try the Frenzel technique with an instructor, and never dive with a cold or congestion.
what do i do if i get swept by a current after jumping

Stay calm and don't swim directly against the current. Swim parallel to shore or across it until you're out of the flow, then head in. If you're tiring, float on your back and signal for help. Before any jump, check the current and plan your exit route, because a strong current is one of the main reasons not to jump at a spot.
what PSI for sand

For sand, most riders run around 12 to 13 psi front and rear for good traction and float. Running too low makes pinch flats and rolled tires more likely, especially with a standard tube, so if you want to go lower, use heavy-duty tubes or a mousse. Check pressure cold before you ride, because a few psi makes a big difference in how the bike feels.
Why do cave divers die even when they're experienced?

The usual pattern is complacency: skipping a guideline, stretching gas rules or going a little deeper and farther each time because nothing has gone wrong yet. Experience also brings more ambitious dives, with deeper gas, longer penetrations and tighter spots, where small errors snowball. The best cave divers stay boringly disciplined about the basics no matter how many dives they have.
I feel like I'm stuck at the same level. Any advice?

Plateaus happen to everyone, and the fix usually comes from changing your routine, not just repeating the same tricks. Try skating with people slightly better than you, filming your attempts to see what you're doing wrong, or learning tricks switch or fakie to build general board feel. A session with a coach can also spot small technique issues you can't feel yourself.
pregnant, 10 weeks, can I still dive on our honeymoon?

The standard advice is no scuba during pregnancy. Nobody knows how nitrogen bubbles affect a developing baby, and the risk isn't worth it. Snorkeling is a lovely alternative, and on a lot of reefs you'll still see turtles, rays and plenty of fish from the surface. Save the dive trip for after the baby, as an anniversary trip maybe.
I'm 16, can I go to the river by myself on weekends?

Paddling whitewater alone isn't a good idea at any age, because you need people to help if you pin, swim or get hurt. Look for a local paddling club or youth program, since many welcome teen paddlers and teach good safety habits. Make sure your parents know your plan and that you're always boating with a capable group.
how do I find closed road events near me

Search for local downhill skate or luge clubs, regional racing associations, and longboard community groups online, since they post events and freerides. Local skate shops that sell longboard gear often know about sessions too. Many events welcome beginners and require basic gear like a full-face helmet and gloves. Contact organizers ahead of time to confirm requirements.
I keep casing jumps. What am I doing wrong?

Usually it's not enough speed, letting off the throttle on the face, or leaning back too far. Try staying on a steady throttle all the way up the face, with your body centered and your knees gripping the bike. Back down to smaller jumps until you're clearing them consistently, and have someone film you or watch from the side so you can see what's happening. A coaching session can usually fix casing habits fast.
tingling lips and dizzy after surfacing just now, felt fine underwater

Those can be early signs of hypoxia, meaning you came close to a samba or blackout. Stop for the day and rest out of the water with your buddy until you feel completely normal. Next time cut your dive times back and lengthen your surface intervals. If the symptoms don't clear quickly, or you get confusion or chest pain, get medical help.
I'm 42, overweight, and want to try parkour. Am I ridiculous?

Not at all, and plenty of parkour gyms run classes aimed at older beginners. Start with the basics: quadrupedal movement, low balance work, safety vaults over knee-high obstacles, and lots of landing practice to build up your joints. Your tendons and knees will adapt more slowly than your muscles, so keep impact low for the first few months. If you have any heart or joint issues, get a quick check-up with your doctor first.
BMX, heel pain every morning for a month, landing drops kills it. Ice or heat?

Morning heel pain that's worst on the first steps often points to plantar fasciitis. It can also be a heel bone bruise or a stress reaction from hard landings, so get it checked if it's very tender on the bone itself. Ice after riding helps settle it. Calf and foot stretches, rolling the arch, and supportive shoes off the bike tend to help more over time. Cut out big drops for a few weeks and stick to flat or flow riding while it calms down.
Is it actually dangerous to paddle a class III river solo if I've done it a bunch of times with friends?

Yes, solo paddling removes your rescue system, and on class III that matters because a pin, a swim into a sieve or a foot entrapment can turn fatal in minutes with nobody there to help. Knowing the run well lowers the odds of trouble but doesn't change what happens when trouble finds you anyway. If you really want to go light, take one competent partner instead of none, and carry a throw bag and a whistle every time.
chest protector or roost deflector what's the difference

A roost deflector mainly protects you from rocks and dirt kicked up by other bikes, while a chest protector offers more impact protection for crashes and often covers the back as well. For general motocross riding, a full chest protector or a body armor jacket is the better choice. Some riders use lighter deflectors in hot weather, but you give up some protection. If you wear a neck brace, make sure your chest protector is compatible.
do BASE jumpers wear helmets?

Most do, and you should too. A helmet protects you from object strikes, rough landings and rocks in a cliff landing area. Many jumpers also wear knee pads and good boots with ankle support, since rough landings cause a lot of BASE injuries. Pick a helmet that fits well and doesn't block your vision or hearing.
Friend in our group is acting drunk at high camp, slurring, can't walk straight but says he's fine. We're at 5,600m. What do we do??

Treat this as possible HACE, which is an emergency, and start getting him down right now, even at night if it's safe to move, because he can deteriorate fast. Don't trust what he says, since confusion and denial are part of the condition. Give oxygen if you have it, use dexamethasone if someone has it and knows the dose, use a Gamow bag if one is available, and contact your guide, outfitter or rescue service immediately. Keep him with at least two people the whole way down and never leave him alone.
I'm 38, overweight, and want to try parkour. Am I too old? Be honest.

You're not too old, and plenty of people start parkour in their 40s and 50s; there are even classes built for older beginners. Your main job early on is conditioning your joints, ankles and tendons, so expect a lot of crawling, balance work, low step-ups and landing practice before any real jumping. A quick check-in with your doctor is smart if you have any heart or joint concerns, and a beginner class with a coach will scale everything to where you are now.
My buddy says you can BASE jump with like 50 skydives if you have a good mentor. legit?

Some people do start with that few jumps, but it isn't a good idea, and most reputable instructors won't take you. A mentor can teach you BASE technique, but they can't give you the canopy reflexes and stability that only come from hundreds of skydives. Build those skills where you have a reserve and lots of altitude, then go to a mentor who sets a high bar.
I keep going over the bars on steep rolls. What am I doing wrong?

Usually it comes down to grabbing too much front brake and having your weight too far forward. On steep rolls, drop your heels, bend your knees and elbows, and keep your hips back over the rear of the bike without locking your arms straight. Brake smoothly with both brakes before the steepest part, and don't stab the front. Practice on a mellow roll until the position feels natural before returning to the steep one.
I want to do my first rail tomorrow. Should I go switch onto it so I don't catch an edge?

Ride onto your first rail in your normal stance, because that's where your balance is best. Approach straight on, ollie onto it with a flat board and keep your knees soft and your weight centered. Catching an edge usually comes from tilting the board, not from your stance. Pick a low, wide beginner rail or box and do some confidence laps watching others first.
Is bungee jumping actually safe or am I crazy for wanting to try it?

You're not crazy. Commercial bungee at a reputable operator has a very good safety record, and serious incidents are rare. Nearly all of the risk comes down to the operator, so choose one with a long track record, certified jump masters and visible equipment checks. If they seem rushed or sloppy, walk away and book somewhere else.
Should I learn backmount doubles or sidemount for cave?

Both work, and the right choice depends on the caves you plan to dive and your body and preferences. Sidemount is great for tight restrictions and easier on the back on land, while backmount doubles are stable, streamlined and simpler for gas management on long dives. Try both with an instructor if you can, and learn one well before switching.
Is there a way to tell if a jump is legal?

Look for posted signs at the site, and check the local park, council or land management website, since many popular spots ban jumping after past injuries. Quarries and reservoirs are often private or restricted, and trespassing there can mean fines on top of the risk of no rescue access. When in doubt, ask a ranger or local authority, because legal spots also tend to be safer and better monitored.
can i ride street luge on a normal open road if i go early morning when theres no cars

I'd skip it, because early morning is exactly when a single car, delivery truck or cyclist appears around a blind corner and you can't stop in time lying flat at speed. Being that low also makes you nearly invisible to drivers. If you must ride a road that isn't closed, use spotters with radios at every blind corner and a chase car behind you, but the right move is to join organized freeride sessions where the road is actually closed.
I have type 1 diabetes, can I do AFF?

Many people with type 1 diabetes skydive, but you'll need medical sign-off, and in the US a valid medical or a signed statement is required for students. Talk to your endocrinologist about managing your blood sugar around the adrenaline, which can cause unpredictable swings. Plan on checking levels before every jump and keeping fast carbs on hand, and let your instructors know so they understand the situation.
whats a coleman slide

The Coleman slide is a classic hands-down slide named after Cliff Coleman, a pioneer of downhill skateboarding. You crouch, put your gloved hand down on the pavement, and rotate your board sideways so the wheels break traction, scrubbing speed and letting you turn or stop. It's one of the first slides most downhill riders learn because it's stable and easy to control once you have it. Practice it at low speed on a smooth, mellow hill with slide gloves.
There's a tombstoning spot off a harbour wall in the UK, kids do it all the time, tide was low last time though

Check the tide times before you go, because harbour walls that are fine at high tide can drop into knee-deep water at low tide, and many tombstoning injuries in the UK come from exactly this. Look out for hidden hazards like chains, ladders, boat traffic and submerged debris near walls. If you're not sure of the depth at that moment, wait for the tide or skip it.
Is it dumb to run a class III river solo if I've done it with a group like five times?

Not dumb to want to, but it's a real jump in risk, because on a solo run a missed roll or a pinned boat has no backup at all. Five group runs on one stretch is a decent start, but levels change, wood moves, and you haven't been tested without someone ready with a throw bag. Keep paddling it with at least two others until your roll is bombproof in cold, aerated water, and if you ever do go solo, pick a much easier section.
Can I just watch YouTube videos and teach myself to paraglide? Lessons are crazy expensive.

Videos are great for theory, but they can't teach you how a wing actually feels in your hands, and most serious accidents happen to self-taught beginners who misread conditions or mishandle a launch. A proper course with a certified school (USHPA, BHPA or your national equivalent) usually runs 8 to 12 days and includes training gear, so you don't buy anything until you know what suits you. If cost is the issue, ask schools about off-season discounts or splitting the course over several weekends.
Deep water soloing — is that a safer way to get into solo climbing?

Yes, deep water soloing is the most forgiving form of ropeless climbing, because you fall into the sea instead of onto rock, and it's a great way to train commitment and climbing at your limit without a rope. It still has its own hazards: check the water depth at the tide you're climbing, watch for submerged rocks, learn to fall feet-first in a tight body position, and avoid falls above about 15 to 20 meters. Go to established venues like Mallorca or the UK's south coast with locals who know the spots. Never go alone, and have someone ready on the water or the shore.
lanyard yes or no for line diving

Yes for deep line diving. A lanyard keeps you attached to the line, so you can't drift off in a current or lose the line in poor visibility, and it lets your safety team pull you up if something goes wrong. Use a quick-release so you can unclip it fast. For shallow recreational diving without a line, it doesn't really matter, but once you're doing proper depth training on a line, wear one.
Pacing for a hot ultra? I usually go out hard.

In the heat, going out hard is the most common way to blow up. Start noticeably slower, maybe 10 to 20 percent off your cool-weather effort, and use heart rate or breathing rather than pace to keep yourself in check. Heat stacks up, so the minutes you bank early get paid back with interest later.
We're getting married and want to do a tandem skydive together on our honeymoon in Hawaii. Any tips?

Great idea, and Hawaii has some stunning dropzones, so book early and plan it near the start of the trip in case the weather delays it. Each of you will jump with your own instructor, and many places can put you on the same plane so you exit close together. Don't scuba dive in the 24 hours before you jump, because of the risk of decompression sickness, and plan your snorkeling days accordingly.
my son is 11 and wants to do the black runs with his older cousins. he's decent on blues. yes or no

Not yet. Let him get completely smooth and in control on the blues first, ideally with a kids' coaching session at the park, then try one black with an adult riding just behind him. Black runs usually have mandatory drops and gaps where a kid who's chasing older cousins is most likely to overcommit. A full-face helmet, goggles and body armour are non-negotiable at that level.
What's the deal with off-heading openings? How scared should I be

Off-heading openings are one of the biggest killers in object jumping, because a canopy turning toward the wall or cliff gives you only a second or two to react. You manage the risk with a symmetrical body position at pull, a careful pack job, and a practiced reaction: grab the rear riser and steer away from the object immediately. Your FJC instructor should drill this until it's automatic, and you should keep rehearsing it on the ground before every jump.
How much water per hour in hot ultras? Just give me a number.

Most runners land somewhere between 500 and 750 ml per hour in heat, but drink to thirst rather than forcing a fixed number. Overdrinking plain water is how people get hyponatremia, which can be just as dangerous as dehydration. Pair your fluids with sodium and weigh yourself before and after a long hot training run so you know your actual sweat rate.
I want to swim to that island about 2km off the coast. Done 5k in the pool. Good to go?

Your fitness probably covers the distance, but the sea adds currents, chop, cold and boat traffic that a pool never prepares you for, and conditions can change fast. Don't attempt it without a kayak or boat escort. Check the tides and the forecast, and get local advice about currents around the island. Do a few shorter coastal swims first so you know how you handle it.
should i fly alone at a remote site to get some quiet time

Avoid flying completely alone at remote sites, because if anything goes wrong there's nobody to help or raise the alarm. At minimum, tell someone your plan, carry a phone or radio, and have a GPS tracker if you can. Flying with another pilot or a ground buddy is the safer choice. You can still get plenty of quiet time with someone just watching from below.
is it ok to ride the day after a concussion if I feel fine

No, feeling fine the next day doesn't mean your brain has recovered, and a second hit during that window can be far worse than the first. See a doctor, then follow a graded return-to-sport plan, which usually takes at least a week or two. Replace the helmet you crashed in, too.
how long should i spend on the summit of kili

Keep it to about 10 to 20 minutes, which is enough for photos and a moment to take it in. At almost 5,900 meters your body is barely coping, and most problems start or get worse the longer you hang around up high. Head down as soon as you're done, because descending is what actually makes you feel better.
Terrified of heights but my friends are all doing it. I don't want to be the one who bails. Help.

Plenty of people with a real fear of heights do jump. Plenty of others decide not to, and the crew sees both every day without anyone caring. On the platform, look at the horizon instead of down, breathe slowly and go on the first countdown, because hesitating only makes it harder. Decide in advance that walking back is a perfectly fine outcome, which takes a surprising amount of pressure off. Your friends will be too busy with their own nerves to judge you.
Crashed and my wrist is swollen but I can still move it. Probably fine to keep riding right?

Stop riding for the day and get it looked at, because wrist fractures, especially of the scaphoid bone, often still allow movement and get missed. Downhill puts huge force through your wrists, so riding on a fracture can make it much worse. Ice it, keep it elevated, and see a doctor if there's swelling, tenderness at the base of the thumb, or pain that hasn't faded within a day or two. An X-ray now is a lot easier than surgery later.
Broke my wrist 4 weeks ago, cast came off yesterday. Doctor said take it easy. How about some light skating?

Light skating feels harmless, but falling onto an outstretched hand is exactly how wrists break, and a bone fresh out of a cast is still weak. The wrist will also be stiff, so your instinct to catch yourself won't work properly yet. Spend the next few weeks on the mobility and strength exercises your doctor or hand therapist gives you. Once you're cleared, come back with wrist guards and stick to flat, easy terrain at first.
Can I learn tricks on a rental board or do I need my own?

You can definitely start on a rental, especially for butters, ollies and small jumps. Ask for something a little softer and shorter if the shop has it, because that makes presses and spins easier. Once you're hooked and riding park regularly, a twin-tip park board will feel noticeably more forgiving, but there's no need to buy one before then.
Can I just watch YouTube tutorials instead of paying for lessons? Lessons are $150.

YouTube is great for understanding technique, but it can't see what you're actually doing wrong, and that's where a coach earns their money. One lesson often fixes a habit, like bad braking or weight too far forward, that you'd otherwise practice for months. If $150 is steep, look for group clinics, which are often much cheaper, and use videos between sessions.
I have a bad back, herniated disc two years ago, mostly fine now. Risky?

Yes, this is genuinely one to clear with your doctor or spine specialist first. The jerk at the bottom of the fall and the rebound load the spine hard, and that can aggravate an old herniation even if it feels fine day to day. If they okay it, ask the operator for a body harness rather than ankles only, because it spreads the force more evenly.
whats the difference between cavern and cave diving

Cavern diving stays in the daylight zone near the entrance, usually within about 40 metres of linear penetration from the surface, with natural light always visible and no restrictions you can't easily swim through. Cave diving goes beyond that into total darkness, often with restrictions, long penetrations and complex navigation, and needs full cave training plus redundant gear. A cavern course is the normal first step if you're curious about overhead environments.
Mouthfill technique — how do I learn it?

Mouthfill is an advanced technique for equalizing beyond your residual volume, usually past 30 to 40 meters. Learn it from an experienced instructor rather than from videos, because you need to master Frenzel first and getting it wrong at depth is risky. Many coaches teach it with dry drills and shallow sessions before taking you deeper. Expect it to take weeks of practice.
im 13 and my dad says i can just borrow his gear and he'll teach me in the pool, do i need a course

Yes, you really do. Even pool diving has risks like lung overexpansion injuries if you hold your breath while ascending, and a proper instructor teaches you the habits that prevent them. At 13 you can take a Junior Open Water course, and your dad can come along or dive with you once you're certified. Borrowed adult gear often won't fit you properly anyway, so the dive shop can sort that out too.
whats the fastest way to learn a 540 i only have a weekend

Honestly, one weekend isn't enough for a 540 unless your 360s are already dialed both ways. A 540 means landing switch or blind, and rushing it on snow is a fast way to land on your head or back. If you're already solid on 360s, spend the weekend on a medium jump working clean 360s and maybe try a 540 into an airbag if your resort has one. Otherwise put the weekend into perfecting your 360 and save the 540 for next season.
Is it fine to skip the avalanche course if I just watch a bunch of YouTube videos? Courses are expensive.

Videos are a decent primer, but they can't replace the field day where you practice companion rescue under time pressure and dig real snowpits with an instructor correcting you. A recreational Level 1 or AIARE 1 course is the single best investment you'll make in backcountry skiing, and many shops, clubs and avalanche centers offer discounts or scholarships. Use the videos to prep so you get more out of the course, not to replace it.
what's the quickest way to get over my fear of heights so I can solo

There isn't a safe shortcut here, because in soloing your fear works as a gauge that tells you when your margin is too thin. You can train it into something calmer through lots of exposure on rope, like leading routes well below your limit and taking practice falls, so height feels familiar rather than paralyzing. Aim to feel calm and in control on rope, not to switch the fear off entirely, and expect that to take seasons rather than weeks.
how do pros tuck so low

A good tuck comes from flexibility and practice: your front knee goes into the back of your back knee, chest down on your front thigh, and arms tucked behind your back. Practice it on flat ground and gentle slopes until it feels natural and you can hold it without wobbling. Keep in mind a tighter tuck means more speed, so only work on it once your braking can handle the extra speed.
What's the deal with not holding your breath? Like why exactly

As you ascend, the air in your lungs expands, and if you hold your breath it has nowhere to go. That can overexpand and tear lung tissue and push air bubbles into your bloodstream, which is called an arterial gas embolism and can be fatal even from a few meters. Keep breathing slowly and continuously, and if you're ever without a regulator, exhale gently the whole way up.
My 19yo son wants to start AFF and I'm a wreck. How can I tell if a dropzone is legit?

In the US, look for USPA Group Member status, which means the dropzone agrees to follow basic safety requirements. Check that instructors hold current ratings, that student gear has AADs, and that the place looks organized rather than rushed. Visit with your son, watch a few loads, and ask about their student-to-instructor ratio and ground school length. A good dropzone will happily answer all of that.
My dive computer died mid-trip. Can I just follow my buddy's computer?

Not really, because a computer tracks one diver's exact depth profile and nitrogen loading, and yours will never match your buddy's exactly. The safer route is to rent or buy a replacement. Most dive centers recommend sitting out 24 hours before you start diving with a fresh computer, since it doesn't know about your earlier dives. Keeping a cheap backup computer on future trips avoids this headache.
I froze halfway up an easy solo yesterday and had to downclimb shaking. Does that mean I'm not cut out for it?

It means your brain gave you an honest warning that your preparation and margin weren't enough for that day, which is valuable information rather than a character flaw. I'd stop soloing for now and go back to climbing that terrain on rope until it feels boringly routine, then think hard about whether soloing is giving you something you can't get elsewhere. Downclimbing safely while shaking was the right call, and that judgment is worth more than any send. Talking it through with an experienced climbing partner could also help you understand what happened.
Can I surf big waves with asthma?

Plenty of athletes manage asthma in demanding sports, but big-wave surfing puts huge pressure on your breathing and breath-hold. Talk to a doctor, ideally one with sports medicine experience, about whether your asthma is well controlled and how to manage it in the water. Carry your inhaler on the beach or boat and let your crew know about it.
do i need to be strong before starting

Nope, parkour itself builds strength, and beginner classes scale everything to your level. That said, adding basic strength work like squats, push-ups, and hanging from a bar will make progress quicker and help protect your joints. Start where you are and let strength grow alongside your technique.
Is it ok to tie myself to my kayak so I don't lose it when I swim?

No, never tie yourself to your boat or anything else in moving water. If the boat pins or gets caught in a hydraulic, a tether can drag you under and hold you there. Let the boat go, take care of yourself first, and gear can be recovered later.
how do i clear a double jump faster, im scared of casing it

Casing comes from not carrying enough speed, so the fix is building up gradually rather than going for it all at once. Roll the jump a bunch of times to learn the face and landing, then start hitting it with a bit more speed each lap until you're landing just short of the backside, and only then commit to clearing it. Watch a rider who clears it consistently and note what gear and where they start their run, and if you're unsure, ask them to pace you.
My friend soloed a route last weekend and wants me to come next time. I've only climbed in a gym for 6 months.

Say no to soloing, and suggest climbing that same route together on a rope. Six months of gym climbing doesn't prepare you for outdoor rock, which has loose holds, polished sections, and route finding that gyms never teach. A good friend won't pressure you, and if they do, take that as a red flag. Ask them to teach you outdoor leading or anchor building, which gets you outside together safely.
I got held down two waves at Waimea last week and now I'm scared to go back. Is that normal?

Totally normal, and honestly it's a healthy response to something genuinely dangerous. A lot of big-wave surfers say a two-wave hold-down changed how seriously they trained afterward. Build your confidence back with breath-hold work, fitness and some smaller days at the bay before you charge again. If the fear sticks around, talking to experienced surfers or a sports psychologist can help a lot.
What's the fastest way to heal a mild wrist sprain? Climbing trip in 2 weeks

For a genuinely mild sprain, rest it from loading for the first few days, then start gentle range-of-motion work and light grip exercises once the sharp pain eases. Ice early on and a compression wrap can help with swelling. Ease back with easy routes and open-hand grips before you try crimps or underclings. If the pain is still sharp, you have trouble gripping, or the pain sits on the thumb side of your wrist, get it checked, because scaphoid fractures often masquerade as sprains.
short answer: free solo or no?

If you're asking, then no, at least not yet. People who solo responsibly have years of roped experience, rehearse routes thoroughly, and climb far below their limit. Build that base on a rope first. The climbing will still be there.
Is it okay to do parkour in running shoes or do I need special ones?

You don't need dedicated parkour shoes to start, but standard running shoes with thick foam heels and slick tread are a poor match. Look for something with a flat, grippy rubber sole and a fairly thin midsole so you can feel edges, which is why lots of traceurs use cheap skate shoes or minimalist trainers. Bulky heels make precision landings wobbly and can roll an ankle on rail and wall work. Expect to burn through shoes quickly, so cheap and grippy beats expensive and cushioned.
im 14 and really good at bouldering, like V6. can i start soloing easy routes

V6 at 14 is seriously impressive, but soloing tall routes is a different skill from bouldering. Outdoor rock brings loose holds, weather, and route-finding decisions that strength can't solve. Join a youth climbing team, learn to lead and climb outdoors with coaches, and keep pushing bouldering, where your talent could take you a long way. The climbers you look up to built years of roped experience first.
hey so I hit my head pretty hard skating an hour ago, I had a helmet, feel kinda foggy and nauseous but I'm fine right? gonna keep skating

Please stop skating for today, because fogginess and nausea after a head hit are classic concussion signs, even with a helmet on. Have someone stay with you, and get seen by a doctor today, and go to the ER right away if you vomit, get worse headaches, feel confused or very drowsy, or notice unequal pupils. A second hit while concussed can be really dangerous, so give it rest and get cleared before you ride again. Also replace that helmet, since most are designed to take only one serious impact.
my 9 year old wants to drop in on the 6 foot quarter pipe at the park after one week of skating, should I let him?

Not yet. A week in, most kids haven't built the balance or the habit of committing their weight forward, and leaning back is how drop-in falls turn into hard slams onto the coping or the tailbone. Have him practice on a 2 to 3 foot ramp first, with a helmet and pads. He should only move up once he's landing it every time without hesitating, and a few lessons from a park coach will speed that up a lot.
Going solo tomorrow on a short tour. Totally low angle. Anything I should do?

Low-angle solo touring can be reasonable if you really stay off and out from under anything near 30 degrees, since runouts from steep terrain above can still reach you. Leave a detailed trip plan with someone and a turnaround time, and carry a satellite messenger if there's no cell service. Still bring your beacon, shovel and probe, because they help searchers find you and let you help someone else you come across.
need a quick answer: can i wingsuit with a student canopy

Generally no. You want a canopy suited to wingsuiting, which usually means a docile, reliable main with good opening characteristics, often a size or two larger than you'd jump otherwise. Student canopies can work in some setups, but you should get a rigger or wingsuit coach to approve your exact gear before your first flight.
I'm good at regular, is it worth learning switch for tricks?

Absolutely. Riding switch makes 180s, 540s, and landing tricks backward way easier, and it improves your balance overall. Start on easy groomers, focus on smooth turns, and keep your weight centered just like when riding regular. Riding switch on mellow terrain for a few runs each day builds it up surprisingly fast.
Can I take ibuprofen during a hot ultra for my knees?

Skip it during the race, because NSAIDs combined with dehydration and heat significantly raise the risk of acute kidney injury and hyponatremia. If you need something mid-race, acetaminophen at standard doses is generally the safer choice, though it's worth checking with your doctor. Better still, figure out what's causing the knee pain in training so you're not masking a problem for 30 hours.
Quick one: flats or clipless for learning downhill?

Flats, with grippy shoes like Five Tens. They let you dab a foot or bail easily, and they force you to learn proper weighting instead of pulling on the pedals. Plenty of pros still race on flats, so you'll never outgrow them. Try clipless later if you want, once your fundamentals are solid.
My teen keeps riding without gloves. big deal?

Yes, gloves matter. Hands are usually the first thing to hit the ground in a crash, and gloves protect against road rash and gravel. They also improve grip and reduce hand fatigue on long runs. Thin full-finger downhill gloves are light enough that most riders forget they're wearing them.
I've been doing static apnea on my bed at night and hit 4:30. Next step is trying it in the bathtub. Thoughts?

Don't do it. Dry static on land is fairly low risk because if you black out you just start breathing again, but in a bathtub the same blackout means your face is underwater with nobody there to lift it out. Once you move breath-holds into water you need a trained buddy within arm's reach every time, so take your 4:30 to a pool session with a club or instructor.
ankle or body harness which is safer

Both are safe when a reputable operator fits them properly, and many sites use the two together as a backup. Ankle attachment gives the classic head-first dive but puts more strain on your legs and back. A body harness spreads the load across your torso, so it's often the better pick if you have knee, ankle or back issues. Tell the staff about any injuries and let them recommend the setup.
My 9 year old is obsessed with bouldering. Is it safe for kids her age?

Bouldering is a great sport for kids and gym injuries are fairly uncommon, especially when the floor is well padded and she climbs routes suited to her level. Teach her to downclimb or jump with bent knees rather than falling flat, and to keep the fall zone clear of other climbers. Many gyms run youth programs with coaches, which is the best way to build good habits early and keep her from overtraining her still-developing fingers.
Can I lift legs with a hamstring strain? Grade 1 apparently.

Yes, with modifications. Grade 1 strains usually do better with early, pain-free loading than with complete rest. Leg press, split squats and isometric hamstring holds at low intensity are generally fine if they stay under about a 3 out of 10 on the pain scale. Avoid heavy deadlifts, Nordic curls and sprinting until you can do them without pain. Build up over two to three weeks, because rushing back to sprinting is the classic way to re-tear it.
Why do cave divers obsess over a continuous guideline to the surface?

Because in a silt-out you can go from perfect visibility to zero in seconds, and the line is the only reliable way back. Keeping a continuous guideline from open water means you can follow it out by touch even blind and without lights. Many fatalities involved a gap in the line or no line at all, so that habit is non-negotiable.
What do I wear for my first tandem??

Wear comfortable, weather-appropriate clothes you can move in, like athletic pants and a fitted top, plus sneakers that lace up securely. Skip sandals, hooded tops and loose jewelry. The dropzone will usually give you a jumpsuit, goggles and sometimes a helmet. It's colder at altitude, so add a light layer on a cool day.
Pregnant, 10 weeks. Already paid for a jump as a birthday gift. Can I still go?

Skip this one, because dropzones universally refuse pregnant jumpers due to the hard opening shock and landing impact. Call them and explain, since most will happily convert it to a gift voucher or postpone it. It'll be a great thing to look forward to after the baby arrives.
Do I really need a continuous guideline if the cave passage is big and obvious?

Yes, every time, no exceptions. Big passages can black out completely in seconds if someone stirs up silt, and a cave that looks obvious going in looks very different on the way out. A continuous line from open water is the single most important rule in cave diving, and many dead divers were in caves they thought they knew.
How do I know if the wind is ok for a cliff jump

You want light, steady wind, ideally coming up the face or crossing it gently. Tailwinds pushing you toward the wall, gusty conditions and rotors near cliff edges are the major hazards. Experienced jumpers use wind meters, streamers and their own knowledge of how a specific cliff behaves at different times of day. If the conditions don't feel right, walking down is always the correct call, and nobody serious will judge you for it.
tides matter??

Absolutely. A spot that's deep at high tide can be dangerously shallow a few hours later, sometimes by several meters. Check a tide chart, scout the depth on the same tide you plan to jump, and keep an eye on surge and swell pushing water away from the base.
I'm at 140 jumps and feel super confident. Can I just buy a beginner suit and teach myself?

Hold off until you hit 200 jumps and then take a proper First Flight Course with a certified wingsuit instructor. Self-taught first flights are where people get into trouble with arm tension during deployment, poor exits that tumble them into the tail, and lost altitude awareness. The course is usually a day or two and a handful of jumps, and it's the cheapest insurance you'll ever buy.
Lost my buddy at 15m in bad viz. What's the right move, keep looking?

The standard rule is to search for no more than about one minute, slowly turning in place and looking for bubbles or lights. If you don't find them, make a normal slow ascent with a safety stop, and they should do the same so you meet up at the surface. Agree on this plan with your buddy during every predive briefing so you both know what to do.
Quick one, flying a wingsuit, which way do I exit relative to the plane?

Exit facing into the relative wind with your head toward the front of the plane, keeping your wings closed until you're clear of the tail. Opening too early can push you up into the tail, which is a serious hazard. Your First Flight Course covers the exit for your specific aircraft, so follow that briefing exactly.
is paragliding more dangerous than skydiving

They're roughly in the same ballpark, though they're hard to compare directly because the risks are different. Skydiving's risks are concentrated in a short window, while paragliding involves longer flights and is much more affected by weather judgement and pilot decisions. In both, the biggest safety factors are good training, conservative choices about conditions, and well-maintained gear. Most accidents involve pilots pushing beyond their skill or flying poor conditions.
whats the fastest way to stop on a longboard going downhill

The most reliable stop at real speed is a pre-drift or Coleman slide, where you turn the board sideways with a gloved hand down and scrub off speed. It takes practice on a mellow hill before you can trust it, so learn foot braking first for lower speeds. If you can't stop from a given speed yet, you shouldn't be going that speed: the hill dictates nothing, your braking skill does.
I've got 30 hours. Ready for an EN-C wing? It looks way faster.

Almost certainly not. EN-C wings require active piloting and react more aggressively to collapses, which takes hundreds of hours and usually an SIV course to handle safely. Most pilots spend a few seasons on an EN-A or low EN-B before moving up. Ask your instructor for an honest assessment, because the speed won't help if you can't manage the wing.
found a guy on facebook doing bridge bungee for $40, way cheaper than the park. worth it?

Skip it. A $40 bridge jump from a random Facebook seller almost certainly means no insurance, no inspected equipment, and no proper calculation of cord stretch for your weight, and those are exactly the things that keep people alive. The price difference at a licensed operator pays for trained staff, retired-on-schedule cords and real safety checks, which is not where you want to save money.
Tire pressure for DH? Running 35 psi front and rear, feels fast.

35 psi is too high for downhill and will cost you grip and control, especially in corners and on roots. Most riders run roughly 22 to 28 psi depending on body weight, tire casing, and whether they use inserts. Go a little lower in front than in the rear. If you burp air or feel the rim hitting rocks, add a couple of psi or switch to a tougher casing instead of pumping the tires back up to road pressure.
what tire pressure for downhill, I weigh about 80kg running 2.5 tires with dual ply casings

A good starting point for you is around 24 to 26 psi in the rear and 21 to 23 in the front, then adjust from there. Go up a couple of psi if you feel the rim hitting rocks or the tire squirming in turns, and down a little if the bike pings off roots and loses grip. Inserts like CushCore let you run slightly lower pressure without risking rim damage, which is worth considering on rough tracks.
do slide gloves really matter or can i use gardening gloves

They really matter. Gardening gloves will wear through in a couple of slides and offer no protection when you put your hand down at speed. Slide gloves have hard plastic pucks on the palm that let your hand glide on the pavement and keep you from losing skin. A cheap pair works fine for beginners.
Had a couple beers, spot is right here and everyone else is doing it. 8 meters, I've done it before sober. Fine right?

I'd wait on this one. Alcohol slows your reactions, throws off your body position in the air and makes cold water much more dangerous, and a lot of serious cliff jumping injuries involve drinking. The spot will still be there tomorrow, and you'll enjoy it more when you can actually control your entry.
Are there any free solo courses?

Reputable guides and schools don't offer free solo courses, since no instructor can make a ropeless fall survivable. What does exist are courses in rope soloing, deep water soloing trips and highball bouldering clinics, all of which deliver much of the same feeling. For a solid base, look for AMGA, IFMGA or national-association certified guides in your area.
What's a silt-out and how bad is it really?

A silt-out is when fine sediment on the floor, walls or ceiling gets kicked up and drops visibility to nothing, sometimes in a single careless fin kick. It's very serious because you lose sight of your buddy, the line and the exit all at once. Trained cave divers prevent it with good trim, frog kicks and careful positioning, and they practice following the line blind, with eyes closed, so a silt-out doesn't turn into panic.
skip the leash or use leashes on tools? beginner

Most people climb leashless now, and it's worth learning that way from the start. It makes placing screws and switching hands much easier. Some beginners like umbilical tethers clipped to their harness so they can't drop a tool on their belayer, which is a reasonable middle ground. Either way, practice on toprope first so you build grip technique and don't overgrip and pump out.
