Look for play in the headset and pivot bearings, oily or leaking suspension seals, worn brake pads and rotors, and dented rims. Factor in the cost of a suspension service, and if you're unsure, pay a local shop to look it over before buying.
quickest way to get good at downhill

Get a few coaching sessions early, then rack up lots of laps on trails just slightly below your limit. Fundamentals like body position, braking and cornering improve faster with consistent clean reps than with scary attempts on features beyond your skill. Filming yourself or riding behind faster friends will also show you your mistakes quickly. Progress steadily, because a big crash can set you back months.
We're a group of four, should we all ski the line together to save time?

No, ski one at a time in avalanche terrain. Exposing all four of you at once means one slide could bury everyone and leave no one to dig. Have each person go to a safe spot out of the runout, ideally where the others can see them, before the next skier drops in. It costs a few minutes but it's one of the simplest, most effective safety habits there is.
I've been climbing 6 months in the gym and I want to free solo something outdoors this summer. Where do I start?

Start by climbing outdoors on a rope, because six months of gym climbing hasn't taught you to read real rock, judge friction or recognize loose holds. Most people who solo seriously have years of outdoor experience and only solo routes far below their roped limit that they've already climbed many times. Spend this summer leading and top-roping outside with an experienced partner or a guide, and you'll find out quickly how different it is from plastic.
I've done my first flight course. Can I jump with friends in a group right away?

Hold off on unorganized group flying for now. Most coaches recommend at least 10 to 20 solo flights, or a few flights with a coach, before trying formation flying. When you do start group jumps, go with an organized load where an experienced leader briefs the plan, spacing and breakoffs.
what's the deal with inflatable vests for big waves, are they actually worth it

Yes, they're worth it and pretty much standard kit for anyone surfing serious size now. A CO2 inflation vest can pull you to the surface after a bad wipeout or help you float if you're knocked out. Practice pulling the cord in the pool so it's instinct, check your cartridges before every session, and remember it's a backup to fitness and breath-hold training, not a replacement.
Are knee braces a good idea for jumps?

If you've had a knee injury, a properly fitted brace can help, and it's worth asking a doctor or physical therapist which kind suits you. For healthy knees, they're not usually needed, and strength and good landing technique matter more. Bend your knees on landing and keep your weight centered so your legs absorb impact rather than locking straight.
My jumps are logged but only 90 of them were in the last two years, older ones are like 8 years ago. Do I qualify?

Technically you may have the total, but USPA recommends 200 jumps within the previous 18 months, and the reasoning is current skills. After an 8-year gap, I'd treat yourself as a lower-jump-count skydiver and build up recent jumps first. Talk to a wingsuit coach at your dropzone, and they'll tell you what you need.
My 9 year old wants to start bouldering at the gym. Is that safe for kids? I'm kind of nervous about the falls.

Bouldering is a great sport for kids, and gyms are about as controlled as it gets, with thick padded flooring and walls built for falling. The main risks are landing awkwardly and someone walking under another climber, so teach your kid to climb down instead of jumping from the top and to keep the fall zones clear. Many gyms run youth intro sessions or kids' teams that teach falling technique properly, and that's worth doing at the start. Stay close and spot for the first few visits until those habits stick.
how long should i wait to climb after spraining my ankle

It depends on how bad the sprain was, but most mild sprains need at least two to four weeks before you can safely land from bouldering or take lead falls. Top-roping with careful foot placements may be okay a bit sooner if walking is pain-free, but avoid jumping off boulders until the ankle is fully stable. If there was significant swelling or bruising, or you couldn't bear weight, see a doctor or physical therapist to rule out a fracture or ligament tear.
My partner wants to ski the couloir solo while I wait at the top as lookout. Good compromise?

Skiing one at a time is good practice, but it only works if the watcher can actually see the whole line and get to the runout quickly with gear. If the couloir doglegs out of view or you'd have to descend the same slide path to reach them, the plan has holes. Agree on safe zones, keep radios on, and if conditions are questionable, the real compromise is picking a different line.
I've got a big race next week but bruised ribs from a crash. Ride or skip?

Get them checked first. Bruised ribs can actually be cracked, and a hard landing on a fractured rib can cause serious damage. If a doctor says it's only bruising, you might be fine to ride a light practice, but be honest about how much breathing and twisting hurts. Racing hurt usually means riding badly and crashing again, so there's no shame in skipping one race to protect the rest of your season.
is it worth paying for an ice climbing course or can I just learn from youtube and friends

Videos are great for reinforcing technique, but they can't watch your feet, tell you a screw placement is sketchy, or show you how to read ice and conditions in real time. A two- or three-day course with a certified guide gives you a solid base in movement, anchors, screws, V-threads, and hazard assessment, and you'll avoid bad habits that are hard to break later. After that, climbing with experienced friends is a great way to keep building skills. Think of the course as the foundation and everything else as practice on top of it.
Buddy's out of air and we're 400ft in, what's the protocol?

Give them your long hose right away, keep your backup necklace regulator in your own mouth, and both head out along the line, with the out-of-air diver usually in front. Move steadily but don't rush, since gas consumption climbs with stress. This is why rule of thirds planning exists, so there's enough gas for both of you to exit. If you aren't drilling this regularly with your team, start now.
Is it legal to BASE jump in national parks in the US?

In most US national parks it's prohibited, and you can face fines, gear confiscation or arrest. A few places allow legal jumping, most famously the Perrine Bridge in Twin Falls, Idaho, which is where many people do their first course. Stick with legal sites, especially early on, because hurrying an illegal jump to avoid getting caught leads to bad decisions.
Can I dive with nitrox without the nitrox course if the shop doesn't check?

Don't. Nitrox has a maximum operating depth set by oxygen toxicity, and going past it can cause a seizure underwater, which is usually fatal. The course also teaches you to analyze your own tank, so you're not trusting a mislabeled fill. It's typically a short course with mostly theory, so just get it done.
How deep can I go on air in a cave?

Many cave training agencies set a ceiling around 30 meters on air, because narcosis gets worse with depth and dulls exactly the thinking you need in a complex overhead environment. Beyond that, trimix with reduced nitrogen is the standard, along with the advanced training to plan it. Gas density is another reason to stay shallow on air, since thick gas at depth makes CO2 buildup more likely.
can i just watch youtube videos and teach myself to lead climb outdoors

Videos are fine for background, but lead climbing outside is where small mistakes get serious. The risky moments are back-clipping, z-clipping, rope behind your leg, and the lower-off at the anchor. You won't notice any of those without someone experienced watching you. Take a lead course at a gym, then spend a few days outside with a guide or a seasoned mentor before going out with only peers.
Feeling really low lately and climbing without a rope is the only thing that makes me feel alive. Is that bad?

I'm glad you said this, and I'm going to take it seriously. When you're feeling low, seeking out risks where one mistake could be fatal is a real warning sign. Please talk to a doctor, therapist, or someone you trust soon, and if you ever feel unsafe with yourself, call or text a crisis line such as 988 in the US. Stick to roped climbing for now with people who care about you, since climbing with others can be part of feeling better.
What's the deal with the altimeter? Instructor kept harping on it.

They harp on it because losing track of altitude is one of the most common ways students get into trouble. Freefall feels timeless, so the altimeter is your only reliable check, and you should glance at it constantly and know your break-off and deployment heights cold. Make checking it a reflex and you'll have one less thing to worry about.
my wrists hurt after practicing vaults, should i just push through

Don't push through it, because wrist pain from vaults is often a sign of overloading tendons that aren't conditioned yet, and ignoring it can turn into a weeks-long injury. Back off on vaulting for a few days and add wrist prep to every session: circles, palm-and-back stretches, and easy weight shifts on all fours. Ease back in with lower volume. If the pain is sharp, swollen, or still there after a week of rest, get it looked at by a physio or doctor.
Detailed one: we're planning a 3-day hut trip in the Alps in February, intermediate tourers, two of us have AIARE 1. Guide or not?

For multi-day high Alpine terrain with glaciers involved, I'd hire an IFMGA guide, at least for this first trip. Navigation in whiteout, crevasse rescue, and unfamiliar snowpack and forecasting systems are all a step beyond what AIARE 1 covers. You'll learn a ton, the guide will adapt routes to conditions, and next time you'll be much better placed to do something similar on your own.
My 17 year old son wants to go ski touring with his friends this weekend. None of them have avalanche training. Should I let him?

Not into avalanche terrain, no. The good news is that's a fixable problem rather than a flat no forever. If they want to go this weekend, steer them toward a resort uphill route or low-angle terrain with nothing steep above or around it. Then get him into an AIARE 1 or equivalent course this season, ideally with a friend or two, and make sure they all own and practice with a beacon, shovel and probe before they head out on real backcountry lines.
Kid swallowed a bunch of lake water and is now coughing a bit. Should I worry?

A bit of coughing right after swallowing water is common, but if water got into the lungs it's worth watching closely for the next few hours. Get medical help straight away if the coughing continues, or if your child seems short of breath, unusually sleepy, confused, or develops a fever. If you're unsure, it's always fine to call a doctor or a nurse line to get them checked.
Is deep water soloing a safer way to get into free soloing?

Deep water soloing is a great way to enjoy climbing without a rope, but it's its own discipline, not a stepping stone. It still has real hazards: shallow water, hidden rocks, bad landings from height, tides, and cold water shock. Go with experienced locals who know the venue, check the depth at the current tide, keep your height modest, and learn to fall feet-first. Treat it as a fun sport in its own right, and it's genuinely one of the best ways to climb ropeless.
Is it okay to BASE jump with a broken pinky finger splinted?

Probably not, because BASE leaves no margin for anything that affects your grip, your toggle control or a fast reach for your pilot chute, and a splinted finger does exactly that. A landing or object strike could also complicate the fracture. Wait until it's healed and your grip strength is back, since a small injury isn't worth compromising a sport with zero room for error.
pads look lame, do pros even wear them?

Lots of pros wear them, especially in vert, bowl and park contests, where pads and helmets are often mandatory. Street skaters tend to skip them, but they also have years of falling experience you don't. Low-profile knee pads can go under pants and nobody notices. Looking cool means nothing if a broken wrist keeps you off the board for two months.
how do I know when I'm ready to climb outside after gym

If you can belay confidently, tie in without thinking, and climb mid-grades at the gym, you're ready to try outside with someone experienced. Outdoor climbing adds anchors, cleaning, loose rock, and weather judgment, and the gym doesn't teach any of those. A guided day or a transition-to-outdoors course is the fastest safe way to bridge the gap.
i solo stuff at my local crag all the time with headphones in, helps me focus

I'd lose the headphones, because they cut off sounds that warn you about rockfall, other climbers shouting, or a hold creaking under your weight. Many soloists also say that hearing their own breathing is one of their best cues for noticing fear or fatigue early. If music helps you focus, use it during your warm-up and approach, then take it out before you leave the ground.
can i mix pump gas with race fuel to save money in my 2 stroke

Usually yes, as long as the mix keeps the octane your engine needs and you use the right premix oil at the correct ratio. Running octane that's too low in a high-compression two-stroke can cause detonation and burn a hole in the piston. If your bike runs fine on premium pump gas per the manual, you may not need race fuel at all. Whatever you run, keep the jetting matched to it.
Is indoor skydiving worth it before doing the real thing?

Definitely. Wind tunnel time is one of the best investments for AFF students, because a few minutes of tunnel teaches body position and stability that would take many jumps to learn in the sky. It's also cheaper per minute of freefall time. Book a coached session and tell the coach you're starting AFF, so they focus on a stable arch and heading control.
Concussion from a mountain bike crash 5 days ago. Headache mostly gone. Ok to ride the easy trails this weekend?

Not yet. Mostly gone isn't gone, and a second hit before the brain recovers can cause much more serious and longer-lasting injury. Concussion return follows a staged process: light activity like walking first, then harder exercise, and technical riding only once you're symptom-free at each stage, ideally with a doctor's clearance. Even easy trails carry crash risk, so give it the full process. Most people are back in a couple of weeks when they don't rush it.
what's a v-thread and should i trust it

A V-thread, or Abalakov, is an anchor made by drilling two angled holes in the ice with a screw so they meet in a V, then threading cord through and tying it off. In good, thick, solid ice they're strong and are the standard way to rappel without leaving screws. They're only as good as the ice, so never trust one in thin, aerated, or rotten ice, and back it up with a screw for the first person down. Practice building them with an experienced partner before relying on one.
Is an airbag pack worth the money or is it just a gimmick

It isn't a gimmick, because airbags do noticeably reduce the chance of a full burial when you deploy them, which is a big deal since burial is what kills most people. They do nothing against trauma from hitting trees or rocks, though, and they won't help in a terrain trap where the debris piles up deep. If the budget allows, buy one, but never let it make you take on slopes you'd otherwise avoid.
If I get caught in an avalanche, should I try to swim?

Yes, fight hard to stay near the surface by swimming and trying to grab trees or rocks. As the slide slows, push one hand toward the surface and use the other to clear an airspace in front of your face. That said, the real goal is to avoid getting caught in the first place, so prioritize good terrain choices and forecast awareness.
Is soloing easy slab safer than soloing steep stuff?

Not necessarily. Slab feels secure because it's low-angle, but you're often relying on friction rather than positive holds, and a single slipped smear can turn into an unstoppable slide or tumble. Heat, dust, lichen and worn rubber can all wreck friction unpredictably. Some climbers actually find slab soloing scarier for exactly that reason, so rehearse any slab on rope in conditions similar to your solo day.
I want to go to 40m next week, I've only got open water. How do I do it without the deep course, any tips?

Hold off. Open water certification limits you to 18 meters, and 40 meters brings much stronger nitrogen narcosis, faster gas consumption, decompression obligations and far less margin for error. Do Advanced Open Water and then the Deep Diver specialty, which takes you deeper step by step with an instructor alongside you. You'll get to 40 meters properly trained, and you'll actually enjoy the dive.
I keep freezing at the exit point. Should I just force myself to go?

No, because a forced exit where your body isn't committed can lead to a tumble, a bad pitch, and a dangerous opening. Freezing is information, so step back, talk it through with your mentor, and work on the process with ground rehearsals or lower, simpler objects. Most experienced jumpers have walked away from exits, and the habit of only going when you're fully ready will keep you alive.
board for mavericks? got a 7'2 i love

Your 7'2 is going to get you nowhere at Mavericks. You'll struggle to get in early enough on those big, fast-moving swells, and late takeoffs there end badly. Most surfers ride something around 9'6" to 10'6" built as a proper gun with extra thickness and glass. Talk to a shaper who knows the spot about matching it to your weight and skill.
Can I jump if I'm 5 weeks pregnant? Nobody would know.

Skip this one until after the pregnancy. Every reputable operator excludes pregnant jumpers because the sudden deceleration and the harness pressure carry real risks, even early on. The jump will still be there later, and you'll be able to enjoy it without the worry.
What's the deal with wind limits for students? The DZ cancelled my jump and it looked fine to me.

Students usually get stood down somewhere around 14 to 18 mph, or less when it's gusty. Your canopy is big and slow, so strong or turbulent wind can push you backward, cause hard landings, or carry you off target. Wind at altitude and gusts near the ground often feel very different from what you notice standing in the parking lot. Trust the call, because instructors would much rather send you up than refund you.
What's the difference between free soloing and free climbing? People keep mixing them up.

Free climbing means you climb using only your hands and feet for upward progress, but you still use a rope and protection to catch a fall. Free soloing means no rope or protection at all, so any fall from height is likely fatal. Most climbers you see on crags are free climbing, and it's one of the safest ways to climb outdoors when done with good technique and gear.
I'm 52 and finally have 300 skydives. Too old to start BASE?

Age alone doesn't rule you out, and people do start BASE in their fifties. What matters is fitness, landing skills and how well your body handles hard landings, since rough landings are the most common BASE injury. Take a First Jump Course, start on a forgiving bridge, and be honest with yourself about your knees and ankles.
I keep soloing the easy approach slabs to get to routes. Like 4th class, 200 ft. That's normal right?

Scrambling 4th class unroped is common on approaches, but common doesn't mean safe, and plenty of accidents happen exactly there. Think about the conditions: wet rock, sand, loose blocks, pine needles and tired legs on the way down. Rope up or short-fix any section where a slip wouldn't end with you stopping yourself, and remember that descending is usually sketchier than going up.
Thunderstorm forecast for late afternoon, can I squeeze in a morning flight?

Possibly, but only with a hard cutoff and a lot of attention to the sky. Storms can develop earlier than forecast, and gust fronts and cloud suck can hit miles ahead of the visible storm. If you fly, land well before any towering cumulus starts building, and if clouds are already growing tall by late morning, don't launch at all. Plenty of experienced pilots have been caught out by 'just one more thermal.'
Is it okay to fly a little hungover? Not drunk, just tired.

I'd skip it. Even a mild hangover slows your reactions, hurts your judgement and leaves you dehydrated, and paragliding needs quick, clear decisions, especially on launch and landing. A lot of incidents happen on days when pilots were tired or off and flew anyway. Rest, rehydrate and fly another day, because the hill will still be there.
wrists hurt after cat leaps

That usually means you're loading your wrists before they're conditioned, or catching with bent-back hands. Take a few days off cat leaps. Use the time for wrist mobility and strength work like wrist circles, rocking on all fours, and light push-up holds on your fingertips. When you go back, start on low walls and focus on absorbing with your feet first. If the pain is sharp or lasts more than a week, have a physio look at it.
is it ok to drink a couple beers before paddling? it's just a chill run

I'd save the beers for the take-out. Alcohol slows reaction time, hurts balance and makes cold water hit harder, and a large share of paddling fatalities involve it. Even a chill run can serve up an unexpected flip or a swim, so you want a clear head when it happens.
how deep can a beginner go?

Most beginner courses take you to around 10 to 20 meters, with AIDA 2 for example targeting about 12 to 16 meters. The real limit is your equalization, comfort and relaxation, not a number to chase. Add depth in small steps and turn around at the first sign of discomfort. Always dive with a trained buddy watching from above.
is mixed climbing just ice climbing on rock

Pretty much. It means climbing on a mix of ice, rock, and frozen turf with ice tools and crampons, using hooks and torques on rock features. It's really technical, the tools can pop unexpectedly, and protection is often trad gear in the rock. Get solid on ice and rock first, then try mixed on toprope or with a guide at a dry-tooling crag before leading anything serious.
I've had heat exhaustion twice on long runs. Should I give up hot ultras?

Not necessarily, but don't sign up for another one until you've seen a sports medicine doctor. Repeated heat illness can point to a fitness, acclimation, medication or underlying medical issue that's worth figuring out. With proper testing, structured heat training and a conservative pacing and cooling plan, a lot of runners do come back and race safely. Go in with a plan rather than hoping it goes better next time.
how to do a nose press

Ride slowly on a gentle, flat slope, then shift your weight over your front foot and bend your front knee until your tail lifts off the snow. Keep your back leg fairly straight, center your shoulders over the nose, and look ahead rather than down. Hold briefly at first, then return to center. Once that feels easy, try it on a wide, low box.
I got really dizzy and confused after a cold swim yesterday, lips were blue for ages. Normal?

That sounds like you got genuinely hypothermic, which isn't something to brush off. Confusion and long-lasting blue lips mean your core temperature dropped. Next time get out sooner, dress quickly in warm layers starting with your torso, sip a warm drink, and rewarm gradually instead of jumping into a hot shower. Be aware of afterdrop, where your temperature keeps falling for a while after you get out. If you had chest pain, fainting or symptoms that lingered, check in with a doctor.
Watched Dawn Wall and Free Solo. Want to do something big before I turn 30, but I've never climbed. Where do I even start?

Go to a climbing gym this week and take an intro and belay course, because a few months of regular climbing will show you how much you love it. From there, join a lead course, then do a guided outdoor day or a multi-pitch trip in a place like Red Rock or Joshua Tree. A big guided objective in a few years, like a classic multi-pitch or an alpine summit, is a realistic goal for 30. That path keeps you safe and actually builds the skills those films show.
Best way to get out of a hydraulic if I end up stuck in one?

If you're in your boat, lean downstream, brace and try to paddle out the side where the hole is weaker. If you're swimming and getting recirculated, ball up or swim down and out with the current at the bottom, or swim toward the edges, and ditch your boat if needed. Your best tool is avoiding them in the first place, especially low-head dams, which are uniformly lethal and should always be portaged.
How long should a spray skirt last? Mine's like 8 years old.

At 8 years, it's worth checking carefully. Look for cracks in the neoprene, a stretched-out tunnel, a worn or loose rand, and especially the grab loop, which must be securely attached and easy to reach because it's your exit. If the deck pops off too easily or the loop is frayed, replace it. A good skirt typically lasts several years with regular use, and swapping out a worn one is cheap peace of mind.
I'm 58 and an active skydiver with 600 jumps. Am I too old to learn wingsuit?

Plenty of people start wingsuiting in their fifties and sixties, and 600 jumps gives you an excellent base. The things that matter are reasonable shoulder mobility, overall fitness and good canopy skills, so get a check-up if you have joint or cardiac concerns. Book a First Flight Course and tell the instructor about any physical limitations so they can adjust the suit and plan.
My 12 year old wants to hit the big jumps in the terrain park after one season. Should I let him?

Not yet. Big park jumps take solid speed control, a reliable pop and clean landings, and most kids need more than one season to build that. Have him own the small and medium jumps first, landing consistently and in control. A park-specific lesson with a coach would also help, because they can tell you honestly when he's ready to move up.
I'm scared of heights but want to conquer it. Is skydiving a bad idea?

It's actually a common choice for people with a fear of heights, and many say it doesn't feel like height at all because the ground is too far away to register as a drop. The scary part tends to be the plane door, not the freefall. A tandem is the ideal way to try it, since your instructor handles everything and you just focus on breathing.
how do you stop on a street luge?

Street luge riders brake mainly with their feet, using shoes with rubber soles, often with added rubber or tire tread glued on, pressing against the pavement to scrub speed. You lower your feet gradually and evenly rather than slamming them down, which can flip you or jam an ankle. Learn this on gentle grades with experienced riders watching, because it takes practice to stop smoothly from real speed.
can i bring my gopro and hold it while i jump

Almost certainly not handheld, because a loose camera becomes a projectile at the bottom of the bounce and could hit you or someone below. Many operators will let you use a chest or head mount they've approved. Others ban personal cameras entirely and sell their own footage, so ask when you book. Don't try to sneak one on, since staff check for loose items for good reason.
I landed kinda flat on my back from like 7m and now my lower back hurts and I peed a bit of blood. Should I just rest?

Get medical attention today, not tomorrow. Blood in your urine after a hard impact can mean kidney or internal injury, and back pain after a flat landing needs checking too. If the pain worsens, or you feel faint or have numbness, go to the emergency room or call emergency services right away.
Pulley injury question. I felt a pop in my ring finger on a crimp last night and now it's swollen and hurts to bend. How soon can I climb again?

A pop, swelling and pain when you bend it suggest a pulley injury, possibly a full rupture, so see a sports doctor or hand therapist before you climb on it again. A partial strain often needs a few weeks of rest followed by gradual rehab, while a full rupture can need several months and sometimes a splint or surgery. An ultrasound is the quickest way to know which you have. Climbing on it too early is how a six-week injury becomes a six-month one, so stay off the wall until you have a diagnosis.
how do i learn a kong vault without eating the box

Start on a low, padded box or a stack of gym mats, at roughly thigh height, so a clipped toe means a soft landing instead of a faceplant. Drill the dive monkey first: two-foot takeoff, hands planted flat near the front of the box, then just pull your knees through and land on the box itself before you try clearing it. Once you're consistently tucking your knees high, push the hands further along and add a stronger shove off the surface. Keep your eyes on your hand placement, and don't move to a hard wall until you've done a few hundred clean reps on soft stuff.
Feel ready to lead my friends down a class II-III run. None of them have done it before. Ok?

Leading total beginners down class II-III is a lot of responsibility, even if you're comfortable there yourself. If something goes wrong, you'd be handling several swimmers and loose boats at once without rescue training. A better plan is to bring your friends to a beginner course or a guided trip first, and run that section with them later once they have basic skills and you have a swiftwater rescue course under your belt.
Riding in 100 degree heat this weekend, any tips?

Start hydrating the day before, and keep sipping water with electrolytes between motos rather than chugging. Ride shorter sessions, rest in the shade, and use a hydration pack if you can. Headache, dizziness, nausea, or chills mean heat exhaustion, so stop riding immediately and cool down.
My kid is 10 and begging. Any way to get her a bungee experience?

Real bungee jumping won't be an option for a 10-year-old at reputable sites, since minimum ages are usually 14 or higher. But trampoline bungee setups at fairs, adventure parks, and some malls are designed for kids, and they give that bouncy, flying feeling with low risk. Giant swings or kid-friendly zip lines can also scratch the itch. Save the real thing for when she meets the age requirement.
is ice climbing safer or more dangerous than rock climbing

It's generally considered more serious, mainly because leader falls are much more likely to cause injury, ice conditions change daily, and falling ice is a constant hazard. Top roping at a well-run ice park with a helmet is fairly low risk, though, and that's where most people start. The danger goes up a lot once you're leading or getting into backcountry routes with avalanche terrain above them.
Is it ok to film my flights with a gopro on my helmet as a newbie?

Most dropzones require around 200 jumps or a camera rating before you jump with a camera, and wingsuit pilots usually wait until they're comfortable in the suit too. Cameras add snag risk and distraction, and helmet cameras can complicate deployments and canopy problems. Get through your first several wingsuit flights without one, then add a camera once flying feels routine.
how do i do a backflip on a snowboard i've never tried flips but i'm good at jumps

Being solid on jumps is a great foundation, but don't throw your first backflip on snow. Learn the motion on a trampoline or an airbag with a coach first, ideally at a trampoline park that offers snowboard binding boards, so you can feel how hard to pop and when to tuck. Once you're landing consistently on the bag, try it on a mellow, well-built jump with a soft landing, never off a kicker you haven't hit straight many times.
Can I just take Diamox and skip the acclimatization days? Trying to save vacation time.

No. Diamox speeds up acclimatization a bit, but it doesn't replace it, and it can't stop HAPE or HACE if you climb too fast. People who use it to compress their schedule tend to get sicker higher up, where descending is harder. Keep the rest days and use Diamox as a preventive backup, ideally prescribed by a doctor who knows your itinerary.
Is there a weight limit for wingsuits?

There's no universal limit, but your weight and size affect suit choice and how it flies. Manufacturers size suits by height and build, and your gear's weight limits, including canopy and reserve, still apply. Get properly fitted through a dealer or instructor so the suit works with your body and rig.
Running solo across Death Valley next month, no crew, carrying my own water. Thoughts?

Don't do that solo and unsupported, especially in hot months. Ground temperatures there can top 70C, water needs can exceed what you can carry, and a single problem with heat or navigation can turn deadly with no one to help. If you want to run Death Valley, do it with a crew vehicle, during cooler months, and with a park permit if you need one. Have a satellite communicator either way.
How do I know if my cave instructor is any good?

Look for someone with many years of active cave diving, a solid teaching record and references from former students you can actually talk to. A good instructor keeps small class sizes, insists on skill mastery over schedules and is willing to delay certification if you're not ready. If someone promises to certify you quickly no matter what, keep looking.
I keep spraining the same ankle every season on trail runs. Just bad luck?

Probably not luck. Repeat sprains usually mean the ligaments have stretched and the ankle's balance reflexes never fully came back after the first one. A focused rehab program can make a big difference, with single-leg balance work, wobble board drills, calf and peroneal strengthening, and hopping progressions. A physio can check whether you have chronic instability. In the meantime, a brace on technical terrain helps while you rebuild.
Is highball bouldering a good step toward soloing?

Highballing does train you to commit to moves where falling hurts, and it's a big step up in mental game from regular bouldering. It carries real injury risk though, especially broken ankles, backs, and head trauma, so use plenty of pads, good spotters, and work the top moves on a rope or with a good inspection first. Treat it as its own discipline rather than as a stepping stone to soloing. Lots of highballers have no interest in going ropeless at height.
Do I need to know self-arrest for Mont Blanc via Gouter route?

Yes, you should be confident with ice axe self-arrest and crampon technique before attempting the Gouter route, since there's exposed snow and ice where a slip can be fatal. Also be aware of the Grand Couloir crossing, where rockfall kills climbers almost every year, so cross it early in the day and quickly without lingering. If you're new to alpine terrain, a short mountaineering course in Chamonix or hiring an IFMGA guide for the climb is a very sensible investment.
Do I need to sign up for anything like insurance for BASE?

Usually, yes. Most regular travel and health insurance excludes BASE jumping completely, so find coverage that explicitly covers it, and include rescue and evacuation cover, since helicopter rescues in places like Switzerland or Norway can cost tens of thousands. Read the fine print and keep your policy details on your phone and with your jump partner.
Is it ok to swim in a river after heavy rain? The water looks fine

I'd skip it for a day or two. After heavy rain, rivers can run faster than they look, carry hidden debris, and have higher levels of bacteria from runoff and sewage overflows. Many local authorities post water quality alerts, so check those before you go. Once the level has dropped and the water has cleared, it's a much safer bet.
Can I just wear a regular life jacket from my fishing boat?

Probably not a good idea for whitewater. Many fishing PFDs are bulky, ride up when you swim, or lack the snug fit and side adjustment of a whitewater vest. Get a Type III or Type V whitewater-specific PFD that's cinched tight enough that it won't slip over your head when someone pulls up on the shoulders.
how do i do a kong vault

Run in at moderate speed, plant both hands on the obstacle shoulder-width apart, and drive your hips up while tucking your knees through between your arms, then push off and land on your feet. Learn it first on a soft vault box or a low padded bench, and start with a half-kong where your feet land on the box before going all the way over. Most face-plants happen from diving too far forward or planting your hands too close to the near edge, so place them in the middle of the obstacle and keep your chin up.
Best clothing for running a hot ultra? Should I go shirtless?

Shirtless feels nice but leaves you exposed to direct sun, which adds heat load and increases sunburn risk over many hours. A loose, light-colored, lightweight technical shirt you can soak with water usually keeps you cooler. Add a wide-brimmed or legionnaire-style hat and sun sleeves you can fill with ice.
what's the best way to build jump strength?

Combine strength training with plyometrics. Squats, deadlifts and lunges build raw power. Box jumps, broad jumps and bounding train you to use that power explosively. Keep plyometric volume moderate, around 50 to 80 jumps a session, and focus on landing softly to protect your joints. Progress gradually, because tendons take longer to adapt than muscles.
Is it safe to do freediving after drinking a couple beers at lunch?

No, skip diving after drinking. Even a couple of beers impair your judgment and coordination, make you dehydrated, and can affect how your body responds to breath-holding, all of which raise the risk of blackout and injury. Save the beers for after you're done in the water.
best way to deal with jellyfish stings

Get out of the water, and rinse the area with seawater rather than fresh water, which can trigger more stinging. Carefully lift off any tentacles with a card or tweezers instead of bare hands. For many species, soaking in hot water (as hot as you can comfortably bear) helps with the pain, and in box jellyfish regions vinegar is the standard first aid. If you have trouble breathing, chest pain or a widespread reaction, call emergency services right away.
I'm asthmatic, mild, use an inhaler maybe once a month. Can I get certified?

Possibly, but it needs a proper medical assessment first. Asthma can raise the risk of lung overexpansion injuries, so many dive physicians want lung function tests and to know what triggers your symptoms, like cold or exercise. Find a doctor with dive-medicine experience, since a well-controlled case like yours often gets cleared.
What do you do if your buddy panics in a cave?

Keep yourself calm first, and stay out of reach of a flailing diver until you can approach from behind or offer your long hose. Get them breathing slowly, make eye contact, establish physical contact with them on the line, and head for the exit as a team. This is why practicing gas-sharing and touch-contact drills during training matters so much, because you want it to feel automatic.
best hat for desert ultras?

Go for a light-colored cap with a neck cape, sahara-style. It shades your neck, and you can stuff ice into it at aid stations. Ice in the hat and a bandana around your neck is one of the most effective cooling tricks out there. Look for mesh panels so heat can escape.
Is it actually dangerous to paddle class III alone if I'm a solid roller? Nobody's free this weekend.

Yes, it's genuinely risky, because a reliable roll doesn't help you if you're pinned, entrapped, or knocked unconscious, and those are exactly the situations where a partner with a throw rope saves lives. Solo boating is something very experienced paddlers choose deliberately on water far below their limit, not a weekend fallback. Post in a local paddling club group or on a regional forum, since there's almost always someone looking for a run partner. If that fails, pick an easier stretch you know well and paddle it conservatively, or just wait a week.
concrete or grass better for practicing jumps

Grass is gentler for learning rolls and practicing landings, but it can hide holes and be slippery when wet. Concrete gives better grip and a truer feel for precision, but it's unforgiving, so keep heights low and reps sensible. Many people learn a move on grass or mats and then transfer it to concrete once it's consistent. Either way, check the surface for debris and wear decent shoes.
Is it dumb to bomb a big hill on my first week skating? My friends do it and say just send it

Yeah, skip it for now, because your friends can already slow down and you almost certainly can't yet. At speed the board starts wobbling, and if you can't foot brake, carve or slide, your only way off is a high-speed fall onto asphalt. Spend the next several weeks learning to foot brake and carve on gentle slopes, then work up to steeper hills gradually with a helmet and slide gloves. The hill isn't going anywhere, and you'll enjoy it a lot more when you can actually control your speed.
We heard whumpfing all morning but the bowl looks so good. Fresh 40cm. Go or no go?

No go. Whumpfing means a weak layer is collapsing under you, which is about the clearest warning the snowpack can give. With 40 cm of new snow on top, that bowl is primed to slide. Stick to slopes under 30 degrees with nothing steep overhead today and save the bowl for when it's had time to settle.
my reserve repack is like 2 weeks overdue, the dz is busy, can i just jump a couple more times

Don't jump it. An out-of-date reserve is legally non-airworthy in the US and most other countries, and your reserve is the one piece of gear you absolutely need to trust. Ask around the dropzone for a rigger, since repacks can often be turned around in a day, or borrow or rent a current rig in the meantime.
How do I deal with getting seasick on dive boats? I barf every time.

Take a non-drowsy motion sickness medication like meclizine the night before and again in the morning, but test it on land first, since some people get drowsy and drowsiness and diving don't mix. On the boat, stay near the middle, look at the horizon, and gear up quickly so you can get in the water, where the nausea usually stops. Eat something light and skip greasy breakfasts. If you need to vomit underwater, do it through your regulator.
We're 300 vertical meters from the summit and the weather is turning but my partner REALLY wants to push. How do I talk him down?

Remind him that the summit is only halfway, and that most mountaineering deaths happen on the descent when people are exhausted and the weather has turned. Keep it concrete: agree on a hard turnaround time or weather threshold and stick to it, since the mountain will still be there next season. If he won't budge, don't let his summit fever pull you along, because staying together and getting down safely matters more than either of your egos.
Can I wear dark clothing, it's what I have

You'll be noticeably hotter in direct sun. A cheap white or light-colored loose technical shirt and arm sleeves are a worthwhile buy for a desert race. If you're stuck with dark clothes, wetting them at every aid station helps a bit.
My friend says if you jump in the ocean you should time it with the waves. Is that a thing?

Yes, it matters a lot. Jump as a swell comes in so you land in the deepest water, not when it pulls back and exposes rocks. Before you go, watch the sets for several minutes, know exactly where and how you'll get out, and skip it if the swell is big or the exit means scrambling onto wave-washed rock. Getting out is often more dangerous than the jump.
best way to learn manuals for rough sections? want to skip some chunk

Practice on flat grass or a gentle downhill car park first. Shift your hips back with straight arms rather than yanking the bars, and cover the rear brake so you can drop the front if you loop out. Once you can hold one consistently, try it over small bumps before using it on real chunk. On steep, rough terrain, staying light and letting the suspension work is often safer than trying to manual over everything.
is downhill skating dangerous?

Yes, it carries real risk because of the speeds and hard pavement, and crashes can cause road rash, broken bones or head injuries. That risk drops a lot with proper gear, skill progression and riding in controlled environments. Smart riders build up slowly and never ride beyond their ability.
Lake I swim in has blue green algae warning. It's a hot day, surely a quick dip is fine?

It's best to skip it, because blue-green algae can release toxins that cause rashes, vomiting and, in worse cases, liver or nerve problems, even after a short dip. Dogs are especially at risk, so keep them out of the water too. Find another venue with clean water for today, or check back once the warning has been lifted.
What's the easiest route to free solo for a first timer? Just looking for a name.

I won't name a route for a first solo, because no specific climb makes it safe, and the right choice depends entirely on your experience, not on the route. What I'd suggest instead is finding a classic, moderate multi-pitch you can lead comfortably and climbing it roped with a solid partner, ideally several times. If you eventually explore soloing, it should be on terrain you've rehearsed so often it feels like walking. That comes from your own long history on that rock, not from a recommendation.
whats the glide ratio on a typical wingsuit

A typical intermediate suit flown well gets roughly 2.5:1, meaning about 2.5 metres forward for every metre of descent. Big advanced suits in skilled hands can push past 3:1. Beginner suits sit lower, and real-world glide drops a lot with wind and pilot technique.
how do i roll a kayak

The roll is mostly a hip snap, not an arm movement. You set up tucked along the deck, sweep your paddle out to the surface, then flick your knee to right the boat while your head comes up last. It's very hard to learn from text, and a few pool sessions with an instructor will get you there far faster than trial and error. Learn your wet exit first so you're never stuck upside down while practicing.
I'm 52 and coming back to downhill after 15 years. What's changed and how should I ease back in?

Bikes are vastly better now: longer, slacker geometry, dropper posts and much stronger brakes make descending more stable but also faster than you'll expect. Spend your first few days on blue trails relearning how a modern bike handles, and consider a skills clinic to update your technique. Protective gear has improved too, so invest in a good full-face helmet and pads, because recovery times aren't what they were at 37.
What's the fastest way to heat acclimate? Race is in 5 days.

Five days won't get you full adaptation, but you can still gain something with daily 60-minute easy sessions in the heat or 20 to 30 minutes in a sauna right after a short run. Don't cram hard efforts in the heat this close to race day, since you'll just arrive fatigued. On race day, your biggest lever is pacing, so start noticeably slower than you'd like, use ice and wet buffs aggressively, and keep drinking and taking sodium.
Going to a flooded mine with my friends this weekend, we all have regular scuba certs. Any tips?

I'd honestly call that trip off as planned, because flooded mines are overhead environments with loose ceilings, old cables, silt and confusing tunnels, which is even riskier than natural caves. Open water certification gives you no training for any of that. If the mine is a known dive site, go with a guide who runs trips there and dive only the areas they approve, and get cave or wreck penetration training if you want to go further.
Detailed one: 300 skydives, completed FJC 3 months ago, 15 BASE jumps all on a bridge. Ready for my first cliff jump in Switzerland?

You're on a good track, but 15 bridge jumps is still very early, and cliffs bring new risks: terrain under your opening, more complex wind, and much less room for an off-heading opening. Many mentors recommend getting to 30 to 50 clean object jumps and doing a cliff progression with them before jumping independently. If you go, start on a low-consequence Lauterbrunnen exit with a local who knows it well, wait for perfect conditions, and keep your delays short.
first tandem jump next week and honestly terrified. is it normal to want to back out?

Completely normal, and almost everyone at the dropzone has felt exactly what you're feeling. Your tandem instructor has likely done thousands of jumps and handles the parachute, the altitude and the landing, so your only real job is to arch and enjoy it. If you show up and still decide not to go, that's fine too, but most people find the fear peaks in the plane and turns into pure adrenaline the second they exit.
I'm 58, decent shape, had a stent put in 3 years ago. Thinking Everest Base Camp trek next spring. Thoughts?

Lots of people in their late fifties do the EBC trek, but with a stent you need a proper conversation with your cardiologist before you book, ideally including a stress test. Thin air at 5,000-plus metres makes your heart work harder, so they may want to adjust your medications or set limits on your exertion. If they clear you, choose an itinerary of at least 12 days with acclimatization days built in, and get insurance that explicitly covers helicopter evacuation and your pre-existing condition.
What's a solid training plan if my long term goal is soloing big walls?

Think in terms of years: build a deep outdoor base in trad and multipitch, aim to climb several grades harder than anything you'd solo, and log lots of mileage on the specific rock type you're interested in. Add the mental side deliberately, through lots of runout leading within your limits and reviewing any time your nerves rattled you. Learn rope-soloing systems too, since many big wall ambitions are better and safer served by self-belayed climbing. Getting coached by an experienced guide on multipitch efficiency and retreat skills will pay off no matter where your goals go.
I'm epileptic, seizures well controlled. Allowed to jump?

Most operators list epilepsy as a condition that excludes jumping or needs medical clearance, because the sudden stress and the head rush can trigger a seizure in some people. Talk to your neurologist about your specific situation before you book anything. Be upfront with the operator too, since a seizure while hanging upside down would be very hard to manage safely.
Is it ok to ride downhill after a couple beers at lunch? Just chill laps

Skip the beers until you're done riding. Even a couple slow your reactions and dull your judgment, and downhill punishes small mistakes at speed. Many bike parks will also pull your lift pass for riding impaired. Save them for the end of the day, when they'll taste better anyway.
my buddy wants to try a gap jump we found off a cat track, said we just need to send it. thoughts?

I'd pass. Unbuilt gaps off cat tracks often have unknown landings, hidden rocks, or flat bottoms, and there's no way to judge speed without scouting it properly. People hiking or riding the track can also end up in your landing. If you want gaps, start with the smaller hits in the resort park, which are built and maintained for exactly that.
should I learn to slide before going fast

Yes, absolutely, because sliding is how you control speed on steep hills. Learn on gentle, smooth slopes at low speed with gloves and a helmet. Only add speed once you can slide predictably every time. It's the most important skill in downhill.
I want to solo something big for my 30th birthday next month. Ideas?

I'd separate the birthday from the solo, because a deadline and a symbolic date create exactly the pressure that pushes people onto routes before they're ready. For a memorable big day out, try a long classic multipitch with a good partner or guide, a deep water soloing trip, or a scenic alpine ridge in good conditions. Big adventures on a rope can feel just as epic, and you'll want plenty more birthdays to celebrate them.
my 9 year old wants a skateboard for his birthday, is it actually safe or am i setting him up for a broken arm

Skateboarding is a reasonable sport for a 9-year-old as long as you set it up right, and most injuries in kids come from falls on the wrist and elbow that good gear largely prevents. Get him a certified helmet that fits snugly, plus wrist guards, elbow pads and knee pads, and have him start on smooth flat pavement away from traffic. A complete board from a real skate shop will roll far more predictably than a toy-store one, which makes him less likely to get thrown. A couple of beginner lessons will also teach him how to fall properly, which is the single most useful skill he can learn early.
My 10 yo is begging to try scuba on our Mexico trip. Is that too young?

Ten is fine for a supervised try-dive or a Junior Open Water course, usually limited to about 12 meters with an instructor or parent close by. The key things are that your child genuinely wants to do it, can stay calm and listen, and isn't pushed if they're nervous. Choose a reputable shop that does lots of kids' programs and has a low instructor-to-student ratio.
What's the best way to sight in open water? I keep zigzagging.

Lift your eyes just above the surface at the start of your breathing stroke, glance forward like a crocodile, then turn your head to the side to breathe as normal. Aim to sight every six to ten strokes, and more often in chop or currents. Choose a big, fixed landmark behind the buoy, such as a building or tree, because it's easier to spot than the buoy itself. Practising bilateral breathing in the pool also helps straighten out a stroke that pulls to one side.
Can I wingsuit off a cliff if I've done 300 skydives but no BASE?

Not safely, because skydiving and BASE are different disciplines and wingsuit BASE requires both sets of skills. The normal path is a BASE first jump course, plenty of slider-up BASE jumps, and then wingsuit BASE at beginner-friendly exits with a mentor. Skipping straight to cliff wingsuit flights is exactly the shortcut that has killed experienced skydivers.
What's the deal with the knuckle on a jump?

The knuckle is where the flat top of the jump transitions into the downslope of the landing. Landing on the knuckle or just before it is hard on your knees and back because you're dropping onto flat or near-flat snow. Ideally you clear the knuckle and land on the sloped part, which absorbs your impact. If you're unsure about clearing it, it's often safer to roll the knuckle at slow speed than to come up short.
bro my leashless tools keep slipping out of my hands, should I just tape my hands to them lol

Definitely don't attach yourself to your tools that way, because you need to be able to let go if something goes wrong, like dropping a tool, avoiding falling ice, or needing to clip. Slipping usually comes from overgripping and getting pumped, wet gloves, or holding the tool too high on the shaft. Try gloves with grippy palms, relax your grip between swings, and use the pinky rest or trigger so your hand naturally locks in. Clipper leashes or umbilicals that attach tools to your harness are a fine option if you're worried about dropping them.
how long till i can fly solo

Most people reach their first solo flights within the first week or so of a beginner course, though they're still guided by radio. Getting a basic license such as a P2 or Pilot rating usually takes 10 to 20 days of training, depending on the weather and how fast you learn. Expect to spend at least a season flying conservatively at familiar sites before you go anywhere independently.
Is it ok to ride on a sprained ankle if I tape it really tight

It's not a great idea. Even taped, a sprained ankle reduces your control on the footpegs and gear shifter, and one hard landing can turn a sprain into a torn ligament or a fracture. Rest it until you can walk and hop on it without pain, and see a doctor or physio if the swelling and bruising are significant. A week or two off now beats months off later.
Night jumps, how do you get approved? I'm at 150 jumps.

You'll generally need a B license or higher and night jump training with a qualified instructor, which covers lighting, visibility, landing area recognition, and spotting in the dark. Your first night jumps should be solo with a light on your rig and a well-lit landing area. Ask your dropzone's S&TA when the next organized night jump is and how to get the training sign-off.
Is it okay to try rails without a helmet if I'm going slow?

No, wear the helmet. Rail falls are exactly when people smack their heads, because your feet go out sideways and you drop straight onto the metal or hard-packed snow, and speed has little to do with it. A helmet is cheap insurance, and a lot of parks require one anyway.
My son (19) wants to start cave diving. I'm terrified. Is this as dangerous as it sounds?

It's a genuinely serious sport, but most deaths involve people with no cave training ignoring the basic rules, and properly trained divers who follow those rules have a far better safety record. The best thing he can do is go through a structured path with a reputable instructor: solid open water experience, then cavern, intro to cave and full cave courses, without rushing the steps. You might ask him to share his training plan and instructor with you, since a good instructor will gladly explain how they manage the risk.
is it okay to ride downhill at night with a headlamp

Night riding is far riskier, because a headlamp won't show you enough of the road at speed to spot gravel, cracks or debris. Drivers also have a harder time seeing you. If you want to ride at night, stick to familiar, well-lit, low-traffic spots and keep your speeds low, or just save the real downhill sessions for daylight.
planning to jump solo at a remote cliff in the alps, no one around. any tips?

Don't jump alone. Even experienced jumpers bring a ground crew or at least one other person, because a broken leg on a scree slope with nobody to call for help can turn survivable into fatal. Jump with locals who know the exit, the landing area and the afternoon winds, and make sure someone has your plan and a way to call rescue. A solo remote jump is all downside for very little gain.
What's the difference between an EN-A and EN-B wing?

EN-A wings are the most forgiving: they resist collapses and recover from them largely on their own with little pilot input, which makes them ideal for training and early solo flying. EN-B covers a broad range, from 'low B' wings that are nearly as docile as an A to 'high B' wings that are fast, demanding and expect active piloting. Most instructors keep students on an A or low B for at least the first 50 to 100 hours. Moving up too soon is one of the classic ways pilots get hurt.
Doing a channel relay leg in August. How should I train for the cold?

Build your cold tolerance gradually from spring by swimming regularly in open water. Add a little time each week, and keep at least one long swim most weeks in water close to channel temperature, which is around 15 to 17°C in August. Do it with your training group or under supervision, not alone, and learn the early signs of hypothermia, like slurred thoughts, clumsy hands and a stroke that's falling apart. Practise warming up properly afterwards with layers and a warm drink, and avoid hot showers right away. Your relay pilot and crew will have their own requirements, so check their qualifying swim rules early.
best way to learn to stop on a skateboard

The foot brake is the one to learn first: keep your front foot planted, take your back foot off and gently drag the sole of your shoe along the ground, increasing pressure gradually. Practice at slow speeds until it becomes natural, then try the tail drag or a powerslide later on. Never rely on jumping off at speed, since that's how plenty of beginners end up face down on the pavement.
Do I actually need a helmet on class II? Feels like overkill.

Yes, wear one. Class II is exactly where people flip unexpectedly in shallow, rocky water, and your head is the first thing that hits the riverbed when you're upside down. A good whitewater helmet is light and comfortable, and every competent paddler wears one regardless of the grade.
Mile 40, stopped sweating, skin feels hot and dry, kinda foggy. Push to next aid at mile 45?

No, stop now, because hot dry skin plus confusion are warning signs of heat stroke, which is a medical emergency. Get into shade, cool yourself with any water or ice you have, and call or flag down race medical or 911 immediately. Don't walk five more miles alone in that state, since you could collapse on trail.
how do i avoid the plane tail on exit in a wingsuit

Clearing the tail is mostly about a calm, compact exit. Keep your legs closed and your arms in for the first few seconds so you drop away before opening the wings, and exit in the order and position your instructor tells you for that aircraft. Different planes have specific techniques, so get a briefing on each new aircraft before you jump it. Never try to fly away from the door with fully open wings.
my kid is 11 and wants to try whitewater kayaking. too young?

Eleven is a great age to start, and lots of clubs and paddling schools run youth programs built for exactly that. Start on flatwater or a pool to learn wet exits and basic strokes, then move to gentle class I to II with a certified instructor and a kid-sized boat and PFD that actually fit. Avoid letting them learn from an uncertified family friend on a 'fun' rapid, because that's where bad first experiences and real scares happen.
Cold water, 12°C. Can I still jump?

You can, but cold-water shock is a real risk at 12°C because the sudden gasp reflex can make you inhale water right after you go under. Get in gradually first to acclimatize, keep jumps short and near an easy exit, and wear a wetsuit if you'll be doing several. Make sure someone on the shore or in the water is watching you surface each time.
Do your ears pop during freefall? I get bad ear pain on planes.

The pressure changes fast, mostly during the climb in the plane and then under canopy as you descend. Swallow, yawn or gently equalize throughout, the same way you would on an airliner. Don't jump with a cold or blocked sinuses, because that's when ear pain can turn into real damage, so reschedule if you're congested.
Forecast is low danger. So I don't need to carry my shovel and probe, right? Trying to save weight.

Low danger doesn't mean no danger, and isolated slides still happen and still bury people. A shovel and probe weigh about a kilo combined, and without them your beacon can only point to where someone is, not get them out. Always carry all three, and find your weight savings in other parts of your gear.
How long does it take to go from first wingsuit flight to wingsuit BASE?

Realistically, it takes years, not months. Common advice is at least 200 or more wingsuit skydives plus a substantial number of regular BASE jumps before even considering wingsuit BASE. Then you still need mentorship on specific objects and starting with exits that give big margins. People who rush this timeline make up a disproportionate share of fatalities.
Do I need a reserve parachute?

Yes, once you're flying solo above training hills. A reserve is your last line of defence if the wing suffers a collapse you can't recover or a midair collision, and it's standard equipment for any licensed pilot. Get it repacked every six to twelve months as the manufacturer specifies, and practise the throw motion so you could do it without thinking.
Salt tabs or no salt tabs. Go.

Usually yes in long hot ultras, but dose them to your sweat rather than chugging blindly. A common starting range is 300 to 600 mg of sodium per hour, adjusted up if you're a salty sweater and down if you're puffy or nauseated. Test your plan in long hot training runs first, because race day is the wrong place to discover your gut hates them.
lost appetite at altitude, does it matter

Yes, it matters, because you're burning a huge amount of energy up high and running on empty drains your strength and judgment. Force down small, frequent snacks you actually like, since carb-heavy, salty foods tend to go down easiest. Stay well hydrated too, and if you can't eat at all and feel nauseous, consider it a sign of altitude sickness and don't go higher.
Gear checklist before launching? I always feel rushed.

Slow down, because being rushed is when mistakes happen. Before every launch, check that your helmet is fastened, all harness buckles including leg straps are closed, your reserve handle is in place and secure, your lines are clear with no knots or twists, your carabiners are locked and the wing is laid out properly. Finally, read the wind and look at the airspace. Many pilots use the same routine every time, or say it out loud, so nothing gets skipped, especially the leg straps.
how do I know if ice is too thin to place a screw

If the ice is thinner than about the length of your screw, or you can see rock, air, or water behind it, treat any screw there as questionable. Tap the ice with your tool first, because hollow or drummy sounds suggest poor attachment or air pockets, while a solid thunk means dense ice. In thin ice, use your shortest screws, look for the thickest bulges or where ice meets rock, and consider rock protection nearby. If you can't get reliable gear, don't keep climbing up hoping it'll improve; that's a good reason to downclimb or back off.
honestly the forecast is always conservative, i usually just bump it down one level in my head

That's a risky habit, because forecasters already factor in uncertainty, and spatial variability means your slope could be worse than the regional rating, not better. Plenty of people caught in slides were sure they knew better than the forecast. Use it as your baseline and then let your own observations push you toward caution, not away from it.
can i put a skateboard on a plane

Usually yes, most airlines let you carry a skateboard on or check it, and many treat it as a personal or sports item. Rules vary by airline, so check yours before you fly, especially for electric boards, because many airlines ban their lithium batteries. Removing or wrapping the trucks can help a regular board fit overhead bins.
My friend has a wing and offered to let me try on a hill without lessons. Fun idea right?

It's tempting, but please don't fly without proper instruction, even on a small hill. Untrained launches and landings are where beginners get hurt, often with back and ankle injuries, even at low height. If your friend isn't a qualified instructor, they can't really teach you safely. Book an intro day at a school, which is cheap and gets you flying properly from the start.
Is highball bouldering basically the same as free soloing?

They share the same core risk, since a fall from a highball can mean serious injury, but highballs usually have pads, spotters and a downclimb or bail option, while a true solo is often above a lethal height with no protection at all. Highballing is a good place to learn how your mind handles committing moves at height, as long as you stack plenty of pads and use experienced spotters. Treat anything above roughly 15 feet with real respect and work it on toprope first if you can.
My son just told me he wants to start wingsuit BASE jumping. I'm terrified. What should I even say to him?

Your fear makes sense, because wingsuit BASE is among the riskiest things a person can do and experienced jumpers die doing it every year. Instead of opening with a flat no, ask him what his progression plan is. The respected path takes years: hundreds of skydives, wingsuit flights out of planes, then a lot of standard BASE jumps before ever combining the two. If he's willing to follow that path with real mentors, you'll know he's taking it seriously, and if he isn't, that's the conversation to have.
I'm 58, a bit overweight, take blood pressure meds. My wife wants us to learn to dive in Bali. Am I too old for this?

Age isn't the barrier. Plenty of people start diving in their sixties and beyond, but your blood pressure meds and weight mean you should get medical clearance first. Fill out the RSTC/WRSTC medical questionnaire honestly and take it to your doctor, ideally one familiar with dive medicine, before you book. Once you're cleared, Bali has calm, warm sites that are ideal for learning together.
avy forecast says considerable but the line I want is only like 30 degrees. good to go?

Thirty degrees is right where avalanches start running, and considerable danger is when the most avalanche fatalities happen, because conditions feel fine but human-triggered slides are likely. Check which aspects and elevations the forecast flags and what the avalanche problem is, because a 30-degree slope in the wrong spot can absolutely release. On a considerable day, the smart move is to stay on slopes under 30 degrees with nothing steep above you and save that line for when the danger drops.
hit my head pretty hard yesterday on a crash, helmet cracked, feel kinda off today. ride tomorrow?

Don't ride tomorrow. Feeling off the day after a hard impact strong enough to crack a helmet is a classic concussion sign, so get checked by a doctor today. A second hit before you've recovered can be far more serious than the first. Retire the cracked helmet too, because it has done its job and won't protect you again. Return to riding only once you're symptom-free and a doctor has cleared you, which often takes a week or more.
best way to learn a backflip on a snowboard fast??

There isn't really a fast way, and rushing a backflip on snow is how people land on their heads. The proven path is to learn the rotation on a trampoline or at an airbag facility first, then progress to snow with coaching, starting off a soft, well-built jump. Lots of resorts and indoor centers have airbag jumps for exactly this, and a few sessions there will get you further than a dozen sketchy attempts on a regular kicker.
dislocated shoulder popped back in on its own. paragliding this weekend??

Don't fly yet, because a shoulder that just dislocated is very unstable for weeks and you need both arms working reliably for brake input and a reserve throw. See a doctor to check for damage like a labral tear or a fracture, since first-time dislocations, especially in younger people, often happen again. Fly once you've rehabbed and have full strength and range, not this weekend.
just hit a 6ft drop on my hardtail, landed flat and my wrists hurt like hell. ride it off?

Don't ride it off. Flat landings send huge force through your wrists and scaphoid fractures in particular often feel like a bad sprain but can heal badly if missed. If there's pain at the base of your thumb, swelling, or it hurts to grip, get an X-ray today. Ice it and stop riding until you know what you're dealing with.
trying to learn butters but i keep catching my edge and slamming. tips?

Edge catches on butters usually come from leaning too far forward or back while your board is still on edge. Flatten your base before you press, then shift your weight smoothly onto your nose or tail while keeping your shoulders over the board. Practice on a gentle, groomed slope at slow speed, and a softer flex board makes presses much easier. Wrist guards are worth it while you learn, since butters cause a lot of backward falls.
My guide says I should descend because of my cough but I feel ok. Should I trust him?

Trust him. A cough that develops at altitude can be early HAPE, and HAPE can go from 'I feel ok' to life-threatening within hours, especially at night. Experienced guides have watched this unfold many times, and descending a few hundred meters often clears it quickly. If it turns out to be a dry 'Khumbu cough' from cold air, you've lost a day, not your life.
Is it worth buying a used street luge?

A used luge can be a great way to start, but inspect it carefully. Check the frame for cracks or bent rails, make sure the trucks are tight and not damaged, and replace worn wheels and bearings before riding. If you're unsure, have someone from a local luge or downhill group look it over, since they'll spot problems a beginner might miss.
Why do people say soloing is selfish?

Critics point to the people left behind if it goes wrong, like family and friends, and to the rescuers who have to recover a body. Supporters argue that adults can choose their own risks, the same as in mountaineering or BASE jumping. Both views have weight, and most soloists who are honest with themselves talk openly with loved ones about it. Some decide to stop once they have kids or dependents.
I've had a few beers, still fine to jump right? It's only like 6 meters

No, skip it until you're sober. Alcohol is involved in a big share of cliff-jumping deaths because it wrecks your judgment, balance and air awareness, and it makes it harder to orient and swim up after a deep entry. Six meters is plenty to get hurt from, so watch your mates today and jump another day.
Riding alone on remote downhill trails tomorrow, any reason not to?

Riding solo on remote trails is risky because even a moderate crash can leave you unable to call for help. If you go, tell someone your exact route and return time, and carry a phone plus a basic first aid kit. Consider a satellite messenger or a crash-detection app, and ride well within your limits. A riding partner is the much safer choice on unfamiliar terrain.
is it a dumb idea to solo an easy WI2 ice route without a rope? i climb 5.11 rock

Yes, it's a bad idea, and rock grades don't carry over the way you'd hope. Ice can fracture under your tool or your feet without warning, and a slip with crampons on means tumbling and catching points, not a clean fall. Even strong climbers die on easy ice because conditions change in ways that are hard to read. Rope up and lead it with screws. If you want mileage, do lots of laps on toprope.
Detailed question: training for a 3.8km Ironman swim, currently doing 2.5km in the pool 3x a week. Water at the race will be around 18°C. How should I adapt for open water over the next 10 weeks?

Move at least one session a week into open water, and build up to swimming the full 3.8km continuously in your wetsuit a few weeks before the race. Practise sighting, drafting and swimming in a group, ideally with a club, because a chaotic start can use up more energy than the distance itself. Do some swims in water around 18°C so you know how your hands and face cope, and test your race-day goggles and anti-chafe routine. Keep your pool sessions for speed work, and use the lake for pacing and confidence.
Rolled my ankle bouldering yesterday, it's swollen and purple but I can kind of walk. Comp is Saturday. Tape it and send?

Swelling plus bruising that fast usually means more than a minor sprain, and a bouldering comp means hard, unpredictable landings on exactly that joint. Get it examined this week, because if you can't hop on it without pain, an X-ray is worth ruling out a fracture. Tape helps with stability once a sprain is healing, but it won't protect a fresh injury from a bad fall off a top-out. Skip Saturday, ice and elevate now, and you'll be back on the wall weeks sooner than if you aggravate it.

Detailed question: I've been climbing indoors for a year, mostly 5.10 top rope and V3 bouldering. I want to start trad climbing. What's the best path? Can I just buy a rack and start placing gear on easy routes?

Placing gear is a completely separate skill from climbing hard, and bad placements can pull out in a fall, so take a trad course with a certified guide or learn under a very experienced mentor before leading. A great way to practice is mock leading, where you place gear on a route while safely top-roped, and then have your mentor check every piece. Start leading routes well below your top-rope grade, around 5.6 or 5.7, so you can focus on protection rather than hard moves. Hold off on buying a full rack until you've used a few different cams and nuts and know what you like.
Honest question, how does Honnold not die? Is there a secret?

There isn't a shortcut. He prepares for years. For El Cap he rehearsed every move on a rope dozens of times, memorized sequences, and walked away from attempts when conditions or his head weren't right. He also has an unusually calm response to fear, built over thousands of days of climbing. Even with all that, he and others have said it's a serious risk, and several elite soloists have died doing it.
what's the deal with v-threads, are they actually strong

A well-built V-thread in good, solid ice is surprisingly strong and is the standard way to rappel off ice routes. Drill two intersecting holes with a long screw at about 60 degrees to each other so they form a deep V, then thread the cord or webbing through. Use fresh cord, test it with a backup screw while the heavier person rappels first, and then have the last person remove the backup. In rotten, aerated, or thin ice, don't trust it and find another option.
I'm 260 lbs. Will they even take me for a tandem?

It depends on the dropzone. Many set the limit somewhere between 220 and 250 lbs, though some will take you a bit heavier, sometimes with a surcharge or an extra fitness check. The limit comes from the gear's certified load and the instructor's ability to land safely, so it isn't arbitrary. Call around before booking and be honest about your weight, because showing up over the limit just means a wasted trip.
what should be in my pack for a full downhill day at the bike park

Bring water, snacks, a mini tool with a chain breaker, tire plugs, a spare derailleur hanger, a shock pump and a small first aid kit. Pack a light jacket and spare gloves in case the weather turns. Also carry your phone and the park's emergency number, so you can get help fast if you or someone else goes down.
rain all night, trails wet. still ride the black I planned?

Probably not today. Wet roots and rocks turn black trails into ice rinks, and your braking distances go way up. Ride blues or flow trails instead, keep off the brakes on roots, and stay loose. Also check whether the park has closed trails for conditions, since riding saturated dirt can damage them for everyone.
lost my buddy underwater what's the protocol again

Search for no more than about a minute by doing a slow 360 and looking up and down for bubbles. If you haven't found them, ascend slowly with your safety stop and reunite at the surface. Agree on that plan in every pre-dive briefing so you both do the same thing.
Forecast says considerable but the line I want is only like 32 degrees. That's under 35 so we're good right?

No, 32 degrees is right in prime avalanche territory, since most slab avalanches release on slopes between about 30 and 45 degrees. Considerable danger is where a lot of backcountry fatalities happen, because human-triggered slides are likely while the terrain still looks inviting.
