On the day, have a kayak or boat escort alongside, not just her dad swimming next to her, because one adult in the water can't easily help a tired kid. Check the tides and wind, and agree beforehand that getting into the boat is a perfectly fine way to finish.
Thinking of doing a cave dive in a cenote since I'm already certified open water, guide says it's cool

Make sure it's a cavern tour, not a cave dive. Cavern tours stay in the zone where daylight is visible and are fine for open water divers with a qualified guide, while true cave penetration needs full cave training because of silt-outs, getting lost and having no direct way up. Ask the guide exactly where you'll go, and decline anything that goes past the light zone without that certification.
Short version: leashes or leashless tools for a beginner?

Go leashless. Modern tools have good grips and pinky rests, and climbing without leashes makes placing screws and switching hands easier. Some beginners use a lightweight umbilical tether so they can't drop a tool, which is smart above other people. Either way, keep your grip relaxed so you don't burn out your forearms.
Got my A license last month. Buddy says I should downsize to a 150 canopy already, I'm currently on a 210. Thoughts?

That's far too aggressive. Jumping from a 210 to a 150 that soon would put your wing loading well beyond what new jumpers can handle, and canopy accidents are the leading killer of licensed skydivers. Downsize in small steps of about 20 to 30 square feet, and only after you've proven you can land consistently and handle off-field landings. Take a canopy course and talk to your S&TA before you change sizes.
track is closed for rain but gate is open, my friend says lets just go ride

Respect the closure. Tracks close in the rain because riding soft dirt tears up the jumps and landings, and the owner could ban you or have you charged for trespassing, which could also ruin the track for everyone. There's also no one there to help if something goes wrong. Wait for the track to dry and reopen, or call the owner and ask when they expect to open.
My friends hitch rides holding onto cars to get back up the hill. Safe enough if the driver goes slow?

Skitching is one of the most dangerous things you can do on a board, and it kills skaters every year, even at low speeds. One pothole, pebble or sudden brake throws you under or behind the car with no way to react. Have someone drive you back up in the car instead, which is how most downhill crews handle shuttling anyway.
we got a rescue question: if someone breaks an ankle mid-route on ice, what do we do

Make the climber safe first, either by lowering them on the rope or securing them to a solid anchor, then call emergency services with your location and details. Keep them warm and insulated from the snow, because cold sets in quickly when someone's immobile. Don't try a complicated rescue you haven't trained for. A self-rescue or wilderness first aid course before your next trip is a smart investment.
What's the difference between parkour and freerunning?

Parkour focuses on moving efficiently from one point to another, using vaults, jumps and climbs to get past obstacles as directly as possible. Freerunning grew out of parkour and puts more emphasis on creative expression, so you'll see more flips, spins and stylistic moves. In practice the two overlap heavily, and most communities train both under the same roof.
is it ok to ride the track alone if nobody's around on a weekday

It's better not to, because if you go down hard and get knocked out or break something, there may be nobody to call for help. At the very least, tell someone exactly where you are and when you'll check in, keep your phone on you rather than in the truck, and skip the big jumps and new obstacles. Many tracks require a flagger or a buddy anyway, so check their rules.
concussion 5 days ago skating, feel fine now. back on the ramp tomorrow?

Too soon, because feeling fine at rest isn't the same as your brain being healed, and a second hit before recovery can be far worse than the first. Concussion return works in stages, from light activity to sport-specific drills to full contact, with no symptoms at each stage, and a doctor should clear you before you drop in again. Give it the time, because getting rocked twice in a row can cost you a season or more.
is it bad to kick really hard with my crampons

Kicking harder isn't better. Big kicks shatter the ice, waste energy, and tire your legs fast. Aim for a controlled, precise kick with your heel slightly low, and look for natural pockets and featured ice where the points slot in easily. A good placement usually takes one or two clean kicks, not five.
what is a nose press

A nose press is riding with your weight over your front foot so your tail lifts off the snow, balancing on the nose. Bend your front knee, straighten your back leg slightly and keep your shoulders lined up with the board. Try it on flat ground first, then on a gentle groomer at low speed.
do i need to sharpen brand new ice tools?

Usually no, new picks come with a good factory edge, but give them a quick look since some brands ship them a bit blunt. After a few days out, especially if you've hit rock, file them by hand with a flat file, following the original bevels and never using a grinder because the heat can ruin the temper. Sharp picks and crampons make placements far more secure and less tiring.
do i REALLY need a helmet just cruising to school on a longboard? it's like 10 min

Yes, and cruising is exactly when people get caught out, because a pebble or a crack can stop your wheels dead and pitch you forward with no time to react. Most serious skateboarding head injuries come from ordinary falls at modest speed, not from tricks. A light, well-ventilated skate helmet takes about two seconds to put on and won't make you sweaty over ten minutes. Wear it every time and you never have to think about it again.
50 yo, never climbed, out of shape. dumb idea?

Not dumb at all. Plenty of people start in their fifties, and climbing builds strength and balance gradually. Begin with a gym intro session on top rope or easy bouldering, and keep sessions short at first to let your tendons adapt. If you have heart, joint, or blood pressure concerns, run it by your doctor first.
Skydiving coach here. Student landed hard and twisted her ankle, she wants to jump again this afternoon to not lose her nerve. Allow it?

No. A student with a fresh ankle injury may not be able to run out or PLF properly, and a second bad landing could be much worse than the first. Get the ankle assessed before she jumps again. Tell her the nerves are better handled with a solid debrief and getting back in the air as soon as she's cleared, not by jumping hurt. You might help her rebuild confidence through ground drills and canopy review meanwhile.
how do i find a mentor in base

Start through a reputable First Jump Course, because instructors often stay in touch with students and connect them with local jumpers. You can also spend time at legal sites like the Perrine Bridge, where experienced jumpers often help newer ones. Look for someone conservative who's willing to say no to you and has a long, clean safety record.
My partner keeps belaying from right under the climb. Should I say something?

Yes, say something, because standing straight under a climber is the easiest way to take falling ice to the face or shoulders. A belayer should stand off to the side, out of the fall line, and close enough to the wall that they won't get pulled in hard if the climber falls. Frame it as a quick tip rather than a lecture and most partners will happily move.
I'm 58 and getting into winter sea swimming because everyone says it's good for you. Anything I should know?

It's great to get into, but check with your doctor first, especially if you have any heart issues or high blood pressure, because cold water puts a real load on the heart. Start in autumn while the water's still mild so your body adapts gradually, and keep early dips to just a few minutes. Always swim with others, never dive in, and have a warm hat, layers and a hot drink ready. Joining a local winter swimming group is the easiest way to learn the ropes safely.
Is nitrox safer than air?

It can be, if you use it correctly. Nitrox has less nitrogen, so diving it on air tables gives you a bigger margin against decompression sickness. The extra oxygen brings a new limit, though, because exceeding the maximum operating depth risks oxygen toxicity, which can cause seizures underwater. Take the nitrox specialty course, analyze every tank yourself and know your MOD before you dive.
First time flying with others in wingsuits next weekend. Any tips?

Keep it small and simple: two or three people, with a clear leader and an agreed flight plan, heading and break-off altitude. Fly to the side and slightly behind, never directly above or below anyone, and give yourself more space than you think you need. At break-off, turn away, de-arm and make sure you're clear before you pull. A coached group jump with an experienced flyer is the best way to learn this.
can I rap off a single ice screw if I'm in a hurry

I wouldn't, even in a rush. A single screw can melt out, fracture the ice around it, or fail if it was placed in poor ice, and rappelling puts all your weight on the anchor with no backup. A V-thread takes a few minutes to build and is far more trustworthy when backed up during testing, or use a two-screw anchor if you're willing to leave gear. Those extra minutes are well worth it compared to staking your life on one point.
I had a bad deployment last week and I'm nervous to go back up. Normal?

Completely normal, and it's actually your brain doing its job. Talk through what happened with a coach or experienced wingsuiter so you understand the cause and have a fix. Then consider doing a couple of regular skydives first to rebuild confidence before getting back into the suit. If the nerves stay strong, take more time off, because there's no shame in that.
I'm 42 and just started park riding. Is it dumb to try boxes and rails at my age?

Not dumb at all, plenty of people pick up park riding in their 40s. Start on wide, low, flat boxes with a straight approach, ride across them with a flat base and loose knees, and don't try to turn or press yet. Wear a helmet and wrist guards, and consider padded shorts because slips on boxes usually land you on your hip or tailbone. Recovery takes a bit longer at our age, so keep it progressive and ride when your legs are fresh.
Tweaked something in my ring finger on a crimp yesterday, heard a little pop. Can I just tape it and keep projecting?

A pop on a crimp usually means a pulley injury, most often the A2, and taping it so you can keep projecting is how a partial tear becomes a full rupture. Stop hard climbing now and get it checked by a hand specialist or a physio who knows climbers, especially if there's bruising, swelling or the tendon looks like it's lifting away from the bone when you bend the finger. Mild strains often heal in four to six weeks with a gradual return through open-hand grips. Taping plus a proper progression is part of the comeback once it's been assessed, not a way to skip the rest.
Should I wear a helmet for big waves or is that overkill?

It's not overkill, especially at reef or rock spots where a hit to the head can knock you out underwater. More and more big-wave surfers wear water helmets for that reason, and it's an easy safety upgrade. Pick a light, purpose-built surf helmet that drains well and doesn't catch too much water.
found a guy online who does bridge bungee jumps for cash, half the price of the commercial place. worth it?

I'd skip it. Bungee safety comes down to properly rated, inspected cords and harnesses, an accurate weight-to-cord match and trained staff who double-check every connection. An unlicensed cash operation gives you no way to verify any of that. The price difference is small compared with what's at stake, so go with an established, insured operator that has a track record you can look up.
Detailed question: I want to solo a 5.7 multipitch I've done 15 times roped. Dry season, solid rock, known descent. Anything else to consider?

You've covered the big ones. Also think about other parties above you, which brings rockfall and congestion, plus wildlife or nesting birds, morning dampness on shaded sections, and how you'll feel if fatigue or a cramp hits at pitch four. Plan to rehearse it roped again close to the attempt. Experienced soloists often carry a short rope or have a bail plan, and they treat any doubt that day as a firm reason to walk away. Nothing removes the core risk, so make the decision with clear eyes.
Our guide cancelled because of high danger but the sky is blue and the snow looks perfect. Can we go ourselves?

Your guide made the right call, and you should respect it. Blue skies right after a storm are the classic setup for avalanche accidents, because new snow is sitting on a weak layer and people feel tempted by the perfect conditions. If you want to ski today, take laps at the resort or on truly low-angle terrain with nothing steep above it, and let the snowpack settle before you go back out.
Worried my 11 yo will freak out underwater. Should I try a discover scuba first?

That's a smart move. A Discover Scuba or Bubblemaker session in shallow, calm water lets your kid try breathing underwater with an instructor right beside them, with no commitment to a full course. If they love it, sign them up. If they get anxious, there's no harm in waiting a year or two, since kids who dive because they want to are the ones who stick with it.
my buddy says I can skip the first flight course since I've done tracking dives. true?

No, tracking is useful preparation but it doesn't teach you the wingsuit-specific exit, wing collapse and deployment sequence. Most dropzones won't even let you jump a suit without the course, and for good reason. Take the course; it's short and the instructor will tune your suit and flying in ways your buddy can't.
my roll works in the pool like 100% of the time. ready for class 3?

A pool roll is a great start, but it often falls apart the first time you flip in cold, aerated, moving water while getting knocked around. Practice rolling on flatwater, then in easy class II current, and do it until it works when you're surprised and tired, not just when you set it up. Once you're hitting combat rolls on class II and reading water well, step up to class III with experienced paddlers who can show you the lines.
how fast can you go on a downhill board before speed wobbles kill you

There's no magic number, because wobbles come from the board setup and your technique more than from one speed, and they can start at 25 mph on loose trucks or hold off past 50 on a dialed setup. Tighter bushings, a lower and stiffer deck, and keeping your weight on the front foot all help, and so does staying relaxed instead of locking up. The real rule is never to ride faster than you can confidently slide or stop. Build speed a few mph at a time on hills you know.
I panicked a little on my cavern dive when my mask flooded. Does that mean I'm not cut out for caves?

Not necessarily, it means you've found the skill you need to practice. Go back to a pool or calm open water and repeat mask removal, replacement and no-mask swimming until it's boring. Cave training includes no-mask exits and plenty of stress drills, and a good instructor will tell you honestly when you're ready. Be truthful with yourself before going further, because caves don't leave room for panic.
is chalk necessary

It isn't strictly necessary, but it helps a lot once your hands start to sweat, especially on slopers and small crimps. Most climbers find their grip much more consistent with it. Use a chalk ball or liquid chalk if your gym wants less dust in the air, and brush off the holds you've caked up when you're done.
Can I wear my glasses during a tandem?

Yes. The dropzone will give you goggles designed to fit over glasses, so wear your normal pair and the goggles go over the top. Tell your instructor beforehand so they can make sure the fit is snug. Contacts also work fine if you prefer them, and the goggles keep them from drying out.
how cold is too cold to go ice climbing

There's no hard cutoff, but once it's well below about -20°C (-4°F) with wind, frostbite risk climbs fast and the ice gets brittle and shattery. Many climbers find the sweet spot is a bit below freezing, where the ice is plastic and tools stick well. On very cold days, keep pitches short, watch your fingers and toes closely, and don't hesitate to bail if anyone starts losing feeling.
do i need to pack my own chute as a student

Not at first, because student gear is packed by licensed packers or riggers at the dropzone. You'll learn to pack your main as part of your progression toward your A license, under supervision until you're signed off. Reserves are always packed by a certified rigger, never by you.
is a half shell helmet fine for downhill if it's a nice one

No, for actual downhill you want a full-face, ideally one certified to ASTM F1952, the downhill-specific standard. Faster speeds and steeper terrain mean face-first crashes are common, and a half shell does nothing for your jaw and teeth. Plenty of riders who broke their face learned that the expensive way, so save the half shell for mellow trail rides.
I'm 52, fit, 600 skydives. Am I too old to start BASE?

Age itself doesn't rule you out, and 600 jumps is a strong foundation, probably better than most people bring to an FJC. What matters more is your landing tolerance, because BASE landings are often rough, off-field, and harder on your knees, ankles and back than drop zone landings. Be honest about old injuries, choose a course that starts on forgiving objects with good landing areas, and plan to progress slowly.
I'm 52 and want to wingsuit. Too old?

Not at all. Plenty of people start in their 50s and 60s, and age matters less than fitness, flexibility and current skydiving skills. Make sure you can comfortably hold an arched, strong body position for a couple of minutes, and that your shoulders and back can handle it. Getting a checkup if you have any health concerns is a sensible step. The prerequisites are the same as for anyone, so focus on getting your jump numbers and staying current.
Is there anywhere legal to BASE jump in the US?

Yes. The Perrine Bridge in Twin Falls, Idaho is legal year-round and is where many people do their first jumps, and Bridge Day at the New River Gorge in West Virginia allows jumping one day a year in October. Some BLM land also allows jumping, while it's banned in most national parks. Check current local rules before you go, because access can change.
Just tell me the fastest way to heat adapt. Race is in 5 days.

Five days won't get you fully adapted, but you can still gain something from daily 30 to 45 minute sessions of easy running in heat or hot baths and saunas after workouts. Taper the intensity so you're not exhausted on race day. More important, plan a slower pace and lots of cooling at aid stations to make up for what you lack.
What's the best weather for a beginner to fly in?

You want smooth, steady wind of about 5 to 15 km/h straight up the slope, with no strong gusts and no thunderstorm risk. Early morning and evening tend to be calmer because the sun is too weak to drive strong thermals. Avoid midday in summer, overdeveloping cumulus clouds and strong wind aloft even if it feels calm at launch. When in doubt, ask local pilots or your instructor.
should I turn off my beacon on the drive home

Turn it off once you're back at the car and fully out of avalanche terrain, not before, since that saves the battery and keeps it from interfering with anything else. Keep it on and in transmit for the whole time you're in or near the terrain, including on the exit. Check the battery level before every tour and replace the batteries well before they get low.
is ibuprofen good for altitude headache

Yes, ibuprofen or paracetamol works well for a mild altitude headache, and studies suggest ibuprofen may even help prevent AMS a little. Take it with food, and don't use it to keep climbing higher while you have symptoms. If the headache doesn't respond to medication, rest and fluids, treat that as a signal to stop ascending or go down.
what's the best way to land so it doesn't hurt?

Go in feet first with your body straight and tight, legs together, toes pointed, and arms either crossed over your chest or pressed to your sides. Squeeze your glutes and keep your head neutral, looking at the horizon rather than down, because looking down tips you forward into a painful slap. Many jumpers also exhale slightly or keep their mouth closed and clench their jaw to avoid water rushing up the nose.
Weather looks perfect tomorrow and I feel strong, finally gonna solo my project. Wish me luck!

Feeling strong is great, but your project is by definition at your limit, and that's the worst possible place to go ropeless. Even dedicated soloists stay far below their max on solos. Take that strong day and send it on rope, then celebrate a clean redpoint. That's a real accomplishment, and you'll be around to enjoy it.
sleep is terrible at altitude, I keep waking up gasping. normal?

Some periodic breathing, where you pause and then gasp, is normal and very common at altitude. Diamox often improves it, and avoiding sleeping pills like benzodiazepines matters because they can suppress your breathing. If you're breathless even while resting during the day, coughing or getting worse, treat it as possible HAPE and descend.
is it fine to just tie a figure eight and skip the follow through if im in a hurry? gym is closing soon

No, a figure eight without the follow-through is just a loose knot around your harness and can fail completely under load. A properly finished retraced figure eight takes about fifteen seconds once you've practiced it, so there's no real time to save. If the gym is closing, take one fewer route instead of cutting the step that keeps you attached to the rope.
Whats the fastest way to get good enough to jump between rooftops

Honestly, there's no fast track to that, and roof gaps are where parkour injuries turn fatal, so most experienced traceurs never do them at all. The real skill is a precision jump that's consistent at ground level, at a distance well below your maximum, repeated hundreds of times. If you want the challenge of height, train with a coach at a gym and keep the risks where a miss means a bruise, not a hospital stay.
fastest way to learn to jump tabletops

The fastest way is the boring way: roll the tabletop, then hit it with a little more speed each pass, so you clear a bit more of the top every time while keeping your body neutral and your knees soft. Stay on a steady throttle up the face rather than chopping it, because chopping the throttle is what sends the front end down. A couple of hours with a coach will fix your body position faster than a month of guessing. Tabletops are forgiving because you can come up short safely, which is exactly why you learn on them before doubles.
can kids get altitude sickness

Yes, at about the same rates as adults, but young kids often can't tell you what's wrong, so watch for fussiness, poor appetite, unusual sleepiness or poor sleep. Follow the same slow-ascent rules as adults, and descend at the first sign of trouble rather than waiting to see if it improves.
im 13 and my dad says i can dive with him even tho im not certified, he's done it for years. is that fine

Your dad's experience is great, but it doesn't replace you learning the skills yourself. Things like clearing your ears, controlling your ascent and handling an out-of-air situation need to be taught and practiced in a pool first. At 13 you're old enough for a Junior Open Water course, so get certified together and then you can dive with him properly.
What's the difference between EN-A, EN-B and EN-C wings?

The ratings describe how a wing reacts to collapses and stalls and how much pilot input it takes to recover. EN-A wings are the most forgiving and often recover on their own, which makes them right for students. EN-B covers everything from easy intermediate wings to demanding high-end ones, and EN-C needs active piloting and quick recovery skills. Move up slowly and with your instructor's input, because flying a wing above your skill level is a well-known cause of accidents.
can i cliff jump if i'm not a strong swimmer

It's not a good idea, because you need to get to the surface and back to shore quickly, often in cold or moving water. If you're set on it, wear a buoyancy vest, start from very low heights and have a strong swimmer with you in the water. Better still, take some swimming lessons first so you can enjoy the jumps properly.
What are signs I'm actually ready to solo something easy?

Real readiness usually looks like this: years of outdoor lead climbing, having climbed that exact route many times on rope, the moves feeling effortless and boring, and not getting any adrenaline spike when you look down. You should be able to downclimb every section confidently. Just as important, you should feel no outside pressure from an audience, friends, or a camera. If you're asking someone else whether you're ready, the honest answer is probably not yet.
do i need knee braces at 19 or is that overkill

They're not overkill. Knee ligament tears, especially ACL injuries, are among the most common serious injuries in motocross, often from a foot catching in a rut. Quality braces like Asterisk or CTi aren't cheap, but they cost a lot less than ACL surgery and a year of rehab. If braces are out of your budget, decent knee guards are better than nothing, but they don't stop the knee from twisting.
My buddy says leashes are dangerous in big waves and I should go without. True??

Some big-wave surfers do debate leashes because a board can drag you down in a heavy wipeout, but most still wear one. A leash keeps you near your board, and your board helps rescuers find you. Use a heavy-duty big-wave leash and get comfortable with your vest and quick-release options instead of ditching it. At most big-wave spots, losing your board means a long, dangerous swim through the impact zone.
is head first or feet first better

Feet first, every time, unless you're a trained diver at a spot you know perfectly. A head-first entry means your head and neck take the impact and hit anything hidden underwater first, which is how spinal injuries happen. Even the professionals at 27 meters enter feet first for exactly that reason.
I'm a lifeguard and I want to start surfing big waves. Where should I start?

Your rescue skills and water comfort are a big head start, but big-wave surfing is its own world. Start at friendly, well-known intermediate spots during their bigger swells, get a proper gun and do a dedicated big-wave safety course. Above all, link up with an experienced crew who'll show you the lineup and let you build up gradually.
I'm on caffeine pills every hour to stay awake in a desert ultra overnight. Fine?

Hourly is too much. Caffeine in big repeated doses can cause nausea, a racing heart and GI trouble, which gets worse on top of heat stress. Keep it to small doses, around 50 to 100 mg, every couple of hours during the low points of the night, and keep your total under about 400 to 600 mg for the race unless you've safely tested more in training. Plan your caffeine strategy in training runs rather than improvising.
My son is 19 and says he wants to get into BASE. I'm terrified. What should I actually know?

Your fear makes sense. BASE is one of the most dangerous sports there is, but the risk depends a lot on how someone gets into it. The responsible route is a long one: a few hundred skydives first, then a formal First Jump Course, then years of conservative jumping on easy objects. If he's willing to follow that path patiently, that's a good sign, and asking him what his plan is and who will mentor him is a fair, non-confrontational way to find out.
what's a two wave hold down actually feel like

Most people describe the first wave as violent and disorienting, then a growing panic when they surface and a second wave lands before they can breathe. Survival comes from staying relaxed, protecting your head, and saving oxygen rather than fighting. Training under supervision builds the calm that gets you through it.
what injuries are most common

The usual ones are bruising and back strain from landing at a slight angle, ruptured eardrums, broken ankles or legs from hitting the bottom, and compressed or fractured vertebrae from bad entries at height. The worst injuries come from striking rocks or shallow bottoms, so checking the landing zone prevents a lot of them. Many deaths happen after the jump, from drowning in cold water or currents, so have a buddy watching every time.
can i just watch youtube videos instead of paying for an avalanche course?

Videos make good prep, but they can't replace a course, because the important skills are hands-on: digging pits, timing yourself on a multiple-burial beacon search, and making terrain calls in the field with an instructor checking you. Most avalanche accidents come from decision-making errors, and you learn good decisions by practicing them with feedback. Watch the videos, then take the course, which will make far more sense afterwards.
My partner says we don't need helmets for toproping ice. That's wrong, right?

Your instinct is right, and your partner is wrong. Ice climbing showers everyone with chunks of ice, even on toprope, and the belayer at the base gets hit the most. Climbers also swing tools near their own heads and can pendulum into the ice. Wear a helmet the whole time you're near the climb, and pick a belay spot off to the side of the fall line.
My computer died mid-dive at 25m. What should I have done? Buddy was close.

The usual move is to signal your buddy, end the dive, and make a slow ascent with them, staying on their computer's profile and doing a longer safety stop than normal. Afterward, don't dive for 24 hours, because a new computer has no record of your nitrogen loading. Going forward, carry a backup computer or at least a depth gauge and timer.
can i lead my first ice route right after an intro top rope day

That's way too soon, because ice leading is a whole different game where you really, really can't fall, and the gear placements need to be second nature. Spend a full season or two top roping lots of routes until you can climb a couple of grades above what you'll lead without feeling sketchy, then take a lead course with a guide. Lots of good climbers mock-lead on top rope first, placing screws while protected, which is a great bridge.
is downhill skating more dangerous than snowboarding

Generally yes, because asphalt is far less forgiving than snow and open roads add traffic. That said, the risk drops a lot with full gear, closed or quiet roads, spotters, and solid slide skills. Many injuries come from riding past your skill level, not the sport itself. Treat it like motorsport-level risk and gear up accordingly.
best avalanche airbag?

The top options are close enough that fit and system type matter more than brand. Mammut, Black Diamond, Ortovox and Scott all make solid packs. Canister systems are lighter and cheaper but need refilling to practice. Electric or supercapacitor systems like the Black Diamond JetForce let you test-fire freely and fly more easily, at a weight and price premium. Pick one that fits your torso, practice pulling the handle, and remember an airbag reduces burial risk but doesn't replace a beacon, shovel, probe or good decisions.
just bought a beacon, do I really need a shovel and probe too or is that overkill for day tours?

You need all three, every time, even on short day tours. The beacon only gets you to roughly where someone is buried, the probe pinpoints them, and the shovel is how you actually dig them out, which is usually the slowest part of a rescue. Without a shovel and probe, a beacon mostly helps rescuers find a body, so treat the three as one inseparable kit.
Just crashed and my wrist is swollen and kind of bent looking. I think I can ride back to the truck.

Don't ride. A wrist that looks bent is likely broken or dislocated, and you can't safely work the clutch or front brake with it. Immobilize it with a splint or a rolled-up jersey, keep it elevated, and have someone else move the bike or come back for it later. Get it X-rayed today, because scaphoid fractures in particular heal badly if they're missed.
best way to climb ice in Canada as a total beginner, any specific spots?

Canmore and the Banff area in the Rockies are classics. Ouray in Colorado and the Ice Park there are also great if you can head south. In the Rockies, start with a guided intro day through a local ACMG-certified guide service, since they know which routes are in condition and safe from avalanche exposure. Many Canadian Rockies routes sit under avalanche terrain, so going with a guide is especially worth it there.
I'm 19 and pretty fit. Do I really need to slow down in the heat or is that for older runners?

You need to slow down too, because heat illness doesn't care about age, and young, fit runners often get hit hardest by pushing at a pace their body can't cool. Your core temperature climbs with effort no matter how fit you are. Expect to be 10 to 20 percent slower in serious heat, run by effort or heart rate instead of pace, and you'll likely pass people at the end who went out hard.
Is it legal to street luge on public roads?

It depends heavily on where you live, and many cities and states restrict or outright ban skateboarding and luging on certain roads, especially steep ones. Check your local traffic codes, because fines and liability can be serious if something happens. The cleanest route is joining organized events that secure permits and close the course.
Can I wear sneakers for street luge braking?

Regular sneakers wear through fast and don't give consistent braking, which can be dangerous at speed. Most luge riders glue rubber or old tire tread onto the soles of sturdy shoes to create durable braking surfaces. Make sure the shoes fit snugly and are securely laced so they don't slip or come off when you put your feet down.
how do i do a parkour roll? ive tried and it hurts my shoulder

That pain usually means you're rolling straight over the point of your shoulder instead of diagonally across your back from one shoulder to the opposite hip. Tuck your head toward the opposite side, place your hands down first to guide you, and let the roll follow that diagonal line. Practice on grass or mats from a kneeling position before you try it from standing or out of a jump, and lay off for a few days if the shoulder stays sore.
how to ride steep loose chutes

Before you ride a chute, walk it to check the line and runout, then commit with your weight back, heels dropped, and elbows bent. Keep both brakes lightly modulated and avoid locking the front, because a skidding front wheel on loose terrain will wash out instantly. Look ahead to the bottom, and if the chute feels beyond your level, use the ride-around until you've built confidence elsewhere.
I'm 58 and my shoulder's been aching for months, worst when I paddle my whitewater kayak overhead. I've been pushing through with ibuprofen. Is that ok?

Months of pain that's worse with overhead paddling sounds a lot like a rotator cuff problem, and at 58 there's a real chance of a partial tear that ibuprofen is only hiding. Masking it while running rapids is risky because a weak or painful shoulder is exactly what dislocates on a bad high brace. See a sports physician or physio for a proper assessment, possibly with imaging. Paddle flatwater with a low-angle stroke in the meantime. Targeted cuff and scapular strengthening fixes most of these, but it needs a correct diagnosis first.
im 52 and out of shape, can i still learn to ice climb

Absolutely, lots of people start in their 50s and beyond, and good technique matters far more than strength in ice climbing. Start with a guided intro day on easy top rope routes, and build general fitness, especially calves, forearms and shoulders, beforehand if you can. Go at your own pace and you might be surprised how quickly it clicks.
how much do i need to weigh minimum

Most operators set a minimum somewhere around 35 to 40 kg, and a maximum often between 100 and 150 kg, but it varies by site and cord system. Below the minimum, the cord doesn't stretch properly and the rebound can be harsh. Check the specific operator's limits before you book, and expect them to weigh you on the day.
How do I stop my hands from cramping up on long descents? It's getting scary near the bottom.

Arm pump usually comes from death-gripping the bars, so brake with one finger and let your legs and elbows absorb the hits instead of your forearms. Check that your levers are angled so your wrists stay roughly straight in the attack position, and consider thicker, softer grips. Take a short break partway down the longer runs, because riding the bottom section with weak hands is exactly when crashes happen.
I'm 58 with mild high blood pressure and want to do a 50K in Arizona in June. Bad idea?

It's not automatically a bad idea, but it's one you need to clear with your doctor first. Some blood pressure meds, especially diuretics and beta blockers, change how your body handles heat and fluids, so ask specifically about racing in 100°F plus. If you get the green light, pick a race with frequent aid stations and early start times, and train in heat gradually over several weeks.
Just bought a wetsuit. Can I go straight out to sea for a long swim this weekend?

Ease into it rather than heading straight out for a long swim, because a new wetsuit feels restrictive and the sea brings swell, currents and cold. Do a short swim close to shore at a lifeguarded beach first, so you can check the fit, get used to the buoyancy, and practise getting the suit off. Once that feels easy, build up the distance with a buddy and a tow float, and check tide times before each swim.
how much does a bungee jump cost

A standard jump usually costs somewhere between 80 and 250 US dollars. Famous high sites like the big bridge and dam jumps run toward the top of that range or beyond. Photo and video packages often add another 30 to 60. Be suspicious of a deal that's dramatically cheaper than others in the same area, because that money sometimes comes out of equipment and staffing.
rolled my ankle pretty badly landing a drop yesterday, it's swollen and purple. can i train tomorrow if i tape it

No, swelling and purple bruising after a bad roll means a serious sprain or even a fracture, and taping it won't change that. Get it checked by a doctor or physio, especially if it hurts to put weight on it or if you have pain right on the bone. For now, rest it, ice it, and keep it elevated. Training on a damaged ankle is how a two-week sprain turns into chronic instability that dogs you for years, so let it heal and work on upper body or core in the meantime.
Can I use nitrox for cave diving?

Yes, nitrox is commonly used in cave diving because it can extend bottom times and reduce decompression obligations, as long as you stay within the maximum operating depth for your mix. You'll need nitrox certification and to analyze your gas yourself before every dive. Many cave courses use it, so it's worth getting certified before you start.
is it true you should relax and not fight during a hold down?

Yes, relaxing during a hold-down saves oxygen, because fighting the turbulence burns through your breath fast and rarely gets you up any sooner. Stay calm, protect your head, and once you feel the turbulence ease, swim toward the light or follow your leash up. Practice this mindset in safety courses and controlled breath-hold sessions so it's automatic when it counts.
back twinges when deadlifting, also do a lot of whitewater kayaking. keep going?

Ease off both until you know what's going on, because kayaking means hours of twisting and bracing in a flexed position and could be feeding the same problem. Drop the deadlift load, avoid big rapids where a hard brace or capsize could aggravate it, and see a physio who can check your form and screen for disc involvement. Get it checked urgently if you notice pain shooting down a leg, numbness or weakness.
do i really need leathers or can i just wear jeans

Jeans wear through in about a second of sliding at 30-plus mph, and then it's your skin on the asphalt. For casual carving, jeans plus pads are okay, but once you're hitting real downhill speeds, leathers or at least kevlar-reinforced pants and a proper jacket are the difference between getting up sore and a skin graft. Used motorcycle leathers are a cheap way in.
We're on a boat trip in Egypt and the guide says we can freedive off the reef without any training. Good idea?

Snorkeling and easy shallow duck dives are fine. Real depth without training is risky, especially since you won't know the signs of blackout, how to equalize properly or how to rescue each other. Many Red Sea spots like Dahab have excellent freediving schools, so a one-day intro course would make the trip a lot safer and more fun. Until then, stay shallow, stay close to a buddy and keep your dives short and relaxed.
How do I know if I'm drinking too much water vs too little?

Sloshing stomach, puffy fingers, weight gain during the race and headache with nausea all point to overdrinking and possible hyponatremia. Dark urine, heavy thirst, dizziness on standing and noticeable weight loss suggest you're behind on fluids. Weigh-ins at aid stations are a good check, and losing about 2 to 3 percent of body weight is roughly normal. If you're confused, vomiting repeatedly or swelling, get medical help, since the two conditions need opposite treatment.
best boots for a beginner on a budget

Get a real motocross boot with a buckle closure, a stiff sole and shin protection, even if it's a last-generation model on sale. Entry-level boots from established brands like Alpinestars, Gaerne and Fox usually run around $200 to $300. Don't ride in work boots or hiking boots, because ankle and lower-leg injuries are some of the most common crashes in motocross and boots are your main protection.
What happens if I freeze up on the platform and can't jump?

That's really common, and the crew deals with it all the time. They'll give you a calm countdown and usually let you take a moment, but they won't push you, and most places allow a limited number of attempts before they unhook you. If you back out, you typically don't get a refund, so it helps to commit mentally before you step to the edge and go on the first 'bungy'.
how long do you bounce for

Usually around four to six big bounces, slowly getting smaller over about 20 to 40 seconds. After that, you'll either be lowered to a boat or the ground or pulled back up to the platform, depending on the site. The whole thing is faster than you expect, so try to look around and enjoy it.
How many skydives do I need before I can start wingsuit flying?

The common standard is at least 200 skydives within the past 18 months, and many dropzones and instructors expect a USPA B license or equivalent too. That number exists because you need solid canopy skills, stable freefall and good awareness before you add a suit that changes how you exit, fly and deploy. Once you're there, book a proper First Flight Course with a qualified wingsuit coach rather than borrowing a suit and figuring it out.
Can I just use my regular hiking boots with strap-on crampons for vertical ice?

Not for vertical ice. Flexible hiking boots let strap-on crampons shift and pop off, and your calves will be fried within minutes of front-pointing. Vertical ice needs stiff mountaineering boots with technical crampons, usually step-in or hybrid bindings. Most guide services and gear shops rent both, which is the smart move until you know you're hooked.
My 15 year old son wants to go cliff jumping with his friends at a quarry this weekend. Should I be worried?

Some concern is fair, because quarries are among the riskiest places to jump. They often hide submerged machinery and rock ledges, and the water stays dangerously cold even in summer, which can trigger cold shock. Many are also on private property where swimming is banned for exactly those reasons. If he's set on jumping, steer him toward a known, supervised spot or a clinic where the depth is verified, and agree on a few rules: feet first, no jumping alone, and someone stays on shore.
what's a terrain trap

A terrain trap is any feature that makes an avalanche far worse than it would otherwise be. Common examples are gullies, creek beds and depressions where debris piles up deep, along with cliffs you could be swept over and trees you'd hit. Even a small slide can bury you several meters deep in a gully. The same slide on an open slope might leave you on the surface. Always ask what happens if this slope slides, and avoid traveling above or through traps when the snowpack is questionable.
Need a quick yes/no. Climb Cotopaxi solo?

No. Cotopaxi has crevassed glaciers, and Ecuador's park rules require climbers to go with a certified guide anyway. Book an ASEGUIM guide, and acclimatize first on peaks like Rucu Pichincha and Illiniza Norte.
Buttering keeps making me fall on my face. What am I doing wrong

You're probably leaning too far onto the nose and letting the tail get stuck on its edge. Keep the board flat on the snow, lean onto the nose only until the tail lifts slightly, and keep your weight centered over the board rather than out ahead of it. Practice slow nose and tail presses on a gentle slope before adding rotation, and soft snow makes falls far more forgiving.
fell on my wrist skating yesterday, its swollen and hurts when i twist it but i can move my fingers. probably fine right

Being able to move your fingers doesn't rule out a fracture, and swelling plus pain when you twist after a fall onto your hand is the classic pattern for a scaphoid break. That bone is notorious for being missed and healing badly when it goes untreated, so get it X-rayed at urgent care today. Pain right in the hollow at the base of your thumb is an especially strong reason to go. Until it's checked, keep it iced, elevated and off the board.
My 12 year old wants to hit the big jumps in the terrain park this weekend because his friends do. He's been riding one season. Should I let him?

One season is usually too early for the big jumps, and the injury risk comes from speed and air time he hasn't learned to manage yet. Steer him to the small or medium features first and have him show he can land straight airs cleanly and control his speed on approach. A park-focused lesson is a great investment here, because a coach will tell him honestly when he's ready to move up, and he'll often take that better from a coach than from a parent.
best way to train for paddling into big waves??

Long paddle sessions on your big board build the specific shoulder and back endurance you need. Interval work, like hard sprints to simulate getting into position and catching a wave, is just as important. Add swimming, especially open water, and core plus shoulder stability work in the gym to stay injury-proof. Practice paddling into waves on progressively bigger days so your timing improves alongside your fitness.
I've got a stress fracture in my foot and my skydiving course is next week. It's not like I'm running, just jumping out of a plane??

Landings are the problem, because even a good parachute landing puts real impact through your feet, and students often land hard or need to run it out. A stress fracture that takes a bad landing can become a complete fracture, which means months off instead of weeks. Talk to the dropzone about rescheduling, since most will happily move a course for a medical reason, and wait until your doctor clears you for impact.
Slider up or slider down for a 400 foot bridge jump

For a low object like a 400 foot bridge, most jumpers use a slider-off configuration with a short delay so the canopy opens quickly. Exact setup depends on your gear, delay, and the object, so confirm it with your instructor or a mentor who knows that bridge. Don't guess on configuration, because using the wrong one on a low jump leaves almost no margin.
i hit a rock and fell and now my head hurts and im kinda dizzy

Stop skating right now, because a headache and dizziness after a fall can mean a concussion. Get someone to stay with you and see a doctor today, and go to the emergency room immediately if you start vomiting, getting confused, feeling very drowsy, or if the headache gets worse. Don't skate again until you've been checked and fully cleared.
Chain keeps coming off. Just tighten it more?

Too tight is bad too, since it strains the bearings and can snap, so set it to your manual's slack spec, usually measured with the rear suspension compressed or a gap of about three fingers. A chain coming off often points to worn sprockets, a bent chain guide, or misalignment, so check those. Riding with a chain that keeps derailing is dangerous, so fix the root cause before riding again.
how cold is too cold without a wetsuit

There's no single cutoff, but for most people who aren't acclimatized, water below about 15°C (59°F) starts to get serious, and below 10°C (50°F) you're in genuinely risky territory where swim failure can come within minutes. Cold-water regulars build up tolerance over weeks of short, frequent dips, not by toughing out one long swim. Get in slowly, control your breathing through the initial gasp, and keep your first swims to a few minutes close to shore.
im 13 and my dad says i can do the PADI open water with him this summer, is that allowed

Yes, you can. Kids from 10 to 14 can earn the PADI Junior Open Water certification, and it upgrades automatically to the full Open Water when you turn 15. Junior divers have some limits, like a maximum depth of about 18 meters and needing to dive with a certified adult. Doing it with your dad is a great setup, so take the theory seriously and you'll have a skill for life.
My 13 year old is begging to do a bungee jump on our holiday in New Zealand. Is that even allowed?

At many New Zealand operators, yes. AJ Hackett's Kawarau Bridge, for example, generally accepts jumpers from about age 10 who meet a minimum weight, with a parent or guardian signing consent. Check the specific site's age and weight rules before you book, because they vary and they're strictly enforced. Kids who meet the requirements are jumping on the same gear and the same procedures as adults. Let your teen watch a few jumps first so the choice is really theirs.
do i need a bigger canopy for wingsuit jumps?

Many wingsuiters choose a moderately sized, docile canopy with reliable openings rather than a small high-performance wing. Openings in a suit can be less clean, and you want something forgiving if you land off or open off-heading. Talk to your rigger and instructor about wing loading, and ideally open conservatively while you're new.
My friend died soloing last year. Part of me wants to do it to understand him. Is that crazy?

That's not crazy. It's grief looking for a way to stay close to him, and I'm really sorry you lost him. Soloing won't give you his mind, though, and it puts the people who love you at risk of exactly what you're going through. Climbing with his friends, visiting his favorite routes on rope, or talking with a grief counselor who understands climbing culture can keep that connection without repeating the loss.
Is solo cave diving ever okay?

Some very experienced cave divers do dive solo, but it's an advanced practice that demands full redundancy and years of conservative diving, and they accept the added risk knowingly. It's not something to step into because you lack a buddy. For anyone newer, a well-matched team is one of the strongest safety tools you have.
whats an FJC and is it actually worth the money

FJC stands for First Jump Course. It's a multi-day course where an experienced BASE instructor teaches you gear, packing, object assessment, malfunctions and off-heading openings, then supervises your first jumps, usually from a bridge or a low-consequence object. It's worth every cent, because the people who try to teach themselves BASE are heavily overrepresented in accident reports.
how long to learn a roll

Most people get a combat-reliable roll in about 5 to 15 pool sessions with good instruction, though some click in one evening and others take a season. The key word is reliable: rolling in a calm pool is very different from rolling upside down in a cold, pushy eddy line. Take a roll clinic, then practice in moving water with a buddy nearby before you count on it in rapids.
My wing is 9 years old but looks fine. Still ok?

Age alone doesn't ground a wing, but at nine years it definitely needs a professional inspection before you trust it. Cloth porosity, line strength and trim all degrade over time and with UV exposure, often invisibly. A shop check will tell you if it's airworthy or needs relining. Ideally, wings should get inspected every year or two anyway.
Just to be clear, I need a yes or no. Can I learn parkour from YouTube alone?

Mostly yes for the basics, but not for the risky stuff. Videos are great for precision jumps, rolls, low vaults and conditioning, especially if you film yourself and compare. Flips, big drops and anything at height really need in-person coaching or at least an experienced friend who can spot you and correct mistakes you won't notice. A few drop-in classes early on will save you months of bad habits.
What happens if the main parachute doesn't open?

You cut away the main and deploy the reserve, which is a separate parachute packed by a certified rigger and inspected on a strict schedule. Modern rigs also carry an automatic activation device that fires the reserve if you're still falling fast at low altitude. Malfunctions do happen, but this layered system is why they very rarely turn into tragedies.
quick one: max depth on open water cert?
18 meters, or about 60 feet. Advanced Open Water qualifies you to 30 meters, and the deep specialty goes to 40, the recreational limit.
Bought a used DH bike and the fork feels kind of gritty and makes a clunk. Can I ride it a few weekends then service it?

I wouldn't, because a clunk and gritty feel can mean worn bushings, low oil, or a loose part, and a fork failure on a downhill run is a nasty crash. Get it to a shop or suspension service center before you ride it hard, and have them check the headset and rear shock while it's there. On a used bike, a full suspension service up front is money well spent anyway.
Thinking of swimming out to the buoy at the reservoir, there's no swimming signs but everyone ignores them.

Reservoir signs are usually there for good reasons, because the water often stays dangerously cold well below the surface and there can be hidden machinery, steep drop-offs and strong currents near intakes. Many drownings happen in exactly these spots, often to confident swimmers. Look for a managed open-water venue or a lake with lifeguard cover nearby, which gives you the same sense of freedom without the hidden hazards.
do i need to wear shoes cliff jumping

Water shoes or old sneakers are a good idea for the climb up and the exit, since wet rocks are sharp and slippery. For the jump itself, lightweight water shoes are fine at moderate heights and actually protect your feet on entry. Avoid anything heavy or loose that could come off or drag you down.
My 9 year old wants to drop in on the big bowl at the skatepark this weekend. He's only been skating a month. Should I let him?

A month in is too early for a big bowl, and a botched drop-in from that height is exactly how kids end up with wrist fractures or a knock to the head. Have him learn on a small quarter pipe first, two or three feet, and work up only once he's dropping in smoothly and committing his weight forward every time. A helmet, wrist guards and knee pads are non-negotiable for this stage, and a lesson or two with a local skate coach will speed things up a lot.
Is it safe to use a figure 8 device for belaying? Saw it in an old book.

Figure 8 devices can work for rappelling, but they're outdated for belaying and offer less control and friction than modern tube or assisted-braking devices. Most gyms and guides recommend devices like an ATC or Grigri, which are easier to learn and give more reliable catches. If you're unsure, ask a gym instructor to show you current belay methods.
hurt my wrist on a mountain bike crash 2 weeks ago, still sore at base of thumb

Get that X-rayed, because lingering pain at the base of the thumb after a fall is a red flag for a scaphoid fracture. These often don't show up on the first X-ray and can heal badly if missed. Keep it immobilized and off the bike until it's been ruled out.
should i wear a life jacket while cliff jumping

Generally no, because a buoyant vest can hit your chin or ribs hard on entry and cause injury above very low heights. A wetsuit gives some buoyancy and warmth without that problem. Instead of a life jacket, keep a spotter in the water or on shore with a float they can throw if something goes wrong.
How often should I check my bike before riding?

Do a quick check before every ride: tire pressure, chain tension and lube, brakes, throttle return, controls, spokes and any loose bolts. Check oil and coolant levels regularly and follow the manual's service intervals, which come much sooner on race bikes than on trail bikes. Many crashes and breakdowns come from loose parts or worn components that a quick inspection would catch. A clean bike is easier to inspect, so washing it often helps too.
How often should I practice beacon searches? I did it once in my course two years ago.

You should be practicing at least a few times every season, and ideally at the start of each one before you head into real terrain. Search skills fade fast, and under the stress of a real burial you'll fall back on whatever you've drilled. Plenty of trailheads and ski areas have beacon parks where you can run timed searches, so try to get a full find, probe and dig done in under five minutes.
Is it dangerous to do pool static apnea with friends who aren't trained?

Yes, it can be. An untrained buddy may not recognize a blackout, which in static can look like calm stillness, or know how to protect your airway and get you breathing. Many pools also ban breath-hold training for this reason. Either do static with a trained buddy and a set protocol of signals, or join a freediving club session.
my kid is 9, can they do the lift-served bike park?

Many bike parks welcome kids that age, but check the park's minimum age and height rules, and make sure your child can already handle confident braking, standing on the pedals and riding small bumps. A properly sized bike with good brakes matters more than fancy suspension, along with a full-face helmet, gloves and knee pads. Kids' camps or lessons at the park are excellent, and staying on green trails together is the right starting point. Let them set the pace and end the day before they get tired.
my screw went in kinda crunchy and white, is that fine

Crunchy, white ice usually means it's aerated, rotten, or full of air bubbles, so screws there are weaker than they'd be in clear, dense blue ice. Treat that placement with suspicion, and if you can, clear away the poor surface ice or find a better spot nearby to place another screw. Hearing the ice crunch, seeing white powder come out, or feeling the screw turn too easily are signs to place more gear and shorten the distance between screws. If the ice is bad throughout, consider backing off or toproping the route instead.
Just bought touring gear. Can I learn avalanche stuff from YouTube or do I really need a class?

Videos are a great supplement, but they can't teach you to actually find a buried beacon under pressure or read real snowpack, and that hands-on practice is what saves lives. Take an AIARE 1 or your region's equivalent, plus a separate companion rescue course, before heading into avalanche terrain. Until then, tour on low-angle slopes with no steep terrain above or connected to them.
teach me how to pump in a bowl

Pumping is about compressing as you go up the transition and extending as you come down, kind of like pumping a swing. Stay low in your knees, and as you start up the wall push down through your legs and stand taller as you roll into the flat to pick up speed. Start on a shallow mini ramp or bowl doing small back and forth runs, wear knee pads, and focus on feeling where the curve begins rather than trying to go high.
tl;dr is free soloing worth it

For a tiny number of extremely experienced climbers, it's a deeply meaningful practice they've chosen with full awareness, but for almost everyone else the risk of death far outweighs what it adds beyond roped climbing. Most of the flow, mastery and adventure people want from soloing is available through trad, alpine and deep water soloing without the zero-margin downside. If you're asking, the honest answer for you right now is probably no.
Does training finger strength make soloing safer?

More strength gives you more margin on a given grade, but it isn't what protects soloists. Rock quality, rehearsal, mental control, and conservative choices matter far more. Plenty of strong climbers have fallen because of a broken hold or a moment of distraction. Train strength because it makes you a better climber, and don't count on it as a safety system.
I have epilepsy, controlled with meds, no seizures in 3 years. allowed?

Many operators list epilepsy as an exclusion regardless of control, so check their policy directly. Medically, the adrenaline spike, sleep disruption from travel nerves and the inverted position are all things your neurologist should weigh in on. Get a written opinion from them, be upfront with the operator, and respect their decision if it's a no.
Kinda want to get into cave diving after watching the Thai cave rescue doc. Where do I start?

Start by getting comfortable in open water, ideally 50 to 100 dives with good buoyancy, plus advanced and nitrox certifications. Then find a reputable cavern course from an agency like NSS-CDS, NACD, GUE, IANTD or TDI. Take your time moving through the levels, because the divers in that rescue had decades of experience behind what they did.
My buddy says we don't need to retreat when it starts raining on the ice, just finish the route. Thoughts?

Rain on ice is a pretty clear sign to bail, because it weakens the ice and screws fast, increases falling ice, and soaks you so you get hypothermic quickly. If you're near the top and the descent is easier from there, finishing might be fine, but generally it's smarter to rap down while things are still good. Nobody regrets turning back on a wet day, but plenty of people regret pushing on.
Best way to train breath hold at home?

Dry training on land is great. CO2 and O2 tables done lying down are the classic approach, and apps like STAMINA or Apnea Trainer will guide you through them. Never do breath-hold training in water alone, including the bathtub, because blacking out there can kill you. Train lying on a couch or bed where losing consciousness is harmless, and pair it with relaxation and flexibility work.
I crashed yesterday at maybe 35mph, I feel fine but my helmet has a crack. still ok to use?

Replace the helmet, no question. A cracked shell means the foam has likely compressed, and it won't protect you the same way in a second impact. Also, a crash at 35 mph that cracked your helmet means your head took a real hit, so if you have headaches, nausea, confusion or unusual tiredness, get checked for a concussion before riding again.
whats a good first trick after ollie

A frontside 180 or a pop shove-it is the natural next step, since both build on your ollie timing without requiring a flip. The shove-it teaches you to scoop the tail, and the frontside 180 teaches you to rotate your shoulders, both of which matter for nearly every trick later. Get those consistent on flat ground before moving to kickflips.
no leash at big waves cool or no

Wear one. At many big-wave spots a strong leash helps you find your board and stay afloat after a wipeout. Some surfers worry about getting dragged or snagged on reef, so the real answer is a heavy-duty big-wave leash, checked for wear before every session, plus knowing how to quickly release it. Going leashless out there is just adding risk.
Why do people say never dive within 24 hours of freediving? I want to do both on my trip.

It's mostly about combining nitrogen loading from scuba with rapid, repeated deep freedives, which can raise your risk of decompression sickness. The usual advice is to freedive first, then scuba, or leave a day between scuba and deep freediving. Plan your trip so the freediving comes earlier, and you'll get the best of both safely.
how do i know if a bolt outside is safe

Look for rust, cracks around the hanger, a spinning or loose hanger, a bolt that shifts or sticks out unevenly, and homemade or very old hardware like quarter-inch buttonheads. Stainless glue-ins and modern expansion bolts in solid rock are generally trustworthy, while anything that looks corroded, especially near the sea, deserves suspicion. Never rely on a single bolt at an anchor. Report anything sketchy to your local climbing coalition or rebolting group, since they track and replace bad hardware.
I get really anxious in the water. Can freediving still work for me?

It can, and many people actually find freediving helps them get calmer in the water, since the whole sport is built on slow breathing and relaxation. Start with a patient instructor in a pool, where you can stand up anytime, and go at your own pace without pressure to reach any depth or time. Anxiety does use more oxygen, so treat relaxation as the main skill you're working on and progress only as you feel comfortable.
quick q - can i use a single carabiner for my anchor when top roping outdoors

Use two locking carabiners at the master point with the gates opposed and reversed, because a top-rope anchor holds every fall and lower, so it needs redundancy. The anchor should also be built from two or more solid, independent points that are equalized. If you haven't been taught anchor building, take a course or climb with an experienced mentor, since anchor failure is the one mistake you can't come back from.
Detailed one: I'm planning a trip to Jaws in Maui next season. I've surfed 15-18ft at Waimea twice. What should I prep?

Waimea at that size is a solid foundation, but Jaws is a heavier, more wind-affected wave with a long, tricky channel and much more push behind it. Give yourself months of breath-hold and fitness training, get a properly shaped 9'6" to 10'6" gun from a Maui shaper, and make sure your inflation vest is serviced. Most importantly, plan with locals who know the spot and set up water safety on skis before you arrive, since paddling Jaws without a rescue plan isn't an option at that level.
trying to ollie down a 7 stair tomorrow, only ever done 3 stairs. hype me up

Love the energy, but jumping straight from a 3 to a 7 is a big leap in height and impact, and that's where ankles and wrists get destroyed. Try to find a 4 or 5 stair first, or a gap that matches that distance, so you can build up how you commit and land. When you go for the 7, wear a helmet, check the runout for cracks and people, and roll up a few times to dial in your speed before you actually pop. Landing it after working up to it will feel way better than limping home.
can i drink a couple beers before a sunset swim, it's chill

Save the beers for after the swim. Alcohol makes you lose heat faster, slows your reactions and makes you overconfident, and it's a factor in a large share of drowning deaths. Swim sober, then crack one open on the beach when you're warm and dry. Watching the sunset from there is just as good.
First ultra ever is a 50K in July in Arizona. Thoughts?

It's doable, but you're making your first ultra a lot harder than it needs to be. If you're set on it, train specifically in the heat, practice your fueling and hydration on long runs, and plan to go much slower than your road pace. Also check the cutoffs, since early heat races can be generous. You might honestly enjoy a cooler first 50K more and save Arizona summer for your second.
is a street luge race safe to spectate up close

Stay behind the barriers or hay bales and well back from the outside of corners, because that's where a rider who loses control will go. Sleds can carry momentum surprisingly far after a crash. Race organizers mark spectator zones for exactly this reason, so follow marshal instructions and you'll have a great view safely.
My 9 year old wants to start bouldering. Is that safe for kids or should I wait until she's older?

Nine is a great age to start, and lots of gyms run youth programs built for exactly that. The main things to teach early are how to fall, which means landing on her feet, bending her knees and rolling back instead of reaching out with her arms, and keeping clear of the mats underneath other climbers. Keep sessions playful and short, and skip hard fingerboard training or crimpy max efforts because her finger growth plates are still developing. A kids' intro class is the easiest way to get her the right habits from day one.
is it ok to dive headfirst if the water looks deep enough

No. "Looks deep enough" is how people break their necks, because water depth is very hard to judge from above and rocks or logs can sit just below the surface. Always check the depth yourself first by swimming down to the bottom of the landing zone, and check again each season since sandbars and debris move. Even then, go feet first unless you've had proper headfirst diving training, because a headfirst entry leaves almost no margin for error.
dehydrated and tired after 6 hours at the park, one more run?

Call it a day. Fatigue is one of the biggest factors in downhill crashes, and the classic "last run" injury happens exactly when you're tired, dehydrated and less sharp. Drink plenty, eat something, and come back fresh next time. If you really want one more, make it an easy cruise on a green, not your hardest line.
My 15 year old son wants to try ice climbing this winter. I'm terrified. Is it actually safe for teens?

With the right setup it's much safer than it looks, and plenty of teens climb ice. The key is toproping with a certified guide or an established program, not leading and not going out with friends who are learning themselves. A good guide will pick conditions carefully, handle the anchors, and teach him how to swing tools and kick without wrecking his shins. If he loves it, a multi-day youth course is a great next step before he ever thinks about leading.
First jump next week and I'm terrified. Any tips??

Totally normal, and almost everyone who jumps was scared too. Listen closely to the briefing, look out at the horizon instead of straight down, and when they count, go on the first try, because hesitating only builds the fear. Breathe out as you leave the platform, and trust that the crew does this hundreds of times a week.
how fast should i be going into a jump

It depends on the jump, so don't guess. Watch a few riders who land in the sweet spot of the landing and notice where they start and whether they check their speed. Do a slow roll-over pass first to feel the lip and landing, then match the speed of the people landing well. Coming in too fast is usually more dangerous than too slow, but both hurt, so build up gradually.
Bouldering is basically free soloing right? So I already do it.

Not really, because in bouldering a fall usually means a pad landing from a few meters, while in soloing a fall means death. The mental game is completely different once a single slip carries no second chance, and that changes how your body moves and how fear shows up. Bouldering does build great strength and technique, so keep at it. Just don't let it convince you that you're ready for real height without a rope.
best way to sight in choppy water?

Lift your eyes just above the surface as you begin your breath, and pick a big, high landmark like a tree, building or tall buoy rather than a small marker. In chop, time the sight for when you're on top of a swell, and sight more often, every 4 to 6 strokes. Practice this in calm conditions first so that it feels automatic when it gets rough.
Is there any free solo gear I should buy, like chalk or special shoes?

Soloists use ordinary climbing shoes and chalk, and the idea is that no gear catches you. That's why it's so serious. If you're shopping, put your money toward a harness, belay device, helmet and a course on outdoor climbing basics. That kit actually keeps you alive while you build the experience that soloing would demand.
how long does it take to learn ice climbing well enough to lead

Most people need at least a season or two of toproping and following before leading even easy ice. You need to be completely solid on easy terrain, placing screws efficiently and never feeling close to falling. Many climbers take an intro to leading course with a guide and do mock leads on toprope first. There's no rush, and slowly building mileage is the best way to stay safe.
felt really chilly and goosebumpy at mile 40 even though it was like 35 degrees out. weird right?

That's not weird, it's a red flag. Chills and goosebumps in serious heat can be a sign of heat exhaustion moving toward heat stroke, as your body's temperature regulation starts failing. If it happens again, stop, get into shade, cool yourself aggressively with ice and water, and get medical staff to look at you. If you also had confusion or nausea that time, it's worth mentioning to a doctor now.
best way to learn tricks without paying for lessons

Watch good tutorial videos, film yourself and compare, and practice each skill on easy terrain until it's automatic before moving up. Ride with friends who are a bit better than you, since they can spot what you're doing wrong. That said, one park lesson is worth it if you're stuck or about to start bigger jumps, because a coach can fix habits that are hard to see yourself.
should i run flats or clips for dh

Most beginners and intermediates do better on flat pedals with good sticky shoes, because they teach proper technique and let you bail easily in a crash. Clips give extra control and are what many racers use, but only switch once you're comfortable and have practiced unclipping until it's automatic. Plenty of pros still ride flats, so there's no rush.
best hill for first ever downhill run?

Pick a gentle slope with a long flat or uphill runout at the bottom, good pavement and no traffic, like an empty parking garage ramp or a quiet cul-de-sac. You want a hill you can confidently foot brake on from top to bottom. If you're asking yourself whether it's too steep, it is, so start smaller.
First tandem jump next week and I'm honestly terrified. Is it normal to want to back out?

Completely normal, and almost everyone on that plane feels the same knot in their stomach. Tandem skydiving has a strong safety record because your instructor is certified, the gear is inspected, and there's a reserve parachute with an automatic activation device as backup. Focus on the briefing, ask every question you have, and remember you can still say no right up to the door without anyone thinking less of you.
what's a coleman slide and when do I need it

A Coleman slide is a heelside slide where you drop your back hand to the pavement and kick the board sideways to scrub speed or stop. You need it the moment your hills get steep enough that foot braking can't keep up, because it's the base slide most downhill riders use for control. Learn it on a gentle, smooth hill with slide gloves and a helmet, starting slow and adding speed only once it feels automatic. A local crew or a clinic will shortcut a lot of painful learning.
what happens if a cave diver gets lost

Lost divers usually run out of gas trying to find their way out, which is why the guideline, gas reserves and lost-line drills exist. Trained divers stop, stay calm, tie off and search methodically for the line, often along a set pattern. Prevention is the real answer: a continuous guideline to open water, proper gas planning and staying within your training.
I have a bad shoulder from an old dislocation. Downhill a dumb idea?

Not necessarily, but talk to a physio or sports doctor first, since a previously dislocated shoulder is prone to popping again in a fall. They can tell you if strengthening work or a brace would help, and when you're cleared to ride. Stick to flowier trails while you build confidence, and consider a padded upper-body protector. Learning to fall and roll well also really matters here.
I'm thinking wingsuiting might help me get over fear of heights lol

Fear of heights often doesn't show up much in skydiving, since you're so far up that it doesn't feel like height in the usual sense. That said, wingsuiting is something you only reach after hundreds of skydives, so it's a long route to a therapy session. If you're curious, try a tandem skydive first and see how it feels.
can kids scuba? my son is 9 and obsessed

Yes, there are programs for his age. PADI's Bubblemaker and Seal Team run in very shallow water, about 2 meters, and junior open water certification starts at 10 with depth limits. Choose an instructor who's experienced with children and keep the pace set by his comfort, not his enthusiasm. Kids' ears and judgment are still developing, so short, shallow and fun is the right approach.
is highballing considered soloing? asking for a debate with my friend

Technically highball bouldering is unroped, so it overlaps with soloing, but climbers usually treat it as part of bouldering. It's done over pads with spotters, typically around 15 to 25 feet. Soloing usually refers to roped-length routes where a fall is very likely fatal. So you're both partly right, but the consequences and culture are pretty different.
How far can you actually fly on a paraglider?

Skilled cross-country pilots regularly cover 100 km or more in a day, and the world record is over 600 km in places like Brazil with strong, long-lasting thermals. Most pilots in their first few years fly local flights near the site, then gradually push to 20 or 50 km as their thermalling and weather judgment improve. Distance comes from experience, so build it gradually.
Does slope angle measuring actually matter? I can eyeball it.

Even experienced skiers tend to misjudge slope angle by 5 degrees or more, and that error is the difference between 28 and 33 degrees, which is where avalanche danger kicks in. Use an inclinometer or a slope-angle map layer such as CalTopo to check your guesses. Make sure to look at the steepest part of the slope and what's above it, not only where you're standing.
How windy is too windy to jump? Dropzone said it's on hold but forecast looks fine to me.

Trust the dropzone over the app, because they're reading real conditions at altitude and on the landing area.
