i've got about 40 jumps. buddy says i should downsize from a 190 to a 150 to make landings more fun. good idea?

That's a big jump in wing loading for 40 jumps, and it's exactly how a lot of low-timers get hurt landing. Downsize gradually, roughly one size at a time, and only once you're consistently landing accurately and can handle the current canopy in all conditions. Take a canopy course and talk to an S&TA or a canopy coach before any change, because your buddy isn't the one who'll pay for a bad landing.
First time out with my new splitboard. Any tips?

Start on mellow terrain close to the road so you can get comfortable switching between ride and tour modes and skinning efficiently. Practice transitions at home first so you're not fumbling with cold hands. If you're heading anywhere near avalanche terrain, make sure you've got rescue gear and training before you go.
honestly do avalanche courses help or is it a money grab

They genuinely help. Besides beacon skills, they teach you to read forecasts, recognize warning signs and manage terrain, which is where most real accidents are prevented. Training doesn't make you invincible, and some trained people still make bad calls, but going without it means guessing in terrain where guessing kills. An AIARE 1 or equivalent is worth every dollar.
is it ok to ski a chute if i go first and my buddy watches from the top

Going one at a time is exactly right, but where your buddy watches from matters. Make sure they're in a safe spot out of the slide path and not on top of the slope or cornice that could release with you. Ski to a safe zone off to the side at the bottom, out of the runout, then watch them ski with your beacon in search mode-ready and a plan if something goes wrong. Before any of that, make sure the avalanche forecast and conditions actually support skiing a chute that day.
two jumps in one day, crazy?

Not crazy at all, and many sites sell double-jump deals. Take a proper break between them, stay hydrated and eat something. If the first one left you with a headache, neck soreness or dizziness, skip the second and call it a great day.
How long should I wait between dives?

A common rule of thumb is to rest on the surface for at least twice your dive time, and longer as you go deeper. Many instructors suggest a recovery time in minutes of about one-fifth of your depth in meters, so roughly four minutes after a 20 m dive. Rest until your breathing is fully relaxed rather than going by the clock alone, and shorten your session if you feel tired, cold or lightheaded.
is a used rope from facebook marketplace safe if it looks fine?

I'd skip it. You can't see chemical contamination, a past big fall, or poor storage, and "looks fine" tells you very little about a rope's history. Used carabiners and quickdraws from people you don't know carry the same risk. Ropes are cheap compared to what they protect, so buy new and keep track of its history yourself.
my beacon battery says 40%. fine for a day tour right?

Most manufacturers recommend replacing batteries at around 40 to 50 percent, because performance and range can fall off quickly in cold weather. Swap in fresh alkaline batteries of the type your manual specifies (usually not lithium or rechargeable, since they can throw off the battery reading) and you're set. That beacon is the one thing your partners rely on to find you, so don't cheap out.
Pregnant, 8 weeks. Planned a dive trip next month. Can I still dive shallow?

The standard advice is not to dive at all during pregnancy, even shallow. There's very little data on how nitrogen bubbles affect a fetus, and the fetus isn't protected by the lungs' bubble-filtering, so it isn't worth the risk. Snorkeling on the trip is a great alternative, and check with your doctor about that too. Diving can wait until after.
Gonna swim to that island, looks like 800m. Tide's going out but should be fine

I'd wait for slack water, because an outgoing tide can pull you sideways or out to sea faster than you can swim, and 800 m always looks shorter than it is. Check a tide table, plan to go around high or low slack, and have a kayak or boat escort with you. Also make sure you can land on the island and swim back once the tide turns. Getting stranded or swept off course is how these swims go wrong.
Can I swim in a wetsuit I bought 10 years ago? Still fits

If it still fits and the seams and neoprene aren't cracked, it should be fine. Check the zip and stitching, and look for thin or brittle spots, because old neoprene can lose some buoyancy and warmth over time. Do a short test swim close to shore to see how it feels before you take it anywhere longer.
do I really need a helmet at the crag?

Yes, wear one, because rockfall and dropped gear from climbers above happen even at popular crags, and flipping upside down in a fall can hit your head on the wall. Belayers should wear them too, since they stand right in the fall zone. A light modern helmet is comfortable enough that you'll forget you have it on.
What happens if I get a malfunction in a wingsuit?

You handle it with the same cutaway and reserve procedures you already know, but the suit adds complication if your arm wings are still open. Practice collapsing your wings fully before reaching for handles, and keep handles in places you can find by feel in the suit. That's a big reason for higher pull altitudes, and your instructor will drill emergency procedures in your suit on the ground first.
Is it cheaper to just buy a used rig and teach myself from YouTube?

That's genuinely one of the most dangerous ideas in the sport, and no legitimate dropzone will put you on a plane without formal training anyway. Skydiving's real risks come down to emergency procedures, canopy control and judgment, and none of those can be learned from video. Do AFF or a static line course, rent gear while you train, and buy a used rig later with a rigger's help once you're licensed.
can i do downhill on my hardtail xc bike or will it explode lol

It won't explode, but an XC hardtail isn't built for lift-served downhill. Steep geometry, short travel, light wheels, and small brakes make it sketchy on rough black trails and hard on the frame. It's fine for easy flow trails at a moderate pace. For real DH, rent a downhill or enduro bike at the park, which also lets you see what the right bike feels like.
I heard you can save gas by skipping a safety stop after cave dives. True?

No, cutting decompression or safety stops to save gas is how you end up with decompression sickness, which can be crippling far from medical help. Plan your gas so you finish with your reserve intact and complete all required stops. If gas is consistently tight, the fix is bigger cylinders, a stage, or a shorter penetration, not skipping deco.
do i need a wetsuit hood at nazare

Depends on the season, but winter water at Nazaré runs around 14 to 15°C, so most surfers wear a 4/3 or 5/4, often with a hood, plus booties. Staying warm keeps your breath-hold and reaction time sharp. Check with local surf shops for current conditions.
what's SIV and do I really need it

SIV is simulated incident training, where you fly over water with an instructor on the radio and deliberately practise collapses, stalls and other emergencies so you learn to recover from them. It isn't legally required, but it's one of the best things you can do once you're flying regularly in active air. Knowing how your wing reacts, and how you react, makes a real difference when things go wrong for real. Do it with a reputable school, with a rescue boat and good conditions.
I got knocked out briefly after a fall but I feel fine now, can I keep riding?

Stop riding for the day and get checked by ski patrol or a doctor right away. Any loss of consciousness means a concussion, and symptoms can show up hours later, while a second hit now could be really dangerous. Rest, avoid screens and alcohol, and have someone keep an eye on you tonight. Don't return to the park until a medical professional clears you.
Can I take a long hot ultra on keto or low-carb?

You can technically do it, but it's harder and riskier in heat. Without carbohydrate you'll have less fuel available at higher intensities, and fat adaptation doesn't help with heat stress itself. If you're committed to low-carb, at least practice your exact race-day plan in long hot runs, and consider adding some carbohydrate during the race, since it's one of the easiest ways to stay sharp late.
how do you even read big-wave sets

Spend a long time watching before paddling out: count waves per set, time the intervals, and note where the biggest waves break compared to landmarks on shore. Locals line up using fixed points so they stay out of the impact zone, and you can ask them what they use. Watch for out-of-sequence clean-up sets, which are the ones that catch people inside.
best way to learn rolling fast

Book a lesson or join a club pool session, where an instructor can catch mistakes before they become habits. Start with hip snaps holding a pool edge or a partner's boat, then add the sweep and head position. Consistent short sessions work better than cramming, and paddling with a nose plug and mask helps you stay relaxed while learning.
I'm 115 kg. Can I still paraglide?

Yes, but you'll need a wing sized for your all-up weight, meaning your body weight plus harness, reserve and gear, which for you is around 130 to 135 kg. Larger EN-A wings come in that range, and many schools keep big training wings in stock, so mention your weight when booking. Flying a wing too small for your load makes it faster and less forgiving, so getting the size right really matters.
cheapest way to get my own tank filled? can i just use a paintball compressor

No. Breathing air has to meet strict purity standards, and compressors not built for it can deliver carbon monoxide, oil or moisture, which are dangerous at depth. Get your tank filled at a dive shop that tests its air. Most charge only a few dollars, and your tank also needs a current visual inspection and hydro test before they'll fill it.
what helmet for downhill

Get a full-face helmet certified to a motorcycle or downhill mountain bike standard such as DOT, ECE 22.06 or ASTM F1952, not an open skate bucket. Your face and chin are what hit first in a lot of downhill crashes, and an open helmet leaves them exposed. Make sure it fits snugly with no wobble, and replace it after any significant impact even if it looks fine.
Can you freedive while sick with a cold?

Skip it. A cold makes it hard to equalize, which raises your risk of ear and sinus barotrauma, and congestion can get forced around in painful ways. Decongestants can wear off mid-dive and leave you with a reverse block on the ascent. Rest up and get back in once your head is clear.
how do i know when my climbing rope needs to be retired? it's like 4 years old but looks fine

Age alone doesn't retire a rope, but use and history do, so check the whole length for flat or stiff spots, a fuzzy or glazed sheath, exposed core, and any section that feels mushy when you bend it. Retire it right away after a very hard fall, any contact with acids or battery fluid, or core damage you can feel. With regular weekend use, four years is around the point where most climbers start seriously considering a replacement. Manufacturers typically cap rope life at about ten years even if it's never used, so check the tag or the manual for your specific rope.
how do i do the frenzel thing

Pinch your nose, close off your throat by locking it like you're about to lift something heavy, then push your tongue up and back like a piston. That compresses the air into your ears. You shouldn't be using your chest or stomach muscles at all. Practice it dry on land until you can feel your ears pop gently, and use a nose clip or mask while you learn. A short session with an instructor can save you weeks of guessing.
i'm 62, been resort skiing forever, want to try backcountry. too old?

Not at all, and plenty of people start touring in their sixties and love it. Make sure your fitness is up for long uphill days, and start with guided tours or a course. That way you learn efficient technique and avalanche basics from the start. Your years of skiing are a real asset, and touring at a sensible pace in good terrain is a great way to keep enjoying the mountains.
There's a closed trail at our park with a sign saying under construction but it looks done. Worth a sneaky lap?

Skip it, because closed trails often have unfinished features, loose dirt that hasn't packed in, or equipment around a blind corner. Getting hurt on a closed trail also means patrol isn't expecting you there, and some parks will pull your pass. Ask the trail crew when it opens, since you'll have way more fun riding it once it's dialed.
Skated a 10 stair today first try lol. Should I try 12 next?

Nice, but one clean try on a 10 doesn't mean you're ready to jump up, since bigger sets punish your ankles, knees, and heels a lot more than the extra two steps suggest. Land the 10 consistently and comfortably first, wear a helmet, and use good shoes with impact insoles to save your feet. When you do step up, film it and have a friend there in case something goes wrong.
do I need knee pads for the bowl or is that for beginners

Wear them, even really good bowl skaters wear knee pads because knee sliding is the standard way to bail out of a transition safely. Without pads, your options are falling on your hips, wrists or head, which is much worse. A solid pair of skate knee pads with hard caps is one of the best investments you can make for transition skating.
Ear hurt really bad after a jump yesterday and there's a bit of ringing. Normal?

That could be a perforated eardrum, which is a common injury when water hits the ear at an angle. Keep the ear dry, don't put anything in it, and see a doctor or urgent care soon, especially if you notice discharge, dizziness or hearing loss. Hold off on swimming and jumping until it's checked, and next time keep your head level and use earplugs or a hood.
Is it okay to run a hot ultra while I'm getting over a stomach bug?

I'd skip it or drop to a shorter distance. A recent stomach bug leaves you short on fluids and electrolytes, and heat makes all of that dramatically worse, which raises your risk of collapse and kidney trouble. If you were vomiting or had diarrhea within the last few days, a DNS is the wise call.
Shark circled us on a dive and my buddy wanted to swim at it for a video. What's the right move?

Your instinct to hold back was right. Stay calm, stay close to the reef or your group, keep eye contact with the shark and don't chase or crowd it. Most sharks are curious and will move off, but pursuing one for footage is how you get an unnecessary defensive encounter. If it seems agitated, like hunching or making jerky movements, end the dive calmly and slowly, without bolting for the surface.
We're behind schedule on Everest Base Camp. Can we skip the Dingboche rest day and make it up?

Skipping the Dingboche rest day is one of the most common ways people end up evacuated by helicopter from Lobuche or Gorak Shep. It's better to shorten the trip at the end, like cutting out Kala Patthar or flying out of Lukla on a later day, than to compress the climb. If time really is fixed, consider turning around at a lower point rather than gambling with your health.
My 17 year old son wants to go ski touring with his friends this weekend and none of them have taken an avalanche course. Should I let him go?

I'd hold off on avalanche terrain until at least one of them, ideally all, has taken an AIARE 1 or equivalent course, which usually runs a weekend and teaches route choice, forecasting and rescue. In the meantime they can tour on low-angle slopes under about 30 degrees with nothing steep above them, or ski a resort's uphill routes. You could also book them a day with a certified guide so they learn from someone good right from the start.
Best fins for a beginner?

Start with mid-length plastic or polymer long-blade fins with a medium-soft stiffness. They're forgiving, affordable and teach good kick technique. Brands like Cressi, Leaderfins and Mares make solid entry options. Hold off on carbon fins until your technique and budget call for them, and make sure the foot pocket fits snugly without pinching.
Is it okay to paraglide with a cast on my arm? It's my non-dominant one

I'd wait. Paragliding needs both hands for brakes, risers and reserve deployment, and launching and landing can involve stumbles or falls where you'll instinctively use both arms. If you couldn't throw your reserve with that hand, you're giving up a critical safety margin. Ask your instructor or club, but most will tell you to wait until the cast is off and your grip strength is back.
is soloing a 5.6 dangerous if i climb 5.11

Yes, because a fall on a 5.6 kills you just as surely as a fall on a 5.11. Grade margin helps, but most soloing accidents come from things grades don't capture, like a snapped hold, a wet patch, a bee, or a foot slipping off polished rock. If you want that free, flowy feeling, try roped soloing with a backup system or a long, easy route with a partner and minimal gear. Those give you the movement without betting your life on every hold staying put.
Quick, belay device recommendation for ice

A standard tube-style device or an assisted-braking device like a GriGri works well, as long as your rope fits it. A lot of ice climbers prefer guide-mode tube devices because they let you bring a second up from the top on multipitch routes. Whatever you use, practice with gloves on, since thick, wet gloves and icy ropes change how the brake hand feels. Dry-treated ropes help a lot with icing up.
is a 450 too much for a first bike if i'm 6'3 and 230lbs

Being big doesn't make a 450 any easier to control. A modern 450 makes a lot of power, which is tiring and punishes mistakes, and most beginners ride them badly and learn bad habits. A 250F will carry your weight fine and let you learn proper technique, and plenty of bigger riders spend a season or two on one before moving up. If you really want a 450, consider a mellower model or have the power mapped down, but a 250F is the smarter first bike.
My son is 16 and wants to go to Nazaré next winter. Should I let him?

Watching from the lighthouse cliff is an incredible experience and completely safe. Paddling or towing into Praia do Norte on a real swell is a different matter. That place has hurt and nearly killed world-class pros, and no 16-year-old has the ocean hours for it. If he's serious, a structured path makes a great compromise: a big-wave safety course, mentoring with an experienced crew, and building up on medium-sized reef waves over the next few years.
best way to practice cliff diving technique without a cliff?

A public pool with 3, 5 and 10 meter platforms is ideal, and many have lifeguards and sometimes diving coaches who can fix your form. Practice feet-first entries until you're consistently vertical and tight, then add height slowly. Some diving clubs run adult classes, which is the fastest way to build good habits.
My suit feels unstable on the exit and I keep flipping. Should I just push through it?

Don't push through it; get it diagnosed. Flipping on exit often comes from suit fit, unzipped or unbalanced wings, poor exit timing, or tension in your body, and an experienced coach can usually spot the cause from a video quickly. Until it's sorted, a clean, relaxed exit with the arm wings closed until you're clear of the plane will help a lot.
What's a strainer and why does everyone freak out about them?

A strainer is anything that lets water through but not you, usually a fallen tree, branches or a fence across the current. People freak out because the current can pin a swimmer or boat against it with enormous force, and those pins are among the leading causes of whitewater deaths. Scout for wood, portage anything questionable, and if you're swimming toward one, get aggressive, go headfirst and try to climb over it rather than getting swept under.
whats a method grab

A method is a grab where you reach your front hand to the heel edge between your bindings while bending your knees and pulling the board up behind you. The style comes from tweaking the board up and arching your back a bit at the peak. Learn it on a medium jump where you have enough air time, and let go early enough to set up for landing.
thinking of doing a sneaky jump off a building downtown at night, tips?

Skip it, because it's illegal, you risk trespass and other charges, and a night urban jump is one of the hardest jumps you can make, not a beginner adventure. Darkness hides wires, wind patterns between buildings are unpredictable, and landing areas are full of traffic and obstacles. If you want that kind of jump eventually, build experience on legal objects with mentors first.
best board length for big waves?

For paddle surfing in the 15 to 25 foot range, most people ride guns between about 9'6" and 11', scaled to their weight and the wave. Longer boards help you get in early, which matters because late takeoffs are where many wipeouts happen. A good shaper who knows the specific break is your best resource, so tell them where you're surfing and your size.
how long after a broken collarbone can I ride again

That depends on the break and whether you had surgery, so your surgeon's clearance is the real answer. Many collarbone fractures take about 6 to 12 weeks before they can handle the impact of riding, and a crash on a bone that isn't fully healed can mean surgery or a much longer recovery. Ask for follow-up X-rays to confirm the bone has healed, and do some physio to rebuild strength and range of motion in your shoulder. Start back with easy laps before working back up to jumps.
How long does it take to pack a BASE canopy and can I learn it from YouTube?

A careful BASE pack usually takes 30 to 60 minutes once you're competent, and longer while you're learning. With no reserve, your pack job decides whether you get a clean opening, so this isn't something to learn from videos. Learn it in person during an FJC, have every pack checked by an experienced jumper for your first dozens of jumps, and keep checking it yourself on every one.
I'm 70 and want to run my first hot ultra. Too old?

Plenty of people in their 70s finish ultras, so age alone isn't a reason not to. Older bodies sense thirst less and cool more slowly, though, so get a medical checkup and do careful heat training first. Choose a race with generous cutoffs and shade, and drink on a schedule rather than waiting for thirst.
How long can someone survive buried in an avalanche?

Survival odds are high for roughly the first 15 minutes, mostly because the victim still has some air. After that they drop steeply as asphyxiation sets in, and by around 35 minutes most people completely buried have died. That's why companion rescue matters so much: your partners are the realistic rescue, not search and rescue crews who might take an hour or more to arrive. Practice beacon searches regularly so you can find and dig someone out fast.
can i skydive while pregnant, it's early, nobody would know

Please don't. Opening shock, harness pressure and the risk of a hard landing are real hazards to a pregnancy even early on, and dropzones and medical guidance are clear that it isn't recommended. Spend these months in the wind tunnel or on ground school if your doctor clears it, and come back to the sky after you've recovered.
Planning Aconcagua solo, no guide, first time above 6000m. Thoughts?

Aconcagua is non-technical on the normal route, but its weather and altitude kill people every season, and making it your first 6,000 m peak solo stacks the risks. Strongly consider a guided expedition or at least joining a team, because a partner who notices your HACE symptoms before you do can be the difference. If you're set on going independent, get real experience first on a peak like Huayna Potosí or Chimborazo, register with the park, carry a satellite messenger, and be ready to turn back when the Viento Blanco rolls in.
My kid broke her wrist on her first try at a jump. Wrist guards worth it?

Yes, wrist guards are absolutely worth it for kids and beginners in the park, since wrist fractures are one of the most common snowboarding injuries. Get snowboard-specific ones that fit under or over the glove. Also teach her to fall on her forearms or roll rather than reaching out with straight arms. Once she's healed, a kids' lesson focusing on falling and small features is a great reset.
just bought tools and crampons, gonna teach myself on a frozen waterfall near my house this weekend

Love the enthusiasm, but don't climb above the ground alone untrained. Unknown ice can be thin or have water running behind it, and a short fall onto crampons breaks ankles fast. If you want to play this weekend, practice low-angle footwork and tool swings right at ground level with a friend nearby. Then book a guided intro day so you learn belaying and anchors properly.
can i fly with a hangover lol

No. Alcohol slows your reactions and impairs judgment, and it can leave you dehydrated, which makes things worse at altitude. Paragliding demands quick responses during launch and in turbulence, and a slow reaction can lead to a crash. Take the day off, have some water and fly tomorrow.
how tight should climbing shoes be

For beginners, snug but comfortable enough to wear for a full route: toes flat or slightly curled, with no dead space at the heel. Aggressive, painfully tight shoes help on hard overhangs but slow your technique learning and can cause foot problems. Try several brands in person, since fit varies a lot between them.
torn calf mid-season, do I need to see anyone or just rest?

See someone, because a calf tear can range from mild to serious, and an Achilles rupture can feel similar and needs urgent treatment. A physio can grade the injury and give you a loading plan, which gets you back faster and lowers the risk of a re-tear. Seek care urgently if you felt a pop or can't push up onto your toes.
is it ok to ride alone at the local track on weekdays when nobody's there

I'd avoid riding completely alone, because if you go down hard and get knocked out or pinned, nobody may find you for hours. If you do go solo, make sure the track has staff on site, tell someone your plan and your check-in time, and keep your phone on you, not in the truck. Even better, bring a friend who sits out and watches, which is a lot safer than riding by yourself.
my buddy says real riders don't use spotters

Your buddy is wrong; pros and event organizers use spotters and radios constantly because blind corners and driveways are where cars appear. A spotter turns an unknown into a known, and it's standard practice on any shared road. Set clear signals beforehand and agree that the rider stops if there's any doubt. Real riders want to keep riding next week.
Forecast for my zone is 'no rating' because the avalanche center hasn't started the season yet. Fresh snow last week. Thoughts?

No rating doesn't mean no danger, and early-season snow often builds weak layers on top of old snow or shallow cover. You'll have to assess conditions yourself, so look for recent slides, cracking or collapsing and wind loading, and check any early-season observations posted by the avalanche center or local community. Keep it conservative with low-angle terrain until you have better information.
Is freediving in a lake different from the ocean?

Yes. Lakes are usually colder below a thermocline, often darker, and fresh water is less buoyant, so you'll need less weight than you would in the ocean. Low visibility makes it harder for your buddy to keep an eye on you, so stay close and use a line. If the lake is at altitude, be extra conservative, because that changes the physics of your dive, and get some guidance before you go deep.
Is it worth learning on a rebreather straight away for caves?

Generally no. Most instructors recommend becoming a solid open-circuit cave diver first, because rebreathers add complexity and failure modes that are much harder to manage when you're also learning the cave environment. Once you have real cave experience, a rebreather course and a careful build-up make sense, especially for long dives or exploration.
How long does it take to acclimatize to cold water?

The cold shock response starts to soften after about five or six short immersions, often within a couple of weeks of regular swims. Real tolerance builds over a season, which is why many people start in late summer and keep swimming as the water cools. Consistency matters more than duration, so frequent short dips beat occasional long ones. Acclimatization doesn't make you immune to hypothermia, though, so keep respecting your time limits.
We found a little underwater opening in a lake. I'm gonna poke my head in with a spool, I'll be fine right?

I'd skip it. Even a small opening can lead into a silty, confined space where a stuck tank or silt-out turns deadly fast, and a spool without training won't save you. Lots of untrained deaths start with 'just a quick look'. Note the spot and come back after cavern training with an experienced cave diver who can assess it properly.
I'm on an SSRI for depression. Anything to know before a hot ultra?

Yes, have a quick talk with your prescriber or a sports doctor first. Some antidepressants can affect how your body regulates temperature and sweating, and SSRIs are linked to a higher risk of hyponatremia, which is already a concern in long hot races. You don't necessarily need to change anything, but knowing your risk lets you plan your sodium and fluid intake carefully. Don't stop or adjust your medication on your own to prepare for the race.
Drinking a couple beers before paddling isn't a big deal right?
It is a big deal. Alcohol slows your reactions, impairs judgment and makes cold-water shock and hypothermia more dangerous. Save the beers for the takeout.
neck stiff after a wipeout surfing, no other symptoms. surf tomorrow?

If it's just muscle stiffness, with full range of motion and no numbness, tingling, weakness or headache, a gentle session could be fine. But if the wipeout involved hitting the bottom or being compressed hard, get it checked before you go back out, because neck injuries aren't worth gambling on. Seek care immediately if any nerve symptoms show up.
pulled at 2500 on my last student jump instead of 5500, felt fine tho. big deal?

Yes, it's a big deal, so report it honestly to your instructor if you haven't already. 2500 feet is right around where your AAD fires and leaves almost no margin to deal with a malfunction. Something pulled your attention off your altimeter, and your instructor needs to work through that with you before you jump again. It's very fixable, but only if you treat it seriously.
is it ok to drink alcohol at base camp to sleep better

Skip it. Alcohol suppresses your breathing during sleep, which makes the already-low oxygen levels at altitude worse. It also dehydrates you and can mask early AMS symptoms. Wait until you're back down, and use a good pillow and earplugs to help you sleep up there.
My girlfriend wants to learn big wave surfing with me. Where should we start?

Do a big-wave safety course together first so you both learn rescue and breath-hold basics. Then surf progressively bigger days at manageable spots with experienced friends. Learning as a team means you can look out for each other.
can i just jump off a bridge with a climbing rope instead, its basically the same

No, it's very much not the same. Dynamic climbing ropes are designed for short falls, not the long, repeated deceleration of a bungee jump. Using one for a big free fall can deliver crushing force or simply fail to stop you in time. People have died trying homemade rope jumps. If you want the feeling, book a commercial bungee, or look into an organized rope swing run by professionals with engineered rigging.
My 9 year old wants a skateboard for his birthday. Is that too young? I'm honestly kind of nervous about it.

Nine is a great age to start, and plenty of kids begin even younger. Get him a properly sized complete from a real skate shop rather than a toy-store board, plus a certified helmet that fits snugly and wrist guards, since wrist fractures are the most common kid skate injury. If you can, book a lesson or two at a local skatepark so he learns how to fall safely and how park etiquette works from the start.
Teenager wants to ride without supervision at our private property. He's 15 and pretty good.

Fifteen and skilled is a good start, but having someone nearby when he rides is still smart, since even good riders crash and may need help. If you can't be there, set rules like no jumps without someone present, phone on him, and regular check-ins. A buddy system with a friend works well too.
quick q how do i get over my fear of heights so i can solo

Fear of heights is useful information, so the goal is to calibrate it rather than switch it off. The proven way is gradual exposure on rope, like leading outdoors, taking practice falls, and spending lots of time on multi-pitch, so your fear starts matching the actual risk. If that fear is still loud on a rope, it's telling you something important about being without one. Lots of climbers find that the fear simply fades with experience, and some of them still decide soloing isn't worth it.
what's the deal with v-threads, are they actually strong enough to rap off

A well-made V-thread in good, solid ice is surprisingly strong and is a standard way to rappel off ice routes. Use a 22cm screw if you can, make the two holes meet cleanly at about 60 degrees, keep the thread at least 15cm across, and back it up with a screw that the first person down removes. Practice building them at ground level with an experienced partner first, and never trust one in rotten, aerated or thin ice.
How do free soloists deal with fear? I want to train my mind for it.

Experienced soloists don't so much defeat fear as build huge amounts of familiarity, through endless roped practice and visualization, until a specific route stops feeling scary. That mental training is useful for any climber, and you can do it safely by practicing lead falls with a good belayer, climbing near your limit on rope, and learning breathing control on hard moves. Treat fear as a useful signal rather than something to switch off. The people who stopped listening to it are the cautionary tales.
how fast do street luge riders actually go? like is 60mph real

Yes, 60 mph is real and pretty routine on good courses for experienced racers, and top speeds on long steep hills have been clocked above 90 mph. Those riders are on closed roads with hay bales, full leathers and full-face helmets, which is the only reason those speeds are survivable. If you're starting out, 20 to 30 mph will feel terrifyingly fast lying a few inches off the pavement.
My regulator has been free-flowing a little at the surface. Probably fine underwater right?

Don't count on it, because a free-flow often gets worse at depth or in cold water and can drain your tank fast. Have a qualified technician look at it before you dive again. Rent a regulator in the meantime if you need to. Regulator servicing is cheap compared to an out-of-air situation.
How do I know if a river is too hard for me?

Read the guidebook rating and flow range, and compare it to rapids you've run cleanly with control, not just ones you survived. If you can't confidently catch eddies, ferry and roll reliably on the grade below, wait. Talking to locals and paddling with people who know the river is the most reliable way to judge.
do i really need a probe if i have a beacon

Yes, without a probe you'll waste precious minutes digging in the wrong spot, because a beacon only gets you close, not to an exact location. The probe pinpoints the burial and depth so you can start shoveling efficiently. The beacon, shovel and probe work as a set, and missing any one of them dramatically slows a rescue.
What's the deal with off-heading openings, how bad are they?

They're one of the main killers in BASE, especially off cliffs and buildings, because the canopy can fly you straight back into the object within a second or two. Good packing, a symmetrical body position at deployment and a stable exit reduce the risk a lot. You also need a practiced reaction: grab the rear risers and steer away right away instead of reaching for toggles. A good first jump course drills this until it's automatic.
Can you skydive with asthma?

Many people with well-controlled asthma skydive without problems, but the cold, thin air at altitude and the adrenaline can trigger symptoms. Talk to your doctor first, keep your rescue inhaler handy before boarding, and tell your instructor about your asthma. If your asthma is poorly controlled or you've had recent attacks, wait until it's stable.
Is a swiftwater rescue course actually worth it or just a cash grab?

Worth it, especially if you plan to paddle class III or above. You learn how to handle pins, entrapments, swimmer rescues and rope systems in a controlled setting, which makes you a much more useful member of any group. Many paddling clubs and outfitters offer good courses, and a lot of experienced boaters retake them every few years.
do i need a reserve for base

No, BASE rigs don't have a reserve because jumps happen too low for a second parachute to deploy in time. That's exactly why packing, gear checks, and a clean exit and pull matter so much, because your main has to work every time. Learn to pack under supervision until an instructor signs off, and never rush a pack job.
Wind is gusting 25 km/h at launch but my buddies are going. Should I?

If you're asking, the answer is probably no, especially if you're a newer pilot. Gusty air at 25 km/h is well beyond what most low-airtime pilots should launch in, and the gust factor matters more than the average speed. Watch how the experienced pilots handle it, and if they're getting yanked around on launch, pack up and fly another day. Nobody worth flying with will think less of you for sitting out.
whats the easiest way to stop on a longboard going fast

At real speed, a slide is the most effective way to stop. A standup or Coleman slide sets the board sideways and scrubs off speed quickly, but each one takes practice at low speed first while wearing slide gloves. Foot braking is easier to learn and works well at moderate speed, but it gets sketchy and wears out your shoes fast once you're really moving. Don't ride any hill faster than the speed you can confidently stop from.
Been drinking a few beers, the cliff is only like 8 meters, we're good?

Skip the jump today. Alcohol slows your reaction time, messes with your body position in the air and makes cold water shock much more dangerous, and a lot of serious cliff jumping injuries involve drinking. Eight meters is high enough to knock the wind out of you or break something on a bad landing, so swim, hang out, and save the jump for a sober day.
I'm 14 and want to start parkour. My parents think it's just jumping off roofs. How do I convince them?

Show them what beginner parkour actually looks like: precision jumps on low curbs, quadrupedal movement drills, safety rolls on grass, and vaults over waist-high rails. Better yet, find a local parkour gym or a coach certified by Parkour Earth or ADAPT and invite your parents to watch a class, because seeing structured progression usually ends the rooftop fear fast. Agree to train only at ground level until a coach says otherwise, and you'll earn their trust much quicker than by arguing.
what conditioning should i do as a total beginner

Focus on squats, lunges, push-ups, pull-ups or rows, planks, and calf raises, since those build the leg strength and grip that protect your joints when you land and climb. Add quadrupedal movement like crawling on all fours, which sounds silly but builds shoulder and wrist strength quickly. Do two or three sessions a week alongside your parkour practice, and give yourself rest days because tendons adapt slower than muscles. Consistency beats intensity in the first few months.
I'm 41 and haven't skated since high school. Any tips for getting back into it without wrecking myself?

Ease in and respect that your body recovers slower now. Start on flat smooth ground for a few sessions to get your balance back, and wear a helmet, wrist guards and knee pads, because wrist fractures are the classic comeback injury. Warm up properly and keep early sessions short. Learn to fall by rolling onto pads rather than reaching out with straight arms.
Is it fine to dive solo if I'm really experienced? Buddies slow me down.

Solo diving is a legitimate practice, but only with specific training like PADI Self-Reliant or SDI Solo Diver and a fully redundant air source such as a pony bottle. Without that, you're one free-flow or entanglement away from a situation with nobody to hand you air. If buddies slow you down, look for a more experienced buddy or get the proper solo certification instead of just going alone.
how do I get over fear of jumping, I freeze at the edge every time

Drop to a height where you can jump without much hesitation, even if it feels too easy, and do lots of reps there so your body learns the motion. Use a set countdown and go on the number, because the longer you stand at the edge the louder the fear gets. Some fear is healthy, so don't let anyone pressure you into jumping before you're ready.
My 10 year old wants to try scuba on our holiday. Is that safe?

Yes, kids 10 and up can do Junior Open Water or a supervised try-dive with a reputable shop. Depth limits are lower for kids, around 12 meters for 10 to 11 year olds, and good instructors keep it relaxed and shallow. Pick a shop with experience teaching children, and make sure your kid actually wants to do it rather than being nudged into it.
brakes started fading halfway down a long run and the lever went to the bar. wtf happened

That's classic overheating: dragging the brakes on a long descent cooks the fluid, and the lever goes soft or hits the bar. Stop riding that bike downhill until it's sorted, because it's a serious crash risk. Have a shop bleed the brakes with fresh fluid, check the pads for glazing, and consider bigger 200 or 220 mm rotors. On the trail, brake hard and briefly before corners rather than dragging all the way down, and give the brakes a rest if you feel them fading.
can I use my skateboard in the street to commute

Lots of people do, but check your local laws since some cities ban skating on certain roads or sidewalks. Ride like a cyclist would, predictable and visible, and wear a helmet plus lights at night. Choose routes with bike lanes or quiet streets, and use soft wheels so cracks and pebbles don't stop you suddenly.
There's a 6 foot drop on the black line I keep walking around. Everyone says just send it with speed. Should I?

Don't send it on a dare. Speed only works if you know how much the drop needs, and too little speed is how people case or nose in. Build up on smaller drops until you can roll off them neutral and land both wheels together, then watch a few confident riders hit this one to see their speed and line. If you can, have a coach or experienced friend check your technique first. Walking around it is fine until you're truly ready.
I'm 52 and want to start freediving. Am I too old?

Not at all, plenty of people start in their fifties and dive well into their seventies. Get a medical check first, with particular attention to heart health, blood pressure and your ears and sinuses, since those matter most for breath-hold and equalization. Then take an entry-level course like AIDA 2 or PADI Freediver so you learn proper technique and rescue skills from the start. Progress at your own pace and you'll do great.
can i free solo with climbing shoes from decathlon or do i need expensive ones

Gear isn't really the question here. If you're at the stage of asking which shoes to buy, you aren't ready to solo, because readiness comes from years of roped climbing. Budget shoes from Decathlon are totally fine for learning in the gym and on roped routes outdoors. Put the money you save toward a course or a few days with a guide.
first time at a bike park next weekend, rented a full suspension DH bike. anything i should know?

Start on the easiest green flow trail for your first two or three runs so you learn how the rental bike's brakes and suspension feel at speed. Ask the rental shop to set your sag and lever reach before you leave the counter, because a bike set up for someone else feels twitchy and unpredictable. Wear a full-face helmet and knee pads at minimum, and save the black lines for another visit no matter how good you feel by lunchtime.
Is cliff diving in the ocean different from a quarry?

Yes, quite a bit. In the ocean you have to worry about tides changing the depth by meters, swells pushing you toward rocks, and currents making the exit harder, so you need to time your jump with the waves and know your climb-out route beforehand. Quarries have calm water but are often very cold, can hide submerged machinery or debris, and sometimes have sheer walls that make getting out difficult. Either way, scout the depth and the exit before you go up.
friend says the trick to clearing the big tabletop is to just straightline it with max speed. true?

No, too much speed is how people overshoot the landing and flat-bottom their knees and back. Watch a few riders who land in the sweet spot and match their speed, or do a few roll-overs to feel the takeoff before you send it. Size up gradually, and if you're unsure, go a little slow and land on the knuckle instead of blasting past the landing.
SIV course worth it or overkill for a recreational pilot?

Worth it, even if you only fly on weekends. Experiencing collapses, stalls and spirals in a controlled setting over water, with an instructor on the radio and a rescue boat below, means your first real collapse won't be your first collapse ever. Most pilots come back calmer and much more confident in their wing. Choose a well-reviewed operator with a boat team and do it on your own glider.
is it ok to lead WI3 after only toproping ice for one season? I feel solid on TR

Feeling solid on toprope is a good start, but leading ice is a different game because falling is not an acceptable outcome; crampon points catch, ankles break, and screws placed while pumped can be marginal. Before you lead WI3, spend days mock leading on toprope, placing and clipping screws while still protected by the rope above. When you do start, pick a fat, low-angle WI2 or easy WI3 with good ice and lead it well within your toprope grade. Many climbers lead a full grade or two below what they can toprope for their first season on the sharp end, and that margin is what keeps them healthy.
how tight should my knee pads be

Snug enough that they don't slide when you pedal or crash, but not so tight they cut off circulation or pinch behind your knee. Try them on and do a few squats; they should stay centered on your kneecap. If they twist down your shin on a run, size down or try a different design with straps. Loose pads fail exactly when you need them.
Wrist is in a cast from a skate slam. Thinking of rolling with a wrist guard over it just to cruise. Dumb?

Pretty dumb, honestly. Anyone can slip even while just cruising, and putting a hand down onto a healing fracture can displace it and turn a six-week cast into surgery. Wrist guards also don't fit or work properly over a cast. Use the time for leg strength, balance board work without falling risk, or filming your friends, and skate again once your doctor clears the bone.
is paragliding dangerous

It carries real risk, but most of it is controllable. Accidents cluster around pilots flying in conditions beyond their skill, flying on worn-out gear, or skipping proper training. If you learn at a certified school, fly a beginner-rated wing and stay conservative with weather, it's a lot safer than its reputation. A tandem flight with a licensed pilot is a low-risk way to see if you like it.
my buddy dared me to hit the big jump with zero practice. it's just snow how bad can it be

Pretty bad. Hit a big jump too slow and you case the knuckle; hit it too fast and you overshoot onto flat ground, which is basically a car crash for your spine and wrists. Snow in a park is often hard-packed, not fluffy. Skip the dare, lap the medium jump a few times to learn your speed, and you'll look way better doing it right.
what's the safest way to enter the water feet first

Keep your body straight and vertical, with legs together, toes pointed and arms pressed tight to your sides or crossed over your chest. Squeeze your glutes and core so you don't fold on impact, and keep your head neutral, looking at the horizon rather than down. Once you're under, spread your arms and legs to slow down so you don't drive into the bottom.
I'm 16 and want to run a summer 50K with my dad. Is that dumb?

Not dumb, but check the race's age minimum first, because many 50Ks require runners to be 18. If you're allowed in, get a sports physical, build up your long runs gradually over several months, and practice hydrating and fueling in the heat with your dad on training runs. Run together and agree beforehand that either of you can call it if things go wrong.
I'm 16, can I do a tandem if my parents sign?

In the US the answer is almost always no, because USPA member dropzones require jumpers to be 18 regardless of parental consent. Some countries, including the UK and parts of Europe, allow tandems from 16 with a parent's signature, so it depends on where you are. Call the dropzone directly to confirm, and if you have to wait, indoor skydiving at a wind tunnel is a great way to learn body flight in the meantime.
best shoes for parkour? running shoes ok?

Running shoes are fine to start, but you'll get on better with something flatter and grippier with a flexible sole, since thick heels and high stacks make precision landings and wall runs harder. Look for a shoe with a gummy, mostly flat outsole that wraps a little up the sides, and avoid smooth soles that slip on rails. Brands like Feiyue are a cheap classic, and some companies make parkour-specific shoes if you want to spend more. Replace them once the tread wears smooth, since grip is what keeps you safe on walls and rails.
I'm 42 and haven't skated since high school. Too old to try downhill?

Plenty of people start or return to downhill in their 40s and beyond, so you're not too old. Your body just won't bounce back from slams like it used to, so start slow, wear full pads and a quality helmet, and spend time relearning balance and basic stopping on mellow hills before chasing speed. Joining a beginner-friendly group session or clinic is a great way to rebuild skills safely and meet riders your age.
do you need a dry suit for cave diving

It depends on water temperature and dive length. Mexico's cenotes around 25°C are fine in a good wetsuit for most divers, while Florida's springs around 22°C often push people into drysuits for long dives, and cold European caves almost always need one. Being cold degrades your thinking and gas consumption, so err on the warmer side for longer dives.
Our group summit push is 2 hours behind schedule but we're close. Turnaround time was 1pm, it's 1:15. Keep going?

Turn around. Turnaround times exist precisely because summit fever makes 'we're close' feel true when it isn't, and most high-altitude deaths happen on the descent, in the dark, with no reserves left. The mountain will still be there, and you'll be alive to come back.
quick q: wingsuit in high winds ok?

Usually no for beginners. High winds make your exit spot and landing harder and affect your flight path and canopy approach. Follow your dropzone's wind limits, which are often stricter for wingsuits and students. If you're unsure, sit it out.
how do i land switch without wobbling

The wobble usually means your switch riding isn't comfortable yet, so spend whole runs riding switch on easy terrain. On landing, keep your knees soft, your weight centered and your eyes looking down the hill, not at your board. Once switch feels natural, the wobble usually disappears by itself.
Is paragliding statistically more dangerous than skydiving?

They're broadly in a similar risk category, but they're hard to compare directly, because flights vary wildly in length, conditions and pilot experience. Paragliding risk depends heavily on decisions: flying in strong conditions, on a wing above your level or without training pushes it up a lot. Pilots who train properly, choose conservative days and fly within their limits lower their risk considerably. Treat it as serious, and respect the weather above all.
Can I skip supplemental oxygen on Everest if I'm really strong? Want the purist ascent.

Only a tiny handful of elite climbers with years of 8,000 m experience pull that off, and the death rate without oxygen is noticeably higher, partly because cold and poor judgment hit much harder. Strength at sea level doesn't predict how your brain and lungs will cope above 8,000 m. If the no-oxygen style matters to you, work up to it over several seasons by doing peaks like Cho Oyu without bottled oxygen first, and even then carry an emergency bottle with your Sherpa team.
I'm 58, a bit overweight and on blood pressure meds. Is scuba still realistic for me?

It very likely is, since plenty of people start diving in their fifties and sixties. You should get a proper dive medical first, because blood pressure medication and cardiovascular fitness genuinely matter for diving. Ask a doctor to go through the RSTC or UHMS medical questionnaire with you, and they can clear you or flag anything to adjust. Once you're cleared, a patient instructor and some work on general fitness will make a big difference.
do i need a different canopy for wingsuiting?

Usually you want a docile, reliable canopy with consistent, on-heading openings. Many people stay on a moderately loaded main they already know well rather than anything aggressive. Wingsuit deployments can be a little less clean, so a lightly loaded elliptical-ish or nine-cell all-rounder with good opening manners is ideal. Ask your rigger to check that your pilot chute and bridle are suited to wingsuit pulls.
Is an inflatable vest actually necessary or is it just a crutch?

It's necessary safety gear, not a crutch, and it's now standard at basically every serious big-wave spot. A flotation vest gets you to the surface faster after a heavy hold-down or if you're knocked unconscious, and that's exactly when it matters. Learn how your vest works, check the CO2 cartridges before every session and practice pulling the toggles. Just don't let it make you take waves you'd otherwise pass on.
honestly just want the fastest way to acclimate, race is in 5 days

Five days won't get you full acclimation, but it's not nothing. Do short daily heat sessions, like a 30 to 45 minute easy run in the heat or a hot bath afterward, and keep the intensity low so you don't arrive fatigued. The bigger win at this point is pacing: plan to start slower than you'd like, use ice aggressively, and adjust your goal time to the conditions.
hurry up i'm at the exit point. pc feels a bit loose in the pouch, jump or not?

Don't jump. A loose pilot chute can come out early and drag you into a premature deployment right at the edge, which is one of the worst failures in BASE. Step back, re-stow it properly, and have someone check it before you go. The exit isn't going anywhere.
first time ice climbing next week with a guide, what should I wear

Dress in layers: a synthetic or wool base layer, a fleece or light insulating midlayer, and waterproof shell jacket and pants to handle dripping ice. Bring a big puffy for standing around and belaying, because you'll cool off quickly when you stop moving. Pack a warm hat that fits under your helmet, thin climbing gloves plus warmer gloves, and wool socks that aren't so thick your boots get tight. Your guide will usually provide boots, crampons, tools, harness, and helmet, but confirm what's included when you book.
can i drink a couple beers between dives on a liveaboard

Save the beers for after your last dive of the day. Alcohol dehydrates you, dulls your judgment and may raise your decompression risk, and none of that mixes well with another dive a couple of hours later. Most good liveaboards have a rule that once you drink, you're done diving for the day, and that's a smart rule to follow.
My girlfriend thinks I'm reckless for cliff jumping. how do I convince her it's safe?

Rather than convincing her, show her you take it seriously: you check depths, never jump alone, skip it after drinking and stick to heights you've built up to. Cliff jumping does carry real risk, so her worry isn't unreasonable. Inviting her along to watch how careful you are, or choosing a lower and well-known spot, will do more than any argument.
Is creeking way more dangerous than regular river paddling?

Yes, generally. Creeks are steep, narrow and often have big drops, sieves, undercuts and wood, so the consequences of a mistake are much higher and rescues are tougher. Most people paddle class IV rivers solidly for a while before taking on creeks, and they do it with experienced creekers who know the specific run.
My 17 year old son wants to take a paragliding course this summer. I'm terrified. Is this a reasonable thing to let him do?

It's a reasonable thing to let him do if he trains with a properly certified school, because structured instruction is where most of the risk gets managed. A good course keeps students on gentle training hills, uses radio guidance, and only moves to higher flights once the basics are solid. Ask the school about instructor ratings, their safety record, and how they decide when conditions are too strong to fly. Then talk with your son about respecting the instructors' calls, since patience is what keeps beginners safe.
quick q can i jump alone if im a strong swimmer

I'd skip it. Swimming ability doesn't help if the impact winds you, you hit something underwater, or cold shock makes you gasp a lungful of water. Always have at least one person watching who can reach you or call for help.
I keep getting nervous before launch and my legs shake. Is that normal or am I not cut out for this?

Completely normal, and many good pilots felt exactly the same early on. A bit of nerves keeps you careful, and it usually fades as launches become routine. Work through a consistent pre-flight checklist to steady your mind, and ask your instructor for extra ground handling time, since confidence with the wing on the ground carries over into the air. If the fear keeps getting worse instead of better, talk it through with your instructor rather than forcing yourself.
Wetsuit or no wetsuit for a 3km lake swim in June? I hate how restrictive they feel.

It depends on the water temperature more than the month. Below about 16°C a wetsuit is the smart call for 3km, because you'll be in long enough for your arms to stiffen up and your judgement to slip. A sleeveless suit or a proper swim-specific suit with thin shoulder panels feels far less restrictive than a surf or budget suit. If the water's warmer and you've done long cold swims before, skins is fine, but don't go without one just to prove a point.
best way to practice launches without flying?

Ground handling is the answer, and it's one of the best things you can do to improve as a pilot. Find a flat open field with steady, light wind and practise inflating, controlling and kiting your wing. It builds feel for the glider and makes launches much safer. Do it with a helmet on, and stay out of strong wind, which can drag you.
Going solo touring tomorrow, just mellow stuff. Anything I should do differently?

Keep it truly mellow: stay on slopes under 30 degrees with nothing steeper above you, and avoid gullies or terrain traps where even a small slide could bury you. Leave a detailed plan with someone, including your route and turnaround time, and carry a way to call for help, like a satellite messenger if there's no cell coverage. Remember your beacon only helps others find you, so when you're alone, conservative terrain choice is your whole safety system.
I'm 52, overweight, and have never climbed. Am I too old/heavy to start?

No, plenty of people start climbing in their fifties, and top-rope climbing at a gym is especially friendly to beginners of any size. The rope and belayer take your weight when you rest or fall, so you can go at your own pace and build strength over time. Start with an intro class and easy routes, and warm up your shoulders and fingers to avoid tendon strain. If you have heart, joint or blood pressure concerns, check with your doctor first, then go enjoy it.
my friend wants to tow me behind his car on my longboard. how fast is safe?

Honestly, no speed is safe for that one. If you fall, you'll be on the road behind a car with no way to stop, and the driver can't react fast enough to you. Plenty of riders have been badly hurt skitching. If you want speed, find a proper hill and learn to slide.
My kid (14) wants to keep doing skate park sessions with a wrist that's been hurting for 3 weeks after a fall. He says it's fine.

Three weeks of pain after a fall is worth an X-ray. At 14 he still has open growth plates, and scaphoid fractures in the wrist are notorious for looking like sprains and then healing badly if they're missed. Keep him off the board until a doctor clears it, since another fall onto the same wrist could make things much worse. If it turns out to be a sprain, wrist guards and a gradual return are perfectly reasonable.
honestly how cold is too cold to go ice climbing

Below about minus 15 C (5 F), ice gets brittle and shatters into dinner plates, and frostbite risk climbs fast, especially with wind. A lot of experienced climbers just call it a day at those temps unless they're on a very sheltered route. Mid single digits below freezing is often the sweet spot, with plastic, chewy ice and manageable hands. Whatever the number, bring a big belay parka and warm spare gloves, and bail if anyone's fingers or toes go numb and won't come back.
I want to try my first 360 tomorrow. I just learned 180s last week. Good idea?

Probably give it a little more time. Get your 180s rock solid both ways, including landing switch, and practice 360s on the ground or off small rollers first. When you do go for it, pick a small jump with a long gentle landing, wind up before takeoff and spot your landing around the full rotation. Rushing a 360 off a bigger jump usually ends in an under-rotated slam.
just bought a downhill bike, never rode one. go straight to the hardest run to test it?

No. Spend your first few runs on easier trails to learn the bike, because downhill geometry, powerful brakes and long-travel suspension feel very different from what you're used to. Set your suspension sag and tire pressure first, then work up through the trails as the bike starts to feel natural. Going straight to the hardest run on unfamiliar equipment is a common way to get hurt on day one.
I'm a strong swimmer and scuba diver, can I skip beginner freediving stuff?

Your water comfort will help, but take the beginner course anyway. Freediving has its own risks that scuba doesn't cover, like hypoxic blackout, LMC and breath-hold rescue. Some scuba instincts don't transfer, such as how you equalize and ascend. You'll probably progress fast, but those basics are the part that matters most.
Is a tracking suit worth it for BASE progression?

Tracking pants or a tracking suit can help you get more separation from cliffs and objects once you're experienced and ready for terrain jumps. Work on tracking skill in skydiving first, then bring it into BASE gradually with good coaching. Don't treat the suit as a shortcut, because body position and a clean exit matter more than the gear.
My 15 year old son wants to do Kilimanjaro with me next summer. Is that too young?

Fifteen is fine. Most operators accept kids from 10 and up, and Tanzania's park rules set the minimum summit age at 10. The bigger issue is that teens often underreport symptoms because they don't want to slow the group down, so make it clear he has to tell you about headaches or nausea, no matter what. Pick a longer route like the 8-day Lemosho, which gives you both much better odds of summiting safely than the rushed 5-day Marangu itineraries.
can i practice wall runs on my garage wall

Maybe, if the wall is solid and the ground in front of it is level and clear. Check that it's brick or concrete rather than plasterboard or siding, and make sure there are no windows, gutters or sharp edges nearby. Keep the first attempts low, focusing on a single strong kick and a firm hand grab. Wear shoes that grip well, because sliding down a garage wall onto concrete is no fun.
Planning Kilimanjaro on the 5-day Marangu route to save money. Good idea?

It's the cheapest option on paper, but the five-day itinerary has one of the lowest summit success rates on the mountain because it gives your body almost no time to acclimatize. Spending a bit more on a seven- or eight-day route like the Lemosho or Machame dramatically improves your odds of summiting and of not getting altitude sick. If budget is tight, Marangu with an extra acclimatization day at Horombo Hut is a reasonable middle ground.
pulled a rib muscle (i think) doing a big wall climb. hurts to breathe deep. push on to summit tomorrow?

Pain on deep breathing after a big effort could be an intercostal strain, but it could also be a cracked rib, and at altitude or deep into a committing wall, that matters. If the pain is sharp, you're short of breath, or you're coughing up anything, retreat and get it checked, because a rib injury can occasionally affect the lung. If you choose to continue, you need to be confident you can safely haul, jumar and self-rescue, and your partner needs to know. When in doubt on a big wall, going down is the smart call.
is it bad to lean back when landing jumps? i always do that

Yes, it's one of the most common mistakes and a big cause of tailbone and wrist injuries. Try to land with your weight centered or slightly forward, with your knees bent to absorb the impact. Spotting your landing early in the air helps, and practicing on small jumps until centered landings become natural will make bigger jumps safer later.
can i solo an easy route i've done 20 times? it's like 5.6

I'd strongly advise against it. Free soloing even easy terrain leaves zero margin for a broken hold, a slip on wet rock, or a moment's distraction. Familiarity breeds the complacency that causes those accidents. Rope up and enjoy it as a fast, flowing lap instead.
We're going rafting... I mean kayaking... on a river after heavy rain tomorrow. Should be epic right?

It might be, but rivers after heavy rain bring higher, faster and colder water, new debris, floating wood, and sometimes flash-flood risk, so it really depends on the river and your group's experience. Check the gauge before you go and compare it to the run's known safe range. Keep an eye out for strainers that weren't there before, and be ready to bail if levels are rising or anything looks off. For newer paddlers, a river after a big storm is usually one to skip.
can i use my old helmet from 2012 its still in good shape

I'd retire it. Most manufacturers recommend replacing a helmet every five years or so because the foam liner degrades with age, sweat and heat even if the shell looks perfect. A 2012 helmet also misses newer safety tech like rotational impact systems. Your head is worth a new lid, and there are solid certified options at reasonable prices.
suspension setup for a total noob? bike has a coil shock and air fork

Start with sag. Set the fork around 20 to 25 percent and the rear around 25 to 30 percent with you in full gear, using the right spring rate for your weight on the coil. Set rebound in the middle of its range, then fine-tune so the bike doesn't bounce or pack down on repeated hits. Most bike shops or park rental desks will do a baseline setup for you in a few minutes, which is well worth it.
I've got a guide booked for heli skiing. Do I still need to know any avalanche stuff?

Your guides will make the terrain calls and give you a beacon, shovel and probe plus a briefing, so you're in good hands. Still, pay close attention to that briefing and practice the beacon drill, because in an accident you may be the one searching for someone. Follow the guide's instructions exactly about spacing and where to stop, as those rules exist for a reason.
whats the fastest way to acclimatize, I only have 10 days off for aconcagua

Honestly, there isn't a fast way, and ten days isn't enough for Aconcagua, where most successful expeditions take 18 to 20 days. Pre-acclimatizing at home in a hypoxic tent can help a bit, but it doesn't replace real time at altitude, and rushing a 6,961 m peak is how people end up with HACE or HAPE. Either save up for a longer trip or pick a lower objective that fits your window, such as a guided climb of a 5,000 m peak in Ecuador.
What's the deal with samba? My buddy got twitchy after surfacing.

That was a loss of motor control, or samba, and it means your buddy was very close to blacking out. Support their airway out of the water, talk them through recovery breathing, and stay with them until they're fully clear. They should stop diving for the day and dial back depth or time next session, because samba is a clear warning sign.
Sprained thumb from a snowboard fall — fine to keep riding with a glove on?

Be careful, because a fall-onto-hand thumb injury is often a skier's thumb, meaning a torn ligament at the base, and it can need a splint or surgery if it's a full tear. Get it examined before your next session, especially if it feels loose or pinching is weak. Wrist guards and avoiding falls onto outstretched hands will help once you're cleared.
I want to go to 40m on my next trip. I've got open water cert and 20 dives.

Open Water certifies you to 18 meters, and 40 meters is the recreational limit, which normally takes Advanced and a Deep specialty. At 40 meters, nitrogen narcosis, rapid gas use and very short no-deco times make mistakes much more costly. Do the Advanced course and then the Deep specialty, building depth gradually with an instructor.
how do i know if im getting heat stroke vs just tired

The red flags are confusion, slurred speech, stumbling, irritability, stopping sweating, or feeling cold and goosebumpy while it's hot out. Being tired and sore is normal, but your brain shouldn't feel scrambled. Because heat stroke impairs judgment, ask a crew member or another runner to check whether you're making sense. If those signs show up, stop, get to an aid station, cool down fast and let medical staff decide.
can someone with asthma surf big waves

Some people with asthma do surf big waves, but you need to talk to your doctor first and get your asthma very well controlled. Long hold-downs and intense exertion can trigger attacks at the worst possible moment. Work with a doctor who understands extreme sports, ask about breath-hold training, and make sure your crew knows your condition and has a plan if something goes wrong.
I'm 24 and got caught in a small slide last week. Wasn't buried but I'm kind of shaken. Normal?

Completely normal, and it's good you're taking it seriously instead of brushing it off. Go back over what happened with your partners, or write it up and send it to your local avalanche center, since they collect observations and it'll help you understand what went wrong. Ease back in on low-angle terrain, and if the anxiety lingers or affects your sleep, talking to someone about it is a smart move.
What color should my pee be during a desert stage race?

Pale yellow is the goal. Dark amber means you're dehydrated, and if you're not peeing for several hours you're well behind on fluids. Watch out for brown or cola-colored urine, especially with muscle pain, because that can mean rhabdomyolysis or kidney trouble, which is a reason to stop and see the medics right away. Completely clear, frequent urine combined with bloating or a headache can mean you're overdrinking.
my partner wants to climb in a frozen river gorge where the ice is over moving water. thoughts?

Be careful there. Ice over moving water can look solid but be thin or undercut from below, and breaking through into a current can be fatal. Ask local climbers or a guide about how established the route is and how thick the ice is, and stay off it after warm spells or if you see open water or slush. When in doubt, pick a route with solid footing at the base.
do i need avalanche gear for ice climbing

Often, yes. A lot of ice routes sit in gullies or below slopes that can avalanche, especially in the Rockies and alpine areas. If the approach or the route has avalanche exposure, carry a beacon, probe and shovel, check the avalanche forecast, and make sure your partner knows how to use theirs. Taking an avalanche course is a good idea if you plan to climb beyond roadside crags.
I'm 42, out of shape-ish, used to skate as a teen. Too old to get into downhill longboarding?

Not at all, plenty of people start downhill in their forties and fifties and do great. The main difference is that you'll heal slower, so take your progression seriously: relearn carving and foot braking on mellow hills, then add slides before chasing speed. Leg and core strength work pays off fast because tucking and sliding are surprisingly demanding on the thighs. Buy proper pads and a full-face helmet from the start rather than treating them as optional.
Whats a good warmup before park laps

Take a couple of easy groomer runs first, adding a few butters, ollies and carves to wake your legs up. Before strapping in, do some leg swings, squats and ankle circles to loosen your joints. Then hit your easiest features first and build up, since most park injuries happen when people jump straight into big stuff cold.
is wall running bad for your knees

Not if you build up to it properly, but the impact of jumping off and dropping down from a wall can stress your knees and ankles if you rush. Start with short runs on a low wall, focus on stepping into the wall with the ball of your foot rather than kicking it, and practice soft landings when you come back down. Pain in the front of the knee that lingers after sessions is a sign to cut volume and strengthen your quads and hips.
My boyfriend wants to take me multipitch for my first time outdoors. He's climbed 2 years. Good idea?

Start with single-pitch sport climbing first. Multipitch adds hanging belays, rope management, retreat planning, and complex communication, and that's a lot to take in on day one. Two years of experience may or may not include solid multipitch rescue skills. A guided multipitch day for both of you would be a great next step after a few single-pitch outings.
Quick q, how many lights should I carry for a cave dive?

Three is the standard: one primary and two backups, each able to last the full planned dive on its own. Losing your only light in a cave is a true emergency, and lights fail more often than people expect. Clip the backups where you can reach them by feel, and test all three before every dive.
how do you get out of a collapse

For a typical asymmetric collapse, the first job is to stop the turn by shifting your weight to the open side and applying measured brake on that side, then pump the collapsed side out if it doesn't reopen on its own. Overreacting with too much brake can stall the wing, which is worse than the collapse. The only real way to learn this is an SIV course over water with a qualified instructor, where you practise collapses under controlled conditions. Book one once you have some airtime.
My spray skirt keeps imploding when I hit waves. Fix?

That usually means the skirt is too loose for your cockpit or the deck material is too stretchy. Check that it's sized for your boat's cockpit rim, and consider a neoprene skirt with a tighter fit. Always make sure the grab loop is outside and easy to reach so you can still pull it for a wet exit.
Do I need to do hot weather long runs or is short heat exposure enough?

Short daily heat sessions of 60 to 90 minutes drive most of the acclimation, so you don't have to do all your long runs in peak heat. Do at least a few longer runs in heat though, to test your hydration, salt and fueling plan and see how your stomach handles it. Do those during cooler parts of the day at first, and bring plenty of water so you're not stranded.
what fins for a beginner

Start with mid-length plastic or composite long-blade fins with a soft to medium stiffness. They're affordable, forgiving and don't wreck your calves while your technique develops. Make sure the foot pockets fit snugly without pinching, since good fit matters more than the brand. Save carbon blades for later, once you know what stiffness you actually like.
do I have to sign a waiver? feels sketchy

Yes, every legitimate operator requires one, and that's normal rather than sketchy. Read it, especially the medical declaration, and answer honestly, since hiding a condition can put you at risk and void any coverage. What should worry you is an operator that doesn't ask about health or weight at all.
Is my old deck safe? it has a small crack near the back truck

A crack near the truck is a real concern, because that's where the board takes the most load, and decks tend to snap there without warning. Use it for light cruising at most, and retire it from tricks or jumps completely. Grab a new deck soon, since a snapped board mid-ollie is a great way to land on your tailbone.
How long does it take to go from open water to full cave certified?

For a motivated diver it usually takes several months to a year or two. You'll typically want solid open water experience, often 50 or more dives, plus advanced and nitrox training, then cavern, intro cave and full cave courses, each over a few days. Don't rush it; the time between courses spent diving and refining buoyancy is what makes you a safe cave diver.
Weather looks gusty at the DZ but I've only got today off. Should I still do my wingsuit jumps?

If the winds are gusty, sit it out. Turbulence makes wingsuit exits and deployments harder and adds risk to your landing under canopy, which is still part of every jump. Talk to the drop zone staff. If they're putting wingsuits on hold or you'd be at your personal limit, wait for a better day. Losing a day off is frustrating, but it's the right trade.
my 14 yo wants to start street luge, is that insane

It's not insane, but it does need structure, because street luge puts your body inches off the pavement at real speed. The safest way in is through an organized event or club that runs closed roads with hay bales and experienced riders, where kids can start on gentle courses. Make sure the gear is non-negotiable: a full-face helmet, full leathers or a proper abrasion suit, gloves with sliders, and solid boots, since your feet are the brakes. Skip any sessions on open public roads, because traffic is the danger no amount of skill fixes.
do you need to be strong to start or does it come with training

Strength mostly comes with training, so don't wait until you feel strong enough to begin.
