Start with basic movements at your current level, like low vaults, balance and short jumps, and add conditioning like squats and push-ups so your body adapts as you progress. Pull-ups and climb-ups take time, so use negative reps or assisted variations until you can do them fully. Beginner classes are designed for exactly this.
Quick q: is static apnea in the bathtub safe to train?

Breath-hold training in a tub alone is genuinely dangerous, because people black out without warning and drown in very little water. Do dry static tables lying on your bed or couch, where a blackout just means you start breathing again. Save any in-water static practice for a pool session with a trained buddy who is watching you the entire time.
wingsuit base after like 20 base jumps, reasonable?

No, that's far too early. Most experienced mentors want something like 200 or more skydives in a wingsuit plus a solid BASE background, often 50 to 100 or more jumps, before you take a suit off an object. Wingsuit BASE has one of the highest fatality rates in the sport, mostly from proximity flying and bad decisions about terrain clearance. Build both skill sets separately and get a coach before combining them.
I'm 52 and haven't ridden much since my 20s. Too old to try downhill?

Not at all. Lots of riders take up downhill in their 50s and love it. Ease in with a lesson at a bike park and stick to green and blue trails while your skills and reflexes come back. Bones and joints heal more slowly now, so wear good protection, including a full-face helmet, knee pads and ideally a back protector, and stop before you're tired, since late-day fatigue is when most crashes happen. If you have any heart, joint or balance concerns, a quick check-in with your doctor first is sensible.
How much does a BASE rig cost, roughly?

A new container and canopy setup usually costs roughly $3,000 to $5,000, depending on the manufacturer and options, plus pilot chutes and accessories. Used gear can be cheaper, but have a qualified rigger or experienced jumper inspect it carefully, since unknown history matters a lot with parachutes. Many FJCs include gear rental, which is a smart way to learn what you like before buying.
What's the difference between free soloing and bouldering?

Bouldering is ropeless climbing on short problems, usually under about 15 feet, with crash pads and spotters, so falling is a normal part of it. Free soloing means climbing tall routes without a rope, where a fall is very likely fatal. Bouldering is built around trying hard and falling safely, while soloing is built around never falling. If you love the pure, gear-free movement, bouldering is the place to get it.
how many skydives do i need before i can try a wingsuit

The standard benchmark is 200 skydives, and USPA also recommends those come within the previous 18 months so your skills are current. On top of that you'll take a First Flight Course with a qualified wingsuit coach and start on a small beginner suit. The 200-jump rule exists because you need rock-solid canopy skills and stability before adding a suit that restricts your arms and complicates deployment.
How often should I service my suspension if I ride the park a lot?

A good rule is a lower-leg service roughly every 50 hours of riding and a full damper service around every 100 to 200 hours. Hard park riding sits toward the frequent end of those ranges. Wipe your stanchions after every ride and watch for oil residue, a harsh feel or loss of travel, which are signs it's due sooner. Unless you're confident working on suspension, a shop or the manufacturer's service center is the safe call.
whats a good warmup before parkour

Spend ten minutes getting warm and mobile: light jogging or skipping, then joint circles for your ankles, knees, hips, wrists and shoulders. Add some dynamic moves like lunges, leg swings, and quadrupedal crawling, and finish with easy versions of the techniques you plan to train, like small jumps and gentle rolls. Skipping the warmup is how a lot of tweaked ankles and pulled hamstrings happen.
is it normal for fingers to swell during long hot runs

Mild swelling is pretty common and usually harmless, often from your arms swinging and from heat. But marked swelling combined with headache, nausea, confusion or weight gain during the race can signal hyponatremia, especially if you've been drinking a lot of plain water. If your hands are puffy, ease off the fluids, take some sodium, and get checked at the next aid station if you feel off.
How tight should my trucks be?

Start in the middle and adjust to feel, since loose trucks turn easily but can cause speed wobbles, while tight trucks feel stable but stiff. A good test is that you should be able to lean and carve smoothly without the board feeling twitchy at a jogging pace. If you plan to ride downhill or go faster, lean toward tighter, and always make sure the kingpin nut still has enough thread showing to be secure.
friend says i should ride without a helmet to 'feel the trail more' lol thoughts

Ignore that one completely. Head injuries are the most serious risk in downhill and a helmet costs you nothing in trail feel. If you want to feel the trail better, work on looser arms and looking further ahead.
What's the difference between wingsuit skydiving and wingsuit BASE?

Wingsuit skydiving is done from an aircraft at high altitude with open sky around you, a reserve parachute, and usually an AAD. Wingsuit BASE is launched from cliffs or mountains with lower altitudes, no reserve in most cases and terrain close by, so mistakes are much less survivable. That's why BASE is considered a separate and far more serious discipline requiring its own training.
Should I pack my own rig or have someone else do it?

Learn to pack your own rig, and pack it very well, because in BASE your one canopy has to open cleanly every time. Have your instructor or a very experienced jumper check your pack job until you're consistent. Never cut corners when packing just because you're in a hurry before a jump.
My son has epilepsy, controlled with meds, seizure free 3 years. Can he do it?

It's possible, but the decision has to start with his neurologist, since epilepsy is on almost every operator's medical exclusion list. Some sites will accept a jumper with written medical clearance and others won't at all. Call ahead with the specifics before he gets his heart set on it. If the answer is no, a supervised zipline might be a decent alternative to discuss with his doctor.
I'm 22, decent skier, and I want to ski a big couloir I saw on Instagram. Can I just go for it?

Big couloirs are serious avalanche and fall terrain, and the photos don't show the hazard, the conditions they waited for, or the skills behind them. Get an avalanche course and build up through smaller lines with experienced partners first, or hire a guide for that objective. That couloir will still be there when you've got the skills and the right conditions.
Is it true that fit people get altitude sickness more?

Not exactly. Fitness doesn't protect you from altitude sickness, and it doesn't make you more prone to it either. The trap is that fit people feel strong and tend to climb faster than they should, which is what really drives the illness. Your genetics and your ascent rate matter much more than how fast you run a 10K, so pace yourself even when your legs say you could go faster.
how far apart should spotters be from the climber

Stand close enough to touch the climber's hips with your arms slightly bent, with your feet staggered and thumbs tucked against your fingers. You aren't catching the climber's full weight. Your job is to guide their hips and torso so they land on their feet on the pad and their head doesn't hit the ground or rock. Move as they move, and reposition the pads as they traverse.
honestly do I need a course? I've watched tons of youtube and I'm a strong swimmer

Yes, take the course. Swimming strength has almost nothing to do with freediving safety, and videos can't teach you to spot a blackout or perform a rescue under pressure. A two or three day beginner course gives you supervised practice with rescues, equalization and breath-up technique. It usually adds meters to your dives too, because you learn to relax properly.
Quick q - is it fine to ride alone at the track on weekdays when nobody's there?

It's best to avoid riding completely alone. If you crash and get knocked out or hurt, there may be nobody to help you or call for help. Bring a buddy, or at least ride when track staff are on site. If you really have to go solo, tell someone where you are, keep your phone accessible, and ride well within your limits.
Wind is gusting 25 km/h at launch but everyone else seems to be flying. I've got about 15 flights. Go or not?

Don't go. Gusty 25 km/h is strong for a pilot with 15 flights, and the people launching may have hundreds of hours or be making their own bad call. Gusts are what cause collapses and nasty launch drag-outs. Pack up, watch how the experienced pilots handle it, and fly on a calmer day, because sitting it out is a skill too.
Planning my first lake swim this weekend, never done open water before, only pool. Any tips?

Go with a buddy or an organised session rather than alone, and stay parallel to the shore in water you could stand up in so you can stop whenever you like. Expect it to feel colder and darker than the pool, which makes your breathing speed up, so wade in slowly and let yourself adjust for a minute or two before you start swimming. Wear a bright swim cap and tow a swim buoy so boats and other people can see you. Keep the first swim short, around 10 to 15 minutes, even if you feel great.
how do I learn to jump a 6 foot gap without practicing smaller stuff, I'm short on time this season

There isn't a safe shortcut here, because coming up short on a gap usually means a casing crash or going over the bars. You can build the skill quickly on tabletops, though: your speed and pop transfer directly, and a short landing just rolls out. Spend a few sessions hitting progressively bigger tables, and a coaching day can compress weeks of learning into one afternoon. Once you're consistently landing past the deck of a table that size, the gap is a reasonable next step.
I soloed a 30 foot route yesterday on a whim and it felt amazing. Planning a 200 footer next. Good idea?

That jump is a big red flag, because going from a whim at 30 feet to 200 feet skips the years of buildup that keep soloists alive. The rush you felt is exactly what makes people escalate faster than their skills, and a fall from 30 feet can already kill you or leave you badly hurt. Climb that 200-foot route on a rope with a partner and see how it feels with real exposure. Be honest with yourself about how close you came yesterday to things going wrong.
I keep crashing on the same corner, should I just send it harder

No, more speed on a corner you can't handle just makes the crash worse. Slow down before the corner with a slide or footbrake, pick a clean line, and look at the exit instead of the curb. Practice that corner at lower speed until it's smooth, then add a little speed each run. If you can, ride it with someone experienced who can watch your line and tell you what's going wrong.
Worried mom here. My 24yo son just told me he's going to Nazaré this winter. What should I actually be asking him?

Ask whether he'll surf with an experienced jet ski safety team, because at Nazaré that's non-negotiable. Ask what his experience is in 20 foot plus surf and whether he's done breath-hold and survival training. Find out whether he has a flotation vest and a plan for which days he'll paddle versus watch. If he has clear answers, he's likely approaching it seriously. If he's vague, that's the conversation to have before he goes.
best way to learn to jump on a dh bike

Learn on small, smooth tabletop jumps in a jump line or pump track, not on gap jumps. Roll them first, then pump the lip by pushing down into the takeoff while keeping your body centered and letting the bike come up to you. Aim to land both wheels together or slightly rear first on the downslope, and keep your speed consistent so you can repeat it. Never jump into a blind landing you haven't walked.
can i just learn to belay from youtube videos lol

Videos are great for understanding the motions, but belaying is a hands-on skill where small mistakes, like letting go of the brake strand for a split second, can drop someone to the ground. Take a belay class at a gym, which usually costs little and takes about an hour, and you'll get supervised practice plus a belay check. After that, YouTube is a fine way to refine technique.
Any trick to running a strainer if I can't avoid it?

The real trick is never being forced into one: scout ahead, stay in control, and portage when trees block the main flow, because strainers are one of the deadliest river hazards. If you do get swept toward one as a swimmer, flip onto your stomach and swim aggressively head-first at it, then try to climb up and over so you don't get sucked under. In a boat, lean toward the obstruction and grab the branch so the current doesn't pull your upstream edge down.
how do i know if the ice on a frozen waterfall is too thin to climb

Look for dark patches where water is showing through, gurgling or running water behind the ice, and areas that sound hollow or drummy when you tap them. If your screws hit rock or water before they're fully in, or the ice is thinner than a screw length, it's not good enough for protection even if it holds your tools. When you're new, go out with a guide who can show you how to read ice in person, because this is hard to learn from descriptions alone.
what's a good first week routine. like specifically

Do three sessions of about 45 minutes, each starting with a 10-minute warm-up of jogging, joint circles and crawling. Spend 15 minutes on landings and precision jumps between lines on the ground, 10 minutes on safety rolls on grass, and 10 minutes on simple vaults over a low wall or bench. Finish with squats, push-ups and calf raises for conditioning. Keep it low and controlled, and if your shins or knees ache, take an extra rest day.
I'm 58 with well-controlled high blood pressure and want to do my first hot-weather 100K. Anything special I should think about?

Go for it, but book a visit with your doctor first and specifically mention the heat and the distance. Some blood pressure medications, especially diuretics, ACE inhibitors and beta blockers, change how you handle fluids, sodium and heat, and your dose or timing may need adjusting for race day. Build up your heat training gradually, practice your exact fueling and sodium plan in long training runs, and know the signs that mean you stop, like dizziness, chest discomfort or confusion.
I'm 41 and out of shape but parkour looks amazing. Too late?

Not at all, plenty of people start in their 40s and beyond, and lots of gyms run adult or beginner-specific classes that move at a sensible pace. Expect your first months to focus on strength, mobility, balance and landing mechanics rather than big jumps, which is exactly what protects your knees and Achilles. A quick checkup with your doctor is smart if you've been inactive for a while, and then just commit to showing up consistently.
Is cliff diving at night a cool idea? Full moon planned with friends.

Skip the night jumps. You can't see the water surface well enough to time your entry, judge the landing zone or spot someone who's in trouble after a jump. Swim and hang out under the full moon, and save the jumping for daylight when you can see everything.
My husband does cave dives every weekend and I worry every time he goes. How can I feel better about it?

Your worry is understandable, and asking him about how he manages risk usually helps a lot. Find out his training level, who he dives with, his gas planning and whether he leaves a dive plan with an expected return time. Knowing he's trained, conservative and diving with solid buddies can make it much easier, and you can always ask him to check in after each dive.
how often should I actually practice beacon searches

At the start of every season, then at least a few times through the winter, and always with partners you tour with. Practice multiple burials and timed drills, aiming to locate, probe and start digging in under five minutes. Many resorts and trailheads have beacon parks that make this easy.
I'm 52, fit, about 400 skydives. Too old to start wingsuiting?

Not at all, plenty of people start wingsuiting in their 50s and beyond, and 400 jumps is a solid foundation. Just make sure your shoulders and back are in good shape, since a suit adds load during exits and flight, and be honest about your flexibility for reaching handles. Take a First Flight Course, start with a beginner suit, and progress at your own pace.
I'm 16 and really want to skydive for my birthday. Can I just lie about my age at the dropzone?

Don't do that, because lying voids the waiver and insurance, and if anything went wrong it would land on the instructor who trusted you. Most US dropzones require you to be 18, but some countries allow tandems from 16 or younger with parental consent. Look up dropzones that legally take your age with a parent's signature, or start counting down to 18 and do it properly.
River's flooding after rain, gonna be epic. Going tomorrow, thoughts?

Flood stage changes a river completely: eddies wash out, strainers and debris appear, the water gets cold and fast, and swims become long and dangerous. Check the gauge against guidebook flow ranges, and if it's above the recommended maximum, give it a day or two to drop. High water is something you work up to gradually with experienced paddlers, not something to chase on a whim.
detail-oriented here: how do operators actually calculate cord length for me?

They start with your weighed mass and the height of the jump, then pick a cord grade or adjust the number of strands to match your weight. That way the cord stretches enough to slow you smoothly while leaving a safe clearance above the ground or water. They factor in the cord's known stretch characteristics and how many jumps it has done, plus your height and how you're attached. Good operators record your weight on your hand or ticket and recheck it on the platform to avoid mix-ups.
Can I use a reel line from my wreck kit in a cave?

Possibly, if it's proper braided nylon line on a reel that won't jam. But you need to lay it correctly, using placements and tie-offs that prevent line traps, and that's taught in cave training rather than wreck training. Cave lines also follow specific conventions with arrows and cookies, so take the course before you go running your own line.
Had back surgery two years ago, fully recovered, gym five days a week. Still a problem?

It might be fine, but check with your surgeon first. The deceleration and rebound load your spine in ways the gym doesn't. Most operators ask about previous back surgery and may require written medical clearance. If you're cleared, a body harness rather than an ankle attachment is usually kinder to your back.
Which is better for a first 6000er, Island Peak or Mera Peak?

Mera Peak is usually the better first 6,000er because the summit route is mostly a non-technical glacier walk, although at 6,476 meters it's the higher of the two. Island Peak is lower, but it has a steep headwall that needs fixed lines, ascenders, and some comfort on exposed ground. Whichever you choose, go with an experienced guide and practice crampon and rope skills before the trip, since crevasses and altitude deserve respect even on the easy ones.
best shoes

Look for thin, flexible soles with good grip and a bit of cushioning at the heel, something like a light running shoe with a flat sole. Parkour-specific brands like Feiyue or Ollie are popular. Avoid thick, chunky soles, because they hide what your feet are feeling and make it easier to slip off edges.
I'm 42 and thinking about starting skating. Too old?

Not at all, plenty of people start in their 40s and have a blast, you just want to be smarter about falls since recovery takes longer. Wear a helmet, wrist guards and knee pads, and consider a slightly wider deck with softer wheels for stability. Spend your first sessions rolling, pushing and turning on smooth flat ground, and practice falling forward onto your knee pads at the skatepark so it becomes instinct.
do i need gloves for street luge

Yes, gloves are essential, both for protection and because many lugers use their hands for balance and minor corrections. Most racing bodies require leather gloves as part of your gear, and you'll want something durable with good grip. Pair them with full leathers, a full-face helmet and shoes with solid rubber soles for braking.
Can I jump solo or do I always need someone with me?

Don't jump alone, especially early on, because if you're injured in a remote landing area, a ground crew or partner may be the difference between a quick rescue and a disaster. Experienced partners also catch gear and packing mistakes and help you assess conditions. Even veterans jump with others, so treat the buddy system as standard.
What's the best way to practice beacon searches?

Bury a transmitting beacon in a pack or bag at a park or practice area, and have a partner time you from switching to search through probing and digging. Many ski areas have beacon training parks where you can practice with buried transmitters and get instant feedback. Practicing multiple burials and rough terrain makes you much faster when it counts.
Ears hurt on the way down, what do I do

Stop descending, go up a meter or two until the pain eases, and gently equalize by pinching your nose and blowing softly, or try swallowing and wiggling your jaw. Equalize early and often, about every meter on the way down, before you feel any pressure. Never force it with a hard blow, and if one ear just won't clear, end the dive, because pushing through can rupture your eardrum.
first time at a bike park next weekend, rented a downhill bike. what trail should I start on?

Start on the easiest green flow trail, even if it looks too easy, and ride it two or three times to learn how the bike feels, especially the brakes, which are far stronger than on a normal bike. Rental downhill bikes are long and slack, so they handle differently at low speed and in tight turns. Once you can ride the green smoothly without grabbing the brakes in a panic, move up to the next blue. If the park offers a beginner lesson, take it on the first morning, because it's the fastest way to learn the lift, the lines and the basics.
ok so how long do you actually have to dig someone out

Survival odds drop sharply after about 10 to 15 minutes for a fully buried person, mostly because of asphyxiation, so companion rescue is everything and outside help almost never arrives in time. That's why you practice beacon searches until you can find and probe a target in a few minutes, and use strategic shoveling, digging in from the downhill side rather than straight down. If you haven't practiced this season, set up a drill at a beacon park before your next tour.
beacon battery at 40%. good enough for tomorrow?

Swap them. Most manufacturers say to replace below about 50%, and cold drains alkalines faster than you'd expect, which can cut your transmit time and search range. Put in a fresh set of the battery type your manual specifies, usually alkaline rather than lithium, and keep the old ones for your headlamp.
What does 'considerable' danger actually mean on the forecast? Sounds kind of medium.

Considerable is level 3 of 5, and it's where most avalanche fatalities happen, so it's not medium in any comforting sense. It means dangerous conditions on specific terrain and likely human-triggered slides. On considerable days experienced parties stick to conservative, low-consequence terrain and avoid the aspects and elevations the forecast calls out. Read the avalanche problem section, not just the color.
What's the cold shock thing people mention?

Sudden immersion in cold water, roughly below 15°C, triggers a gasp reflex and fast, uncontrolled breathing for the first minute or so. If your head is underwater during that gasp, you can inhale water. It also spikes heart rate and blood pressure. Wear a wetsuit in cold water, keep your mouth closed on entry, and float calmly until your breathing settles before you swim.
best way to survive getting caught inside by a big set?

Stay calm and take a deep breath before each wave hits. If no one's behind you, ditch the board and dive deep under the whitewater to dodge the worst of the turbulence. Between waves, conserve energy and try to get toward the channel. If you have an inflatable vest and you're running low on air, pull it.
How do I learn a Coleman slide without eating it every time?

Start on a gentle, smooth slope at low speed with slide gloves, knee pads and a helmet, and practice the motion until it feels natural before adding any real speed. Pre-drift your shoulders, plant your hand early, and let the board come around rather than kicking it out. Use softer wheels with rounded lips or slightly worn-in wheels, since they break traction more predictably. Expect to fall a bit at first, which is exactly why the slow hill matters.
Doing my first 50K in July, forecast says 95F. Any quick tips?

Start slower than feels right, because heat punishes early pacing more than anything else and you can't claw it back later. Drink to thirst, and take sodium in some form, whether capsules, chews or salty food, roughly every hour. Use ice in your hat, bandana and sports bra or shirt at every aid station, since external cooling buys you a lot. If you get dizzy, stop sweating or feel confused, sit down in shade and tell aid station staff right away.
ok be honest, how do pros jump from 27m and survive

They spend years building up through diving, acrobatics and gradually higher platforms, and they land feet first with near-perfect vertical alignment and huge core tension. Competitions also have rescue divers waiting in the water and carefully checked depths. Even with all that, pros pick up injuries, so it's not something to try outside that setting.
how do I wheelie

Start in an open, flat dirt area in second gear at a slow roll, cover the rear brake with your foot, and practice small lifts using a quick blip of throttle combined with a slight pull on the bars. The rear brake is your safety valve, so tap it if the front gets too high. Work on small, controlled lifts for a long time before trying to hold one. Always wear full gear, because flipping a bike backward is a real risk if you go too big.
forecast says considerable but the slope I want is only like 35 degrees, that's fine right

No, 35 degrees is right in the sweet spot for avalanches, and considerable danger is the rating where the most people die in North America. Natural slides are possible at that level, and human-triggered slides are likely on the problem aspects and elevations. Keep to slopes under 30 degrees with no steep terrain connected above you, and save that line for a day when the danger drops.
My son is 19 and just announced he's doing a full cave course in Mexico. I'm terrified. Should I try to stop him?

Your fear makes sense, but a full cave course from a reputable instructor is the responsible way into this sport. Nearly all cave diving deaths involve people with no cave training, not people who took the course. Help him check that his instructor is certified through an established agency like NSS-CDS, GUE, TDI or IANTD and has a solid local reputation. Ask him to promise he'll dive within his training once he's certified, because that is where the real risk lies.
Should I run and jump out or just step off?

A couple of strong steps and a push outward is usually right so you clear the base of the cliff, especially if the rock slopes or has ledges below. Before you go, look at exactly how far out you need to land. Don't sprint, though, because that makes it harder to control your body position in the air.
First wingsuit jump next week. Any tips?

Focus on a clean exit, a relaxed body and a disciplined deployment, and don't chase performance. Fully collapse your wings and keep your arms symmetric as you reach for your pilot chute, since that's where first-flighters get unstable. Pull at your planned altitude no matter how good the flight feels, and enjoy it, because the first flight is usually a big grin.
reservoir near me has no swimming signs but its so calm and nobody is ever there lol

Those signs are usually there for good reasons. Reservoirs often have very cold water just below the surface, hidden machinery, intake currents and steep underwater drops, and nobody being around means nobody to help if you get into trouble. Look for a nearby lake or managed open-water venue with safety cover, which can be just as peaceful and won't risk a fine or worse.
Is it fine to free solo an easy route with a sore finger? It's way below my grade.

No. Soloing with any injury is a bad combination, because the whole safety margin depends on your body doing exactly what you expect on every single move. A sore finger can buckle on a hold that would normally be trivial, and on a solo there's no second chance. Rope up or wait until the finger is fully healed and you trust it completely.
my 9 yo daughter wants to try rails. she's fearless lol. how do i keep her from getting hurt

Start her on the smallest, widest ride-on boxes in the beginner park, not rails. Kids' park lessons are great for this because the coaches teach the basics, like approaching straight and keeping a flat base. Make sure she has a helmet and wrist guards, and padded shorts help too. Fearless kids progress fast, so the main job is keeping her on features that match her skills.
Is it okay to do a deco dive in a cave the day after flying?

Flying before diving isn't the problem, it's diving before flying that carries the risk. Still, travel days leave you dehydrated and tired, which raises your decompression sickness risk and dulls your judgment for a demanding dive. Many cave divers do an easy checkout dive on day one and save the deco dives for once they're rested and hydrated.
Can I skate in the rain? I really want to get a session in today.

Better to skip it, because wet pavement and painted lines get dangerously slick and urethane wheels lose grip with almost no warning. Water also ruins bearings fast and makes a deck soggy and delaminated. If you're itching to skate, find a covered parking area or an indoor park, or use the day to practice balance and board flips on carpet.
Honest question, is solo diving actually that dangerous if I'm experienced?

It's riskier because a buddy is your backup air source and your help if you get entangled or have a medical problem. Experienced divers do dive solo, but they take specific self-reliant diver training and carry fully redundant gear like a pony bottle with its own regulator. If you want to go that route, do the course and carry that gear rather than just heading out alone.
I'm 45, fit, and always wanted to ride a really big wave before I'm too old. Realistic?

Plenty of people surf big waves into their 40s and 50s, so it's realistic if you train for it properly. Start by honestly assessing where you're at, then build gradually with a lot of cardio, breath-hold work, and progressively bigger days at forgiving breaks. A big-wave safety course and a good crew are non-negotiable. Give yourself a couple of seasons rather than aiming for one heroic session.
What wheels should I get for downhill longboarding?

For downhill you generally want wheels in the 70 to 80 mm range with a durometer around 78a to 83a, which gives grip and a smooth roll at speed. Lips matter too: sharp-lipped wheels hold grip in corners, while rounded lips break into slides more easily. Many riders keep a grippy set for racing and a slidier set for freeride. If you're just starting, a mid-grip wheel with slightly rounded lips is forgiving and teaches you control.
Can I skip the ground school for AFF if I've already done like 5 tandems? Seems redundant.

No, and you really wouldn't want to, because tandems don't teach you the things that keep you alive on a solo jump. In ground school you learn body position, altitude awareness, deployment, malfunction recognition, and emergency procedures, and on a tandem the instructor handled all of that for you. Your tandem experience will make the course feel more familiar, but do the whole thing.
How long should I wait to surf again after nearly drowning?

See a doctor first, because near-drowning can cause lung complications for days afterward. Once you're cleared, ease back in on small days and give yourself time mentally too. Some surfers work with a coach or counselor to rebuild their confidence.
What's the best way to avoid road rash?

Wear long sleeves and pants made of tough material, or leathers if you're going fast, along with knee and elbow pads and slide gloves. Learning to slide and fall properly also helps you avoid scraping your skin. The more gear between you and the pavement, the less skin you'll lose when you slam.
is it chill to climb under other parties at the ice park

It's best to avoid it, because climbers above will knock down ice whether they mean to or not, and the base under a busy route is a real hit zone. Pick a line out of the fall path, or wait until they're done, and always keep your helmet on near any climbing. If you have to pass, say something so they can warn you before they clear loose stuff.
What's the deal with board sizes? I'm a size 11 shoe.

With size 11 feet, most people feel good on a deck around 8.25 to 8.5 inches wide. Narrower boards flip more easily for technical street tricks, and wider boards feel more stable for transition and bigger stuff. If you can, stand on a few at a skate shop and pick the one that feels comfortable for how you want to skate.
How do I do a 50-50 on a box? Detailed please, I've watched videos but keep sliding off.

Approach straight on with a flat base and moderate speed, ollie or step lightly onto the box so your board lands parallel to it, and keep your weight centered over both feet with knees soft. Most people slide off because they're riding on an edge or leaning back, so keep your shoulders lined up with the board and your eyes on the end of the box, not your feet. Ride off the end with a flat base and bent knees. Pick a wide, low box to start and you'll lock it in quickly.
What if my wingsuit flight goes into a flat spin?

Most spins can be stopped by de-arching symmetrically and bringing your arms and legs into a neutral, balanced position, then flying back out. If you're still spinning when you reach your hard deck, deploy anyway or follow emergency procedures your coach taught you. Practice spin recovery scenarios on the ground and talk through them with your coach so they're automatic.
how many years before i can do real cave diving

There's no fixed timeline, but most people spend at least a year or two building solid open water experience, often 50 to 100 dives, before starting cavern and then full cave training. The progression usually runs cavern, intro to cave, then full cave, each with real dives in between to consolidate skills. Rushing it is the classic mistake, so focus on rock-solid buoyancy and trim now because that's what instructors care about most.
Can I wear my GoPro on my first solo jumps?

Hold off, because most dropzones follow the USPA guidance of no cameras until around 200 jumps and a C license. Cameras add snag hazards and a lot of distraction, and new jumpers have been hurt while worrying about footage instead of altitude. Buy the instructor's video package for now, and add your own camera once you've earned it.
Ran low on gas in a cavern yesterday, came up with like 300 psi. No big deal right?

That's actually a big deal and worth taking seriously. At 300 psi you had almost no margin to share air if your buddy had a problem, and in an overhead you can't just bolt for the surface. Go over what happened: whether you planned your turn pressure, checked your gauge often and accounted for stress or current. Next time plan by thirds and turn at the first signal.
Is Lauterbrunnen good for a beginner?

Lauterbrunnen in Switzerland is legal and popular, but many exits there are better suited to jumpers with solid object experience, and the valley has seen many fatalities, mostly in wingsuit flying. If you go as a newer jumper, stick to the easier exits, register as the local rules require, and hire a local guide or mentor. Most people do their first jumps on a bridge before taking on alpine cliffs.
Do I really need a leash in big waves? Some old guys say no.

Use a heavy-duty big-wave leash. Losing your board means a long, exhausting swim through the impact zone with nothing to float on. Some old-school surfers rode without leashes, but modern big-wave safety practice keeps you attached unless the leash itself becomes a drowning hazard. That's why some people use quick-release systems. Get a proper thick leash rated for big surf and check it for nicks before each session.
Is it bad for your back? I've got a herniated disc.

With an active herniated disc, I'd hold off until a doctor or physio clears you, because the hard deceleration and rebound put a lot of load through your spine. Back and neck problems are on most operators' list of medical conditions for that reason. If you get cleared, a full-body harness spreads the force more evenly than an ankle setup.
Booked a shark dive in South Africa, cage-free. I've only done 6 dives. Bad idea?

It depends on the dive. Baited tiger shark or oceanic blacktip dives with reputable operators like those in Aliwal Shoal take fairly new divers, but they'll expect solid buoyancy control and calm behavior in mid-water. Email the operator with your exact dive count and conditions to confirm you qualify, and do a few practice dives before the trip to tune your buoyancy. If they're vague about experience requirements, pick a different operator.
Is an airbag pack worth it or is it mostly marketing?

Airbags are useful, with research suggesting they meaningfully improve survival chances by keeping you near the surface in many avalanches. They don't prevent trauma or deep burials in terrain traps, though, and they can tempt people into riskier choices. Think of one as a solid addition to beacon, shovel, probe and good decision-making, not a substitute for any of them.
Why do so many experienced BASE jumpers die, not just beginners?

Many fatalities come from complacency and progression instead of inexperience. Experienced jumpers push into more extreme lines, especially wingsuit proximity flying, where small mistakes or misjudged terrain leave no margin. Pressure from sponsors, social media and fatigue also add up. The people who last tend to have strict personal limits, walk away often, and treat every jump like it matters.
My daughter is 14 and wants to try ice climbing. Is that okay??

Yes, 14 is a great age to try it, and lots of guide services run youth or family programs. On a guided top-rope day the risk is well managed: helmets, proper belays, and controlled terrain. Make sure she has warm layers and decent gloves so she stays comfortable, since cold and wet is the main thing that sours kids on it. Pick a reputable, certified guide and she'll likely have a blast.
What's base jumping like compared to skydiving? Thinking of trying it after like 50 skydives.

BASE is a completely different risk level, with lower altitudes, objects close by and almost no margin for error, which is why its fatality rate is much higher. Fifty jumps is far too early, and the community standard is at least 200 skydives, with many experienced BASE jumpers recommending 500 or more plus solid canopy skills. If you're serious about it, build your jump numbers, take canopy courses, and do a proper first-jump course with a reputable mentor instead of learning on your own.
whats the rule of thirds in cave diving

It's gas planning: you use one third of your starting gas going in, one third getting out, and keep the final third as reserve for your team in an emergency. You turn the dive as soon as anyone hits their first third, not when it's convenient. Many cave divers go more conservative in siphons or with mismatched tank sizes, because pushing against the outflow on the exit burns more gas than the trip in.
Found an old BCD and reg in my uncle's garage, probably 15 years old. Good to use after a rinse?

Don't dive it as-is. Regulators that sit for years get degraded seals and corrosion, and old BCDs can have leaking bladders or stuck inflators, which are exactly the failures you don't want at depth. Take it all to a dive shop for inspection and a service, and be prepared for them to say it isn't worth fixing.
is it true bungee cords snap all the time

No, cord failure at reputable operators is extremely rare. Cords are replaced after a set number of jumps or a time limit, and inspected regularly. Most serious bungee accidents historically came from setup errors like the wrong cord for someone's weight, miscalculated length, or attachment mistakes, not cords randomly snapping. That's why choosing an experienced operator with strict procedures matters most.
My 14 year old wants to join an open water club. I'm terrified. Is that crazy of me?

Your worry is completely normal, but a good club is one of the safest ways for a teenager to get into open water, much safer than swimming at a beach with friends. Look for one with qualified coaches, safety kayakers or lifeguards on every session, and a junior section that checks pool ability first. Go along to the first session and ask how they handle cold water and how they count swimmers in and out. If they answer clearly and confidently, that's a very good sign.
Just got held down for two waves at a 12 foot day and I can't stop thinking about it. Should I just go back out tomorrow to get over it?

Going back out is fine, but there's no need to force it on a big day tomorrow while it's still rattling you. Ease back in on a smaller, comfortable day so your confidence rebuilds on good experiences rather than gritted teeth. A session with a breath-hold or surf survival coach can turn that scare into actual skill. If the anxiety sticks around or affects your sleep, talking to someone about it is a smart move, not a weak one.
worried. my partner wants to try highballs this weekend and I'm the only spotter

Your worry makes sense. Highballs need several pads and ideally more than one spotter, because one person can't safely redirect a fall from that height. Ask your partner to pick lower problems this weekend, or wait until you have more pads and another friend. A good spotter's main job is guiding the climber onto the pad and protecting their head, not catching them.
Going to Whistler solo for a week. Anything I should know safety-wise?

Ride trails one grade easier than you would at home for the first day or two, because Whistler's grades are stiffer and the trails are longer and rougher than most parks. Carry a phone, tell someone your plans, and consider a guided session or lesson to learn the mountain. Get proper insurance that covers mountain biking, since rescue and treatment can be expensive. Pace yourself across the week, as fatigue on day four catches a lot of people.
is it ok to toprope ice on screws alone or do i need a tree anchor

You can absolutely build a solid toprope anchor on ice screws alone, and it's done all the time. Use at least two good screws in solid, bubble-free ice, placed roughly a foot or more apart and offset so they don't share a fracture plane, then equalize them with a sling or cordelette. Check them through the day, because sun and warm temps can melt screws out faster than you'd think. If a bombproof tree is right there, there's no shame in using it and saving your screws.
Sauna training: how many minutes and how hot? Don't want to overdo it.

Start with 15 to 20 minutes at around 80 to 90°C right after a workout, and work up to about 30 minutes over a week or two as you tolerate it. Get out immediately if you feel dizzy, nauseated or have a pounding headache, and rehydrate afterward with something salty. Don't do it alone if you can avoid it, and skip it entirely if you're sick or already dehydrated.
My 19 year old son just told me he wants to start BASE jumping. I'm terrified. What should I even say to him?

Ask him how he plans to get there before you argue about whether he should. A careful path means hundreds of skydives first, a first jump course with an established instructor, and a slow progression on big, forgiving objects. If he's committed to that route, he's taking it seriously, and you can encourage him to stay patient and conservative. If he's talking about learning from YouTube or jumping with friends right away, say clearly that's the part that scares you, because that's where the real danger sits.
what's a strainer

A strainer is any obstacle that lets water pass through but stops a body, usually a fallen tree, branches, or a fence across the current. They're among the deadliest hazards on a river because the current pins you against them underwater. Avoid them at all costs, and if you're swimming toward one, get aggressive, swim hard, and try to climb up and over it rather than going under.
My dive computer died mid cave dive, I just finished on my buddy's. Fine right?

It worked out, but next time carry a backup computer or bottom timer, because relying on your buddy's computer leaves you guessing about your own decompression. Get yours checked or replaced before diving again, and be conservative for the next day or so since your profile data is incomplete. Most cave divers run two computers for exactly this reason.
How expensive is it to get into cave diving realistically?

Plan for a few thousand dollars in training, often $2000 to $4000 from cavern through full cave, plus gear that can easily run $3000 to $6000 for doubles or sidemount rigs, regulators, lights, reels and drysuit if you need one. Travel to places like Florida or Mexico adds up too. Buying gear after talking with your instructor saves you from replacing the wrong stuff.
how do you do a safety roll properly

Roll diagonally across your back, from one shoulder to the opposite hip, never straight over your spine or the top of your head. Start kneeling on grass or a mat, place your hands on the ground, tuck your head toward the opposite side, and push off gently so you roll over your shoulder blade. Practice both sides until it's smooth, then do it from a crouch, then from walking, and only later from small drops. A good roll spreads the impact so your knees and ankles don't take all of it.
Running Badwater next summer. How do I heat acclimate if I live in Seattle?

Use passive heat exposure. Twenty to forty minutes in a sauna or a hot bath right after your runs, five or six days a week for the last two to three weeks, gets you most of the plasma volume and sweat-rate gains. Layer up on some easy treadmill sessions in a warm room too, and keep a close eye on how you feel, because it is surprisingly easy to overcook yourself. If you can, arrive in the desert a week early to finish the job in real conditions.

Detailed question: I'm 34, been climbing 8 years, lead 5.12 sport and 5.10 trad. I've been toprope soloing a lot on a local crag with a Micro Traxion. I'm considering soloing a 3-pitch 5.7 there I know very well. What's your honest take?

Your experience puts you where some people make that call, and the toprope soloing has given you real familiarity with the rock. Still, a three-pitch route has a lot more exposure, and the multiple belay ledges add places where fatigue, a loose block, or a moment of doubt can catch you. If you go ahead, rehearse it on your Traxion setup that same week, check every hold you'll weight, go on a cool dry day, and give yourself permission to bail at any point. Many experienced climbers stay at the toprope solo stage indefinitely because it gives about 90% of the feeling with a fraction of the risk.
Is wingsuit flying worth it given the risk?

That's a personal call, but wingsuit skydiving at a dropzone, done with training and conservative habits, is far less risky than wingsuit BASE or proximity flying. Many people get years of joy from skydive wingsuiting without ever going near terrain. If you try it, be honest about your skills, choose the safest version of the sport that satisfies you, and talk with experienced pilots about the risks.
Should I wear gloves for parkour?

Generally no, since gloves reduce your grip and feel on walls and rails, and most traceurs train bare-handed and let their hands toughen up over time. The exception is rough or cold surfaces that are temporarily trashing your skin, where thin fingerless gloves can help. Start with low volume on rough surfaces and moisturize calluses so they don't tear.
I get really bad headaches after hot long runs. normal?

Mild headaches after a hot run usually come from dehydration, low sodium or just the heat, and they should ease once you rehydrate, salt up and cool down. If they're severe, last more than a day or come with confusion, vomiting or vision changes, see a doctor promptly. Weighing yourself before and after runs can show whether you're under or overdrinking.
honestly is bungee or skydiving more dangerous

Statistically both are very safe at professional operations, with fatality rates in the range of a few per million jumps. Skydiving involves more variables like weather, landing and equipment deployment. Bungee is more controlled but depends heavily on correct cord calculation and rigging. Either way, the operator's quality matters far more than which one you choose.
thinking of buying a used yz125 that sat for 3 years. what should I check

The fuel system is the main concern, because old gas varnishes the carb, so plan on a full carb clean and fresh premix before trying to start it. Check compression with a gauge, since a low reading means a top end job is coming, and look for leaking fork and shock seals, dry rotted tires, a seized or rusty chain, and old brake fluid. Ask whether the top end was done and when. Factor these costs into your offer, and a bike that sat for three years can still be a great buy.
tips for swimming in waves? i keep getting smashed getting in

Time your entry by watching a few sets, then go in during a lull. Once the water's about waist deep, dive under breaking waves rather than standing up to them, and keep going until you're past the break. Coming back in, check behind you and let waves carry you rather than fighting them. If the surf is bigger than you're comfortable with, stick to a calmer beach or a lifeguarded area that day.
how high can paragliders legally fly

That depends entirely on the airspace where you fly. In many places you're limited by controlled airspace boundaries, which can be anywhere from a few hundred metres to several thousand metres above the ground. Cloud base is also a practical limit, and flying into cloud is both illegal under visual flight rules and dangerous. Learn to read airspace charts and use an instrument with airspace warnings, and ask local pilots about specific restrictions at your site.
my 16 yo son keeps watching Free Solo and says he wants to do it. should I panic

No need to panic. Wanting to be like Alex Honnold is common, and it's a great hook for getting into climbing safely. Channel it by signing him up at a climbing gym or for a youth team where coaches teach proper rope work and respect for risk. Have an honest talk about how Honnold spent over a decade roped up before his big solos, and that most of his climbing still uses a rope.
I'm 19 and just watched Free Solo for the third time. How do I start training to free solo big walls like Alex Honnold?

Start by becoming an excellent roped climber, because that's exactly what Honnold did for years before he ever soloed anything serious. He had a huge base of mileage, climbing thousands of pitches with ropes, and he rehearsed El Cap routes dozens of times before going ropeless. Get into a gym, take a lead climbing course, then move outside with experienced partners and build a decade of solid trad and sport experience. Most people who go down that road find the roped game is plenty rewarding, and that's a good outcome.
rooftop gaps. how far is too far for a beginner

For a beginner, any rooftop gap is too far. A fall from two stories can kill you, and roofs bring loose gravel, weak edges and skylights you can't see. Build your jump distance at ground level until you can consistently clear well beyond what you'd ever attempt at height. Even experienced traceurs only commit to height when a missed jump wouldn't be catastrophic.
Found a cheap used BASE rig online, like half price. Worth it?

Only if a qualified rigger who knows BASE gear inspects it thoroughly and it fits your skill level and the objects you'll jump. Used gear can have hidden wear, outdated components or a canopy size that's wrong for you, and you don't get a reserve to fall back on. Ask your instructor or a BASE-experienced rigger before you pay. Most of the time it's smarter to buy gear that matches what your course recommends.
I dive fine in the pool but get claustrophobic in my mask in open water. tips?

That's common and fixable. Make sure your mask fits well and doesn't leak, since water creeping in is a huge anxiety trigger, and try a low-volume mask with clear side windows for a more open feel. Stay shallow in calm, clear water at first, and focus on slow, long exhales to calm your nervous system. A few guided dives with a patient instructor who knows you're working on this will make a big difference.
Had a hard opening last weekend, neck's been sore since. Jumping again Saturday, should be ok?

Get it checked by a doctor before you jump again, since hard openings can cause real neck injuries that a second opening shock might make worse. If you still have pain or limited movement, sit this weekend out. Also have a rigger or an experienced jumper look at your packing and slider, because a hard opening often has a fixable cause.
Worried mom here. My 15yo crashed and says he's fine but he hit his head. His helmet has a crack. What now?

Treat it as a possible concussion and get him checked by a doctor today, especially if he has a headache, nausea, confusion, drowsiness or blurred vision, and go to the ER if any of those get worse. Teens often downplay symptoms because they want to keep riding, so don't rely on him saying he's fine. He shouldn't ride again until a doctor clears him. The helmet has done its job and needs to be replaced, even if the crack looks small.
Is backcountry kicker building a good idea if the resort park is too crowded?

It can be fun, but it's a big step up in risk. Outside the resort you're dealing with avalanche terrain, no ski patrol, and landings that usually aren't as well shaped as a groomed park jump. If you go, take an avalanche course, carry a beacon, probe, and shovel, ride with partners who have the same gear, and check the avalanche forecast. For crowds, early mornings or weekdays at the resort park are a safer fix.
is it true you should break the surface of the water by throwing something first

Some divers do it, especially at greater heights, because a broken surface helps you spot the water and can make it feel softer. It doesn't meaningfully reduce impact forces, though, so don't count on it as a safety measure. Good form, enough depth and sensible heights matter far more.
friend wants to do a backflip off a 12m cliff, he can do them on trampolines. good idea?

Not a good idea. Trampoline flips don't translate to heights where you're falling for over a second and a half and hitting water at 50+ km/h, and one under- or over-rotation can mean landing on your back or face. If he really wants flips, he should learn them with a coach at a pool starting from 3 to 5 meters.
should I run flats or clipless for dh

Start on flat pedals with grippy shoes if you're new to downhill. Flats let you step off easily when things go wrong and teach good technique because you have to stay weighted on the pedals. Clipless can add control at speed for experienced riders, but bailing takes practice. Many World Cup riders use clips, but many skilled park riders stay on flats.
shins keep hurting after training

That sounds like shin splints or impact overload, which usually means you've ramped up jumping and landings faster than your lower legs can adapt. Cut back on drops and running for a week or two, make sure you're landing softly on the balls of your feet instead of slapping down flat, and train on softer surfaces where possible. Calf raises and tibialis raises can help build resilience. If the pain is sharp and in one specific spot on the bone, or it hurts even when resting, see a doctor, because that can be a stress fracture.
ok be honest how dangerous is BASE compared to skydiving

Much more dangerous, by most estimates somewhere in the range of tens of times riskier per jump. You have no reserve parachute, often only seconds to deploy, and objects to hit if your canopy opens facing the wrong way. Experienced, careful jumpers still die, which is why the people who last in the sport are conservative about weather, objects and their own skill level. Go in with clear eyes about that.
My buddy says you don't need knee braces they're for pros. Thoughts?

Your buddy has it backwards. Knee injuries like ACL tears are among the most common in motocross, and they happen to beginners as often as pros, often when a foot drags or gets caught in a rut. Proper knee braces can help reduce the risk, but if those are out of your budget, hard-shell knee guards are still far better than nothing. Learning to keep your feet up on the pegs also helps a lot.
Is paragliding dangerous? My wife is freaking out about me starting.

It carries real risk, but the risk depends heavily on how you fly. Most serious accidents come down to flying in poor conditions, flying gear beyond your skill or skipping proper training, and those are all things you control. Training with a good school, staying on a forgiving wing and being willing to stay on the ground on doubtful days makes a big difference. It might help to bring her to the school to meet your instructor and hear how they manage safety.
can i wingsuit in my jumpsuit rig or do i need a special container

Most modern containers work for wingsuiting, but you need to check with your rig manufacturer and make sure the suit is compatible. A big factor is the pilot chute and bridle length, since a short bridle can get caught in the burble behind the suit. Ask your rigger and coach to look at your setup before your first flight instead of guessing.
my son is 13 and wants to jump off the rocks at the lake with older kids. should I let him?

It can be fine if the jump is low, roughly under 4 or 5 meters, he's a strong swimmer, and an adult has actually confirmed the landing zone is deep and clear. The real risks with teens are peer pressure pushing them higher than they're ready for and nobody checking the water first, so going with him the first time is the best move. Set a clear height limit together and make feet-first the non-negotiable rule.
How do I know if a big wave is going to close out?

Read the swell direction, the wave shape and how the set lines up with the reef or sandbar. A wave that walls up in a straight line across the bay is far more likely to close out than one that peaks and peels. Watch a lot of waves from land before paddling out, and ask the locals, because they know the spot's patterns better than any app.
Is it ok to drink alcohol at base camp to help me sleep?

It's best to skip it, especially in your first days at a new altitude. Alcohol depresses your breathing during sleep, which is exactly when your oxygen levels are already lowest, and it also dehydrates you and can mimic or mask the symptoms of altitude sickness. If sleep is a real problem, ask your doctor before the trip about options that are safe at altitude, and save the celebration beer for after you've come down.
Is it safer to jump with a running start?

A short controlled step or two can help you clear the cliff face, which matters when the base slopes outward. A full sprint usually throws off your body position and makes a flat, rotating landing more likely. Figure out how far out you need to land, then use just enough momentum to get there cleanly.
My 14 year old has shin splints but wants to keep training for his motocross races. Is this harmful?

It can be, because untreated shin pain in a growing teen can turn into a stress fracture. Racing itself loads the legs less than running, but if his pain is pinpoint on the bone or there at rest, he needs to see a doctor and maybe get imaging before training continues. Cut back his running and jumping conditioning, and check his footwear and training jumps, because kids often ramp up too fast.
I'm 41 and out of shape, is parkour even realistic for me

Completely realistic, and there are plenty of traceurs who started in their forties and fifties. The key is spending your first couple of months on conditioning rather than jumps: quadrupedal movement, squats, step-ups, low balance work, and lots of easy landings from knee height to toughen up your tendons. Lots of parkour gyms run adult beginner or masters classes that scale everything properly, which is the fastest and safest way in. Your joints and connective tissue adapt slower than your muscles, so progress gently even when you feel strong.
is it bad to drink a couple beers before jumping? just to calm nerves

Yes, skip the beer. Alcohol slows your reaction time and dulls judgment, which matters a lot when you have only a few seconds to deal with an off-heading opening or line twist. Nerves are normal and actually keep you careful. Save the drinks for after you've landed and packed.
sport climbing fall, lip bashed into rock and tooth loose. its been an hour

Get to an emergency dentist today, since a loose tooth after trauma has the best chance of being saved within the first few hours. Bite gently on clean gauze, don't wiggle the tooth, and skip hot or hard food. If the tooth comes out, hold it by the crown, not the root, and keep it in milk or tucked inside your cheek on the way there. If you hit your head too or feel dizzy or nauseous, go to the ER instead.
I'm 17 with 50 skydives, can I do a BASE course this summer?

Not yet. Courses require you to be an adult, and 50 skydives is well short of the typical 200-plus minimum. Use the next couple of years to build jumps, take canopy courses, and get really good at accuracy landings. When you're old enough and experienced enough, you'll learn far more from the course.
skied a slope yesterday no problem, so it should be fine today too right?

Not necessarily, because the snowpack changes with new snow, wind, warming or sun, and a slope that held yesterday can fail today. Plenty of slopes also get skied many times before they finally slide, since the weak layer can sit there waiting for the right trigger point. Read today's forecast and assess today's conditions instead of trusting yesterday's tracks.
Flying into La Paz then trying Huayna Potosi two days later. Doable if I'm fit?

Fitness won't protect you here, because acclimatization is about time, not cardio, and La Paz already sits around 3,600 m. Give yourself at least four to six days around the city and on nearby hikes like Chacaltaya before heading up a 6,088 m peak. Most reputable Bolivian guide outfits build in a rest day at high camp for exactly this reason, so book one of those rather than squeezing it.
how high can a beginner safely jump off a cliff into water?

Start low, around 3 to 5 meters, and only move up once your entries are consistently clean and controlled. Most injuries at beginner level come from bad body position, not height, so nail a straight feet-first entry with arms tight to your sides before going higher. Even 10 meters is a big step up because you hit the water at roughly 50 km/h, which is why many experienced divers stay below that height.
I froze at the edge last time and felt like an idiot. how do I get over it?

Freezing is your brain doing its job, so don't beat yourself up about it. Drop down to a height where you feel nervous but not panicked, do a bunch of jumps there until it feels routine, then step up a meter or two at a time. Count yourself down out loud and commit on a set number, because standing at the edge thinking is what makes the fear grow.
Climbed 3 years in gyms only. Never outside. Thinking of soloing outdoors to make it 'pure'. Good idea?

No, and the gym-only background is the main reason. Outdoor rock behaves very differently: holds break, friction changes with temperature, and the route isn't marked with tape. Hire a guide or take an outdoor transition course, learn to place gear or clip bolts on real rock, and spend a few seasons outside on rope. The rock will still be there.
Is a regular skate helmet fine for downhill or do I really need a full face?

For real downhill speeds you want a full-face helmet, because slides gone wrong and highsides tend to put your chin and jaw into the pavement first. An open-shell skate helmet is built for low-speed falls at the park, not 40 mph impacts. Look for one with a proper certification like DOT or ECE, and pair it with a visor or goggles so bugs and grit don't blind you mid-run.
Watching a freediving doc made me want to try deep stuff fast. How quickly could I get to 40m?

Plenty of recreational divers reach 40 meters, but it usually takes several seasons of steady training. A first course gets most people to 20 meters, and progressing safely means slowly adapting your lungs, mastering equalization and building solid rescue habits. People who rush depth are the ones who get lung squeezes and blackouts. Take a structured course, and let your body set the timeline rather than the documentary.
Gonna fly into La Paz and climb Huayna Potosi two days later, it's only 6,088m

That's too fast. La Paz itself sits around 3,600 meters, and most people need about a week acclimatizing in the area before they're ready for 6,000 meters. Spend those days on day hikes and smaller peaks like Chacaltaya or Pequeño Alpamayo, and book a guided three-day itinerary for Huayna when you're ready. You'll actually enjoy the climb instead of grinding up it with a pounding headache.
can i just take diamox and skip the acclimatization days lol

No. Diamox speeds up acclimatization a bit, but it doesn't replace it, and people who use it as a shortcut still get altitude sickness, sometimes badly. It can also hide early symptoms just enough that you push higher when you should be resting. Use it the way it's meant to be used, as a preventive alongside a sensible ascent profile, and get a prescription from a doctor who knows your health history.
is it normal for eyes to go bloodshot after jumping

Mild redness can happen from the pressure in the head during deceleration, and it usually clears within a few days. Seek medical attention promptly if you notice vision changes, floaters, a curtain over your sight, severe headache or eye pain. If it's just a bit of redness and you see fine, rest and keep an eye on it.
do i need to bring anything for my first jump

Wear comfortable, weather-appropriate clothes and sneakers with laces, not boots or sandals with hooks. Bring photo ID, water and snacks, since weather delays can stretch the day out for hours. Leave jewelry and loose items at home or in the car, and the dropzone supplies everything else.
How often should I practice beacon searches?

At the start of every season and at least a couple of times during it, and ideally a quick drill with your touring partners before trips. Skills fade fast, and a buried friend doesn't have time for you to remember how the beacon works. Many areas have beacon parks at trailheads that make quick practice easy.
how long should i be able to hold my breath before paddling into 20 foot waves

Static breath-hold numbers matter less than you'd think, because a real hold-down happens with your heart rate spiking and your body getting tumbled. Most big-wave surfers aim to comfortably handle two-wave hold-downs, which means training for calm 3 to 4 minute static holds and doing CO2 tolerance tables under exertion. Take a proper freediving or big-wave survival course such as BWRAG or Surf Survival rather than training alone, and never do breath-hold practice in water without a trained buddy watching you.
Wind tunnel worth it for wingsuit progression?

Yes, especially for body awareness and flying on your back. Some tunnels even offer wingsuit-specific sessions, though most training will be in regular freefly. It won't replace actual wingsuit jumps, but it can make your sky time far more productive.
what does 'lip' 'knuckle' and 'landing' mean on a jump

The lip is the top edge of the takeoff ramp, where you leave the ground. The knuckle is the rounded transition at the top of the landing slope, and landing on it or before it is harsh because it's nearly flat. The landing is the downhill slope after the knuckle, and that's where you want to touch down, since the angle absorbs your impact.
We found a wreck on sonar while fishing. I have open water cert. Can I just drop down and poke around inside it?

Diving the outside of it within your depth limit with a buddy is fair game, but don't go inside. Wreck penetration kills untrained divers through silt-outs, entanglement and getting lost with no direct path to the surface. You'd need a Wreck Diver course at minimum, plus a guideline and redundant air for real penetration. Also check the depth and currents first, because an uncharted wreck is an unknown site.
Guide says my oxygen sat is 78% at 4,900m. Is that bad??

Saturation in the high 70s or low 80s can be normal at 4,900 meters, so the number alone isn't a reason to panic. What matters more is how you feel and whether the reading trends downward over the next few hours or days. If it keeps dropping, or you get breathlessness at rest, confusion, or a worsening headache, take those as signs to descend and don't talk yourself out of it. Keep checking in with your guide, who sounds like they're paying proper attention.
Fastest way to learn a frontside boardslide?

Make sure you're comfortable sliding a box straight with a flat base, then practice popping 90 degrees on flat snow. On a low, wide box, approach at a slow, consistent speed, pop so the box is under the middle of your board, and keep your shoulders lined up with the feature. Keep your base flat and your knees bent, and look at the end of the box. Rushing to rails before this is consistent on boxes is how people get hurt.
operator says my cord weight bracket is fine but I lied by 8kg on the form lol

Tell them the real number before you jump. Cord length and tension are set based on your weight, and 8 kg can shift how far you stretch, which matters a lot near the ground or the water. They'll just adjust the setup, nobody cares about the number, and it's a two-second fix that keeps the jump safe.
rib still sore 4 weeks after surfing wipeout. paddling hurts. keep surfing or not

Ribs can take six weeks or more to heal, and pain while paddling means it isn't there yet. If you push it, you can delay healing or worsen a crack. If it's very tender to touch or breathing still hurts, get an X-ray to rule out a fracture. Ease off for another couple of weeks and swim easy if that doesn't hurt.
teen hiker here, 17, going to Peru with my dad to do Huayna Potosi, how hard is it really

Huayna Potosi is one of the more accessible 6,000 meter peaks, but it's a real mountaineering climb with glacier travel, crampons, an ice axe and a steep final ridge, usually starting at night. Most people who succeed have spent a week or more acclimatizing around La Paz and maybe doing smaller peaks or treks first. Go with a reputable local guide service, take the practice day on the glacier seriously, and turn back if either of you feels unwell, since it'll still be there.
skipping the safety course, I've watched like 50 hours of youtube on hold downs. fine?

Fifty hours of video is great for spotting lines and reading sets, but it can't teach your body how to stay calm while being ragdolled in the dark. A big-wave safety course has you practice rescues, sled pickups and CPR in real conditions, and those are the skills that keep you or your buddy alive. Do the course. It's a weekend, and it pays off for the rest of your surfing life.
I'm terrified of getting stuck upside down in my kayak. Can that happen?

It's a really common fear, and the good news is that in a properly fitted kayak you'll slide out easily by pulling your spray skirt's grab loop and pushing out. Practise wet exits in a pool or calm water with an instructor until it becomes automatic, and you'll feel much more confident. Always make sure the grab loop is outside your skirt before launching. Entrapment is rare and mostly happens from pins on rocks, which is why good boat fit and scouting matter.
Got the flu-ish thing last week, feel better now. Asthma acting up a bit. Diving Saturday?

With your asthma acting up, I'd sit this one out. Narrowed airways can trap air in your lungs during ascent, which raises the risk of lung overexpansion injury, and cold, dry tank air can trigger symptoms. Check in with your doctor, and wait until your breathing is back to your normal baseline before you dive.
How long should I be able to hold my breath before surfing 15-20 ft waves?

Static breath-hold numbers matter less than how long you can hold your breath while your heart is pounding after a paddle and a wipeout. Many experienced chargers can do two-plus minutes static, but the real goal is staying calm through 20 to 30 seconds of violent hold-down after hard exertion. Train this with a certified freediving or big-wave breath course like Performance Freediving or the XPT style programs. Never do breath-hold work in the water alone, because shallow water blackout gives no warning.
Tell me straight: what kills most wingsuiters?

Most wingsuit deaths happen in wingsuit BASE and proximity flying, usually from hitting terrain after a navigation error, misjudging glide or flying lines without enough margin. Wingsuit skydiving from planes has a far lower fatality rate, and the problems there tend to be deployment issues or collisions. The common thread is people pushing beyond their experience. That's why experienced flyers keep big margins.
Landed hard yesterday, back is a bit sore but fine. Flying again tomorrow ok?

Get it checked first. Compression injuries to the spine from hard landings can feel minor at first and get worse with another impact, so a doctor's look is worth it, especially if the pain is sharp, radiating or getting worse. If you get the all-clear, ease back in with an easy flight in calm conditions. Also consider a harness with a good back protector if yours is old or thin.
I'm a big guy, 240 lbs. Does that change heat stuff?

Yes, larger runners generate more heat and usually sweat more, so you're likely to overheat sooner than lighter runners at the same pace. Plan for higher fluid and sodium intake, and test your sweat rate in training. Be extra aggressive with ice and pacing, since your heart rate will climb fast in heat.
First time ice climbing next weekend with a guide. Do I need to buy my own crampons or will they provide them?

Most guide services include technical gear like crampons, tools, harness and helmet in the price, but confirm when you book so you're not scrambling the night before. What you'll almost always need to bring is a pair of stiff, crampon-compatible mountaineering boots, and many outfits rent those too. Don't buy crampons until you know you like the sport and which boots you'll pair them with, since fit between boot and crampon matters a lot.
My 16 year old son wants to start freediving after watching YouTube videos. He's a strong swimmer. Should I be worried?

A little caution is warranted, but this can be a great sport for him if he learns it properly. Strong swimmers are often the ones who push breath-holds too far, because they feel comfortable in the water and underestimate blackout risk. Sign him up for an entry-level course like AIDA 1 or 2, Molchanovs Wave 1, or PADI Freediver. Many agencies accept teens with parental consent, and he'll learn buddy rescue and the rule of never diving alone, which matters most.
is it dumb to paddle out at Jaws on my first big swell if I've surfed 10 footers at home?

Not dumb to want it, but Jaws is a different animal. A 10-foot beach break doesn't prepare you for 30-plus feet of open-ocean energy breaking over a reef. Spend a season or two at intermediate big-wave spots like Sunset or Waimea on smaller days, do a breath-hold and big-wave safety course, and only go out at Peahi with experienced locals and a dedicated ski driver watching you.
Cheapest way to get cave certified fast? On a budget

Cave training isn't the place to cut corners, but you can save money sensibly by training locally, buying good used gear checked by a technician and taking courses in stages. Many people take cavern first, then save up for full cave instead of bundling everything at once. Choose your instructor based on reputation and safety record, not price, because that's the training your life will depend on.
it snowed 2 feet last night, bluebird today, when's the best time to go out

Bluebird after two feet is the classic setup where people get caught, because the snow looks perfect but the new load hasn't bonded yet. Give it at least a day or two to settle. Today, stick to low-angle slopes under 30 degrees with nothing steep overhead and avoid runout zones. Check the avalanche forecast first, and watch for warming as the sun hits slopes, which can quickly trigger wet slides.
Is wearing black gear really that bad for heat races?

Yes, in direct sun black absorbs noticeably more heat, so light colors are a real, if modest, advantage over many hours. The bigger wins are a wide-brimmed or legionnaire hat, light sleeves you can soak, and loose breathable fabric. Wear whatever you'll actually wet down and keep ice in, since active cooling matters more than shirt color.
Solo-ed a route today and a hold broke. I caught myself. Still shaking. What now?

Glad you're okay, and the shaking is totally normal. Your body is processing a near miss, so rest, eat and talk it through with someone you trust tonight. Take a real break from soloing while you reflect on what happened, including whether that route had loose rock you could have spotted and whether it changes how you think about the risk overall. Lots of experienced climbers have walked away from soloing after a moment like this, and plenty of others came back with stricter rules. Both are respectable outcomes, but decide once the adrenaline is gone.
can I hit the jumps without a helmet? i hate how it feels and I'm only doing small ones

I'd wear one, especially in the park. Small jumps still give you enough height to slam your head on hard-packed or icy snow, and most park head injuries happen on lower features. If yours feels bad, it's probably the wrong fit or model, so try on a few at a shop. A well-fitted helmet with a good liner barely feels like anything.
