I'm 52 and a bit overweight, want to try freediving on holiday. Anything to check?

Plenty of people start freediving in their fifties, but see your doctor first, especially about your heart, blood pressure and lungs. Breath-holding and cold water stress the cardiovascular system. Then book a beginner course or guided intro session at your destination rather than going it alone. Instructors will start you shallow and relaxed, which is exactly right.
can i rent ice climbing gear or should i buy

Rent for your first few outings, boots, crampons and tools especially, so you can figure out what you like before spending a lot. Most guide services and mountain shops rent full kits, and guided days often include gear. Buy your own helmet and harness early if you want, but hold off on technical tools and screws until you know you're sticking with it.
Considering wingsuiting. I have 120 jumps. Where do I start?

At 120 jumps you're close, since most organizations recommend at least 200 jumps, and many dropzones require it. Use the time to get really solid at tracking, navigation and emergency procedures. When you hit the number, take a proper First Flight Course with a qualified wingsuit coach, using a beginner suit.
Worried mom here. My 13 year old son keeps asking for a neck brace. Are they worth it or a gimmick?

Neck braces aren't a gimmick, and the fact that your son is asking for one is a good sign. Research suggests they can reduce the risk of certain neck injuries by limiting extreme head movement in a crash, though they aren't a guarantee and won't prevent every injury. Get one sized for his height and weight from a known brand like Leatt or Atlas, and have it fitted properly so it works with his helmet and chest protector. For a teen riding regularly, it's a reasonable addition to his gear.
I wiped out at Puerto Escondido and my eardrum feels weird and muffled. Can I surf tomorrow?

Hold off on surfing until a doctor looks at it, because a heavy wipeout can rupture an eardrum, and getting water in a perforated ear can cause infection and balance trouble. See a clinic and get an otoscope check. If it's ruptured, you'll usually need a few weeks out of the water.
Teen son tore ACL skiing, surgery done 5 months ago, he feels great and wants to race this winter.

Five months is early. Most surgeons and research point to at least 9 months before returning to pivoting sports like ski racing, because the graft is still maturing and re-tear rates are much higher with an early return. Feeling great isn't the same as being ready. Strength and hop tests showing the leg is within about 90% of the other side are a better measure. A free-ski season building back up, with racing the following year, is the safer path.
planning a trip to do wingsuit BASE in Switzerland next summer, I've got 250 skydives and 30 wingsuit jumps. good to go?

Not yet. Most experienced wingsuit BASE jumpers recommend a few hundred wingsuit skydives plus a solid base of regular BASE jumps before trying wingsuit BASE. Lauterbrunnen is not a place to learn, and plenty of fatalities there involve pilots with more experience than you have now. Make the trip about building skills at a dropzone, or take a reputable BASE first jump course if that's your long-term goal.
My buddy says frostbite blisters should be popped. True?

No, leave them intact in the field, because popping them invites infection. Rewarm the area only if there's no chance of it refreezing, using warm water around 37 to 39°C rather than fire or rubbing, then protect it and get to medical care. Refreezing tissue after thawing does much more damage than staying frozen a bit longer while you get down.
Quick q: lanyard needed for 20m line dives?

Yes. A lanyard clipped to the line means you can't drift away from it, so your buddy can pull you up if something goes wrong. It's standard practice in deep training for good reason, so use one with a quick-release.
What's roped soloing and is it a reasonable middle ground?

Roped soloing means climbing alone while protecting yourself with a fixed rope and a self-belay device such as a Silent Partner, or with a mini-traxion on toprope. It's a legitimate way to climb alone, but the systems can fail if they're rigged wrong, so learn from an experienced mentor and back everything up. Toprope soloing on a fixed line is the most common starting point, using two independent devices and a well-built anchor. Practice low to the ground first until the system is second nature.
my 9 year old wants to ride his cousin's 125 two stroke this weekend, he's ridden a PW50 a few times, thoughts?

That's too big a jump, because a 125 two-stroke makes several times the power of a PW50 and hits hard in the midrange, which can throw a small kid off the back or into a tree before he knows what happened. Kids his size and experience usually move to a 65cc, or a 110 four-stroke with a clutch, and spend a season there learning throttle and clutch control. Let him sit on the 125 with the engine off if he's excited, but keep him on something he can actually manage.
How do I know when I'm ready to move from small jumps to medium?

You're ready when you can land the small jumps cleanly almost every time, with control and no skidding or arm-flailing, at a consistent speed. You should also be able to grab or add a basic trick on the small one without losing that control. Watch a few people hit the medium jump first to judge the speed needed, and do a test pass rolling over it before you go for real.
what's a v-thread / abalakov and can I trust one to rappel

A V-thread, or Abalakov, is an anchor made by drilling two angled holes with an ice screw so they meet, then threading cord through and tying it off. In thick, solid ice it's very strong and is the standard way to rappel off ice routes. It's only as good as the ice and your technique, though, so learn it from a guide, practice building them at ground level, and back it up with a screw while the heavier climbers test it. Always inspect any old V-thread cord you find and replace it if in doubt.
Detailed one: I've been bouldering for 4 months and keep seeing people do dynos. My shoulder sometimes clicks. Should I start practicing dynos?

Hold off on dynos for now, because they put big, sudden loads through your shoulders and fingers, and a clicking shoulder is worth getting checked by a physiotherapist first. Four months is still early, and building shoulder stability with exercises like scapular pull-ups and controlled static climbing will set you up better. Once you're cleared and stronger, start with small dynos to big, positive holds before attempting dramatic ones.
What's the difference between a wet slide and a dry slab?

Dry slab avalanches happen when a cohesive layer breaks off a buried weak layer, and they're often triggered by people even on cold, stable-looking days. Wet slides happen when melting water weakens the snowpack, usually with warm temps, rain, or strong sun, and they tend to come later in the day. That's why spring touring means starting early and getting off sun-baked slopes once the surface turns punchy and soft.
60 y/o, had knee replacement a year ago, want to try skydiving. Landing worries me.

That's a reasonable worry, because landings are where most skydiving injuries happen and a replaced knee isn't great at handling hard impacts. Talk to your surgeon first. If they're comfortable with it, a tandem jump is the way to go, since an experienced instructor controls the canopy and many operators can do a sliding seated landing. Let the dropzone know about your knee ahead of time so they can plan for it.
planning to spearfish solo off the rocks tomorrow, conditions look calm. tips?

Honestly, the best tip is not to go solo. Spearfishers are one of the groups most often killed by shallow water blackout, because chasing a fish makes you push your dives past your limits. If you absolutely can't find a buddy, stay much shallower than usual, rest at the surface for at least twice as long as each dive lasted, and never hunt hard at your max depth. A buddy watching from the surface is still the thing that actually saves lives.
found an old cam at a garage sale for $10, no idea of its history. good to lead on?

Treat that one as a decoration, not protection. You don't know if it's been dropped onto rock, stored near chemicals, or had its slings and trigger wires degrade, and the sling on an old cam is often past its rated life anyway. Some manufacturers will inspect and re-sling their cams, so look up the brand and model before trusting it. Until a pro has checked it, keep it off your lead rack.
I'm 15 and want to start freediving this summer. My parents are nervous. Is it actually safe for teenagers?

It can be very safe for teenagers if you learn it properly, and many agencies like AIDA, PADI and Molchanovs run courses for people your age, sometimes with parental consent. The real risk comes from teaching yourself and diving without a trained buddy, because shallow water blackout can happen to anyone. Ask your parents to look into a beginner course with you so they can see how much of the training is about safety and rescue. That will probably calm their nerves more than anything you say.
Line cut or lost in zero vis. What do I do

Stop and stay calm, keep breathing slowly, and don't swim blindly. Tie off your safety spool where you are, then search in careful sweeps until you find the line. Once you're touching the line, form an OK sign around it and follow it out, using line arrows to confirm which way is out. This is exactly the drill a cave course makes you practice until it's automatic, so if you haven't trained it, you shouldn't be beyond the light zone.
just tell me the best shoes for free soloing, not a lecture

Most soloists pick a comfortable all-day shoe with a stiff, supportive edge over an aggressive downturned one, because comfort and consistent footing matter more than peak performance. The La Sportiva TC Pro and Scarpa Maestro are popular choices for long trad and slab, and you want a pair that's broken in but not worn through at the toe. Whatever you choose, wear it on those exact routes with a rope first so nothing about the fit surprises you up high.
what suit should i buy for my first wingsuit

Don't buy anything yet. Your first flight course will put you in a small beginner suit from the school, something like a Squirrel Sprite, a Phoenix-Fly Shadow or a Tony Suits Trac. After 20 to 50 flights in small suits, your coaches can tell you what fits your flying style. That's when buying makes sense, ideally a used beginner suit sized by the manufacturer.
I have a crew for my first 100 in the heat. What should I tell them to watch for?

Tell them to watch for confusion, slurred speech, irritability, stumbling, vomiting that won't stop, swelling or dark urine, and to take those seriously even if you insist you're fine. Give them your planned fluid, salt and calorie amounts so they can check you're on track, and agree ahead of time that they can call medical staff. A good crew also has ice ready, swaps wet clothes, and keeps you moving out of aid stations without lingering in the shade too long.
Can I practice breath holds in my pool by myself? My buddy is never free.

Don't do breath-hold training in water alone, ever, because shallow water blackout hits without warning and you won't know you're going under. Dry static tables on your couch or bed are safe to do solo and build most of the same tolerance. Save the in-water work for when your buddy or a freediving class can actually watch you from arm's length.
What's a combat roll

A combat roll is a roll you pull off for real when you flip in a rapid unexpectedly, as opposed to setting it up in calm water. It's what actually keeps you in your boat, and most paddlers find it falls apart at first under stress. Practice in moving water, flipping at random times, so it becomes reliable.
is it okay to wear glasses?

Yes, the dropzone will give you goggles that fit over glasses. Make sure the goggles fit snugly, and consider wearing a sports strap on your glasses. Contacts are often easier, if you have them, and they work fine under regular goggles.
can I drink alcohol at base camp to celebrate

A small drink after you're well acclimatized and resting won't usually wreck you, but alcohol worsens dehydration, disrupts already poor sleep and can blur the early signs of altitude sickness. Skip it entirely during the first days at a new altitude or before any push higher. Save the real celebration for when you're back down.
I want to film a rooftop gap jump for my channel. Any tips for making it look good?

Before you think about the shot, you need to be able to do the same distance on the ground, landing with a margin to spare, dozens of times in a row. Rooftop gaps have hidden dangers like crumbling edges, wet surfaces and skylights, and there's often no legal access, so many experienced athletes film a creative ground-level line instead. If you go ahead anyway, walk and inspect both sides first and have someone with you who can call for help. For the footage itself, a low angle and a wide lens make modest gaps look dramatic, so you can get a great shot without pushing your limits.
Ran a half with a sore hip, now it's worse and aches at night. Ugh. Next steps?

Night ache after running on a sore hip is a red flag, because it can point to a femoral neck stress fracture, which is serious and can need surgery if it progresses. Stop running and see a sports doctor soon, and ask about an MRI, since X-rays often miss these. Until you have a diagnosis, avoid impact, and keep walking to a minimum if it hurts. It might be something less serious, but this is one to get properly checked.
What's the difference between a three-wing and a mono-wing suit?

A three-wing suit has separate wings under each arm and between the legs, which is the classic design used by most pilots. Mono-wing suits connect everything into a single surface and are rarer, but some coaches like them for certain training purposes. For beginners, a small three-wing suit is the standard choice. Your coach can help you pick when you get there.
Anyone ever just push through dizziness? I usually do and it goes away.

Plenty of people do, and it often passes, but dizziness in the heat can be the early edge of heat exhaustion or hyponatremia, so it deserves a pause rather than a push. Slow to a walk, get shade if you can, cool down, and take fluid with sodium. If it doesn't clear within a few minutes, or it comes with confusion, headache or vomiting, get to the aid station and medical staff. Pushing through works until the one time it really doesn't.
what does nitrogen narcosis actually feel like

People often describe it as being tipsy, with a mild euphoria, slowed thinking, tunnel focus or sometimes anxiety. It usually becomes noticeable around 30 meters, but it varies from person to person and day to day. The tricky part is that it impairs your ability to notice it. If you feel off, ascend a few meters and it clears quickly.
How long does it take to get hypothermia in 12 degree water?

True hypothermia in 12°C water usually takes longer than people expect, often more than half an hour, but your body starts losing strength and coordination well before that. Cold shock in the first minute and swim failure after 10 to 30 minutes are the bigger dangers. Keep your swims short, stay close to an exit, and warm up gradually afterwards with dry layers and a warm drink rather than jumping straight into a hot shower.
what's the world record for cliff diving and could a normal fit person work up to like 20m?

Laso Schaller's 58.8 meter jump in 2015 is generally cited as the record, but that's an extreme outlier done with careful preparation and safety divers. A fit amateur can realistically progress toward 20 meters, but it takes years of structured training, ideally through a diving club or a high-diving coach. At 20 meters you're hitting the water at roughly 70 km/h, so self-teaching at that height is how people get badly hurt.
I'm 42 and want to learn to skate. Am I crazy?

Not at all, adult beginners are everywhere now and lots of skateparks run adult-only sessions or lessons. Your bones don't bounce like a teenager's, so wear a helmet, wrist guards, and knee pads, and wear hip pads too if you're nervous about falling. Start with pushing, turning, and stopping on flat ground before dropping into anything, and progress steadily rather than trying to keep up with the kids.
I keep flipping in eddy lines. What am I doing wrong???

Almost certainly you're not tilting your boat downstream as you cross. When you hit the eddy line, the water grabs your upstream edge and flips you, so lift that edge by dropping your downstream hip and keep the boat tilted until you're fully in the new current. Cross with good speed and an angle of about 45 degrees rather than drifting in sideways. Practise peel-outs and eddy turns over and over on an easy rapid, and it'll click quickly.
what should I do if someone hits the water badly and doesn't come up

Get to them immediately, but only swim out if you can do it safely, and send someone else to call emergency services right away. If you suspect a neck or back injury, support their head and neck in line with their body, keep their face out of the water, and move them as little as possible. If they're not breathing once they're out, start CPR. Taking a first aid or water rescue course before your next trip is a great idea.
Should I buy a 450 as my first bike? Im 6'2 and 210lbs

Even at your size, a 450 is a lot of bike for a beginner. The power comes on hard, and it's very easy to whisky-throttle into trouble. A 250F would fit you fine physically and let you learn throttle control and technique much faster. Lots of big riders start on a 250F, and it's a smarter path even if you move up to a 450 after a season or so.
I'm heavier than my wing's weight range by about 8kg. Big deal?

Yes, it matters. Flying overloaded makes the wing faster and more dynamic, with harder, more energetic collapses and reactions that can be beyond a pilot's level. It can also void certification and insurance. Get a wing sized for your all-up weight, including gear, and ask your instructor or a dealer to confirm the fit.
I fell during a practice and hit my head on concrete. I feel fine now, can I keep training today?

No, stop training for today and keep an eye on yourself, because concussion symptoms often show up hours later and a second knock while your brain is vulnerable can be serious. Tell someone what happened so they can watch for warning signs like headache, nausea, confusion, drowsiness or blurred vision. If any of those appear, or if you lost consciousness at all, see a doctor promptly. Return to training only once you are completely symptom-free, and with medical clearance if you got any symptoms.
How do I stop being scared of falling when I lead climb? It's ruining my progress.

Fear of falling is normal, and the most effective fix is structured fall practice: start with tiny falls with the bolt at your waist, then gradually work up to falling with the bolt at your knees and feet. Do it with a trusted, experienced belayer who gives soft catches, on overhanging or vertical terrain where there's nothing to hit. A lot of gyms offer falling clinics, and a coach can make the progression much faster and safer.
What's the difference between paddle-in and tow-in for a beginner to big waves?

Paddle-in means catching waves under your own power on a long gun, so you're limited to waves you can actually paddle into. That naturally keeps you in a more manageable size range. Tow-in uses a jet ski to sling you onto much bigger, faster waves on a short, heavy board. It needs a highly skilled driver and serious rescue skills on both sides. Start with paddling. Tow surfing is an advanced team discipline, not a shortcut.
can I free solo an easy 5.6 that I've done like 50 times on top rope

Knowing the route well lowers the risk but doesn't remove the things you can't control: a hold that breaks, a slip on damp rock, a sudden cramp. Any of those means a fatal fall with no margin at all. Fifty laps make it a great route to lead or to run quick laps on with a rope. The consequence is death, so keep the rope.
My friend says you should drink 6 liters of water a day at altitude to prevent AMS. Legit?

Hydration helps you feel better and keeps your body working, but it doesn't directly prevent altitude sickness. Around 3 to 4 liters a day is a sensible target for most people, adjusted for exertion and heat. Overdoing it can dilute your blood sodium, which causes confusion that's easily mistaken for HACE. Aim for pale yellow urine rather than a fixed big number.
Is it fine to touch turtles if they swim up to me?

Just enjoy watching them and keep your hands to yourself. Touching stresses turtles, can spread bacteria to them, and is illegal in many marine parks. Hold still, keep good buoyancy, and they'll often stay close longer anyway.
can i fly my paraglider near the airport? its a small one

Not without checking the airspace rules first, because even small airports usually have controlled or restricted airspace around them. Get the local aviation charts or an airspace app, and talk to local pilots about what's allowed. Flying into controlled airspace without permission is illegal and genuinely dangerous given traffic. Often there are clear corridors and altitude limits that make legal flying possible nearby.
I bouldered V5 today with no crash pad and felt amazing. Ready for highballs and maybe soloing next?

Glad it felt good, but skipping pads is how people break ankles and wrists even on short problems. Highballs and soloing raise the stakes much further. If highballs interest you, build up gradually with several pads, experienced spotters, and problems you've worked thoroughly at lower heights. Soloing should stay off the table until you have years of roped outdoor climbing behind you.
What's a good fingerboard routine for a beginner who's been climbing 2 months?

At two months you're better off skipping the fingerboard, since your tendons and pulleys adapt much more slowly than your muscles, and early hangboarding is a common way to injure fingers. Spend that energy on climbing more, varied problems and technique like footwork, which will make you better faster. Most coaches suggest waiting about a year or more, and then starting with conservative open-hand hangs on large edges.
im 52 and want to start backcountry skiing. too late?

It's not too late at all, and plenty of people start at your age or older and go on to love it. Start with an avalanche course like AIARE 1 and a few days with a guide, and get your fitness up beforehand, since skinning uphill is the hard part. Strong resort skiing ability makes the transition much easier, so make sure you're comfortable on off-piste terrain first.
Want to solo Denali without a guide. I've done Rainier twice. Thoughts?

Rainier is great preparation, but Denali is a big step up, with weeks of hauling loads, brutal cold, and storms that can pin you down for days at 5,000-plus meters. Most rangers strongly discourage true solo climbing, mostly because of crevasse risk on the lower glacier, where falling in without a rope partner is often fatal. Join a rope team, either guided or with experienced partners, and consider taking an expedition skills course before you go. Get some big-mountain experience under your belt first, like Aconcagua, and Denali will be far more fun and much safer.
Dive computer says I'm fine but my buddy's says we need deco. Whose do we follow?

Follow the more conservative one. Computers use different algorithms and settings, and the standard practice for a buddy pair is to dive to whichever computer is most restrictive. Do the stops your buddy's computer is calling for, and before your next dive agree on how you'll handle disagreements like this.
My husband just booked us a tandem jump and I'm terrified. What are the actual odds something goes wrong?

Tandem skydiving has one of the best safety records in the sport, with fatalities running at roughly one in half a million tandem jumps in recent USPA data. Your instructor has done hundreds or thousands of jumps, the rig has a reserve canopy, and it has an automatic activation device that deploys the reserve if needed. Feeling scared is completely normal. Tell your instructor you're nervous, because they deal with it every day and will talk you through each step.
I'm going on a cenote dive trip and the operator says I don't need any certification. Legit?

For a guided cavern tour in the daylight zone, many reputable operators accept open water certified divers, as long as the guide is cavern- or cave-certified and the group is small. What you shouldn't do is go past the daylight zone or into real cave sections without full cave training, no matter what anyone says. Ask about the guide's credentials, group size and route before you book.
Is it legal to do parkour on buildings and stuff?

It depends on where you are, but climbing private buildings or roofs without permission can count as trespassing, and some cities have bylaws about public structures too. Public parks, dedicated parkour parks, and gyms are the stress-free options. If you're unsure about a spot, ask permission, and if you're told to leave, be respectful and go, because that keeps the community's reputation good.
do i need to know how to swim for a water-touch bungee?

It's a good idea, and some operators require it or ask you to declare it, though in a water-touch jump you're still attached and usually just dip in briefly before being lowered to a boat. If you can't swim, tell the staff so they can decide whether to do a dry jump instead. Never hide it to get the water dip, because things like a slow pickup do happen.
Is it fine to drink a beer or two before running the river?

Save the beers for the takeout. Even a couple of drinks slows your reactions, worsens your judgment, and speeds up hypothermia if you swim, and alcohol shows up in a lot of river fatalities. A clear head makes for a better run and a better celebration afterward.
my ears always hurt after jumping, normal?

Some pressure is common, but repeated pain isn't something to ignore, because hitting the water can rupture an eardrum, especially if you land slightly sideways. Try keeping your head perfectly straight on entry, and consider snug earplugs made for water sports. If you get sharp pain, hearing loss, dizziness or fluid draining, stop jumping and see a doctor.
can i reuse the gym's rental harness strap if it looks frayed
No. Hand it back and ask for a different harness. Frayed webbing, especially at the belay loop or tie-in points, is a retirement sign. Gyms want to know so they can pull it from rotation.
The slope already has tracks on it so it's safe right?

Tracks don't prove stability. A slope can take many skiers and then release on the next one who hits the weak spot or adds enough load, and plenty of slides have happened on tracked slopes. Make your call from the forecast, recent weather and what you're observing, not from other people's tracks.
My chain is really loose and I'm in the middle of a ride day, no tools. Can I just keep going?

Stop riding it. A really loose chain can jump off the sprockets, lock the rear wheel, and damage the cases or your leg. Ask around the pits or at the track office, because someone will almost always lend you the wrench and a minute of help. Set the slack to the spec in your manual, and check that the rear wheel is aligned before you head back out.
What's a good warm up before bouldering? I usually just jump on my project

Jumping straight onto your project with cold fingers is a common way to tweak a pulley. Spend ten minutes on light cardio and shoulder and wrist mobility, then climb five or six easy problems that gradually get harder, working up to moves close to your project's intensity. Your first attempts on the project will actually go better too, because your skin, tendons and coordination are ready.
Is it ok to surf big waves after a few beers to calm nerves?

No, because alcohol hurts your breath-hold, judgment, and reaction time, and it increases blackout risk. Calm your nerves with breathing drills, good preparation, and by surfing within your limits. Save the beers for after.
What's the right body position to land from about 10m without getting hurt?

Enter perfectly vertical, feet first, with legs squeezed together, toes pointed, glutes and core tight, and arms locked against your body or crossed over your chest. Look at the horizon during the fall rather than down, so you don't tip forward. Ten meters is a big step up, so get plenty of clean entries from 5 to 7 meters first, and ideally have someone experienced watch your form.
Huayna Potosí from La Paz - i heard you can do it in 3 days. too fast?

The 3-day itinerary is standard and fine, because it assumes you've already spent several days acclimatizing in La Paz at about 3,600 m. If you fly straight in and head up the next day, you're asking for AMS on a 6,088 m peak, so spend at least four or five days in La Paz and the surrounding high country first. Go with a reputable agency, since equipment and guide standards vary a lot there.
Can I take my GoPro on a cave dive?

Sure, as long as it's securely clipped and doesn't take your attention away from the line, your gas and your buddy. Avoid big lights and housings dangling where they could snag or stir up silt. Camera fixation is a real hazard, so let the footage be secondary and turn around at your gas limits even if the shot is perfect.
Quick q - the best boots for Island Peak?

You'll want proper double boots or insulated single mountaineering boots rated for 6,000 m, like the La Sportiva G2 Evo or Scarpa Phantom Tech, that take step-in crampons. Summit day starts in the cold dark and frostbitten toes are common on cheaper three-season boots. Break them in properly before the trip, or rent good ones in Kathmandu and fit them carefully.
is it dumb to buy a used wing off facebook to save money? its like half price

Not dumb, but don't fly it until a paragliding shop has checked it, which usually means a porosity test, line strength and trim check, and an inspection of the cloth for damage. A wing that looks fine can have saggy trim or degraded cloth that changes how it handles in a collapse. Also make sure the size and certification class actually match your weight and skill level. A cheap advanced wing is a terrible deal for a newer pilot.
can I ride downhill alone in the woods? nobody else is free

Riding alone is risky on downhill trails because a crash can leave you injured and unable to get help. If you go, stick to well-traveled lift-served runs rather than remote trails, tell someone your plan, and carry a phone with signal. A small first aid kit helps too. Holding off on hard features and riding conservatively makes a big difference.
is it ok to do tricks without wrist guards

Plenty of riders skip them, but wrist injuries are among the most common snowboarding injuries, especially when you're learning tricks and putting your hands down a lot. Guards are cheap and low profile, so they're worth wearing while you're still falling often. It also helps to practice falling with your fists closed and rolling onto your forearms rather than catching yourself on straight arms.
Can I touch the formations in the cave? Just once for a picture?

Please don't. Speleothems take thousands of years to form, and even a light touch transfers skin oils that stop their growth, or breaks off pieces that will never grow back. Keep good buoyancy and stay off the walls and ceiling entirely; your photo will look better with untouched formations anyway.
what do I do if I get caught in an avalanche

Shout so your partners can see you, deploy your airbag if you have one, and fight hard to get to the side of the slide, or grab a tree if you can. As it slows, push a hand toward the surface and get the other arm in front of your face to make an air pocket. Once it stops, stay calm to save oxygen and trust your partners to search, which is exactly why carrying gear and practicing matters.
What should be in my pack for a full DH day?

Bring water, snacks, a multitool, tire plugs, a spare derailleur hanger, and a small pump or CO2. Add a basic first aid kit, your phone, ID, and any medical info or insurance details. A light jacket is smart in mountain weather. If you're riding big remote descents, carry a whistle, and don't ride alone if you can avoid it.
My friends ride way faster than me and I keep pushing to keep up. Tips to go faster quick?

Chasing friends is the fastest route to a crash, so ride your own pace and let them wait at the junctions. Real speed comes from braking less, not riding braver. Learn to brake before features, look further ahead, and stay loose so the bike can move under you. A single coaching session will make you faster than a month of trying to keep up.
quick q, inflatable kayak ok for class III?

Some purpose-built whitewater inflatables, often called duckies, handle class III just fine, but cheap recreational inflatables will fold, puncture, or flip and are dangerous there. Make sure yours is rated for whitewater with self-bailing floors, thigh straps and tough material. Even with good gear, take a guided trip first to learn how to read rapids.
Guide says weather's iffy for summit day but I paid $45k. Can I push for it anyway?

You can ask, but listen to your guide, because they make those calls based on forecasts and experience, and a lot of deaths on big mountains happen when people push on in marginal weather. Paying a lot doesn't protect you from wind, storms or a missed turnaround time. If the trip allows, ask about waiting for a later window, and remember that coming home safe and maybe trying again later is a much better use of the money.
Want to get into wingsuit BASE ASAP. Fastest path?

There isn't a safe fast path, and rushing this kills more people than anything else in the sport. The usual advice is at least 200 wingsuit skydives and around 200 BASE jumps before you combine them, and many experienced flyers say more. Start with progressive wingsuit training in skydiving, then build slick BASE experience, then do a wingsuit BASE course on big, forgiving exits. Proximity flying should wait years beyond that.
honestly do I need to do a refresher? haven't dived in 3 years but I remember it all

Three years is long enough that a refresher is worth it, even if you remember the theory. What fades is the hands-on part: buoyancy control, assembling gear by feel, clearing your mask and handling an out-of-air situation calmly. A short pool session or refresher dive takes half a day and makes your first real dives much more enjoyable. Most reputable operators will ask for one anyway.
honestly just tell me it's fine to paraglide with my bad knee

I can't promise that. Paragliding landings and launches can put sudden, hard loads on your knees, and a bad knee is more likely to give way at exactly the wrong moment. Talk to a doctor or physio about what's actually going on with it, and ask your instructor about technique, since a good landing approach takes a lot of strain off. With a properly assessed knee and maybe a brace, you may well be able to fly safely.
Thinking of soloing as a way to deal with stress, it's the only thing that makes my brain quiet.

That focused quiet is real, and a lot of climbers find it. You can get much of it from roped climbing, especially leading near your limit, long multipitch days, or hard bouldering sessions. If you're reaching for high-consequence activities mainly to manage stress, it's worth talking to a therapist too. Feeling better shouldn't depend on risking your life.
Do I need to take a swiftwater rescue course or is youtube enough?

YouTube is great for getting familiar with concepts, but it can't replace hands-on practice in moving water with an instructor correcting you. Things like rope work, tethered swimmer rescues and pin extraction can hurt you or your friends if done slightly wrong. Take a certified course, then refresh it every few years.
quick q, how much does an AFF course cost

In the US, a full AFF program typically costs around 2,500 to 3,500 dollars through the 25-jump A license, depending on the dropzone and how many levels you repeat. The first jump with ground school usually runs 300 to 450 dollars. Budget a bit extra for repeats and gear rental, because almost everyone repeats something.
Detailed question: 32, surfing 15 years, comfortable at 15 ft, want to step into 25 ft paddle. What's the progression look like?

At your experience level, the next step is to spend a season at a well-known big-wave spot with an established crew and water safety. Start on the shoulders on 18 to 20 foot days and pick waves conservatively. Do a recognized big-wave survival course, get a properly fitted gun and a flotation vest, and work on breath-hold under exertion. Build relationships with the locals, because their knowledge of the lineup and rescue dynamics is worth more than any gear.
Friend wants to film me doing a cat leap onto a ledge over a canal. I've done cat leaps at the gym. Should be fine?

Gym success is a good sign, but outdoor walls are rough and sometimes crumbly, and a missed cat leap over water risks hitting the wall or edge on the way down and then being stunned in cold water. Check the ledge in person first, test the grip, and try the exact same distance somewhere with flat ground below. If you still do it, make sure the water is deep, there's an easy way out, and your friend is ready to help, not just filming.
I want to get my breath-hold up to 4 minutes in a month. Fastest way?

Four minutes in a month is unrealistic for most people. Pushing that hard mostly leads to blackouts rather than progress. Do structured CO2 and O2 tables dry on land, never in water alone, a few times a week, and focus on relaxation. With good coaching and consistency, real progress usually takes a few months, so enjoy the gains rather than chasing a number.
There's this canyon road near me with almost no traffic at 5am. Good spot to bomb solo?

Riding solo on an open road is one of the riskier setups in downhill, because "almost no traffic" still means a car can appear around a blind corner and nobody is there to help if you go down. If you ride roads at all, bring a crew with a spotter at blind turns and a follow car, and know the local laws, since many places ban it. Better yet, look for organized freerides or closed-course events where you can push speed safely.
i landed a jump and felt a pop in my knee. its swollen now. walk it off?

Don't walk it off. A pop followed by swelling is a classic sign of a ligament or meniscus injury, possibly an ACL tear. Ice it, keep it elevated and avoid putting full weight on it. See a doctor or sports physio in the next day or two, because training on an unstable knee can make the damage much worse.
My kid snapped his board in half doing a jump. Should he use my old board till we get a new one?

Check that your old board suits him first. If it's much longer or stiffer than his was, it'll be harder to control and can mess up his landings in the park. A board that's too big is risky on jumps, so rent one his size in the meantime. Also check that the bindings fit his boots properly and the edges aren't cracked.
how long do climbing ropes last

There's no fixed date, because it depends on how the rope has been used. A rope with heavy use and regular falls might last one to two years, while an occasional weekend rope can last much longer, and most manufacturers cap even an unused rope at around ten years. Retire it right away after a severe fall, contact with chemicals like battery acid, a core shot, or if the sheath feels mushy, flat or stiff when you run it through your hands. If you're unsure, retire it, because a rope is cheap compared with what it protects.
my buddy is offering to let me hit his triple on my first day riding. good idea?

Definitely skip it, because a triple needs speed and precise technique, and coming up short is one of the most common ways riders get seriously hurt. Spend your first days learning throttle control, braking, cornering, and standing, then work through rollers and small tabletops. That triple will still be there when you've earned it, and you'll actually enjoy it then.
quick q: what wheels for downhill beginner

Go for 70 to 75mm wheels around 78a to 80a durometer with rounded lips. They grip well, roll over rough pavement, and break into slides predictably once you're learning to slide. Avoid hard, small street wheels; they slide out unexpectedly at speed.
Is it safe to swim across the lake alone early in the morning before anyone's around? It's only about 800m.

Swimming alone is the one habit most worth breaking, because cramp, cold shock or a sudden dizzy spell can turn 800m into a serious problem with nobody to see it. If you can't find a swim buddy, at least have someone paddle alongside in a kayak or watch from shore with your planned route and finish time. Wear a bright cap and tow a swim buoy so boats and rescuers can spot you. Early mornings are lovely, but they're also when fewer people are around to help.
My 13 year old daughter wants to start downhill. She's fearless which honestly scares me. What do I do?

Get her into a youth coaching program or kids' camp at a bike park. Coaches are great at turning fearless energy into good technique and teaching kids when to back off. Fit her out properly with a full-face helmet, goggles, knee pads, gloves, and ideally a back protector, and make sure the bike fits her rather than one she'll grow into. Kids who learn skills early tend to ride safer than adults who teach themselves.
quick: how fast should i ascend

No faster than 9 meters (30 feet) per minute, and slower is better. Go about as slow as your smallest bubbles or slower, and keep an eye on your computer's ascent alarm. Finish with a 3 minute safety stop at 5 meters on every dive.
What's the deal with foot entrapment?

Foot entrapment happens when someone stands in fast water and their foot wedges between rocks, then the current pushes them under. The fix is prevention: never try to stand in moving water above knee depth, and swim in the defensive position on your back with feet up and downstream. Swiftwater rescue training teaches techniques for freeing someone if it ever happens.
What gas do cave divers use for deep dives?

For deeper cave dives, divers often use trimix, a blend of oxygen, helium and nitrogen, which reduces narcosis and oxygen toxicity risk compared to air at depth. Deco gases such as high-oxygen nitrox or pure oxygen are staged for the shallower stops. Each of these needs separate technical training on top of cave certification, so learn the gas side properly before going deep.
Wetsuit or no wetsuit for warm tropical water?

Even in warm water, a thin wetsuit, around 1.5 to 3 mm, is a good idea. Staying warm keeps you relaxed and helps your breath-hold. It also protects you from sun, stings and scrapes. If you skip it, just remember you'll need to adjust your weighting.
Can I take an ice bath right after finishing a hot 100K?

If you're overheating or showing signs of heat illness, rapid cold-water immersion is exactly the right treatment, ideally with medical staff there. If you're just tired and sore, a cool shower and getting into shade with fluids and food is plenty. Have someone with you either way, because people can faint after a long hot effort.
My 16 year old son keeps talking about free soloing after getting into climbing. I'm terrified. What do I do?

Take it seriously but don't ban climbing outright, because that often pushes teens toward doing it secretly and badly. Get him into a proper climbing gym team or youth program where coaches he respects can talk honestly about risk and channel his ambition into competition, bouldering, or lead climbing. Ask him calmly what draws him to it, since it's often the mental challenge he's after, and roped climbing offers plenty of that. Make it clear that ropeless climbing is off the table while he lives with you, and give him plenty of support for everything else.
My buddy wants to build a kicker on a closed run at night. Seems sick, any tips?

Skip the closed run at night, because grooming equipment and winch cables run after hours, and people have been killed by them. You'd also lose your pass if patrol catches you. If you want to build features, ask about a resort that allows it, or build one in daylight on legal terrain with a good landing slope.
Thinking about cave diving. I'm advanced open water with 80 dives. Where do I start?

Eighty dives is a solid base, but caves are a whole different sport, so start with a Cavern course, then move on to Intro to Cave and Full Cave with a dedicated cave instructor, ideally in Florida or Mexico. Most untrained cave fatalities happen to experienced open-water divers, so don't go past the daylight zone without that training. Work on rock-solid buoyancy and frog-kick trim now, because you'll need them on day one.
Can I use my regular hiking boots with strap on crampons for WI3?

For WI3 you really want stiff, insulated mountaineering boots with automatic or semi-auto crampons, because floppy hiking boots let the crampon twist and pop off on steep ice. Strap crampons on soft boots are fine for glacier walking but not for front-pointing vertical sections where your feet hold your weight. Rent proper boots and crampons from a guide shop for your first outings, it makes a huge difference to both safety and how tiring it feels.
We're travelling in Croatia and found a spot locals jump from but there's no signage. How do I assess it?

Watch the locals jump a few times and note exactly where they take off and where they land, since the safe line is often narrower than it looks. Then swim the landing zone with goggles to check depth and look for rocks, and ask someone about currents and swell, which can change the depth and push you toward the cliff. Also make sure you know how you'll climb out before you go up.
how do pros prepare before a downhill race?

Pro downhill racers walk or ride the course in practice runs to learn every turn and bump, and they check their gear and board setup carefully. They also warm up their bodies and practice their braking and slides. Mental preparation helps them stay focused and relaxed at high speeds.
rappelling without a backup knot on the ends, is that actually a big deal

Yes, rappelling off the end of the rope is one of the most common causes of serious climbing accidents, including among experienced climbers. Tie stopper knots in both ends unless there's a specific reason not to, such as rappelling into moving water or high winds, and in those cases manage the ends deliberately. Pair the stopper knots with a friction-hitch backup like an autoblock. It takes thirty seconds.
Is a 450 too much for a first bike? I'm 6'2 and 210 lbs, used to ride street bikes

Even at your size, a 450 is usually too much for a first dirt bike, because the power arrives fast and is hard to control on loose ground, and street experience doesn't transfer as much as people expect. A 250F, or a 350 if you want a bit more grunt, will help you learn throttle control and body position much faster, and you'll actually ride better. Many riders who start on 450s end up scared or injured and quit. If you still want to move up later, you'll be a much better rider when you do.
Where can I learn street luge?

Look for local downhill skate or street luge groups on social media or forums, since many organize beginner sessions on safe hills. Some skate parks or events host luge clinics too. Learning with experienced riders is the best way to get proper technique and safety tips.
I've got patellar tendinitis from skiing moguls. My coach says ski through it. Thoughts?

Tendons respond badly to being ignored but do well with smart loading. Skiing moguls through it at full intensity tends to turn a manageable tendinopathy into a chronic one. A physio-guided program, often built around isometric and slow heavy squats, can calm it down while you keep skiing groomers at a lower intensity. Back off the bumps until the pain during and after skiing stays low, around 3/10 or under, and doesn't get worse the next day.
Can I fly home the same afternoon after my last dive? Flight's at 4pm and I finish diving around 11.

That's cutting it too close. The standard guideline is a minimum 12 hours after a single no-decompression dive and 18 hours after multiple dives or multiple days of diving, because the lower cabin pressure can trigger decompression sickness from nitrogen still in your tissues. If you can't move the flight, skip that last morning dive and spend the time snorkeling instead.
ugh my goggles keep fogging and I can't see the buoys. help

Rub a drop of baby shampoo or a proper anti-fog spray on the inside of the lenses, rinse lightly, and don't touch the inside with your fingers afterwards. Tinted or mirrored goggles help a lot on bright days, and keep a spare pair in your kit. If they fog mid-swim, stop, tread water and give them a quick rinse, because swimming blind toward a buoy is how people drift off course.
Just did my first solo of a 5.5 and felt amazing. How fast can I progress harder?

I'm glad you're okay, but slow down here, because that amazing feeling is exactly what leads people to push grades too fast. Experienced soloists usually stay far below their roped limit and add difficulty over years, not weeks. Focus your progression on roped climbing, where getting stronger is safe. Ask yourself honestly whether you need to solo at all, since the high comes back on hard roped climbs too.
quick q - can I use my recreational single tank setup in a cavern dive?

Many cavern courses do allow a single tank, as long as you have a long hose or redundant regulator setup, a backup light and good trim. Beyond the cavern zone you'll need redundant gas, usually doubles or sidemount. Check with your instructor or the dive operator before you go, since requirements vary.
My 14yo son has shin pain from cross country but insists on racing regionals. Should I let him?

Get it checked by a doctor or sports physio before regionals, because in teenage runners shin pain can be a stress reaction that turns into a stress fracture if he keeps racing on it. A quick test is pain in one specific spot on the bone, pain while walking, or pain at night, all of which are red flags and mean he shouldn't race. If it turns out to be simple shin splints, he may be cleared with reduced training around the event. Getting a professional opinion also takes the argument off your shoulders.
I'm moving to Hawaii. How do I get into big wave surfing there respectfully?

Start by surfing smaller local spots, showing respect in the lineup, and getting to know the community before you head to heavier breaks. Locals care about humility and safety, so take a water-safety course and connect with established crews. Respect patience and the pecking order, and acceptance comes with time.
What altitude should I pull at in a wingsuit?

Most dropzones require wingsuit pilots to open no lower than about 4,000 to 5,000 feet, which is higher than typical skydiving pull altitudes. You need extra time to collapse the wings, deploy cleanly and handle any malfunction while your arms are less free. Follow your dropzone's specific rules, and use an audible altimeter so you're never relying on memory.
My 9 year old wants to start bouldering. Is that too young? I'm nervous about falls.

Nine is a great age to start, and lots of gyms run kids' bouldering sessions with coaches who teach falling technique before anything else. The main thing is teaching her to land on her feet, roll back onto her bottom and back, and never put her arms out to catch herself. Have her stay on the lower problems at first and climb down rather than jump from the top. Keep the mat under her clear of other kids and bags.
rain all night, bike park open. go or skip?

You can go, but adjust. Wet roots and rocks get slick, so slow down, brake more gently, and avoid sketchy features until you see how things ride. Mud tires help a lot. If the trails are badly torn up or you're not comfortable, a dry-day trip is fine.
climbing gym or outdoor boulder for first time? going alone

Go to the gym. You'll get an orientation, staff nearby, padded floors, and graded problems to learn on. Bouldering alone outdoors as a beginner means no spotter and no help if you sprain an ankle far from the car.
first tandem jump next week and honestly i'm terrified. is it normal to want to back out?

Completely normal, and most people who jump feel exactly the same way the night before. Tandem skydiving is very safe because your instructor has done this hundreds or thousands of times and handles the deployment and landing. Get a good night's sleep, eat a light breakfast, and tell your instructor you're nervous, because they're great at talking people through it. If you truly decide on the day that you don't want to go, that's okay too, and most dropzones will let you reschedule.
Is it worth paying for a motocross coach or can I just watch YouTube

YouTube is great for learning the basics, but a coach can see what you're doing wrong in person, which is much harder to figure out alone. Even one or two sessions can fix bad habits before they get ingrained and speed up your progress. Many riders combine both, taking lessons and using videos to reinforce what they learn.
My daughter (9) keeps trying jumps off the side of the run that her friends built. Is that ok?

I'd steer her toward the official terrain park instead. Homemade side jumps are often badly shaped, with steep lips or flat landings, and sit where other riders aren't expecting someone to launch out. Most resorts have a beginner or kids' park with small features made for learning. A kids' freestyle lesson would give her the thrill with a lot less risk.
wanna try deep water soloing in thailand, ever done that? how safe

Deep water soloing in Tonsai and Railay is a classic, and it's reasonably safe if you respect it. Go with a local guide outfit that knows the tides and water depth, because entering wrong or landing in water that is too shallow is the main hazard. Climb only as high as you're comfortable falling from, aim to land feet first with your body vertical and arms tucked, and be a confident swimmer. Avoid flat landings from high up, which hit like concrete.
ok so theres this railing over a stairwell, like 3 floors down. balancing on it would be sick for a vid. thoughts?

Don't do that one. A single slip over a three-story drop isn't a sprain, it can kill you, and even pros with years of rail balancing don't treat filming as a reason to take that risk. Practice the exact same balance on a rail at knee height, where a slip just means stepping down, and you'll get a clean shot without betting your life on it.
Motocross, broke my collarbone 3 weeks ago, no surgery. Bone feels solid-ish. Back on the bike next week?

Three weeks is too early. A collarbone typically needs at least six to eight weeks to be strong enough, and motocross crashes load it in exactly the way that broke it. Feeling solid-ish isn't the same as healed. Get a follow-up X-ray and clearance before riding. A re-break or nonunion could put you out much longer.
Is it worth taking skate lessons or just watch youtube

YouTube is great for specific tricks, but a few lessons early on are really worth it, especially for learning to fall correctly, stand properly, and drop in. A coach catches small mistakes in real time that you'd never spot in yourself and that can take months to unlearn later. A handful of lessons followed by self-practice with videos is a smart, budget-friendly combo.
Weather looks gusty, about 15 to 20 mph at the exit. Friends still want to jump the cliff. Thoughts?

Gusty 15 to 20 mph is a good reason to stand down, especially at a cliff where rotors and turbulence near the wall can collapse or turn your canopy. Gusts are worse than steady wind because they change your heading and landing approach without warning. Skip this one. The cliff will be there on a calm morning, and plenty of experienced jumpers have died ignoring exactly these conditions.
I want to learn tricks but I'm on a budget, should I skip lessons and just watch YouTube?

YouTube is great for understanding what a trick should look like, but it can't spot bad habits like leaning back or opening your shoulders too early, and those habits lead to injuries. If money's tight, even one or two group park lessons are worth it to get your fundamentals checked, then use videos to keep practicing. Many resorts have cheaper group sessions or early-season deals too.
my 12 yo wants to start whitewater kayaking. too young?

Twelve is a great age to start, and lots of kids pick it up faster than adults because they're flexible and fearless. Get them into a proper youth course with a certified instructor, where they'll learn wet exits, swimming in current and basic strokes on flat and gentle moving water first. Make sure they have a kid-sized boat, a well-fitted PFD and a helmet rather than borrowed adult gear. Plenty of clubs run junior programs, and those are a fantastic way to build skills with peers.
can i skip the leash on huge days so i dont get dragged under by my board

Most big-wave surfers keep a heavy-duty leash on, because losing your board means a long swim in dangerous water with nothing to float on. Getting dragged by the board happens, but that's why many people use quick-release leashes, which let you choose to detach. Practice using the release until you can do it by feel underwater.
what's the safest way to try a tail press on a box

Choose a low, flat beginner box and ride onto it with your board flat and your weight centered. Once you're stable on it, gently shift your weight onto your back foot to lift the nose, keeping your shoulders lined up with the box and your knees soft. Don't press too hard at first, because leaning back too far can shoot your board out. Practice the tail press on flat snow before taking it onto the box.
We're snowmobiling into a zone to ski. Any extra avalanche stuff to think about?

Sleds let you cover a lot more terrain quickly, which means you can end up in more avalanche-prone areas than you'd realize, and they're heavy triggers on slopes. Everyone still needs a beacon, shovel and probe on their body, not stashed on the sled, and never have more than one person on a slope at a time. A sled-specific avalanche course is worth it because rescue and terrain dynamics differ from human-powered touring.
I'm 19, been surfing 3 years, mostly head-high beach breaks. Swell is forecast at 20 feet this weekend at the local reef. Can I just paddle out and see how it goes?

Don't make a 20-foot reef your first step up from head-high beach breaks, because the jump in hold-down time, current and consequences is enormous. Spend this swell watching from the cliff or channel, studying where the sets break and how the experienced crew positions themselves. Build up through 8 to 12 foot days first, and do a breath-hold and water safety course before you even think about the big ones.
Thinking of riding the closed trail since it looks fine and nobody's around. Quick lap, no harm?

Skip it. Trails get closed for reasons you can't always see, like washed-out sections, machinery, or a broken feature. If you crash there, patrol isn't looking for you, so help could take a long time to arrive. You can also lose your pass. Plenty of open trails are just as fun.
I'm pregnant (first trimester), can I still do the tandem I booked?

I'd postpone it and talk to your doctor first, because most operators won't fly pregnant passengers anyway. The main concerns are the harness pressure and the impact risk on landings, which can occasionally be firm. It's not worth the risk when you can reschedule for after. Many operators will happily move your booking.
Do I really need a reserve parachute? It's heavy and I only fly small ridge sites.

Yes, carry one every time. Collapses and mid-air collisions can happen even on gentle ridges, and low-altitude ridge soaring next to terrain leaves you very little time to recover. Modern lightweight reserves and harness containers have made the weight penalty small. Get it repacked every six to twelve months, and practice the throw so your hand knows where it is.
My 9 year old wants to start motocross. What bike should we get him?

For most 9 year olds a 65cc two-stroke or a small four-stroke like a CRF110 or KLX110 is the sweet spot, but fit matters more than age, so he should be able to touch the ground with the balls of both feet while seated. If he's brand new to riding, an automatic or semi-automatic 110 lets him learn throttle and braking before adding a clutch. Budget for a proper helmet, boots, goggles, gloves and a chest protector alongside the bike, and look for a local youth training day so he picks up good habits from the start.
Is it actually worth buying a beacon if I'm only skinning up groomed resort runs before the lifts open?

If you're staying on groomed, open runs inside resort boundaries, a beacon isn't really necessary, since that terrain is avalanche-controlled. What matters more for uphill travel is following the resort's uphill policy, wearing a headlamp and something reflective, and staying well clear of grooming machines and winch cats, which are the real hazard at that hour. Hold off on the beacon until you're ready to step past the ropes, and buy it along with a shovel, probe and an avalanche course.
best age to start base? i'm 52 and fit

There's no upper age limit, and plenty of people start in their 40s and 50s. At 52, focus on your landings, since bad landings cause many BASE injuries and recovery takes longer as you age. Get your skydiving numbers up with lots of accuracy work, keep your joints and core strong, and choose a course that's honest with you about your readiness.
Just did my first jump and now my eyes look kind of bloodshot and I have a headache. Normal?

Small burst blood vessels in the whites of the eyes are fairly common after jumping head-first, and they usually fade within a week or two. A mild headache can also come from adrenaline and the pressure change. Get checked by a doctor promptly if you notice blurry vision, floaters, flashes of light, a severe or worsening headache, or any neck pain, because those can point to something more serious.
I'm 52 and want to try cliff jumping for the first time on holiday. Am I too old?

Not at all, plenty of people start later, but go in with a modest goal. Begin with low jumps of 2 to 4 meters, and if you have any back, neck, heart or joint issues, check with your doctor first, since the landing jars the spine. A guided coasteering trip is a great way to try it with an instructor who knows the safe spots.
So the rule is climb high sleep low? How much per day?

That's the core idea, and the common guideline is that above about 3,000 m you shouldn't raise your sleeping altitude by more than 300 to 500 m per night. Add a rest day every three to four days, or after every 1,000 m of gain. Daytime climbs higher than where you'll sleep help you adjust, as long as you come back down for the night.
what's the best weather for a beginner to fly

Smooth, light and steady wind straight up the slope, usually around 10 to 15 km/h, with no gusts or strong thermals. Early mornings and late afternoons tend to be calmest. Avoid days with building cumulus, strong wind forecasts or approaching fronts. Your instructor will help you learn to read conditions, which is honestly one of the most important skills in the sport.
Quick q: can I fly with a hangover? Nothing crazy, just tired
Skip it. Even a mild hangover slows your reactions and decision making, and paragliding punishes both. Fly when you're sharp, because the mountain will still be there tomorrow.
im scared of heights but want to do it to get over it. dumb idea?

Not dumb, and lots of people do it for exactly that reason. Bungee can be a good way to face that fear because it's over quickly and the crew handles the technical part. Start with a smaller jump in the 40 to 50 m range rather than a monster bridge, and don't look down too long before you go.
My son just told me he wants to start wingsuiting. I'm terrified. Is it as insane as it looks on YouTube?

Most YouTube clips are wingsuit BASE or proximity flying, and that's a very different risk level from skydiving with a wingsuit. Learning to wingsuit from a plane, with proper prerequisites and a certified first flight course, is far more controlled. It's still a serious sport. The most helpful thing you can do is ask him about his jump numbers, his instructor and his plans, and encourage him to stay on the structured path rather than rush.
how do i deal with a frontal collapse? asking for real, had one last week and froze

Freezing the first time is really common, and it's a sign you'd benefit a lot from an SIV course where you practise collapses safely over water. In general, a frontal on a beginner wing often recovers on its own once you stop overreacting. A light, symmetric brake input as the wing reinflates can help, but avoid big stabs that risk a stall. Talk it through with your instructor, since they can tailor advice to your wing and how it happened.
Thinking of taking ibuprofen before my hot 100K so my legs hurt less. good idea?

Skip it, because NSAIDs during hot ultras raise the risk of acute kidney injury when you're already dehydrated and your muscles are breaking down. They also contribute to hyponatremia. If you really need something, acetaminophen in normal doses is safer during the race. Heat-adapting and pacing smart will do more for your legs than any pill.
Doing Mera Peak, guide wants rest days, I want to save time and skip them. I feel fine.

Feeling fine on day four doesn't tell you how you'll feel at 6,476 m, and acclimatization often lags behind how good you feel. Mera's rapid climb out of Lukla is notorious for causing altitude sickness, which is exactly why guides build in those days. Keep them, use them for short hikes higher, and you'll have a much better summit day.
Bought a used cam set online. How can I tell if they're safe?

Inspect each cam for frayed or kinked cables, bent or worn lobes, and slings that are faded, stiff or worn, and check that the trigger and springs return smoothly and the lobes stay symmetric. Look up the model and age, since slings on older cams often need replacing. Some manufacturers will reinspect or reseal cams, and a local guide or shop can give them a look if you're unsure. Retire anything with cable damage or a cracked component.
Cold water, any tips?

Cold water is genuinely dangerous because the gasp reflex can make you inhale water and your muscles weaken fast. Get in gradually from the shore first to acclimate, keep sessions short, and consider a wetsuit or neoprene shorts and shoes. If the water's below about 15°C, keep jumps low and make sure your exit is quick and easy.
Is it okay to cross under a big avalanche path quickly if I'm careful?

Moving quickly does reduce your exposure time, but it doesn't make the crossing safe, since slides can release naturally or be triggered by someone above you. If you have to cross, go one at a time, keep the others watching from safe ground, and don't stop in the runout. When the danger is elevated, choose a route that avoids that path altogether.
Heat rash and chafing during hot ultras, ugh. Prevention?

Use an anti-chafe balm generously on thighs, armpits, the sports bra line and anywhere your pack rubs, and reapply midrace. Wear seamless, quick-drying fabrics and swap into dry socks and shorts at drop bags if you can. For heat rash, loose clothing and cooling the skin with water help, and it usually settles once you cool down.
Is it fine to freedive alone if I stay shallow, like 5 meters?

No. Shallow water blackout happens most often in the last few meters of ascent and at shallow depths, and you get no warning before you lose consciousness. Depth doesn't make solo diving safe. Always dive with a trained buddy who watches you from the surface through your whole dive and for at least 30 seconds after you surface. One up, one down is the rule, even in a pool.
my boyfriend says he wants to free solo a 5.8 at our local crag this weekend. he's been climbing 8 months. should i be worried

Yes, it's reasonable to be worried. Eight months is very early, and 5.8 doesn't feel easy when there's no rope. The usual killers on easy terrain are a loose hold, a wet patch or a sudden pump, not a hard move. If you can, encourage him to lead that route a bunch of times on rope, or channel the urge into highball bouldering with plenty of pads and spotters, and be honest that the plan scares you.
I'm 15, climbing on a youth team. My middle finger knuckle has hurt for weeks and my coach says to push through. Should I?

Don't push through this one. In teen climbers, ongoing pain at the middle finger joint can be a growth plate stress fracture, which is common in young climbers and can cause permanent problems if you keep crimping on it. Tell your parents and get an X-ray from a doctor who knows sports injuries. Cut out crimping and hard board climbing until it's sorted. Missing a few weeks now is a tiny price compared with a damaged finger for life.
how steep does a slope need to be to avalanche

Most slab avalanches release on slopes between 30 and 45 degrees, and the 35 to 40 degree range is the sweet spot for trouble. Slopes under 30 degrees rarely release, but you can still get caught if you're on flat ground beneath or connected to steeper terrain above. Carry an inclinometer or use a phone app, because people routinely misjudge angle by several degrees.
My friend says we don't need to do partner checks because we're both experienced. Thoughts?

Experience is exactly why people get complacent and skip them, and many of the worst climbing accidents involve experienced climbers with an unfinished knot or a misthreaded belay device. A partner check takes about fifteen seconds: check the harness buckles, the tie-in knot through both tie-in points, the belay device and locked carabiner, and the knot in the end of the rope. Make it a habit that neither of you ever questions.
Got about 40 jumps. Thinking of downsizing from a 190 to a 150. Good idea?

That's a big jump for 40 jumps, and canopy downsizing is where a lot of serious injuries come from. Most coaches recommend stepping down gradually, maybe one size at a time, and only once you can consistently land accurately, do flat turns and handle rear-riser landings on your current canopy. Take a canopy course and talk to your S&TA or a canopy coach about your wing loading before you buy anything.
how to do a tail press

Shift your weight back over your rear foot until the nose lifts, keeping your back leg bent and your front leg a bit straighter. Hold your arms out for balance and keep your eyes looking forward. Practice on flat, gentle terrain first, and don't lean back so far that the board shoots out from under you.
do i really need a helmet for just rails? theyre low to the ground

Yes, wear one. Rail falls are notorious for slamming your head on the metal edge or catching an edge and whipping backward onto hard snow, and a low height doesn't help you there. A helmet costs far less than a concussion and you'll forget you're wearing it after a few runs.
I just broke my wrist skating, how soon can I get back on the board?

That really depends on the type of break and how it heals, so your doctor or orthopedist should give you the green light, usually after follow-up X-rays. Rushing back risks a re-break or a long-term problem, especially since a fall puts your hands right back in the line of fire. When you do return, wear wrist guards or slide gloves with built-in support and ease back in on mellow hills.
bearings making grinding noise

That usually means dirt got inside or they've dried out. Pop the shields off, soak the bearings in isopropyl alcohol or citrus degreaser, spin them dry, and add a drop or two of skate-specific lubricant rather than WD-40, which strips oil and attracts grit. If they still grind after cleaning, they're probably damaged, and a decent set costs about as much as a pizza.
Any advice for riding wet roots? Total beginner and the forest is always damp here.

Cross wet roots as square to them as you can and stay off the brakes while you're actually on them. Do your braking before the root section, then roll over loose and light. Lower tire pressure and a softer-compound tire make a huge difference. Ride a little slower than feels necessary until you learn how much grip there really is.
do i need a helmet in the gym

Helmets aren't usual in indoor gyms because rockfall isn't an issue there, and they're mostly worth it for kids or anyone learning to lead who might flip upside down. Outdoors is a different story: wear one for climbing and belaying at the crag, since falling rock and dropped gear are common hazards there.
how do i stop going over the bars on steep rolls

Drop your heels, bend your elbows and knees, and shift your hips back so your weight sits over the rear wheel rather than your hands. Lower your saddle all the way or use a dropper so it isn't pushing you forward. Brake mostly before the roll and feather both brakes on it instead of grabbing the front. Practice on a short, mellow roll until it feels automatic, then work up to steeper ones.
What altitude should I deploy at on a wingsuit skydive?

Most drop zones want wingsuiters to wave off and deploy around 4,000 to 5,000 feet, which is higher than a typical solo skydive. You need margin for a clean pitch, possible line twists, and getting into your flight pattern away from other traffic. Ask your local drop zone what their rules are and stick to them, especially early on.
I'm 16, my parents don't know I downhill, how do I hide the scrapes

Honestly, the better move is telling them, because if you get hurt on a hill they'll need to know fast, and hiding it makes that harder. You can make it easier by showing them your gear, the hills you ride, and the crew you skate with, which shows you're taking it seriously. Scrapes also mean you need more protection, like full pads and slide gloves. Being upfront often gets you more freedom, not less.
how long should a climbing rope last

With occasional weekend use a dynamic rope usually lasts about three to five years, while heavy daily use can wear one out within a year. The age matters less than its condition: retire it if you see core showing through the sheath, flat or mushy sections, glazing from a hard fall, or any contact with chemicals like battery acid. Most manufacturers also give a maximum lifespan of around ten years even for a rope that has never been used. When in doubt, cut it up for gear slings and buy a new one.
I've done 80 skydives and a buddy says he can teach me BASE this weekend. He's done like 50 BASE jumps.

I'd pass on that. Eighty skydives is well short of where you should be, and a jumper with 50 BASE jumps isn't experienced enough to teach, however good his intentions. Keep building skydives and canopy skills, then book a real first jump course with a professional instructor. Your buddy can still be part of your BASE life later, once you've been trained properly.
quickest way to get faster on downhill?

Work on cornering and line choice, which make the biggest difference. Look ahead, brake before turns, and carry speed out of corners rather than into them. Ride a few runs repeatedly to learn the lines, and follow faster riders at a safe distance. A skills clinic gets you there faster than just pushing speed.
Do I need lessons for downhill skateboarding or can I just watch youtube

YouTube is great for understanding technique, but you can't see your own mistakes, and bad habits in downhill tend to show up at speed. Even a few sessions with an experienced local rider or a downhill camp will speed up your progress and help you avoid the common crash patterns. Pair video learning with real coaching or a crew that will give you honest feedback.
what psi should my tires be for mud

Many riders run around 12 to 13 psi for most dirt, and some drop a pound or so in mud to get a bit more grip. Be careful going too low, because you risk pinch flats and rim damage, especially without rim locks. Check your tire manufacturer's recommendations, and check pressure cold before you ride. In real mud, fresh tires with good knobs matter more than chasing pressure.
Is a combat roll really that different from rolling in a pool?

Very different. In a pool you're calm, warm and set up, while in a rapid you're disoriented, getting tossed around, and probably not in your ideal starting position. That's why many people with a perfect pool roll swim on their first real flip. Bridge the gap by practising rolls in moving water at an easy spot with friends standing by, practising from awkward positions and with your eyes closed, and staying tucked and patient until you're set up. It takes repetition before it holds up when you're stressed.
Is it smart to film tricks with a gopro on a chest mount?

Chest mounts are generally fine and actually safer than helmet mounts for crashes, since helmet cameras can snag or add rotational force to your head. Make sure the mount is tight and doesn't dig into your ribs if you fall forward. Just don't let filming push you into a trick you wouldn't try otherwise.
How do I know the jump master isn't messing up? I read about that one accident

You're right that human error causes most bungee accidents, so it's worth watching. A good team weighs you, double-checks your weight against the cord, and has a second person verify every connection out loud before you jump. Don't hesitate to ask them to walk you through the checks. If they get irritated by that, or skip steps when they're busy, take that as your cue to leave.
ice climbing next to a lake, it's thick enough to walk out to the base yeah?

Don't assume it is, because ice near waterfalls and inlets is often much thinner thanks to moving water and spray. Clear ice is generally strongest, and you want at least 10 cm (4 inches) of solid clear ice for walking, but check it with an axe or auger as you go and stay away from areas near flowing water. If there's a shoreline approach to the base, take it even if it's longer. Getting soaked or falling through in winter is far more dangerous than any climbing move.
what size board should my 6 year old get

For most 6-year-olds a deck around 7.0 to 7.5 inches wide works well, since it's easier for small feet to control. Get a complete from a real skate shop rather than a toy-store board, because cheap ones have bad bearings and wheels that stop dead on small pebbles. Pair it with a properly fitted helmet and pads. Ask the shop staff to check the fit while your kid stands on it.
how cold is it really at everest summit

On a typical May summit day it's usually around minus 25 to minus 35 Celsius, and wind chill can push the feel well below minus 50. Frostbite on exposed skin can happen in minutes, which is why climbers use 8,000 meter down suits, triple boots and heavy mitts instead of gloves.
