The low oxygen makes it worse, since your body cuts blood flow to fingers and toes, so keeping hydrated, eating and using supplemental oxygen helps you stay warm as well as move.
I'm 19 and just watched Free Solo. How long until I could realistically start soloing stuff?

Honestly, years, and that's the right timeline. Alex Honnold had roughly a decade of near-daily roped climbing before his notable solos, and he rehearsed Freerider on rope for two years before going ropeless. For now, put that energy into getting really good on lead with a rope, because solid technique and mileage are what actually make you a strong climber. Free solo is a choice very few experienced climbers make, and there's no point at which it stops being deadly if something goes wrong.
what board length for mavericks

Most surfers paddling Mavericks ride guns somewhere between about 9'6" and 11', depending on their weight and the size of the day. More length gives you the paddle speed to get in early on those steep, ledgy drops. A shaper who knows the break can dial it in for you. If you're asking this for the first time, spend a few seasons riding bigger days elsewhere before Mavericks becomes a realistic goal.
is it safe to touch stuff underwater like turtles or coral

Keep your hands to yourself. Coral is a living animal that dies when touched, and some species sting or cut, which can leave nasty infections. Touching turtles stresses them and is illegal in many places. Good buoyancy control is the real skill here, and staying a little off the reef makes you a better diver.
Tore a callus open, blood everywhere lol. Keep going?

Call it for the day. Climbing on a flapper gets the hold bloody and makes the tear worse. Clean it, trim the loose skin with nail clippers, and keep it covered until it heals. Afterward, file your calluses down regularly so they don't catch and rip again.
What do I do if my wing collapses mid-flight?

For small asymmetric collapses, keep your weight away from the collapsed side and use opposite brake to keep flying straight, then let it reopen or pump the collapsed side. Don't overreact on the brakes, since that can cause a stall. If you're spinning or losing control near the ground, throw your reserve without hesitating. Do an SIV course to actually practice this safely.
my husband wants to start motocross at 52. am I right to be scared?

Some worry makes sense, but plenty of people start in their 50s and ride safely for years, mostly by taking it slow and staying in control. A few things help a lot: proper gear including a quality helmet, boots, knee braces and a chest protector, a beginner-friendly bike like a 250F or trail bike rather than a 450, and a few lessons with a coach instead of learning by copying the fast kids. Getting fit beforehand also matters, since tired riders are the ones who crash.
My son is 19 and wants to climb Kilimanjaro on the 5-day Marangu route. Should I be worried?

Your instinct is reasonable, because the five-day itinerary is one of the main reasons Kilimanjaro has such a high rate of altitude sickness and failed summits. It goes from the gate to 5,895 meters too fast for a lot of bodies, no matter how fit or young the climber is. Encourage him to book a seven- or eight-day option like the Lemosho or Machame route, which costs a bit more but greatly improves both his safety and his chances of reaching the top. Also make sure he picks a reputable operator whose guides carry oxygen and a pulse oximeter.
My 13 year old wants to hit the big jumps in the terrain park after one season. He's pretty good on blues. Should I let him?

Not yet. Big park jumps are a different skill from carving blues, and kids who go straight to them tend to overshoot the landing or come up short on the knuckle. Have him progress through the small and medium features first, and a park-specific lesson or camp is well worth it at his age. Make sure he's wearing a helmet, and that he can land straight airs and 180s cleanly on smaller jumps before sizing up.
Had heat exhaustion last year. Can I race the same hot event again?

Probably, but treat last year as a warning to rework your plan, not just to try again harder. Get checked by a doctor first, especially if it was severe or you needed IV fluids, since a past heat illness can raise your risk. Do a proper heat-acclimation block, pace far more conservatively and lean hard on ice cooling.
Water's 45 degrees but air is 70, can I just wear shorts?

No. The water temperature is what matters, and at 45°F a swim can trigger cold shock and lose you strength within minutes. Wear at least a thick wetsuit, ideally a drysuit, with insulating layers, plus neoprene booties and a skull cap. You'll probably end up in the water at some point, so dress for that rather than for sitting in the boat.
My son just told me he wants to start cave diving and I'm honestly terrified. Is it as deadly as I think?

It has a frightening reputation, but most deaths involve people with no cave training who ignore basic rules like running a continuous guideline, keeping enough gas in reserve and staying within their depth limits. Properly trained cave divers who stick to those rules have a much better safety record. Encourage him to train with a reputable agency like NSS-CDS, NACD, GUE or TDI, and to progress slowly. Asking him about his gas plan and his instructor is a good way to stay involved without trying to talk him out of it.
How long does it take to get a paragliding license?

A basic licence, like a P2 in the US or a club pilot rating elsewhere, usually takes about 8 to 15 days of flying-suitable weather, which in practice can stretch over a few weeks or months. Intensive courses in reliable-weather destinations can get you there in one or two weeks. Expect around 25 to 40 flights plus a theory exam.
I've surfed overhead waves a few times. Can I just paddle out at Mavericks on a medium day to see what it's like?

Even a medium day at Mavericks has cold water, heavy rocks, strong currents, and waves that break with power far beyond normal overhead surf, so going out just to see is a bad way to learn. Start by watching sessions from the cliff and talking to locals, then build experience at heavier spots like Ocean Beach on solid days. When you do eventually paddle out, go with experienced surfers who know the lineup and have water patrol around.
what should I wear

Wear comfortable, fitted clothes and closed shoes that strap or lace on securely, and empty your pockets. Skip skirts, dresses and loose jackets. Tie back long hair and leave jewelry and hats in a locker. Dress for the weather at the top, since platforms are often colder and windier.
i keep getting speed wobbles what do i do

Speed wobbles usually come from loose trucks, uneven weight or tense legs. Tighten your trucks a bit or use stiffer bushings, keep more weight on your front foot and relax your knees. Practice at slower speeds to build control, and if wobbles start, scrub speed gently with a footbrake or slide rather than fighting the board.
Is it okay to boulder outside without a crash pad if the problem is short?

Even short problems can produce nasty ankle sprains, broken wrists, or worse, because rocky, uneven landings are far less forgiving than gym mats. Bring at least one crash pad and a spotter whose job is to guide your fall onto the pad and protect your head and back. If you don't own a pad, many climbing shops rent them cheaply for the weekend.
Water temp's 9°C. I'm planning 45 mins in skins to toughen up. Good plan?

That's too long without proper adaptation. At 9°C even acclimatised cold swimmers often limit themselves to around 10 to 20 minutes, and without a wetsuit you could lose control of your hands and develop hypothermia before you realise it. Toughening up works by gradually building time over weeks, not by forcing one long swim. Start with a few minutes, stay close to shore with a buddy, and add time slowly as your body adapts.
Pinched a nerve? numbness in my hands after riding for an hour. normal?

Some arm pump is common, but numbness lasting after riding isn't something to just push through, so see a doctor if it persists or keeps returning. Commonly it's from gripping too tight or a poor bar and lever setup, so try loosening your grip, gripping with your legs instead, and adjusting your levers so your wrists stay straight. Some riders find relief with bar-end weights or different grips too.
my board feels loose at speed. should i tighten trucks all the way

Tightening helps, but don't crank them all the way, since too tight makes the board hard to turn and can actually cause you to lose control in corners. Tighten a bit at a time and test on a slow hill until it feels stable but still turns. Harder bushings are often a better fix than overtightening.
My daughter (9) wants to do parkour. Is it safe for kids that age?

It can be, and a kids' parkour class is a great way to build strength, coordination and confidence, often safer than many team sports. Look for a gym that runs age-specific classes with padded equipment, qualified coaches and low ratios, and ask how they teach progressions and falling. Kids that age should mostly be doing obstacle courses, balance work, rolls and low vaults rather than big drops or flips. Watch a class first so you can see how they manage safety.
honestly how dangerous is base

Very. It's one of the deadliest recreational activities, with a fatality rate many times higher than skydiving, and wingsuit BASE accounts for a big share of the deaths. Disciplined jumpers who stick to conservative objects, good weather and slow progression lower their risk a lot, but they can't remove it. Anyone who tells you it's safe if you're careful is underselling it.
is a back protector necessary

It isn't mandatory at most parks, but it's worthwhile for downhill, where falls onto rocks and roots at speed are common. A lightweight vest-style protector certified to EN 1621-2 gives solid spine coverage without much heat or bulk. If you ride steep, fast trails or jumps, treat it as standard kit along with your full-face helmet and knee pads.
My 22-year-old son just told me he's taking a BASE course next month. I'm terrified. What should I even ask him?

Ask him how many skydives he has, who is running the course, and whether he'll keep jumping with experienced mentors after it ends. A good answer sounds like 200+ skydives, an established first jump course with a known track record, and a plan to progress slowly at forgiving objects. Those three things separate careful jumpers from reckless ones far more than any single jump does. It's also fair to tell him you'd sleep better knowing he'll be jumping with people more experienced than he is, not chasing YouTube lines with friends.
How long until I can move up from a beginner suit?

Plan on 50 or so wingsuit jumps or more in a small suit, then step up to an intermediate suit with your coach's agreement. The key signs you're ready are clean, stable exits and openings, good navigation, and consistent flight skills in group flights. Moving up too soon is a common route to scary openings and spins.
Track day tomorrow, haven't changed oil in like 15 hours of riding. Will it be fine?

Change it tonight if you possibly can, since many four-stroke MX bikes call for oil changes every five to ten hours and the engine works hard under racing conditions. Cheap oil is far cheaper than a damaged engine, and it's a quick half-hour job with a new filter. While you're at it, check your air filter, chain tension, and that everything's tight.
18f trying to learn skating but im embarrassed at the skatepark around guys who are way better. tips?

Totally normal, and most skaters remember what it's like to be new, so they're more supportive than you'd think. Try going at quieter times like weekday mornings, or join a beginner meetup or girls' skate night if there's one near you. Learn the basic park etiquette of waiting your turn and not cutting people off, and you'll fit right in.
How do I know if it's heat exhaustion or heatstroke during a race??

With heat exhaustion you're usually still sweating heavily, weak, nauseous and dizzy, but you're thinking clearly. Heatstroke is marked by confusion, slurred speech, stumbling, irritability, or collapse, and the skin may be hot. The key sign is a change in mental state, and that is a medical emergency needing rapid cold-water immersion and help right away. If a runner near you seems 'off' mentally in the heat, get them to medics immediately.
screws are expensive. ok to buy used ones off marketplace?

Used screws can be fine, but only if you can inspect them closely, because bent tubes, dull or damaged teeth, and sticky hangers all matter a lot. Avoid any with dents, rust inside the tube or damaged threads, and favour sellers who can tell you their history. If the price seems too good or you can't check them in person, buying new from a shop is worth the extra money for something your life depends on.
can i street luge on a public road if theres no cars around

Even if a road looks empty, a car can appear around a blind corner in seconds, and at luge speeds you can't stop in time. Riding open public roads is also illegal in many areas. Stick to closed-course events, organized freerides or private roads where someone has secured the route and spotters are watching for traffic. Local downhill groups often know where and when those sessions happen.
what's the best beginner wingsuit

Look for a small, forgiving suit designed for first flights, like the Squirrel SWIFT, the Phoenix-Fly Shadow, or the Tony Suits Tracker-style beginner models. They're stable, easy to exit and easy to deploy from, which matters far more than glide performance when you're starting out. Your First Flight Course instructor will usually provide or recommend one sized for you, so get their input before you buy anything.
Can i skip scouting if my friend ran it last week?

Rivers change week to week, especially after rain, when new wood or shifting rocks can turn a clean line into a hazard. Your friend's description helps, but scout anything significant yourself or have someone you trust check it that day. Paddling blind is how people find strainers the hard way.
hit my head snowboarding this morning, felt dizzy for like 10 min but fine now. good to go back up after lunch?

No, call it for the day. Any dizziness after a head hit counts as a possible concussion, and a second impact before your brain has recovered can be far worse than the first. Get checked if you have a headache, nausea, confusion, light sensitivity or drowsiness, and go to the ER right away if any of those get worse. The usual return is a few days of rest, then easing back in step by step once you're symptom-free.
is it legal to luge on public roads

It depends heavily on where you are; some places ban skating or luge on certain roads, others have no specific rule, and police often treat it as unsafe use of the road anyway. Even where it's technically allowed, open roads mean cars, so the real answer for luge is closed courses and permitted events. Check your local laws and look up nearby clubs, which often know the legal spots and run sanctioned sessions. That keeps you out of tickets and out of traffic.
Thinking of taking ibuprofen before a hot 100k so my legs hurt less. Good idea?

Skip it. NSAIDs like ibuprofen during long, hot efforts are linked to kidney injury and may raise the risk of hyponatremia, especially when you're dehydrated. If you need pain relief, acetaminophen (paracetamol) is generally considered safer during races, at normal doses. Better yet, look at your pacing and training to address why your legs hurt.
What altitude should I deploy at with a wingsuit?

Most dropzones require wingsuit pilots to begin deployment no lower than 4,000 to 5,000 feet, which is higher than standard because you need time to stabilize, deploy, and unzip. Your coach and dropzone will set the exact number, so follow their rules. Leave yourself extra margin early on, since problems at opening are where wingsuiting gets dangerous.
Oxygen on Everest — cheating or necessary?

For almost everyone it's necessary, because without supplemental oxygen the summit has roughly a third of the oxygen available at sea level, and the risks of HACE, frostbite and bad decisions climb steeply. A tiny number of elite, highly acclimatized climbers summit without it, but they have years of 8,000 meter experience and still accept much higher risk. Whether it's cheating is a style debate, while survival is a separate question, so plan to climb with oxygen and a solid supply.
Is it worth flying a big suit early to get longer flights?

No, step up slowly. Big suits are harder to exit cleanly, slower to recover from instability and more demanding at deployment. That's why the usual advice is lots of jumps in a small beginner suit, then intermediate, before anything big. Skilled flying in a small suit beats wobbly flying in a big one, and coaches will tell you when you're ready.
can I do a backflip off a 10 meter cliff? I can do them off a 3m board

Flips from 10 meters are a big jump in difficulty, because you're in the air much longer and a slight over or under-rotation means hitting flat on your back or face at high speed. Work your way up gradually, landing the flip cleanly and consistently at 5 and then 7 meters first. If you're serious about it, a diving club with high platforms and a coach is the safest place to build that skill.
I'm 16 and my parents don't know I've been jumping my friend's bike. How do I keep it from them?

I'd honestly tell them instead. If you get hurt, you'll need them for the hospital and the insurance, and finding out after a crash is the worst way for them to learn. You could come to them with a plan: a proper helmet and gear, riding at a real track, maybe some lessons. That plan shows you're serious and makes a yes much more likely. Parents tend to respond better to a kid asking to do something safely than to finding out it's been happening behind their backs.
teen here (16), my parents won't let me go to the crag with my 17 yr old friends alone, they're being dramatic right?

Your parents aren't wrong to worry, because outdoor climbing involves anchor building and rope management that gyms never teach, and mistakes are unforgiving. You could suggest a compromise, such as a guided day, a youth club trip, or going with an experienced adult who can show everyone the systems. That route lets you climb outside soon and gives your parents a reason to trust you with more independence later.
found my old board from 15 yrs ago in the garage, can i just ride it?

Check it over first, because old parts fail in ways that throw you. Look for cracks or delamination in the deck, flat-spotted or hardened wheels, rusty or seized bearings, and make sure the bushings aren't cracked and the truck bolts are tight. Wheels and bushings harden with age, so they'll often grip badly, and replacing them plus the bearings costs little and makes a huge difference. If the deck is cracked or soft, retire it, and either way take it slow until you've got your legs back.
How long is the free fall usually?

On a typical 50 meter jump you get roughly two to three seconds of real free fall before the cord starts taking the load. The very high jumps, around 200 meters, can stretch that to five or six seconds. It feels much longer than it is, and the rebounds afterward add a lot more to the ride.
What's dry tooling and can I do it at home

Dry tooling means climbing rock or artificial holds with ice tools and crampons, and it's a great way to train and stay sharp off-season. Some gyms have dedicated dry-tool walls, and a few people build home setups with hard wooden or plastic holds. Don't hook tools on regular gym holds or your house, since that can damage the equipment and the tools can pop violently. Wear a helmet and eye protection, and use a proper belay or mats.
How do I get more pop on my ollies? Mine feel weak.

Pop comes from loading the tail, not just jumping. Shift your weight back as you go, bend your rear knee to flex the tail, then spring up and lift your front leg first, followed by your back leg. Tuck your knees up once you're airborne for extra height. Practice on flat ground or gentle slopes until the timing becomes automatic.
Haven't dived in 4 years. Can I just jump on a boat dive in Thailand next week?

Do a refresher first. Most shops offer a ReActivate or scuba review that takes a few hours in a pool or shallow water. After four years, setting up your gear, managing buoyancy and handling problems are all rusty, and a boat dive in current is a bad place to rediscover that. Many reputable operators will ask for one anyway, so book it ahead and enjoy the trip properly.
First wingsuit jump tomorrow. Nervous. Any tips?

Feeling nervous is normal and keeps you sharp. Focus on the basics from your briefing: a clean exit, staying symmetrical and relaxed, holding your heading, watching your altitude and deploying at your planned height. Don't worry about performance, because a calm, stable first flight with a good deployment is a great success. Get a good night's sleep and listen closely to your coach.
best way to not burn through air so fast? i'm always first back up

Slow everything down. Breathe slowly and deeply, get your weighting right so you're not constantly finning and adding air, and get into a horizontal trim so you glide instead of fighting the water. Keep your hands still and kick from your hips, and you'll see a big improvement as you get more relaxed with practice. Doing a buoyancy course speeds that up a lot.
I'm 58 with mild high blood pressure, controlled on meds. Considering Island Peak. Am I crazy?

Not crazy at all, since plenty of people in their late 50s and 60s climb Island Peak, but you should see your doctor first, ideally one familiar with altitude medicine. Blood pressure often rises at altitude, so ask whether your medication and dose suit the trip and whether you should bring a home monitor. Choose a longer itinerary that includes Everest Base Camp or a good acclimatization loop before the climb, and pick an operator whose guides are trained in altitude illness.
I'm 7 weeks pregnant and we booked a Red Sea dive trip before we found out. Can I still dive carefully?

Congratulations, but the standard advice is no diving at all while pregnant. There isn't good evidence that it's safe for the fetus, and bubble formation and decompression risk can't be ruled out. Snorkeling the Red Sea is spectacular, so you'll still have a great trip, and your partner can dive while you explore the reef from the surface.
what's the deal with two wave hold downs

A two-wave hold-down is when you get pushed down by one wave and the next wave hits before you can surface, leaving you under for two waves in a row. It's one of the most dangerous situations in big surf, and it's the main reason people train breath-holds, wear inflation vests and surf with water safety on skis. Staying calm, protecting your head and using your vest early are what get you through it.
can i ride my yz250 without a helmet just around the backyard lol its like 2 minutes

No, wear the helmet. A YZ250 two-stroke hits hard and fast, and most serious head injuries happen at low speed in familiar places, not on big jumps. A tip-over onto a fence post or hard-packed dirt is all it takes. Putting the helmet on takes twenty seconds, and that's a small price for those two minutes.
I fell while roped on easy terrain yesterday, foot just slipped. Makes me rethink my plan to solo. Overreacting?

Not at all, that's exactly the kind of signal worth listening to. Feet slip on easy terrain all the time, from a bit of grit, a damp patch or a moment of inattention, and on a rope that's a non-event. Without one, the same slip could kill you. Plenty of excellent climbers have reached the same conclusion and chosen to keep the rope.
Is it okay to drink a beer at Namche?

One beer in Namche probably won't hurt if you're feeling fine, but alcohol can worsen sleep quality and breathing at altitude and dehydrate you. It can also mask early symptoms of altitude sickness. Many trekkers wait until they're heading back down to celebrate. If you drink, keep it to one, drink plenty of water and skip it completely if you have a headache or poor appetite.
Wanna try free soloing a 5.6 I've done like 20 times on rope. Easy for me, no big deal right?

It is a big deal, because even an easy route you know well has hazards you can't control without a rope, like a broken hold, a slip on dirt or lichen, a wasp, or a sudden cramp. On rope those are non-events, and soloing turns them into fatal falls. The rope costs you almost nothing, so keep using it. If you want a similar feeling with a safety margin, go bouldering or try faster, more flowing climbs on toprope.
What do I put in my ice bandana? Just ice?

Yep, plain ice cubes or crushed ice wrapped around your neck works great, and refilling at every aid station is the move. Add ice to your hat and sports bra or shirt too, and dunk your buff in cold water when you can. Just don't let your neck go numb for hours at a time, so shift it around occasionally.
I keep going over the bars on drops, what am I doing wrong

You're likely leaning forward or letting the front wheel drop first, often by freezing up at the lip. Approach with enough speed, stay centered, and push the bike slightly forward as the front leaves the lip so both wheels land together or the rear lands first. Practice on small drops with good runouts until it's automatic, and consider a lesson, since a coach can pinpoint the fault in minutes.
Friend at mile 60 is slurring and stumbling but says he wants to keep going. He's always a bit out of it late in races. Let him go?

No, get him to medical now. Slurred speech and stumbling in the heat can signal heat stroke or severe hyponatremia, both of which can kill and both of which come with impaired judgment, so his opinion isn't reliable right now. Start cooling him with ice and water, keep him from drinking large amounts of plain water, and get race medics or emergency services. A DNF is nothing compared to what's at stake.
36F, 300 skydives, considering my first wingsuit course. Is it ever too late to start?

Not even close. Plenty of people start wingsuiting in their 30s, 40s and beyond, and 300 jumps gives you a solid base. What matters more than age is current, consistent skydiving and good canopy skills. Book a first flight course and enjoy it.
My son is 16 and obsessed with Nazaré videos. He wants to go out at our local reef when it gets big. I'm terrified. What should I say?

Your fear is reasonable, and the best move is to channel his obsession into the proper path instead of only saying no. Big-wave surfers who last get there through years of progression, breath-hold training, a solid water-safety partner and coaching, and you can frame it that way with him. Find a reputable local coach or big-wave safety course, and agree that he only surfs the reef on big days with experienced surfers and a safety plan in place.
What's the right way to hold your arms when you jump feet first?

For most recreational heights, cross your arms tight over your chest or press them firmly against your sides so they don't slap the water and dislocate a shoulder. Keep your legs locked together, toes pointed, and squeeze your glutes and core so your body enters as one rigid line. Look at the horizon rather than down at the water, since dropping your head tends to tip you forward.
is headfirst or feet first better

Feet first, almost always, unless you've had proper diving coaching. Headfirst entries from height put your neck and spine at risk if your angle is even slightly off or the water is shallower than you thought, and that's how people end up paralyzed. Even professional high divers enter feet first from big platforms.
My 14yo wants to start downhill racing. I'm terrified. Is this insane?

It's not insane. Plenty of teens race downhill safely when they come up through a proper club or coaching program instead of figuring it out alone. What actually keeps them safe is a full-face helmet, a neck brace or at least a good back protector, knee and elbow pads, a properly serviced bike, and coaches who move them up in difficulty gradually. Look for a junior program at your local bike park, and go watch a session so you can see how controlled the progression really is. Most of the scary crashes happen to riders pushing past their skill with no guidance, which is exactly what a club prevents.
Do I need a jet ski safety team or is that just for pros?

At truly big spots with heavy hold-downs, a jet ski safety team is about the most important protection there is, and that isn't just for pros. Many dangerous incidents only ended well because a ski got there within seconds. If you can't arrange a ski, surf only when experienced people with water safety are around, and stay well within your limits. Many big-wave crews share ski teams, so ask around your local scene.
Women-specific heat tips for ultras? I'm in my luteal phase on race day.

In the luteal phase your core temperature runs a bit higher and you may sweat a little later, so the heat can hit sooner. Lean into pre-cooling, start conservatively, and be generous with ice and sodium. If you've noticed bigger symptoms in past races during this phase, adjust your pacing expectations ahead of time.
is it legal to do parkour on random buildings in the city

It varies by location, but in most places climbing on private buildings counts as trespassing, and security or police can move you along or fine you. Public spaces like parks, plazas, and schoolyards after hours are usually more tolerated, though you can still be asked to leave. Respectful traceurs leave immediately when asked, avoid damaging anything, and stay away from rooftops and anywhere you could fall from height. Many cities also have dedicated parkour parks, which take care of the legal question and are designed for it.
can i just watch youtube and teach myself

No. Self-taught paragliding is how a lot of serious accidents happen. Videos are great for supplementing lessons, but they can't correct your launch technique in real time or tell you that today's wind is too strong for you. A proper course with a certified instructor usually takes one to two weeks for the basic rating, and it's the single best investment you'll make in the sport.
Can I learn wingsuit from YouTube videos? Courses are expensive.

Videos are great for theory and visualizing exits and flight positions, but they can't replace a First Flight Course. A coach checks your gear and suit fit, briefs you on your specific dropzone, flies with you, and debriefs your mistakes, and that feedback is what keeps beginners from getting into trouble with deployment or traffic. A course usually costs about the same as a handful of jumps, which is cheap insurance for a discipline this unforgiving.
Can I skydive if I had a few beers the night before? Not drunk now, just a bit hungover.

Most dropzones have a strict rule against jumping within 8 to 12 hours of drinking, and a hangover is a good reason to wait regardless. Dehydration and fuzzy thinking slow your reactions, and that matters most during deployment and landing. Be honest with the staff and reschedule if you feel off, because the sky will still be there next weekend.
i keep swimming at the bottom of rapids. tips?

That's usually a sign you're paddling passively or leaning back when the water hits you. Keep your paddle in the water, lean slightly forward and downstream when you cross eddy lines, and practice braces until they're reflexive. A lesson with an instructor watching you on a few rapids will spot the issue faster than trial and error.
ankle rolled pretty bad landing a trick, how soon can i skate again

That depends on how bad the sprain is, so if you can't put weight on it, it's badly swollen or bruised, or the bone itself is tender, get it X-rayed first to rule out a fracture. A mild sprain usually needs one to three weeks, while a moderate one can take four to six, and coming back too early is how people end up with chronically weak ankles. Use rest, ice and elevation for the first couple of days, then start gentle mobility and balance work. Wait until you can hop and jog on it without pain before you skate, and an ankle brace helps for your first sessions back.
Is riding downhill with a slightly cracked carbon rim fine if it still spins true?
No, a cracked carbon rim can fail suddenly and completely under a hard landing, often without warning. Replace it before your next ride. Have the shop check the tire and hub while they're at it.
What should I wear for a desert ultra? Thinking just shorts, no shirt.

Go shirtless in a desert and you'll likely regret it, because direct sun on bare skin heats you up and burns you fast. A loose, light-colored, long-sleeve sun shirt plus a hat with a neck flap actually keeps you cooler, especially when it's wet. Add sunglasses and sweat-proof sunscreen on any exposed skin.
Is proximity flying something I can work up to on my own if I'm careful?

Not safely without mentorship, because proximity flying leaves almost no margin and most fatalities come from misjudged lines and terrain. People who last in it usually log several hundred wingsuit skydives, then many BASE jumps, then wingsuit BASE with open, conservative lines for a long time before going near terrain. Find experienced mentors who know specific exits, and accept that the progression takes years, not a season.
I dislocated my shoulder last year. Can I still jump?

Probably, but talk to your doctor or physio first. The rebound can jerk your arms around, and a shoulder that has dislocated before is more likely to go again. Tell the operator about it, and ask whether they can attach you at the ankles with a body harness, keeping your arms tucked in. If your shoulder still feels unstable, wait until it's properly strengthened.
What's a cavern vs a cave dive, exactly?

A cavern dive stays within the daylight zone, usually within around 60 meters of the surface entrance and at limited depths, so natural light is always visible. A cave dive goes beyond that into total darkness where you depend entirely on your lights, guideline and gas planning. Cavern training is the standard first step before full cave work.
Can I teach myself paragliding from YouTube videos? Lessons are expensive.

Don't do it. Most self-taught crashes happen during launch and landing, which are exactly the skills videos can't give you. A proper course with a certified school like a USHPA or BHPA one usually runs a week or two and includes gear use, radio guidance and supervised flights. Save up for the course and use YouTube to supplement it, not replace it.
my 12 yo wants to do the black runs at whistler because his friend does them. he's been riding greens and a couple blues for one summer. thoughts?

I'd hold him on blues until he's riding them smoothly and in control, braking before features rather than on them. Whistler blacks have big rock rolls, steep chutes and drops where a mistake at speed gets serious, and one summer is usually too early. A kids' lesson or camp with the park's coaches is a great way to progress him faster and safely, and they'll tell you honestly when he's ready. Peer pressure is the most common reason kids end up over their heads.
Wave pool or ocean to train for big surf?

The ocean, no contest, because big-wave surfing is mostly about reading swell, currents, positioning and surviving wipeouts, and no pool teaches that. Wave pools are useful for squeezing in more turns and pop-up reps, but they won't prepare you for a 20-foot set on the horizon. Use the pool as a bonus, and spend your real training time in increasingly challenging ocean conditions.
How long before I can jump solo without an instructor?

In AFF you're usually jumping on your own, with no instructor holding on, within the first week or two of training. To earn an A license in the US you need 25 jumps plus a checklist of skills, after which you can jump unsupervised. Most motivated students finish in a few weeks to a few months, depending on weather and budget.
how do i know if a surface is too slippery to jump on

Test it before you trust it: press and twist your shoe on the exact spot where you'll land, and treat anything wet, dusty, mossy, painted or polished as suspect. Brushed concrete and rough stone usually grip well, while marble, metal rails and painted lines can be dangerously slick, especially in the morning dew or after rain. When in doubt, choose a different spot, since a slipped landing is one of the most common ways traceurs get hurt.
Can I take my 9 year old on a tandem with me? I'm P3.

Not on your P3 alone. Flying tandem, especially with a passenger, requires a specific tandem rating in most countries, along with a proper tandem wing and passenger harness. Kids are also lighter and less predictable on launch and landing, which takes real tandem experience to manage. If you want your kid to fly, book a certified tandem pilot who regularly flies children. You can be right there to share the experience.
I'm 52, tore my calf playing tennis 3 weeks ago, and want to get back to trail running before my 50k in 10 weeks. Physio says go slow. How slow is slow?

Slow usually means pain-free walking and calf raises first, then short flat runs, and only after that hills and trails, with each stage held for about a week without symptoms. At 52, calf tears are prone to re-injury, so I'd plan to finish the 50k comfortably rather than race it, and treat a smooth return to 30-plus kilometre long runs by week seven or eight as your green light. Have your physio set the exact progression, because downhill running loads the calf hardest and needs the most patience. If the timeline slips, dropping to a shorter distance is a far better outcome than a re-tear.
whats the deal with flagging, like what do yellow flags mean

A yellow flag means there's a hazard ahead, usually a downed rider, and it means no jumping and no passing until you're past the hazard. Ignoring a yellow flag is how riders land on people, so race tracks penalize it hard. Watch for flaggers on the landings of blind jumps. A red flag means the race or practice is stopped, so slow down and get off the track safely, and a white flag means one lap to go.
Is wearing shoes a good idea when cliff jumping?

Grippy water shoes or old trainers are a good idea for climbing wet rock and getting out over barnacles or sharp stone, and plenty of coasteering guides require them. Make sure they're snug enough to stay on at impact, and keep your feet pointed so the soles don't slap. Flip-flops are useless and will just fly off.
How do I know if my track is too advanced for me?

If you're getting passed constantly, unable to clear the jumps, or feeling scared on most of the lap, it's probably too advanced. Many tracks have a beginner or vet section, and riding those builds skills without forcing big jumps. It's fine to roll jumps you're not ready for, as long as you hold your line so you don't get in the way. Ask staff or experienced riders which tracks suit your level.
Dad here. Son (22) announced he's going to free solo. I don't climb. How do I even talk to him about this?

Start with curiosity rather than an ultimatum. Ask what draws him to it, what route he's thinking about, and how he prepared, because people tend to dig in when they feel judged. Tell him plainly that you'd be devastated to lose him, and ask whether experienced climbers he respects think he's ready. Many climbing mentors will talk him down more effectively than a parent can.
can i just use a static rope i found in my garage for lead climbing, its basically the same

No, this is one of the few true dealbreakers in climbing. Static rope barely stretches, so a lead fall on one sends a huge shock load into your body, your gear and the anchor, and that can break bones or pull protection out. Lead climbing requires a dynamic rope rated to UIAA standards, and an old rope of unknown history from a garage shouldn't be trusted for anything life-safety anyway. Buy a new dynamic rope, as a decent one costs far less than an ER visit.
What's the best way to get out of a hydraulic if I swim into one?

If you get recirculated, stop fighting toward the surface current and swim hard for either end of the hydraulic, where the backwash weakens. If that's not working, try balling up or diving deep to catch the downstream current under the boil. The best defense, though, is scouting and portaging any low-head dam or uniform river-wide hole, because those can hold people indefinitely. Take a swiftwater rescue course to practice this in a controlled setting.
Headache at 4,200m, mild, ibuprofen helped. Keep going up tomorrow?

A mild headache that goes away with ibuprofen is common and may just be ordinary acclimatization, but it's also the first sign of acute mountain sickness. The safe move is to stay at the same altitude tomorrow and see how you feel, rather than climbing on the assumption that it's fine. If the headache comes back, or you get nausea, unusual fatigue or trouble sleeping, don't go up, and descend if things get worse.
What's the rule of thirds?

It's the standard cave gas plan: use one third of your starting gas going in, one third coming out, and keep one third in reserve for emergencies like sharing air with a buddy. You turn the dive as soon as anyone on the team hits their turn pressure. Many divers use even more conservative margins for siphons, downstream flow or deeper dives, so treat thirds as the maximum, not the target.
I'm 68 and fit, walk 10k a day. Too old?

Plenty of people your age and older jump, and many operators have no upper age limit, though some ask for a doctor's note past a certain age. The real questions are your blood pressure, heart health, back, neck and any osteoporosis, so a quick check with your GP is worth it. If you're cleared, a body-harness option can be gentler on the joints.
Just got my P2. My buddies are heading to a thermal site with strong spring conditions this weekend and want me to come. Ready?

Probably not yet, and that's normal for a fresh P2. Strong spring thermals are punchy and turbulent, and they call for active piloting you only build with lots of hours in milder air. Go with your buddies, but fly in the calmer morning or evening windows, or just watch midday and learn how the air behaves. Ask an experienced local or instructor to tell you honestly when the site suits your level, because building up slowly is how pilots stay in the sport for decades.
Is it cheaper to just buy gear online and teach myself from youtube?

No, and you couldn't get air fills or join dive boats anyway. Shops require proof of certification. More importantly, things like gas management, emergency ascents and buoyancy have to be practiced under supervision, because the mistakes can kill you. Take a proper course, rent gear at first, and only buy your own mask, fins and computer once you know what you like.
dude just tell me how to free solo without all the safety lecture

Here's the short version from people who actually do it. They spend years climbing far harder routes on a rope, solo only terrain well below their limit, rehearse the exact route repeatedly on a rope, and back off without ego when anything feels wrong. There's no shortcut version of that, and skipping steps is how people die. If you want the ropeless feeling now, bouldering gets you there immediately.
is there a way to get experience faster than 200 skydives? i want to start BASE this summer

Not really, and trying to rush it usually means arriving underprepared. You can make your skydives count by doing canopy courses, accuracy work and hop-and-pops, and by staying current through the season. Taking a canopy piloting course and doing plenty of low-altitude practice openings at the dropzone builds exactly the skills BASE needs. If summer slips to next year, that's fine; the sport rewards patience far more than enthusiasm.
My dad is 68 and wants to do Everest Base Camp with me. He's fit for his age but has high blood pressure. Am I crazy to let him?

Plenty of people in their sixties and seventies reach Everest Base Camp, so his age alone isn't a dealbreaker. The blood pressure is the real question, since altitude can push it higher, so he should see his doctor, ideally one familiar with travel medicine, before you book anything. If he gets the all-clear, pick an itinerary with extra acclimatization days and make sure your insurance covers helicopter evacuation above 5000 m.
I run ultras and have Achilles pain every morning that warms up after a mile. Normal?

Common, yes, but not normal, because morning stiffness that eases as you warm up is classic Achilles tendinopathy, and it tends to get worse if you keep piling on the miles. Cut your volume and hills, and start heavy slow calf raises, which have good evidence for tendon rehab. See a physio if it isn't improving within a few weeks, or straight away if you feel a sudden snap or pain like being kicked.
best surface for a total beginner to practice on

Look for smooth, flat concrete with no traffic, like an empty basketball court, a tennis court if allowed, or a quiet parking lot. Avoid rough asphalt, because small rocks stop your wheels and throw you. Grass is great for practicing balance and pop while standing still, but you can't roll on it. A skatepark's flat sections also work during quiet hours.
my friends want me to drop in on the big bowl tomorrow. never dropped in before. how do i do it

Don't make the big bowl your first drop-in. Learn on a small quarter pipe or mini ramp first: set your tail on the coping with your back foot, put your front foot over the front bolts, then commit by leaning forward and stomping the front trucks down. The classic mistake is leaning back, which shoots the board out and slams you on your tailbone, so wear a helmet and pads until it feels automatic.
my friends are all jumping off a bridge near our town, is that fine

Bridge jumping is riskier than it looks. River depth changes, debris collects around the bridge supports, currents can be strong, and there may be boat traffic. It's also illegal in many places. If you go anyway, check the depth and obstacles yourself first, never jump during high water, and make sure someone is watching from the shore. A known cliff spot or a supervised lake platform is a much better choice.
gonna duck the ropes at the resort to hit the closed bowl, patrol never checks. how bad is that

Bad idea, closed terrain is closed for real reasons, often because patrol hasn't done avalanche control yet or it's actively unstable. Ducking ropes can also get your pass pulled, lead to fines, and put patrollers at risk if they have to rescue you. If you want that kind of terrain, wait for it to open or take an avalanche course and learn to tour properly with the right gear.
can i use a gym rope outside?

Only if it's a dynamic rope in good condition that you own, and most gyms won't let you take theirs. Gym ropes see a ton of falls and abrasion, and you'd need one long enough for the routes you plan to climb, usually at least 60 meters, plus a stopper knot in the end. Bring your own rope you know the history of.
Had a line twist on my last wingsuit jump and freaked out a bit. normal?

Line twists are more common on wingsuit jumps, especially with an asymmetrical body position at deployment, so yes, it's a known issue. The standard fix is to unzip your arm wings first if needed, grab the risers, and kick out of the twist while staying aware of your altitude and hard deck. If you can't clear it above your decision altitude, cut away. Go over that jump with your coach, because an uneven pitch usually points to a body position problem you can fix.
how do I find people to train parkour with

Search for a local parkour gym or academy, since almost every big city has one, and they often host open sessions and community jams. Look for local parkour groups on social media, which regularly organize free meetups at parks and other good spots. Training with experienced traceurs is hugely valuable for safety, since they'll correct your technique and tell you which spots and moves are risky. Don't be afraid to show up as a beginner, the parkour community is generally really welcoming.
What's the deal with low-head dams? Look harmless.

They're nicknamed drowning machines for a reason. The uniform recirculation below a low-head dam can hold a person, even in a PFD, and the hydraulic is often hard to spot from upstream. Never run one or paddle close to the backwash below one. Portage well around it.
Can I tow in at Jaws with my friend driving his new jetski? He's had it a month.

Not with a driver who's had the ski for a month. At Jaws your driver is your lifeline: they have to read sets, position you, and pull you out of the impact zone under enormous pressure. Driving and rescue sled pickups in big surf are skills people train for years, and drivers usually take water safety and rescue courses first. Have your friend log serious hours in smaller surf and take a PWC rescue course. Hire an experienced team for any Jaws session in the meantime.
Whats the best way to learn to whip

Start with small, mellow tabletops, so a mistake means landing on the deck instead of in a gap. Begin by just leaning the bike a few degrees off the lip with your hips and legs, and build up the angle only once you're bringing it back straight every time. Focus on getting the bike straight before the landing, because landing crossed up is how most whip crashes happen. Filming yourself or riding with a coach speeds this up a lot.
wanna try a 540 but i only just landed my first 360 like an hour ago

Give it some time. Land the 360 consistently for a few days, on both sides if you can, before adding another half rotation. A 540 needs more height, more speed and a confident landing switch, and rushing it is how people catch edges at full speed. Once your 360s feel automatic, a session with a coach or on an airbag is a smart way to try your first 540.
can I cave dive solo once I'm certified? my buddies are flaky

Solo cave diving does exist, but it's an advanced practice for very experienced divers with fully redundant gear and a lot of cave time, not something to start right after certification. Your first hundred or so cave dives should be with a competent team so you can build judgment safely. Look for dive partners through local cave diving groups or shops; that community is usually happy to bring in new divers.
What should I eat and drink on a big park day?

Eat a solid breakfast with carbs and protein, then snack every hour or two on things like bars, bananas or sandwiches, because chairlift laps burn more energy than you'd expect. Drink water steadily throughout the day and add electrolytes when it's hot. Most bad crashes happen late in the day when riders are tired, so treat fuel and rest as part of your safety plan.
My son just told me he wants to start BASE jumping. He's 24 and has around 400 skydives. I'm terrified. What should I know?

Your fear makes sense, because BASE carries far more risk than skydiving. With 400 jumps, though, he's at the point where serious jumpers make the move. What helps most is a structured First Jump Course, a long stretch on simple, forgiving objects like big bridges, and staying away from wingsuit proximity flying for years. Ask him who is mentoring him and what his progression plan looks like. A thoughtful answer to that is a good sign.
I'm overweight, about 120 kg. Can I still learn?

Absolutely, many pilots your size fly happily. Contact schools in advance so they can supply a wing sized for your weight, since flying overloaded or underloaded affects handling and safety. Launches and landings require some running, so working on your fitness and ankle strength will help. A tandem flight first is a good way to try it.
Is it safe to swim after heavy rain? The river looks fine

I'd wait two or three days after heavy rain. Runoff and sewage overflows can push bacteria levels way up even when the water looks clear, and rivers can also be faster, colder and carrying debris after a downpour. Check your local water quality reports or sewage overflow alerts before going in. If you do swim, cover any cuts and shower afterward.
Plantar fasciitis killing me. Still hiking 15 miles every weekend. Advice?

Cut the mileage for a few weeks, because long hikes on an irritated plantar fascia keep it inflamed. Calf and foot stretches, supportive shoes or insoles, and rolling your arch can help, and so can night splints. If it's still bad after a month or two, see a podiatrist or physio, and go back to long days gradually.
can i do freediving tables on my phone app while lying in the pool

Do your CO2 and O2 tables on land, lying on a couch or bed, never in water, unless you're in a supervised pool session where a trained buddy is watching you hold by hold. Tables are specifically designed to push you toward your limits, which is exactly when blackout happens. On land that's harmless. In water alone it can kill you.
how long does full cave cert take

Most people go through cavern, intro to cave, then full cave, which is usually 8 to 12 days of training spread over months or even a year or two. You'll want solid buoyancy and trim before you start, and plenty of dives between levels to consolidate skills. Rushing it through back-to-back courses is possible but rarely makes better cave divers.
Sprained my ankle two days ago bouldering, it's swollen and purple. Comp is Saturday. Can I tape it and send?

Two days out with that much swelling and bruising, you're likely looking at a moderate sprain at minimum, and taping won't stop a bad landing from turning it into a torn ligament. Bouldering means repeated drops onto a joint that can't stabilize itself yet, which is exactly how a two-week injury becomes a three-month one. Get it checked to rule out a fracture, keep elevating and icing, and treat this comp as a skip. There will be another one, and you want to show up to it with two working ankles.
can i just skip skydiving and go straight to base if i take a course

No, and no legitimate course will take you without a skydiving background. BASE gives you seconds instead of minutes to deal with a problem, so you need hundreds of skydives first to make deployment, canopy control and malfunction handling automatic. Get your skydiving license, build your numbers, then look for a First Jump Course.
Do free soloists wear helmets?

Most don't, partly because a helmet won't save you from a long ground fall. Rockfall from above is still a real hazard, though, and some people do wear one on choss or busy routes. For roped climbing outdoors, a helmet is a smart default, since it protects against falling rock and against hitting your head in a fall.
My girlfriend wants to try DH with me. How do I not scare her off?

Book her a lesson with a park coach rather than teaching her yourself, because instruction from a stranger is often less stressful and more effective. Start on the easiest trails, let her set the pace, and don't push her toward features she's not comfortable with. Make sure she has rental gear that fits well, including a full-face and pads, and keep the day short so it ends on a good note.
is it fine to top rope off two ice screws or do i really need a tree/bolt anchor up top

Two good screws in solid, well-bonded ice can make a perfectly sound top-rope anchor, and that's how a lot of ice routes get set up. The catch is that top-roping loads them for hours while sun and body heat soften the ice around them, so place them at least a foot apart, check them between climbers, and back them up to a tree or bolt whenever one is available. If the ice is wet, hollow-sounding or getting sun, treat screws as a backup only.
What's a good number of jumps to do in a day as a newbie?

Keep it low, often just a few jumps, because fatigue, rushed packing and lapses in focus build up fast. Quality matters more than quantity, so debrief each jump and pack carefully. Your instructor will set the pace on a course, and after that it makes sense to keep the same conservative approach.
There's a 20ft swell coming and no water patrol at my spot. I've surfed it big before. Should I go?

Without a water patrol, a 20 foot day carries a lot more risk even if you know the spot. If you do go, surf with an experienced crew who'll actively watch each other. Consider whether you can organize a ski with a trained driver for the session. If neither happens, picking smaller sections or sitting out the biggest part of the swell is the smart call.
It's been above freezing all week and now it's sunny. Ice should still be fine to lead right?

I'd be cautious. A week of thaw followed by direct sun can leave ice detached, hollow, or rotten, and pillars and free-hanging features can collapse outright. Leading on questionable ice means your screws may not hold either. Look for shaded, well-frozen routes, top rope instead of leading, or wait for a solid cold snap to refreeze things.
how do people die in base most often

The most common causes are object strikes from off-heading openings, bad landings, wingsuit proximity flying, and jumping in conditions or at objects beyond the jumper's skill. Many deaths involve people pushing too far too soon or ignoring warning signs. Good training, conservative choices, and a willingness to turn around and walk down prevent a lot of accidents.
Is the AAD worth it or can I skip it to save money on gear?

It's absolutely worth it, and most dropzones won't let you jump without one anyway. An AAD fires your reserve automatically if you're incapacitated or lose altitude awareness, and it has saved thousands of lives. Save money elsewhere, such as by buying a used container or a used main canopy that's been inspected, but don't cut corners here.
can i just wear jeans for downhill

Jeans shred in seconds on asphalt and offer almost no abrasion protection, so they're fine for mellow cruising but not for real speed. Once you're going fast enough to need slides to stop, get leathers or at least kevlar-lined riding pants. Road rash through denim hurts and can leave lasting scars.
my light died during a cavern dive and my buddy didn't notice. what should I have done

Switch to your backup light straight away, then signal your buddy, ideally by grabbing their attention directly or using a light signal once your backup is on. Lights failing is normal, which is why you carry backups and agree on signals before the dive. Talk to your buddy about staying aware of each other's lights so problems get spotted faster.
can i skate in the rain if i dry my bearings after

You can, but it's the grip more than the bearings that should worry you, because wet pavement, painted lines and metal covers get slick and your wheels lose traction without warning. Water also soaks into the deck and makes it soft and warped, and griptape loses its bite when wet. If you do ride in the rain, go slow, skip tricks, and avoid hills and painted surfaces. Afterward, pop the bearings out, dry them, re-lube them, and let the deck dry flat indoors.
I'm 62 and just got cleared by my cardiologist after a stent last year. Is it realistic to learn to dive?

Yes, plenty of people your age with a cleared cardiac history dive happily. Ask your cardiologist to fill out the RSTC/WRSTC diver medical form specifically, and ideally have a dive-medicine physician look it over too, because diving puts particular demands on the heart. Start with a patient instructor, keep dives shallow and relaxed at first, and be honest with yourself about fitness for surface swims and currents.
Can I land in water on purpose if the landing zone looks sketchy?

Water landings are dangerous. Your gear soaks up water fast, currents can drag you, and you can get tangled in the canopy and lines, which has drowned jumpers. If the landing zone looks bad, the safer call is usually not to jump. If water is a possible out, arrange a boat or swimmers in advance and consider flotation. Never plan on water as a casual backup.
Tried a backside 180 and keep catching my heel edge on landing. Help??

Heel-edge catches on backside 180s usually come from landing with your board still turning or tilted onto that edge. Try to finish the full rotation in the air so your board is pointed straight down the landing when it touches. Keep your knees bent and land with a flat base and weight centered over the board. Practice the rotation on flat ground at low speed until the timing clicks.
My 12 yo skateboards every day and complains of knee pain below the kneecap. Normal growing pains?

It might be Osgood-Schlatter disease, which is common in active kids during growth spurts and causes pain and sometimes a bump just below the kneecap. It's usually not serious, but have a doctor confirm it to rule out anything else. Most kids keep skating while doing less jumping, icing after sessions, and stretching their quads. Ease back if the pain stops them from skating normally.
My ears hurt on the way down last time and I kept going anyway. Is that bad?

Yes, pushing through ear pain is how people end up with barotrauma, including perforated eardrums and sometimes inner ear damage. Next time, equalize early and often, starting at the surface and every meter or so. If it hurts, ascend a little and try again rather than forcing it. If you still have pain, muffled hearing, dizziness or ringing now, see a doctor, ideally one familiar with diving, before your next dive.
What do I do if I lose my buddy underwater?

The standard procedure is to look around for about a minute, turning slowly and checking above and below you for bubbles. If you still can't find them, ascend slowly with your safety stop and meet at the surface. Your buddy should be doing the same, so you'll usually find each other quickly. Agree on this plan in your pre-dive briefing so neither of you starts searching deeper.
I'm writing a story where my character free solos. What would realistically go through their head?

Realistically, a good soloist's mind is narrow and calm. They focus on the next foothold, the feel of the rock, and their breathing, with fear present but held at arm's length. Before the climb there'd be rehearsal memories, weather checks and a deliberate go or no-go decision. Mid-route, a small surprise like a hold that feels greasy could spike real terror they have to manage. Many soloists describe the top as relief more than triumph, and that kind of honesty will make your character believable.
Can wind tunnel time replace actual wingsuit jumps?

Tunnel time is great for body flight but doesn't replace real wingsuit jumps, since you can't practice gliding, navigation, or deployments in a tunnel. Some tunnels offer wingsuit-specific sessions which help with body position. Use it as a supplement, not a shortcut around experience requirements.
Feeling dizzy and stopped sweating at mile 40 last year but pushed through and finished fine. Can I just do that again?

Please don't treat that as a strategy. Dizziness plus stopping sweating is a classic warning sign of heatstroke, and you may have just gotten lucky. Next time, stop at the aid station, get in shade, cool down with ice, and let the medical staff assess you, even if it costs you your finish. It would also be smart to mention last year's episode to a doctor before you race in heat again.
Riding alone tomorrow on trails, anything I should know?

Riding alone is riskier, so tell someone your route and when you'll be back, and carry a charged phone, water, basic tools and a small first aid kit. Pick trails you already know and ride at about 80 percent so you have margin for mistakes. Some riders carry a satellite messenger or GPS beacon for areas with no signal. If something feels off, turn around early rather than late.
quick q, can I use nitrox in caves

Yes, nitrox is very common in cave diving because it gives longer no-decompression time at typical depths. You must analyze your gas and respect the maximum operating depth for your mix, since oxygen toxicity underwater can cause a convulsion and drowning. Always label your tanks clearly and plan depth limits before you dive.
Why do people even do this? It seems insane.

For most soloists it's about total focus and the purity of moving over rock with nothing but your body, and people describe a flow state that's hard to find anywhere else. The ones who last tend to be extremely methodical, soloing well below their limit on terrain they know intimately. It's still among the deadliest activities in climbing, and many respected climbers have died doing it. You can admire the commitment and still think the risk is too high, and plenty of climbers feel exactly that way.
ok so im in the air and suddenly see big dark cloud growing fast nearby. what do i do

Get away from it and land as soon as you safely can, because a fast-growing dark cloud can be developing into a thunderstorm with violent lift that can suck you up. Fly away from it toward a safe landing area, and use descent techniques you've trained like big ears if you need to lose height. Don't hang around to see what it does. Afterwards, look at the forecast you flew on, because overdevelopment is usually predictable.
Should I take a park lesson or just watch YouTube?

YouTube is great for understanding a trick, but a lesson spots what you can't see yourself, like where your weight really is or why you're under-rotating. One or two park lessons usually save you weeks of building bad habits. Do both: watch videos for ideas and use a coach to fix your technique.
my 14yo son wants to start parkour after watching youtube videos. should i be terrified?

Not terrified, just involved. Parkour taught properly is mostly about control, landing mechanics and conditioning, and the injury rate at coached gyms is lower than many parents expect. The flashy rooftop clips are the part to steer him away from. Find a parkour gym or certified coach near you, ideally one with ADAPT or similar credentials, and let him build skills on mats before he takes them outside.
what should i bring for a basic beach swim

Bring a bright swim cap, goggles, a tow float, and a wetsuit if the water's cool. Pack a towel, warm layers you can pull on quickly (a changing robe is great), a hat, and a flask of something warm. Bring some water and a snack too, and let someone know where you're swimming and when you'll be back.
pregnant, 14 weeks, signed up for a hot 50K before I found out. still run it?

Talk to your OB before deciding, because overheating in pregnancy is a real concern, especially in the first trimester. Many runners keep running easily while pregnant, but a 50K in heat is a much bigger stress than training runs. Most races will let you defer for pregnancy, and that's likely the safest choice here.
My shins hurt every time I run and jump, could this be shin splints?

It could be, since shin splints are common when people ramp up jumping and running faster than their legs can adapt. Cut back on impact work for a week or two, use cycling or swimming to stay fit, and strengthen your calves and the muscles in the front of your shin before easing back in. If the pain is in one specific bony spot or gets worse with rest, see a doctor, because that can point to a stress fracture rather than shin splints.
best way to learn grabs?

Start with an indy grab: front hand reaching down to the toe edge between your bindings, done on a small jump or even just an ollie. The trick is bringing your knees up toward your chest so the board comes to your hand, rather than reaching down and losing your balance. Let go early enough to spot your landing. Once indy feels natural, try melon and stalefish.
Mavericks is supposed to be huge this weekend and I'm flying in. I've never surfed it. I'll just paddle out and figure it out.

Mavericks on a big day is not a place to figure out on arrival, because the rocks, currents and the way the peak shifts have injured and killed very experienced surfers. Use this trip to watch from the cliff or a boat, talk to locals and learn the lineup and the channel. If you want to surf it, come back on a smaller day with someone who knows it well and a water safety team around.
best stretches for parkour?

Focus on calves, hamstrings, hip flexors, wrists and shoulders, since those take the most load from landings, vaults and climbing. Do dynamic moves like leg swings, lunges and wrist circles before training, then hold static stretches for about 30 seconds afterward. Deep squats and pike stretches help your mobility for vaults and climbs over time. Consistency matters more than intensity, so a few minutes daily beats one long session a week.
Is it worth buying a park-specific board?

If you spend most of your time in the park, yes. Park boards are softer and usually true twin, which makes butters, presses and riding switch much easier and more forgiving. If you split time between park and all-mountain riding, a softer all-mountain twin is a good compromise. Rent or demo one first so you know what you like.
my son is 13 and wants to try street luge. am i crazy for considering letting him

Not crazy, as long as he starts in the right setting. Many organized luge and downhill events have youth or beginner categories on closed courses with hay bales, marshals and required leathers, which is very different from bombing a public road. Find a local club or race organization that runs beginner sessions, get him proper gear, and let him learn speed control from experienced riders before he ever goes fast.
I'm 67 and had a knee replacement 9 months ago. Wanting to get back to ski touring. Too ambitious?

Not necessarily. Plenty of people get back to touring after knee replacements, but it's a decision for your surgeon, since high-impact skiing can affect how long the implant lasts. Uphill touring is actually gentle on the joint, while the descent, falls and twisting forces in variable snow are where the risk sits. If you're cleared, start on mellow terrain with consistent snow and stick to conservative descents. Pair it with a strength program from your physio first.
what is a shifty

A shifty is where you twist your board about 90 degrees in the air by counter-rotating your upper and lower body, then return it straight before you land. It's a great early trick because it teaches body control without full rotation. Learn it on a small jump and bring it back straight well before touching down.
Can I go bungee jumping right after scuba diving? Doing both on my trip

Leave a gap, ideally the next day or longer. After diving your body is still off-gassing nitrogen, and the sudden pressure and blood flow changes of a jump could raise decompression sickness risk, similar to why you shouldn't fly too soon after diving. Plan the bungee first, or give it at least 24 hours after your last dive. That keeps both activities in the safe zone.
Never surfed before but want to start with big waves, is that dumb?

Yes, start with small waves first. Big-wave surfers spend years building their skills, fitness and ocean knowledge in normal surf before stepping up. Take lessons at a beginner-friendly beach and learn to read the ocean. Big waves can be a long-term goal once you've built the foundation.
Detailed question: I'm 6'2, 190 lbs, I've done 20 hours of indoor tunnel and I'm starting AFF next month. Will the tunnel time let me skip levels?

Tunnel time will make you much more stable and relaxed in freefall, but it usually won't let you officially skip AFF levels. The levels also cover pulling at the right altitude, emergency procedures, canopy flight and landing, and none of that can be practiced in a tunnel. What it often does is help you pass each level on the first try, which saves you money, so ask your dropzone whether they offer a tunnel-specific progression.
I keep getting a squeeze feeling in my chest around 25m. Normal?

Feeling pressure is normal, but anything that hurts, or coughing up blood or tasting blood afterward, can be a lung squeeze. That's a real injury, so stop diving and get it checked. The usual fix is to back off to a depth that feels comfortable and build up in small steps. Work on flexibility stretches for your diaphragm and chest, and stay relaxed rather than tense on the bottom phase. A coach who can watch your dives is worth a lot at this stage.
My goggles keep fogging and I can't see buoys. Help!

Rinse the lenses with a bit of baby shampoo or spit, then rinse lightly, or use a proper anti-fog spray; and never wipe the inside, because that strips the factory coating. Tinted or mirrored goggles help a lot on bright days when you're sighting into the sun. If they still fog, a new pair is worth it, because not being able to see where you're going in open water is a real safety issue, not just an annoyance.
spearfishing solo off rocks this weekend, conditions look ok. any tips

The biggest tip is not to go solo, since spearfishing is where a lot of freediving deaths happen. People chase a fish too long, push their breath-hold and black out with nobody nearby. Bring a buddy who watches you from the surface, tow a float with a flag and keep your dives short with long rests. Also have a clear exit plan off those rocks for when the swell picks up.
lol is it dumb to jump down a 7 stair on my second month

Yeah, pretty much. Second month is the time to land ollies up and down curbs and small 2 to 3 stairs consistently, because a 7 stair hits your ankles and knees hard and bails get ugly fast. Work up gradually, and only try bigger sets once smaller ones feel boring. Wear a helmet when you do.
Can I skydive with a GoPro on my first solo jumps? Want footage lol

Hold off. USPA recommends at least 200 jumps and a C license before you jump with a camera, because cameras add snag hazards and pull your attention away from altitude and emergency procedures at exactly the wrong moment. Most dropzones won't let students jump with one anyway. If you want footage now, pay for a camera flyer to film your AFF jumps.
Someone at my hostel says dexamethasone lets you climb higher faster. Should I bring some?

Dexamethasone is an emergency drug for treating HACE and severe altitude sickness so a person can get down safely, not a way to climb faster. Using it to push higher can hide dangerous symptoms, and if it wears off when you're up high, you can crash badly. It's worth carrying in your group's medical kit for emergencies, but only on a doctor's prescription and with guidance on when to use it.
Ice looks a little wet and the temps are around 5°C today. Still worth going?

I'd skip it or pick a shaded, high-elevation route that's been cold overnight. Above freezing, ice loses strength, screws hold poorly, and pillars and daggers can collapse without warning. Wet, dripping ice and running water behind it are clear signs to back off. Come back after a few days of solid cold and the same route will be safer and more fun.
Is it okay to fly alone at a site nobody's at? Conditions look perfect.

Solo flying at a quiet site adds real risk, because if you land badly in trees or rough terrain, nobody may know to come looking. If you're experienced and know the site well, carry a charged phone, a radio and ideally a satellite tracker, and tell someone your plan and expected landing time. If it's a site you've never flown or you're still fairly new, wait for company. Local pilots know rotor spots and hazards that can't be seen from launch.
What's the highest bungee in the world?

Height records shift as new sites open, but the big names include the Macau Tower at around 233 meters and the Bloukrans Bridge in South Africa at about 216 meters. Both are run by established operators with strong safety records. If you're new, start with a lower jump to see how your body and nerves handle it before chasing a record.
my mates reckon if you go in pencil straight it doesn't matter how high you go lol

Your mates are wrong on that one. A good pencil entry helps a lot, but impact force climbs steeply with height, and above roughly 15 to 20 meters even a clean entry can compress your spine, damage your organs or knock you out. The pros who jump from those heights train for years and have rescue divers waiting in the water.
honestly whats the death rate in street luge

There's no reliable official statistic, but deaths are rare in organized street luge, largely because events use closed roads, hay bales and full protective gear. Most serious injuries and fatalities in gravity sports happen on open roads with traffic or among riders without proper gear. The risk is real, but racing in controlled settings is a very different thing from bombing hills alone.
how long should i hyperventilate before a dive to get more bottom time

Don't hyperventilate at all. It blows off CO2, which is the signal that tells you to breathe, so your oxygen can run out before you feel the urge and you black out with no warning. Do a calm breathe-up instead: slow, relaxed breaths for a couple of minutes, then one full final inhale. You'll gain more bottom time from relaxing and good technique than from any breathing trick.
how fast can i go up if i feel fine

Feeling fine doesn't mean you're acclimatized, because symptoms often lag behind altitude gain by several hours. Above about 3000 m, the standard guideline is to increase your sleeping altitude by no more than 300 to 500 m per night, with a rest day every three to four days. Day hikes higher are fine as long as you come back down to sleep.
Im 52 and want to try downhill for the first time. Am I too old for this?

Not at all, plenty of riders start in their 50s and have a great time, and lift-served parks make the climbing irrelevant. Book a lesson with a park coach on your first day, because learning proper body position from the start helps you avoid crashes, and recovery takes longer as we age. Wear full protective gear, stick to green and easy blue trails at first, and take more breaks than you think you need, since fatigue is when most crashes happen.
Just tell me the best bungee spot in Europe, no essay
The Verzasca Dam in Switzerland is the classic choice. It's a 220 meter drop made famous by the GoldenEye opening scene, and it's run by an established operator. Book well ahead in summer.
Mate says I can skip helmet for just ridge soaring cause it's mellow. True?

No, always wear the helmet. Ridge soaring often means flying low near terrain, and most injuries happen on launch and landing, exactly when you're close to the ground. A gust or bad landing on a mellow day can still put your head into rocks or the slope. Wear a certified paragliding helmet every time, and back protection in your harness matters too.
is it ok to put regular car gas in my 2 stroke without oil, just for a quick ride?

No, never run a two-stroke on straight gas, even for a short ride. The engine gets all of its lubrication from the oil in the premix, and without it the piston can seize in minutes, which can lock the rear wheel and cost you a full top end rebuild. Mix the ratio your manual recommends, often around 32:1 or 40:1, using quality two-stroke oil and fresh premium fuel.
Is a regular skate helmet okay for downhill?

For mellow hills a certified skate helmet is the bare minimum, but once you start going fast you really want a full-face helmet, ideally one certified for high-impact use like a motorcycle- or downhill-rated lid.
