At speed, crashes often involve sliding face-first or hitting your chin, and a half-shell does nothing for your jaw or teeth. Most serious downhill riders consider full-face non-negotiable above roughly 30 mph.
Got a mild heart murmur since childhood. cardiologist never worried. Do I need a note?

Probably worth getting a quick confirmation anyway, since heart conditions are on almost every operator's declaration form. Benign murmurs are usually harmless, but your cardiologist can confirm that it's the innocent type and that the adrenaline and blood pressure spikes won't be an issue. Getting a short note also saves you any hassle on the day.
Just bought a 450 as my first bike, 28 years old, never ridden. Tips?

A modern 450 is a lot of bike for a first-timer, with brutal power that can loop you out or yank the bars out of your hands, so many experienced riders would recommend swapping to a 250F or even a trail bike while you learn. If you're keeping it, ask a dealer about a power map or throttle settings that soften delivery, and take a beginner course before you go to a track. Stay in open fields at low speed until clutch, throttle and braking feel automatic. Full gear is non-negotiable from day one.
I keep getting line twists on deployment. How do I fix this??

Line twists in wingsuiting usually come from an asymmetric body position at deployment. A dropped shoulder, uneven legs or turning your head while pitching are the usual culprits. Stay flat and symmetrical, keep your eyes forward, and stay level through the pitch until the canopy is fully open. Have a coach watch video of your deployments, because they'll spot the cause faster than you will.
There's a cornice on the ridge I want to walk along. How close can I get?

Keep well back from the edge, because cornices can break much farther back than you'd expect, often several meters behind the lip. Walk along the windward side, on rocks or terrain you can see clearly, rather than on the flat snow near the edge. Don't travel underneath cornices either, especially when it's warm, since a collapsing cornice can also trigger a slide on the slope below.
Been doing 8m jumps all summer and I'm ready for 20m. Any tips?

Going from 8 to 20 meters isn't a small step. At 20 meters you hit the water at around 70 km/h, and the forces involved can cause compressed vertebrae or ruptured organs even when your entry is only slightly off. Work up in stages through 10, 12 and 15 meters, and get coaching from a high-diving club or instructor before you attempt 20. Your form needs to be close to perfect at that height, and it's hard to see your own form without someone watching.
is night jumping a building ok if nobody's around

Urban night jumps are about as advanced as BASE gets. You have poor visibility, tight landing areas, hidden obstacles like wires, and you're almost certainly trespassing, which brings serious legal trouble. A trespass jump also leaves no one around to help if you get hurt. Stay on legal, well-known objects until you have a lot of experience, and even then most seasoned jumpers think hard before trying this.
whats the deal with standing vs sitting

Stand for most of the track, especially through rough sections, whoops and jumps, since your legs act as extra suspension and you can move your weight around. Sit in corners, sliding forward toward the tank with your inside leg out, which lets you keep the front wheel planted. A good rule is if it's bumpy or you're going straight, stand, and if you're turning, sit.
Just did a dive and now there's a little blood when I cough. Normal?

It isn't normal, and it often points to lung squeeze, which is bleeding in the airways or lungs from the pressure of depth. Stop diving for now and get checked by a doctor, ideally one who knows diving medicine. Get help urgently if you're short of breath, have chest pain or are coughing up more than a few streaks. Even mild squeezes need several weeks off and a gentler return to depth.
Is Kilimanjaro dangerous? My friends say it's basically a hike.

It is technically a hike, which is exactly why it catches people off guard. At 5,895 m, altitude sickness is the main risk, and many people suffer serious AMS each year, mostly on rushed itineraries. Choose a route of at least 7 or 8 days, like Lemosho or Machame with an extra day, and descend as soon as symptoms get bad.
I panicked a bit in a restriction during training. Should I quit?

Not necessarily, since lots of good cave divers had a moment like that early on, and noticing it is part of learning. Talk honestly with your instructor about what happened, practice the skill in easier settings, and only move back into tight spots when you feel calm. If restrictions keep feeling overwhelming, you can still enjoy wide, open cave passages, and plenty of divers choose never to do tight sections at all.
My partner always wants to push harder lines than I'm comfortable with. How do I handle that?

Raise it before you leave the trailhead and agree that anyone in the group can veto a slope without having to justify it. Heuristic traps like group pressure and the desire to reach a summit play a part in a lot of avalanche accidents, so you're right to take this seriously. If your partner won't respect a veto, find other partners, because you're the one carrying that risk.
rain tomorrow, should i still go ride?

Wet roads cut your grip dramatically and make braking unpredictable, so skip fast downhill in the rain. Some riders do slow rain sliding for fun on familiar, closed spots, but bearings and decks take a beating. Save the speed runs for dry pavement.
Been sending it all week and my knee feels kinda unstable on landings now. ride through it?

No, take a break, because an unstable knee after landings can mean a ligament or meniscus injury, and riding through it risks making it much worse. Rest, ice and see a doctor or physio if it keeps feeling like it gives way, or if there's swelling or locking. Coming back properly is the fastest way back to sending it.
Highballing a 20 foot boulder with one pad, my buddy says it's fine if I don't fall lol

Twenty feet onto one pad is a real injury risk, and "just don't fall" is the plan that ankle and back fractures are made of. Bring several pads to cover the whole fall zone and have at least one or two attentive spotters. Rehearse the moves near the top, or check it on a top rope first if the problem allows. If you can't get that setup, wait for a day when you can.
I keep spinning on exit. Should I just open my wings faster to stabilize?

Probably the opposite, as opening early can make you unstable or hit the tail; a clean, symmetric exit with wings held closed is key. Spinning often comes from uneven arm or leg pressure or a twisted body position. Ask an instructor to watch video and coach your exit, and practice on the ground in your suit.
I'm 52, haven't ridden since my 20s. Too old to get back in?

Not at all, many riders come back in their 50s and have a great time. Your reflexes and recovery won't be what they were, so start on a manageable bike like a 250F or trail bike and work on fitness, since motocross is physically demanding. Spend time riding easy trails or a beginner track before tackling bigger jumps. Modern protective gear is much better than what you remember, so invest in it.
is indoor skydiving worth it before real skydiving

Yes, it's one of the best investments you can make before AFF. A wind tunnel builds body position and stability in a controlled setting, so your real freefalls feel calmer and you're less likely to repeat levels. It won't teach you canopy skills or exits, but for freefall control it's excellent value.
I'm terrified of falling backward on rails. Any tricks to feel safer?

Stick to wide, low boxes first so falls are short and the surface is forgiving. Keep your knees bent, your weight centered, and your eyes on the end of the feature, because looking down is what makes people fall back. Impact shorts and a helmet help a lot with the fear. Move to rails gradually, and only once you feel steady on boxes.
How do I know if the launch wind is too strong for me?

For most beginners, anything over about 15 to 20 km/h, or any gusts, is a good reason to stay down. If you're struggling to control the wing during ground handling or getting dragged, that's your answer right there. Watch whether experienced pilots are penetrating forward easily once airborne. Set personal limits with your instructor and stick to them even when it's tempting to bend them.
My 14 year old son wants to start downhill skateboarding and I'm honestly terrified. Is there any way to make this not insane?

Your fear is reasonable, but downhill can be done in a fairly controlled way if he builds up properly. Insist on a certified full-face helmet, slide gloves, knee and elbow pads, and have him learn foot braking and the standup slide on gentle hills before he goes anywhere steep. A local downhill crew or a skate camp with downhill coaching is the best thing you can find, because experienced riders teach progression and won't let a kid jump onto hills beyond his skill. Make closed roads or quiet, well-scouted spots with a lookout a firm rule from day one.
hyperventilating before a dive gives you way more bottom time right? why does everyone say not to

It feels like more bottom time because hyperventilating blows off CO2, which is what triggers your urge to breathe, but it barely adds any oxygen. So your body's warning system is switched off while your oxygen keeps dropping, and you can black out with no warning at all. That's the classic recipe for shallow water blackout. Breathe slowly and calmly before a dive with a relaxed final breath, and let your breath-hold improve through training instead.
